en: The *Sarasvatīkaṇṭhābharaṇa*, together with the commentary named *Ratnadarpaṇa* composed by Śrī Ratneśvara. First Chapter:
He, the ascetic, shines with one half of his body like a woman, and with the other half like a man.
Now, may that Lord who wields the thunderbolt [Śiva]— who, through the sequence of reality, increases the welfare of both women and men— grant you prosperity.
This *Kaṇṭhābharaṇadarpaṇa* (Mirror of Neck-Ornaments) for the King of Avanti is being composed by Śrī Rāmasiṃhadeva, whose arms have crushed his enemies like mountains.
May the Goddess of Speech behold, upon this priceless necklace resting on the lap of the jeweled mirror of her own eloquence, the concealed beauty of all its limbs revealed; thus,
at the commencement of his work, he follows the conduct of the learned by performing a salutation to his chosen deity.

We worship that Goddess of Speech, whose fourfold locus consists of sound (*dhvani*), phonemes (*varṇa*), words (*pada*), and sentences (*vākya*), distinguished by categories such as the subtle (*sūkṣma*) and so forth. 1.
*Dhvani*... [etc.]
How is the goddess Bhāratī— the presiding deity of speech, radiant, and whose nature is the self-luminous Śabdabrahman—
to be worshipped? This salutation is intended according to the distinctions of the subtle [levels of sound] and so forth, as well as the distinctions of resonance (dhvani) and so forth.
There are four divisions of Śabdabrahman: Sūkṣmā, Paśyantī, Madhyamā, and Vaikharī;
among these, the state of non-modification is Sūkṣmā.

For she indeed, abiding within the interval between the out-breath and the in-breath of all beings, and free from appearance and disappearance, is rightly attained through the yoga of action— which consists in the repeated practice of correct application— and through the yoga of knowledge, such as reflection and so forth.
"Though this [power] is constantly being overwhelmed by adventitious impurities,
it is the final digit of the moon that is never entirely eclipsed."
"When that [sixteenth part] has been merely recognized, the [soul's] qualification ceases;
they call that the immortal part within the sixteen-part person."
Due to the power of beginningless ignorance (avidyā), that Brahman undergoes its first transformation in the form of Paśyantī;
for she is without sequence because there is no differentiation of phonemes (varṇa) and is self-luminous.
She is called Paśyantī because she perceives her own prior and subsequent states.

Thereafter, due to the material cause of supreme ignorance (*paramavidyopādāna*), a third transformation arises in the form of the *madhyamā* speech; it possesses an internal sequence consisting of conceptualization (*saṃkalpa*) and is devoid of the manifestation of phonemes (*varṇa*) perceivable by the ear.
Indeed, because it always exists between those two transformations, it is called "middle" (*madhyamā*).

When ignorance has extended far within, a third transformation arises in the form of *vaikharī*; it is manifested through the effort of the articulatory places and organs (*sthānakaraṇaprayatna*), corresponds to what is perceived by the ear, and consists of a collection of phonemes such as indistinct forms, stammering, and the like, resembling the sounds of a lute or a drum.
The aggregate of the body and the senses is called *vikhara* because it bestows (*rāti*) the distinguished space (*viśiṣṭam kham*), that is, the ether (*ākāśa*).
Thus says the Śruti: "Indeed, for one who possesses a body, there is no removal of the pleasant and the unpleasant;
but for one who is bodiless, the pleasant and the unpleasant do not touch him."
Thus,
among these, the state known as Vaikharī is the last; however, the first three of these states are eternal and transcend the senses.

As it has been said: "Vaikharī speech, which assumes the form of articulated phonemes when the vital air is expanded through the [articulatory] places, is dependent upon the activity of the breath of speakers; it follows solely the sequence whose material cause is the intellect."
Having transcended the function of the vital breath (prāṇa), the middle speech (madhyamā-vāk) proceeds; however,
because it is undivided and has withdrawn all sequential order from every side, the visionary speech (paśyantī) is within, consisting solely of the light of its own nature, subtle and imperishable.
Thus the Śruti also says: "Speech has been measured out in four quarters; those Brahmins who are wise know them.
Three, hidden in the cave, do not stir; the fourth quarter of speech is what humans speak."
This and other such points are to be understood from the *Āgamasamuccaya* itself.
Furthermore, as to what those "words" (vācas) are which she presides over, it is said: "Sound, phonemes, words, and sentences—these are her fourfold locus."
The locus (*āspada*), the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*), or the delimitation (*avaccheda*):
*parā vāk*, when delimited by sounds (*dhvani*) and so forth, is the cause of linguistic usage.

Since the capacity to effect the linguistic usages known in literary tradition—characterized as denotation (*abhidhāna*), suggestion (*dhvanana*), and indication (*lakṣaṇā*)—cannot be attributed to a single phoneme (*varṇa*), the plural number is employed.
Since both the word (*pada*) and the sentence (*vākya*) possess that same nature individually, the singular number has been employed for them;
this, then, is the summary of the intended meaning here:
indeed, this commencement of the treatise is for the purpose of defining the essential nature of *sāhitya*.
Literature (*sāhitya*) is the relationship between word and meaning.
In that regard, when the inquiry arises as to what exactly the "word" is, this classification beginning with *dhvani* [is provided];
as for the "meaning," characterized by such things as pillars and jars, it is well-known both in common parlance and in the technical treatises.
There is a certain beginningless relationship that, while appearing as its own essence, does not exist elsewhere;
it depends upon this [work], and it is fourfold: the abandonment of defects, the adoption of excellences, the application of ornaments, and the cultivation of aesthetic flavor (rasa).
He demonstrates the connection and the purpose, which are prerequisites for the engagement of a discerning person:
"The poet, composing poetry that is faultless, possessed of excellences, adorned with ornaments, and imbued with aesthetic flavor (rasa), attains both fame and pleasure. (1.2)

"Flawless" refers to *prīti* (joy), which is the bliss arising from the relish of the complete meaning of the poem; this joy occurs during the state of contemplating the meaning of the poem, as even the poet is accepted as a member of the audience,
or it arises from the praise of connoisseurs— this is the visible purpose (*dṛṣṭaprayojana*).
Fame results in heaven through the medium of the unseen (adṛṣṭa); as for the unseen, it has been said: "They say fame has heaven as its fruit.
By thus describing the purpose of the primary work, poetry, the connection with the purpose of this [treatise], which is a subordinate part of it, has been stated.

Although the word *kāvya* denotes only word and meaning as qualified by the absence of defects and other such qualities, it is nevertheless employed in the sense of word and meaning alone through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*). The purpose of this indication is the enumeration of the subjects to be treated;
for the body of a treatise is threefold: "enumeration (*uddeśa*), definition (*lakṣaṇa*), and examination (*parīkṣā*)."
Our teachers maintain that the text of the *Udāharaṇavyākhyā* is intended for examination (*parīkṣā*) throughout;
since the "enunciation" (*uddeśa*) is obtained from that which is concerned with the purpose and the connection, there is no contradiction.
For this very reason, the chapters follow the sequence of the enunciation of defects and so forth.

"Faultless" means possessing an absolute absence of defects; for even a defect that pertains merely to the color of a beloved’s body—like a vitiligo spot affecting only one part of a limb—necessarily causes a distaste for the poetry.
For this very reason, defects that are generally inauspicious are mentioned first;
indeed, the primary function of an ancient poet is precisely what is called the "elimination of defects."
The suffix *matup* is used here in the sense of abundance (*bhūman*) or praise (*praśaṃsā*), as in the word *guṇavat*.

Although it would have been sufficient to say simply "adorned" (*alaṃkṛta*), the use of the term "ornaments" (*alaṃkāraiḥ*) is intended to include those ornaments that are well-known [in literary tradition].

Although it would have been sufficient simply to say "tathālaṃkāraiḥ" (likewise by ornaments), the word "alaṃkṛta" (adorned) is used for the purpose of including only those ornaments that are well-known and will be discussed hereafter.
[The phrase] "rasānvitam" means "always connected with rasa.
According to the Kashmiris, there is no such thing as poetry in which, even indirectly, there is no ultimate convergence upon the excitants (*vibhāva*) and so forth.
By this, the definition of poetry (*kāvyalakṣaṇa*) is also indicated: such is poetry; and by saying "one who composes that is a poet," the definition of a poet (*kavi*) is also provided.
Now, following the order of enumeration, he states the general definition and classification of the defects:
"The defects of words, sentences, and sentence-meanings are sixteen, which are to be abandoned by the lords of poets in poetry; those very ones we shall first explain. (1.3)
The faults of words are to be abandoned; by this [statement], the general definition is established, based on the intention that "those which are to be abandoned are faults."

That which acts as an obstacle by obstructing the intended comprehension is always to be rejected in poetry; this very thing is what others intend by the term "defect" (doṣa), defined as "the impairment of the primary meaning. And that [defect] was previously shown to be threefold, according to whether its locus is a word, a sentence, or the meaning of a sentence.

Since a sentence is preceded by its constituent words, and the meaning of a sentence is preceded by those words, the sequential order is logical; however, he disregarded the fault of mentioning merely individual phonemes.
But when making a further internal division, he stated "sixteen," because each [word] is crowded with sixteen limiting adjuncts (upādhi).

The intention here is that those additional [figures] mentioned by the author of the *Kāvyaprakāśa* and others are included within these; however, if they were not so included, they would simply not constitute defects at all. This is not, however, a revelation of one's own doctrine according to the maxim of "local dialects" (*deśīyarāga*), because those factors which create an interval in the immediate apprehension are always of that nature [i.e., defects].

The underlying intention has already been stated—that [the defects] "beginning with those very [words]"—because the specific definitions cannot be introduced without such a classification. He now classifies the defects of words:
that which is ungrammatical (asādhu), unidiomatic (aprayukta), harsh (kaṣṭa), and meaningless (anarthaka).
That which has a different meaning, that which has an improper meaning, and likewise that which is non-significant;
furthermore, that which is unintelligible, the labored, the obscure, the one whose meaning must be inferred,
the doubtful, the contradictory, and that which is stated to be purposeless.
The defects residing in words— such as being provincial (deśya) or vulgar (grāmya)— are clearly evident;
likewise, the term "ungrammatical" (asādhu) refers to the loss of the primary meaning through the indication of mutual independence, which results in compounding.

For this very reason, anticipating the objection as to why brevity is disregarded and why the defects of individual words are not counted, he says: "The [defects] based on words are clear," meaning they follow the presence and absence of the words.
Thus, this same state of being dependent applies to sentences and so forth, as well as to qualities and so forth.
He states the purpose for distinguishing them:
"Now, their definitions are correctly stated along with examples. (6)

Now, with the words "athaiṣām" (now, of these), he proposes the examination: "properly" means free from defects in definition; for the very meaning of the term "examination" (parīkṣā) is the determination that removes the impossibility of a definition.
To explain how this will be accomplished, he says: "With examples.
With the intention that the first defect to be rejected is defined by the nature of the word itself, he states the definition of *asādhu* (incorrect speech), which was previously mentioned:
"That which is contrary to the science of grammar is declared to be *asādhu*."
For example:
"O you who are oppressed by the weight of a heavy burden, this shoulder of yours does not cause such pain as that which it causes when it is truly pained. (1)
In this regard, because the root *bādh* is conjugated in the middle voice (*ātmanepada*), the form should be *bādhate*, and not *bādhati*.

Since grammatical rules (*śabdāḥ*) are taught—that is, made known—through the conceptual analysis of base and suffix, that science of words, namely the *Vyākaraṇa* of the Three Sages (*trimuni*), is contradicted [by such usage]. Therefore, because it abandons the specific individual rules prescribed therein, there is no lack of correctness (*asādhutva*) regarding regional (*deśīya*) words.

And so it has been stated by the ancients: "O Lord, do not cover your pair of breasts with leaves"—this illustrates the futility of another agent; and likewise, the example "bearing [the lotus] whose copper-colored petals were made to dance upon the stalk swaying from her two playful hands" is cited as being of that same kind.

On this point, some say: "The term *bādhatibādha* means 'that which obstructs the root *bādh* by causing its displacement through refinement' (*saṃskāra*); the vocative address to you is *bādhatibādha*, meaning 'O You who are such an obstructor'."
The phrase "the word" is to be supplied as the ellipsis; that [interpretation] is incorrect because it would entail the fault of being of interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*).
Others, however, read: "the word *bādh* means 'it sublates' (*bādhate yathā*)."

This is the truth: when the meaningfulness of an existing [word] is not intended to be expressed—as in "gavity ayam āha" and similar cases—the designation of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) does not apply;
that which is not employed by poets is said to be "unemployed" (*aprayukta*). || 7 ||
For example:
"Kāmacīka, you have become weary; who are these who wish to make you tongueless?
He sleeps; what are these saying? Will Kamba swallow Śamba? (2)

In this context, although the words *acīkamathāḥ*, *ajihvāyakīyiṣan*, *sasti*, *vacanti*, *ghariṣyati*, *kambaḥ*, and *śambam* are established by the science of grammar (*śabdānuśāsana*), they are not employed by poets;
for there exists certain usage where a word is to be rejected precisely because it is unfit for poetic employment.
If this were so, it would follow that whatever is used in common worldly speech must necessarily be correct; therefore, it was said: "by poets.

This means that in poetry (*kāvyam*), that very fact of not being employed is the seed of its defectiveness. And such a class of words is understood from the convention of the authors of the treatises on poetic ornaments (*alaṃkāra*).

And so, while one [author] has cited the word *puṃdaivata* and another the word *cīrṇa*, the author, intending to show that other such unattested forms exist as well, cites an example: "kāmacīkamathā.
Because this is intended merely as an illustration, one need not search for a single complete verse here.
The venerable teachers maintain, however, that the employment of even a single word [from a prohibited list] should be avoided because it does not violate the rules of grammar;

thus, *acīkamathāḥ* is the form derived from the root *kam* with the suffix *ṇiṅ* in the *luṅ* tense, after which, following the application of *caṅ*, there occur reduplication, the *saṃvadbhāva* substitution, lengthening, shortening, and the elision of *ṇi*.
Its meaning is: "Which heroine did you desire? (*kāṃ nāyikāṃ kāmitavān asi*).
And who are these people who desired to seek you out as one who summons [them]?
The suffix *kyac* is applied after the word *hvāyaka*.
From that [root], with the suffix *san* and then the *laṅ* [augment], the form *ajihvāyakīyiṣan* arises; he,
a certain person, *sasti*, meaning "he sleeps."
The form *svapne* is from the verbal root *pasa* (meaning "to sleep");
*kambaḥ* and *śambam*— the words *kaṃ* and *śaṃ* being denoters of water— are derived from those two.
By the rule “*kaṃśaṃbhyāṃ vabhayustitutayasaḥ*,” the possessive suffix *vap* is applied;
therein, by the first [suffix], the meaning is that the cloud (*jaladhara*) will pour water (*jala-āśaya*).
In some places, it is read as “*śambaḥ kamban*.”
In this context, the meaning should be understood as "the one possessing auspiciousness will sprinkle the wearer of the skull";

for the form *ghariṣyati* belongs to the verbal root *ghṛ* in the sense of "to sprinkle," and the ancient teachers have stated that this root is employed in no sense other than "clarified butter," "compassion," or "heat."

By the phrase "by poets," he indicates that the suspicion of being ungrammatical is dispelled, stating: "Even those [words] established by the science of grammar are called 'difficult' (kaṣṭa) because they do not please the ear.
For example:
"Wherever the cloud pours down rain, there the cātaka bird finds it difficult to endure;
the nīpa tree blossoms—this very season grinds my heart.
(3) Here, the verbal roots such as *varṣ* ("to rain") and others are heard, which are unpleasant to the ear when uttered.
"Padam," and so forth: a word composed of difficult-to-articulate phonemes is called "kaṣṭa" (painful) because it is difficult to pronounce;
thus, the disclosure of the seed of its defectiveness is that it does not provide pleasure to the ear.

For the author of the *Kāvyaprakāśa* has stated that when the power of the Vedic revelation (*śruti-śakti*) is strained by such usage, it becomes incapable of apprehending the meaning of that sentence; thus, he designated as "harsh" (*kaṣṭa*) a single part of a word, as in the examples ‘tadgaccha sidhdyai’ and ‘apekṣate pratyayamaṅgalabdhyai’, where the syllables ‘dhyai’ and ‘dhyai’ are used. To this, [the commentator] replies: "It is the word (*pada*)," for a word does not incur the status of being harsh merely through the pungency of its constituent parts taken as a whole.

The sense is that since [the fault] is absent in examples such as *kārtārthya*, where it has been cited, the status of being a "fault of the word" (*padakaṣṭatva*)— on the grounds that it is difficult to understand only in one part— is not barred here by a staff [i.e., it is indeed a fault]. Furthermore, *varṣati* means "it rains again and again."

The form *dardharṣṭi* is the form of the root *vṛṣ* with the *yaṅ*-lopa suffix; it means "he becomes bold again and again," being the form of the root *dhṛṣ* (in the sense of "boldness") in that very same context.
In the reading ‘dardraṣṭi’, it is a form derived from the root *dṛś* with the *yaṅ*-luṅ suffix and the augment *am*; furthermore,
the *nīpa*, that is, the *kadamba* tree, beholds [it] again.

*Pophullūti* is a form of the root *phulla* in the sense of "blooming" (*vikasane*); such is this rainy season that it tears at— or repeatedly and excessively cuts— my heart, from which my beloved is far away.

Regarding the form of the root *kṛtī* in the sense of "cutting," one might mistakenly think that a syntactical fault (*vākya-doṣa*) arises from the juxtaposition of many difficult words; to address this, he says: "the verbs.
To the question, "How is such a distinction determined? he replies: "they are heard."
The meaning is that, because it proceeds by means of mere words through auditory perception alone, its difficulty is experienced;
thus, what is cited as being meaningless is for the sake of merely filling out the meter.
For example—
“He who bears his beloved upon half his body and the moon upon his head—he indeed is the God, the destroyer of Madana; may he purify you! (4).
Here, the words *ca*, *hi*, *vai*, *khalu*, and *tu* merely serve to fill out the metrical quarters.

An indeclinable (*avyaya*) employed without a meaning to be expressed, [merely] for the purpose of filling out a line (*pādapūraṇa*), is considered to be meaningless (*anarthaka*). For this very reason, the Easterners (the Prācyas) state that words such as *ca* are indeclinables; this is for the sake of explaining the basis for their usage, for a usage that lacks a root cannot possibly be capable of sustaining a poetic composition (*vṛtti*).
Generally, one fills out the verse by inserting indeclinable words.
As it has been said: "Like the composition of a bad poet, it possesses a dense arrangement of words,
yet it is manifest with a mass of frost and crowded with people"— thus [the mountain] bears [these qualities].

The particle *ca* is well-known in its usage in four senses, such as conjunction (*samuccaya*) and so forth; yet none of those [four] is possible here, nor does it have a meaning that is "high and low" (*uccāvaca*). Thus, by the statement [of its absence], another meaning (the sense of exclusion) is also to be understood in the case of *eva* and other such particles.

By this, the following view is also refuted, which some have asserted: that because specific words and so forth are not employed, even a single constituent part of a word is intended to be meaningless;
and thus [they cite]: "First, of eyes whose forms were smeared with a mass of collyrium, and then tormented by the spreading fire of separation fanned by the wind of their sighs..."

In the verse, "Right now the deer-eyed woman performs, as she pleases, the act of moistening with the water of her tears the discharge of the god Cupid, as if they were the points of his arrows," the plural number in the word *dṛśām* ("of glances") is redundant, because only a single woman— the deer-eyed one— is mentioned.

Furthermore, the word *dṛk* does not denote the act [of looking] here, for otherwise there would be the consequence of a lack of syntactic connection (*ananvaya*) with the ointment-paste and other items.

Likewise, the statement that the ātmanepada in "kurute" is meaningless because the fruit of the action does not intend for the agent (*akartrabhiprāya*) is itself a delusion on the royal road; furthermore, the claim that both [the *parasmaipada* and *ātmanepada*] would be ungrammatical in the absence of a fruit intended for multiple agents is likewise a delusion.
For nothing whatsoever can be either improper or proper by its very nature; rather,
that word which has fallen from its conventional usage is heard as having another meaning,
as for example:
‘Those who do not divide [the land] do not obtain the earth; those who do not sacrifice [an animal] do not bring prosperity; they do not forget suffering, nor do they [forget] their beloved.

(5) Here, the word *vibhajati* is conventional (*rūḍhi*) in the sense of partitioning (*vaṇṭana*), *ālabhati* in the sense of killing (*māraṇa*), *āvahati* in the sense of bringing about (*karaṇa*), and *prasmarati* in the sense of forgetting (*vismaraṇa*).
But it is not [the case] in the sense of "exclusive service," "gain from all sides," "carrying on all sides," or "excellent recollection"; thus,
that which has fallen from conventional usage (*rūḍhicyuta*) is so called because it is employed without regard for its conventional power.

For this very reason, that which one intends when applying [a term] is not in any way its [literal] meaning; thus, the names *anvartha* (etymologically meaningful) and *anyārtha* (having another meaning) are applied.

This very point has been stated by others through such expressions as "possessing a connection" (*yogavān*) due to the application of specific prefixes (*upasarga*) to a specific verbal root (*dhātu*), and so forth—thus they analyze it.

The root *bhaj* has the meaning "to serve," while the prefix *vi-* serves to illuminate a specific distinction pertaining to that [meaning]; therefore, just as in the expression "it flashes forth" (*vidyotate*), there is a designation of a usage corresponding to a specific verbal root, so it will be here as well—this is the seed of the delusion. However, due to the very nature of the power of words, in some cases a verbal root functions with a completely different meaning through the addition of a prefix.
As they say: "The meaning of a verbal root is forcibly led elsewhere by a prefix,
as in the cases of *prahāra* (striking), *āhāra* (eating), *saṃhāra* (destroying), *vihāra* (wandering), and *parihāra* (avoiding)."
Regarding this, he says: "In this case, [the fault lies] with the root *vibhajati*, etc.
Now, Vāmana maintains that if there is a dependence on the meaning, such a thing is a defect of the word-meaning (*padārtha*);
but this is not so.
Since it is the word alone that possesses positive and negative concomitance,
there is no fault whatsoever here in the logical connection; rather, it is the word itself that incurs the fault through such things as a lapse in its function.
If a fault of meaning were to occur merely by depending on the meaning, how could even ungrammatical words (*asādhu*) and the like be considered defects of the word?
For they are not such [defects] by their very nature; rather, it is the specific meaning that constitutes the distinction, just as in the case of "horse" (*aśva*) and "wild ass" (*gośva*).
As for how faults of meaning actually come to be, we shall explain that later.
That which has a trivial subject matter is called "devoid of substance" (apuṣṭārtha).
For example:
‘He whose arms are fifty, and whose eyes are six.’
"May the Destroyer of Madana purify you—He whose heads are twenty times half of half [ten].

Here, the denotations "ten-armed," "three-eyed," and "five-faced" are expressed by words that are not themselves trivial (atuccha), even though the objects they denote are trivial; thus, this is *apuṣṭārtha* (insignificant meaning).
As for the point that "the denotation is trivial," it refers to the following:
The meaning is that when a matter can be expressed by a few words, it is [faulty] if it contains an abundance of many words;

for being composed in such a manner does not nourish even the slightest degree of excellence, such that it would not be something to be abandoned—this is indicated by the term "un-nourished" (apuṣṭa). For example, half of a hundred is fifty, and the fifth part of those is ten.
In a compound, there is the elision of the ordinal suffix;
that word which is disconnected is traditionally known as "asamartha" (semantically deficient),
as for example:
“The water that the cloud rains down is salty;
this is the roar of elephants, and this is the neighing of horses.
Here, it is well known in the world that *jaladhara* means a cloud, *vāridhi* means the ocean, *bṛṃhita* refers to the trumpeting of elephants, and *hreṣita* refers to the neighing of horses.

In this context, when [the word *samudra*] is employed with reference to a cloud, a horse, or a bull, it is "inefficacious" (*asamartha*) because it does not express the intended meaning; thus it is "incoherent" (*asaṃgata*).
But how is this different from [the fault of] "having another meaning" (*anyārtha*)?
In this context,

when [a word] is to be understood in another sense, conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) is stronger than etymological derivation (*yoga*); however, when [the conventional meaning] is not applicable, *yogarūḍhi* (a combination of etymology and convention) prevails over mere etymology.
Others criticize this, saying:
"Even so, the loss of conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) remains common [to both]; therefore, that [distinction] is merely another pair of internal particulars.
This is not correct.
Due to a lack of understanding of the underlying reality,
a certain word— even when understood through the force of a reason for negation— occurs in a particular sense without regard for its etymological derivation (*yoga*),
as in the case of the word "cow" (*go*).

For it is not possible for the act of going to enter into the meaning of the sentence; moreover, since there is no cause for sublation, one who understands [the word] cannot abandon its primary sense, and thus it denotes the substrate as qualified by the connection [with the action],
just as in the case of the word "paṅkaja" (lotus).
In that regard, in the first type, conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) alone is the essence; therefore, when that is abandoned, it is "fallen from convention" (*rūḍhicyuta*).

In the second type, however, the meanings are distinct: [a word] used merely in its etymological sense (*yoga*), used inappropriately (*asaṃgata*), used where the primary power (*śakti*) is absent, or used for only a portion of the power. He clarifies all of this through the following explanation: here, in the phrase "jaladhara," words such as *jaladhara* possess the denotative power (*abhidhāna-śakti*) established by convention (*rūḍha*) with respect to things like clouds, which are characterized by the holding of water.
If it is asked, "How is this determined? he says in response: "It is well-known in the world.
The sense is that the relationship between word and meaning is determined based on worldly convention (*lokādhīnāvadhāraṇatvāt*).
Consequently, there is no conventional designation (*saṃketa*) for that specific yoga which falls outside the scope of [the word's] expressive power (*śakti*).

And where there is usage regarding the ocean and so forth, the convention is not established through the combined power of its adjuncts such as "ocean-ness" (samudratva) and so on; rather, usage regarding the ocean and so forth is inferred by the addition of words such as "salty" (kṣāra). Thus he says: "Therefore here... The summary is this: for this very reason, a word is not the designator (*vācaka*) of that state [of the object]; and for this very reason, because it is incapable and ineffective, it is designated by the technical term "ineffective" (*asamartha*). This is the concise point.
That which is not well-known [to the general public] but is established within the treatise itself is designated as *apratīta*.
For example:
"What is the use of much speaking? There are no qualities in my aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*)."
"Since love is inseparable from its qualities, you have no grounds for reproach.

(8) Here, because the terms *rūpaskandha* and *nāntarīyaka* are technical terms well-known in the treatises (*śāstra*) and are not understood elsewhere, their employment constitutes the fault of *apratīta* (the unintelligible).
The meaning is that it is established solely by the treatise, being a convention designated by those who engage in the discourse of the treatise.

For a sentence consisting of the juxtaposition of both well-known and unfamiliar terms, when employed as a subject for one ignorant of the treatise, is unable to produce the cognition of the intended meaning;
in such a case, the fault lies precisely with those [terms] that are unfamiliar, and thus its defectiveness arises from causing distress through stumbling over them.

Therefore, the conventional expression "aggregate of form" (*rūpaskandha*) is well-established in the Buddhist tradition [as meaning]: "What is the use of speaking of that which exists externally to what is not employed [in cognition]?"
Their [constituents] are the five aggregates: form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
Among these, the category of the aggregate of form consists of eleven categories:
the five sense faculties, the five objects, and representation as the eleventh; such is the system.

The word *antara* is listed in the *gaha*-group [of Pāṇini 4.3.60] in the sense of "absence. In the case of the suffix *cha* (forming *āntarika*) and the self-referential suffix *kan*, when a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*) is formed, the absence of *n*-elision occurs by virtue of its belonging to the *pṛṣodarādi* class; this is the meaning of the *Bhāṣya-ṭīkā*.

The sense is that qualities which pervade love do not exist in me, and since that which is pervaded cannot exist without its pervader, the absence of love is necessitated by the non-perception of its pervaders; thus, there is no fault to be imputed in this manner.
By the restrictive particle *eva* in the phrase "in the treatise alone" (*śāstra eva*), that which is excluded is stated: "elsewhere," meaning in the world;
for that [cognition] whose apprehension of an object is remote is considered afflicted and is not desired by the wise.
For example:

"A person who has conquered his own self and has been struck by the feet of his preceptor, who is the enemy of the birth of worldly existence, rejoices in the sky pervaded by the clouds, which are the enemies of the fire that consumes snow. (9)
In this verse, Indra was defeated by one other than Garuḍa; his son was Arjuna; his enemy was Karṇa; his teacher was the Sun; and the world, struck by his rays, welcomes the sky—of what sort?

[The sky] is filled with those clouds which hold that water which is the enemy of fire, which removes the cold. This is *kliṣṭa* (obscure), as it requires the comprehension of a remote or indirect meaning.
"Far" (*dūra*) means "at a distance" or "for a long time," which are synonymous;
affliction (*kleśa*) is of two kinds: that pertaining to words (*pada-viṣaya*) and that pertaining to sentences (*vākya-viṣaya*).

The first [type] is the employment of a general term in a specific intended sense without depending on context and so forth; when this occurs, even though the denotative power is present, comprehension does not arise immediately, but rather takes a long time through the consideration of mutual syntactic connection, resulting in a lack of aesthetic appeal (*virasatva*).

As it has been said: “For that is not desired by those who are intent [on the goal]”; this very meaning was expressed by Vāmana and others through the word *vyavadhāna* (obstruction), whereas the second [type of fault] will be described otherwise by means of the words *vyākīrṇa* (confused) and so forth. In the phrase *vijitā*, the word *vi-*—which denotes birds in general—is intended to signify its specific instance, namely Garuḍa.
Even when constrained by that, it is indeed a specific distinction;
likewise in other cases as well,
and here too there is no cause for restriction that would conform to an immediate cognition— thus, an intervention is entirely logical.
The form *himāpahaḥ* (fire) is derived from the root *han* with the suffix *ḍa*;
thus Candragomin formulated the rule simply as *hanter ḍaḥ* in the section on *ḍa*-suffixes.
However, having observed the irregularity (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of *himāpahaḥ* when formed with the suffix *kvip*, Candragomin formulated the rule beginning with *brahmabhrūṇa-*.
The wise say that a *prayoga* (poetic usage) has a hidden meaning when its sense is not well-known,
as for example:
"Your army, like that of the Thousand-eyed One, is unbearable to enemies."
"Like Hari's, other splendors do not shine within your splendor.
By the word *sahasragu*, "thousand-eyed" is expressed;
however, the word *go* does not have a more established usage in the sense of "eye."
And by the word *hari*, the thousand-rayed sun is meant; yet since he is not addressed by that name by many people, there is "obscurity" (*gūḍhatva*).
Regarding "of obscure meaning":
when a word has two meanings, one established and one unestablished, and it is employed in the sense that is less well-known, then it is "of obscure meaning."

The term *aprasiddhārthaprayogam* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound based on its capacity to convey meaning (*gamakatvāt*), signifying "that which has an application to an unestablished object. The construction is:
"In your splendor, the splendors of others do not shine."

He states that even though the word *go* is prescribed [in the lexicon] as meaning "arrow," "eye," "milk," "heaven," "cattle," "goat," and "speech," it is not employed with respect to the eye in the same way as it is with respect to the various types of cattle and so forth: "And not [in the case] of the word *go*...

He further states that even for the word *hari*, which is conventionally established by one's own [lexicographical] agreement as meaning "the black [color]," "lion," "cloud," "sun," and "serpent," its renown is not as great with respect to the sun as it is elsewhere: "That too is not [the case].
That which has its meaning constructed through one's own convention is called *neyārtha* (of interpretable meaning).
For example:

"Having mounted [the chariot] possessing the splendor of his face, he who has released the multitude of animals, who desires to consume the names of many people in rows, has conquered the conqueror of owls. (11)

Here, by the word *paṅkti* is meant the number ten; by *anekajanāmā* is meant the discus (*cakra*); and by *taṅra* is meant the chariot (*ratha*). From these two [words], *daśaratha* is formed; his son is Bālaka, namely Lakṣmaṇa. By him was conquered Ulūka-jit, that is Indrajit.
Having done what?
Having mounted Hanumān, who possesses a radiant face.
By what kind [of person]? By one for whom the rows of cattle have been released (*vimuktapaśupaṅktinā*).

Here, the word *paśu* (cattle) indicates the word *go* (cow); by that, arrows are meant. Thus, this is called "interpretable meaning" (*neyārtha*), because its referent is constructed through one's own conventions.
Having formulated the sūtra "svasaṃketa" as "the imagined meaning is the interpretable meaning," Vāmana explained it thus:
"The imagination of a meaning not found in the [original] scripture is 'imagined meaning' (kalpitārtha)."

The meaning of this is as follows: some maintain that a term which is led, by way of its own synonyms and secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), to the point of conveying the intended object—that term has a "conceptualized object" (*kalpitārtha*).
This is incorrect, because the phrase "by its own synonyms" (*svaparyāya*) is both redundant and too narrow (*avyāpaka*).
Therefore, the meaning is simply that it is employed through indication (*lakṣaṇā*) without a specific purpose (*prayojana*).

As the author of the *Kāvyaprakāśa* said: "Because of the power of the limit of 'non-primary' (*neyārtha*) meanings"—that is, where the indicative is prohibited [as a fault], there is no defect in employing indication when it is conventional (*rūḍha*), provided it is not for a specific purpose.

And likewise, since the application of words such as *dvirepha* (two-repha), *rathāṅga* (chariot-part), and *nāma* (name) to [the meanings] "bee," "discus," and "name" respectively—by way of denoting the words *bhramara* (bee), etc., which are followed by two *rephas*—follows the tradition of the usage of the elders (*vṛddha-vyavahāra-paramparā*), their employment [in such senses] is indeed improper.

For this very reason, the Kashmiris maintain that expressions such as "having pierced the water, she rose up like the flame of the fire from the mouth of the horse's beloved" are also of forced meaning (*neyārtha*).
He has demonstrated this very point by means of his own words.
Here, the jaw is intended as a part of the face;
"row" (*paṅkti*) refers to the meter consisting of ten syllables, by which the number ten is indicated.

"Born many times" (*anekaja*) refers to the twice-born *cakravāka* bird; its name is "wheel" (*cakra*), meaning a part of a chariot. [The term *cakradhara*] is formed with the suffix *ka* because it belongs to the class beginning with *mūlavibhuja*, according to the rule for the root *dhṛ*.
The phrase "from those two" refers to the *paṅkti* meter; "of whom [the name] is 'born of many'" means that it has such a name.
Furthermore, *tuka*, *toka*, and *tokman* are synonyms for offspring (*apatya*).
By way of illustration, he explains a single part:
"In this context, by the word *paśu* (animal), the word *go* (cow) is indicated"; the remainder of the sense is that, with respect to the *pṛt* (omentum), arrows are thereby implied.
The wise know that a word which does not produce certainty is "ambiguous" (saṃdigdha).
For example:
"He whose form is blue and red burns the three worlds at the end."
"For this very Mahādeva is worshipped in the three worlds" (12). Here, it is not determined whether [the one referred to by] "that word" (*yatpada*) is Vahni, Arka, or Śiva.
The very nature of the words here is subject to doubt;

for instance, in the phrase "sa eṣa hi mahādevaḥ," one might wonder whether the division should be made as "sa kiṃ eṣa hi mahādevaḥ" or as "mahādevaḥ. Since there is an absence of both supporting and subverting evidence, doubt arises, and there is no cause for restricting the specific application of the qualifiers.
For even fire and the sun, though they are forms of the Lord Nīlalohita and are destroyers of cold, do not produce certainty; this demonstrates the seed of the fault [of doubt].
When one says, "He is a *sādhucara* when one is intended," there is a fault:

regarding the word *sādhucara*, does it mean "one who was previously good" (*sādhupūrva*), with the suffix *caraṭ* according to the rule "in the sense of what occurred previously" (*bhūtapūrve caraṭ*), or does it mean "one who moves among the good" (*sādhuṣu carati*), with the suffix *ṭa* according to the rule "after *car* [the suffix ṭa occurs] in the sense of moving"? Thus, the very word is doubted, and therefore the claim made by some that "the constituent part of the word is doubted" is also refuted.
The contrary is said here to be the fabrication of a contradictory meaning,
as for example:
“Of him whose majesty is unsurpassed and whose power is concealed even from others...”
"Your praises are unprecedented for us, who have no friends worthy of such deeds.

Here, by the word *anuttamāḥ* (unexcelled), just as it implies "excellent," it also implies "inferior"; and by the word *apihitam* (covered), just as it implies "not concealed," it also implies "concealed."

By the phrase "a friend in misdeed" (*akāryasuhṛd*), just as one is called a "friend" (*suhṛd*) even when there is no [ordinary] purpose, so too is one who is a friend in misdeed (*akārye*) called a "friend. By the phrase "unprecedented glories" (*apūrvāḥ kīrtayaḥ*), just as glories are marvelous, so too are infamies (*akīrtayaḥ*) called "glories.
This is the opposite case.
A contrary construction of meaning is that which subverts the intended subject matter;

for instance, in passages such as "unsurpassed" (*anuttama*) and so forth, once it is established through context and other factors that the intent is praise, it is impossible to resolve the passage upon a contradictory meaning such as the absence of superiority.
Furthermore, there is no contradiction even if there is a simultaneous desire to express doubt.

In this case, however, the simultaneity of praise and censure is impossible; therefore, when one is present, there must necessarily be the sublation of the other, as for example: “The beloved suddenly seizes the neck of her lover, who has long been granting her eyes the joy of his sight.”
Thus, when the word *galagraha* is intended to mean "that which is the opposite of seizing the throat" (*kaṇṭhagrahapratidvandvin*), its previously established quality of bestowing bliss is sublated.

Here, the term *anuttama* is [interpreted] through both *bahuvrīhi* and *tatpuruṣa* compounds; according to the rule beginning with *vaṣṭi bhāguriḥ*, the elision of the vowel *a* is optionally prescribed, so that in one alternative it is *apūrvāḥ* (meaning "preceded by *a*"), while in another alternative it is *apūrvāḥ* (meaning "without a preceding *a*").
But when there is a restrictive factor (*niyāmaka*), it is indeed a merit;

for example: "That unprecedented object which manifests itself without a collection of causes. Here, the very change in the form of the word conveys a contradiction; thus, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), its status as a verbal defect is established.
They say that what is "unmotivated" (*aprayojaka*) is that which prescribes without distinction. (13)
For example:
"This Hanumān leaped across the salt ocean, which was dark as the *tāla* tree, exceedingly clear, and full of foam, with his forehead. (14)
In this context, some say that epithets such as "dark as the tamāla tree" applied to the ocean do not indicate Hanumān’s excellence in leaping, and are therefore irrelevant;
for only that which nourishes the excellence of the sentence-meaning is to be adopted by poets.

Otherwise, if the "bodiless one" (the Wind-god) were not mentioned, it would be a case of stating the inexpressible; for, since it would possess meaning yet lack syntactic connection, it could not have the mere purpose of completing the meter. Thus, there is no exaggeration; rather, the excellence of Hanumān is to be expressed by way of his leaping across the ocean.
Furthermore, qualifiers such as "dark like a tamāla tree" do not in any way contribute excellence when [the object] is at a distance and so forth; thus, they are not employed.
That which is indicated as "belonging to that place" (tad-deśya) is a word that lacks conventional usage (avyutpattimat), for example:
‘O friend, your cheeks are pits of loveliness; your arms are charming and plump; and your eyes, O friend, are the companions of the full-blown blue lotus’s playful smile.
(15) Here, words such as *gallatalla* and others are seen to be non-etymological regional (*deśya*) terms.

Regarding the term "tad-deśyam" (that which belongs to that region): a word that is unanalyzed, devoid of the distinction between stem and suffix, and used solely by common people, becomes unacceptable;
it is of two kinds: partless and having parts.

The division is such that the first [type of word] is regional (deśya) and the second is vulgar (grāmya). For those who are highly refined, the aesthetic impression (chāyā) is of one kind, whereas for those from the regions it is not so; thus, when words known in regional dialects are employed together, there generally occurs a discordance in the aesthetic impression of the composition. This is the seed of the defect, as witnessed by the hearts of connoisseurs. Examples include: *tallama* (a small lake), *laḍaha* (charming), *maḍaha* (slender), *vosaṭṭa* (blossomed), *kandoṭṭa* (blue lotus), and *moṭṭāyita* (amorous playfulness).
Vulgar (grāmya) is said to be that which has a meaning that is indecorous, inauspicious, or loathsome.

Here, it is taught that the indecorous is threefold: that which has an indecorous meaning, that which has another indecorous meaning, and that which causes the recollection of something indecorous. (14–15)
Among these, an example of improper meaning is as follows:

"May the great banyan tree protect you—that tree with a parasol-shaped crown, with thick trunks as supple as lotus stalks, possessing a vast expanse like the son of the Sun (Yama), the clouds, and the ocean;

which, when the two [Viṣṇu and Śiva] lie upon the earth in a single body, draws the splendor of the waist of the one who has a crescent moon as his crest and the one conquered by Kaiṭabha, as their massive thighs are spread wide apart. (16)
Because expressions such as "one with a head shaped like a parasol" (*chatrākāraśiras*) and "a crow" (*kāka*) possess vulgar meanings,
that which is used only by common people— excluding regional dialects— and is characterized by such vulgar meaning is termed *grāmya* (vulgar), specifically as *aślīla* (indecorous).
That is threefold: because it causes shame (*vrīḍā*), disgust (*jugupsā*), and fear (*taṅka*).
Among these, the first is *aślīla* (indecorous). That which possesses *śrī* (prosperity/beauty) is *ślīla*;
since the group beginning with *sidhma* is a class-name (*ākṛtigaṇa*), the suffix *lac* [is applied].
Due to the inclusion of "kapilaka" and others in the list of words, there is the substitution of *l* for *ś*.
"Inappropriate" (*aślīla*) means that which is offensive because it causes shame; this is the meaning.

The second [type] has a loathsome meaning, being that which causes disgust; the third is that which conveys an inauspicious meaning, being that which makes known a cause for alarm; thus, it is called an "unrefined word" (*asabhya-śabda*), a synonym for the indecorous (*aślīla*).
In order to demonstrate that even by him [Patañjali] the term is used in the treatise in the sense of "proper in an assembly," he explains the word *aślīla* by means of the word *asatya*,
stating "therein, the indecent (*asabhya*).
Since the meaning is indecent, the word itself is also indecent.

And that meaning—whether contextual or non-contextual, presented through *śleṣa* (paronomasia), or merely ascended to memory from a single part—is, in its respective order, of three kinds: the indecorous (*asabhya*) and so forth; likewise, there are also those beginning with the inauspicious (*amaṅgala*).
The Yamunā is the daughter of the Sun,
and the Gaṅgā is the river of the clouds;

the term *apāre madhye* (in the middle of the non-bank) is an avyayībhāva compound according to the rule "the word following [another] in the sense of the locative case ending (*ṣaṣṭhyā vā*) may optionally form such a compound."

Regarding the statement "Half belongs to Hari, half to Hara," since the word *kāṭa* (half) has an indecent meaning when used for the unity of the body, the qualifiers of that word would also become indecent; therefore, taking those [qualifiers], he explains: "here, 'having the shape of a mushroom'.
An example of another indecent meaning is as follows:
"The one who comes at night while you are practicing your studies is the one dear to you."
"How could there be a binding of the hair on the private parts of women for you?"—

this [objection] is because the word *pelabandhana*, which refers to the hair on the private parts of those dear to you, possesses an indecent secondary meaning (*asabhyārthāntara*), and thus it is understood as having an indecent secondary meaning.
That yakṣiṇī who comes to you at night while you are practicing your lore and reciting your mantra—
how then could your wealth be "pelava," meaning delicate, soft, or, in other words, meager?
However, the meaning is that by the grace of the Yakṣiṇī, much wealth is appropriate for you;

yet, the words used here have indecent secondary meanings. Having extracted those [words], he explains them: "That which is dear to you"—the very revelation of this indecent meaning constitutes the "insult" (ākrośa) expressed by the genitive case.

"That which is dear to you" is one word; since sexual intercourse is dear to him who possesses it, it follows that the meaning refers to the vulva of the woman. The word *pele* is well known to denote the testicles.
In this context, "bondage" refers to that which causes improper recollection, such as:
"O mango tree, why do you make me tremble with the harshness of the cuckoo's song?"
"Your foot has been placed upon the nape of your neck by my departing life-breath.

Because this [verse] causes the recollection of vulgar things—namely, the anus, the nape of the neck, and the feet—it possesses the quality of being a cause for the recollection of the vulgar; thus, it makes one tremble.
O mango tree, since the cuckoo’s voice causes pain through its bitterness, why do you frighten me?

Indeed, having placed my foot upon your nape—the back of your neck—my life-breaths have departed; therefore, I have won, and this effort of yours is in vain. This is the intended meaning of the statement.

In the word *kāṭava*, *kāṭa* is a partial form; in the word *kṛkāṭikā*, there is the elision of *kāṭika*. Thus, *kāṭa* and *kāṭikā* [are used] in common parlance for that which has an inauspicious meaning and for another thing that has an inauspicious meaning.
And the cause of an inauspicious recollection is likewise threefold for the sake of an ill-omened meaning. Among these, an example of an inauspicious meaning is as follows:
"In the village of Kheṭaka, [there was] rice-gruel and soup, and of the city of Valabhī..."
‘I shall die unsatisfied, O Hēhale, with what has been spoken.
Here, the word *mariṣyāmi* (I shall die) has an inauspicious meaning; [the word] *kheṭaka* is [an example of]...
One is never satiated with happiness because there is no limit to its measure;

thus, regarding the rice and soup that are produced in the village of Khaṭaka, it is inferred from the indicative mark (*liṅga*)—namely, the prohibition of the genitive case when used with a word meaning "satiated" (*su-hita*)—that the genitive case occurs when used with a word meaning "satiety" (*tṛpti*). In the phrase "the turret (*valabhī*) of that town or city," the genitive is used because it expresses the sense of being satisfied.

Others, however, explain it as follows: In the southern region (Dakṣiṇāpatha), there is a district named Bhaktasūpapada; in its village (kheṭaka) called Valabhī, which is a seat of Virūpākṣa, there is a certain city. There, the speech of women—which contains an excessive mutual love that is free from guile—is [the subject].
An example of this having an unintended meaning is as follows:
"She who sends her beloved away while he is staying at home during the spring..."
‘By giving a path to destruction, she is a *piśācī*, not a woman.

Here, through the words *pravāsayati* (banishes), *saṃsthitam* (established), *vināśapathadānena* (by giving a path to destruction), and *piśācī* (demoness), there is a shift toward an inauspicious meaning; thus, it means ‘she banishes [him].’

Without administering an oath, she banishes him—that is, sends him away elsewhere—even though he is dear and properly situated in the house; the intended meaning is that she acts improperly like a *piśācī* (demoness). "Banishing elsewhere" means expulsion (*uccāṭana*); "destruction" (*saṃsthāna*) means ruin (*vināśa*). It is the giving of the path to that destruction.
She is a *piśācī* because she eats flesh (*piśita*).
Because it belongs to the *pṛṣodarādi* group [of irregular formations],
he explains it as follows: here, "he causes to dwell abroad" (*pravāsayati*) refers to that which is a cause for the recollection of what is inauspicious, as for example:
“This is the sage Mārīca, whose *kṛtyā* (magical spell) brought about the birth of sons for Saṃkrandana and others from their wives, destined to bring about the end of Time at the abode of Death.
In this instance, the words *mārīca*, *kṛtyā*, *kāla-antaka*, and *saṃkrandana* serve as causes for the recollection of inauspicious meanings.
"Mārīca" means the son of Marīci; Kāśyapa produced twelve sons, the Ādityas, beginning with Saṃkrandana (Indra).
This is the meaning: it is the fruit of those *kṛtyās*—ritual acts consisting of the worship of the Lord—which were performed in the abode of the Blessed Mahādeva, the Ender of Time (*Kālāntaka*).

In the word *mārīca*, the part *māraka* is a [synonym for] *kṛtyā*; in the nominal form *kṛtyā*, the word *kṛtyā* itself is a part; in *kālāntakālaya*, the word *antaka* is a part; in *saṃkrandana*, the word *śabdakrandana* is a part.

That which expresses a meaning possessing compassion (*ghṛṇāvat*), that which expresses a different meaning, and that which is a cause for the recollection of something possessing compassion—these three types here are called "possessing compassion" (*ghṛṇāvat*). (17)
Among these, an example for the purpose of disgust is as follows:
“This suckling cries out, gapes, and vomits milk; the newly-wed bride, having conceived again, repeatedly belches and spits. (22)
The words *pardate*, *hadate*, *vamati*, and *niṣṭhīvati* have a loathsome meaning; *pardate* means he vomits, that is,
he performs an eructation.
"She spits and makes a *thūtkāra* sound, for the bride has conceived"—this indicates the cause of the infant's vomiting of breast milk and so forth;
for this very reason, the medical treatise states: "One should not drink the milk of a pregnant woman, for that [milk] causes the fetus to fall."
An example of a different meaning involving disgust (*ghṛṇāvat*) is as follows:
"These two cheeks of yours, drenched with tears and pale from putrefaction, stand before your beloved, O daughter; he honors them with the radiance of his smiles. (23)
In this context, for the words *klinnagaṇḍa*, *vipūya*, *āviṣṭhita*, *varcas*, and *pada*, there is another meaning that is loathsome: *bāṣpa* (tears),
*vipūya* (pus), and *muñja* (a type of reed).
"Viṣṭhitaḥ" means standing out prominently; "smitavarcaḥ" means the luster of a smile.
The meaning is that your beloved, standing before you and looking at your cheeks, performs a kind of worship with the moonlight of his smile upon your cheeks while offering a gentle laugh.
In another sense, "gaṇḍa" refers to a boil or ulcer that has become softened and moistened by tears and heat.
The pus is distinguished as *vipūya*; by that it becomes pale-white (*pāṇḍara*).
That which is stuck together is *viṣṭhā* (excrement); its feces are called *varcas-purīṣa*.

He explains that very thing separately, [showing] how the recollection of it causes a state of loathing in one who feels disgust: here, the word "klinna" (moistened) is the cause for the recollection of what is loathsome, as in:
"Moistening our healed wounds from the arrows of Love..."
"These great trees moisten the heart with the moisture of the dung-heap of an old wound.

Here, the words "moisture" (*kleda*), "dung-heap" (*purīṣaṇḍa*), and "great trees" (*mahaddruma*)—which refer respectively to the moisture of a healed wound, a heap of excrement, and large trees—are causes for the recollection of something loathsome; thus, [the poet] makes them fresh once again.
A cluster of trees growing closely together is called a *ṣaṇḍa*.
By the use of the word "healed" (*rūḍhāni*), he intends to specify that these are wounds from the arrows of Love;

thus, by excluding the portion belonging to the arrows of Love and retaining only the portion consisting of the wounds, he wishes to convey that the memory of the healed wounds arises almost immediately.
In the word *purīṣaṇḍa*, *purīṣa* is a single part [of a compound].
Thus, having characterized the defects of words (*pada-doṣa*), the defects of sentences (*vākya-doṣa*), which follow in due order, must now be characterized; therefore, he classifies them:
"That which is deficient in sound, that which has lost its proper sequence, that which has faulty euphonic junction (*visaṃdhi*), and that which contains a tautology."

18–19. *Vyākīrṇa* (disordered), *vākyasaṃkīrṇa* (intermingled sentences), *apada* (without a word), and *vākyagarbhita* (sentence-embedded); two types of *bhinnaliṅga* (different genders) and *bhinnavacana* (different numbers); two types of *nyūnopama* (deficient simile) and *adhikopama* (excessive simile); two types of *bhagnacchanda* (broken meter) and *bhagnayati* (broken pause); *aśarīra* (bodiless) and *arītimat* (unrefined).

These sixteen great defects of a sentence have been proclaimed; specifically, the compound consisting of a *dvandva* within a *bahuvrīhi* is [considered defective] for the very reason already stated regarding "being devoid of words."
In this way, the purpose [of the definition] should also be understood in sentences concerning the classification of qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth.

However, in cases such as "having different genders and numbers" (*bhinnaliṅgavacane*), the words "different" (*bhinna*) and so on—which precede the compound characterized as a *dvandva*—are each connected individually. Some maintain that "broken meter" (*bhagnacchandaḥ*) means "broken rhythm" (*bhagnayatiḥ*).
And thus the meaning would be confused;
[the term] *arītimat* means "that which possesses *rīti*," where the suffix *matup* is used in the sense of an eternal connection (*nityayoga*).
For the demonstration of constant conjunction serves to expose the seed of the fault;
therefore, even though there is brevity in the case of a *bahuvrīhi* compound, no regard is paid to it here.
Now, their definitions are stated concisely along with illustrations. (20)
Since the status of being a non-scholar (*asādhummatta*) is characterized primarily by the speaking of what is incorrect, he states its definition:
that sentence which is devoid of correct words is said to be "ungrammatical" (*apaśabdavat*); for example: [text follows].
‘When the Lord of Beings had caused the stone-canopy to reach total destruction with his arrows,

the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva struck the chest of the Three-eyed One— which resembled a slab of gold— with his two arms. (25) Here, the forms *gamitavati* [for *gamite*] and *ājaghne* [for *ājaghne*] are ungrammatical (*apaśabda*), because the suffix *ktavat* is used in the passive sense and the Ātmanepada ending is used for an action where the body is not the object.

Furthermore, those two defects of a sentence (*vākya-doṣa*) arising from the connection between the stone canopy and the chest of the Three-Eyed One are distinct from the defect of a word (*pada-doṣa*) known as "incorrectness" (*asādhu*).

It is said that incorrectness (*apaśabdatva*) is restricted to the word alone; since the application of grammatical refinement (*saṃskāra*) does not extend to the sentence, incorrectness is not a defect of the sentence.
To explain: because of the rule "kṛt-affixes [denote] the agent" (*kartari kṛt*), the suffix *ktavatu* in the sense of the object (*karmani*) is ungrammatical;

and since the phrase "and from an intransitive verb" (*akarmakācca*) is understood [in the subsequent sūtra], the ātmanepada ending prescribed by "after *yama* and *hana* preceded by *āṅ*" (*āṅo yamahanaḥ*) would apply only to intransitives. Furthermore, considering the syntactic unity with the statement "also after [verbs having] a limb of one's own as the object" (*svāṅgakarmakācca*), [the ātmanepada] is ungrammatical when a limb of one's own is the object. One might object: "How can there be a defect in the sentence merely by being included within it? For that [status of being a sentence-defect] is not appropriate merely by such inclusion, as it would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Anticipating this, it was said:

Regarding the phrase "and those two," it is not the case that there is ungrammaticality simply because the root *bādh* ends in the *parasmaipada*; rather, here, even though dependence on the proximity of another word is determined— as in the case of "the stone-canopy of the Lord of Beings"— as long as one does not reflect upon it, the doubt as to whether [the form] *gamitavatī* refers to the agent (*kartṛ*) or the object (*karman*) is not removed.

Similarly, in the case of "the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva [struck] the chest of the three-eyed one," having understood only this much, one wonders how he struck it; thus, the Ātmanepada ending is appropriate for an action directed toward a part of one's own body (*asvāṅgakarmaṇi*).

Indeed, this very thing constitutes a syntactic defect (*vākya-doṣa*), namely, that which must be determined through multiple words. Regarding the word *bādhate*, there is doubt as to whether it is derived from the root *bādh* with a *kvip* suffix followed by *tip*, or from the root *bādhṛ*; such a criticism is misplaced, for that doubt does not cease even when words such as *skandha* (shoulder) are in proximity.
The example from this very work, beginning with “‘Therefore your pair of breasts entreats you,’” was written among the word-faults by the author of the *Kāvyaprakāśa* through oversight;
likewise, Rudraṭa [cited] “Who is not humiliated by one who has risen up? (udapūtitaḥ).

For in that case, there is a prohibition of the suffix *tasi* by the rule "apādāne cāhīyaruhoḥ," and it should be observed by oneself that this [prohibition] occurs only through the proximity of another word;
the expression "the chest of the Three-Eyed One, which is like a stone canopy" is merely an illustration.
The terms *adhipati* and *gāṇḍīviśabda* are also to be understood [in this context].
Wherever the meaning or the expression deviates from its proper sequence, that is "Sequence" (krama).
For example: [Example omitted per instructions]
"Give him a horse and an elephant languid with rut; your beauty and majesty are equal to those of the sun and the moon.
(26) Here, although one should have said "an elephant and a horse," the meaning is expressed as "a horse and an elephant."
Having stated that the radiance and majesty of the sun and moon are equal, a verbal violation of sequence (*kramabhraṃśa*) is observed; this is called "violation of sequence" (*kramabhraṣṭa*),
whereas the sequence arrived at through the sense (*artha*) is the "semantic sequence" (*ārtha*).
That which comes from words is "verbal" (*śābda*).
How can the non-corruption of the meaning be a defect of the word? To this he says:

[the fault lies] in the fact that one ought to have said, "Let the elephant be given," yet instead one says, "Then let the horse be given. In this case, it is merely the inversion of the arrangement that constitutes the offense, provided there is no lack of capacity to give that [elephant].
It is logical that this constitutes a defect of sound (śabdadoṣa), because it is not meaningful; that whose sandhi is disjointed or discordant is "disjointed sandhi" (visaṃdhi),
as for example:
"In this forest on the mountain, this earth, filled with young trees whose buds are beginning to emerge, is being shaken by this cloud-wind.
Here, the intention to speak [the phrase] "by this cloud-wind" (*meghānilena amunā*) as a non-compound (*asaṃhitayā*) is a *visaṅgi* (a discordance).
In such instances as "mañjaryudgamagarbhāsau," however, there is a discordant junction known as *visaṃdhi*; here,
the prefix *vi-* signifies both departure and contrariety.
Thus, two meanings are established:
"the closest proximity is *saṃhitā*," and by that [definition], its grammatical operation is indicated.
*Saṃdhāna* means *saṃdhi*; it is an interval of half a *mātrā*, and thus the meaning is:
"that in which there is a joining (*saṃdhāna*) devoid of the effects of *saṃhitā*."
"According to the rule that 'euphonic combination (*saṃhitā*) is obligatory within a single word,' there is an option (*vikalpa*) elsewhere;
therefore, it is not included among the [types of] non-euphonic junction (*asaṃdhāna*).
There are two kinds of dissimilarity (*vairūpya*)."
Regarding "difficult to speak" (*durvacakatva*) and "indecorousness" (*aślīlatva*), the first is cited as an illustration by way of indication;
the second is as follows: "Flying far into the sky, moving with terrifying movements..."
"This bird flies up; therefore, take pleasure right here.
Now, one might ask: "If the composition of a *saṃdhi* (euphonic junction) is optional, how can there be a fault here? To this he says: "Not a *saṃhitā*...

If there were a prohibition against *saṃhitā*, then by forming a single *asaṃdhi* in such a way, the resulting deformity (*vairūpya*) would not be considered the poet's fault. However, if there is no prohibition, or if it is employed more than once, then because the deformity is clearly manifested, how could it not be a fault? This is the meaning.

The phrase "not the intention to speak" (*na vivakṣām*) is an elliptical expression; for even when there is an intention to speak, repeated usage is indeed distasteful, as in: “Then [the moon] rose, possessing noble gestures and movements.”
We shall explain the specific [category] in the Vaiśeṣika [system].
However, where the word and its referent are non-different, that is characterized by tautology (punarukti).
For example—

"These deep thundering clouds, accompanied by lightning, are making those longing [for their lovers] restless. (28) Here, the phrase "making those longing restless" constitutes a redundancy of meaning (*arthapunarukta*).
The phrase "the thunders are deep" is a repetition of sound; however, the distinction is that where both word and meaning are identical,
the word is non-different, having a non-different intended meaning as its denotation.
Therefore, there is no fault in *lāṭānuprāsa* when there is a difference in intended meaning (*tātparya*), nor in *yamaka* when there is a difference in the expressed meaning (*abhidheya*).
The remainder is that the word-meaning is conveyed by words that are non-synonymous;
thus, it differs from the former [type].

Both the repetition of a word whose intended meaning has already been expressed and the employment of a synonym are considered verbal redundancy (*śabda-punarukta*). Accordingly, there is a Sūtra of the Great Sage: "The repetition of two words is redundant, except in the case of a restatement (*anuvāda*).
And this is logical.

To state a single subject twice is a fault; and since that repetition may occur either by means of the same word or by means of a synonym, its definition is established by taking the word itself. Thus, "repetition" (punarukti) occurs here with respect to this very word. To the question, "What then is the sense of the possessive suffix (*matvartha*) here?", it is said: "Where that [is]"—that is, where within a composite whole a constituent part has the form of a repetition, that is the sense of the possessive suffix.

Therefore, the meaning is clear: the defect of the sentence (*vākyadoṣa*) consists in its being analyzable through various constituent words (*pada*). Furthermore, although this definition has been examined [in detail], it is capable of bearing the burden of refuting any single instance;
however, for the sake of brevity, only one example is provided.

Intending to demonstrate that a restatement made after the meaning has already been conveyed constitutes "repetition" (*punarukta*), and thus following the reverse order of the definitions, he first provides an example of "repetition of meaning" (*arthapunarukta*).
Bearing this intention in mind, and adhering to that same sequence even in his commentary, he says: "In this context, *utkān* means *utka*, which is to say, longing (*unmanāḥ*)."
"Unmanayantīti" means "they make [the mind] *unmana*"; this form is derived from the causative (*ṇic*) with the application of the *iṣṭhavad-bhāva* rule and the elision of the suffix *ṭi*.

"Ambhodharāḥ" is the noun being qualified (*viśeṣya*), while the remaining terms are its qualifiers: "deep and full," "thundering" (making sound), and "possessing lightning" (endowed with excellent lightning).
*Vyākīrṇa* (the disjointed) is that in which there is an inconsistency of case endings among words;
for example:
"When the swan kisses the stalk of the lotus, [he touches] its rough thorns."
"Making a sweet sound with its mouth while rubbing its limbs against [the stalk]," (29).

Here, when it should have been stated that "the swan, rubbing its limbs against the staff-like stalk of harsh thorns, kisses the face of the lotus," it is *vyākīrṇa* (disordered) because of the application of a construction involving displaced case-endings (*vighaṭṭitavibhaktika-yukti*).
That is what constitutes *vyākīrṇa*.

Even when words are free from affliction (*kleśa*), they are not capable of generating knowledge of a qualified object (*viśiṣṭārtha*) because of the intervention of case-endings (*vibhakti*) and the proximity of case-endings that do not create expectancy (*anākāṅkṣita*). This must be understood as the intended meaning of our venerable teachers who state that words characterized by such distinctive "afflictions" are causes of error. However, the affliction caused merely by the intervention of case-endings generally arises only in the case of word-sentences (*padaikavākyatā*).
The term "staff" (daṇḍa), being a locative case expressing the locus, requires a nominative case expressing the agent located therein; however, the verb "he kisses" (cumbati), being an action,
requires a case expressing its grammatical factor (kāraka).
In that context, it should be understood that "of the lotus-lake" (*padminyāḥ*) is indeed a genitive case expressing a relationship;
the intended meaning, which is understood here with some effort, is conveyed by the word "rough" (*karkaśā*).
For this very reason, there is no confusion due to meaninglessness, because the collective sense of the whole is perceived.

Is there some distinction between two utterances by which the comprehension of the sentence-meaning occurs directly in one case but not in another? That very distinction is explained as "proximity" (*saṃnidhāna*) and "separation" (*vyavadhāna*).

Intending to show that [the nature of a sentence] is inferred from the observation and non-observation of its effect, he says: "They know that to be *saṃkīrṇa* (intermingled) when it is mixed with words from other sentences in the manner previously described.
For example: [Example follows]
‘Hungry, he eats the crow; excessively enraged, he vomits the rice; shouting, the old man seizes the dog by the neck and strikes it with his staff. (30)
The elder seizes the dog by the neck and calls out to his grandson.

Here, although one ought to say "he throws the crow," "he eats the rice," "he seizes his grandson by the neck," and "he frightens the dog," the arrangement of words as stated is intermingled with the words of other sentences.
Words embedded within another sentence, by intruding into that other sentence, obstruct understanding in such a way that the entire collection becomes corrupted—just as when one says:
"An old man, being hungry, eats rice with crows; being intensely angry, he throws away the crow; he wards off the dog; and he seizes his grandson by the neck."
It is indeed understood that a certain word is connected to a certain sentence according to the sequence of expectation;
thus he says: "In this case, 'he throws the crow' reveals the verbal defect"—this is what ought to be stated.
By the phrase "the arrangement of words as stated," the intended meaning is that it is "intermingled"; the sense is that such a form constitutes an intermixture (*saṃkara*).
In common worldly usage, the term "intermixture" is applied to the blending of heterogeneous elements.
The wise know that a word which is inappropriate due to its connection with another word, such as one belonging to a different *prakṛti* (grammatical base), is a fault;
for example:
“Even though my husband is beaten by a dog... (*āujjaa piṭṭiae jaha kukkuli ṇāma majjha bhattāle*).

Thus, this word— which, when misapplied among words that are natural, soft, harsh, urban, semi-urban, or rustic— is termed "out-of-place" (apada)—
is of six kinds: the natural, the soft, the harsh, the rustic, the urban, and the semi-urban.
In this context, a word that possesses the weightiness produced by multiple long vowels or the weightiness produced by a single consonant cluster (*saṃyoga*) is said to be in its *prakṛti* state.
Examples include: *nīhāratārānīkāśasārasī* and so forth; *hastapallavakaṅkaṇakarpūra* and so forth;
as well as *pāḍiva āmāṇa siṇivaṃ ālagoḷa* and so forth, and *tyajjhatujjhauttāvilavihatthiatiaccha* and so forth.

That which possesses gravity produced by a single vowel, or is devoid of gravity, yet remains soft—such as *kareṇu*, *tāraka*, *saroja-nikara*, and so forth; or that which is sweet, smooth, succulent, and graceful, such as *madhura*, *masṛṇa*, *sarasa*, *sarala*, and so forth—for example:
*nīhāra-bāṇa iva āṇaveṇī* and so on, or *parakuala-ḍahataliṇa* and so on.
Drink that speech which is harsh— weighed down by the heaviness of nasalized sounds (*anusvāra*), visargas, and long vowels, and abounding in conjunct consonants (*saṃyoga*)—
just as [the fire] boiled pure water; as in "piba" (drink), "āhiṣātām" (let them two strike),
and "acchācchatatrasthavyūḍhoraskapracchanna" (covered by those standing in rows of bright armor with broad chests).
And just as the triad beginning with *grāmya* arises by taking conventional usage as its basis— as in "ā ī i e" and so forth, or "uppiccha uppupua ekkamekka" and so forth.

Renown is threefold: that which is universal, that which pertains to learned people, and that which pertains to a few worldly people who depend upon the former; among these, that which is renowned among all the world is the vulgar.

All regional words (*deśīpadāni*)—such as *hasta*, *vivāha*, *bhaginī*, *hāraka*, *kaṅkaṇa*, and so forth, as well as *tuṃbha*, *aṃbha*, *haliddā*, *sāhajja*, and so forth—are well-known in the same manner as Apabhraṃśa.

It is said that what is "not very well-known" (*nātiprasiddha*) is "urban" (*nāgara*), because it is the opposite of "rustic" (*grāmya*). This is based on the analogy with a city (*nagara*); thus, the comparison is made by virtue of its lack of extreme commonality.
This very [type of Prakrit], which is not overly well-known, is called *upanāgara*, as for example:
*ādyāśakiṃśārukhuralīlātaṅka* etc., and *sudevaacchevaguppantī vivalāā* etc.
However, in the *Śṛṅgāraprakāśa*, it is stated that even among the languages (*bhāṣā*), there is a distinction of *pada*.
But here, the author’s intention is that [the matter] has been resolved by discerning the propriety of the word and its genus;
such being the case, poets must maintain a certain sequence at every step, and one should not abruptly employ a state that is either incomplete or disjointed.
This is what he says with the words beginning "vibhinna" (distinct), and so forth.

The "logical and pleasing arrangement" (yojanā) refers to the fact that the [qualities] such as those abiding in their own nature (*prakṛtistha*) and so forth have been arranged differently; this amounts to what is called "exaggeration" (*atyukti*).
This he will state [later] with the words: "because of the illogicality" (*ayukteḥ*) and "having abandoned" (*ujjhia*).
Having seized him by the hair and bent him down,
and having rebuked him according to the reading "āujjhie," he is beaten with a stick.
Just as the word "kukkuli" (a female dog) is used for clarity— meaning it was struck in plain sight—
so too is my husband being watched by those with ears like winnowing baskets.
The genitive case is used here in the sense of disregard; the meaning is "disregarding those appointed to the royal court who were looking on.
The word *hā* expresses grief.
"To whom shall I cry out? To whom shall I shriek?"—this is the meaning.
Here, in the first quarter, the word *āujjhie* is both *upanāgara* (semi-refined) and in its natural state (*prakṛtistha*).
In the reading ‘āujjhī’, it is rustic (*grāmya*) and natural (*prakṛtistha*);
likewise, *bhattāla* is also so;
and in the third quarter, *pekkhantaha* is harsh (*kaṭhora*) and refined (*upanāgara*).
*rāulakaṇṇiā* is both vulgar (*grāmya*) and natural (*prakṛtistha*); *he* is both vulgar (*grāmya*) and soft (*komala*);
and *kasse* is both natural (*prakṛtistha*) and refined (*upanāgara*).
"Vulgar" (*grāmya*) refers to that which is common and natural;

here, when the speaker is vulgar—such as a laborer or a servant’s wife—and the meaning of the sentence is likewise uniform, and there is an absence of the brilliance of sentiment (*rasa*) that could conceal all defects, then just as the intermingling of dialects is a fault, so too is the case with vulgar expressions and the like. This path is to be known by the sensitive reader (*sahṛdaya*) alone, and therefore one must be attentive.
