The meaning is that [the statement] lacks connection as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
An example of what is contrary to propriety (*aucitya*) is: "A commoner fans a commoner woman with a silk upper garment."
‘With his upper garment of fine silk, the commoner wipes the face of the low-born woman, which is moistened with sweat from the burden of the exceedingly heavy and cruel water-jar. (70)

In this case, because it is improper for a commoner to have silk garments, upper cloths, and ornaments, this is "contrary to propriety" (*aucityaviruddha*). Here, "propriety" (*aucitya*) means fitness; when that [fitness] is being considered, its resulting in a conclusion opposite to what was intended constitutes another form of contradiction with inference (*anumānavirodha*).

For instance: when a low-born man has his face moistened with sweat wiped by a low-born woman using a fine silk upper garment, while he carries the burden of an exceedingly heavy and harsh earthen jar— here, as before, there is an absence of any means of valid cognition to establish a necessary relation,
since such a thing could possibly occur through royal favor or similar circumstances.

However, when considering what is appropriate for a commoner (*pāmara*), being veiled in fine silk (*paṭṭāṃśuka*) is improper; indeed, it is precisely the lack of acquaintance with the urban conduct (*nāgaravṛtta*) consisting in the adoption of refined attire and the like that constitutes "commonerness.
Therefore, the meaning is this: she is unfit for association with fine silk because of her commonerness.
Rice and boiled grain in a pot or jar, as in the case of that which contradicts one's vow:
‘“As long as I live I shall remain silent; my father and mother were barren; you are like the god of love, incomparable.

Here, because the speaker himself utters such phrases as “as long as I live I shall remain silent,” this is an instance of *pratijñāviruddha* (contradiction of one’s own proposition), due to the contradiction with his own declaration.
"Contrary to one's own proposition" (pratijñāviruddha) refers to a statement of commitment (abhyupagamavākya);
for example, the proposition: "Whatever my master commands, that I do without hesitation."
And the statement of the probandum is: ‘This is that hand which used to pull up the girdle, press the full breasts, touch the navel, thighs, and hips, and loosen the knot of the lower garment.’
Both [of these] are intended by the term "proposition" (*pratijñā*);
regarding the first, the example is "I shall remain silent for as long as I live," where silence (*mauna*) consists in non-speaking (*avyāhāra*).
This is understood precisely by the very statement of that admission;

for instance, having admitted that "this man is not silent because he possesses speech," it results in the negation of silence. This is the third contradiction with inference. Regarding the fourth example, which accepts the second alternative: "My father is a celibate student (brahmacārī) and my mother is barren"—the one who is the biological son is intended by the word "father," and for him, being a celibate student is impossible.
A mother is designated as such precisely because she gives birth; it is impossible for her to be barren.
This mutual contradiction is a conflict by way of a pervader, and this is the fifth type of contradiction.
For example: "He is incomparable, resembling the god of love.

For resemblance to the god of love is not well-known in the world; rather, by speaking of his similarity to the god of love, one accepts a state of being comparable, which is contradictory to the claim of being incomparable.
Therefore, this is a contradiction with the pervader (*vyāpakavirodha*),
as in the case "fire is not hot";
by the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the contradiction with inference (*anumānavirodha*) by way of an example is subsumed.
The wise declare that whatever contradiction there may be with the treatises on Dharma, Artha, Kāma, and so forth, that is the defect known as "contradiction with scripture" (āgamavirodha).
Among those, an example of contradiction with the treatises on Dharma is as follows:
‘Even though uninitiated, he mastered the Vedas from his teacher;
a crystal naturally pure does not require refinement.
Here, because one who is uninitiated lacks the qualification for Vedic study, there is a contradiction with the *Dharmaśāstra*.
Regarding the phrase "for the sake of dharma and artha," it is because [the child] lacks the qualification for Vedic study; as it is said:
"But when the guru has passed away without having performed the binding of the vows..."
"One should not utter the Veda except when performing the offering of the *svadhā*"—
this is a rule of Dharmaśāstra;
an example of its contradiction with Arthaśāstra is as follows:

“‘The conquest of the earth by kings has as its fruit the full enjoyment of sensual pleasures; enemies are conquered by egoism—what need is there for the glory of policy? Here, since the authors of the treatises on statecraft (arthaśāstra) do not approve of the enjoyment of sensual pleasures as the fruit of conquering the earth, and since egoism is not the cause for the defeat of enemies, there is a contradiction with the arthaśāstra.”
Regarding the word "kāma" here, it is established in the treatises on political science (*nītiśāstra*) that for Mahījaya, dharma is the fruit [of his action].
Egoism is pride; it is not a means for conquering enemies.
For the abandonment of the group of six internal foes, there must likewise be mastery over the senses and a desire for victory.

And as for what he said regarding "humiliation by an enemy"— beginning with the passage "that Raghu, together with his kingdom, rejoiced," the teacher Kauṭilya [points out] contradictions with the *Kāmaśāstra*, such as: Rāvaṇa’s pride in not returning another's wife, and Duryodhana’s refusal to give up a portion of the kingdom.
“O lady with lips like the *bimba* fruit, this tooth-mark shines upon your upper lip;
it is like the full scale of the seven notes, proceeding through distinct *grāmas*.
(74)” Herein, because the authors of the treatises on erotics (*kāmaśāstra*) do not authorize a tooth-mark on the upper lip, there is a contradiction with the *kāmaśāstra*.
Furthermore, since it is impossible for separated villages to possess the full seven musical notes (saptasvara),
even though there is a contradiction with the *kalā-śāstra*, you yourself face a contradiction with the *kāma-śāstra* precisely because [the villages] are parts of that [system].

Regarding this, the *Kāmasūtra* states that, excluding the upper lip (the upper lip being the "uttaroṣṭha"), the interior of the mouth, and the area up to the corners of the eyes, there are places for biting with the teeth similar to kissing.

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "of those with distinct musical scales" (*bhinnagrāmarāgāṇām*), it means that a combination of the seven notes (*saptasvara*) has not been established within the different musical modes (*mārga*).
And likewise: "The *dhaivata* leading [scale] (*nyāsa*), devoid of *pañcama* and *ṛṣabha*, with *ṣaḍja* as its *yati*, is declared to be *bhinna-ṣaḍja*";
on this, Aṅga also says: "The two *jātis* that are *ṣāḍava* and *auḍuvika* are declared to be of the *bhinna-grāma*."
Furthermore, in the *bhinnagrāma* scale there are either six or five notes, but not seven.
To the question, "In the context of discussing contradictions with the *kāmaśāstra*, how can a contradiction regarding the arts (*kalā*) be cited?", he says: "Because they are its parts.

This means that since the sixty-four arts, such as music and so forth, are taught by the authors of the *Kāmasūtra* as being limbs of love (*kāma*), a contradiction regarding them constitutes a contradiction with the *kāmaśāstra*.

By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), one should cite examples such as "liberation comes from devotion to a deity, not from the attainment of knowledge of reality," which contradict the scriptures concerning liberation and other goals.
Having first presented this enumeration of defects, he clarifies it under the guise of a specific summary:
"Thus, that poet who [knows] the words, the sentences, and the sentence-meanings..."
He who knows the defects as things to be abandoned is fit to compose poetry.

Even if it is adorned, a poem devoid of the *guṇas* is not worth hearing; therefore, the connection with the *guṇas* is primary between the two types of connection: that with the *guṇas* and that with the *alaṃkāras*.
And there are three kinds of qualities (*guṇa*) recognized by poets in poetry:
the external, the internal, and those that are specific (*vaiśeṣika*).
Among these, the external are the qualities of sound (*śabda*), while the internal ones reside in the meaning (*artha*). (60)

Indeed, those which are called "qualities" even though they are actually defects are certainly Vaiśeṣika categories; among them, those that depend upon sound will now be described according to their definitions and characteristics. (61–62)
Cohesion (śleṣa), clarity (prasāda), evenness (samatā), sweetness (mādhurya), delicacy (sukumāratā),

explicitness of meaning (arthavyakti), as well as loveliness (kānti), nobility (udāratva), loftiness (udāttatā), vigor (ojas), as well as another, namely forcefulness (aurjitya), the beloved (preyas), and phonetic excellence (suśabdatā). || 63 ||

Likewise, there are *samādhi*, subtlety (*saukṣmya*), depth (*gāmbhīrya*), expansion (*vistara*), brevity (*saṃkṣepa*), proportionality (*saṃmitatva*), reality (*bhāvikatva*), movement (*gati*), style (*rīti*), expression (*ukti*), and maturity (*prauḍhi*); these are their definitions and illustrations. (64–65)
In this context,
the quality of having well-connected words is designated as *śleṣa* (cohesion), as for example:
‘If two separate streams of the waters of the celestial Gaṅgā were to fall from the sky,
then [his chest], dark as a tamāla tree and adorned with a string of pearls, might be compared to them.
Here, because the composition is so well-knit that even distinct words appear as a single word, this is the verbal quality named *śleṣa* (coalescence).
"Thus"—
in this way, since the definition of defects has been completed, the qualities (guṇas) that follow in order must now be defined;
thus, the qualities such as *ojas*, *prasāda*, and so forth [are to be explained].

Since it is already established that figures such as *yamaka* and others are ornaments (*alaṃkāra*), it is now considered: what is the basis for their mutual distinction? And why are the excellences (*guṇa*) mentioned before the ornaments? For there is a reason for their posteriority, namely that rasa only attains its manifestation when refined by the triad beginning with the absence of defects (*doṣābhāva*). Regarding this, he says: "Even though it is adorned...
The Kashmiris hold that the excellences depend upon rasa, whereas the ornaments depend upon word and meaning (*śabdārtha*).
That [distinction] is not informative;
for instance: if this classification is based on the premise that poetry has rasa as its primary essence, then the ornaments (*alaṃkāra*) must likewise be directed toward that [rasa].
Alternatively, if there is no such rule that rasa is always primary, then how can there be a restriction regarding their dependence on that [rasa] even in the case of the qualities (*guṇa*)?

Furthermore, just like *prasāda* (clarity) and other qualities, *śleṣa* (conjunction) and the rest are also recognized here as belonging exclusively to word and meaning; so how can this distinction [between word-based and meaning-based] hold?

If it is argued that although word and meaning are perceived, they nevertheless incline toward *rasa*, then what is this "inclination toward *rasa*"? It cannot possibly mean "being dependent upon *rasa*."

Furthermore, since the culmination in the apprehension of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) is equally present in poetic figures (*alaṃkāra*) regardless of how they are constructed, this path is merely "delightful when left unexamined.

A certain specific excellence, transcending the conventions of worldly life and scientific treatises, constitutes what is designated by the term "beauty" (*śobhā*); this excellence falls within the scope of the science of poetry as residing in the audible word.
Consequently, the *guṇas* (qualities) are the causes for the production of such beauty, while the *alaṃkāras* (figures) are the causes for its enhancement.

As for what others have said—"Qualities (*guṇas*) are those properties that produce the beauty of poetry, while ornaments (*alaṃkāras*) are the causes of their excellence"—that too is not correct, because this [definition] lacks pervasion (*avyāpti*), just like the case of *rasa* and so forth;

for no one accepts that they (the ornaments) are included within the body of the *rīti*. Therefore, a quality such as *śleṣa* (conjunction) and others, which conforms to the conventions of the *ālaṃkārikas*, [is what constitutes a quality].
The classification is that an ornament (*alaṅkāra*) is any one of the [categories] beginning with *jāti*;
for that very reason, he will later include even the *guṇas* within the category of ornaments by virtue of their producing beauty.
However, a work in which the *guṇas* are prominent brings about aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*) even if it is clearly devoid of ornaments.
For example: "Who are you, O auspicious one? Whose wife are you? Or what is the reason for your coming to me?
Speak, considering that the minds of the self-controlled Raghus are by nature averse to the wives of others.
Since the possession of virtues is the primary [criterion], this [quality] was mentioned first and characterized here.
While the general qualities remain [unspecified], he divides the specific qualities: the word "and" [in the sūtra] indicates that they are threefold.
Sound is external, as it occupies the body, because it is that which is to be presided over and because it is the first to be perceived;
consequently, the qualities dependent upon it are also external.

But the *artha* (object) is internal because it is like the self (*ātman*) in its role as the substratum and because it is subsequently grasped; therefore, the qualities (*guṇas*) residing within it are also internal.
Now, some [schools], having reached a distinction—namely the Vaiśeṣikas—[assert that] those which were previously considered defects later become qualities.
With the intention that even defects may become virtues through specific application,

he refutes the view of the author of the *Dhvanyāloka*— who held that "there are only three virtues: sweetness (*mādhurya*), vigor (*ojas*), and clarity (*prasāda*)"— by stating "twenty-four," the implication being that this is due to the mutual intermingling of the limiting conditions (*upādhi*).

And this is not a mere conceptualization on our part; thus he says: by the use of the suffix *niṣṭhā* (the past participle) in the word *ākhyātāḥ*, the state of being "for the first time" (*idaṃprathamatā*) is indicated.
Precisely because of the aforementioned qualification, he states that the qualities of sound exist prior [to the words]: "in them" (*teṣu*).

He states that expression is twofold according to its division: by way of name and by way of characteristic—in the phrase "through the application of name and characteristic. Since this concerns the arrangement of words, one must investigate other qualities; therefore, he first states the definition of *śleṣa* (punning conjunction), beginning with "therein."

Where words are "śliṣṭāni" means they are joined; the state of being so is "tattā. One should not suspect that mere joining constitutes a poetic quality (guṇa), for "supada" means a beautiful joining.

The excellence of *ghaṭanā* (structural arrangement) consists in smoothness and the capacity for the appearance of unity. In this regard, the seed [of this excellence] is the presence of alliteration (*śrutyanuprāsa*) and the unperceived seam (*alakṣitasandhi*), as in the example "brahmaṃ sūtram uraḥsthalam," where both the vowel *u* and the consonant *bh* belong to the labial class. Thus, in the cited example, both the *u* and the *bh* are labials.
If the *v* and *y* at the beginning and end of "avya," etc., are palatal (*tālavya*),
this is not an alliteration of phonemes (*varṇānuprāsa*),
because of the difference in their degree of contact (*īṣatspṛṣṭatva*) and so forth.
In the middle [of the sequence], the letters *da* and *va* are dental-labial;
in the word *amni*, it should be understood that the letter *ma* is homophonous with *bha*, and the letter *na* is homophonous with *da*, and so forth.

Likewise, in the phrase *pṛthakpravāhau*, the letter *ka* appears as having attained identity through its transition into the *pa*-group (*pavarga*). In the phrase *pravāhāvākāśa*, the letter *au* results in another phoneme through its substitution by *ā*.
In the same way, this should be inferred for expressions such as "let them fall from the milk" (*payasaḥ patetām*);
by the word "separately" (*pṛthak*), meaning on both sides,
it is understood that the necklace consists of two strings hanging from the right and left portions of the chest.

In the phrase "his chest" (*asya vakṣaḥ*), the word *asya* (his) implies that there is no one else whose necklace is thus incomparable, nor any other chest that is as lofty and expansive as the sky; this suggests the Blessed One's uniqueness in contrast to the entire world—thus say the venerable teachers.
When a word possesses its well-known conventional meaning, that is called *prasāda* (clarity). || 66 ||
For example:

"Let the buffaloes plunge into the water of the drinking-trough, repeatedly striking it with their horns; let the herd of deer, gathered in groups in the shade, practice rumination; let the lordly boars unrestrainedly root up the *musta* grass in the pool; and let this bow of mine find rest with its string slackened. (76)
In this context, *prasāda* (clarity) arises from the employment of words with well-known meanings, such as in the verse beginning "Let the buffaloes plunge into the water of the pool";
the meaning of this [definition], namely that it consists of "well-known meanings," has already been explained previously.
Grace (*prasāda*) is twofold: that which has the expressed meaning as its object and that which has the suggested meaning as its object.

Among these, an example of that which has the suggested meaning as its object is as follows: “While the divine sage was speaking thus, Pārvatī, with her face cast down beside her father, began counting the petals of her play-lotus.”
In this regard, from the very sentence heard and understood, bashfulness and other such qualities manifest as if placed directly in one's hand;
the subject matter of the sentence becomes twofold— either vulgar or refined— depending on whether it is carried out through vulgar or refined words.

The first is as follows: "A stain upon the moon, poverty among the virtuous, flickering splendor in the lotuses, and a perpetual lack of favor in the faces of the wealthy—they tell us that the Creator’s fame is broken. He illustrates the second type with the verse beginning "Let them plunge... (gāhantām).
In this first quarter, "gāhantāṃ mahiṣāḥ" is vulgar;
"nipānasalilam" is Upanāgara;
and "śṛṅgaiḥ" is vulgar.
"muhūrttyupanāgaram tāḍitam" is vulgar because of the word "tāḍita" [in the first pāda];
in the second pāda, the words "kadamba" and "karomantha" are refined (upanāgara), while the remaining words are vulgar.

And thus, even in the case of the last two [syllables], the analysis (*vivecana*), the immersion (*gāhana*), and the churning (*viloḍana*) performed by themselves become entirely free from doubt; this is the suggestion of confidence (*visrambha-dhvani*).
Precisely because there is no fear, there is a return to the natural state (*prakṛti-pratyāpatti*).
Striking the water alternately with its two horns is the nature of the buffalo;
seeking shade and forming herds is the nature of the deer.

Because they were long unacquainted with one another's news, their chewing of the cud during the daytime was as if unfamiliar; the implied meaning is that it should now be practiced so that familiarity may arise through the process of training.
By the phrase "by the lords of boars," it is revealed that such creatures as these are not within the scope of our hunting frenzy;
for is it not the case here that the discrepancy in the grammatical subject (*kartṛprakramabheda*) constitutes a fault?
This is not so.

This [hero] does not exert such fury against buffaloes—who are intoxicated by the onset [of battle] yet fearful of its consequences—nor against deer—who are timid by nature—as he does against boars, who are skilled in returning [to the charge] and experts in various maneuvers;

and thus, it is now suggested that he could not endure their mere agency (*kartṛtā*) in performing their appropriate actions. Therefore, when the third case-ending (*tṛtīyā*) is employed to indicate this fitness, even a break in the symmetry of expression (*prakramabheda*) is entirely appropriate; this is the path approved even by the author of the *Vyaktiviveka* and others.

By the word "ca" (and) in the phrase "idaṃ ca," it is implied that if our bow is either strung or unstrung, then at that very moment there would be both fear and confidence among those within the range of our fury; this indicates the intensity of our anger.
For this reason, the plural form "asmat" (our) is used to signify that [the bow] is strung.
This refers to the method of composing the arrangement of syllables, which are soft, distinct, and intermingled.
The expression of meaning without inequality is called *samatā* (evenness).
For example:
"That which wandered upon the tawny mass of matted locks of Hara, which bore the weight of the buds of the rays of ten million moons..."
"May that water of the celestial river (Surāpagā), resounding with the grand resonance of the *jhāṅkāra* [gurgling] from the bowers on the rocks of the snowy mountain (Himaśaila), purify you.
Here, there is "evenness" (*samatva*) because the clear composition is maintained consistently from the beginning until the conclusion.

The Path has been explained by means of the term *pratītya* (in dependence). By the phrase "speaking without unevenness," the classification of speech is indicated: among vowels, the short ones and the final ones are soft; among consonants, the final letters of the classes (*varga*) and those beginning with *da* are soft and gentle syllables.

Among vowels, the long ones are distinct; among consonants, with the exception of the letter *ṇa*, the *ṭa*-class, *ra*, *śa*, *ṣa*, and *ha*, as well as conjuncts not beginning with *da*, are distinct.

The remaining consonants, the dental conjuncts, and the intermediate letters mixed [with others]—the method of composition involving any of these letters, when expressed through a process that is uniform in its commencement, conclusion, and so forth, is what constitutes *samatā* (evenness).

This is not merely the absence of a defect; rather, it is the accomplishment of the entry into and the conclusion of a composition through the familiarity with letters of a single type, which culminates in the excellence of the primary element by way of being a manifestation of innate power (*śakti*) and cultivated proficiency (*vyutpatti*).
Nor has such a nature of the absence of defects been denied by anyone.
For this very reason, the status of *śleṣa* (paronomasia) and *prasāda* (clarity) as *guṇas* is also established.

Now, consider this: "O slender-waisted one, where has she gone, leaving behind her devoted lover? Why do you vainly shake your head, overcome by the wind, when she is not seen? Without the touch of her feet, how could there be this emergence of flowers for you, whose petals are bitten by the swarm of bees gathering in their longing? In this verse, the paronomasia (*śleṣa*) between the meanings of "slender-waisted" (*kṛśodarī*)—referring both to the woman and the Aśoka tree—and the other words is present. Furthermore, the clarity (*prasāda*) of the sense is evident; thus, these two are indeed *guṇas*. However, if it is argued that the paronomasia here is merely a figure of speech (*alaṅkāra*), then it would follow that *prasāda* also becomes a mere figure of speech, which is undesirable. Therefore, both must be accepted as *guṇas*. Moreover, since the paronomasia is subordinate to the suggested meaning (*dhvani*), it is established that it functions as a *guṇa*. Thus, the status of *śleṣa* and *prasāda* as *guṇas* is proven.
In this case, there would indeed be the fault of inconsistency;
for here, in the state of liberation, there is no manifestation.
Therefore, this [objection] is trivial.

Thus, because it is accomplished through these three types, *samatā* (evenness) is of three forms: *grāmyā* (vulgar), *paruṣā* (harsh), and *upanāgarikā* (polished). Among these, *grāmyā* occurs when the composition is mostly carried out with a mixture [of the aforementioned qualities], as for example: "First pale in hue, then marked by a brownish tint, and thereafter its form increased by the quality of redness due to the excess of ripening..."

In the forest, uneven with its own rugged buttresses as it slowly begins to form its hollows, the jujube fruit attains a state of sapless dryness while its fragrance is swallowed up—just as [the poet] says: "O Moon," [referring to] the Himālaya groves where the creeper-like matted locks of the Supreme Lord are still entangled in the clusters of buds from the rays of the young moon; there, due to the illusion of wandering, the water of the Gaṅgā is perceived even now as if it were still gurgling—this is a case of *pratīyamānotprekṣā* (implied poetic fancy).

The *upanāgarikā* style is as follows: “Clad in soiled garments, her face emaciated by religious observances, bearing a single braid, and pure in character, she reveals my long suffering of separation from that utterly merciless man.
Here, our fellow students consider only the first half-verse to be an example of the *upanāgarikā* style.
For in the latter half [of the verse], because of the placement of descriptive words such as "viṣka" and so on, there is indeed a lack of intermingling;
this is another type of composition called "unmixed" (aparonmiśrā), which consists in a conclusion through the equalization of soft and harsh phonemes.
Furthermore, that state of separate words within a sentence is known as "sweetness" (mādhurya).
For example:

"The first drops of rain, having rested for a moment on her eyelashes, striking her lower lip, and being pulverized by falling upon the elevation of her breasts, finally reached her navel after stumbling across her folds. (78)
In these words, because there is an absence of *saṃhitā* (euphonic combination), there is sweetness (*mādhurya*) through the state of separate words (*pṛthakpada*).
That composition in which the words appear as if they were separate is called "separate-worded" (*pṛthakpada*); this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound containing a simile (*upamā*).

The state of that [word] is its "tattā," which is the nature of sweetness as previously described; when that [sweetness] residing in the word is not interrupted by being separated into distinct words,
then that very [word] is endowed with sweetness.

For by propriety (*aucitya*), either compound (*samāsa*) or non-compound (*vyatireka*) is drawn forth; sometimes there is a non-compound, which is "non-elaborate" (*anuddhata*), meaning "without elaboration" (*anullekha*).
As it has been said: "In the quality of sweetness (*mādhurya*), the arrangement (*ghaṭanā*) is likewise either without compounds or with moderate compounds."
For this very reason, Vāmana stated that "this [verse] aims at the avoidance of compounds.
However, when a certain compound, drawn by the propriety of the sentiment (*rasa*), is contemplated by the wise, it becomes a cause of aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra*).

For example: "May there be well-being for those bower-huts on the banks of the daughter of Mount Kalinda (the Yamunā), which were friends to the dalliances of the cowherd women and witnesses to the secret trysts of Rādhā."
"Now that the utility of soft-cutting for fashioning love-beds has ceased, those sprouts, their dark luster fading, will surely become withered.

Here, the word *tat* (those) does not refer to just any woman, but specifically to one related to a cowherd (*gopa*), who is entirely dependent on her mastery of the arts of cowherd conduct; this is because the speaker intends to emphasize the particularity [of the subject] by avoiding a compound and thus leaving the conclusion unabbreviated, implying that the experience of these sprouts—which have attained excellence through the abundance of her playful charms—is itself the witness.

Affection does not exist elsewhere except in that which is somewhat devoid of flavor; rather, it is indeed a form of amorous play (*vilāsa*), and even that is not just any kind of play, but specifically one related to the cowherd women. Thus, with the intention of expressing the collective nature of many elements, a compound (*samāsa*) alone is appropriate;
by this much alone, a break (*viccheda*) [in the verse] is also entirely fitting.
Since everything is being surrendered, it is appropriate to state separately the specific quality produced by that connection;
thus, even in the phrase "of the witnesses of Rādhā’s secret," the compound is formed as before.

Although a compound does not appear fitting here because the primacy of the connection with Rādhā is merely intended for the sake of expression, nevertheless, considering that another [term] would be capable of being placed in the secret of Rādhā, he abandoned the word "friends" (*suhṛdām*) and spoke instead of "witnesses" (*sākṣiṇām*).
For a witness functions as one who stands on the sidelines;
therefore, it should be understood that because the intention is to emphasize the necessity of being a witness, a contradiction is possible,
[as expressed by the phrase] "they remain."

By specifying the agency of the water droplets as they remain upon her eyelashes, strike her lower lip, fall upon the slope of her breasts, slip across the folds of her waist, and reach the depth of her navel, her absolute freedom (svācchandyam) is revealed. And thus—it is suggested that Gaurī is devoid of external perception; by this, the intensity of her passion directed toward the Lord is indicated in the first quarter-verse. Furthermore, it is implied that she is a source of wonder even for the three worlds: by dispelling the heat of the summer season, by removing the dust [of worldly passion], by manifesting fragrance, and by causing the peacock’s cry and other such wonders.
Furthermore, regarding the perception of those [phonemes] as they actually are, the intended meaning remains the same:
in the form "tāḍitā," there is the emergence of the [syllable] *cha*; in "payodhare" and so forth, there is the vowel *o*; and [in other cases], the phonemes *dha* and *ta*.
That which consists mostly of non-harsh syllables is known as *sukumāra* (the delicate).
For example:
"Having formed circles with their plumages, with throats [emitting] sweet songs..."
"The peacocks dance at the time when the sky is garlanded with clouds.

(79) Here, because there is no harshness of sound—due to the absence of the defects of *śleṣa-viparyaya* (inversion of alliteration) and *śaithilya* (flaccidity), and because of the abundance of syllables—the quality of *saukumārya* (tenderness) is present;
thus it is said, "not harsh" (*aniṣṭhurā*).

The opinion of the ancients is that even in an entire composition, two or three, or three or four, clearly articulated syllables are inserted; this, by way of the analogy of an occasional relish, results in a variegated aesthetic experience and is thus called *sukumāra* (the delicate).
For this very reason, it is a variety of *samatā* (evenness).
Furthermore, the *bhṛṅgīkāpāka* (the ripening of the grape) will be described as being of a different kind.
In the world, a practice that is gentle and delicate is observed;

for instance, in the first quarter of the verse beginning with *maṇḍalīkṛtya*, the three conjuncts (*saṃyoga*)—*maṇḍe-ti*, *kṛ-tye-ti*, and *bar-he-ti*—are presented, while in the second quarter, the two conjuncts *ṇṭhe-ti* and *rm-e-ti* are introduced. By employing these and incorporating long vowels within the melody, a different form is achieved, which serves as the cause of its particular beauty.

In the third quarter, there are long vowels, visargas, and conjuncts in the words *keti*, *na*, and *pranṛtyanti*; in the fourth quarter, there are likewise long vowels in the phrase *antarāntarā*. This is indeed the same *vāsanā* (poetic impression).

Now, since it should have been stated that "suavity (*saukumārya*) consists in being composed of non-harsh syllables," for what purpose is the word *prāyas* (mostly) used? To this he says: "In this [verse]... (*atre*).
Furthermore, this [quality] is not a quality of meaning, for that is determined with respect to the sentence-meaning as the substratum (*dharmin*);
however, since this [quality] pertains to a collection of words, its inclusion among the qualities of sound is appropriate.
Otherwise, it would be "appropriateness" (*saṃmitatva*).
That in which they speak of the completeness of the sentence and the clarity of meaning is as follows:
"Speech and meaning, joined together like speech and meaning for the sake of understanding speech and meaning..."
"I revere Pārvatī and Parameśvara, the parents of the world.
(80) Here, because the sentence is complete and the meaning is fully realized, there is *arthavyakti* (clarity of meaning), as in the example "like speech and its meaning."

Here, by the very use of the first-person pronoun in the word "I venerate" (*vande*), the sense of "I" is already established, since the rule "the first person is used for 'we'" (*asmadyuttamaḥ*) specifies that this is the substitute for the original form. When the object is required, [it is supplied as] "Pārvatī and Parameśvara.
Furthermore, when asked what these two are like, [it is said] they are "the parents of the world."

Therefore, by virtue of this distinction from cases such as Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, the state of being worthy of salutation is the meaning of the word "mother" (mātṛ) expressed through the single-remainder compound (*ekaśeṣa*);
for it is appropriate that [the term] refers to both female and male, just like the expression "word and meaning" (*vāgarthau*).
Regarding the question "For what purpose do you pay homage?", [the answer is] "for the comprehension of word and meaning" (*vāgarthapratipattaye*).

Thus, whatever kind and however many varieties of qualifier and qualified are intended, all of them are understood without impediment by the mere collection of words employed in the phrase beginning with "speech" (*vāk*). He clarifies this through the explanation of the meaning of the term *arthavyakti*—that is, the manifestation of meaning—by stating "because it conveys the meaning" (*arthasamarpakatvāt*), thereby revealing that [speech] is a quality of sound (*śabda*).
That brilliance which belongs to the poetic bond is called *kānti* (loveliness).
For example:
“Joyless in the jasmine, distressed by the honey of the young *bakula*, not lingering even for a moment on the *sāla*, nor finding delight in the *lavaṅga*...”
"The bee does not alight on the *priyaṅgu* flower, nor does it frequent the mango tree; remembering its drinking of the honey from the *lakṣmī*-sport-lotus, it [remains elsewhere].
Here, the brilliance (*ujjvalatva*) of the composition, by virtue of its luster, is what is called "loveliness" (*kānti*).
Furthermore, what is this so-called "brilliance" (*ujjvalatva*)?

Some say it is an abundance of alliteration (*anuprāsa*); that is incorrect—for instance: "From her two eyes flowed water born of the anger of love, just as dew-water flows from the petals of a lotus."
In such passages as these, an abundance of alliteration is indeed possible; for they declare that the "ancient luster" (*purāṇacchāyā*) consists precisely in the opposite of [modern] brilliance.
For example: "It moves through the sky, resembling the leaf of the *bhallātaka* tree.
For this very reason it is said: "The poet's speech is as barren as a painting in an old scroll.
Therefore, the beauty of composition lies precisely in its beginning with unblemished words.
For example: "the bow of Kusuma" is *prahata* (struck/derived), while "of Kusuma" is *aprahata* (unstruck/un-derived);
likewise, "in the ocean" is *prahata*.
"Having overcome the ocean, [he] has cast off heaviness"—
thus "cast off" (*prahata*) is not cast off (*aprahata*), and so forth.

For this very reason, the quality of being "wonder-inspiring" (*camatkāritva*) consists in its capacity to delight the connoisseur. Indeed, even though words possess the same denotative power (*vācakatva*), there exists a certain intermediate distinction among them, by virtue of which great poets employ only specific words and not all;
for example, instead of saying *pallava* (sprout), one uses *kisalaya*.
Where one should say "woman" (*strī*), they say "beloved" (*kāntā*);
where one should say "lotus" (*kamala*), they say "rājīva," and so forth;
this very practice is adopted by the great poets.
“O noble one, this is the truth: for poets, truth is equal toward all;
having established a boundary within falsehood, one is not deceived by truth.”
Considering that even a pleasing alliteration (*kāntavarṇānuprāsa*) becomes truly charming, he provides an example where alliteration is predominant: *nirānanda* (joyless).

Here, the word *prahatam* (struck) refers to the fact that although there is honey in the *kunda* flower, it is not of the same species as that in the lotus; thus, the bee, being attached to the *kunda*, did not obtain joy.
The word *kaundam* (of the *kunda*), however, is *aprahatam* (unstruck/unemphasized).

By the word *vidhura* ("distressed"), it is suggested that because there was no appearance of honey on the *bakula* flowers during their youth, he did not find pleasure at that time; furthermore, since honey is never produced on the *sāla* tree even at other times, he had no support—not even a mere bond of hope—for it. By the word *lava* ("a little"), it is intimated that, failing to obtain the essence after momentarily alighting within due to the intensity of the fragrance, he pursues the *lavaṅga*.
In this way, the natural sense of the words in the latter half [of the verse] must also be sought.

Intending precisely the aforementioned distinction, he explains: "In this context," the meaning is that *chāyā* (shadow), *ujjvalya* (brilliance), and *kānti* (beauty) are well-known in the world as synonymous; however, one must discern here how they cohere within the context of sounds (*śabda*) according to the established usage of the ancient masters.
The noble ones describe "grandeur" (*audārya*) as the quality of being composed of striking syllables,
as for example:
"He climbs a tree, enters a chasm, vies with mountains, reaches the sky, gapes, tosses about on the surface of the earth, and hides within the hollows of forest thickets."
"It wanders within, it sports in the hollows, and it clings to the creepers; what is there that the fire in the forest does not do when it has come under the power of the wind?

(7.82). Here, because of the arrangement of harsh-sounding syllables (*vikaṭākṣara-bandha*), the composition of the sentence with words that seem as if they were dancing is what is called "Vikaṭodāratā" (the grand style characterized by the striking).

Some explain that when there is a composition consisting of striking syllables, its very nature (*tattva*) is such that, for sensitive readers (*sahṛdayas*), there arises the common usage regarding a certain meaning that "the words seem to be dancing";
and since this [usage] has neither no object nor is it a mere particularity [of something else], another distinct quality (*guṇāntara*) exists, established by that very [usage] as its authority.
However, in that way, its own essential nature is not revealed by breaking through [the surface] in any manner;
others, however, say that what is intended by this is the density of alliteration (*visarga-anuprāsa*) and so forth,
but that too is not correct.
Because there would otherwise be the undesirable consequence of excluding vigor (aurjitya),
this must be stated here: "vikaṭa" means extensive,
that is to say, abundant.
Such syllables, consisting of long vowels, *anusvāra*, and so forth, are to be experienced by those with aesthetic sensitivity (*sahṛdaya*);
for this very reason, there is a similarity to dance.
For just as in dance, the limbs such as the fingers possess a quality of enchantment through the sequence of contraction and extension, so it is here as well.
For instance: in the first quarter of the verse beginning with "ārohati," there is expansion (*prasāra*) through the vowels *ā* and *ū*;
in "hatyave," there is contraction (*saṃkoca*); and in "nīruhaḥ," there is expansion again through the vowel *ī* and the visarga.

The expansion [of the meaning] through the *visarga* and diphthongs (saṃdhyakṣara) in the phrase "competing with mountains" (*nagaiḥ spardhate*) is also initiated by the unfolding [of syllables] in the second quarter; thus, there is no internal descent (*avaroha*) in the middle of the conclusion (*nirvahaṇa*),
nor is the arrangement of caesuras (*yati*) intended here.
By the phrase "fallen under the power of the wind," it is understood through the force of the resonance (*anusvāna*) rooted in the word that he is seized by the disease of insanity (*unmāda*).
Furthermore, one who is seized by insanity performs improper and unstable acts such as climbing trees;
by the word "in the forest," it is shown that since no remedy whatsoever is possible there, it further intensifies his unrestrained, insane behavior.

"He rivals the elephants" means he imitates the height of mountains; "his madness extends far" means he licks the sky—it is with this same intention that [the author] says, "What is it that... meaning that the activities of his madness cannot be counted, as they manifest through the breaking of knots in the text.
The culmination of expansion is contraction, which enters through the word "śveti" (white);
for this very reason, the continuous insertion of two *parasmaipada* endings is indeed commendable because it produces a particular luster.
Thus, that connection with praiseworthy epithets constitutes what is called "exaltation" (*udāttatā*). || 70 ||
For example:

"Having heard that he had suddenly arrived, the women of the enemy's harem, fleeing in terror from their own city, cast glances with eyes blinking as drops of water trickled down, toward the white palace, the leafy grove, the pond with its fresh lotuses, and the pleasure-mountain with its grassy slopes, their necks turned back. (83)
In this verse, "In this bright, leafy new lotus," and so forth, there is the quality of *udātta* (loftiness) due to the employment of praiseworthy qualifiers;
for in common usage, that which possesses excellence is known as *udātta*.
He who is praised in the midst of many is pre-eminent;
thus, being praiseworthy constitutes the definition of the *udātta* (the exalted).

Here, in this poetry, because it serves to nourish the meaning of the sentence and is capable of winning over the hearts of connoisseurs, it is the object of praise and the substantive (*viśeṣya*). Therefore, the excellence (*utkarṣa*) of the aforementioned nature intended in the adjectival words [qualifying that subject] is what is meant by this *guṇa*. Furthermore, this quality is "non-exalted" (*anudāra*), and it differs from the "wonderfulness" (*camatkāritva*) inherent in the body of *kānti* (loveliness) due to its specific essential character.
And since no delay is desired here, not even a single form of beauty exists;

for this very reason, he cites an example of "ancient luster" (purāṇacchāya): "Having heard"—by the mere hearing of this, such a state arises, whereas in actual sight it is not known how it will turn out.
The word "yam" (which) implies that such a possibility of power could not have arisen instantaneously for anyone who has merely heard of it;
rather, it is suggested that even the time required to take leave of one's playmates, the white palaces, and so forth— according to their affection— was not obtained.

By using the past passive participle suffix (*niṣṭhā-pratyaya*) in the word "āgatam" (arrived), he indicates that the arrival was indeed accomplished; this suggests that even in dreams, the idea of anyone else violating her had never entered his mind,
and that despite the presence of calamities, there was never, under any circumstances, any abandonment of her.

By the use of the word *nirgacchatām* (of those going out) with the present participle suffix (*śatṛ*), it is illuminated that the departure of those who repeatedly stop is an impossible form [of action].
By the plural number in *śatrūṇām* (of the enemies), it is made known that when he sets out for a single simultaneous assault, this same condition applies to all of them;
for this very reason, the compound is not formed and remains alive [with its full expressive power].

The word *lava* (a drop) suggests that for those whose minds are distressed by the pain of separation, even tears that have welled up are cut off within before they can flow out. Some maintain that the secret of the word *lava* is the suppression of tears by those who, longing for reunion, fear inauspiciousness;
otherwise, it would be impossible for any tears to emerge, resulting in nothing more than a mere moistening of the eyelids.

The word "śubhra" (bright/white) indicates that where the splendors are made to blossom by the moonlight, they enhance an indescribable measure of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) during the playful diversions of the night; immediately following that, he says "vyāpyām" (pervading), and with "navāmbhoruhī" (the two fresh lotuses), there is an expression of sexual union as before.
By the phrase "covered with grass," it is revealed that for those who were longing with curiosity for amorous play and exhausted by climbing the mountain peaks, that very [grass] served as their bed;
furthermore, by the description of their necks being turned back, it is suggested that they were merely fleeing on foot and not even turning their bodies,
thereby implying that the prevailing rasa is the Terrible (bhayānaka) rather than the Erotic (śṛṅgāra).
Intending all of this, he says: "In this context," referring to what was stated regarding the absence of *arīti*, he states the definition of *ojas*: "Ojas is an abundance of compounds (*samāsa*)."
For example:

“Victorious is the Vedic chant of the many Brahmās who have completed numerous kalpas, as it is immediately bound upon the head of Śiva—the Lord of the Cities—by his cheeks, whose affection has been restored by the nectar flowing from the moon when it is squeezed by the knot of the serpent-king’s coils. (84)

Here, by means of the compound "bhujagarajjugranthi" and so forth, there is *ojas* (vigorousness) due to the abundance of compounds; for the word *bahu*, when the suffix *iyasun* is added to express extensiveness (*vaipulya*), it takes the form *bhūya*.
And thus, "abundance of compounds" means their extensiveness and complexity;
nor should it be said that this is merely the Gauḍīya style,
because in certain instances, even the mere abundance of compounds brings about a particular beauty by virtue of propriety.
For example: "vādyanti diggajagaṇḍakaṣaṇairbhagnasrastāḥ" (They sound, broken and fallen by the rubbing of the temples of the world-elephants).
Nor is the absence of a compound improper;

for it is not the case that only a single compound, by assuming a particular form, can simultaneously cause both the status of a subordinate element (*guṇatva*) and the status of not being an ornament (*analaṃkāratva*). What, then, is untenable?
Likewise, in the present example as well, it is thus:

"the creators of many kalpas" (pariṇatāḥ) means those who have undergone transformation; when the four word-meanings are taken as a collective whole, the four words form a *samāhāra-bahuvrīhi* compound. The metaphor (*rūpaka*) using the phrase "with serpent-ropes" is employed to convey the firmness of the knots through conventional usage.

For this very reason, the prefix *ni-* in the word *nivīti* is purposeful; by the phrase "immediately fashioned praise," it indicates the unique function of the skull-caps (*kapāla*). Indeed, the bond, which consists of the nature of Brahman, cannot be produced without the palate and other such organs.

The word "immediately" (*sadyaḥ*) indicates the Lord’s unimpeded power in seizing the three worlds, as the sound of the *brahma-ghoṣa*, consisting solely of praise, issued forth from him out of a surge of terror immediately after his birth;

or else, it signifies that the ultimate purport of the Vedas and Āgamas concludes in the form of praise for the Supreme Lord. By this, the poet intends to show that all scripture is inclined toward the Supreme Lord and is characterized by a devotion that is unique and bowed in surrender.
By the term "of the Ancient Enemy" (*purāreḥ*), the Lord’s nature as the Destroyer is revealed, which is consistent with the nourishment of the subject at hand.
Vigor (*aurjitya*) is the state of firm binding,
as for example:
"In this [garland], slightly turned, extended, somewhat severed and curved, and here and there gracefully gathered and spread, it is both bunched and uplifted."
"The smoke, dark as the shoulder of a young buffalo, rising from the forest fire and spreading freely, creates fleeting cloud-like fragments in the sky.
Here, because the firm construction of the words is clearly manifest, there is *aurjitya* (firmness);
thus it is called *aurjitya*.

"Ūrjita" means possessed of great vital energy (*mahāprāṇa*); its state is "aurjitya. In this context, the "great vitality" of the composition consists of density and a certain curvature produced by occasional, non-delayed applications [of phonemes]. There is no over-extension [of the definition] from the general characteristic of a *guṇa*, for instance, in the example under discussion, in the first quarter of the verse at the word *vicchinnabhugna*, there is a pair of palatal sounds (*tālavya*).
In the second quarter, the conjuncts of gutturals and dentals are clearly mixed;
others are soft.
The conjuncts of labials, the upadhmānīya, and the four palatals are clear.
Durgasiṃha maintains that the reading of the *visarga* among vowels and consonants is intended to give it both designations;
therefore, its substitute also possesses the nature of a consonant.
Others hold that in the third quarter, the conjuncts consisting of dentals, labio-dentals, dentals, and gutturals are mixed.
Others are soft;
in the fourth foot, there are conjuncts ending in *r* and the soft *ya*, so no harshness whatsoever appears.
And thus: here, the second and fourth feet possess greater density than the first and third.

Likewise, in such passages as "In her hand is a play-lotus, and her hair is interwoven with young *kunda* flowers," even though the first and third syllables are not deeply established, their retention and great breath-force (*mahāprāṇatā*) are clearly manifest; thus he says:
"In this context, that which is employed in flattering speech is called 'the more beloved' (*preyas*).
For example: [text follows].

"O ocean of kindness, beloved of the wise, rampart of virtues, sprout of the tree of Dharma, affectionate toward those who have sought refuge, great renouncer, abode of discernment, dwelling place of Fortune, O venerable Muñja, teacher in the initiation into the amorous arts of noble-minded women, why do you not deign to touch this person even with a glance?
(86). Here, the employment of words such as "ocean of kindness" and others, which convey endearing meanings, constitutes the figure *preyaḥ* (the charming).

*Preyaḥ* (the "pleasing") is the expression of what is dear to another; that which is prescribed therein is the quality named *preya*. However, as for the question "what is it that is performed?", he says: "the narration of what is more dear. The emphasis lies on the suffixal portion (*pratyaya*). The meaning is this: when something is called "dear" (*priya*) in common worldly usage, that which is understood there as an extraordinary excellence (*prakarṣa*) is [the quality].
By this, the suffix *īyasun* in the word *lakṣaṇa* is explained.
Whether the matter be augmented by fragments of well-spoken words, be it existent or non-existent, the well-spoken word (*sūkti*) alone is the preeminent abode of abundant waters in the three worlds;
likewise, you too are perceived as such an abode for the excellence of goodness (*saujanya*).
The term *vudhapriyā* conveys two meanings through its analysis as both a *bahuvrīhi* and a *tatpuruṣa* compound.

It bestows excellence by means of the resonance of "delight" (*prīti*), which arises from being illuminated by the reflection of subtle qualities and from granting everything desired— just as in the expression *guṇaprākārā*,
where, as stones and other materials are placed one upon another in a rampart, so too do your qualities exist within you in a spirit of competitive excellence.
Alternatively, just as a rampart is a place for observing the defenses, so too are you said to be the "sprout" (*praroha*)— meaning a shoot or sprout— of the tree of dharma, specifically of virtues.

Therefore, you are the foremost descendant, the support, and the new sprout of the tree of Dharma—which has many branches such as Vikramāditya and others—and which is now broken and decaying; or rather, you are the upward-turning growth of a creeper that was previously hanging downward.

Furthermore, since the tree of Dharma has its vast expanse established above in the world of Brahmā and other realms, the fact that a sprout in the form of your venerable self now stands upon the surface of the earth brings about an unsurpassed degree of joy.

"Affectionate toward those who approach him": one who has approached for the sake of receiving assistance is "accepted" (svīkṛta); toward such a person he is "affectionate," meaning his inner heart is instantly moistened with love. It is not merely that he accepts [the petitioner] out of fear of breaking his word—as Indra and others do—nor is it through a combination of union and separation, as in the cases of Bali and Karṇa; rather, you act like the ocean by providing assistance such as fulfilling desires and so forth. This is identical to the previous epithet, "O Great Renouncer."

He who is worthy of worship even among those who practice renunciation is a "great renouncer" (mahātyāgī); therefore, it is certain that even those such as Dadhīci and others, though they bestowed their wealth, are not able to equal you. As before, regarding the phrase "having discernment as its support": discernment (viveka) is the knowledge of what ought to be done; if you were not its support—that is, its resting place—then upon what could the palace of discernment establish its footing? You should infer for yourself such points as these. Indicating all of this, he says: "of words whose meanings are dear."

That which is called "suśabdatā" (the excellence of words) is the proficiency in the application of nominal and verbal suffixes for the sake of beloved meanings— that is, for the sake of intensifying the sense of delight—
as follows:

"O Mother, let there be no life for him; let there be no living for one who lives, or rather, O Mother, what is the point of his being born? For what is the use of the birth of a creature whose life is in vain—he who does not salute you, does not worship you, does not approach you, does not behold you, does not praise you, does not honor you, does not reflect upon you, does not contemplate you, and does not meditate upon you? (87) In this verse, the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) and the excellence of the words (*suśabdatā*) are seen in the nominative forms such as *ajīvaniḥ* and *ajananiḥ*, and in the verbal forms such as *vandate* and *yajate*.
"Vyutpatti" means distinguished production (viśiṣṭā utpattiḥ).

It refers to the capacity to produce aesthetic charm by bestowing excellence upon the composition of many words, both nominal (subanta) and verbal (tiṅanta), even in the absence of particles such as "ca" (and). This is the meaning.

To the question, "For what purpose is this [negation] sought in the case of verbal abuse? he says: "Insult while living"—the meaning is that there should be no humiliation for one who is alive; even death would be better than that.
If it is argued that one will live even in such a state due to the force of the karma of lifespan (*āyuḥkarman*), then there would simply be no birth or non-arising at all;

why? To this he says: "Why [should there be] birth?"—the use of the masculine gender (*puṃliṅga*) here is to be considered, since the suffix *ika* is prescribed in the section dealing with feminine forms.
Since "birth" (*januḥ*) implies "origination" (*utpatti*), and because of their association, one might ask:
for whom is all this desired? To this he says: "He who [worships] you alone.

By stating that birth and so forth are fruitless for one whose devotion is directed toward a deity other than you, it is inferred that there is a certain excellence of devotion toward the Blessed Lady.

Others, however, explain it as follows: the meaning of the definition is that *sauśabdya* (grammatical excellence) occurs where a poet’s proficiency— consisting in familiarity with words— and the word itself— which is twofold, being either a nominal stem (*sup*) or a verbal root (*tiṅ*)— are employed, whether one or both, in such a way that they manifest that proficiency.

For instance: having introduced "non-living" (*ajīvanir*) as a *kṛdanta* form established with an adjunct (*sopādhi*) denoting the act of living, he then introduced that very same "living" (*jīvitam*) as a *kṛdanta* form established without an adjunct (*nirupādhi*) denoting the object of the proposition, namely the living being itself (*jīvasya jīvataḥ*).

In the second quarter, he conceived of "motherhood" (*mātṛtvam*) in two ways, introducing it as "like the life of birth" (*janijīvamiva*), and then took up that very same concept in two modes by means of the word "birth" (*janinā janma*).

He has composed this work by bringing together the various grammatical expansions (*prapañca*) of individual nominal stems (*subanta*), which were difficult to integrate into a single coherent composition, through their connection with appropriate verbs; thus, "the derivation of nominal stems" (*subantavyutpatti*) is the general direction [of this work].
The word *avamā* (inferior) is to be supplied with the sense of "let it be," and like the word *vṛthā* (in vain), it may also be connected with what precedes.

Now follows the analysis of verbal forms (*tiṅanta*) in the latter half [of the chapter]. Since a distinction of types as previously described is not applicable there, that [type of *utprekṣā*] which consists in the imagining of things possessing intention is the "expressed" (*vācyā*).
For instance: by the phrase "you are to be saluted," her status as the Mother of the Three Worlds is established through being worthy of homage from the very moment of birth;
by the phrase "you are to be worshipped," she assumes the form of all the deities;
and by the phrase "you are approached by all," she is the refuge of the world through being accessible to everyone.

"It shines" praises its universal pervasiveness up to its captivating nature; "it bestows" signifies its capacity to grant all that is desired; and "it is thought" denotes its being the very essence of all that is knowable.
By the phrase "he knows," she is praised as being of the nature of reality (*tattva*) by virtue of her being that which is to be ascertained;
by "he studies," she is praised as being manifested through various difficulties such as wildernesses and the like, as that which is to be remembered;

and by "he meditates," she is praised as being the form of the inner light (*pratyag-jyotis*) by virtue of being the object of profound contemplation (*nididhyāsana*). Thus, the Blessed Lady is praised through her division into the supreme (*parā*) and the non-supreme (*aparā*).
Just as *manate* and *manute* denote both the general and the particular, so too do *adhyeti* and *dhyāyati*;
and although the mutual connection between these verbal forms (*tiṅanta*) is difficult to establish, it should be understood—as in the previous case—to be established by some means or other.
This is what he expresses with the words "here," etc., which are connected with both.
Therefore, the "section on life" (*jīvitavarga*) and the "section on birth" (*janivarga*) are accepted;

the "section on intellect" (*mativarga*) is not mentioned because it turns back only once. The resolution is that in the world, designation is generally seen to follow the majority of cases. This [superimposition] is the attribution of the properties of one thing to another. (72)
For example:

“The lower lip, by its paleness, assumes the likeness of a young sprout; the cheek, due to its whiteness, takes on the appearance of a *tālī* leaf; the gaze, being almost faded, imitates the lotus; thus she touches upon sweetness and yet attains thinness. (88)

In this context, he accepts [the following]: "samādhi" is the metaphorical superimposition (*adhyāropaṇa*) of the properties of conscious actions—such as "accepting," "descending," "repeating," and so forth—upon insentient things like the earth;
"samādhi" means "proper placing" (*samyag-ādhāna*), that is, superimposition.
And correctness (*samyaktva*) consists in the state of transcending the light of the moon; it is not the mere absence of that [light].
This is clear from the definition, as well as from the lack of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in cases such as: "The lotuses close and the night-lilies open."
Therefore, "being connected" (*saṃbandhitā*) is not intended here as a qualifier of the property (*dharma*);

the distinction from *alaṃkāra* will be explained in the fourth [chapter]. "Accepting" (*pratyeṣaṇa*) means the taking of what is being given, which is a property of sentient beings; that [property] has been superimposed upon the lower lip, which is insentient, in the case of one suffering from separation.

The fading of the luster of the fresh sprouts indicates that the giver has departed and moved elsewhere; furthermore, because the act of returning [the gift] has been accomplished, the lower lip possesses a soft rosy hue even more delicate than the *aśoka* sprouts— thus, its sweetness is enhanced.
Turning toward that [object] is indeed a property of a conscious being; yet, when superimposed upon the insentient cheek, it manifests a certain paleness.
This is not a grasping in its entirety, as in the case of recognition, but rather intends merely the state of being oriented toward the object;

thus, it nourishes sweetness just as before. Furthermore, repetition is also a property of a conscious being; when superimposed upon the insentient gaze, it makes known here the unbroken shade of a withered lotus.

Even in a case of separation (*vipralambha*) that is directed toward the excellence of another, it is indicated by the word "generally" (*prāyaḥ*) that beauty may sometimes arise in the gaze when the life-partner is present through mental construction;

for since the sweetness of touch is impossible [in such a state], the metaphorical expression "she touches" (*spṛśati*) reveals the manifestation of the splendor of her first embrace— this is what is meant by "the action of a sentient being."

Because there is no similarity between the action and the agent of the action with respect to their primary nature, this is not metaphorical (*gauṇī*), but rather purely figurative (*aupacarika*); thus he says, "by way of figurative usage" (*upacāreṇa*).
By this, the distinction from metaphors (*rūpaka*) and the like is established.
The subtlety (*saukṣmya*) of words is said to consist in their internal nature as mental discourse (*saṃjalpa*).
For example:

"In this [verse], the verbal roots *sṛji*, *saṃhṛ*, and *śās* take only suffixes denoting the agent and never those denoting the object; here, however, the root *stu* functions with its grammatical roles reversed. (89)

In this context, for one who has understood the meaning of the sentence through hearing, the words such as "creates," "destroys," "governs," and "is praised" exist in a subtle state by way of internal monologue; they are subtle because they reside "within.

Just as the forms of elephants, horses, and so forth, which are manifested in stone or rock, remain in a subtle state, so too do these words—even while being heard—exist in a subtle form. Otherwise, how could there be the emergence of the remaining [words] according to their fixed order at the stage of contemplating the meaning of the sentence?

In the passage beginning with "kevalam," when the meaning of the sentence is considered—that the verbal roots *sṛj* (to create), *saṃ-hṛ* (to withdraw), and *śās* (to govern), when employed in reference to the Lord as the agent, trigger suffixes [indicating the agent] and not the object—then these words shine forth as "He creates, He withdraws, He governs," and not as "He is created, He is withdrawn, He is governed. In this way, the root *stu* (to praise) functions with reversed grammatical roles.

In this context, the suffix in the verb *stauti* (he praises) functions only with respect to the object (*karman*) and not the agent (*kartṛ*). Thus, at the very moment of the realization of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha-bhāvanā*), words emerge to the effect that "this [agent] does not praise anything at all, but rather is praised by everyone.
This is what is stated: "In this case, as much as is heard and understood from the scripture...

This supports the analogy of the banyan seed (*vaṭabīja-nyāya*), meaning that the sprout of the productive urge (*bhāvanā-pallava*) is subsequently determined only after the entire sentence has been heard and comprehended.
This very matter is witnessed by the perception of those with aesthetic sensitivity;
its "possessing of resonance" (dhvanimattā), however, is its profundity, as for example:
"Place the immeasurable lotus upon your head; display your own prowess; bear on your pair of feet the marks of the discus; lift up the earth with your arm;
establish Lakṣmī upon your chest; become the elder brother of the Lord of the Gods—O sole thief of the hearts of all! Even so, it is known that you are indeed Hari.

Here, the mention of bearing a lotus on the navel, having limited prowess, having hands marked by the discus, lifting the earth with a tusk, having Lakṣmī seated upon the chest, and being the younger brother of Indra suggests [other meanings], which constitutes profundity (*gāmbhīrya*).
Regarding the term *dhvanimat*: "resounding" (*dhvanana*) refers to *dhvani*, which is the function consisting of suggestion (*vyañjanā*);
that [function] is of two kinds: verbal *dhvani* and objective *dhvani*.

Some maintain that "the sound of words" (śabdadhvani) is intended as that by which the word itself is manifested; however, this is not correct, because it is not accepted that the word itself is what is manifested,
and because it would entail the contradiction of the explanatory text [of the commentary] stating, "the holding of a lotus by the two [arms]," and so forth.

Therefore, it should be stated that *dhvanana* based on words is "verbal *dhvani*" (*śabdadhvani*), while that based on meaning is "meaning-based *dhvani*" (*arthadhvani*). Alternatively, *dhvani* is that collection of words which possesses a verbal essence (*śabdātmaka*) that causes [the meaning] to resound; its profundity consists in its connection with an abundance of such *dhvanis*.

For instance, in the context of the word *puṇḍarīka*, that which possesses a fixed denotative power toward a white umbrella is observed to produce the manifestation of a white lotus, which stands in the place of the resonance of a bronze cymbal;
and because it possesses a fixed denotative power toward multiple meanings, he says: "When the denotative function of a word with multiple meanings is restricted..."
"By means of conjunction and so forth, there is the coloring [of the mind] through the operation that produces the cognition of an inexpressible object"—
thus it is in the case of *vikrama* and the rest.
Nevertheless, valor, manliness, the remaining strides, the wheel— the mark of a universal monarch consisting of the configuration of lines as well as a specific weapon—
and the lifting up— the attainment, protection, and securing of rightful gain— remain.

*Lakṣmī* refers both to the goddess of fortune and to one who is superior—meaning more praiseworthy or elder in age; with this very intention, he explains the passage ending with "of the lord of the dwellers of heaven" as follows: "In this [context]..."

By the word "also" (*api*) in the phrase "tadapi," which indicates a contradiction, it is understood that [the author] is practicing the state of being Hari (*haribhāva*). Since the wearing of the *puṇḍarīka* mark and so forth are common to both [Śiva and Viṣṇu], the mention of "on the head" (*maulau*) and so on would be contradictory; therefore, by suggesting through resonance (*dhvani*) a location opposite to that [of Śiva]—namely, the navel and so forth in Viṣṇu—he suggests this very point by the force of conventional usage (*prasiddhi*).
For even in the context of discussing the resonance of words, he has explained it otherwise, intending that conventional usage is indeed a cause for the comprehension of a specific meaning.
Otherwise, due to the suspicion of inconsistency with the subject matter at hand, there would be no enrichment of the expressed meaning (*vācyārtha*).
This sentence-meaning, rooted in contradiction and characterized by suggested contrast (*pratīyamānavyatireka*), has verbal suggestion (*śabdadhvani*) as its life-breath here.

By the phrase "the sole thief of the inner hearts of the universe," there is a suggested poetic fancy (*pratīyamānotprekṣā*): that he steals the minds of the three worlds day and night, and as if through the skill of practice, conceals the extremely well-known marks of Nārāyaṇa.
Now, some do not consider *vastudhvani* (the suggestion of a fact) to be rooted in the power of words (*śabdaśaktimūla*).
How then [is the following verse to be understood]? "O traveler, there is no bedding here in this village of stone slabs;
yet, having seen her high breasts, if you wish to stay, then stay."

In such passages as these, is there not a description of a factual reality (*vastu-varṇana*)? For here, neither the principle of *śleṣa* (paronomasia) nor the principle of *samāsokti* (speech of brevity) is possible.
Furthermore, even in the case of *alaṃkāra-dhvani* (suggestion of figures of speech), it is the power of the word itself that is employed; thus, *śabda-dhvani* remains intact.
As for those who claim that a function of the word other than *abhidhā* (denotation) does not exist at all—for them, even *lakṣaṇā* (indication) would have to be rejected.
Nor should it be said that this [secondary meaning] need not be admitted;
for in the case of "gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ" ("a hamlet on the Ganges"), there would otherwise result a lack of syntactic connection (*ananvaya*) with the locative case-ending.

Since it is a well-established rule of grammar that case-endings denote their own meanings as inherent in the base noun (*prakṛti*), some meaning capable of functioning as the locus relative to the hamlet must be expressed by the word "gaṅgā."
And thus, what other [function] could it be but indication (*lakṣaṇā*)?

The cognition of qualities such as merit (*puṇyatva*) arising from that very [indication] brings forth suggestion (*dhvanana*); this and more has been explained by us at length in our commentary on the *Kāvyaprakāśa*, but we desist here for fear of making the book too voluminous.
The statement by Vyāsa is "elaboration" (vistara).
For example:

"By means of merits, may a person attain the state of being water in the ocean; and may the clouds, through their auspicious natures, place him in that very condition within the mouths of oyster shells."
"Therefore, O full-breasted one, may he attain that maturity through blessings so that, manifesting his desire, he may roll upon your heart.
Here, because the intention— "How might I roll upon the slope of your breasts?"— is revealed in detail, this is *vistara* (elaboration) by way of expansion (*vyāsa*).

Where even a slight matter to be expressed is rendered striking by the blossoming of expression (*ukti-pallava*), it alone is capable of ascending to the rank of a poetic quality (*guṇa*); therefore, it is appropriate to discern this among the verbal qualities.

For this very reason, in examples such as "janaḥ puṇyaiḥ" and so on, the speaker points to the *ukti* itself as the subject of predication. In examples such as "katham aham," even though the intended meaning—consisting of the speaker's crooked intention—is already indicated, it is brought to excellence by the blossoming of the expression.
To illustrate: by the use of the word "jana" (person) in a detached manner, [the speaker implies] that such misfortunes do not belong to me, such that my mind could bear them directly.

By the use of the plural "by merits" (*puṇyaiḥ*), it is indicated that this fruit belongs only to those merits acquired over many lifetimes. By the optative suffix in "might go" (*yāyāt*), which expresses possibility, it is revealed that even the attainment of ocean water suitable for the transformation into pearls is possible only for someone of exceptionally fortunate birth; thus, a certain excellence of cause is manifested. Furthermore, by the term "clouds" (*jalamucaḥ*), it is shown that for these beings, their function is not merely the giving of water, but rather, being intent on benefiting others and dispelling the world's distress, they even carry [the water] as far as the opening of the pearl-oyster shell.

By the phrase "in such a state," it is meant that at the very moment the state of love arises, the drinking by the clouds becomes the object of mere hope (*āśaṃsā*) and no longer merely the object of possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*) as before; for this very reason, the word "auspicious" (*śubhaiḥ*) is used, since the delay in time is caused by the power of previous merit, and so forth should be understood by oneself.

By this, that which has been called another quality (*guṇa*) by others—namely, "the composition of a sentence within a single word"—is shown to be merely an expansion of the excellence of construction (*ghaṭanāsauṣṭhava*) alone; however, we shall describe it under the specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) in the section on *pallava*.

"Rolling upon the slope of your breasts is not possible for one of very meager merit"—this much alone is the intended object of expression. Since it is the expansion of the effect itself that possesses the power to impart aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*), it is appropriate here to employ *parisaṃkhyā* (exclusive specification) by making the word the primary element; this is what is illustrated as *saṃkṣepa* (abridgment), which is expressed in a concise manner, as follows: [Example: "The moon is not the thief of the night-lotus; the sun is not the thief of the day-lotus; nor is the fire the thief of the lotus-stalks. But, O slender-waisted one, you alone are the thief of the entire world. In this verse, the intended meaning is that "you alone are the thief of the entire world," yet by means of the exclusion of others through the word "alone" (*eva*), the excellence of the speaker's poetic skill is revealed. This is called *saṃkṣepa*. It is distinct from *parisaṃkhyā*, because in *parisaṃkhyā* the exclusion of others is the primary focus, whereas here the primary focus is the excellence of the speaker’s artistry. Furthermore, it differs from *samāsokti* (speech of brevity), because in *samāsokti* the suggested sense is more prominent than the expressed sense, whereas here the expressed sense is more prominent. Thus, it is distinct from both *parisaṃkhyā* and *samāsokti*. Therefore, it is established that this is indeed *saṃkṣepa*. This is the end of the section on *saṃkṣepa*. Now, the section on *bhāvika* begins. This is the end of the chapter on *alaṃkāras* based on the excellence of words. Now, the chapter on *alaṃkāras* based on the excellence of meaning begins. Among these, the first is *udātta* (the noble). Its definition is as follows: The description of the greatness of someone who is already great, or the description of the greatness of something that is already great, is called *udātta*. It is of two kinds: that which is based on wealth and that which is based on valor. An example of the former is: "The king, having seen the daughter of the mountain-king, whose waist was slender like a lotus stalk, became so agitated that he could not even look at her face, though she was standing nearby. In this verse, the greatness of the King of Mountains is described through the greatness of his daughter. An example of the latter is: "The King of Mountains, seeing the daughter of the ocean-king, whose waist was slender like a lotus stalk, became so agitated that he could not even look at her face, though she was standing nearby. In this verse, the greatness of the Ocean is described through the greatness of his daughter. This is the end of the section on *udātta*. Now, the section on *udāttālaṃkāra* begins. Its definition is as follows: The description of the greatness of someone who is already great, or the description of the greatness of something that is already great, is called *udātta*. It is of two kinds: that which is based on wealth and that which is based on valor. An example of the former is: "The king, having seen the daughter of the mountain-king, whose waist was slender like a lotus stalk, became so agitated that he could not even look at her face, though she was standing nearby. In this verse, the greatness of the King of Mountains is described through the greatness of his daughter. An example of the latter is: "The King of Mountains, seeing the daughter of the ocean-king, whose waist was slender like a lotus stalk, became so agitated that he could not even look at her face, though she was standing nearby. In this verse, the greatness of the Ocean is described through the greatness of his daughter. This is the end of the section on *udāttālaṃkāra*. Now, the section on *atiśayokti* (hyperbole) begins. Its definition is as follows: The description of something as being greater than it actually is, or the description of something as being less than it actually is, is called *atiśayokti*. It is of two kinds: that which is based on identity and that which is based on difference. An example of the former is: "The lotuses are the eyes of
"‘Having had his pain removed by the great medicinal herbs brought by Māruti,
he once again acted as a teacher of lamentation for the women of Laṅkā with his arrows.

(92) Here, because the matter to be set forth in detail according to the narrative has been stated in merely half a verse for fear of interrupting the sentiment (*rasa*) of the ongoing battle, this is *saṃkṣepa* (abridgment)."
