Regarding the term "in brief" (*samāsena*):
there exists a particular case where the condensation of a sentence, by virtue of its suitability to the context, becomes a cause of aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*).

For instance, in the verse beginning with *sa mārutī*, both the bringing of the herb by Mārutī and the removal of the pain by her are presented here in merely half a verse, whereas they would have been explained at length in an epic narrative (*itihāsa*). Although this merit consists primarily in the emphasis placed on the word, nevertheless, a condensation of meaning must be understood as occurring within the form of poetry (*kāvyarūpa*) which includes only what is intended to be expressed.

And since that very contraction occurs precisely through such *vakrokti* (indirect speech), when it is said that "contraction is indicated," he asks: "How is this contraction attained as the appropriate state? He replies: "By the context (*prakṛta*)," etc.

For this very reason, although the matter of the historical narrative (*itihāsa*) had been introduced, the poet—overcome by haste—abandoned it and composed only the second half-verse for the subject at hand; yet, for the sake of consistency between the first and second halves, even the subject matter was stated in an abbreviated form.
And being measured is said to be the quality of having as many words as are necessary for the meaning.
For example: "Some [poets] are [skilled] in the subject matter but not in speech; some in speech but not in the subject matter."
"Others [excel] both in expression and in subject matter, while others excel neither in expression nor in subject matter.
(93) Here, the meaning and the words are "measured" (*saṃmita*) by their being equal, like [objects] held on a balance scale (*tulāvidhṛtavat*). This is the extent [of the definition].
To the extent that words cannot follow the natural flow [of expression] without [deliberate] coloring, to that same extent the sentence possesses *saṃmitatva* (appropriateness).
Therefore, due to this conciseness,
there may arise at times a distinct charm of composition from the poet’s power and proficiency, even in the absence of elaborate ornamentation.
As was previously cited: "Who are you, O auspicious one? Or whose wife are you? and so forth;
by this very [explanation], even the suspicion of confusion regarding the clarity of meaning is refuted.
Some cite [the verse] beginning with "There is a divine being in the northern direction," but that is incorrect.

One should disregard the statement in the section on *vyabhicāriguṇas* (transitory qualities) which asks how there can be "manifestation" (*ābhāsatva*) when there is no equality between the name and the word because they exist in the form of blossoms; for by the power of context, the conclusion that the pronoun "some" (*kecit*) refers specifically to the intended poet is possible, so there is no room for the suspicion of an ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*). Furthermore, the verb [“is”] is also understood through the force of context. Having all this in mind, he says: “like what is held on a scale” (*tulāvidhṛtavat*).
That mode of expression which proceeds from an internal state of being is called *bhāvika*.
For example:
"Come, come, my child, joy of the Raghus, full moon! I shall kiss you on the head and embrace you for a long time."
"Or, having placed [thee] in my heart, I carry thee day and night; or else, I bow to thy two lotus-feet.

Here, because of the influence of joy, even though it is improper, such expressions as "or else, I bow to thy two lotus-feet" have been uttered; therefore, this is *bhāvikatva* (the state of being manifest), so called from *bhāva* (intentional state).
The mental modification (*cittavṛtti*) that has entered into the state of contemplation (*bhāvanā*) is "being" (*bhāva*);
*bhāvanā*, *vāsanā*, and *vyāpti* (pervasion) are synonymous.
For it is said: "Everything is permeated by this fragrance or this flavor."

For when the mind is permeated by emotions such as joy, various types of expressions arise that are like waves, through which the underlying emotion (*bhāva*) is manifested without any obstruction. This is what has been stated: the very occurrence—that is, the production—of speech in the form of poetry (*kāvya*) from an emotion (*bhāva*), is itself *bhāvika*;
this is an expression where the suffix denotes the predominance of the state (*bhāva*).

For instance—in the example under consideration: (1) once the act of turning [the person] toward oneself has been accomplished by the single word *ehi* ("come"), which is inseparable from the meaning of *yuṣmad* ("you"), the employment of a second [vocative]; (2) the mention of *pūrṇacandra* ("full moon"), which is not required for the subsequent actions; (3) the use of the present tense (*cumbāmi*) even though the action of kissing is yet to be performed; (4) the employment of the qualifier *ciram* ("for a long time") in the phrase *pariṣvaja* ("embrace") without providing a corresponding qualifier for *cumbāmi*; (5) the use of *tvam* ("you") even when the referent is already established, as if competing with the subsequent action; (6) the mention of "carrying" (*vahana*) alone, treating it as equal in status to all other parts of the speech; (7) the contradictory statement of saying *vatse* ("child") and then commanding *caraṇau bandasva* ("bow at her feet"); and (8) the utterance of *te* ("your"), even though its meaning is already understood—all of these are established by *adharmasiddhi* (establishment through non-merit), and because the intended meaning is thus brought to completion, they become a cause for aesthetic relish (*svāda*).

For the worldly, words characterized by longing for objects of affection arise and are relished, as in: "She is the goddess Lakṣmī in this house; she is an ambrosial ointment for the eyes; her touch upon the body is like thick sandalwood paste.
Having this in mind, he explains [the verse] with the word "atra" (here).
Because it is prominent, he indicates the remaining [elements] by that term: "Even through impropriety, there is a 'descent' (vanda);
such is the sequence known as *gati*, which occurs here in the ascent and descent [of sounds].
(75) For example:

"May that Boar grant you prosperity— he upon whose tusk-tip the Earth rests, which is untouched by the masses of waves from the four oceans that, out of fear of being displaced by his strides, coalesce with one another, becoming as beautiful as millions of fragments of the moon.
In this verse, there is *gati* (movement) because of the ascent of vowels (*svarāroha*) in the first half and the descent of vowels (*svarāvaroha*) in the second half.

Some explain "gati" as referring to the ascent and descent of ascetics; however, due to the power of the poet's creative genius, they appear in certain instances as if they have already ascended and descended.

For example: "As it falls lower and lower into the series of pits on the earth, the crest-jewel of serpents appears closer and closer to all the world; yet, for men who occupy ever-higher mountain peaks, this divine sun becomes further and further away. Here, the ascent and descent appear as clearly distinct as sesame seeds and rice grains.
This propriety of conduct, however, will be explained [later], and thus it would be consistent with the second [chapter];

therefore, this is the meaning: the realization of the vowels beginning with *a* in their successive order is the "movement" (*gati*), which is the manifestation of them as if they were closely proximate.
And he will explain it thus: "of the vowel" (*svarasya*).

For instance, in the example under discussion, having pointed out two vowels of the same class in *varāhaḥ kalyāṇam*, and having—as it were—established a state of elevation by means of the *u* in *sa vo*, a succession of rises of the same class is established at the beginning of the second quarter in *kalākoṭīkāntam*;
however, such is not the case in the latter half.

Even here in the phrase "he lies," there is no such prominent ascent; this is an aesthetic quality (*guṇa*) based on experience, which occurs in the manner of a verse-half, a single verse-quarter, or a portion of a verse, like the form of Narasiṃha.
Here, he provides the first example by way of illustration: "In the first half [of the verse]," etc.

Some say that it is by means of the fear (*bhīḥ*) arising from the inability to lift up—that is, the failure to recover—the feet as they slip away due to the movements of shifting them hither and thither.

Others, however, say: that in which there is fear of bursting and so forth when the upward gaze is directed with the fear of being pulled out gradually fading away— that is called *upakrama-nirvāha-rīti* (the style of carrying through the commencement),
as for example:

"‘You were not wounded by the pressing-stone from the mountain; you were not distressed by the water; you did not wither; you were not exhausted by the breaths of the serpent; nor were you ever weary while following Him—thus, as the two Lords of Śrī and the Śārṅga bow returned to their own abode, may that long series of pairs of questions and answers, full of longing, protect you.
Here, because the negative particle (*nañ*) is placed after each individual word, the *rīti* (style) is characterized by the absence of monotony in sequence."
Regarding the phrase "of the commencement":
when a composition is commenced with a certain arrangement of words, maintaining that same [arrangement] throughout the verse sometimes brings about a particular beauty;
for this very reason, complete consistency is not intended here.

Even though it is one of the eleven types of *vṛtti* (speech-styles), because this [*paripūrṇā*] alone constitutes the essential life-force of poetry when all its intended elements are complete, there is no over-extension [of the definition]. Thus, in the example at hand, Kṛṣṇa—having beheld the natural, all-encompassing beauty of the Daughter of the Ocean as she first appeared—felt that his eyes had achieved their purpose; he now thinks, "If I can hear even a single syllable of speech issuing forth by the breaking of her seal upon her lower lip, then my ears will have attained their fruitfulness."

The conversation of charming young women does not proceed in this very manner; rather, it is out of fear when in the presence of the hero that she asks first: "Were you not wounded by a stone from the mountain?
And immediately thereafter, knowing that if she did not speak, he would perceive her as bold, she gives two answers appropriate to the occasion—a shake of the head and a single syllable.
Of these, the former (the shake of the head) was employed by Kālidāsa: "He gave this answer with a nod of his head."

The second [verse] was composed by the poet: "Not so"—thus, one who has been filled with the talk heard [from others], considering himself as if his purpose were accomplished through that connection, asks while reminding [the listener] of the cause of excessive fear:
"By milk," and this is what was said: "Afflicted," etc.
Since it was impossible to provide an answer in any other way, he spoke again: "No.
Immediately following that, eager to hear even a few more words from her who possesses the essence of guile, he asks—reminding her of all the causes of fear well-known to the world—"Is she withered?
He did not say, "I have seen her," because one does not allow an undesirable thing concerning a beloved object to attach itself even in a dream.
Thus, although this is well known, he asks by means of an elaborate verbal expansion—a mode of opening the seal of speech familiar to all charming women: "Your follower...

[and so on]. Considering all of this—that he, being recognized as supreme in every respect, was arrogant and went back to his own house rather than asking for directions—the author explains it with the word "atra" (here).
That which is a distinguished mode of speech, poets know as *ukti*.
For example:
"Is she well? I ask after her welfare; 'She lives,' was the reply. (76)

“Once again you speak of that very same thing; shall I say she is dead? She who yet breathes. Here, when asked “Is she well?”, instead of saying “She is well or not well,” this manner of demonstrating that she has nothing left but life—expressed through the artful turn of phrase beginning with “she lives”—receives the designation *ukti* (artful expression) among the verbal excellences (*śabdaguṇa*) in poetry because it is distinguished.
Indeed, there are indeed supramundane modes of expression well-known in the world,
such as when, in response to the question "Are you asleep?", one replies, "In my house" or "In the temple," and so forth.
However, any expression whatsoever that is drawn forth by the creative intuition (*pratibhā*) of a poet, by departing from these worldly conventions, becomes supramundane.
And thus, because it is striking due to being drawn forth by poetic intuition (*pratibhā*), it possesses the status of a "quality" (*guṇa*);
for this very reason, [the author] says "poets," since such familiarity with expression is possible only for poets who are connoisseurs (*sahṛdaya*).

For instance—in the example under discussion, when inquiring after someone's welfare, it is well known in the world to say "Is it well? (kuśalaṃ vā); therefore, one ought to say that very thing. Yet, having set that aside, the word "is he living? (jīvati) is employed; and since this is likewise stated in other inquiries as well, it is understood as being intentional (sāmiprāya), drawn forth by the speaker's genius (pratibhā). Thus he says: "In this case, 'is it well' or 'is it not well,' etc. Now he defines the quality of a sentence characterized by the highest degree of excellence (prakarṣakāṣṭhā):
The mature culmination of expression is termed "prauḍhi" (maturity),
as for example:
"The earth was uplifted, the chests of enemies crushed, and the royal fortune of Bali swallowed in rapid succession."
"Whatever this youth accomplished in a single lifetime, the Ancient Puruṣa performed that in three lifetimes.

(98) In this context, *prauḍhi* (maturity) is said to be that ripening of a sentence—such as "the ripening of a coconut" (*nālikerapāka*) or "the ripening of a grape" (*mṛdvīkāpāka*)—which arises from habitual practice through the insertion (*āvāpa*) or removal (*udvāpa*) of words. This refers to the beauty of arrangement resulting from the substitution of words that are either natural, soft, or harsh, or those that are urban (*nāgara*), semi-urban (*upanāgara*), or rustic (*grāmya*), or a combination of both types of words.
Thus, this particular sentence is called "the ripening of a coconut."
In this way, examples such as the ripening of mangoes and grapes are also to be cited;
for it is said that "this ripening of the utterance"— that is, of the sentence— is what constitutes *prauḍhi* (maturity).
The "maturation" (*pāka*) of words is their inability to withstand the substitution of synonyms;
as it has been said: "That wherein words truly abandon their capacity to endure such substitutions, the experts in the logic of language declare that to be the 'maturation' of words."
Thus,

"the mature" (*prauḍha*) is established through the consistency between the opening and the conclusion; and this very [mature] is proclaimed as being of three kinds, characterized by the coconut, the mango, and the grape.

For example—a ripe coconut fruit is hard in its rind, mostly soft and tender in its fibers, and even harder in its shell; likewise, a certain composition is hard at the beginning, then mostly soft, and then harder still, which is called "the ripening of a coconut. To illustrate this in the present example: in the first quarter, the four syllables beginning with *abhyuddhṛtā* are hard; the six syllables *vasumatī dali* are soft; and the four syllables *taṃ ripūraḥ*, containing the anusvāra, the letter *r*, and long vowels, are the hardest.

Regarding this, our venerable teachers maintain that by employing the word "that" (*tam*) in a manner that is predominantly soft, [the poet] confirms the resemblance to the surface of a tender earthen shard (*komalakapālikāmukhabhāga*).

Thus, in the three feet beginning with the second, the similarity to a coconut fruit (*nālikeraphala*) is to be inferred through the sequence of four, six, and four [syllables]. To the question, "How, moreover, is such a ripening possible? he says: "In this case. (*atrāpi*)
That which is produced by practice is "practiced" (*ābhyāsika*).
Practice is the repeated engagement in composing and analyzing poetry through the instruction of those who know how to do so.
How does even this [practice] result in a particular excellence of flavor (*pāka*)? To this, he says: "by means of the beauty of its arrangement."

"Arrangement" (sanniveśa) means composition; as for how there is beauty in that, he says: "by means of insertion and deletion" (āvāpodvāpābhyām). Insertion (āvāpa) is the introduction into the context.
Regarding the question of whose extraction (*samuddharaṇa*) or removal (*udvāpa*) occurs thereafter, it is said: "of the words" (*padānām*),
meaning those that have been extracted, i.e., mentally separated.
To answer the question "From what [is this derived]?", it was said: "from that which stands in its own nature" (*prakṛtisthāt*), and so forth.

By this, the following meaning is intended: even from words such as *prakṛtistha*, precisely this [quality] must be extracted—that which, due to the excellence of its composition, does not tolerate the substitution of synonyms; for there is a common saying among connoisseurs (*sahṛdayas*) to the effect that "there is no other word [that can take its place]."

This specific excellence in composition—how else could a word of that very same type, when placed in another context, not yield such aesthetic pleasure? For this very reason, it is a quality of the sentence (*vākya-guṇa*);
and harshness arises from conjunct consonants (*saṃyoga*) or long vowels (*svara*).

Just as in this very example, such as *ripūraḥ* and so forth, some have spoken of a "cooking of the *suptiṅ* [inflected words] according to their grammatical derivation" (*vārtākapāka*); however, that is indeed merely the quality (*guṇa*) characterized by euphony (*suśabdatā*). Thus it is.

Just as a grape fruit is soft starting from the skin toward the interior, yet possesses a certain hardness produced by two, three, or four seeds, so too a certain composition that is soft at the beginning and the conclusion but hard in the middle—wherein there is no harshness caused except by conjunct consonants or long vowels—is called the *mṛdvīkā-pāka* (grape-ripening).
For example: "O, the sprouts of the creepers that cling to these [trees], nourished by the water poured forth by you..."
"Since her lip, which has long been parted from the rosy hue of lac, rivals the color of ivory;

and as it is said: 'The fawn-eyed women bear faces upon which the musk-patch has been washed away by the incessant falling of drops of tears, and the deer-scented unguent has vanished like the rays of the moon.'"
For this very reason, the author of the *Kavikalpalatā* and others have stated that a fourth kind of "ripening" (pāka), namely the "blue wood-apple ripening," does not exist.

Just as a mango fruit, when fully matured, is soft from its very beginning yet becomes mostly hard at the stone, so too another composition is called "mango-ripening" (*sahakārapāka*) because it is soft starting from the opening and becomes harder within;
for example: "O lotus, may you be well; O ruddy geese, may there be a fair dawn! O night-lily, once the moon has risen, may you take your delight!"
"Friend, the night has passed; the darkness has been consumed"—thus do the birds cry out with their wings fluttering wildly.
Even in this very example, a twofold harshness is to be understood.
These three alone are examples of pure *pāka*.
However, those arising from the combination [of causes] are numerous;
these very "ripenings of meaning" will be presented in the fifth chapter by way of another method.
The author of the Sūtras himself establishes their connection in the section on the qualities of meaning (*arthaguṇa*).
These twenty-four qualities of word have been described as pertaining to the sentence.
Now we shall explain these very same qualities as being qualities of the sentence-meaning; among them, *śleṣa* (conciseness) is said to be the state of being well-arranged in their coordination.
For example:
"Seeing her two beloveds seated together on one seat, the rogue approached from behind and, under the pretext of playful persistence, closed the eyes of one with respect;
then, with his neck slightly bent and his hair standing on end, he kissed the other, whose cheeks were radiant with inner smiles as her heart overflowed with love. (99)
Here, while the two beloveds are seated upon a single seat, one is deceived by the lover through the playful act of closing her eyes,
while the other is gratified by a kiss upon the face; such is this well-contrived arrangement.
"Cohesion" (*śleṣa*) is a quality of the meaning of a sentence;
the statement "have been stated" is a reference to what has already occurred, intended to demonstrate its causal status.
"Of these very ones named Śleṣa and so forth"—here the genitive case is used in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*). [The meaning is:
"Among these, Śleṣa, which constitutes the body of the sentence-meaning, is characterized first."
Having formulated the rule "ghaṭanāśleṣaḥ" (the union of connection), Vāmana explained it as: "Ghaṭanā is the conjunction of sequence, artfulness, non-excessiveness, and feasibility.

The meaning of this is as follows: "Having done this, one should do that" constitutes sequence; therein, "artfulness" (kauṭilya) refers to a curvature that transcends worldly norms, because words and meanings, being devoid of curvature, consist of mere utterance.
The absence of excessive manifestation due to extreme intensity is "non-excess" (*anulbaṇatva*).

How does this meaning cohere? The "justification" (*upapatti*) consists in the introduction of a qualification that serves to resolve such an apparent inconsistency. Thus, the "fusion" (*śleṣa*) is the joining of a meaning with non-excess through a sequence of justifications by means of *kauṭilya* (crookedness). In that context, since the word "sūtra" is used as a term for the arrangement of the sequence, "crookedness" is expressed by its own word; the sense of the sentence is that there is a "joining" of a sentence-meaning that was, as it were, unjoined, through the cleverness of the intellect.
Having seen this,
one heroine and her friend, the other heroine who is the object of the secret lover's affection, sit together on the same seat with him.

Thinking that pleasing her alone was the very essence of his life, he acts simultaneously with great care, moving his feet so softly as not to make a sound; thus positioned, he covers both eyes at once with his two hands—a pastime well-known in the world.
"Slightly" means only the neck moves, but not even the body.
Otherwise, in the cognition of movement, there would be no state of agitation in the heroine;
rather, from the disclosure of her restrained passion, there arises a thrill of horripilation.
For this very reason, the exhilaration of the mind is its oscillation through various waves of emotion by means of love, which takes the form of the conceit that its own object is transcendent.
The phrase "he does not know how to deceive the virtuous" implies that he has a suppressed smile arising from the cultivation of reproach directed toward his co-wife;
"shrewdness" (*dhūrtatā*) is the accomplishment of one's own desired aim through skill in deception,
which the author explains here with the words "on a single seat."
That which is the manifestation of the object is called *prasāda* (clarity),
as for example:
"Here rises the breaker of the seal of the lotuses, the young *mandāra* flower from the forest groves of the Sunrise Mountain."
"Splitting the darkness, [the sun]—the kinsman of the pair of *kokila* birds distressed by separation, and as copper-red as the cheeks of an angry monkey—" (100).

Here, although not explicitly stated, the meaning characterized as the "sun" is clearly perceived in its manifestation regarding the causing of the lotus-bed to bloom, its descent upon the mountain of sunrise, the removal of the grief of the *kokila* pair, and the dispersal of darkness;
this is what is meant by "manifestness" (*prākaṭya*).

The clarity of meaning (*arthaprasāda*) is the manifestation, within the sentence-meaning—which consists of the connection between the word-meanings uttered together—of the intended object even though it is not explicitly mentioned, like a reflection on the surface of a mirror.

Nor is this a matter of inference, because [the intended object] is perceived through the same cognition [as the expressed meaning]. Thus he says: "Even though the object characterized by the sun is not stated, it is clearly perceived."
The absence of disparity among things occurring in succession is celebrated as "evenness" (samatva).
For example:
"In front stands the *kurabaka* flower, pale-red like a woman’s fingernail; on two sides the young *aśoka* tree, beautiful with its emerging passion, remains poised on the verge of blossoming. (79)

“O friend, the fresh cluster on the mango tree, tawny at its tips by the slightly clinging particles of pollen, stands between childhood and youth; so too does the beauty of spring stand between them.

Here, because there is no disparity among the qualifiers—caused by the abandonment of childhood and the onset of youth—of the beauty of spring, there is *samatā* (symmetry), which is defined as the absence of disparity.
The expression of that object in the world exactly as it is perceived through its form, without deviating from it, constitutes "evenness" (samatā);
here, "crookedness" (vakratā) is to be understood as a qualifying attribute. Otherwise, what difference would there be [between this] and the statement "she goes having released [her garment]"?

According to the *Mugdha-koṣa*, the first stage of the beauty of spring (*madhuśrī*) is when the *kurabaka* bud, just beginning to burst open at its tip, becomes as pale-red as the fingernail of a beloved; this is its childhood.
Then, as the buds reach maturity, the dark portion at the base remains distinct because it has not yet split open; this is its youth.
In this way, in the passage beginning with "the grief of a child" (*bālāśoka*), one should understand that the characteristics of childhood and youth are shown in succession.
Sweetness (*mādhurya*) has been described by the Teachers as the absence of intensity even in states such as anger,
as follows:

"Even when a frown suddenly arose, her face was brought to a state of extreme humility; she smiled slightly toward me, yet uttered no harsh word; her eyes, dulled by internal tears, were not dilated by their usual brilliance, and while her anger was made manifest, her courtesy was not abandoned. (102) Herein, the sweetness (*mādhurya*) consists in this concealment of the signs of anger through the maintenance of decorum, even amidst the anger of the character Vāsavadattā.

"Sweetness" refers to the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) and pathetic (*karuṇa*) sentiments, for these two are sweet; therefore, the meaning that manifests them is also sweet. Its sweetness is akin to the taste of sugar and the like. For just as the taste of sugar—whether presented to a connoisseur or a non-connoisseur, or to one who is healthy or unwell—immediately brings about a sense of wonder (*camatkāra*) when placed upon the tip of the tongue, so too does the meaning that manifests the aesthetic flavor whose sole life-breath is the savoring of the essence of the melting of the heart. Thus, the final meaning is that the sweetness of the sentence-meaning consists in the singular fulfillment of the power to manifest that [flavor].

In that regard, although the mental fluctuations (*cittavṛtti*) are characterized by arising and passing away and remain wakeful due to the ripening of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), a state of opposition is established through the subordination of all others; thus it is said that even in anger and the like, there is an absence of intensity.

For instance, in the verse beginning with "the knitting of the brows" (*bhrūmede*), when the hero has somehow offended her by stumbling over his limbs and so forth, the manifestation of a transitory emotion (*vyabhicāribhāva*) characterized by jealousy and rage—which is the very nature of love—is suppressed by a feigned indifference (*avahittha*) arising from the excellence of passion.
Indeed, in the victory over a contrary state, the excellence of the other [the dominant emotion] becomes even greater.
For this very reason, it was stated as "supreme" (*parām*).
Likewise, in such instances as "this smile directed toward me is slightly divisive," sweetness (*mādhurya*) is to be inferred;
this is what he says: "here, of that which is characterized by Vāsavadattā."
That which they call freedom from harshness is termed *saukumārya* (delicacy). For example:
"Sītā, as tender as a *śirīṣa* flower, though having walked only three or four steps with speed even within the vicinity of the city—"
"‘How much further is there to go?’— repeating this again and again, Sītā brought about the first descent of her tears.

Here, hearing Sītā’s words asking how much further there was to travel even on the outskirts of the city, Rāma’s shedding of tears upon seeing her limbs as tender as *śirīṣa* flowers expresses her extreme delicacy (*saukumārya*) and lack of hardness (*aniṣṭhuratva*).
Even when the causal conditions are present, one who does not attain a melting of the heart (cittadruti) is called "insipid" (nīrasa) or "hard" (kaṭhora);

however, one who is not thus, whose internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) is capable of immediately becoming identified with that [object], is called "delicate" (sukumāra). This is what is meant by the term "non-hardness" (aniṣṭhuratva).
By the phrase "they say," he indicates its established usage—as in the word "sadyas" (immediately).

Though she was being restrained with the words, "How will you, who are so delicate by nature, endure such wildernesses? and though she was eager to go along, she—her heart turned away from [staying] yet deluded by affection, thinking "I shall go very quickly on foot"—struck out three or four steps with speed. The first descent of tears, which became the ground for the subsequent flow of a succession of tears and spoke of her delicacy, reveals the melting of the heart (cittadruti)—the cause of the tears—as clearly as a myrobalan fruit in the palm of the hand through that shedding of tears. This is an instance of the *anubhāva* (consequent emotion) revealing the *vibhāva* (causal condition).
Clarity of meaning (*arthavyakti*) is said to be the direct description of an object's own nature, as for example:
"Upon the backs of the peacock feathers, which possess the luster of fragments of conch shells, there are lines marked with the redness of lac."
"The white water-lily, with its exterior petals yellowish-brown like cow-gallstone, rejoices in the pond-water.
Here, because the very nature of the white water-lily is perceived as if directly present, this clear description constitutes *arthavyakti* (clarity of meaning).
This is what is meant by *arthavyakti*.

Its own nature (*svarūpa*) is unique, accessible solely to the poet’s creative intuition (*pratibhā*), and consists of a form that produces aesthetic wonder (*camatkārin*). The direct description of this nature is the quality (*guṇa*) called *arthavyakti* (manifestation of meaning), which belongs to a literary composition (*saṃdarbha*) by virtue of the poet’s power; it consists in possessing words that generate a cognition similar to direct perception.
"Meaning" (*artha*) refers to what has been described above; its "manifestation" (*vyakti*) is its appearing as if directly perceived.
The distinction between species will be explained in the third chapter regarding the "backs" (*pṛṣṭha*).

On the backs of the petals of a slightly blooming night-lily (*kumuda*)— petals that are somewhat opening outward and are extremely clear due to the absence of contact with cold or heat— one observes surfaces marked by reddish-brown lines resulting from ripening (*pāka*).
For this very reason, she rejoices slightly with a face that is beginning to blossom, releasing the fragrance concentrated within her womb;
thus, *kānti* (loveliness) would be the state of having radiant aesthetic flavor (*dīptarasa*), as for example:
"Do not harbor pride, thinking: 'The cluster of blossoms written by my beloved’s own hand shines upon the cheek of my rival.

O friend, is another woman not also a fit vessel for such things, provided that trembling—the internal obstacle—does not arise? (105) Here, the *kānti* (brilliance) of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*), characterized by the heroine's passion for her lover as expressed through her jealousy toward a co-wife, constitutes its state of being a "blazing sentiment" (*dīptarasa*).

"Radiance" (*kānti*) is the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) consisting of self-consciousness, namely the *śṛṅgāra* (erotic) sentiment. Its "intensity" (*dīptatva*) is the reaching of the highest pitch by the permanent emotion (*sthāyibhāva*), which has been thoroughly stirred by the determinants (*vibhāvas*), consequents (*anubhāvas*), and transitory emotions (*vyabhicāribhāvas*), and is thus continuously accumulating. For instance, in such verses as "Do not be proud," where, through the manifestation of a state characterized by the non-obscuration of external objects—composed of many subtle nuances within the various turns of speech—the hero’s lack of luster (*vicchāyabhāva*) is expressed regarding his passion for a rival wife.

However, through the sudden manifestation within her own self of a *sāttvika* state, there is the revelation of the *sthāyibhāva* (permanent emotion) consisting of the pride that regards love as the very essence of life; in its state of mutual dependence, the heroine is likewise perceived to be in that same condition.
This is what he says: "By the passion for her beloved...
It is characterized by passion (*anurāga*), for it increases like a seven-flamed fire by means of its own radiance; thus, it is defined by passion.
Nobility (*udāratā*) is the excellence of prosperity.
For example:
"In a forest where the wish-fulfilling trees abound, the maintenance of life is performed by the wind; the rite of holy ablution is performed in waters browned by the pollen of golden lotuses."

"In the jeweled stone mansions, amidst the presence of celestial nymphs, they practice meditation and self-restraint—that very thing which other sages long for through their austerities; therein these [ascetics] perform penance.

Here, the excellence of the majesty of Mārīca’s hermitage is established through words such as "excellent wish-fulfilling trees," which constitutes the quality of *audārya* (magnificence), characterized by prosperity and so forth.

*Bhūtiḥ* is prosperity; its *utkarṣaḥ* (excellence) is a transcendental pre-eminence. Because it alone is capable of ascending the height of the qualities (*guṇa*) by imparting aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra*) to the connoisseurs (*sahṛdaya*), it is fit for the vital breaths (*prāṇa*). Thus, it is "appropriate" (*ucitā*), meaning worthy of ascetic practice (*tapas*).

The forest’s excellence lies in its connection with the wish-fulfilling trees (*kalpavṛkṣa*); therein, by the word "excellent" (*sat*), there is a further distinction indicated by pearl clusters, ruby blossoms, Chinese silk, sprouts, and so forth.
The excellence of the water lies in the abundance of lotuses; therein, the excellence of the lotuses consists in their being made of gold.
The excellence of the stone dwellings lies in their multiplicity; therein, the excellence consists in their being composed of jewels.
"Abundance" (*saṃnidhi*) is the perfection consisting in the state of being the counterpart to beauty; therein lies the excellence of "the wise" (*vibudha*).
He expresses this with the words "by means of such terms as 'the excellent wish-fulfilling tree'.
The elevation of the intention is what is intended by the term "nobility" (*udātta*).
For example:

"When the Lord of the Universe stood before him as his recipient, yet the gift to be given was but a tiny morsel of earth, the smile of modesty that appeared on his face at that moment was such that even the God himself was struck with wonder. (107)

Here, even when offered the gift of the entire circle of the earth, Bali’s intention is shown to be superior because he feels shame; thus, there is the quality of *udātta* (nobility) regarding his intention,
and its excellence is as explained before.

He whose noble intention is renowned in the world as "Sublime," who is known as the "Vessel" and "Lord of the Universe," and under whose command the three worlds are obedient— even he prays for this; by the word "even" (api) in the phrase "even for a bracelet," it is implied that he feels shame even at giving a mere portion of his own, which is famous as the cause of the destruction of the Kurus and Pāṇḍavas.

Even this entire manifestation of the moving and stationary world, beginning with gods, asuras, and kinnaras, is a mere play of his breath; thus, the excellence not explicitly stated in the words is the intended meaning.
*Ojas* (vigour) is that specific quality of firm resolve which arises toward objects.
(82) For example:
‘If those very elements are [his weapons] and if those very powers are [his],
then we do not perceive the defeat of Paraśurāma.
Here, the power (*ojas*) consists in the expression of one’s own firm conviction regarding the fact that Paraśurāma is indeed victorious.
*Ojas* (vigor) is the determination or certainty; in that regard, the specific quality is— as before— intended by the speaker to be expressed by its own term.
The word "those" (*tāni*) refers to those very [beings] if they belong to the same class as those to be killed and have not undergone any transformation.
Likewise, if his powers— born of majesty, energy, and counsel— which were renowned for their proficiency in destroying enemies and whose fame was celebrated, had not fallen into dissolution;
[he] who, through the severing of Arjuna’s thousand arms and so forth, and by the granting of boons from Paraśurāma, became famous even throughout the three worlds, and so on.
An example of audacity born of established egoism is as follows:
"Umā is the bride, you are the giver, and we here are the suitors."
"Śambhu is indeed the supreme boon-granter; he is the very ordinance for the prosperity of your lineage.

Herein lies *aurjitya* (excessive pride), arising from the manifestation of a mature egoism through the thought "we are here" and the performance of vows associated with one's own self, as indicated by the word *rūḍha*.

The word *ūrjita* (exalted) is well-known in the context of *ahaṃkāra*. When an immediate cause occurs, due to the expansion of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), there is a piercing through the state of darkness; like one who has awakened from sleep, this self-conceit (*abhimāna*) which has first appeared, not yet mingled with the stable emotions (*sthāyibhāva*), is called *ahaṃkāra* in its conventional sense.
That which has reached the second stage of manifestation from its subtle state is *rūḍhāhaṃkāra*; the state of being such is *tattā*.
An easily understood example follows.
The state of being most desired among objects of affection is as follows:
"Nectar is full of rasa; of this there is no doubt. Honey is likewise not otherwise. Even the fruit of the mango, with its clear juice, is exceedingly sweet."
"Let even a neutral person, well-versed in other flavors, say once more if there is anything here sweeter than the lip of the beloved.
Here, the demonstration of the beloved’s lip being more desirable than nectar and the like is *preyas* (the "more pleasant"). Thus ends the section on *preyas*.
Regarding the quality of sound (*śabdaguṇa*), it was stated that words produce delight in the form of the produced description;
here, however, the distinction is that the meaning of the sentence is said to be the object of the speaker's delight. "Delight" (*prīti*) has been mentioned previously.
In that very context, excellence is indicated by the prefix *abhi-*;
"desirability" (*preyatā*) is the basis for the application of the term *preyas*,
while "possessing rasa" (*rasavat*) [is the basis for the term *rasavat*].
The suffix *matup* is used here in the sense of praise (*praśaṃsā*):

"immortal" (*amṛta*) implies that it is by his grace alone that the thirty gods attained immortality, and not otherwise; thus, regarding a matter witnessed by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), there is no need to seek further means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
"Possessing a pleasing flavor" (*prasannarasa*) refers to a transformation resulting from the departure of the poetic meaning characterized by acidity, and so forth.
The use of the word *su* (well) in the sense of "not cruel" (*adāruṇa*) when applied to things that are actually cruel;
for example:
"When Devavrata desires the long sleep [of death], and Droṇa and Karṇa remain only as a memory..."
"O child, today this son of Droṇa, full of affection, is the companion of you, whose companion is Lakṣmī.

Here, the expression of harsh matters such as the desire for death or dying through synonymous terms like "long sleep" (*dīrghanidrā*) and "remaining only as fame" (*yaśo'vaśeṣa*) constitutes *suśabdatā* (the quality of beautiful words).
And because this involves a transposition of the primary meaning (*mukhyārtha-vyatikrama*) as the sense of the sentence, it is not a verbal quality (*śabda-guṇa*).

Regarding the passage beginning with "not cruel" (*adāruṇa*), that which causes immediate distress is "cruel. If this were expressed directly, there would arise the distress of a failure in the intended comprehension; therefore, the object conveyed by that [term]—either through superimposition (*adhyāsa*) upon it or mediated by such superimposition—constitutes the meaning of the sentence.
For in every case of indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the superimposition of a meaning is accepted.
Since this characteristic is worldly (*laukikī*), there is no need even to seek its purpose; thus, the example is easy to understand.
As for that which relies on a pretext, it is known as *samādhi*.
For example:

“Thinking her foot was wounded by a blade of darbha grass, the slender maiden stopped midway after taking only a few steps; she stood with her face turned back, as if trying to disentangle the bark garment from the branches of the trees, even though it was not caught. (112)

In this context, when the departure occurs, Śakuntalā’s recourse to pretexts— such as the injury to her foot by a blade of darbha grass and the entanglement in her bark garment— while longing to behold her beloved, constitutes *samādhi*.

When mental states arise forcibly and become manifest and unavoidable due to their intensity— which conflicts with the propriety of the prevailing sentiment— the justification of those states through some other means is "recourse to a pretext" (*vyājāvalambana*), because it consists of a resolution appropriate to the subject at hand.

For instance: first, for one rendered helpless by shame and trepidation due to prior passion, it is appropriate to withdraw from the presence of the hero; subsequently, however, for one agitated by longing, there arises the thought, "How might I achieve my purpose even by a mere glance? and thus she turns back.

Then, fearing the loss of her maidenly innocence (*maugdhyabhaṅga*), she resorts to pretexts such as treading upon sprouts of *darbha* grass; this alone appears to be the very essence of her entire undertaking.
That which is called subtlety (*saukṣmya*) is the perception of subtle meanings;
for example:
"Mutually blended with the luster of full, white teeth, joyfully shimmering with closely set half-glances..."
"In the pleasure-chamber, at every moment during their amorous sports, the couple shines with modesty alternately yielding.

(113)" Here, because the subtle meaning—characterized by the mutual passion of the husband and wife—is perceived in the sentence beginning with "the dense luster of their intermingled teeth," there is subtlety (*saukṣmya*).
This is called subtlety.

The object that is the exclusive domain of such statements as "subtle" (*sūkṣma*) and so forth is "subtle" (*sūkṣma*) by virtue of requiring an intellect as sharp as the tip of a blade of *kuśa* grass. Its "vision" (*darśana*)—which, due to the distinctness of the means employed, consists in its appearing as if directly perceived despite possessing various specific qualities—is distinguished from the figure of speech "Subtle" (*Sūkṣmālaṃkāra*), which will be discussed in the third [chapter].
Furthermore, this [vision] is both to be cultivated (*bhāvya*) and to be infused with latent impressions (*vāsanīya*).
That which is to be cultivated is to be understood through cultivation alone, as for example:
“Come up, come closer;
my young wife, who is perspiring, with her limbs trembling, and her face like a ripening mango fruit, is letting out a soft sigh.”
He illustrates that which is to be cultivated and accessible through the excellence of one-pointed concentration: "Mutually," etc.

In a pleasure-chamber from which their attendants have been discreetly removed, a clever couple, experiencing the agitation of love-kindled at that moment, attains a distinctive radiance at every instant like the new moon, as their shame and trepidation are successively cast aside.

Through the unpredictable manifestation of joy, weeping, smiles, and so forth during their various and infallible mutual penetration, there arises the blossoming of the erotic sentiment known as *kilakiñcita*, characterized by its incongruous mixture of emotions.
Profundity is defined as the state of being in accordance with the meaning of the scriptures,
as follows:
"Having cultivated the mind through friendliness and other [immeasurables], those who know the method, having abandoned the afflictions here and attained yoga together with its seed..."
"Having attained the discernment of the difference between the intellect (*sattva*) and the Spirit (*puruṣa*), those who maintain meditative absorption desire to suppress even that [discernment].

Here, the profundity of the terms such as "friendliness" (*maitrī*) and so forth arises from their dependence on the meaning of the treatise; thus, it is the meaning of the treatise [that is profound].

The profundity of the meaning of the sentence consists in the exposition of categories that serve the single human goal, which results in the understanding of injunctions and prohibitions; it is the dependence upon that [exposition] for its own purpose, or rather, the fact that the determination of the sentence-meaning is contingent upon the determination of the process described therein.
Furthermore, there are four purifiers of the mind: loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*).
Ignorance, egoism, attachment, aversion, and the will to live are the five afflictions (*kleśas*).
Yoga is the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind. That [cessation] is "with seed" (*sabīja*) when it cannot be overwhelmed by the causes of emergence.
Sattva is *pradhāna* (primordial matter), and Puruṣa is of the nature of consciousness; the distinction between these two is discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*). Such is the Sāṃkhya method.

In this context, regarding the phrase "of the words such as *maitrī* (friendliness) and so forth," since the meaning of the sentence itself possesses the aforementioned nature, it will be explained that the words expressing that meaning must necessarily possess that same nature; otherwise, there would be a distinction from the Vaiśeṣika school, and the detailed exposition would result in a deviation from the intended meaning.
For example:
“O King, listen! When you arrived on the field of battle and strung your bow, see what was suddenly attained by each:
the bow [attained] arrows; the arrows, the head of the enemy; he, the circle of the earth; the earth, you; you, stainless fame; and that fame, the seven oceans. (115)

In this context, because the meaning— that fame, by destroying the adversaries, has been acquired as something pervading the seven oceans— is unfolded in many ways, it is called *vistara* (expansion).

This *vistara* is a literary quality (*guṇa*) consisting of the spreading out of various specific aesthetic delights for the connoisseurs (*sahṛdaya*), which act like the unfolding of petals upon the core meaning of the sentence, much like the opening of a folded cloth.
"Vistara" means "like a spreading out," in the sense of being like a verbal proliferation;
otherwise, it would simply be "vistāra.

However, in cases such as "saṃgrāmāṅgaṇe" (on the battlefield), the sentence-meaning—that you have acquired fame extending across the seven oceans by severing the heads of enemies—is a source of aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*) because it is common to worldly experience. Thus, the connection with the "battlefield" itself is not as striking as the fact that this is appropriate for a hero alone; furthermore, the mention of "fixing the bow" implies some extraordinary power of energy (*utsāha-śakti*).

Therefore, since that which was concluded by the slaying of the plunderer who had attached himself to a powerful patron is attained by that very act, it is precisely this expansion through the elaboration of the agent and the object—including its supplementary details—that is the seed for attaining the status of poetry.
This is what he says: "Because it is expanded in many ways.
Thus, excellence here does not depend on the expansion of words; this is the distinction from mere verbal prolixity.
Its summary is conventional truth (saṃvṛti).
For example:
"Listen to the essence of all dharma, and having heard it, let it be firmly grasped."
"One should not do to others what is disagreeable to oneself.
(116) Since the dharma explained at length in this treatise has been stated here by means of half a verse, this contraction of meaning is called "the summary" (*saṃkṣepa*).
Thus, it is the "summary."

The reflective apprehension (*parāmarśa*) of that referent (*artha*), even though it has become a subordinate element (*guṇībhūta*) within a compound, occurs by means of mental analysis (*buddhyā vibhajya*), as for example: "Now follows the instruction on words (*śabdānuśāsana*);
of which words? ("*keṣām*? *śabdānām*").

"Or, by way of presenting every particular detail, let the concise statement of the meaning of the sentence be heard, like a cloth that is both open and closed: 'Whatever is disagreeable to oneself, one should not practice toward another. In this regard, regarding a dharma that is to be explained in detail through various particulars, such a general statement—asserting that "one must not do to another what is contrary to one's own self"—appears exceedingly beautiful as it skillfully incites one who has not yet engaged in virtue.
In this context, poetry is not defined by being established through the compression of composition; rather, the distinction lies in the excellence of sound (*śabdaguṇa*).
Where both word and meaning are equal, that is called "balancedness" (*saṃmitatva*), as for example:

“May that pair—the moon on the head of Śiva and the curved nail-mark on the breast of the Mountain’s Daughter—grant you prosperity, as they mutually emulate one another: the former through its resonance with the *praṇava* (the syllable Om) which, when it unfolds, brings about the unity of their bodies; and the latter by being meditated upon in the heart as the form of the upper aperture (*ūrdhvadvāra*).
Herein, the quality of *saṃmitatva* (correspondence) consists in the proper distribution and placement of the meanings characterized by the *praṇava* based on their equality.
Regarding the phrase "the word and its meaning":

some hold that "conformity" (*saṃmitatva*) is the distinct placement of these two—the word and its meaning—after having analyzed them; however, that is not correct, because it would entail the redundancy of including the mention of the "word."
And because there would be the undesirable consequence of not intending to express duality [in the case of the plural], [the following verse is cited]:

"The lady's loveliness has put forth buds, as it were, with her sprout-like hands; it has blossomed, as it were, with her moon-bright faces; and it has borne fruit, as it were, with her full breasts."
In such cases, the non-distinct placement of two or more meanings is intended;
therefore, "word and meaning" (*śabdārthau*) refers to the word and the meaning, and their equality extends as far as the term "subject matter" (*uddeśa*).
"Proportionality (*saṃmitatva*) is the precise correspondence of the meaning, like that of one holding a scale after having divided it.

With respect to this, the weighing of the word with reference to the meaning is the verbal quality (*śabdaguṇa*) which is the seed of poetic sentiment (*kāvyabhāva*); whereas the weighing of the meaning with reference to the word is the semantic quality (*arthaguṇa*).

For instance: "The young moon upon the head of the Supreme Lord; the nail-mark upon the breast of Pārvatī"—having designated these separately by distinct words, their fitness for comparison through the unity of the body consists in the simultaneous presence [of the two] within the meditation upon the opening of the fresh lotus-heart, like the designation of a *praṇava* (the syllable *oṃ*) that has been properly divided and weighed.
This is what he says:
"here" (*atra*), "according to reality" (*yathāvat*) means in whatever manner things are connected; thus, it means "without deviating from that."
The employment of speech with intentional phrasing is called *bhāvikatva* (vividness).
For example:
"O neighbor, will you perhaps grant this child a moment's glance here in our house? His father will likely not drink the tasteless water from the well."
"Even alone, it is better that I go from here to the riverbank thick with tamāla trees; let the hard joints of the reeds, cutting deeply, scar my body.

Here, the *bhāvika* (poetic suggestion of the future) consists in the meaningful speech of an unchaste woman who has made an appointment on the riverbank encircled by rows of *tamāla* trees, as she conceals the future nail-marks of other men upon her own body under the pretext of them being the scars of reed-joints.
It is "meaningful" (*sābhiprāya*) because...
The "Arrangement" (*nyāsa*) is the specific deployment of words that expresses the meaning of a sentence bound by a particular intention (*abhiprāya*).
While in the quality of sound (*śabda-guṇa*) the arrangement consists of words whose meanings are already accomplished, here it is the arrangement of the meaning itself; this is the distinction.

For instance, in the verse beginning with *dṛṣṭim* ("the sight..."), by the statement "let the knots of the reeds, though worn out by cutting, scratch their bodies," the very act of arranging the future meaning—the painting of the reed-knots—reveals immediately to the perceiver, whose mind is intent on contemplating the nature of the unchaste woman, the concealment of the marks of her own amorous wanderings.
Inference (*gati*) is the comprehension of one object from another, as for example:
"O auspicious lady, who is this old man, the master of the house? Is he your father? No, he is not my husband; for at night his sight has failed, and moreover, he is deaf."
"Huṃ huṃ! I am weary and wish to sleep right here in this inner chamber. Where are you going in the middle of the night? Go to sleep, for it is indeed free from gadflies and mosquitoes! (119).
Here, having understood the meaning through the question, the understanding of another meaning through the answer is *gati* (logical transition); thus it is called *gati*.
From the meaning, that is, from a specific meaning— namely, from that which resonates with the heart—
from such a different meaning.

Therefore, the meaning of the definition is this: where, by the force of the primary sense, another such meaning is understood through the principle of the resonance following a bronze cymbal (*kāṃsyatāla-anusvāna*), that is *gati*.

Having understood from the question a meaning agreeable to the heart—that "who is this old man?"—namely, that he does not deserve even the state of a slave for one who is in every way faultless—the answer given was "the master of the house" (*gṛhaparivṛḍha*).

Even from this [statement], one should ascertain the meaning that accords with the heart—that "this is not anyone at all to me, but rather the master of the house"—and thus there is no need to search for a chain of questions and answers such as "Who is he? or "Whose son is he?";
this is what he explains by the words "from the answer," meaning from the statement consisting of the answer and the counter-answer.
The subsequent word, however, is the very word of the question; that is the *rīti* (mode) which consists here of the sequence of actions such as the production of objects.
For example:

‘First having the hue of dawn, then the luster of gold, thereafter possessing the brilliance of the cheek of a slender woman distressed by separation, and finally at the onset of night capable of destroying the darkness— the moon, with the splendor of a slice of a juicy lotus-root, comes forth. (120) Here, the sequence of actions beginning with the rising and continuing through the birth and so forth of the moon constitutes *rīti*.
*Rīti* is the sequence of actions such as origination and so forth; it is a *guṇa* (poetic excellence) because it brings beauty to poetry.
This is distinct from *jāti* (genus) and *arthavyakti* (manifestation of meaning), as it is not a description of the inherent nature of an object.
The example is easy to understand:
"Suggestion" (*ukti*) occurs when one's own purpose is expressed through a clever turn of phrase,
as for instance—
“You possess such beauty, and he is the very epitome of charm; you two alone here have reached the ultimate limit of the arts.
O fortunate one, by good fortune this pair is thus in harmony—if only the remainder were also so, then victory would truly belong to excellence.
Here, the desired union of the hero and heroine is expressed through an indirect manner of speech (*ukti*).
"Utterance" (ukti) refers to one's own intended meaning, which is "one's own purpose" (svārtha).
Since the direct expression of that purpose is considered improper, its presentation through the artifice of another meaning constitutes the quality of meaning (arthaguṇa).
The hero is Bhavya-manohara;
the rest is easily understood as referring to the union of the hero and the heroine.
The intensification of mutual longing between the hero and the heroine, and between her and the hero, is intended;
therefore, a single-remainder compound (*ekaśeṣa*) is not employed, for the successful accomplishment of the intended meaning is known as "maturity" (*prauḍhi*) in poetry. (88)
For example:
"The Creator, his mind distracted by the sight of the moon of your face, deposited your own splendor among rival kings; thus you have been filled with the fortune of the learned.
Therefore these [kings] are surely impoverished, yet this [fortune] is seen in their houses. You do not honor her, but she runs after you alone. (122)

In this matter, the Creator, distracted by the sight of your face, has placed your own fortune among your enemies and transferred the fortune of the learned onto you; therefore, you honor the fortune of your adversaries and she follows after you,
while you are filled with the fortune of the learned, and thus they have become poor.
For this very reason, you do not respect her,

and she is seen only in the houses of the learned; because such a vast amount of meaning is established through multiple sentences, the successful execution of the intended meaning is *prauḍhi* (maturity), as the term "intended" (*vivakṣita*) implies.
*Prauḍhi* (mastery) is the expression of even a vast amount of intended meaning by a poet through a very brief statement;

for instance—in the passage beginning with "Having fashioned you, the Creator, amazed by his ability to produce a being so unique in the world, [performed] the beholding of your moon-like face..."; here, a great deal of meaning—such as the Creator’s creation of you, his wonder at producing a thing unlike anything else in the universe, his gazing upon your moon-like face, his wandering through rival kingdoms in search of the Goddess of Fortune (Śrī) who was created for your sake, and his drawing Lakṣmī away from the learned by the power of reassembling her previous and subsequent parts—is conveyed in a single, concise sentence.
Now, in order to prevent over-extension, the specific qualities (*vaiśeṣika-guṇas*) that follow in sequence must be defined;
these are also called "faults" (*doṣas*) when they have attained the status of being subordinate qualities.
Regarding this, there is this saying among poets:
"Even lack of discipline brings forth the grace of those beautiful as ascetics; indeed, smoke is highly esteemed from fragrant woods that are ablaze.
Showing the suspicion that even harsh qualities may constitute virtue, he says:
Those defects which depend on word-initials and others, as well as those which always become merits in cases such as imitation (anukaraṇa), are remembered here as "defects that are merits.
These three types are further divided by the wise into twenty-four kinds.

It is now stated how that which was previously declared as a defect by virtue of its being a flaw is, when analyzed according to its specific qualities, considered a merit. (90) That lack of grammatical correctness (*asādhutā*) which was defined among the defects of words—such as in the case of indistinct or barbarian speech—attains the status of a merit when it occurs in imitation (*anukaraṇa*). (91)
For example:
"When the beloved, lifting her face by seizing her hair, kisses her with forceful intent, the soft murmuring of the proud women—'Hum! Hum! Let go! Leave me alone!'—is triumphant. (123)

In this context, words such as *huṃ*, *hu*, *mamama*, and *iti*—even when used by the wicked, or in the case of the indistinct speech of barbarians (*mliṣṭa-mlecchita*)—are considered merits because they are imitations (*anukaraṇa*).

The connection [of the verse] is as follows: those defects of words, sentences, and sentence-meanings which always occur under the heading "beginning with a word" (*padādi*) and which result in the attainment of merit, are known as "defects that become merits" (*doṣaguṇāḥ*) among instances such as imitation.

Although imitation and the like are not themselves *guṇas*, nevertheless, by means of the metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*) of the imitation with that which is being imitated and so forth, it is stated that among the defects of words (*padadoṣa*), when the final syllable is divided ninefold, there are twenty-four varieties, as follows.
The various distinctions of those specific conditions by which the subordination [of a word] was established by the Teachers will now be demonstrated;
thus, regarding the term *mliṣṭā*, there are here two types of defects: permanent and non-permanent.

In this context, the connection is as follows: those word-faults such as *cyutasaṃskāra* (corrupted formation) and *aprayukta* (unemployed), which consist merely in imitation and lack the status of irreproachable faults, are permanent;
whereas faults such as *śrutikaṭu* (harsh to the ear), which are caused by the imitation of what is to be imitated and the non-contradiction thereof, are impermanent.

Regarding those word-faults in which ungrammaticality (*asādhutā*) has been established for forms such as *mliṣṭa* and *mlecchita*, that very ungrammaticality attains the status of a poetic quality (*guṇatva*) when occurring in imitation.
That which has a missing portion is *mliṣṭa*;
that which is indistinct in form is *mlecchita*.
By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), [other defects such as] *grasta*, *nirasta*, *upaghnātaka*, *kampita*, and so forth are intended.
In the second *huṃ* uttered as "huṃ hu," because of the smudging of the *bindu*, it is indistinct; whether it is "muñca muñca" (release, release) or "mama" (mine), it is not certain,
and due to its being an imitation, it possesses the quality of being indistinct (*guṇatva*).

For it has been stated that the status of grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) is established based on specific meanings; thus, even that incorrect form which arises from incapacity is accepted as correct when it is an imitation (*anukaraṇa*). However, that which is being imitated, by virtue of being an imitation of a word in its own form (*svarūpa*), remains correct because it does not abandon its original meaning. Furthermore, due to its function as an imitation of the words of a woman who was impassioned at that moment, it possesses the capacity for poetic excellence (*guṇīkaraṇa*) through its imitation of that very imitation.

The status of being a *guṇa* (poetic figure) applies even to that which is not actually employed, as in the case of imitation (*anukaraṇa*), for example: "Those who speak thus, 'divaṃ patkāṣiṇo yānti ye'cīkamata bhāṣiṇaḥ,' go to heaven."
"Even those who limp do not go [to hell] if they speak and employ [such words].
Here, although words such as *acīkamata* and *vacanti* have not been employed by poets, they possess the status of a merit (*guṇa*) because they are imitations; thus, they are a merit.
"Patkāṣiṇaḥ" means those who even scrape their feet;
the substitution of "pad" for the word "pāda" occurs according to the rule "himakāṣihatiṣu ca. The form "vacanti" from the root "vac" is unattested.
But it is not otherwise, because [the Buddha] has accepted such statements as "I do not speak what is called truth," and so forth;
this is said with the intention of providing another example for the phrase "and so forth."
Wise men consider even that which is harsh and unpleasant to the ear to be a merit in the case of *durvaca* (difficult-to-speak) words and the like, provided it possesses alliteration (*anuprāsa*).
For example: [92] (Note: The verse following "For example—" is not provided in the source text.)

"‘The sons of Tvaṣṭṛ [the Tvaṣṭras] are in the kingdom of the enemy of Tvaṣṭṛ [the Rāṣṭra], but not in a frying pan; there are no people without fangs among the Dhārtarāṣṭras [sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra] in Surāṣṭra, nor are there camels in Mahārāṣṭra.
(125) Here, although there is harshness due to the unpleasantness of the sounds heard, it is considered a merit because of the difficulty of expression."
Regarding the statement "because of what is heard," the employment of *durvacaka* (puns) is permitted within the sixty-four worldly poetic conventions;

when such usage serves as a constituent of alliteration (*anuprāsa*), it becomes subordinate because it is capable of accomplishing the poetic figure (*alaṃkāra*) and thus manifests the poet's creative power.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādipadena*), the entry of sentiments such as the Furious (*raudra*) is intended,
as it has been said:
"The letters *śa*, *ṣa*, and *sa* in conjunction with *ra*, as well as the *ṭa*-group, occur most frequently [in the Furious sentiment]."

In the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*), these [sounds] would be contradictory; therefore, those very same sounds that have fallen away from that sentiment are employed when they are placed within the loathsome (*bībhatsa*) and other sentiments.
In that case, they indeed intensify that [new] sentiment; thus, those sounds are "fallen away from the sentiment" (*rasacyuta*).
"Thus,
in the realm of Indra— the enemy of Vṛtra, who was the son of Tvaṣṭṛ and whose offspring were the Tvaṣṭra Rākṣasas—
there are no blunt fangs, neither in heaven nor in the frying pan, which is the place for roasting chickpeas and the like."
There exist *dhārtarāṣṭra* swans with black beaks and feet that are golden; there are also camel-keepers who subsist on camels.
That which has been cited as meaningless for the purpose of filling out a verse-line or similar reasons is [an example of] *pādapūraṇa*.
They also acknowledge its status as a poetic quality (*guṇa*) in cases such as *yamaka* (paronomasia), for example:
"The limbs of women were not at all diminished by the scratching of nails; indeed, they were not diminished because of their radiant beauty. (126)
"She shone with an incomparable face, surpassing even Menakā, who is superior among the most beautiful.

Here, although the purpose of the words *khalu* and *ca* is merely to fill the meter, they possess the status of a poetic quality (*guṇa*) because of their role in the *yamaka* (rhyme). This is what is meant by "that which fills the meter."
It has been stated that an indeclinable word employed without a meaning to be illuminated is meaningless;
however, the reason for its being a defect is its serving merely to fill out the verse (pādapūraṇa).
By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (ādi), the filling out of prose (gadyapūraṇa) is also implied.

But when there is a functional utility for it, because that [fault] lacks its seed, there is an absence of the presence of the fault; and in the commencement of an ornament (*alaṃkāra*), it possesses the status of a quality (*guṇa*).
This is what was stated: "In *yamaka* and so forth"—the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) refers to alliteration (*anuprāsa*), *citra*, and the like.

The status of being for the purpose of sentence ornamentation (*vākyālaṃkārārthatva*) is precisely the initiation of word-ornamentation (*śabdālaṃkāra*), as he said: "The causes of ornamentation for the sentences of the Ṛṣis, the sons of the Ṛṣis, farmers, Vaidikas, and so forth, are those things intended for the purpose of sentence ornamentation.
Therefore—
“O Gaurī, you whose radiance is as fair as the pollen of the filaments of a full-blown lotus, may my desire indeed be fulfilled through your grace, O Blessed One.”
For here, it has already been largely stated that the words *pra* and *iti* do not function as mere ornaments of the sentence.

In the verse beginning with *yoṣitām*, although the first half-verse is sufficient by itself to convey "the limbs of women are not at all diminished because they are radiant," the second quarter-verse—being composed of a *yamaka* (rhyme)—is employed for the sake of the subject at hand and out of the poet’s mastery; thus, it abandons its status as a defect and assumes the status of a merit. As for that which was previously described as "deviation from convention" (*rūḍhicyuta*), it is designated as having another meaning.
In riddles (*prahelikā*) and the like, its status as a poetic quality (*guṇa*) is generally appropriate.
For example:
"O Kani, at that time your *khātayaḥ* were *sphātayaḥ*, with *sphārhavalgavaḥ*."
"In this [context], when the moon is present, the winds become my sustainers.

Here, in cases such as "khātaya" (you dig) and so forth, there is no conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) for the root *dhṛ* (to hold/sustain) in the sense of a water-pot (*ghargharikā*) or similar objects, nor in the sense of non-stability;
however, in the case of hidden meanings such as riddles (*prahelikā*), this is not a fault. Thus, these possess the nature of both defects and merits.
The phrase "that which," however,
by virtue of its departure from conventional usage, employs a second designation:
the *prahelikā* (enigma), which is useful for purposes such as crowded assemblies and invitations.

And likewise—in conversation with those possessing such knowledge, there is no fault because the seed of the definition (namely, "not conveying one's own intended meaning") is absent due to the cleverness of the presentation; rather, it becomes a merit.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), things such as imitation (*anukaraṇa*) are included; [in this context], *khātayaḥ* refers to small flutes (*ghargharikāḥ*).
*Kanī* is an address to a young girl (*kanyā*). *Kāla* means "foot" according to the language of the Karṇāṭaka country. *Sphātayaḥ* means "expanded" (*sphītāḥ*).
The sound was vast, captivating, resonant,
and as delightful as the moon.
The vital breaths (*prāṇas*) are sustaining winds that are unstable;

thus, this is the meaning of the sentence: "O little girl, these *ghargharikās*—bound to your delightful feet and possessing the aforementioned qualities—are becoming manifest and are being perceived directly by the ear."

In this context, he states that my vital breaths (*prāṇa*), unable to endure the intensity of the stimulus (*uddīpana*), are unstable and cannot be sustained; thus, words such as *khāti* and so forth have their conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) in places like the site of a wound-healing, but not in things like a *ghargharikā* (a small water-pot).
This is explained in two ways, depending on whether one intends to interpret it as a noun (*nāman*) or a verbal root (*dhātu*).

That which was previously declared to be "vapid expression" (tucchavācya) or "insubstantial meaning" (apuṣṭārtha) is determined to possess the status of a poetic quality (guṇatva) when it occurs at the beginning of a verse for the sake of conforming to the meter.
For example: [verse follows]
“They desire this tree, which has the form of one sixteen years of age, as the fulfillment of the wishes of supplicants;
they call it the one who destroys the meaning of the word ‘Indra,’ and that which preceded the golden skin of Hari.

Here, although the phrases “having the form of one sixteen years of age,” “the tree with the prefix ‘kalpa’,” and “that which preceded the golden skin” have a trivial meaning, they possess the status of a merit (guṇa) due to compliance with the meter.

Regarding the term *tuccha* (insignificant): although it would normally be considered a defect because the proliferation of words is inconsistent with the intended aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), it is sometimes produced by a poet as a last resort. For instance, in the verse beginning with *bhinna-sargāntaiḥ*, since the standard practice for cantos is to maintain a single meter throughout, there is no fault in the expansion of words here; rather, it is indeed a merit. This is because the aforementioned concise wording has not been employed, and the intended meaning is expressed through a different form. Thus, in such cases, the expansion of words does not constitute a defect, but is actually a quality.
In the present example, they consider "dviraṣṭavarṣākṛtim" (having the form of a sixteen-year-old) and "kalpopapadaṃ mahīruham" (a tree with the prefix 'kalpa') to be instances [of the rule],
because even words such as "ṣoḍaśa" (sixteen) enter into the *vaṃśastha* meter and thus lack any other alternative recourse; however,
the expression "hiraṇyapūrvaṃ kaśipum" (a bed preceded by gold) is consistent [with the rule].
The word "Hiraṇyakaśipu" does not actually enter into this [definition];
rather, two others have been included for the sake of illustration,
with the intention that such an elaboration of words attains the status of a merit (guṇa).

Therefore, this is the meaning: regarding the poetic quality (*guṇa*) called *pallava*, its insignificance is indeed established upon the very burden of being a quality by virtue of its capacity to produce aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*). However, when there arises a desire to know where a specific quality occurs due to its extensive and distinct scope, the requirement of meter (*chandaḥ*) is prescribed;

for it has been demonstrated at the outset that even such a [metrical] constraint—which is occasional—indeed effects the exclusion of the state of being a defect (*doṣa*), namely that which is "incapable" (*asamartha*) or "non-expressive" (*avācaka*).
Indeed, they also consider the quality [of *guṇa*] to reside in sounds such as the hissing *sītkṛta*;
for example:
“Quickly leaping upon the fingertips of her lover, with her gaze half-closed like a bud... (96)
"The lute, its strings struck by the hands of a red-clad musician, cooed beautifully with the resonance of its circular frame.

(130) Here, although the word *kūjita* ("cooing") is not expressive [of the sound] of anything other than a bird, it is established as a merit because it is sanctioned in the treatises on love (*kāmaśāstra*).
There exists a certain subject matter where that which is incapable [of being primary] attains the status of a subordinate quality (*guṇabhāva*) by virtue of its beauty;

for instance, although the word *avyakta* (indistinct) is listed in the *gaṇa-pāṭha* as a synonym for *kūjita* (cooing), it is nonetheless restricted in common usage to the context of birds. Thus, when employed regarding the desired object, it conveys the form of the warbling of birds—as indicated by the authors of the *Kāmaśāstra* in their instruction on the *sītkāra* (the sound of pleasure) starting with the words "the *hārīta* bird, etc. and so forth.
And because the *sītkāra* (the sound 'sit'), as consisting of sixty-four artistic elements (*kalā*), is exceedingly worthy of adoption due to its aesthetic inclination, it is said:
"One should also observe other apprehensions of forms. This is called "unfamiliar" (*apratīta*) because it is understood through the technical treatises (*śāstra*) alone.
The wise know that its quality [of being a *guṇa*] is established through conversation with those who possess such knowledge and other means.
For example:
"In all bodies of action, there is the pentad of limbs and shoulders released from [the body]."
‘For kings, there is no mantra other than that of the Sugatas.

Here, although the term ‘the fivefold group of limbs and aggregates’ is well-known only within the [Buddhist] scriptures, it possesses the quality of being a virtue when used in conversation with those learned in that science; thus, it is a ‘scriptural [figure].’

The failure to produce a clear comprehension of the intended meaning of a sentence by forcibly generating a cognition of terms that are established solely by technical treatises causes weariness and is a seed of various subtle defects;
however, if it were to generate an immediate cognition due to some particular excellence, then how could it be a defect?
And such a particular excellence exists, characterized by the superior nature of the understanding and proficiency [of the audience].
This has been stated: "That knowledge" means that on occasions such as the recitation of mantras, by virtue of propriety, even the subordinate status of various words is maintained;
this is the profundity consisting in the requirement of the scriptural methodology.

Another method is that the status of being a quality (*guṇatva*) belongs to those terms conventionally established in the technical usage of the treatise (*śāstra-vyavahāra-saṃketita-pada*). Its application must be carried out exactly as it is; its "body" (*śarīra*) is the totality of these methods, while its "limbs" (*kāya*) are the verbal expressions. Its "soul" (*ātman*) is the essential element, the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*), and the means for the undertaking of actions. It has five constituent parts (*pañcāṅga*): the excellence of personnel and materials, the distinction of place and time, the counteraction of setbacks, and the accomplishment of the task.
