The five aggregates—form, perception, mental formations, feeling, and consciousness—are remote from producing the comprehension of meaning; however, that which is called "defiled name" follows as a subordinate quality when there is the instantaneous comprehension of meaning. (98)
For example:

"Then, as he who knows the qualities [of things] ascended by means of his celestial chariot to the region of the sky, which has sound as its quality, he beheld the middle station of his father—the place where the girdle-string of the blameless lady was situated. (132)

In this case, because of universal convention—such as "the word *ātman* has sound as its quality" and "the father’s station is the middle one"—and "the girdle-string is located in the region of the hips" and "the waist is located in the region of the buttocks," it produces an immediate cognition. Thus, although this [type of expression] is "obscured" (*kliṣṭa*), it possesses the status of a poetic quality (*guṇa*) because it effects the comprehension of the meaning. Here too, that very same factor is the seed of its being a defect; however, it is remedied when an immediate cognition is produced.
And the means for determining [the intended meaning] are the proximity of other words, extreme renown, or the context.

For instance, in the example under discussion, because of the mention of "Hari" in the second half of the verse, the phrase "the station of the Self" (ātmanaḥ padam) results in "the station of Hari" (hareḥ padam). Although a cognition directed toward the sky cannot arise immediately due to this word's general nature, nevertheless, by the qualifying term "whose quality is sound" (śabdaguṇam), a cognition is produced that is oriented toward the intended object by excluding other possible referents, just as in the case of "the father’s station."

Although "pada" is a general term, since it is well known specifically as the place for placing the middle step of the sky (the atmosphere), there is no delay in the appropriate cognition [of the waist].

Furthermore, in the sequence of description beginning from the feet with the phrase "the site of the girdle-string," the hips alone are the proper location for the placement of the girdle; thus, there is no delay in the cognition [of the intended meaning].

This is the purpose of the three examples: one must seek here many meanings for the sentence beyond the mere example itself. How then does he say "because of universal renown"? He says this because, since the term *śabda-guṇa* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound, one must necessarily follow established usage (*prasiddhi*) in order to reach a specific determination of its meaning.

Necessarily, even in the sequence of description, one must accept the established poetic convention (*aucityaprasiddhi*) among poets that the term "the station of the girdle-string" (*kāñcīguṇasthāna*) in the phrase "of the blameless woman" ultimately refers to the hips. [Objection:
But why does the quality of clarity (*prasāda*) not apply to the statement "the station of oneself is the quality of sound"? [Response:
He says that it does not so apply.

Because an example cannot be a fault, a general term must be understood as terminating in a specific sense; furthermore, there is the reflection of the intended specific meaning within the sentence-meaning—which consists of the connection between the meanings of the co-occurring words—like [a reflection] in clear water.

Due to this conflation of two conditions, that which is known as "obscure" (*gūḍhārtha*) because its connection with the meaning is not well-known is generally accepted as a merit (*guṇa*) in commentaries and the like. (99)
For example:
"Even poets like us are poets; even Halibuddha, Śāli, and others are indeed poets; even frogs and monkeys are lions and serpents. (133)
"Even poets like us are poets; even those headed by Harivṛddha and Śāli are indeed poets;
even frogs, monkeys, and snakes are Hari-sarpasiṃhas.

Here, although the word *hari* has multiple meanings, it is considered a merit because, despite its obscurity due to its unconventional application to frogs, monkeys, snakes, and lions, it is explained by the poet himself.
The phrase "having a relationship with a meaning not well-known" is an explanation of that [fault] regarding the meaning of a subordinate element (*guṇa*).

In this case as well, the seed of the defect must be stated as the failure to produce the cognition of a meaning that is not excessively well-known, even when [the word] is drawn in by an excessively well-known [meaning]. However, that [defect] ceases precisely upon the completion of the cognition [of the intended meaning].

Furthermore, in an exposition, there arises an immediate understanding as if from a dictionary; even poets like ourselves, who possess dull wit, are denoted by the word "poet" (*kavi*), while those endowed with transcendent genius, such as Harivṛddha, Śāli, and others, are designated as its "components. And words are common to both the famous and the obscure;
for example, the word *hari* itself—such is the explanation.

Consequently, there is an absence of fault, and because it culminates in the figure of speech known as *prativastūpamā*, it attains the status of a merit (*guṇa*) by being conducive to the subject matter at hand. He explains this as follows: "The absence of fault is self-evident; however, its status as a merit should be understood as resulting from its intentional conformity to the subject matter.
This refers to that which was described as having a literal meaning (*neyārtha*), whose expressed sense is constructed through one's own arbitrary convention.
In riddles and the like, it is considered by the wise to be a merit.
For example: "The peacock carries its tail-feathers; likewise, [the river] bears its name. (100)
‘The peacock bears its tail; its name is like that of another who, from head to foot, is followed by those who entreat him, just as a boat follows its helmsman. (134)

In this case, although the name "Candra" (Moon), which is conceived through the convention of the eye-spots on a peacock's plumage, is of interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*), it is considered a merit because it functions as a riddle (*prahelikā*);
thus, even here, the underlying impression (*vāsanā*) is the same as before.
In contexts such as crowded assemblies or invitations, the characteristics of the clever and other such features are employed to reveal specific types of riddles (*prahelikā*);
for instance, in the reading *mayūra* as *jianāu*, the meaning remains the same: "one who has conquered ships" (*jitanauka*).
A peacock bears a moonspot (*candraka*) upon its mass of plumage;
by this convention, it receives the name "moon" (*candra*).
The region of the head of one who is lying down is the "head-end" (*ucchīrṣam*), and the region of the feet is the "foot-end" (*pādāntaḥ*).
The eastern direction is indicated by the head,
according to the injunction, "One should sleep with the head toward the east"; by implication, the western direction is indicated by the feet.
Furthermore, in the case of the sentence “The crescent moon has gone west from the east,” the meaning of the sentence is the dawning of the morning;

whereas in the reading “They entreat their husbands” (*aṇuṇenti ajiṇaṇāu*), it is the lamentation of a woman whose lover has been unfaithful, expressing: “I have realized that I was deceiving my beloved who fancies himself handsome.

Since there is no purpose for these [secondary] indications (*lakṣaṇā*), when the consequence of "intended meaning" (*neyārthatva*) arises, the very nature of being a riddle (*prahelikā*) is the cause of its resolution.
Now, let it be granted that this applies to cases such as *ucchīrṣapādāntarapada*; but how can it apply in instances like *mayūrakalāpa*?

For the word *yam* indeed presents itself as being intended as a pronoun (*sarvanāman*). Even if one were to argue that in the case of *barhe* (in the sense of "in the tail-feather"), which is abundant among many, there might be the cognition of a single [quality], this would at best be a strained interpretation of a specific attribute.

There is no need for an interpretive meaning (*neyārthatā*) here; rather, by the phrase "the name similar to that name," what is intended is obtained through the primary sense (*mukhyavṛtti*) itself, namely, the name of the moon as it is conceptually constructed by that convention.
To this, it must be said: by the phrase "of that name," the word *candraka* is presented, and there is no similarity between that [word] and the word *candra*.
In this regard, the basis for the definition must be resorted to;
thus it was said: "of the name 'moon' which is conceptually constructed by means of the convention 'moon'. And this is an explanation of a single part by way of illustration.
That which is declared to be "uncertain" (aniścayakṛt) would become a "quality" (guṇa) if there were a comprehension of the specific [meaning] through context and other such factors.
For example—

"Though the king had many sons, his gaze could not find satiety upon that particular child; may Śauri—whose complexion is like a cloud and who holds the Śārṅga bow, the discus, sword, mace, and lotus in His hands—protect the worlds.
(135) Here, although the specific child is undetermined and remains ambiguous in the phrase "upon that child," it is understood through the context (*prakaraṇa*) to be Gaurī.

Furthermore, in the case of the expression *meghacchaviḥ* ("cloud-complexioned"), even if words such as *nava-śyāma* ("freshly dark") were not employed, because it is connected with Śauri (Viṣṇu), a specific quality—either "having the complexion of a fresh cloud" or "having a complexion dark like a cloud"—is determined; thus, this too possesses the status of a *guṇa*.
As for the phrase *yat*, its capacity to generate doubt, being of a nature that causes uncertainty, is the very seed of its defectiveness (*dūṣakatā*).
If, however, due to some specific factor, the intended comprehension arises without obstruction, then indeed there is an absence of fault.
The "comprehension of a specific feature" (*viśeṣāvagama*) is the perception of a specific feature (*viśeṣadarśana*), for that alone is the opposite of doubt.

In examples such as *mahībhṛtaḥ* ("of the mountain-possessor"), although the word *apatya* ("offspring") and even the word *gaurī* ("the fair one") are of a nature that causes doubt because they have been applied to others, nevertheless, by concluding with the intended specific meaning once that very word has presented its sense, it abandons its status as a fault.
As for how that very word brings about that specific meaning, the context alone remains active here as it were in a waking state.

In the case of the phrase "cloud-like luster" (*megha-chavi*), although the word *megha* (cloud) belongs to a class of words that cause doubt because it has been applied to both dark and non-dark things, nevertheless, due to its co-occurrence with the word *gaurī*, which is well-known to denote a blue color, the proximity of another word also restricts [the meaning] to a specific one; or else, it is the word *chavi* itself that culminates in that specific meaning, because in this case, context and the other factors serve as causes for the recollection of the specific meaning.
For this very reason, since words such as the plural number are not employed in the *sūtra* and are thus not explicitly included, he explains this with the words "here," and so forth.
Just as when it is said, "having the luster of nine clouds," the comprehension of the meaning occurs invariably and without obstruction, so too is it said, "cloud-lustre.
Therefore, its status as a poetic excellence (*guṇa*) arises from the fulfillment of the causal conditions for understanding the specific [meaning] well-established in the conventions of poets.

Furthermore, how is it that this [appearance] does not constitute a specific instance of the afflicted (*kliṣṭa*), or rather, how does it function as a statement? Rather, it is intended that even the appearance of that which induces doubt is eliminated by the aforementioned reasoning; and such a nature is not possible in the case of a specific instance of the afflicted.
Since the power of doubt resides in a single, multiform word, it does not pertain to the meaning of the sentence;
thus, what was called "contradiction" (viruddha) becomes a figure of speech (guṇatva) when it is presented as such through a contrary conceptualization. || 102 ||
For example:
"Having then uttered that unpleasantness, Śiśupāla has fallen into a state of extreme resentment; yet, with a mind set on you, he seeks to pay homage to you while you are still angry. (13.6)
In this case, although there is a conceptualization of a contrary meaning, it is considered a merit because the meanings of the compound and the analysis (vigraha) are clearly expressed as distinct;

for when a sentence is composed with reference to a specific subject matter indicated by "yat-tat" (that which...), the introduction of another subject matter that subverts that [original] is "contradiction" (virodha).
Where both subjects are contextual, or where another subject is itself contextual, how can there be a fault in the absence of the form described above?

For instance, in the messenger's speech beginning with "abhidhāya" (having spoken), although *saṃdhi* (peace) and *vigraha* (war)—which are mutually contradictory—are intended [to be conveyed], that fault exists: "Śiśupāla desires the honor—that is, the worship—of you who are *sarūṣaḥ*, meaning full of wrath."

In the case of the *sandhi* (compound) interpretation, it means "one whose mind is filled with *anuśaya* (remorse) and longing directed toward [you]"; however, in the case of the *vigraha* (analytic) interpretation, *anuśaya* refers to anger, meaning "one whose mind is devoid of fear toward you. Because it is always dependent [on another word], it forms a compound (*samāsa*).

The consideration of honor for one who is angry is useful; thus, in this case, the presentation of both alternatives by the *nisṛṣṭārtha* (fully authorized) messenger—composed with the intention that "let whatever is pleasing be done"—is considered a merit (*guṇatva*) under the view that there is an intention to express both. However, when the messenger is a bearer of a command, then according to the maxim that "messengers speak exactly as they are told even when weapons are raised," the intended purpose is indeed war. Since it is the duty of a messenger to provide encouragement even to the enemy, a peace (*saṃdhi*) occurring at the outset is indeed appropriate as a strategic alternative.
He clarifies this through the following explanation: "In this [context]..."
The meaning in the form of a compound is the "compound-meaning" (*saṃdhyartha*), and the meaning in the form of an analytical expansion is the "analytical-meaning" (*vigrahārtha*);
by the expression of these two, the distinct meaning—the purpose—is indeed made clear.
This explanation is intended according to the purpose stated for both positions.
It has been stated that [the *aprastutapraśaṃsā*] is not a productive cause (*aprayojaka*) because it prescribes something non-distinct;
however, when the mere essential nature (*svarūpa*) is to be expressed, even that [non-productive cause] is accepted as a subordinate element (*guṇa*).
For example: [103] ————
"Those supreme sages also leaped into the sky, which was dark as a sword-blade,

and that high-minded one performed austerities for more than a thousand years. Here, although no specific qualification is stated regarding the sky with the term "dark as a sword-blade," nor regarding the thousand years with the term "more than" (*sāgram*), these function as *guṇa* (qualifying attributes) because they are intended to convey the utility of the long leap and the prolonged practice of austerity.
Regarding the term "inefficacious" (*aprayojaka*):

it is that very [word] which is employed by poets because it establishes the intended connection, yet which, even though it has entered into the sentence-meaning, does not attain such a status; this is what is called "inefficacious."
If its usage culminates in the expression of a specific nature (*viśeṣasvarūpa*), then there is no fault;

for instance, in the case of "the sky" (*ākāśam*) and so forth, [the term] does not manifest even the slightest trace of a specific quality such as extreme blackness in the sky, because the sky never loses that nature.
Likewise, since that which is incomplete lacks the state of being "a thousand," the term "complete" (*sāgram*) also does not impart any specific quality.

Regarding the statement that "of the two thousand *ākāśas*, that which is to be perceived as form" (*rūpa-bhāvedanīya*), there is no fault here if the intention is merely this much; nevertheless, what is the purpose of mentioning these two [qualities] as being inseparable (*nāntarīyaka*), such that their status as subordinate qualities (*guṇabhāva*) is established? To this he says: "At a distance"—in extreme distance, blackness appears more intensely, and because there was not even a moment's cessation [of it], this is the intended meaning of the word *sāgra* (with the top/limit); therefore, there is no tautology here.

If it is argued that these two [words] merely impart a specific qualification to the meaning of the sentence, how can there be any possibility of their being a defect? It is thus: a word is "irrelevant" (aprayojaka) when, even if it were not employed, there would be no deficiency in the intended meaning.

Furthermore, there is the consequence that both [the proponent and the opponent] would incur the fault if [the reason] were of that same class; however, this [consequence] is averted only when one intends to apply it to the subject at hand.
If it is in no way applicable to the subject at hand, its status as a flaw remains unavoidable.

And there exists a very appropriate application here which deserves to be expressed; thus he says: "In the case of intended expression," that which was previously defined as "unrefined and censurable" becomes a merit here when it is composed by a great poet. (104)
For example:

"By whom [the wind] was obtained as it reached the shore, shaking the *piṇḍītagara* trees in the groves, and acting as a kinsman to the lotuses blooming in the ponds that burst open upon the high banks. (138)
"Into the cavities of his cheeks, which rivaled the netherworld (Pātāla), he cast the seven oceans" (139);
"Scattering the spray-drops from the charming waves of the Kāverī" (140).

Here, although words such as *talla*, *galla*, and *laḍahalahari* lack etymological derivation (*avyutpattimat*) and thus ought to be objects of censure (*uddeśya*), they possess the status of a merit (*guṇatva*) because they have been accepted by great poets.

It was previously stated that the cause of "difficulty" (*kaṣṭatā*) here is a disparity in the stylistic tone (*saṃdarbhacchāyāvaiṣamya*) of the composition. If this is refuted by inserting words of identical tone into the midst [of the passage], then how could it be a fault?
For such words, precisely because they serve to sustain the flow of the composition, are what is composed by a great poet.
For this very reason, it attains the status of a poetic quality (*guṇa*) by virtue of being conveyed through words:
the hardness of *piṇḍītagara* flowers is established by their being "tall as a staff," and the maturity of even such things is shown by their being "swaying."

In "uttāla" and so forth, one should understand that the word *talla* is of the same class as the words possessing alliteration (*anuprāsa*), such as *proḍha*; likewise in "galla" and so forth. This is what he says: "here, *talla*, *galla*, etc."
That which is uttered as vulgar, disgusting, indecent, or inauspicious in meaning does not constitute a fault when it is concealed, hidden, or indicated.
(105) Regarding that, an example of the "concealed" is as follows:

"Therefore, strive to unite that self-restrained one with the daughter of the Snowy Mountain who is purified for him; for it was taught by the Self-born (Brahmā) that among women, she alone is fit to be the ground for the sprinkling of his seed.
Here, even though the expression "the ground for the sprinkling of his seed" is indecorous (*aślīla*), it possesses the status of a poetic excellence (*guṇa*) because it is concealed.
As it has been said:
"In this world, it is not appropriate to seek out faults in that which is well-encased; when the Śiva-liṅga is established, who would conceive of it as being indecent?"

Regarding the term "vulgar" (*grāmya*), some explain it according to the sequence [of the three defects]: that for the three starting with "disgusting" (*ghṛṇāvat*), the seeds for the absence of defectiveness are respectively "counting," "concealment," and "characteristics. That is incorrect, because later on, after taking up the triad of "counter-distinction" (*pratisambheda*) and so forth, the triad of "garment" (*saṃvyāna*) and so forth is presented in relation to the mere objects such as "disgusting" and the rest.
It is precisely for the sake of indicating such a correspondence that the "disgusting" (ghṛṇāvataḥ) is mentioned first, even by transgressing the [expected] order of definition.
Therefore, just as with "reckoning" (saṃkhyāna), "reckoning" (saṃkhyāna) refers to public consensus;
for even a certain word of a corrupt class does not lose its nature [of being a word] simply because it is not employed in common usage.

Since poetic theory generally follows worldly conventions, it is stated that because each [type of word] is connected to its own threefold classification, they should correspond respectively; having said this, he provides examples according to the previous order:
"In this case," by which the plural form in "enveloped" (*saṃvīteṣu*) and so forth is explained.

Just as in the phrase "in the configuration of the Śiva-liṅga," although the word *śivaliṅga* is primarily used only in a vulgar sense, it is nevertheless not capable of causing shame because it is associated with usage from time immemorial; likewise here, "that intellect" (*taddhīḥ*).

He states that the same principle applies here as well—that the connection with the Blessed Lord is the determining factor in the case of the term "Śivaliṅga"—by saying "That [is the reason]," for here the well-known fact that the Blessed Lord, as the inner controller of the universe, is opposed to such things must be accepted; and when that is accepted, a perception that would cause embarrassment simply does not arise. He writes down the teacher's view on this very point: "For of one who is clothed... and so forth.
The contemplation as to whose impropriety it is constitutes knowledge common to all the world,
as for example in the case of a secret.
"Even though one's birthplace is difficult to abandon, it was made free from the crowding of elephants;
therefore, this fortunate and proud brother of ours must be conciliated—this is our primary intention.

(142) Here, although the words *janmabhūmi* (birthplace), *saṃbādha* (crowding), *subhaga* (fortunate), and *bhaginī* (sister) possess other vulgar meanings, they are considered a merit because they are concealed by the power of the intended primary meaning.
As it has been said:
"Because a thing that is concealed by the greatness of its subject matter is revealed,
words such as *bhaginī* (sister) and *bhagavatī* (venerable lady) are not perceived as indecent."

When another meaning obtainable through etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) is vulgar, or when another meaning obtainable through syntactic collocation (*samabhivyāhāra*) is so, the concealment thereof is the seed of the resolution (*samādhāna*). That [concealment] takes two forms: either the predominance of conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), as in the case of words like *jaladhara* (cloud); or, by obstructing the inference of the intended meaning, it results in the inference of an opposite meaning, as in the example about to be cited. Thus, since there is no impediment to comprehension, there is an absence of the seed of fault (*dūṣaṇatā-bīja*). Regarding this, he first cites an example by taking the first alternative.

The primary meaning brought forth by conventional usage (rūḍhi) is its "state" (bhāva)—that is, the immediate cognition of the sentence-meaning; the "cultivation" (bhāvanā) of that is its latent impression (vāsanā). By means of that, there is "concealment" (gopana), which is the imparting of aesthetic wonder (camatkāra), a non-obscuration.
He confirms this very point through the authority of the Teacher (Ācārya): "by the majesty of the subject matter," and "due to the lack of discernment."

The contemplation [of an object] is contradictory because it produces shame; however, since that [shame] is absent, there is no fault even if such a state is achieved when employing a particular yoga in certain cases. He clarifies this very point by means of an example: "sister," etc.

By this, the previously unmentioned example "the Blessed Lady" (Bhagavatī) is explained; the second concealment will become manifest in another context of censurable meaning, as illustrated in the following definition:
“I perform this worship for Him who, as the cause of the cosmic egg, deposited His own seed in the waters, and who reclines upon the serpent Śeṣa.

Here, although the words *brahmāṇḍa* (cosmic egg) and *upasthāna* (worship/sexual union) are causes for the recollection of something indecorous, they possess the status of a poetic quality (*guṇatva*) because they are perceived elsewhere [in their conventional meanings].
When a portion of a word follows a vulgar usage, it serves as a cause for recollection;

in that case, sometimes due to the variety of expression, that portion immediately triggers recollection, while in other cases, the whole word itself conveys its own meaning immediately by presenting a contrary sense through its collective power. Of these two, the former constitutes a defect.
But the second [type] is a quality (*guṇa*) because there is no lack of conformity to the class [of the intended meaning].

Thus, the definition is as follows: where there is vulgarity (*grāmyatva*) in the first case, it is a quality in other cases due to its being defined in many ways; this is what was meant by the statement "because it has been defined elsewhere.
In this same way, [the status of] inauspiciousness (*aśasta*) and so forth is also a quality.
For example:

“O auspicious Māri, speak favorably; O Kṛtyā, dance joyfully in the assembly for a moment; O Mṛtyu, arrange a square of jewels; O Kālarātri, perform the nightly lamp-offering; O Cāmuṇḍā, bring the garland of severed heads; O Bhairavī, subdue your excessive jealousy”—may these words of the attendants as they address Queen Bhavānī before the Lord protect you! (144)

In this context, even words with inauspicious meanings, such as *mārī* (disease) and the like, acquire the status of a "quality" (*guṇa*) because they are uttered in connection with the Blessed Lord Viśveśvara, the abode of all auspiciousness.
Furthermore, it manifests the inauspicious [nature of those words] by showing that they become "enveloped" (*saṃvyāna*) in another manner;
for it is well known in the scriptures and histories that the Supreme Lord is the abode of auspiciousness, according to the rule that whatever is merely connected to Him becomes auspicious.

As it has been said: "Nevertheless, O Giver of Boons, you are the supreme auspiciousness for those who remember you. And this mode [of address] pertains specifically to those mothers such as Māyā and others, whose nature is not praiseworthy.
The *ārātrika*— the vessel for the continuous display of the *nīrājana* lamps—
nourishes the connection with the station of the attendants;
it suggests a second mode of concealment, implying another meaning that is not explicitly praised.
Or for example:
“The sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra—possessing strong wings, sweet voices, adorned quarters, and arrogant undertakings—fall upon the surface of the earth under the power of Time. (145)

In this context, although the statement "the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra fall upon the surface of the earth under the power of Time" possesses an inauspicious secondary meaning, it attains the status of a merit (guṇa) because it is concealed by the sentence to be spoken later: "I designate the swans as the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Or, according to another view, the term *pakṣa* refers to both a wing and a retinue (*parikara*).
Āśā means the cardinal direction; pratyāśā means hope;
mada is intoxication; kṣībatā is drunkenness; darpa is pride; nipāta is falling down; āgamana is arrival; and [it also denotes] the contact with the earth of those struck by weapons.

First of all, it is not possible here for the stage-manager—who has already commenced the auspicious rites (*svastyayana*) at the conclusion of the theater’s blessings—to intentionally introduce the subject matter (*vastu*) of the auspicious section; for the intended meaning (*tātparya*) has been restricted by the verse beginning with "I am the swan" (*haṃsānaham*).
However, words manifest other meanings through their own power (*svaśakti*), yet this does not appear as a defect.

In this regard, since the introduction of a specific element of the *vīthī* (theatrical entertainment) constitutes the body of the prologue (*āmukha*), one should understand that the underlying intention is that the insertion [of the subject] is clearly due to propriety (*aucitya*) alone.
The contradiction regarding propriety (*aucitya*) is not universal; thus, there is no over-extension [of the rule]. For example:
"Who was intended by her as being well-proportioned? There is no certainty."
"But this female demon of hope will choose me as her bridegroom.

Here, although the words *abhipreta-susaṃsthāna-āśā-piśācikā-kumārī* are causes for the recollection of inauspicious things, they possess the quality of excellence because they have been perceived by people elsewhere [in a positive sense].
Regarding the phrase "Who is the intended one? and so forth, the latent impression (*vāsanā*) functions exactly as before.
In this way, even qualities such as compassion (*ghṛṇā*) and so forth possess the status of a poetic quality (*guṇa*).
Among these, an example of compassion is as follows:
"Having drunk the sparks of fire spat out by the rays of the sun, the lotuses..."
‘...as if vomiting again through their mouths, which have disgorged ruddy dust.
Herein:
‘Words such as *niṣṭhyūta*, *udgīrṇa*, and *vānta* [should be employed] by resorting to metaphorical function (*gauṇavṛtti*).’”
"Anything else that is exceedingly beautiful falls into the category of the vulgar.
An example of [the fault of] a disagreeable shift in meaning (*ghṛṇāvadarthāntara*) is as follows:
"In my opinion, the moon is but a drop trickling from the cheek of a passionate woman."
"Otherwise, how could his splendor illuminate the world? (148).

Here, because of the power of contemplating the essential nature of the beloved’s cheek and the moon—which serve as the causes for an excess of passion—the contemplation of another meaning is concealed; thus, even though the phrase "drops trickling from the cheek" has a loathsome secondary meaning, it does not constitute a defect.
Now, he describes another method of enumeration regarding a loathsome meaning—with the words "as for example."

When secondary words such as *avāntara* (intermediate) and others—which serve as the substrata for the functions of qualities (*guṇa*) and operations (*vṛtti-vyāpāra*)—are first employed, the non-arising [of faults] due to the manifestation of *samādhi* (poetic concentration) serves as the gateway to the absence of defects, even when the attributes of other actions and so forth are superimposed upon something else. Consequently, he explains by means of the verse of the former teacher how there is a sense of loathsomeness (*jugupsādāyitva*) precisely in the primary locus: "In this case," and so forth.

Intending that it is overwhelmed by the qualities (*guṇagrastatva*), because of the excellence of the intensity (*atiśayasaṃpatti*) and the propriety of the context, there is the appearance of the cheek itself; thus it was said: "Of those two which are the causes of the excess of passion."

And so, it is entirely appropriate that the moon—which is the delight of the eyes of the world and has dispelled all darkness—should appear as nothing more than a drop of the loveliness on the cheek of a desired beloved;
with this in mind, referring specifically to the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the ancients, he cites an example of the cause of memory:
"As for the cause of memory belonging to one who possesses compassion... [as follows].
‘These young twice-born ones, wearing garlands of putrid *vipūya* flowers and bearing *palāśa* leaves as their crowns, go forth endowed with the splendor of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcasvin*).

(149) Here, although the words *vipūya*, *palāśa*, *brahmavarcasa*, and *pogaṇḍa* are causes for the recollection of something loathsome, they are not considered a fault because they have been observed used in other [appropriate] contexts.
"Yathā" refers to the staff of Āṣāḍha; "brahmavarcasinaḥ" means [possessing] spiritual luster.
By the rule "brahmahastibhyāṃ varcasaḥ," a compound-ending suffix is applied, followed by the possessive suffix *ini*; thus, *pogaṇḍa* means a child.
He states that other types of derivations, such as those involving numerals and so forth, should likewise be inferred by oneself.
In this regard, other cases should also be understood as follows:
"Even that which is improper may possess beauty through its connection with a particular substratum."
It is like soot-like collyrium applied to the eyes of a beloved woman.
For example:
“With the sounds of numerous ornaments swaying—consisting mostly of bracelets jingling from the cruel *nalaka* bones of large skulls strung together with entrails—he makes the sky resound. (106)
“With a body terrifying due to the weight of her swaying breasts, which shine with a dreadful mass of thick mud consisting of yellow vomit and blood, she runs about, arrogant with pride.
(150) Here, because the substratum is appropriate for the *bībhatsa* (disgust) rasa, there is no fault whatsoever. Thus it is said.
This objection is not permanent;
for in those cases where there is no defect, since it is included within the causal complex that reveals rasa, how could it not be a quality (*guṇa*)?
And this inclusion is twofold: either by way of the propriety of the context of usage, or by way of the propriety of the verbal expression as a determinant (*anubhāva*).
Therein, he first demonstrates this: "something" [is that which becomes an excitant].
For example, collyrium, even when contemplated hundreds of times as being associated with the collyrium-creeper and so forth, does not become an excitant;
rather, it becomes one when it is perceived as being kissed by the eyes of a beloved woman.
He explains this very point regarding the application [of the term] to both that which is within its scope and that which is not its scope: "In this case,
by virtue of the configuration of the substratum (*āśraya*), even something slightly contradictory appears beautiful."
The dark blue palāśa leaves were fastened in between like garlands;
for example:
“Having suddenly bound on garlands of heart-lotuses, with auspicious amulets fashioned from intestines, and wearing visible ear-ornaments made of red lotuses from women’s hands... (107)

“Here, these delighted female Piśācas, enjoying the saffron-paste of blood-mud, drink together with their lovers the wine of bone-fat from skull-cups. (151) For those possessed by passion perceive even the entire world as consisting of passion; thus, even within a *bībhatsa* (disgustful) sentiment, there is no fault in the inclusion of words such as ‘auspicious amulet’ (*maṅgalapratisara*) among the intervals of the offering of entrails and other parts by Mādhava. He explains the second mode of subsumption: “by virtue of the arrangement” (*saṃniveśavaśāt*).

The arrangement [of words] is the power of speech (*vāganubhāva*), consisting of a composition of words drawn together by propriety (*aucitya*). It is under the control of that [propriety], and is thus drawn by it; for this very reason, even when two heterogeneous elements are joined in opposition, they manifest a particular beauty by virtue of propriety. This demonstrates a resemblance to a garland formed from the intermingling of leaves and flowers—as in the verse beginning with "nīlam" and "antraiḥ," where the intensity of the *bībhatsa-rasa* (the sentiment of disgust) is justified in Mādhava, who beholds the corpse of a woman recently deceased and driven mad by a sudden affliction, through the excellence of the *ālambana* and *uddīpana* excitants.

As for this sudden introduction here of words such as "maṅgala" (auspiciousness) and others that follow upon the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*), how is it to be removed from the status of a defect, or how is its quality (*guṇatva*) to be attained? To answer this, he explains by providing the underlying reason: "In this context, 'the one possessed of the erotic' (*śṛṅgārī*) refers to one whose latent impressions (*vāsanā*) are fixed upon the erotic;

thus, even though there was previously a connection with the loathsome sentiment (*bībhatsarasa*), the poet first made a formal declaration with the words 'For me,' etc., so that there might be no disruption of the intended erotic sentiment, and then established the firmness of those impressions with the words 'As if merged,' etc."

Therefore, in every instance, the metaphor (rūpaka) is indeed imbued with intention; thus, it is appropriate that [the object] consists of the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra), attaining the status of a rasa by virtue of being a constituent of the erotic.
And the mental apprehension of its identity with that [object] occurs through mere similarity of mind.
Consequently, how could there not be the quality of an excitant (uddīpanatā), since the actual physical existence of the object is of no utility?
For this very reason, since the *bībhatsa* (the loathsome) mentioned in the aphorism is sublated by the subject at hand (*prakṛta*), it does not nourish the intended meaning;
[one might ask] "How then was it stated in the enumeration that there are twenty-four types?
for previously only sixteen *doṣas* were classified. To this, he says:
Since these subdivisions of the indecorous (*aślīla*) and other [defects] are each divided threefold,
they become nine; thus, when added to the ten and five previously mentioned,
these are said to be twenty-four varieties based on words (*pada*).
"In brief, for the purpose of establishing the excellence of the previously mentioned defects—
this has been declared as the non-defectiveness of word-defects such as the indecorous (*aślīla*) and so forth. (109)
The phrase "thus the twenty-four" has been explained by the commentary:

from ten onwards, a number denotes the thing numbered; since it expresses both the number and the thing numbered, it is established that—as in the case of "twenty cows"—it depends on the word [itself] as a mere expression of the number.
Now, the status of defects of sentence as merits is being stated.

(110) He introduces the exposition of how the defects of sentence, which follow in the sequence, can become subordinate: "Now," etc.; therein, in some cases, that which is devoid of words [becomes a merit] by virtue of the speaker's intention.
The status of being a quality (*guṇatva*) is attributed [to beauty] by virtue of its natural loveliness.
For example:
"O charming one, the lotuses challenge the splendor of your face."
"For those who possess both treasury and army, what indeed is difficult for them?

(152). Here, although the genitive case is prohibited for the agent and the object by the rule "na lokāvyayaniṣṭhākhalarthatṛnām," the use of the form *kimeṣāṃ duṣkaram* (what is difficult for them? is considered a merit because it expresses the mere relationship [between the subjects and the difficulty], as he says:
"For this treatise appears like mere gibberish to those whose minds are indolent in perceiving its greatness, yet it does not forfeit its elegance.

Since a single entity possesses various forms that are heterogeneous in nature, the diversity of words employed according to the diversity of the speaker's intention regarding those specific forms is logically consistent; thus, there is no fault.

Regarding the statement "she has been brought to such a state," etc., [the author] says "in some cases" to show that this fault of being of a certain nature never exists, whereas in other cases there is a different nature;
let it be so.

To address the question of how this constitutes a *guṇa* (poetic excellence), he says: "By nature... For the intention of great poets regarding a fixed form cannot arise merely by following conventional beauty;

for instance, in the verse beginning with *ākṣipantī*, regarding the word *eṣām* in the phrase *eṣāṃ duṣkaram*, since the genitive case is prohibited by the rule *na lokāvyayaniṣṭhākhalarthatṛnām* when used in conjunction with words having the sense of the suffix *khal*, how can there be a genitive in *eṣām*? The resolution of this difficulty lies in the intention to express a specific residual relation (*śeṣa*) by taking up a particular class of difficult [grammatical] forms.
For the relation denoted by the genitive case has two forms: general relation and specific relation, such as the producer-produced relationship (*janyajanakabhāva*).

Among these, while the prohibition by rules such as *na loka-* applies to the genitive prescribed for a specific relation, by what means could the genitive be prevented when it is employed in the form of a general relation?
This very relationship is called "the remainder" (*śeṣa*);
thus, there is no fault.

Just as for kings who possess a full treasury, once they have seized the fortune of their enemies, nothing that merely pertains to their own kin is difficult to achieve, so too we establish this for lotuses.

Otherwise, how could there be the "stealing of the beauty of the face" (the impossibility of attaining it)? Since this provides nourishment for the subject at hand, it is a merit; he explains this very point [with the words] "herein," etc.

Now, one might object: "Let there be no fault if only a mere relationship is intended, but how can it be a merit? Having in mind what was stated [previously], he writes down the opinion of another: "For this," etc.—namely, the greatness of the scripture consists in the fact that injunctions and prohibitions have non-overlapping domains.
If some effort has been made to ascertain the relationship [between words], then even if there is a transgression of the proper sequence, the learned do not consider it a fault; as for example:
"Abandonment of kin, abandonment of the body, and abandonment of one's country"—in these three... [112]
The beginning and end are long-lasting afflictions, while the middle is a momentary fever;

because the sequence "beginning, middle, and end" is prescribed for the purpose of establishing a connection [between them], there is no fault of violating the verbal order. Furthermore, since the speaker considers the abandonment of the body to be more significant than the abandonment of kinsmen or the abandonment of one's country, even the violation of the logical order [of meaning] constitutes a merit.
Regarding "effort":
for when there is a lapse in the sequence, the seed of faultiness consists in the obstacle to the comprehension of the intended connection;
however, if through some particularity a comprehension arises that is indeed unerring, then, due to the absence of that seed, such [faultiness] is necessarily removed.
And since that specific detail cannot be enumerated step by step, it has been explained in general terms as "some effort";
this is an exception to the rule regarding the sequence of words,
whereas in the case of transgressing the sequence of meaning, there is a specific intention.

For instance, in the passage beginning with "abandonment of kinsmen" (*bandhutyāga*), having first enunciated the abandonment of kinsmen, the abandonment of body, and the abandonment of country in that order, their subsequent reference (*anudeśa*) ought to follow in the same sequence; it is not the case that the last is enunciated after the first, and then the middle one. Although this constitutes a violation of the sequence of the science defined by enunciation and subsequent reference, its faultlessness is established because an effort is made to bring about the knowledge of the relationship [between the items].
And this very effort consists in the mention [of the items] by means of the word *ādi* ("and so forth"), for those words produce a cognition directed toward each of those specific positions.

And it is certainly appropriate to state this in such a sequence here, because the abandonment of the body deserves to be mentioned separately, as it is intended to be of a different nature [from the abandonment of kin]. Furthermore, there is no logical inconsistency, for in the world it is well known that the abandonment of the body is far more grievous than the abandonment of kinsmen. Therefore, the statement “the middle one involves prolonged suffering, while the first and last are momentary fevers” is fitting; thus, how could there not be an absence of deviation from the intended order? To this, he says: "and of the speaker... (vaktuśca).

By the term "desired" (*abhimata*), a specific intention is indicated as the cause for the exception: according to the principle that "the appearance varies according to taste, according to need, and according to proficiency;
thus, even when accomplished through a single unifying synthesis, the appearance is differentiated," this [distinction] is indeed logically established.

That which was previously described as "irregular sandhi" (*virūpasaṃdhi*) and "disjointed sandhi" (*visaṃdhi*) does not generally constitute a fault in cases such as *durvaca* or *pragṛhya*. (113) Regarding that, an example of irregular sandhi in the case of *durvaca* is as follows:

"‘May [the goddess] who is difficult to address when addressed by those who speak ill—she who is "abhenaṅgeḍje khamapograbhograrugdhruḍbhramabruṇmukhi" (O you whose face is like the sun, with its rays, fierce heat, fixedness, wandering, and the moon)—be victorious during the rains and protect us!
(153). Here, although the sandhi (euphonic junction) in the second half-verse is irregular, it is considered a merit by connoisseurs because of the quality of being difficult to pronounce."
As they say:

"In social gatherings, words such as 'durvaca' (difficult to speak) and the like should be uttered for the sake of refining the speech of parrots, women, children, and fools, and for the sake of amusement. (154)
An example of the absence of euphonic combination (*saṃdhi*) at the beginning of *pragṛhya* vowels is as follows:
“These two eyes are like lotuses; the path of his grace clings to them.
He, my beloved, is present throughout the seasons of the year; you do not recite the *Ṛg-veda* nor the *Yajur-veda*. (155)
In this context, the absence of euphonic combination (*guṇatva*) is caused by factors such as *pragṛhya* vowels;
as it has been said:
"When one does not intend to express a *saṃhitā*, that lack of combination occurs between words."
That which is designated as "disjunction" (*visaṃdhi*) is not caused by *pragṛhya* vowels and the like.

[The term] "virūpa" means "ugly" or "ill-spoken. In the case of an ill-spoken [utterance] where the application of *saṃhitā* has departed—that is, where the rule for the application of *saṃhitā* is not accepted because it takes the form of a specific artistic variation (*kalāviśeṣarūpatayā*)—it is called disjunction.
Regarding the second [point], he asks where there is no fault and says: "In the case of *pragṛhya* and so forth.

*Pragṛhya* refers to that for which the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of *pragṛhya* has been prescribed by rules such as "the dual endings of *ī*, *ū*, and *e* are *pragṛhya*. By the inclusion of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), examples will likewise be cited where the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) is prescribed even without the *pragṛhya* designation, or where a pause occurs due to the speaker’s fatigue or other reasons during recitation.
For example: "Who is she with but a single lock of hair?

Thus, he states that such instances as *durvacaka* (unpronounceable words) and *pragṛhya* (non-sandhi vowels), etc., serve as exceptions (*apavāda*) to the rules of *virūpa* (dissimilar form) and *visaṃdhi* (absence of euphonic junction) respectively. He explains:

"In this context, they are employed" (*atra prayujyante*), thus they are called *prayuktayaḥ*; and since they are both *durvacaka*s and *prayuktayaḥ*, the term *durvacakaprayuktayaḥ* is a *karmadhāraya* compound.
"Difficult to utter" (*sudurvacāḥ*) means they cannot be pronounced by another;

having himself vowed this, the poet states the difficult riddles (*durvacakāni*) in the second half-verse beginning with *ameḍ*. O daughter of the mountain king (*nageḍje*), "kham" is the sky, "bheḍ" refers to the stars (*bhānām*), and "īḍ" is their lord, the moon; that [place] where he is absent is [the meaning].
In response to the inquiry—"Since it has vanished, the moon is imagined to be non-existent; by what, then, was it concealed?"—the second qualification is given: *apogre*.

This means where the clouds, denoted by the word *abhra*, are the perpetrators of offense against the sun (*bhā*), which has departed its fierce radiance (*apagatogra-dīpti*) and possesses intense brilliance (*ugra-ruci*).
The term *abruṭ* refers to a lotus that grows in the waters; thus, "O Goddess whose face is like that [lotus]" is an address to the Goddess.
To this, Gaurī replies, "If it is such as this, then may I be your companion (*sadhryaṅ*).

He states that even a discordant union possesses the quality of being a virtue because it is esteemed by those who know the arts (*kalāvidbhiḥ*), owing to its nature as an artistic refinement (*kalārūpatva*).
In examples such as *kamale iva*, because they serve as illustrations [of different cases], a single half-verse is not [the sole example].
In the first half, the triad beginning with *kamale* is an illustration of the *pragṛhya* designation;
in the second half, where the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) is prescribed even without the *pragṛhya* designation, that triad serves as the illustration.
For instance: in the case of *abda-ṛtau* and *na ṛcaḥ*, there is the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) by the rule *ṛtyakaḥ*;
and in the case of *yajūṃṣy ūhasaḥ*, [the preservation of the original form] occurs by the rule *iko’savarṇe śākalyasya hrasvaśca*.
It should be understood that "that" (saḥ) is to be supplied here as well, just as it was previously cited as being implied by the initial words; furthermore,
although this is sanctioned by the treatise, it should be inserted with skillful composition.
But it is not otherwise;
for it was already stated previously that even that which is caused by *pragṛhya* vowels and so forth should not be employed more than once,
unless some excellence of compassion or the like is intended to be expressed.
There is no fault even in a tautology; on the contrary, this is an ornament (alaṃkāra). For example:
"That woman of beautiful hips is being struck by Smara, the enemy who strikes at the unseasonable time."
"She whose every limb is beautiful is being struck; she who speaks so sweetly is being struck" (156).

Here, the repetition of the word *hanyate* is a verbal tautology (*śabda-punarukta*), and the repetition of the sense "she whose every limb is beautiful" as "she of noble form" (*varārohā*) is a semantic tautology (*artha-punarukta*). Both of these, however, are not defects when there is a desire to express an excess of compassion and the like; thus, they possess the status of a poetic excellence (*guṇa*), specifically that of compassion (*anukampā*).
Because repetition of words and so forth is accepted in cases such as agitation—as indicated by the phrase "until awakening" and others—it does not constitute a fault;
rather, because it invariably reveals the intended meaning and is conducive to enhancing the original aesthetic flavor, it is a merit.

For instance: in cases such as *hanyate* (is killed), although the intended meaning of *hanyate* is already expressed [by the preceding context], it constitutes a type of verbal tautology; and although in the case of saying *varārohā* (one with beautiful hips) followed by *cārusarvāṅgī* (one with beautiful limbs in every part), which has the same intended meaning, it constitutes a type of semantic tautology due to being a synonym, nevertheless, its repeated use is justified because of the speaker's intense compassion for one distressed by the pain of separation, following the worldly convention of saying *ahirahi budhyasva* (O snake, wake up!).

Intending to show that such a repetition of words by one who acts out of compassion or fear is indeed capable of ascending to the level of excellence, as it is accomplished through a specific underlying intention, he explains: "Both of those...

[The verse continues: "Where there is an inversion of words, whether in sequence or out of sequence, they know that as *vyākīrṇa* (intermingled); for that, there is no fault whatsoever. For example: || 116 ||

"‘Do not despise him, for his disposition is not corrupt; do not act thus, O you whose virtuous conduct remains unimpaired!’—as if such were the words [spoken], the vital breaths of the Great Sage’s son were restrained by their throats being constricted.

(157) Here, although one ought to say "mā sma jugupsata" (do not despise), the inversion of the word order in "jugupsata smainamaduṣṭabhāvaṃ maivam" constitutes a *guṇa* (excellence), because some authorities maintain that even in the case of transposition (*vyasta*), the specific characteristics of the *luṅ* and *laṅ* tenses apply.
Regarding "of words":

within a single sentence, the displacement of words from their appropriate arrangement is the violation of sequence (*kramabhraṃśa*). This occurs in two ways: either by the removal of such a sequence among words whose status as preceding or following is fixed, or...

Just as "much grass" (*bahutṛṇam*) has one meaning and "grass much" (*tṛṇaṃ bahu*) has another— since these [words] lack a fixed order of priority and posteriority— or just as by such a reversal of utterance, in the cases of "he anoints the potsherd" (*kapālam anulimpati*) and "he puts on the silk garment" (*dukūlaṃ paridadhāti*), a specific sequence is intended.

When one says "he anoints the skull" and "he puts on a garment," because the same meaning is obtained through these actions, yet when it is expressed as "he puts on the skull" and "he anoints the fine cloth (dukūla)," there occurs a reversal of proximity; this is equivalent to what is called "confused" (*vyākīrṇa*) and "mixed" (*saṃkīrṇa*). Thus it has been said: "Whether in sequence or out of sequence."

Now, one might object: since the rule *‘sma-yoge laṅ ca’* prescribes the use of the *luṅ* and *laṅ* tenses where the word *sma* follows the word *mā*, a fixed order of words has been established; how then can that meaning be understood when the expression *sma mama* is used? To this, he says: "The state of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatva*) consists in being specifically characterized (*viśeṣeṇa lakṣyate*) as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa-lakṣaṇa*). [This occurs] where, by way of alternation, there is a sentence consisting of two [parts], such as in questions and answers."
Those learned in the art of dialogue know that such a mixture does not constitute a fault—for example:
"O child! O Lord! O proud one, abandon your anger. What was done by me out of wrath? Why this distress toward us? You have not offended me; all the offenses are mine."
"So why do you weep with a faltering voice? Before whom are you weeping? Is it not this [person] here? Who am I to you? I am not your beloved; it is for this reason that I weep.
Here, although there is a mixture [of sentiments], there is no fault because it is a dialogue (vākovākya) conducted by turns.

In a case where there is a syntactic unity of sentences (*vākyaikavākyatā*) and the cognition of the intended relation fails because the meanings of the words intrude into one another within the intermediate subordinate clauses (*avāntaravākya*), there is the defect of "confusion" (*saṃkara*). However, when the cognition is unerring, there is no fault. This confusion occurs through the mixing of sentence components belonging to different speakers or occurring in succession; furthermore, this mixing may take the form of a question and answer or otherwise. Thus he says: "In questions, answers, and so forth."
This is a locative of object (*viṣayasaptamī*).
In the phrase *vākya-vākovākya*, the form is correct by virtue of its inclusion in the *pṛṣodarādi* group.
Therein, he provides an example of *vākovākya* consisting of questions and answers, beginning with the word "O child" (*bāle*).

In this context, the first question, "O child, abandon your anger toward me," has as its corresponding answer, "Lord, what have I done out of anger? Here, the mention of the opening of the subsequent sentence, "O Lord," immediately after the opening of the sentence "O child," was intended to bring about a blending of the two types [of speech], but it is set aside by the power of the question-and-answer exchange.
If it is argued that *vākovākya* occurs even when two mixed sentences are presented as alternatives (*paryāya*), we say no;
for such an intermingling (*vyatikara*) is distinct (*vijātīya*) because it produces aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*) by manifesting a specific intention (*abhiprāyaviśeṣa*).
It is for this very reason that it constitutes a poetic excellence (*guṇa*).
For instance, the word "fool" (*bāla*) reveals a reproachful address directed at one who places trust in the words of a lowly companion due to ignorance of another's mind;

immediately upon hearing this, the address "O Lord" (*nātha*) is intended with a specific purpose, as it is the appropriate speech of a woman impassioned by jealousy—intending to convey: "You are merely a master [in name], but you have not bestowed your affection upon us, nor do you possess the good fortune of being under our control.
In the same manner, the subsequent parts should be inferred by oneself.
The mention of "both" is illustrative; for even in the case of a single speaker, it is appropriate to employ such discourse in contexts like riddles (*prahelikā*) and the like.

Regarding words situated between two sentences of a different genus (*vijātīya*), there arises a doubt mixed with uncertainty as to whether this word is to be construed with the former or with the latter. The Teachers (*guravaḥ*) maintain that such doubt is indeed included within the category of *saṃkara* (confusion). For example, in the sentence "The king’s son is coming; let the man be removed," the word "king" (*rāja*) falls between two clauses and is thus doubted: is it to be construed with the preceding [son] or with the following [man]?
In cases such as "king's cow-milk," the application of the word *go* (cow) is ascertained through two factors;

therefore, even though there are distinctions such as "rustic" (*grāmya*) and so forth based on whether it is used in its primary sense (*prakṛtistha*) or otherwise, the use of such words—which might otherwise be considered non-words—is permitted in the variety of poetic diction (*bhāṣācitra*). || 118 ||
For example:

“Alas! That which was merely a cloud is not Madana himself appearing directly upon this earth; so why does he appear thus? Is it truly heard that Kāma has been slain? Or is it that he was consumed by the Lord of Beings (Śiva) during the wedding festival of Gaurī? If this is indeed the truth, why then is the bracelet on his hand looking at itself in a mirror? (159)

In this context, a rustic man who has come to the city, upon seeing the king, asks in the vernacular using words that are either rustic or natural: "O, is that the god of love? And the urbanite, desiring to favor him, replies with refined or tender words and through clever speech: "This is not Madana himself manifest on the surface of the earth."

Then the rustic man, his wit provoked by the preceding verse, reproaches him in half-Prakrit using words that are either rustic-civilized (*grāmyopanāgara*) or naturally soft: “Is this true? Is it heard that Kāma has been slain?

Then the civilized man, knowing the rustic’s proficiency, replies in half-Prakrit, likewise following the meter, using words that are either rustic-civilized-civilized (*grāmyopanāgaranāgara*) or naturally soft and harsh: “O messenger, you have been sent by the Lord of Beings for Gaurī’s wedding festival.”

Then the rustic (grāmya), out of regard for the completion of the verse and for the following quarter, speaks three or four words in Prakrit—either rustic or natural—and stops at the very middle of the quarter, saying: "Thus, speak only the truth" (*aiseṃ sacca ji bollu*).

Then the urban (nāgara), appearing victorious, completes the verse and its sequel with words that are rustic, semi-urban, or urban, and natural, soft, or harsh, saying: "Is the hand adorned with bracelets looked upon by means of a mirror?
And in that case, all the Prakrit words are considered rustic.

Among the words used by the questioner, *vapuḥ* is refined (*upanāgara*), while the remaining ones are rustic (*grāmya*); among those of the respondent, *hastavivāha*, *gaurī*, and *pada* are rustic, whereas *bhūtapatinā* is refined and the rest are refined-urban (*upanāgara*). Thus, in such a subject matter, because the commencement was likewise [rustic], this does not constitute a fault, as it remains consistent with the natural style (*prakṛti*).
In the rule *apadalaṅkṣaṇam* (Pāṇini 6.1.134) beginning with the word *vibhinna*, the term "of six" (*ṣaṇṇām*) does not intend a combination [of all six];

rather, it is presented as an option between the triad beginning with *grāmya* or the triad beginning with *prakṛtistha*. The purpose of this presentation is the attainment of permission (*anujñā-saṃpatti*), by which the absence of defect and the presence of excellence are established.
He shows the scope [of this rule] with the words: "in *bhāṣācitra*" (poetic figures based on language).

Since the combination of *saṃskṛta* and other languages is intended as a form of poetic defect (*apada*), it follows that *saṃskṛta*, *grāmya*, *prakṛtistha*, and so forth, are what is meant by the term "language" (*bhāṣā*).

For instance, just as a painted picture is composed of various colors, or as a variegated cloth (*citrapaṭa*) is woven from threads of different kinds, so too a certain poem composed of various languages is called "variegated" (*citram*).
Here, "variegated" (*citram*) means wonderful (*āścaryam*), and that which produces such wonder is also called "variegated."

Anticipating the objection that such a combination of two forms would necessarily involve a reinforcement of logic—namely, that a single entity might arise from the intermingling of various languages drawn together according to propriety—the author provides, in brief, an illustration of the very mixture of all languages: "For example" (*yathā*).
He clarifies both the mixture and the vulgarity through his commentary: "In this context, 'rustic' (*grāmya*) means a village-dweller who is somewhat educated."
Furthermore, those from the countryside are curious about the objects found in cities and possess a sense of wonder; this constitutes the "jāti" (universal).

In that context, the phrase "having seen the king" expresses wonder through the description of a marvelous object, while "he asks" expresses curiosity. Respect and deference arise precisely through that sense of wonder.
Alternatively, there is great respect for those whom he asks about, based on the intention that "Blessed are they who know his name, lineage, and so forth, and who behold him constantly.
Furthermore, since this character is a common villager, it is appropriate for him to ask questions using only Prakrit words.
To demonstrate all of this, the author sets aside the question and shows it: "Hā tā! and so forth.

‘Hā to’— this interrogative intonation in the Mahārāṣṭrī language means “is it?”; the wonder is that he, whose fame is so widely renowned even in our village by virtue of being the leader of this city, is called “Jo Jjhaladeu.”
Furthermore, this question concerns people generally wandering about in the city;
here, all the words—being native to the countryside rather than belonging to a very low class—are Apabhraṃśa words, and their rusticity is universal due to their being regional (deśī) words.
The phrase "hā to" carries weight through its phonetic quality.

The word *‘jo jjaladeu’*, which has acquired gravity through the presence of a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*) and remains in its natural state (*prakṛtistha*), is here employed because it is drawn forth by the propriety (*aucitya*) of both the Prakrit and the rustic (*grāmya*) styles;
for in the case of the natural state, propriety is not merely functional,
but rather it is intended that the composition has been commenced by means of it.
Since there is nothing further to be asked, this is the very occasion for the answer immediately following this question;
therefore, there is no impropriety.
For by their very nature, refined people are opposed to the views of the vulgar and are connoisseurs of *vakrokti* (indirect or figurative expression).
If it is asked, "Since he has a vulgar and inferior intellect, why would he give such an answer?", it is said: "Desiring to favor him"—
he asks the vulgar man with great respect because at that time he felt compassion for him.
Favor consists in generating the knowledge that brings an inquiry to rest.

Although a refined person ought to employ refined words, nevertheless, when it is necessary to favor a rustic person, what is intended is precisely that which is suitable for their understanding, rather than refinement itself.
Therefore, one should not ask why he does not speak using only rustic words.

If one were to act in such a manner all at once, it would contradict the common understanding; moreover, it would lead to the destruction of the refined (*upanāgaraka*) style. Therefore, he says "in the refined [style]," implying that the middle [registers] are the refined ones suitable for usage.
By their very nature, those established in the Prakrit source-language and those established in the Sanskrit source-language attain maturity.

Therefore, although words of a type commonly used in the vernacular (grāmya) would have been appropriate to employ for the sake of achieving uniformity in the composition, nevertheless, if he had respected their natural state (*prakṛtisthatva*) while inserting Sanskrit words obtained through propriety (*aucitī*), there would have been a discordance in the aesthetic tone (*chāyāvairūpya*). With this intention, he stated that only words "mostly soft" (*komalaprāya*) were employed;
for according to the worldly maxim that "the designation follows the majority," he said "with soft [words]" (*komalaiḥ*) even though one word, "directly" (*sākṣāt*), was in its natural state.

And regarding a question that implies a further inquiry, the intended sense is: "For what purpose is Ajjaladeu supramundane (*lokottara*), and why is there no one else like him? In this context, by merely saying "no," a favor would have been shown; however, it is appropriate to say something more as well, and thus he says: "with his witty speech" (*savakrokti*).

By this, it is shown that the conduct of a refined city-dweller (*nāgaraka*) is not at all augmented [by him]. Furthermore, by the restrictive particle *eva* ("only"), it is revealed that he is not even a mere human, let alone someone of such a specific character as Ajjaladeu.

The word "directly" (*sākṣāt*) means being apprehended through perception; since it has been stated that one who is slightly learned is a "rustic" (*grāmya*), the possibility of his being involved in the burning of passion arises through the contemplation of contradictory attributes—namely, the state of direct manifestation which is opposed to [the usual state of] being turned away from desire. Thus, he introduces the rustic's inquiry when the opportunity has arisen with the word "now" (*atha*).
Intellect that touches upon specific instruction is *pratibhā* (inspiration/intuition).

"Do not suspect me as being entirely dependent on a familiarity with the conduct of city-dwellers (*nāgaraka*). With this intention, out of pride, she uses words of the very same kind employed by city-dwellers; yet, a question is appropriate [in this context], and for this reason alone, it is not right to abandon the original nature (*prakṛti*) altogether. Therefore, even those words suitable for her own usage deserve to be employed there, half of which involve a deviation from the original nature (*prakṛtivaiśasa*), half of which is Prakrit, and half of which is rustic (*grāmya*), as these would otherwise be unsuitable for the sentence of the question. She says: "In accordance with the preceding word" (*pūrvapadānurodhāt*);
the preceding word used by the other was considered, and *saccimā* means "truthful."
He presents as much of the common person's proficiency as is appropriate: "It is heard"—meaning this has been thus heard from the mouths of historians, yet even today no final determination exists;
"it is reasoned"—meaning it remains within the realm of nature.
"It is seen" is soft; "it is true" is situated in its natural state;
"its form is destroyed" is soft.
"Kāmaḥ kila... and so forth; likewise, it is heard [in the text] as "prakṛtistham"; immediately thereafter follows the occasion for the *nāgarika* (the refined man).
As for how one who speaks of the ultimate truth (paramārtha) should respond when [the opponent's position] is untenable, this is the method of resolution:

by using the two phrases "it is said" (asti kila) and "it is heard" (śrūyate), the state of being doubtful and slightly enlightened on the part of the rustic [opponent] is inferred; thus, by stating something entirely false that appears as such through cleverness of intellect, deception becomes possible.

Since it is devoted solely to that [the literal meaning], it is capable of directly demonstrating every aspect of superior proficiency (*vyutpatti*); thus, one might conjecture. With the intention of considering how much proficiency a vulgar expression such as *tarkitam* possesses, and how much further proficiency its imitation (*anukaraṇa*) ought to presuppose, he introduces the subsequent verse with "Now" (*atha*).
The foot beginning with *tarkitam* is employed by a vulgar speaker; its conformity (*anurodha*) is the imitation of that proficiency.
*Paścāt* means "afterwards."
O, here he is!
In the reading "ai dūe" (O messenger), "dūa" means a pretext; by this pretext, [the Lord] Paśupati, the Lord of Beings, [is present].

[Objection: "But this is not heard anywhere; how then does the awakening of the rustic occur? To this he says: "In the festival of Gaurī’s marriage. Let it not be thought that this is established merely by hearsay; rather, it is established through reasoning. For if there were no second manifestation of desire (*kāma*), how could the Blessed One have such enthusiasm for taking Gaurī’s hand in marriage? Therefore, the meaning is that he must have been created once again by him whose soul is tranquilized by a continuous stream of compassion. *Paccha* means "natural" (*prakṛtistha*); *ai* means "harsh" (*kaṭhora*); *kialeu* means "soft" (*komala*); and *bhūtapatinā* likewise [indicates the agent]; *gaurīvivāhotsave* is "natural."
In the reading "e~dūe~," both [words] are harsh;
here, the employment of a harsh [sound] is intended to indicate an abundance of *vyutpatti* (linguistic proficiency).
When this much has been stated, no vulgarity appears in the proficiency resulting from the examination.

And since he still does not possess complete confidence, the question is appropriate as it relies upon the authority of the refined city-dweller (*nāgaraka*); with this intention, the author introduces [the next section] with "Now, the rustic," which refers to one who has fallen back into his natural state.

Therefore, just as there was a resolution for the initial question beginning with "Alas, my dear! and so forth, the same applies here; thus, the two [characters] remaining in their rustic nature are presented.

Due to the competition between their respective linguistic styles (*bhāṣācitra*) as they engage in the composition of a single poem, even for a rustic poet, it is entirely appropriate that the completion of one verse and the commencement of the next coincide; furthermore, if this very [rustic style] were to carry the entire work to its conclusion, an answer suitable for dispelling all doubts would have been provided by the urban poet. Therefore, in accordance with that subsequent requirement, even a delay of half a quarter-verse (*pādārdha*) is fitting.
The word *aiseṃ* (in this way) is used here in the sense of *evam* (thus), containing an implied intonation (*kākugarbha*).

The phrase “*sacca ji bollu*” (let him speak the truth) contains the emphatic particle *ji*; thus, it means: “this which has been said is indeed the truth—if you were to speak preceded by the truth, then I would believe it.”

Thus, since the establishment of vulgarity and deception has been achieved, he introduces the answer with the intention that—for a refined person (*nāgara*), when responding to a matter witnessed by all the world, it is more appropriate to merely complete the verse by providing an answer through an indirect expression (*vakrokti*) based solely on the previously established context—saying "Now," "in the hand," which is *prakṛtistha* (contextually situated), "the bracelet," which is *komala* (soft/mellifluous), and "it is seen in a mirror," which are both *prakṛtistha*; because these terms such as *prakṛtistha* and so forth are easily understood, he explains only the vulgar (*grāmya*) and other [faults], beginning with "In that case... (*tatra ca*).

He concludes by stating that since the propriety of both the modification and non-modification of the *prakṛti* (original nature) is established, the commingling of dialects (*bhāṣāsaṃkara*) is indeed a merit (*guṇa*) due to its enhancing beauty: "Therefore, a sentence containing another sentence within it—that is, a sentence embedded within a sentence—is desired when it does not obstruct another rasa; otherwise, it is not desired. (119)
For example:
"The earth, with its four boundaries demarcated by the trunks of the elephants of the quarters, is being conquered; and even as we speak of it as already conquered, our hair stands on end. Behold!
It is now being bestowed upon a Brahmin. What more can be said? Salutations to that Rāma, from whom this wondrous tale emerged and into whom it has likewise returned. (160)

In this context, although it ought to have been stated that "the earth as described is established, and once established, it is bestowed upon the Brahmin," the fact that the phrase "to the Brahmin" and so forth is interrupted by the sentence—"For even as we speak, our hair stands on end; look!"—uttered by one acting under the influence of the heroic and marvelous sentiments (*vīra* and *adbhuta*), is called "the suppression of another sentiment" (*rasāntaratiraskṛti*).
By means of this, the sentence, though containing another sentence within it, does not become a defect, because of the presence of another sentence.

"Another rasa" means a specific rasa that is consistent with the primary rasa; by that, there is a sublation of the state of being a defect. When this occurs, such a sentence is indeed desired by poets and fit for adoption; otherwise, it is not desired and is simply defective.
Therefore, the meaning is as follows: the very seed of defectiveness is indeed the obscuration of the primary rasa, and that is removed precisely by its non-obscuration.

On the contrary, when there is the attainment of the method of composition for sentences containing "the embryo" (*garbha*) and so forth—as will be explained in the second chapter—the result is the acquisition of poetic figures (*alaṅkāra*), and thus it becomes a merit (*guṇa*).

For instance: it is that [earth] which has four boundaries (*āghāṭa*) demarcated and established separately by the array of elephants from the cardinal directions; thus, it is intended that "the earth consisting of seven islands (*saptadvīpā vasumatī*) is conquered.

Regarding those such as Bharata, Bhagīratha, and others, whose excellence of prowess was world-renowned and whose power was perfected in defeating their enemies—it never even reached the range of hearing that the energy of any one of them was sufficient for the conquest of the nine-knotted earth (*navakhaṇḍamedinī*) by uprooting the entire lineage of Kṣatriyas. Thus, the extraordinary energy of Pārashurāma is made known.

By the phrase "and that [aim] was accomplished," the intention—just as before—is that "whatever was desired, that very thing was accomplished; oh, what a desire for victory! This is further illuminated by the word "ca" (and), which indicates that even though he did not set out with the specific intent of achieving success, that success was nonetheless attained immediately thereafter.

When this has been stated, there exists the remainder of the sentence beginning with “to the Brahmin,” and by interrupting that very [sentence] in the middle with the statement “for we, while speaking, were filled with horripilation,” there is an internal fullness (*sagarbhatā*). This is not a defect;
for by this sentence, the intended rasa—which manifests upon the attainment of the *vibhāva* consisting of the contemplation of a supermundane object—is revealed.

And that [rasa], being the cause for the sustained apprehension of the heroic (*vīra*), is characterized by an absence of opposition due to the mutual accompaniment of the heroic and the marvelous (*adbhuta*), which occupy the same ground.

In this regard, just as the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*), the furious (*raudra*), and the loathsome (*bībhatsa*) are not eclipsed by the comic (*hāsya*), the pathetic (*karuṇa*), and the terrifying (*bhayānaka*), even when they are brought together in a single continuous thread (*sūtra*) according to the maxim that "one's own limb does not obstruct," so too here, the heroic (*vīra*) rasa is not eclipsed by the marvelous (*adbhuta*). For this very reason, there is the demonstration of the *anubhāva* characterized by the sprout of a son appearing from the overflowing [marvelous rasa]—[expressed by the stage direction] "Behold! (*paśyata*).

Furthermore, in the example of this fault, a conflict with the natural flow [of the sentence]—as occurs when the expectancy raised by the agentive case ending in "by me" (*mayā*) is obstructed by "protect him" (*rakṣainaṃ*) and so forth—is not possible here. This is because the meaning of the sentence reaches its conclusion even when only "accomplished" (*siddhā*) is shown;
