nor can one say "even while speaking" (*avadanta eva*) and so forth once the rasa is complete, for the wonder of the king's majestic presence depends solely on that [completion].

Thus, for one who is not satiated by the experience of rasa and feels longing for that very same [rasa] again and again, the statement "it is bestowed upon the brahmin" (*viprāya pratipādyate*) serves to highlight the excellence of the recipient obtained through the efforts of one desiring victory.
Since even the hero of generosity (*dānavīra*) is indeed a hero, for this reason, when there is no further duty to be performed, the conclusion begins with "what else remains? and so forth.
He explains all of this as follows:

"In this context, that which was stated to be a discrepancy in gender and that which is a discrepancy in number—these do not constitute a flaw in the simile where they cause no agitation among the wise. (120)
For example: "At other times, self-restraint is the ornament of a man, just as modesty is for a woman; valor [is the ornament] in the face of defeat, just as boldness is during sexual unions. (161)

In this regard, differences in gender are seen in the examples "of a man as of a woman," "tranquility as modesty," and "valor as impudence"; however, in the example "in contempt as in sexual pleasures," both difference in gender and difference in number are observed.

Since these cannot be altered otherwise because there is no other synonym available when one intends to express the mutual relationship of standard of comparison (upamāna) and object of comparison (upameya) among these very terms, they do not offend the sensitive reader; thus, even what is a defect becomes a merit.
This is one example for both [cases];
now, an example of that which has a different gender is as follows:
"He whose days come and go empty of the three aims of life..."
"Though he breathes like a blacksmith’s bellows, he does not live.
Here, as before, because there is no other synonym available, there is no fault in the difference of gender in the phrase "sa lohakārabhastreva," since it is that which is distinct.
Examples of these defects, both collective and individual, should be understood in accordance with the specific category of defect concerned;
for it is by virtue of causing distress to the sensitive reader (*sahṛdaya*) that something constitutes a defect.
However, where such a state does not occur in any way, it is indeed appropriate that the status of being a defect be abandoned.

For instance, when one intends to express the relationship of subject and object (upamāna-upameya-bhāva) between a woman and a man in accordance with the context, it is necessary that either gender or number differ; since the word *dāra* is necessarily plural in number when used as the object of comparison for a single man, the word *kalatra* must likewise be plural.
Furthermore, even among synonyms, a difference in gender is fixed, and there exists no masculine synonym of a similar nature by which this [present] method might be avoided.

And since the nourishment of the intended meaning of the sentence cannot be achieved without such a simile, this lack of grammatical gender agreement or number agreement— which has no other recourse— does not cause distress to those who know the conventions of literary composition; for this very reason, its status as a poetic quality (*guṇa*) is established through its perfection of appropriateness to the figure of speech (*alaṃkāra*).

Intending to show that this same principle should be understood to apply to *śamala* (stain) and *jaya* (victory), as well as to *parākrama* (valor) and *vaiyātya* (boldness), and to *paribhava* (disgrace) and *surata* (sexual union), he explains:

"In this case," [the fact that] all words denoting sexual union—namely *rata*, *rahaḥ*, *śayana*, and *mohana*—are in the neuter gender does not constitute a fault; the reason for this is that they do not cause distress to the hearts of connoisseurs (*sahṛdaya*), and this is intended as a merit (*guṇatva*), which has indeed already been demonstrated.
The word "atha" [introduces] the *trivarga*, which consists of dharma, artha, and kāma.

Just as a bellows (*bhastrā*)—which is a leather bag for fanning a fire—is filled with air and releases air, yet achieves no human purpose whatsoever, so too, although devoid of the *trivarga*, the quality [of this figure] is established through the absence of agitation among sensitive readers (*sahṛdaya*) due to the perfection of the ornament (*alaṃkāra*), since there is no lack of a common gender for the synonym *bhastrā*. Thus he says: "In this case, it is just as before."
The phrase "absence of fault" (*adoṣa*) is an elliptical expression; it should also be understood that there is a "quality" (*guṇa*) as well, even when the words differ in number—as for example:
“He of abundant power, the source of Dharma, whose passion and darkness have subsided... (*prājyaprabhāvaḥ prabhavo dharmasyāstarajastamāḥ*).
"May the liberated soul Nemi grant us auspiciousness, as may the other Jinas as well.

(163) Here, although there is the fault of *vacanabheda* (discrepancy in number) in the phrase "Nemi [singular]... others [plural]," it attains the status of a merit (*guṇatva*) through the power of the *śleṣa* (punning) of the verb "may they grant" (*dadatām*), which is common to both. Nor should it be said that because the particle *iva* or the like is not present here, it cannot be considered a simile (*upamā*).

Because the particle *api*, used here in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*), excludes the [literal] object through word-plays (*vacanaśleṣa*) such as "the source of Dharma" when applied to things possessing common attributes;
just as in a simile, the indicator (*dyotaka*) is elided before the [comparison], as in: "O slender one, your tender and pale-red sprouts and your lower lip.
Now, why is this not also considered a *śleṣa* (pun)?
It is said: "Where there is the expression of two similar things, that is *śleṣa* (paronomasia);

where from a similar thing there is the cognition of another similar thing, that is *upamāna* (analogy); and where the similarity between two things is either expressed or implied, that is *upamā* (simile). We shall explain this in detail further on.
Furthermore, this is merely an illustration: namely, that in the case of *upamā* alone, a discrepancy in gender or number is not a defect.
Since it is common to all ornaments, under the view that similarity alone constitutes an ornament, this is cited as an example of *upamā* (simile): "Prājya... [The verse continues:

May Nemi—the specific Jina named Nemi among the Ārhata [Jainas], whose power consisting of spiritual perfection (*siddhi*) is such that it is abundant (*prājya*) and appropriate—grant auspiciousness (*śiva*). Other Jinas include Ṛṣabhanātha and others. May such a Nemi grant auspiciousness.
Following the root *dada* in the sense of "giving," when there is an expectation as to "to whom," then in our view, regarding the liberated soul (*muktātmā*),
[the phrase] means "may he grant (*dadatām*) welfare (*śivam*) to you (*vaḥ*), i.e., to you all (*yuṣmabhyam*)."
The rim (*nemi*) is the source, the cause of the arising, and the power (*prabhava*) of the Dharma; it is the Jinas who, through their teaching exactly as it is,
have cast away passion and darkness (*rajas-tamasī*), and thus the rim is of such a nature.

Those by whom passion (*rajas*) has been destroyed are "destroyed-passion" (*asta-rajas*); among them, those who are preeminent even in that state are "destroyed-passion-and-darkness" (*asta-raja-stama*).

One whose self (*ātman*) is liberated—that is, free from obscuration—is a "liberated-self" (*mukta-ātman*); the word *ātman* here denotes either the self or one's own nature (*svarūpa*), thus forming a *bahuvrīhi* compound. Such is the "rim" (*nemi*);
it is clear that the Jinas are indeed those with liberated selves.

In this case, since there is no pun (*vacanaśleṣa*) without a difference in grammatical number, a discrepancy in number is necessarily a defect; however, through its integration with the figure of speech known as *śleṣa*, it becomes a merit. Now, it may be objected: "The difference in gender and so forth has been stated to be a flaw in the case of a simile (*upamā*), yet here it is cited as an example of a different figure of speech; how, then, can there be consistency between what precedes and what follows?"

Nor is a simile possible here, because the necessary conditions for it are absent; for it is said that the words expressing the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), the object of comparison (*upameya*), and their common property (*sādhāraṇadharma*) are the constituent parts of a simile.

Having raised the objection—"In this case, since the words *iva*, *vat*, *vā*, and so forth, which connect these three elements, are not employed, how can there be a simile?"—the author refutes it with the words "nor is [a simile] possible."
For words such as *iva* and others are indicators of similarity;

thus, from them, there arises the cognition of a connection in the present context with something well-known elsewhere, by resorting to the analogy of the original object (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*).
And in this way, there is no simultaneous connection with an identical form.
The word *api*, however, conveys a simultaneous relation of identical form [between two things], and thus there is a difference in their objective domains (*viṣaya*).

For it is not the case that similarity is not perceived in the absence of words such as *iva*; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of destroying the entire range of "elliptical similes" (*luptopamā*), since the cognition [of similarity] would be established through other means alone, rendering further devices redundant.

The question remains: why were words such as "nemi" not employed here? To this, the answer is as follows: in the phrase "of the word *iva*" and so forth, the particle *api* in "others also" indicates a conjunction (*samuccaya*), and that conjunction is established only when there is a simultaneous expression of a single relationship.

Therefore, the domain of a word expressing a conjunction (*samuccaya*) is the mention of some single attribute with reference to multiple subjects; however, the domain of words such as *yathā* and *iva* is the prescription of a well-known attribute of another [subject] with reference to one [subject]. Because their domains are mutually exclusive, they are not employed together. This might be argued: "Since the status of being a standard of comparison (*upamāna*) is perceived for that which follows words like *iva*, *vat*, or *yathā*, and since [the comparison] takes the form of a prescription of a common attribute (e.g., 'this is equal to that'), how can it be a simile? To this it is said: "But of those possessing common attributes... [and so forth].

In this case, there is no occurrence of a similarity of attributes based on a pun (*vacanaśleṣa*); rather, because "the dependence upon words" applies only to those things established in such a manner—as in the puns of double meaning found in phrases like "the source of dharma"—if the cognition of a simile were not possible without particles such as *iva*, then the standard examples of well-known similes would be undermined. Therefore, he says "as follows" (*yathā*) [in the fourth chapter].

Here, he anticipates the view of one who does not accept the simile: "Now," [he says]. The intention of the objector here is that, because of the two *ca*s, the simultaneous imposition of a single attribute upon both the sprout and the lip is equal [in both cases]. He refutes this with the aforementioned reasoning: "It is said."
"In that case, there is no simile at all in the example under discussion; how then can the subordination of the difference in number be cited as an instance? To this he replies:
"In which," meaning that even though the expressed similarity does not exist, the sense is that it should nevertheless be treated as an implied simile (*pratīyamānopamā*).
He has disregarded the mere verbal identity as being merely a mixture of *śleṣa* (paronomasia).

Now, one might object: "In cases where a work is designated as poetry by virtue of its simile (*upamā*), even an implied similarity (*sādṛśya*) is accepted; however, in cases where poetry is established solely through the nature of other figures of speech (*alaṃkāra*), that is not the case. To this he replies: the term "indication" (*upalakṣaṇa*) refers to the disparity in cognition, which is common to other figures of speech as well; therefore, a discrepancy in gender or number is indeed a defect even in instances other than simile.
For example, in a metaphor (*rūpaka*) such as "the face is a lotus," in a doubt such as "is it the face or a lotus? and in a denial (*apahnava*) such as "it is not the face, but indeed a lotus"—
and similarly in other cases— the term "simile" (*upamā*) is not included in the definition of that which possesses two different genders or numbers.
If this is so, why is the refutation illustrated specifically regarding the simile (*upamā*)? To this he says: "Only" (*kevalam*).
For the ancient masters, such as the sage Bharata and others, accepted only two figures of speech—*yamaka* (paronomasia) and *upamā*—as being based on the adherence of words.

However, other authors of treatises on poetics have merely elaborated upon these; yet, because the simile possesses a vast range of application and is preeminent, its illustration is made most clear [in this context]. This is the summary.

When the attributes of the standard of comparison (upamāna) are not equal to those of the object of comparison (upameya), it is called "deficient comparison" (hīnopama); however, this is not considered a fault when such a deficiency is well-known [in common usage].
For example:

‘The hero of the Yadus, his yellow garments trembling in the wind, gracefully bearing a lotus that shone like the moon and holding his Śārṅga bow, shone like a cloud accompanied by Indra’s bow (the rainbow).
Here, because only the bow is mentioned in the phrase “accompanied by Indra’s bow,” while the garment and the conch are omitted, it is an instance of *ūnopamā* (deficient simile).
In this regard, because the moon and lightning are so well known, there is no fault;
as it has been said:
"No entity whatsoever possesses complete similarity with everything else."
“Just as the wise employ comparison according to their ingenuity:
‘Where is the moon with its unbroken orb, and where is the face of this beloved with its present radiance?’—
yet, due to some slight similarity in luster, it is compared to the moon.”

In the verse beginning with "yatropamāna," where the objects of comparison (*upameya*) and their qualifiers are equal in number— there being one rainbow (*indrāyudha*) as the object of comparison and three qualifiers as the objects compared, namely "yellow garment," "Śārṅga bow," and "conch"— this constitutes a case of an excess of qualifiers. Consequently, at the very moment of inquiry, the cognition of the two objects of comparison— the moon and the lotus, which are not commonly known [in this context]— is observed to be on the verge of faltering due to the mental association with clouds.
And because it emerges through the operation of resonance (*dhvani*), it attains the status of a poetic quality (*guṇa*).
As it has been said: "In the words of great poets, even when they bear ornaments, this shadow of the suggested meaning (*pratīyamānacchāyā*) is their true decoration, just as modesty is for women."

It should not be argued that this is not the case for thunder and so forth; for even though they are perceived, there is no regard for them because they do not require a location as a means for resolving the discrepancy in their cognition. Thus he says: "Everything by everything."

The meaning is as follows: up to the limit of what arises [from the context], that is, as far as it is led to function as a reflection of the qualifier of the subject of comparison (*upameya*) by way of being a qualifier of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*); beyond that, even by means of a qualifier of the subject of comparison imagined in accordance with a single unified cognition. Otherwise, the comparison of "moon-face" and the like would not reach its conclusion; thus he says, "unbroken," etc.
Applying this very same method to a case where the object of comparison is excessive, he says:
By this sequence, the wise should recognize that which is superior to the simile;
however, the specific excellence of the object of comparison is understood through inference.
For example:
‘Clad in yellow garments and grasping his Śārṅga bow, Kṛṣṇa assumed a form that was both charming and formidable, like a cloud at night accompanied by lightning and Indra’s bow, joined with the moon.
(165) Here, although the moon is an excessive object of comparison due to its inclusion, it is considered subordinate because it is not intended to function as the standard of comparison (*upamāna*).
Alternatively, if one infers the attributes [of the object] through comparison—based on the well-known fact that "Viṣṇu bears the conch, discus, and mace"—the Śārṅga bow may be inferred in sequence.

Where there is an omission of additional qualifiers in the standard of comparison (upamāna), that sentence is called *adhikopama* (deficient comparison). In such a case, a fault arises because the reflection-like qualifiers of the object of comparison (*upameya*) are not immediately recalled.

But how is that very point stated here? It is said: "The distinction, however..."—because a specific qualifier of the object of comparison (*upameya*) is employed, it is understood from the qualifier of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) that [the lightning] is a flash of lightning (*śatahradā*).
"Because it is not intended [by the author] as a standard of comparison (upamāna)"—this is the superficial view.

To demonstrate that the qualifiers of the standard of comparison are not grasped beyond what is actually perceived, he states "or rather," indicating that this is the ultimate established doctrine (siddhānta):
the "unveiling" (uddhāṭana) is the mention of an additional property of the standard of comparison; the "subsequent measurement" (anu-māna) is the cognition following that.

To the question "How is this so?", he says: "Because of established usage"—when scholars say that through intense effort there is no heaviness resulting from [the presence of] a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*) and so forth, nor a violation of the meter (*chanda-bhaṅga*), then [such usage] is considered a fault. (123)
For example:
“Just as one who has entered to bathe has his upper garment and half of his beard washed away, so too have you bathed in the pure ford of the Godāvarī river. (166)
"Just as the edge of your garment became wet and fluttered when you descended to bathe, so too have you bathed at the clear bank of the Godāvarī river.

Here, although the second, eleventh, and twenty-third syllables are heavy because they are followed by consonant clusters (*saṃyoga*), there is no violation of the meter because the preceding syllables remain light due to the intense articulation (*tīvraprayatna*) of the clusters *ṇhā*, *lhā*, and so forth; thus, this is considered a merit (*guṇa*).

"Yadā" (when) refers to *prayatana*, which is effort (*prayatna*), namely the operation of the articulatory places (*sthāna*) and instruments (*karaṇa*); its intensity (*tīvratva*) is its excess (*udreka*). For it is precisely from that [intensity] that the lack of harshness in *piṇḍākṣara* and other such sounds appears. By the inclusion of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the letters *i*, *u*, and *ṛ*—along with their nasal counterparts (*anusvāra*) when standing at the end of a word—are to be understood as occurring within the scope of their respective languages.
For it manifests in that way only in certain phonemes, but not everywhere;
it is merely an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*), as shown in the *Chandoviciti* in such passages as "raha vaṃjaṇasaṃjoe" (i.e., "raha u vyañjanasaṃyoge").
Thus [the word] is "jahā."

When you have descended to bathe, half of your garment has slipped away; since it is soiled and moist, its movement is perceived just as its stillness is. The underlying intention is that you have not merely entered the water for a place of aquatic play, for otherwise how could the clear water of the Godāvarī river be seen? Thus, this is the bathing-place (tīrtha).

In this regard, although there is heaviness due to the preceding element of a conjunct consonant in positions such as the second and eleventh, nevertheless, by the power of the conjunction with letters such as *ś* and *h* which are to be articulated with intense effort, the clarity of the distinct hearing is not defiled;
thus other examples may also be cited,
such as:
‘The white night-lotuses, like nails, fall from the sky toward the white, dark-antimony-like necks.

In such cases, where there is no elision of vowels (*svarasaṃdhāna*) within the portion consisting of nouns and verbal roots, it has been stated that there should be no pause in recitation; yet this [rule] is resolved simply by transgressing it, as it enhances the aesthetic beauty (*śobhā*).

The sentence characterized by "cessation at an improper place" (asthānavirati), which was previously designated under the name *prāgbhagnayati*, is now considered to possess the quality [of being a fault].
For example: [Example follows]

‘This fresh awakening of beautiful women brings forth splendor; the glances of these passionate ladies are somewhat languid with emotion and yet straightforward. Beholding all duties and non-duties through the scriptures alone, this king bears the earth under his control. (167) In this verse, although there is a violation of the pause (*yati*)—since the pause which ought to occur at the fourth position is placed at the fifth, and elsewhere because of the presence of a solitary vowel in the middle of the line—it does not constitute a fault. This is because the violation is caused by the euphonic combination of vowels (*svarasaṃdhi*), and furthermore, the body of the name and the verbal root remains undivided.
As it is said:

For example:
