In this context, since similes are compounded with words expressing commonality (*sāmānyavacana*), even if the established method of composition is not fully sustained, the employment of the word *iva* or its corresponding secondary derivative (*taddhita*)—being intended solely for the purpose of explaining the compound—actually enhances the aesthetic effect (*chāyā*); thus, it constitutes a merit (*guṇa*). "Fatigue" (*kheda*) refers to the failure to carry through to the conclusion the subject (*dharmin*) of the sentence-meaning, which was introduced (*prakrama*) by means of a particular poetic figure (*alaṃkāra*).
However, there is no fault if the comprehension remains unimpeded once it has settled upon a previous ornament;
moreover, that [previous ornament] possesses the status of a poetic excellence (*guṇatva*) because it is suggested (*dhvanana*) through other modes within the primary ornament under discussion.

To explain: having introduced the simile with two compounds—“sweet like the anger of a new bride” (*abhinavavadhūroṣasvādu*) and “cruel like the embrace of a dishonest person” (*asaralajanāśleṣa iva*)—by joining [the objects] with words expressing common properties (*sāmānyavacana*), [the poet] then abandons the compound in the phrase “like the command of one whose wealth has faded” (*malinavibhavasyājñeva*). Furthermore, by superimposing an internal attribute through the phrase “she bears the feminine timidity of a woman separated from her lover” (*virahivanitāvaktraklaibyaṃ bibharti*), he abandons the simile. Thus, even though the *rīti* (literary style) cannot be fully sustained, the resolution lies in the fact that the finality rests upon the simile itself; this states the reason for its being a merit (*guṇatva*). This is expressed by the words: “by virtue of being intended for explanation” (*vyākhyāparatvena*).

When the compound *galitavibhāvājñāmasṛṇā* ought to have been formed, this employment of the word *iva* indicates that the two preceding compounds are to be understood in the sense of *iva*. In the general figure of speech (*sāmānyālaṅkāra*) expressed as "he bears weakness," there is a simultaneous reflection on how one thing can bear the attribute of another. When the internal simile (*antargatopamā*) becomes manifest through the phrase "his crookedness is [like] weakness" (*vakraklaibyam asya*), that simile is also perceived within the words of the comparative compound. Thus, this poetic ingenuity nourishes only the suggested shadow;
this is what has been stated by the words "on the contrary" (*pratyuta*).
That which appears as if transcending the world is considered "excessive" (atimātra) in this context;
by means of it, the discerning are satisfied in subjects such as *vārtā*, but other people are not.
And that [excessiveness] is found both in the narrations of *vārtā* and in poetic descriptions.
That which follows worldly meanings is considered beautiful in the world;
however, that departure which proceeds by transcending worldly meanings is called *atyukti* (hyperbole), for the delight of the Gauḍas' minds. (143–144)
For example:
"O Lord, from this day forward, our home shall be worthy of being honored by Your presence, its every stain washed away by the falling dust of Your feet. (184)

Even in this defect called *atimātra* (excessiveness), when it is mentioned as a subject of discussion (*vārtā*), it is considered a merit because the quality of *kānti* (loveliness) is thereby permitted; for example:
"The Creator fashioned the sky too small, without even considering..."
‘Such as this will be the swelling of your breasts.
Here, although there is exaggeration (*atimātratva*), it is considered a merit (*guṇa*) because it serves the purpose of poetic description.
Now, what is [the figure] that is not exaggerated (*anatimātra*)?
It is said:
first, regarding worldly affairs—as for example:
"Those very houses are indeed a mass of ascetic merit [only] when occupied by one such as you."
"Those very things which they honor with such purifying foot-dust.
Now, for example, in the context of description:
"O lady of faultless limbs, as these two breasts of yours expand..."
“There is no sufficient space within the expanse of your vine-like arms. Thus,
in this world beyond [the mundane],
in the absence of illness, one’s welfare and news are exchanged in pleasant conversation.

In the commentary on the words beginning with "varṇanāsv api," the connection is seen as "it is beautiful" (*kāntam*). That which follows worldly meaning—namely, that which is called "beautiful" in the world—is transcended by the poetic practice of poets; even such a practice is said to be for the delight of the minds of the Gauḍas.

The meaning of the verse is that for those who favor the Gauḍī style, which consists of verbal ostentation, the presence of true poetic qualities (*sadguṇa*) serves as a command for the wise regarding matters of love.
"Dhiṣṇya" means a house.

Now, one might ask: since such compositions of speech exist in both the world and in poetry through descriptions of pleasant conversation, there is no distinction between "excessive" (*atimātra*) and "not excessive" (*anatimātra*); thus he asks—"Now... (*atha*).

However, that which is exceedingly censurable— harsh, cruel in meaning, and contrary to proper characteristics— is not considered a fault when it occurs in such utterances as those characterized by irony (viruddhalakṣaṇā). || 145 ||
For example:
"O friend, consume the hālāhala poison; do not trust in that [ordinary fire], for it is my opinion that you will not be burned by even a small amount of wood. (188)
In this case, even though there is harshness (*pāruṣya*), it is considered a merit because another meaning is indicated through the function of contrary indication (*viruddhalakṣaṇā*).

The expression "harsh" (*paruṣam*) is a worldly instance of contrary indication; for, due to the immediate and inseparable connection with the denotation, the non-harsh meaning is understood from that very expression. Thus, the harshness is not a defect, and by virtue of its inclusion within the scope of indication (*lakṣaṇā*), it becomes a merit.
Regarding this, they say: "That which is called 'indication' (lakṣaṇā)— the cognition of an inseparable connection with the expressed meaning—
is held to be the 'burnt-mouthed' mode of life that constitutes the very vitality of poetry."

The wise declare that a subject matter lacking the intended sentiment is "tasteless" (virasa); however, the learned maintain that this should be accepted when neither the sentiment nor the subject matter is intended as the primary focus.
For example: [text follows]

"Thrust away when he clung to her hand, violently struck even as he seized the hem of her garment, cast off when grasping her hair, and ignored with agitation when falling at her feet—he who was brushed aside while embracing by the young women of Tripura, whose lotus-eyes were filled with tears; may that fire of Śambhu’s arrow, like a lover who has committed a fresh offense, burn away your sins.

(189) In this verse, although the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) is not the primary subject within the context of pathos (*karuṇa*), it possesses the status of a subordinate element (*guṇatva*) because neither of the two sentiments predominates, as both serve as constituent parts of the description of Śambhu’s power, thereby avoiding any sense of discord.

It should be understood that "being irrelevant" (*aprastuta*) and "being subordinate" (*aprādhānya*) are merely indicative characteristics (*upalakṣaṇa*), and thus "being sublated" (*bādhyatva*) must also be included. This applies either to two things that manifest mutually contradictory aesthetic moods (*rasa*),
or to two things that consist of mutually contradictory aesthetic moods themselves.

Regarding this, he says: "When things that are sublated, or those that have attained the status of subordinate members, are not [properly] released [from their functions], it is called *hīnopamā* (an inferior simile) where the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) is inferior and the object of comparison (*upameya*) possesses superior qualities; however, poets say that in some cases this is not considered a fault. (147)
For example:
"Then the eastern quarter was adorned by the moon, the lord of night-lotuses, pale as the cheek of a longing woman, and the delight of the eyes. (190)

In this case, even though there is inferiority of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), it possesses the status of a "quality" (*guṇa*) because it serves as a cause for an excess of passion. Regarding the term *hīna* ("inferior"): that which is inferior by way of both genus and magnitude is called *hīna*. When the inferiority of the beloved’s cheek in relation to the moon is established, it conveys the speaker's own equality [with her]; thus, by demonstrating the excellence of the excitant (*uddīpana*), it will impart intensity to the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) under discussion, and thereby possesses the status of a "quality."

Likewise, even in the case of "excessive comparison" (adhikaupamya), where the object of comparison is superior while the subject of comparison is inferior, that should be known as excessive comparison; yet in some instances, this too is not a defect. (148)
For example:
“O King, you emulate the moon in beauty, the sun in splendor, the ocean in fortitude, and even the god of love in good fortune. (191)
Even though this constitutes an exaggeration (*adhikopamā*), it is considered a merit because the king is honored by the learned as a partial incarnation of a World-Guardian (*lokapāla*).
"Due to the disparity of the standard of comparison, there may be the figure of speech known as *asadṛśopama* (the dissimilar simile)."
In cases such as the *vyatirekopamā* (simile of contrast) and others, they require his permission.
For example:
"I have been sent by the King to summon Mādhava to the field of battle."
"Those of great power do not harm others through deception, like thieves.
Although this simile is dissimilar, it is considered a merit because it serves to establish a *vyatireka* (contrast).
Thus, the excellence lies in the standard of comparison (*upamāna*).
By means of a comparison (*upamāna*), there is indeed a disparity because of the absence of similarity through positive concomitance (*anvaya*).
By the inclusion of the term "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "dissimilar comparison and so forth," the mention of dissimilar examples (*vyatireka-dṛṣṭānta*) and the like is intended.
That for which no comparison is well-known in the world is what is intended [here].
That which is called an "unestablished simile" (*aprasiddhopamā*) is not at all faulty in certain cases. For example:
"The mark on the moon resembles the impression left by the pressing of the high breasts of a pregnant Hūṇa woman, bent down by the weight of her womb. (150)
‘The image [of Viṣṇu’s foot] first reveals His station with its foremost toes, white as the pale and firm stalks of a lotus.

Although this is a defect due to the use of a well-known comparison (*prasiddhopamā*), it possesses the status of a merit because both [the subject and the object] share the common quality of being excitants (*uddīpanavibhāva*) of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*).
This refers to that which serves as the standard of comparison (*upamāna*).

That which is already well-known in the world becomes beautiful as a point of comparison for poets; therefore, when describing a simile with that which is famous in the world, even if it results in an unfamiliar comparison, its lack of renown is subordinated through its entry into aesthetic flavor (*rasa*). The dark spot at the tip of the breast is desired as an imitation of the moon's mark. "Free from ornament" (*niralaṅkāra*) refers to speech devoid of poetic figures.
Even in cases of wealth and power, his [the poet’s] work is sometimes considered faultless, as for example:

“The Ikṣvākus have not been taught a supplication that is associated with wretchedness and humiliation; nor has a folded hand ever been placed upon the crest of the Raghu lineage in a manner joined with servitude. (151)
"Everything was arranged by him accordingly, yet the ocean did not offer any obstruction; now he desires to forcibly seize my hand—what more than this? He even wishes to touch my bow.
(194) Here, although there is no ornament (*alaṃkāra*), it possesses the quality (*guṇa*) of "strength of meaning" (*arthaurjitya*);
thus it is "without ornament."

Because of the connection with such distinguished and abundant qualifiers as "fond of wretchedness and defeat" (*dainyaparābhavapraṇayinīm*), the word *asti* (is) is indistinct; yet, there is no lack of poetic curvature (*vakratā*) in its meaning, for curvature is indeed an ornament (*alaṃkāra*).
Although the sentence-meaning thus appears as if it were without ornament, nevertheless, even when one determines the specific ornament, curvature shines forth by way of generality.
For here, a reversal from the meaning of ordinary or technical (scriptural) speech is not perceived.
This has been stated [in the verse] as "due to the vigor of the meaning" (*arthaurjityāt*).
For when it is said, "We beg," or when it is said, "The begging of those who live on alms is not noticed," there is a specific excellence that manifests the preeminence of the hero; thus he says:
"That which is indecorous because of its vulgar meaning, or which expresses another meaning..."
In this context, its frequent usage is observed and it is not considered faulty—as for example:
“Even now I remember that face of hers, with cheeks rubbed by golden earrings, during the exertion of inverted union. || 152 ||

"In this verse, '...sprinkled with a multitude of pearl-like drops of perspiration clearly manifest from the sweat of exertion during the agitation of her beloved,' it is considered a merit because it is not censured by poets, even though it possesses a vulgar meaning; thus, it is [an example of] a vulgar sense."

In some cases, the very first connection between word-meanings is indecorous (*aślīla*), while in others it is not; even when such a [first] connection exists, there may be another connection [that renders it so]. This is why it was stated by the poets that "that which is indecorous expresses a different meaning," because it is not censured by them.

The meaning is that because the authors of the treatises have declared that love which is contrary to what is not contrary (i.e., natural) is the most excellent, and because poets have favored it as an enhancer (*uddīpana*) of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*);

[the factors are: place (*deśa*) such as mountains, forests, and kingdoms; time (*kāla*) such as night, day, and the seasons; and the arts (*kalā*) such as dance and song, which are based upon the objects of desire and wealth. || 153 ||
The activity of moving and non-moving beings is known as the world; logic consists of the science of causes, while tradition comprises the Smṛtis and the Śruti.
If anything whatsoever proceeds in those [traditions] in a manner that is not established according to reality, [it is invalid]. || 154 ||
It is said that due to a poet’s negligence, there may be a contradiction with place and so forth.
(155) However, through a poet’s skill, such a contradiction sometimes transcends the category of defects and enters the path of merits. (156)
In that regard, an example of the subordination of what is contrary to place (*deśaviruddha*) is as follows:
“By the power of that king, his gardens became the abode of celestial trees with fresh sprouts like moist garments. (196)
In this case, although there is a contradiction with local custom, it is considered a merit because the reason— "by the power of that king"— is adduced;
"country" refers to mountains and so forth, the word "and so forth" (ādi) including islands and other such places.
Those based on desire and wealth; activities based on wealth; specific states [of existence];
the science of causes (hetuvidyā); logic (ānvīkṣikī); that which is not as it is established (ayathārūḍha); and that which is not well-known (aprasiddha).
An example of what is contrary to time (*kālaviruddha*) is as follows:
“A harsh wind, foreboding the destruction of kings, blew, kissing the blossoms of the *saptacchada* trees along with the *kadamba* flowers. (197)

In this case, although there is a contradiction with time, the phrase "foreboding the destruction of kings" constitutes a merit because it takes the form of an ill-omened portent (*utpāta*) indicating an undesirable event; thus,
an *utpāta* is a calamity that contradicts the [proper] time.
An example of what is contrary to worldly experience is as follows:
“A lover, overwhelmed by the agony of separation from his beloved, considers the fire—the very bearer of oblations—to be intensely cool compared to the radiance of the moon. (198)
In this case, although it contradicts worldly convention, it is considered a poetic excellence (*guṇa*) because it is perceived as such by those who are impassioned.
An example of what is contrary to logic is as follows:

"That contraction [of the world] is like that of a cluster of night-lotuses from the moon; that helplessness of the *kokila* birds is like their separation from the sun, wherein all remedy has vanished."
"That these wicked people feel such agitation toward your virtues, which only serve to allay distress, is like death resulting from nectar itself.

Here, although this is contrary to reason, it is considered a merit because of the perception [of the comparison] through the power of *chekokti* (witty speech) and the suggested simile (*saṃbhāvyamānopamā*).
This is *saṃkoca* (contraction).

If the closing of night-lotuses and the like were caused by the moon and so forth, then the agitation of the wicked toward your virtues could be compared to it; however, such a thing is not possible. Therefore, because it is extraordinary and bestows wonder, this presentation is indeed a merit (*guṇa*) due to the enrichment of the sentence-meaning. An example of what is contrary to propriety (*aucitya*) is as follows: "Then, O Lord, by that heat which is difficult to endure, even she who is gentle by name has attained a state of harshness."
Sītā blazed forth, suddenly vomiting sharp and clear rays of speech, like a sun-crystal stone.
(200) Here, although there is a contradiction with propriety due to her being a woman, it is considered a merit because it is appropriate for that specific occasion.
An example of what is contrary to common usage is as follows:
"How can my longing for another's wife be appropriate for a noble man?
When indeed shall I drink from her trembling lower lip? (201).
Here, although there is a contradiction in the words, it is considered a merit because of the speaker’s particular state of being.
Regarding "of that which is contradictory to speech," this refers to the eighth stage of passion;
as for the contradiction with dharma, it is as follows:
"The daughter of the Pañcāla king was the wife of the five sons of Pāṇḍu and the foremost among virtuous women; for such is the decree of fate.
Here, although there is a contradiction with dharma (righteousness), it is not considered a fault because it is stated that "it is the decree of fate."
From the contradiction with dharma, from the saying "for it is ordained by fate," and from the prediction of the Siddhas, the chastity of the princess of Pañcāla is established.
Or rather, the scripture states that it is intended to be fivefold precisely because it is "disregarded.
An example of that which contradicts the *Arthaśāstra* is as follows:
"That one should resort to another in times of distress is a matter of policy; for a proud man, however, it is a source of shame."
"He is like the moon to Rāhu; when full, he is for his festival.

(203) Here, the political maxim (*nīti*) is that an enemy who has fallen into distress should be attacked; however, since this causes shame to a proud man, it is contradictory. Nevertheless, because it is spoken by an arrogant person, it is not considered a fault, and thus it functions as a poetic excellence (*guṇa*) within the science of polity (*arthaśāstra*).
"Because it was spoken by an arrogant man" means that, as a prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), it serves as an introduction to the final conclusion (*siddhānta*).
An example of what is contrary to the *kāmaśāstra* is as follows:
"The song, emerging from the mouths of the womenfolk who were terrified by the excessive swinging of the swing,
increased the passion of the lovers due to its discordance with the rhythmic tempo (*laya*).

(204) Here, although the song is a cause of passion because of the discordance of the tempo arising from their fear, it possesses the quality (*guṇa*) of intensifying passion precisely because it is sung forth from the mouths of the amorous women.

Regarding the objection that the *kāmaśāstra* (treatise on love) is flawed because it describes musical modes (*kalā*) with irregular tempos (*laya*), and since such irregular tempo is unpleasing, how can it increase passion (*rāga*)—this criticism is neutralized by the marvelousness of describing the power of a song sung by a trembling woman on a swing; thus, it is elevated to the status of a poetic excellence (*guṇa*).
Furthermore, love existing in the intervals between emotional states is itself the "tempo" (*laya*).
Thus, the merits, the defects, and those qualities of defect which have been described in poetry have now been clearly explained; we shall now proceed to discuss the ornaments (alaṃkāras).
[Objection: But if word and meaning are already rendered magnificent by the merits alone, what is the use of this effort to analyze the ornaments? To this, he says:

O friend, poetry, like the beauty of a young woman, is delicious when its qualities are pure; yet it becomes exceedingly so when love is bestowed upon it through the continuous employment of various ornaments and poetic fancies. (158) "Like a young woman," etc.
The word *aṅga* is used here for the purpose of an address or exhortation;
it conveys the connection of the intellect with the literature of poetics (*alaṃkārasāhitya*), as well as affection (*praṇaya*).

As for the alternative view (*vikalpa*) that these are specific distinctions, one might ask: "In that case, let the poetic excellences (*guṇas*) be abandoned according to the maxim that 'what is established by the latter need not be [repeated] by the former'? To this, he replies:

If speech should fall away from its virtues, just as the body of a woman loses its youthful charm, even ornaments that are beloved by people will inevitably come to possess a state of misfortune. 159.
"If it should happen," etc.
This has been explained:

he instructs poets that these ornaments, when applied in their proper places, are alone capable of delighting the connoisseur— The beauty of collyrium adorns the pair of eyes with their long outer corners; the pearl necklace is able to grace the high and expansive breasts.
On her slender waist, the beauty of the *sthānaka* (upper garment) is attained; on her heavy hips, the girdle-strap bears its splendor.

(160) The intended meaning is that the classification of ornaments according to the divisions of objects such as sound and so forth is indeed purposeful by virtue of [the distinction between] "long" (*dīrgha*) and so on.
The remainder is not obscure.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Analysis of Guṇas," in the *Ratnadarpaṇa*, a commentary on the *Sarasvatīkaṇṭhābharaṇa* composed by Śrī Miśra Ratneśvara.
This concludes the first chapter, titled "The Analysis of Guṇas," in the treatise on poetics (*alaṃkāraśāstra*) named *Sarasvatīkaṇṭhābharaṇa*, composed by the illustrious Mahārājādhirāja Bhojadeva.
Homage to that granter of desires, who is established in Avimukta, whose beloved Viśālākṣī dwells in the center of his field, the second chapter.
May the Goddess of Speech’s first playful ornament for her throat manifest within me, whose mental disposition is humble as I present this jeweled mirror.

Thus, once faults and merits have been determined, the figures of speech (alaṃkāras) find their proper occasion; therein, having shown the general definition of figures of speech in the first chapter, he connects the three chapters by demonstrating their classification.
The lords of poets instruct upon ornaments— those pertaining to words, those pertaining to meaning, and those pertaining to both— by means of designations for words, meanings, and both.
(1) "By means of designations for words, meanings, and both" means:
The third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used here in the sense of a characteristic mark (*itthaṃbhūtalakṣaṇa*),
and it is a compound with the middle term elided (*madhyamapadalopīsamāsa*);
thus, the meaning is "by means of the designations 'verbal ornament' (*śabdālaṃkāra*), 'semantic ornament' (*arthālaṃkāra*), and 'both-type ornament' (*ubhayālaṃkāra*)."

In the discussion on *guṇas*, externality (*bāhyatva*) and so forth have been explained. Sound (*śabda*), by virtue of being a delimiting factor and because it is the first to be perceived, stands in the place of the body; therefore, the figures of speech (*alaṃkāras*) based upon it are also external. Meaning (*artha*), however, is like the soul (*ātman*) because it is what is delimited and because it is perceived subsequently; therefore, the figures of speech based upon it are also internal. By this, the external and internal [figures] are explained.
The relationship between the substratum and the superstratum has been explained exactly as it is;

the instruction of the masters of poetry has been stated on the basis that the application [of these principles] is generally prevalent among both types of ornaments. This will be analyzed at the beginning of the fourth chapter.
He states the general definition of verbal figures (śabdālaṃkāra):

"Those [figures] such as *jāti* and the rest, which are capable of embellishing words here through etymological derivation and so forth, should be known by the wise under the designation 'verbal figures'. (2)
"Those who [possess] vyutpatti"—*vyutpatti* is distinguished *utpatti* (origination); it is the manifold expansion consisting of elision, augmentation, modification, and so forth.
For this very reason, the classes such as *saṃskṛta* (Sanskrit) and others are established.
By the inclusion of the word "etc. (*ādi*), twenty-three factors such as the arrangement of heavy and light syllables and the delimitations of *gati* (movement) and so forth are included.
He states that this designation is applied because of its similarity to external bracelets and the like: "The designations of verbal ornaments (*śabdālaṃkāra*) are:
*jāti*, *gati*, *rīti*, *vṛtti*, *chāyā*, *mudrā*, *ukti*, and *yukti*."
Bhaṇiti, gumphanā, śayyā, paṭhiti, and yamakas; 3.
śleṣa, anuprāsa, citras, vākovākya, prahelikā, gūḍhapraśna, uttara, adhyeya, śravya, prekṣya, and abhinīti. 4.
And these will be explained individually—the twenty-four types of verbal ornamentation (śabdālaṃkāra) have been mentioned; now their definitions, together with examples, are correctly stated. || 5 ||
Regarding the various types of verbal ornaments (*śabdālaṃkāra*),
it is improper to seek out different forms while they remain in their own essential nature;
therefore, because the genus (*jāti*) is primary, he states the definition first:
In this context, the term "saṃskṛta" and so forth is intended as a class of speech; however, that [class] serves as an ornament for words through propriety and other such qualities.
Regarding the word "tatra":
The term *saṃskṛtam* is an expression where the abstract quality (*bhāva*) is the primary referent;
the inclusion of the word *bhāratī* (speech) is for the sake of clarity.
[An objection: Surely, speech must necessarily be one or another of the refined languages (*saṃskṛta*) and so forth?

In this regard, one might ask: what portion of a poet’s power (*śakti*) and proficiency (*vyutpatti*) is present here such that it could constitute an ornament (*alaṃkāra*)? To this he says: "That [ornament] is precisely that which is drawn forth by propriety (*aucitya*); and the fact that even [the use of] refined language (*saṃskṛta*) and so forth possesses such a character is the intended meaning."
Although propriety regarding the subject matter was appropriate to demonstrate first, nevertheless, in order to indicate its preeminence, he speaks separately of propriety itself:
"Some say [the drama] should be in Sanskrit alone, some in Prakrit alone; some because of its universality and other qualities, and some in the language of the Mlecchas. (7)
He states the propriety regarding the subject matter:

"One should not speak like a barbarian at sacrifices and the like; one should not speak non-classical [Sanskrit] to women; one should not speak mixed [language] to those of noble birth; and one should not speak Sanskrit to the unenlightened. (8)
"One should not speak barbarously," and so forth;
"barbarous speech" refers to ungrammatical words, whether in the vernacular (Prākṛta) or derived from Sanskrit.
"Noble-born" means of pure lineage.
Now, who are those fit to speak in Saṃskṛta and the other languages? To this he says:
"The gods and others speak Saṃskṛta; the Kinnaras and others speak Prākṛta."
The Piśācas and others [should recite] the Paiśāca [language], while those of low birth, such as the Māgadhas, [should recite] the Māgadhī.
By the use of the word "and others" (*ādi*) in the phrase "the gods and others," sages, kings, and so forth are included.
He demonstrates the propriety of expression: "A certain meaning can be composed in Sanskrit alone, another in Prākṛt alone, and yet another arises through Apabhraṃśa. (10)
"By the refined language alone" means as follows:

for instance, in the praise of deities and the like, the refined language (*saṃskṛta*) excels, whereas the vernacular (*prākṛta*) and others do not; and just as in the precise delineation of the nature of subtle objects, the vernacular possesses excellence, whereas the refined language and others do not, and so forth.
One [work] is composed in Paiśācī, another in Śaurasenī, another in Māgadhī;
some are written in two or three languages, while others are composed in all of them as well.
(11) Regarding the term "Paiśācī":
With two or three [verses], someone [expresses] the meaning of a particular poetic riddle (kāvya-samasyā); with all [of them], someone [expresses] the meaning of a section or the like;
and in certain specific cases, he says that it is precisely the fitness of the subject matter that bestows excellence upon the beauty [of the composition].
One who narrates a story in social gatherings using neither exclusively Sanskrit nor exclusively the vernacular language will be highly esteemed in the world.
(12) "Neither exclusively," it is said.
A social gathering (*goṣṭhī*) is a sitting arrangement for the purpose of diversion among those of equal intellect, character, and age;
it speaks of the propriety of place:
"The Lāṭas listen to the charming [speech], while those hostile to Sanskrit listen to Prakrit."
The Gurjaras are satisfied with their own Apabhraṃśa and not with any other;
they listen to it as charming and delightful.
O Brahmin, I, a member of the Gurjara caste, address you with the desire to relinquish my own office:
let the Gauḍa abandon his song, or let Sarasvatī be something else entirely. (14)

By means of the restatement of a censurable meaning in the passage beginning with "O Brahmin, O Brahmin," Rājaśekhara reveals the natural impropriety among the Gauḍas and demonstrates the propriety of social convention.
Who were the speakers of Prakrit in the kingdom of King Āḍhyarāja?
And who were not speakers of Saṃskṛta in the time of the illustrious Sāhasāṅka?
"Who were they? [is the question].
Āḍhyarāja Śālivāhana,
Sāhasāṅka Vikramāditya,
and [the author himself] are designated with the honorific "Śrī" because they were born before the author.
Thus, these six languages—Sanskrit and the others—are mutually intermingled; he concludes this general classification and the purpose of its composition as follows:

"Divine speech that is worthy of being heard, Prakrit which is naturally sweet, the highly graceful Apabhraṃśa, the vividly composed Bhūtabhāṣā (Piśāca), and the eloquent diction of those dwelling in Magadha and Mathurā—which are desired by the connoisseurs—he who has composed [works] in these [languages], that king of poets is victorious here. (16)
*Gira* refers to the divine *saṃskṛta* languages;
*bhūtavacana* refers to the *paiśāca* language.
The speech of those inhabitants of Mathurā is Śaurasenī;

that is a statement of fact, and it is an Apabhraṃśa, as are the [other varieties] such as Divya and so forth; thus, there is a *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) according to the rule "the neuter [remains] when combined with a non-neuter."

The plural number is used optionally, for a poet is indeed one who is skilled in describing living beings according to their individual characteristics; he alone is a king among poets, endowed with the mastery of such expressions that traverse every path. Therefore, he triumphs—that is, he exists with preeminence over all creators of worldly and scriptural discourse.

Thus, he states that *jāti* (genus) is divided into six types, according to its purity and other distinctions as appropriate in Sanskrit and other languages: [He states: "In this way, *jāti* is divided into six types through the distinctions of purity (*śuddha*) and so forth, as applicable in Sanskrit and other languages."
The masters declare that *jāti* is sixfold: pure (*śuddhā*), common (*sādhāraṇī*), mixed (*miśrā*), confused (*saṃkīrṇā*), non-transferable (*nānyagāminī*), and corrupt (*apabhraṣṭā*).
(17) "Pure" and "common" [are explained as follows].

In this context, grammatical refinements (*saṃskāra*) are differentiated according to the distinctions among languages, dialects, and subject matters; it is with reference to these that the instructions of Pāṇini, Vararuci, and others are established.
However, where only a single refinement is recognized through recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), that is considered "pure" (*śuddhā*), because no other refinement is perceived.

But where there is a convergence of various conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) through a blending of characteristics—like milk and water—that is "common" due to the commonality of form; it consists of two parts established as distinct languages like Narasiṃha;
it is "mixed" due to the mixing of forms; and it is "intermingled" according to the analogy of sesame and rice.
In the world, it is precisely through the exclusion of other heterogeneous entities that linguistic usage avoids confusion;
however, that which does not tolerate contact with another language even in its original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) is "non-deviant" (*ananyagāminī*).

Because it does not go elsewhere—whether by being mixed with grammatical refinement (*saṃskāra*) or by remaining in its original form—it is corrupted (*apabhraṣṭā*) insofar as it takes the form of an ungrammatical word (*apaśabda*).
Among these, the pure *saṃskṛta-jāti* (Sanskrit style) to be employed by the highest class of characters is as follows:
“Her face, with one creeper-like eyebrow raised as she takes her steps, proclaims her passion for me through her cheek, which is covered in horripilation. (1)
Among those, the characteristics of a worthy recipient (*pātra*) and the classification into superior and so forth will be explained in the fifth chapter,
beginning with the verse "unnamitaika" (with one raised).
The words were suited to the *anaṅgalekha* (letter of love) and filled with sincere affection;

for this very reason, as her mind was immersed in the process of composing and deleting [the words], there appeared, in the form of an emotional manifestation (*anubhāva*), a movement of her creeper-like eyebrows as if they were dancing.

With one cheek resting upon the palm of her hand, the sight of that single cheek bristling with horripilation revealed that the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*)—consisting of excessive pride (*māna*)—had awakened, as it were, at that moment for the hero as well. Thus, Love itself, having ascended to the stage of "new passion" (*apūrvānurāga*) characterized by mutual attachment, becomes the very essence of the poem.
And here, although some words may be common to other languages, the status of being an illustration applies to the majority; likewise elsewhere,
the *śuddha* (pure) variety of the *Prākṛta-jāti* employed by characters of middle rank is as follows:
‘I do not know your heart, but for me, O pitiless one, love torments intensely day and night,
as my limbs are filled with longing for you.
(2) I do not know your heart, but for me, love [torments] by day and by night.
O merciless one, as you burn intensely, my limbs—though their desires were fixed upon you—are now turned away.
[The word *tujjha* means "towards you";
*valiam* means "forcibly" or "powerfully. They have been forcibly turned away.

An example of Magadhi used by an inferior character is as follows: “O Māṇava Maṃśabhālaka, having taken a jar full of water, I shall constantly drink blood; and with a hundred offerings of flesh, the sacrifice shall be performed. (3)
"A hundred loads of human flesh, a thousand jars filled with fat, and blood I shall drink incessantly for a hundred years; there will be a battle.
[Śada māṇuśeti]
"A hundred loads of human flesh, a thousand jars filled with fat,
and blood I drink incessantly for a hundred years— a battle shall take place.
Here, the longing for battle, driven by the desire to obtain meat and other things, reveals a sense of revulsion and confirms his status as a base vessel.
The Paiśācī language, when used by characters of no very high status, is pure (*śuddhā*),

as for example: “Bow down to the fierce eleven-fold host of Rudra, whose reflection clings to the tips of the moving cowries trembling from the agitation caused by the bowstring across his ten fingernails.”
Bow down to Rudra, who bears eleven bodies, his reflection clinging to the tips of the feet of Gaurī when she is provoked by love, appearing within the ten mirrors of his fingernails.
[The phrase] "not too high" refers to...

Bow down to Rudra, who bears eleven bodies, whose reflection is fixed upon the tips of Gaurī’s feet when she is provoked by love, appearing as neither superior to the highest nor inferior to the middle, yet not exceeding the most excellent, within the ten mirrors of his fingernails.

Thus, in the *Devīkośa*, the Blessed One’s timidity in the face of affection is such that it appears as if he were bowing with all his forms simultaneously; this is an instance of *pratīyamānotprekṣā* (suggested poetic fancy) employed by a character of neither middling nor superior status, using pure *Śaurasenī*, as follows:
"Thou art the mango sprout given by me to Kāma, who has taken up his bow."
"O mango sprout, you have been given by me to Kāma who has taken up his bow; become his fifth arrow, capable of deluding the minds of young women. || 5 ||
"Not too middle" means that from the inferior it is superior, and from the middle it is not inferior;
thus, "not too middle. But why is it so? Because it is excellent.
The meaning is "for the sake of desire";

the genitive case [in *kāmasya*] is used because of the rule: "In the case of the fourth case [dative], when there is a desire to express a general relationship, the sixth case [genitive] may be employed."
Apabhraṃśa that is not employed for an excessively inferior recipient is pure, as for example: “O Vappula, drink the milk! Where could we have buttermilk?
If there were buttermilk even at birth, my hand would have been like that of a god. (6)
"Take it out of compassion and drink the milk; where could we have buttermilk?
If there were ever curds, it was only at the birth of our son.
This is merely a common saying.
Therefore, due to the poet's intention, capacity, and other factors, all [of these] may be employed in every case;
yet, among them, these six alone are pure and not significantly inferior.
Slightly superior to the inferior, not inferior to the mediocre, and not excessively low—
take it, O Vappulā; take it!
"Vappula!"—this is an address of compassion;
"drink the milk.
From where would we have buttermilk, which is designated by the word *chāsi*?

"By my son's life" is an oath; "I swear by my son's head that even at birth, curd was the pervader of the buttermilk"—this is indeed an application of the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*).

Now, since one observes in common usage (*prākṛta*) and other works the mixing of superior and inferior vessels, how is this rule consistent? To this he says: "It is general" (*prāyika*), meaning that where the poet proceeds otherwise by intending a specific purpose suited to the development of the plot (*prakṛti-nirvahaṇa*).

For example, in the *Mālatīmādhava*, there is the passage relying on Sanskrit: "O, here I am; by the force of my purpose and the requirements of the performance, I have become a speaker of the Prakrit language," and so forth;

or where a deviation from linguistic norms caused by the poet’s creative ingenuity is set aside by his power, such as the use of Sanskrit by the *viṭa* (the parasite), even though he is a character of middle status, in the *Mṛcchakaṭika*.

Or, where the linguistic registers such as *saṃskṛta* and others are reversed under the influence of what is appropriate for the specific composition—for instance, in works like the *sarga-bandha*, even for characters of middling status and below, only *saṃskṛta* is used; in works like the *khaṇḍakathā* or *parakathā*, even for characters of the highest status and above, only *prākṛta* is used; in the *bṛhatkathā* and similar works, only Paiśācī is used; and in works based on historical facts (*vastu-bandha*), only Apabhraṃśa is used—in those cases, the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) flourishes through the excellence of the junctures (*sandhi*), the constituent parts of the junctures (*sandhyaṅga*), and the structural arrangement (*ghaṭanā*). This is the path clearly illuminated by the sage Bharata and others;
furthermore, the principles such as universality (*sādhāraṇya*) and so forth are infinite.
Among those, the speech used by a superior character situated at the level of a middling character, which is common to both Sanskrit and Prākṛit, is as follows:
“O simple one, O lady with thighs like plantain stalks, abandon this rash passion; cast off your agitation.
Your heart is not able for me to endure the bitter exhaustion of separation. (7)
Regarding "common" (*sādhāraṇī*):

when Sanskrit is common with Prākṛta and the others, there are five types; when Prākṛta is common with Śaurasenī and the others, there are four; when Śaurasenī is common with Paiśācī and the others, there are three; when Paiśācī is common with Māgadhī and the others, there are two; and when Māgadhī is common with Apabhraṃśa, there is one. Thus, in the case of combinations of two, there are fifteen subdivisions; in combinations of three, twenty; in combinations of four, fifteen; in combinations of five, six; and in combinations of six, one. Summing all these together, the common type consists of fifty-seven varieties.

In this way, even in the case of mixed [languages] and so forth, there are many varieties according to the sequence of examples such as clods of earth; however, since providing all these examples would result in excessive bulk for the text, he illustrates only a mere direction: "In those [languages]," meaning that when there is a mixture of the natures of the speakers in the employment of a language, their linguistic impressions (*saṃskāra*) become intermingled; yet, this mixture of natures is not real, because it would entail the undesirable consequence of a confusion of essential natures (*svabhāva*).
Therefore it is said: "situated in the role of a middle-ranking character. *Bhūmikā* means costume;

it refers to the enactment of passion and so forth appropriate to the nature of a middle-ranking character. One who abides therein—by assuming that role—enters the path of a cognition distinct from the audience's correct, false, doubtful, or similar perceptions regarding three or four cows. Thus, he is "situated in the role of a middle-ranking character. And this is an illustrative indication (*upalakṣaṇa*).

Even though she is situated on the highest plane and employs a middling effort, it is precisely this [state]; thus, the construction is: "My heart is unable to endure the distress of separation from you in the future."
The *sādhāraṇī* (common) form of *saṃskṛta-paiśācī*, employed by a superior character residing on a not-very-high plane, is as follows:
“Then she of the delicate and lovely luster of a campaka bud, who kindles the god of love, whose gait is like that of a lordly elephant, and whose large eyes are tremulous, desires to speak. (8)
In this way, [the rules] should be understood as being common to both Sanskrit and its apabhraṃśas, as well as common to other languages such as Prākṛta;
"not too excellent" (nātyuttamā) refers to this Anaṅgī belonging to Anaṅga.
An example of the mixed type (*miśrā*), which is employed due to the appropriateness of the speaker, the subject matter, and so forth, is as follows:
“Victorious is Giriśa, the wish-granting tree that bestows the fruits desired by the people; and victorious is the daughter of the mountain, the sole petal of his ear-ornament. (9)
"And victorious is the daughter of the mountain, who embraces the Tamāla tree and is a wish-fulfilling creeper for her lover.
In this way, the intermingling of different languages should also be observed according to the speaker and the subject matter.

When a single poetic riddle (*samasyā*) is composed by various speakers regarding subjects such as the "excellent" (*uttama*) and so forth; or when a single poem is commenced concerning a subject to be described in different languages; or when, for the purpose of demonstrating his power, a poet himself begins a poem consisting of various languages—at such times, how could it not occupy the rank of an *alaṃkāra*? Therefore, he says: "mixed," meaning that which is mingling or merging.
An example of *saṃkīrṇā* (mixed) [speech], employed by characters such as the *durvidagdha* (the ill-bred):
“The moonlight is not yet bright; the cuckoo indeed sings sweetly; the southern wind blows repeatedly, O friend, and the red *aśoka* tree is in bloom.
Is it not for your heart’s delight? Not at all! Not at all! Today, because of my pride, I shall not go to meet my beloved. (10)
This very mixture of Saṃskṛta, Mahārāṣṭrī, and Apabhraṃśa is a hybrid (jāti) variety, like sesame seeds mixed with rice;
in this same way, the mixture of Prākṛta and Apabhraṃśa is also to be understood, as in the case of the *durvidagdha* and other such forms.
Having attained the status of a refined gentleman (*nāgaraka*), yet relying on that very ground, the witless man—
beginning with the aforementioned riddles and so forth—
is truly a source of wonder.

The *gumaṭī* is charming, like the flickering sparks of a brandished sword; this is the usage in the Mahārāṣṭra region, as seen in the application of the venerable [poets]: "lavai a vijjūmaṇoharī" (and it is as charming as lightning).
Others, however, say that the meaning is "speaking"; and thus, because the word *kala* flourishes (*puṣyati*),
the southern direction belongs to Yama.
The term *idāvāraka* refers to a rain-covering that is either deceptive or devoid of water;
thus, the prefix *alā-* has been applied.
If pride were not exercised here, there would be the encouragement [of others] based on the thought: "The moonlight and other such things will surely bestow joy upon the mind."
But when the reading is *manonude* (driving the mind away), the word *api* indicates that the power to cause longing belongs not only to the moonlight and so forth, but also to the hero;

therefore, there is no purpose in producing tears [of joy] through *māna*—which is characterized by jealousy and anger and rests upon a contrary state of mind. Consequently, we maintain that it is indeed for the sake of the beloved that one goes there, whether going there oneself or as prescribed [by tradition], for the purpose of diversion in playful gatherings and the like. An example of such exclusive [love] that does not go elsewhere is as follows:
"The words spoken by Bhīṣma rest upon the mouths of the learned; the row of cows has been scattered here and there across the field.
(11) Here, the words of the first half-verse are in Sanskrit alone, while the words of the second half-verse are in Prākṛt alone.
This is called a genus that is unique and not shared by others; however,
among other languages, there is no such uniqueness as there is in *krīḍā*.

The play of poetic *samasyā* (completing a verse fragment), previously mentioned social gatherings (*goṣṭhī*), and therein the diversion of passing the time according to one's pleasure—these are the initial points, as before.

Now, [an objection is raised]: "Surely, let there be no admixture of other languages by virtue of their original nature (*prakṛtibhāva*); however, such admixture will occur when refined forms (*saṃskāra*) meet. And if that is so, how does this differ from the 'common' (*sādhāraṇī*) [style]? To this, he says: "And it is uncommon (*asādhāraṇī*)."
At dawn in the forest, that small lake is a watering place where rows of cranes stand amidst the dust of lotuses.
The [two] halves have been separated and expanded; there is no agreement between the first and second halves here because they serve as distinct examples.

However, the venerable [commentators], by conceiving a simile—just as a line of lotus pollen spread along the shore of a lake shines, so too do Bhīṣma’s words shine in the mouths of the learned—somehow assert a single syntactical unity.

In this context, the term "words from the first half" does not refer to Bhīṣma and others, because there is a prohibition against the status of being a substitute for words located in another language due to their non-mention; likewise, [the compounds] Vācaspati-viśiṣṭa, rasavaśa-pracetas-pota, and so forth, are to be understood in the same way.
"It is indeed Prakrit" because it belongs to the Mahārāṣṭra region, and because regional words (*deśī*) cannot function as substitutes (*sthānin*); furthermore,
this refers to other languages.
Beginning with the instruction, "Success [is achieved] from Mahārāṣṭrī; success from Śaurasenī," it is clear that [the grammatical forms] are indeed of the nature of those [vernaculars];
however, for those [forms] common to both, there is simply a state of shared usage.
Examples of such Apabhraṃśa forms are as follows:
“O innocent one, take this deposit; hold the seal in your own hand. Beautiful lady, I have a promise of sexual union with you. (12)
"O beautiful one, my longing for sexual union with you is certain.

This [speech], though corrupted by the use of ungrammatical words (*apaśabda*), is employed even by the ignorant, such as Vedic scholars (*śrotriya*) and others; thus, it is the *apabhraṣṭā* (corrupted) class [of speech]. Furthermore, its correctness is accepted when it is used as a mere imitation (*anukaraṇa*).
Regarding the term *apabhraṣṭā* (corrupt):
here, because it abounds in vulgar expressions such as "you have a desire for sexual union with me," it is clearly corrupt;
yet, how can that be an ornament? To this, he says: "This very [corruption]... and so forth.
A *śrotriya* is one learned in the Vedic hymns;

by the first word [of the verse], all worldly objects such as children and so forth are intended. Indeed, how could that which has ascended to the level of representation (*abhinaya*), having abandoned its vulgar form and become present within the determinants (*vibhāva*) and other factors, not be an ornament? This is what is meant by the phrase "by means of performance" (*prayogataḥ*).

Nor should it be said that corrupt words (*apaśabda*) are exclusively defects, for they are included within this [category of excellence] by virtue of their subordinate status as a general defect under the rule "but all [are permissible] in imitation" (*anukaraṇe tu sarveṣām*). Thus,
since a single delimited genus does not enter into the body of poetry, he next defines the mode consisting of its various delimitations:

That poetry which consists of verse (*padya*), prose (*gadya*), and mixed form (*miśra*) is known as *gati* (the mode); furthermore, by virtue of the appropriateness of meaning (*arthaucitya*) and other factors, that too is considered an ornament of speech (*vāgalaṃkāra*). [Verse 18] "Verse" (*padya*)... [and so on].
*Gati* (movement) is the transition from one word to another during recitation;
it is regulated by a certain measure of composition that arises through propriety,
and therefore that [measure] is also figuratively called *gati*.

And since poetry also relies upon a measure of syllables (*paṭhitiparimāṇa*), that too is included; furthermore, it is briefly stated that this [measure] is threefold, distinguished by verse (*padya*) and so forth.

For this very reason, some have employed a meter (*vṛtta*) even in prose composition (*gadyabandha*). Now, *vṛtta* means "turning" (*vartana*), which is to say "extent" (*iyattā*); for pronouns (*sarvanāmaśabda*) sometimes take on the gender of the subject (*uddeśya*) and sometimes that of the referent (*pratinirdeśya*). Thus, it is said that in poetry, whatever that extent may be, that is its "course" (*gati*).

In this regard, defining *padya* (verse) as "that which consists of four lines" (*catuṣpadī*) is not a valid definition, because it is absent in forms such as the *ullāla*, which consist of two lines, five lines, and so forth.

Furthermore, defining *gadya* (prose) as "a sequence of words that lacks feet" (*apāda*) is also incorrect; for "lacking feet" means either having a metrical structure that is not recognized as such, or, depending on one's intention, being distinct from the four-line verse.
In the first case, there would be no verse possessing even a trace of metrical structure;
in the second case, however, there would be an over-extension of the definition.
Therefore, the distinction is that poetry is that which possesses metrical constraints, whereas prose is that which lacks them.
Mixed poetry consists of both prose and verse;
it establishes the status of this [manner] as an ornament by means of "appropriateness of meaning" and so forth. Among these, he states the appropriateness of meaning:
Some [poetic meaning] can be composed in prose, some in verse, and some in a mixture;
in poetry, one [meaning] is expressed by two [modes], and another by three. (19) "Some in prose," etc.

For just as prose excels in descriptions such as those of forests and the like, whereas verse does not; and just as verse is capable of sustaining matters appropriate for the completion of poetry or scientific treatises, whereas prose is not—so too, one should observe the propriety of the literary form (*bandhaucitī*) implied by terms such as "prose" in *kathās* and *ākhyāyikās*, or "mixed" in works such as the *campū*.

Let alone the investigation into the propriety of meaning and so forth; even in its very nature, verse and the rest are understood to captivate the connoisseurs (*sahṛdaya*) by making manifest a particular excellence of the poet's creative intuition (*pratibhā*).
How else could there be excellence in only some [works] by someone? Thus he says:
"As Bāṇa is in the composition of prose, so is she in the construction of verse; for this Goddess Sarasvatī is wondrous in every single step. (20)
"Of whatever kind" means in every type of movement—
namely, in verse, prose, and mixed composition.
To establish the systematic application of practice for those whose accomplishments are diverse and unstable, he provides the following:
according to one's intelligence, according to one's power, according to what is appropriate, and according to one's inclination.
The employment of this [work] by the poet and this vessel is appropriate.
"According to one's intelligence" (yathāmati) means according to one's understanding (vyutpatti).
The discernment between what is appropriate and inappropriate— namely,
the innate capacity consisting of a latent predisposition (*saṃskāra*) from former lives that serves as the seed of poetic talent— and propriety have already been demonstrated.
The connection with "taste" (*ruci*) and "conformity to the mind" (*manonukūlatā*) belongs respectively to the poet and the audience;
for indeed, creative power (*śakti*) and proficiency (*vyutpatti*) belong to the poet alone.
Appropriateness belongs to the recipient alone, yet it is pleasing to both;
and this delineation of the composition shines precisely through the arrangement of heavy and light [syllables]. Therefore, relying upon that, he states the classification:
Swift, slow, medium, then swift-slow, swift-medium,
and likewise medium-slow are to be known. (22) "Swift" means...
The first three are pure;
the latter three are mixed due to their mutual intermingling.
To explain how these are established, he says:
Through the combination of the abundance, scarcity, and mixture of light and heavy syllables, it arises in six varieties in verse, prose, and mixed composition.
(23) "It [arises] from light [syllables]," etc.
Abundance, scarcity, and mixture appear as if they were equal;

it is not merely prose and the like that constitute the path, but rather the movement of recitation which serves as their substrate. This he clarifies with the words "in verse, in prose, and in mixed [composition]," wherein they say that *vṛtta* and *jāti* are verse, and then separately [they treat] the others.
This is declared to be even (sama), half-even (ardhasama), and uneven (viṣama).
In this context, "therein" refers to the metrical form (chandas) regulated by syllables (varṇa).
*Jāti* is that which has an indefinite number of *mātrās*.

*Samaprastāva* is "equal," meaning it has an identical opening in both the first and third quarters and in the second and fourth quarters. *Ardhasama* is that which has equal openings in the first two quarters and the last two quarters.
That which lies outside both [prose and verse] is uneven;

it is considered to be of two kinds—namely, that consisting mostly of prose (gadya) and that possessing the scent of verse (padyagandhin)—and it is also regarded as mixed due to the distinctions between prose, verse, and so forth. || 25 ||
"Gadyam" means a prose composition; it consists primarily of "utkalikās," which are like waves,
meaning it appears as if rising and falling in various heights.

For example: "salīlakarakamalatālikātaralavalayāvalīkam" (with the series of bracelets trembling from the clapping of lotus-like hands performed with grace)— this is a portion of a *pratibhāta-vṛtta* (a metre suggested by its appearance) that possesses the character of a *vṛtta*, and it is indicated by the secondary suffix (*samāsānta*) produced after the word *alpā*.
The meaning of this is as follows: movement is generally threefold, distinguished by the divisions of *padya* (verse) and so forth;
within that, it is sixfold according to the distinctions of genus (*jāti*) and so forth;
and those, further, are thirty-sixfold according to the distinctions of speed (*druta*) and so forth.

Now, one might ask: "Since certain authors on poetics have enumerated *lalita* and other varieties of prose (*gadya*), why are they not mentioned here? To this he replies: "The other distinctions—namely *lalita*, *niṣṭhura*, *cūrṇa*, and *āviddha*—will belong rather to the styles (*rīti*) and modes (*vṛtti*) of prose. (26)

*Lalita* refers to a composition that is delicate; for example: "In a certain part of the forest, where lotus stalks have become entangled with the thorns from wandering through the groves of *kamalinī* plants, he places his foot down heavily."
An example of harshness with a clear composition is: "He, with his mass of raised and curled hair, descends into the precincts of the cremation ground.
This is *cūrṇa* (powdered prose), in which no compounds are employed.
For example: "Indeed, practice bestows skill upon an action;
for surely, even a drop of water does not create a hollow in a stone merely by its contact with it"—this was uttered in the assembly of Udbhaṭa.

Just as in the example—"the lion, whose face is radiant with a mass of beautiful manes sprinkled by the spray of rut from intoxicated elephants, which have been split by a fierce slap from a collection of sounds harsher than the tip of a thunderbolt"—the locative case in "rītivṛttyoḥ" (in *rīti* and *vṛtti*) is used in the sense of the locus (*viṣaya-saptamī*), so too *lalita* is included within *kaiśikī* and the like, *niṣṭhura* within *bhāratī* and the like, *cūrṇa* within *vaidarbhī* and the like, and *āviddha* within *gauḍīyā* and the like; thus, the aforementioned varieties are not exhaustively enumerated. This is the meaning.
He provides an example of some of the aforementioned types:
among the varieties of verse, an example of a swift pace in a symmetrical meter (*samavṛtta*) is as follows:

"O fair-limbed one, this rising of the sun is occurring; the cocks are crowing.
Here, because of the greater number of short syllables in the *samavṛtta* meter, there is a rapid tempo (*drutā gatiḥ*).
"O you who fear new union"—this is an address;
from the word *bhīru*, the feminine suffix *ūṅ* is applied, and from that, the form [bhīru] arises through the shortening of the vocative.
If she, staying in the inner sanctum (*garbhagṛha*), does not look out, then he says: "They cry out together."

In this [meter], there are eight short syllables and four long syllables per quarter-verse; thus, due to the abundance of short syllables and the predominance of conjunct consonants, the state of rapidity (*druta*) is quite evident, even as the tempo and rhythm remain constant.
An example of slow tempo (*vilambita*) in an even meter (*samavṛtta*) is as follows:

"The compendium of the properties of categories (padārthadharmasaṃgraha), which brings about great exaltation, shall now be proclaimed.
This [verse], beginning with "having bowed," possesses a slow tempo (vilambita-gati) due to the occurrence of heavy syllables (gurvakṣara) in various places.

In this case, although there is an equal number of heavy and light syllables across the four quarters, nevertheless, because the conjunctions of consonants cause a lack of fluency in recitation at various intervals, the tempo is slow (*vilambita*) due to the predominance of ascent;
likewise, even in the *samānikā* meter, when arranged in reverse order, it is also slow—as in:
"The nets of fish, woven together, awakened by the rays of the sun..."
"Behold, O timid one, the lotuses crowded with intoxicated bees"—
this is what he said: "This very [woman]..."
Therefore, in the *Vibhāgasūtra*, it should be understood that the mixing of heavy and light [syllables] is also of this nature; therein, for example, the middling [type] is as follows:

"Those whose smiles are like white umbrellas speak of the strength of their arms;
this very [speech] is the 'middle' (madhyā) style of delivery because its syllables are not too short. Thus it was.

In this regard, although there are many teachers, the fact that recitation should be neither too fast nor too slow is a matter witnessed by experience; thus he says: "Neither with too light syllables," etc.
An example of the *drutavilambita* meter is as follows:
"May the row of the Sun’s horses protect you—the row in which the leader Aruṇa is situated in the middle of the shimmering [chariot]."
"Having completely surpassed the high clouds, she is like a single emerald creeper belonging to the splendor of the sky.
May this *drutavilambita* meter— which enters between the fast (*druta*) and the slow (*vilambita*) tempos—
protect you.
Aruṇa is the elder brother of Garuḍa; śoṇa means a leader or guide, as well as the central gem of a necklace;
and payodhara refers to clouds, as well as breasts.
Thus, in this meter called *drutavilambita*, the very name itself indicates its form;
for example, the *drutamadhyā* [verse]:
“He did not even take as his arrow’s mark the peacock with its beautiful plumage, though it was flying up from near his horse.”
"His mind suddenly went to his beloved's mass of hair, strewn with variegated garlands and loosened from its binding during lovemaking.
This is the *drutamadhyā* (fast-medium) tempo, so called because it enters between the fast (*druta*) and medium (*madhya*) tempos; it is also called *turaga*.

"How can that peacock—the one whose plumage is radiant and variegated with soft feathers as they emerge from its body, and who at that moment serves as the cause for the blossoming of the beloved’s desire by disheveling her mass of hair through a neck-embrace unrestrained by sincere love, and who is cherished as his very life—how can he endure being the target of Bāṇa's arrows? This is suggested by the *cvipratyaya* suffix.
Here, it is stated that even across all four quarters of the verse, the *druta* (quick) meter is first perceived and subsequently the *madhyā* (medium) meter is recognized in their respective parts:
"This is the *madhyavilambitā* (the medium-slow), as follows: [The verse follows].
“Kettledrums resounded loudly in the sky and the monkeys leaped about with great force;
then, a garland released from the lotus-like hands of the host of Siddhas fell upon the head of Aṅgada.
This is the *madhyavilambitā* (medium-slow) tempo, resulting from the entry into the interval between the *madhyā* (medium) and *vilambitā* (slow) tempos.

Regarding the verse *dundubhayaḥ*, it is shown here as well that within each quarter-verse (*pāda*), first the *madhya* (medium) tempo and then the *vilambita* (slow) tempo appear in distinct segments; this is indicated by the words *seyam*.

Thus, in the case of *ardhasama* and *viṣama* meters among the *mātrā-chandas* (measured meters), when they are mixed with prose (*gadya*), the various tempos such as *druta* (fast) and so forth are to be sought through the predominance of specific arrangements of light (*laghu*) and heavy (*guru*) syllables.
Thus, this very rule is extended to the *ardha-madhyama* and other meters as well; he provides a mere illustration:
therein, in a meter with uneven feet (*viṣamavṛtta*), the fast [tempo] is as follows—
‘Then, at the word of Vāsava, Dhanañjaya, whose face was radiant, performed austerities according to the prescribed rites in order to propitiate the three-eyed Lord who is free from weariness.

Then, having determined that the most weighty speech uttered by his beloved was pleasing to the mind, Vṛkodara addressed these words to the king— a speech supported by reason and based on a formidable resolve:
In the *utkalikāprāya* prose, the *druta* (quick) and *madhyā* (medium) tempos are as follows:
"The vault of the sky appears like a stainless ocean whose thick mass of clouds has vanished;
meanwhile, the nocturnal darkness, dark as a heap of powdered collyrium, spreads abroad.
[This is] the state of being on the verge of longing.
Just as a wave appears through various high and low states—
as in the phrase, "with her necklace trembling from the clapping of her graceful lotus-like hands"—
so too is this very example clear in its application to the present context.

In passages such as "pātāla," there is a semblance of the *vasantatilakā* meter; in passages such as "hara iva," there is a semblance of the *āryā* meter. Thus, in prose possessing the scent of verse (*padyagandhigadya*), there are those with the scent of *vṛtta* (meter) that are moderate, and those with the scent of *jāti* (class of meters) that are rapid, as for example: "Among the Dānavas dwelling in the depths of the surface of the netherworld."
"Like Hara, he has conquered Manmatha; like Guha, his power is unimpeded.
(22) Thus, these two are *madhyā* (intermediate) types, characterized by the scent of *vṛtta* (meter) and the scent of *jāti* (genus).

By the rule "In the case of the third [case-ending] and those following, that which has been stated as masculine is treated like the masculine according to Gālava," the *num* augment does not occur due to the application of the masculine form.
In prose and mixed compositions consisting of both prose and verse, the *drutamadhyā* meter is as follows: "Ah!

I am truly fortunate, since by her—whose eyes beam with joy at my unexpected appearance—I have been bound, as it were, with a dense cord of white lotuses, and bathed, as it were, in a cascade of milk-streams."

‘As if entirely swallowed by my wide-open eyes, I have been forcibly drenched by a thick shower of nectar. The exclamation ‘Hanta! is the expressive state (*anubhāva*) of one who is stunned by wonder; from that arises the manifestation of self-conceit (*abhimāna*), namely, ‘I am a man of merit. Immediately after this, as he hastens due to the description of the extraordinary excitants (*vibhāva*), the verse beginning with ‘yadaham’—which remains unfinished at the point of the word ‘aham’—and continuing with ‘āviralam’ and so forth, emerges.
When there is no reason for an interruption in the middle, a single sentence may consist of both prose and verse;
when mixed at the beginning of the verse, the *drutavilambita* meter is used, as in:

“Asau vidyādhāraḥ śiśurapi vinirgatya bhavanādihāyātaḥ saṃpratyavikalaśaraccandramadhuraḥ” || [He, the upholder of learning, though but a child, has departed from his home and arrived here, now as sweet as the full autumn moon.]
“When the city is in the light, it is as if its windows have been turned into blue water-lilies by the side-glances of women, tremulous with intoxication.
Here, [the word] “this one” (*asau*) refers to that Mādhava by name, who studies the science of logic (*ānvīkṣikī*) together with his childhood friend Makaranda.
In the *Dūtīkalpa*, it is traditionally taught by a certain woman who was to be wooed in secret that "one should lead [the lover] to union.
Here, however, the act of looking—which is charming through its imaginative nature—is described as being rustic (*grāmya*).

Thus, while the subject matter to be described has been recounted at length in verse, she has composed this prose section merely to provide a connection to the current context; therefore, this sequence is appropriate, and there is a unity of the sentences within the larger discourse.
The path established by Vaidarbha and others is known as *mārga* (the way) in poetry;
it is called *rīti* (style) through the etymological derivation from the verbal root *rī*, meaning "to go. [Verse 27] Regarding "Vaidarbha and others":
*Rīti* is the arrangement of words endowed with *guṇas*;
the *guṇas* are the nine qualities beginning with *śleṣa* (cohesion), which are never absent from poetry.

Because they are capable of merging with one another—like the flavor of a *pānaka* drink, or like the sweet, sour, and other tastes of molasses, black pepper, and so forth—their transition into a distinct state through the process of commingling is precisely what distinguishes poetic composition from the composition of ordinary worldly speech and treatises.
For this very reason, it is sought by poets from the beginning of saṃsāra; thus it is called "mārga" (the path).

The Vaidarbha and other styles originate from regions such as Vidarbha and others, and they have been manifested through their being the primary objects of cultivation; however, those specific regions do not contribute anything at all to the path of poetry.
For those who desire to attain the status of great poets indeed establish themselves [upon this path]; thus, this very definition of *rīti* is the opinion of Ānandavardhana and others as well,
and the aphorism has been explained by way of this illustration.
But how is it that the word *rīti* has been introduced as a synonym for *upamā* and so forth? To this he says: [The root] *rīṅ* means "to go.
The word *rīti* is derived from the instrumental sense (*karaṇasādhana*), meaning "that by which they proceed (*riyante*) in succession"; thus, its meaning is a synonym for "path" (*mārga*).
Having thus established the general definition, he states the classification:
The *rīti* (style) is said to be sixfold: Vaidarbhī, Pāñcālī, Gauḍīyā, Āvantikā, Lāṭīyā, and Māgadhī.
[Verse 28] Regarding "Vaidarbhī":
Intending to emphasize the primacy of the Vaidarbha style according to the method to be explained, he says:

"Among those, the Vaidarbha style is held to be that which is free from compounds, woven with all the qualities such as *śleṣa* (punning cohesion) and others, and possesses the beauty of the sound of the lute. (29)
In that context,
"without compounds" means that no compounds are explicitly mentioned; [this applies to] all instances such as *śleṣa* (paronomasia) and so forth.

The nine qualities, beginning with *śleṣa* (cohesion), are woven together; though they merge through mutual conjunction so that no individual distinction among them is perceived, they nevertheless exist by virtue of their mutually distinct essential natures, becoming the object of resonance within the hearts of the connoisseurs (*sahr̥daya*).
Thus, it possesses the beauty of the notes of a lute (*vipañcī*).
Sarasvatī, whose form is speech, is twofold as the *vipañcī* lute through the relationship of the original image (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*).
By virtue of being the substratum for the reflection, even a wooden mechanical instrument is called a *vipañcī*.

Its notes—arising from the strings and the throat, their physical locations inferred from the inversion of the sequence [in the reflection]—are reflections such as *ṣaḍja* and the rest. Even though these exist in the form of blended auditory impressions (*śrutisammūrcchanā*), the individual *śrutis*, having attained the state of notes that delight the ear, manifest themselves as witnessed by those who possess complete knowledge of music (*gāndharva*).
For this very reason, the *vīṇā* alone is primary for the entire range of musical notes (*svarajāta*), since it is therein that the circle of *śruti*s unfolds.
However, when a certain portion arises according to the analogy of a mixed beverage (*pānakanyāya*), then another melodic style (*rīti*) emerges; thus he says:
"consisting of five or six words in total, devoid of vigor (*ojas*) and beauty (*kānti*)."
Poets know the Pāñcālī style to be sweet and delicate;
"samasta" refers to that which is devoid of *ojas* and *kānti*, meaning specifically lacking in *ojas* and *kānti*.
This means that the qualities of *ojas* (vigor) and *kānti* (splendor) have become subordinate;
since their opposites, *mādhurya* (sweetness) and *saukumārya* (tenderness), arise therein, he says this: "sweet and tender.
For this very reason, in the six [types of] compounds exceeding [the usual limit], a compound is not formed so as to manifest *ojas*.
Those expert in the *rītis* recognize that style (*rīti*) which consists of entirely exalted words and is endowed with the qualities of *ojas* and *kānti* as the *Gauḍīyā*.
(31) [The word] "entirely" (*samasta*)...

Because it possesses highly exalted compounds with *ullekha* (repetition of sounds), this *rīti*—in which the other seven qualities are subordinated for the emergence of *ojas* (vigour) and *kānti* (splendor)—is the *Vaidarbhī*.
However, that which stands in the interval between *Pāñcālī* and *Vaidarbhī* is the *Āvantikā*, which consists of two, three, or four words [per compound]. (32)
Regarding the term *antarāla* (intermediate state):

it indicates the conceptualization of an interval either through the slight emergence of sweetness (*mādhurya*) and delicacy (*saukumārya*), or through the predominance of the closing [of the eyes]. This is expressed by the compound *dvitraiḥ*:
"two or three" or "three or four," where the *bahuvrīhi* compound is used in the sense of "or" (*vā*).
The *lāṭīyā* style is said to be a mixture of all the styles;
when the previous styles cannot be maintained, it is the *khaṇḍarīti*, which is *māgadhī*.
(33) [Regarding] "all":

Although there is likewise a failure to carry through the style initiated here, nevertheless, because the latter style— which is the object of the poet’s creative effort and which is blended with the former style like sesame and rice— is distinct from the former style,
this completion of the composition by means of another style after having commenced with one is indeed a different kind of thing altogether.
Nor is "lack of completion" (anirvāha) a defect, because there is an absence of discordance with the *chāyā* (poetic resonance);

for even when the *rīti* (style) is broken, the attainment of the excellence of composition (*saṃdarbhasaubhāgya*) manifests nothing but *śakti* (poetic power), as in the Vaidarbha style: [example follows].
“‘The deities desired by you reside in your home; but where, my child, is penance, and where is your delicate form?
A *śirīṣa* flower, though fragile, may endure the touch of a bee, but not that of a bird.
This is the Vaidarbha style (*rīti*), characterized by the absence of compound words and endowed with all the qualities such as *śleṣa* (paranomasia) and others.”

Regarding the objection raised by some that "how can there be *ojas* here in the absence of a long compound [in the word] *manīṣitāḥ*?"— this is refuted by the very fact that it is a context concerning those who lack discernment (*aparītimat*).
By this, the momentary blending of the nine qualities on an equal footing is established.
"Having no compound words" (asamastapadā) means having no words that are compounds;
"complete and possessing nine qualities" (samagrā navaguṇavatī) uses the suffix *matup* in the sense of constant connection (*nityayoga*).
An example from the *Pāñcālī* style is as follows:

“The sound of jewels became resonant with the clatter of *jhaṇajhaṇa*, produced by gems on armlets shattered against limbs, struck by earrings rolling upon the surfaces of cheeks, and jostled by the tips of crowns bursting open in the agitation. (26)

This is the Pāñcālī style (*rīti*), which—due to the absence of vigor (*ojas*) and brilliance (*kānti*)—possesses a clinging, relaxed, and ancient luster, sweetness, and softness, and consists of five or six words combined; it is characterized by the non-separation of limbs. Here, in the first and third [verses], six words are combined, while in the second, five words are combined.
The phrase "due to the absence of vitality and luster" uses the negative particle *nañ* in the sense of "slightness"; for this very reason, there is the manifestation of sweetness and delicacy.

The analysis of the compound is as follows: "that which possesses a *chāyā* (luster) that is *śliṣṭā* (coherent), *prāptā* (attained) according to the respective order (*yathāsaṃkhyam*), which has its emergence obtained through the closing of *ojas* and *kānti*, and which is *ślathā* (flaccid) and *purāṇī* (ancient).
An example of the Gauḍīya style is as follows:
"Whose neck-joint was bent by the weight raised up by the exertion of crushing the earth, [the weight] being dwarfed by the forceful movement of his army as it swayed in the sport of charging."

The remainder [of the verse] consists of a mass of sparks from the fire hissing from the expanded, blossoming, wide-open, and broad hoods, which causes the fragments of jewels in his formidable circle of crests to flash with uncertainty. This is the Gauḍīya style (rīti), which possesses vigor (ojas) and luster (kānti) and is characterized by entirely bold and abundant words. Thus it is said.
