"Avaskanda," "dhrāṭaka," and "samastodbhaṭabhūripada" constitute *udbhaṭatā*, which is the excellence of maturity (*prauḍhi*).
An example from Āvantikā:

“These faltering footsteps of hers, inconsistent with her exhausted body, betray her mind to be empty; and these trees along the path proclaim her feverish heat by their sprouts, which are drooping, cast aside, and withered. (28)
This is the style named Āvantikā, which exists between Vaidarbhī and Pāñcālī and consists of all [words] combined into two, three, or four *pada*s;
for example,
in the phrases “niḥsahatanorasamañjasāni” and “mārgataravaḥ,” there are two *pada*s each, while in “ālambita-” and so forth, three *pada*s are combined.
A slight manifestation of sweetness (*mādhurya*) and softness (*saukumārya*) constitutes the portion belonging to the Pāñcālī style;
the equal status of the other [qualities] constitutes the portion belonging to the Vaidarbhī style.
The conceptualization of an intermediate state resulting from the blending of these two is indeed evident.
An example from Lāṭa is as follows: “Here rises the sun, the breaker of the seal of the lotuses; the young *mandāra* flower of the forest groves on the mountain of sunrise;
the kinsman of the pairs of *kokila* birds distressed by separation; piercing the darkness, copper-red like the cheeks of an angry monkey. (29)
This is the style named Lāṭīyā, which is a mixture of all the styles;
and by the two compounds "ayam" and "mudrābhañjana," it is Āvantī.

By the group of five beginning with "Udayagiri," the *Pāñcālī* style is recognized through its excellence in sophistication (*prauḍhi*), the *Gauḍīyā* through [the presence of] compounds such as "ayasudayati," and the *Vaidarbhī* through the absence of compounds; thus, there is a convergence of all the aforementioned modes.
An example of Māgadhī is as follows:
"These foothills of the Vindhya mountains terrify one from all sides; their paths are reddened by the leaf-tips of vegetable branches left over from the feeding of elephants.
They are agitated by wild boars startled by the fierce sound of cow-horns blown by the moving Śabara tribes. (30)
This is the "fragmented style" (*khaṇḍarīti*), which is a form of the *Māgadhī* style known as "the elephant's mouthful" (*karikavalanā*), because it fails to carry through the style that was begun.

In this case, having commenced with the aforementioned *Ābhīrī* style in the first half-verse, one does not adopt the *Gauḍī* style in the final half-verse; thus, there is a "fracture" due to the failure to complete the initiated style. Nevertheless, because there is no discordance in its aesthetic luster (*chāyāvairūpya*) and it serves to manifest the poet’s creative power, it possesses the status of an ornament (*alaṃkāra*).

Śāka is a specific type of tree; furthermore, that which directs the mind toward expansion or contraction, as well as toward dispersion or extension, is a mental modification (vṛtti), and that too is of six kinds. (34)
That which is called "expansion" (*vikāsa*) is the function, the operation, or the activity of poetry directed toward aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), because poetry is inclined toward *rasa*.

And that activity— characterized by the emergence of the qualities of *sattva* and so forth, arising from latent impressions (*vāsanā*) cultivated through experiences in previous lives, serving as the primary cause for the state of mind in which the tasting of *rasa* will reach its fullness— is grounded in the meaning [of the poem] and will be explained in the fifth chapter.
Furthermore, that which resides in the word is what is relevant here, because it is the primary cause for manifesting the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) within a literary composition;
as it has been said:
"The poet’s speech and the dramatic performance are held to be its two means."
"However, by the power of the object's own capacity, the first [state] here is distinguished.

Since the mind functions by means of this [power], the word *vṛtti* is derived in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa-sādhana*). This is indicated by the term *vartayitrī*, which emphasizes the activity of the agent.
In that regard, due to the diversity of objects, there are four states of the mind, beginning with expansion (*vikāsa*).
For the object is threefold, distinguished as intense, mild, and moderate;
indeed, by the power of the presentation of the determinants (*vibhāva*) and other factors, the mind— which is capable of becoming one with that [object]— sometimes blossoms,
and this blossoming is the manifestation of *sattva*.
For when the mind has the qualities of *rajas* and *tamas* suppressed, it attains repose in a consciousness consisting of light and bliss through the predominance of *sattva*.
Consequently, the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*), which is established in that portion of *sattva*, even in its manifestation, takes hold of that very same state.
For this very reason, although it arises as a positive entity like the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, it is manifested through the power of poetry solely by virtue of the presence of a defect.

Intending to show that the sentiment of humor (hāsya-rasa) arises from a stage identical to that [of love], the sage Bharata said: "From the erotic (śṛṅgāra), indeed, humor arises. Therefore, the erotic and the humorous have expansion as their ground;
when the mind has fallen away from such expansion and has not yet attained the manifestation of another quality, it is called "distracted" (vikṣipta).

In that state, when the mind—due to the emergence of the quality of *rajas* arising from the diversity of appropriate excitants (*vibhāva*) and so forth—is in a condition of distraction and decline, there is the manifestation of the *raudra* (furious) sentiment.
For this very reason, he says [in the *Nāṭyaśāstra*], "From the *raudra* arises the *karuṇa* (pathetic) sentiment," because they share the same plane.

However, when the mind is established solely in *rajas* through the closing of *sattva* and *tamas*, it then reaches the state known as "expansion" (*vistara*) due to the manifestation of manifold activities.
The heroic sentiment (*vīrarasa*) belongs to that same ground; and the marvelous (*adbhuta*) also manifests by remaining in that very state. Thus it is said: "The marvelous arises from the heroic.

A specific state of the mind in which the quality of passion (*rajas*) has subsided and ignorance (*tamas*) is awakened is characterized by contraction; taking hold of that [state], the loathsome (*bībhatsa*) appears, and the terrifying (*bhayānaka*), sharing its same ground, likewise emerges. Therefore, he says: "From the loathsome, the terrifying.

Having raised the objection as to how these four specific states of the mind arise from a literary composition (*saṃdarbha*) without any further qualification, he provides the answer by means of a distinction:
Kaiśikī, Ārabhaṭī, Bhāratī, Sātvatī, as well as Madhyamārabhaṭī and likewise Madhyamakaiśikī— these are the [styles].
Regarding "Kaiśikī":
Based on purity and mixture, as in the case of *rīti*, there are likewise six varieties here.
Among them, that which consists of a composition of delicate meanings is called *kaiśikī*; whereas that which consists of a composition of mature meanings is the *vṛtti* known as *ārabhaṭī*. (36)

They know *sātvatī* to be speech that possesses both soft and mature composition, as well as soft meaning; or [speech] with mature meaning and soft-mature composition. On the other hand, *madhyamakaiśikī* has soft composition but mature meaning. (37)
The *madhyamārabhaṭī* style is characterized by mature meaning expressed in a tender composition (verse 38).

Regarding the term *sukumārā*: its analysis (*vigraha*) is "that in which the arrangement of meanings is tender (*sukumāra*), whereby tenderness (*saukumārya*) consists in causing the melting of the heart."
Thus, "maturity" (*prauḍhi*) consists in the capacity to produce a brilliance of thought through a composition of mature meaning;
and a composition characterized by the delicacy of meaning and so forth— namely, qualities such as "delicacy" (*saukumārya*)— induces the status of verbal ornament (*śabdālaṃkāra*).
The "soft-mature" (komalaprauḍha) is the middle [type],
and because there is no other category [between them], the "middle-Bhāratī" and so forth do not exist.
Among these, the Kaiśikī is as follows:

“The glances of the tremulous-eyed women fell upon the moonbeams, the leaves of the betel-creeper, the jasmine garland, the delightful sandalwood, the blue water-lilies, the vessel of aged wine, and upon their beloved.
This is the *kaiśikī* style (*vṛtti*), so called because of the delicacy of both its meaning and its composition.

Their glances fell first upon the moonbeams—namely, the leaves of the *nāga-latā* creeper—which were cooled by the breeze and offered a most charming redness to the lips of young women eager for the taste of a kiss; then they fell upon the jasmine garland, beautiful with its fortune of being used to seize the hair of those women seeking specific kisses such as the *valitaka*; then upon the sandalwood paste, the fortune of which was to be applied over all limbs; then upon the wine-cup, desired by those longing for the pleasure of love after all constraints of play had been exhausted by the lingering scent of jealousy and anger; and finally, their glances fell with equal intensity upon the beloved, who was the very life of all their implements and the essence of their existence.
‘Kuvalayini’ is the correct reading;
for in the reading ‘kuvalayita-’, since the intention is to emphasize the predominance of the qualifying attribute over the subject, its subordination within a compound would be inappropriate.
This is the Kaiśikī style, which is employed in smooth (masṛṇa) sentiments such as the erotic (śṛṅgāra).
Ārabhaṭī is as follows:
“Whosoever among the Pāṇḍava armies bears a weapon with pride in his own mighty arms; whosoever of the Pāñcāla lineage is a child, of advanced age, or even lying in the womb;

whosoever is a witness to their deeds and moves against me in battle; and whosoever stands in opposition—blinded by rage—I myself am here the end-maker of that very person, even as the End-maker of the worlds. (32)
This is the style named *Ārabhaṭī*, characterized by mature composition;
"yo yaḥ" refers to a composition that is mature due to its predominance of *ojas* (vigorousness).

Since this *ārabhaṭī* (the forceful style) is employed in the *dīpta* (intense), *raudra* (furious), and other such [rasas], it is appropriate that there be a maturity (*prauḍhatva*) of both word and meaning;
as in the following *bhāratī* (speech):

"Rising at the end of lovemaking, resting the weight [of her body] upon the lord of serpents with one hand, and holding her garment with the other, she carries the mass of her disheveled tresses upon her shoulder."
May the body of Lakṣmī purify you— her arms languidly resting as she was led by Śauri to her bed, which he embraced with redoubled pleasure from the amorous delight of their union at that moment.
(33) This is the *vṛtti* known as *Bhāratī*, wherein the meaning is exceedingly delicate while the composition is not overly delicate,
as in the verse beginning with "uttiṣṭhantyā" (rising).

When the beloved is eager for an embrace covering all her limbs, the behavior of a charming young woman—turning away outward while following inward according to the maxim of the "innocent maiden"—is such that, though her creeper-like arms are languid from the exhaustion of intense play, they remain radiant in their desire to bind the knot of her garment and restrain her mass of hair; yet she is not even able to employ them for that purpose. This constitutes an intense heightening of emotion at that moment.

Here, although the sentiment (*rasa*) is smooth (*masṛṇa*), maturity of composition (*prauḍhi*) is indeed appropriate due to the propriety of the style (*vṛttyaucitya*); for while long compounds are forbidden in the *śṛṅgāra* (erotic) and other sentiments, maturity itself is not.
However, due to the inclusion of phonemes such as *ra* and *ha*, there is softness in the composition;
in this way, the distinction in subsequent examples should also be inferred by oneself.
An example of the Sātvatī style is as follows:
"Both of these are worthy of homage, for both have attained the rise of majesty through noble conduct: Bhīma of terrible prowess, and that sage whose weapon is a sun-bright, blunt-edged spear.
By one, the blood of enemies was drunk after being torn open like nectar with his claws; by the other, he bathed in the lake of the blood of slain foes to pacify his wrath.
This is the *sāttvatī* style, characterized by mature meaning and a composition that is not overly elaborate.
An example of Madhyamakaiśikī is as follows:
“O cursed door-keeper, why has this wicked poison-tree been nurtured by you with a mango sapling?
For when even the slightest change occurs in its blossoming, the terrifying fevers of passion break out. (35)
This is the style known as Madhyamakaiśikī, which possesses a mature composition for a delicate subject; an example of Madhyamārabhaṭī is as follows:
"O King of Serpents, firmly encircle with your coils the broad slopes of Mount Mandara."
"What excessive burden could there be for you, who have endured the practice of binding yourself in the paryaṅka posture during the playful sport of riding upon the unbearable bull?
This is the *madhyamārabhaṭī* style, characterized by delicate composition applied to a mature theme.
Furthermore, the *chāyā* (imitation) of *anyoktis* (indirect expressions) is also sixfold in this context.
Due to the distinctions in the speech of worldlings, clever people, children, madmen, boys, and the intoxicated— among these various types of *anyokti* (indirect expression) in the world,
the reflection (*pratibimba*) is renowned for its aesthetic charm (*camatkāritva*).

For this very reason, he states that "the dramatic (prekṣya) is superior to the audible (śravya)" in the section on verbal ornaments (*śabdālaṃkāra*). It is precisely the imitation of a sentence (*vākyānukaraṇa*) that is designated by the word *chāyā*—which literally means "reflection"—through a figurative application (*guṇavṛtti*).
He then explains that this imitation is established as being of six types based solely on the differences in the object of imitation (*anukārya*): namely, *cheka*, etc.

Since specific classes of people such as *chekas* (clever ones) are mentioned separately because they serve as ornaments, the word "world" (*loka*) by implication refers to the various other diverse types of persons who are the subjects of imitation.
*Chekas* are the clever;
*poṭās* are those possessing the characteristics of both male and female.
The *poṭā* is well known as "innate play" (*sahajakeli*);
others call her a "servant" (*bhujiṣyā*) or a "slave-girl" (*dāsī*).
Here, some say that even poetry born from the shadow of another work is the domain for the application of the figure of speech called "shadow" (*chāyā*).

The five varieties of poetry born from [natural] sources are: *prakṛtipariṇāma* (transformation of nature), *parapurapraveśa* (entering another's body), *khaṇḍasaṃghātya* (patchwork), *cūlikā* (the crest), and *parimala* (the fragrance).
Among these, *prakṛtipariṇāma* is that in which the meaning is slightly modified, as for example:
“The smoke has vanished; the bees have left the trees;
the birds have not abandoned their branches; and the quarters of the sky have returned to their own nature.
And as it is said:
‘The forest thickets, having cast off their dense mass due to the onset of winter, appear as if they have been gathered and spread out by the rays of the sun across the quarters of the sky.

Here, the description of the expansion of the sky and the directions appears slightly unnatural; thus, this is a variety of *yonija* poetry named *prakṛtipariṇāma* (transformation of the natural state).
Entrance into another's body through mere speech,
as for example: "Whether I be the lord of gods, the lord of serpents, or the lord of the earth, may I become a Haihaya."
“May I perform your vision, your praise of virtues, and my service with joined palms.
And as it is said:
“Having attained myself as the son of Viṣṇu, the son of Añjanā, and the son of Mahendra...”

"Seḍaṃ jāladaṃsaṇa guṇakahāmuta ijaṇūpajjattam. Here, only the language is different; thus, this is the variety of *yonija* poetry called *parapurapraveśa*. *Vikīrṇa*, which is a non-composite (*asamāhāra*), is *khaṇḍasaṃghātya*.
For example:

"Two or three lotus petals rest upon the bosom of the lakes; the *kiṃśuka* trees bear three or four buds on their crests; five or six flowers form within the internal joints of the mango trees; and the waves of warbling have arrived and become manifest in the throats of the female ospreys."

In this case, four lines have been extracted from four separate poems and woven together; thus, this is a variety of *yonija-kāvya* (poetry born from a source) named *khaṇḍasaṃghātya* (composite of fragments).
An example of *cūlikā* (the appendix), which takes up that much meaning or even more, is as follows:
"A lotus in waterless ground, and there a blue water-lily; these upon a golden creeper, and that creeper itself so delicate and beautiful—what is this succession of marvels?
And as it is said:

"Two plantain-stalks inverted above two lotuses; above those, a certain inscrutable gem-stone surface; then two jars, followed by two fresh lotus-sprouts, and then a kandalī-shoot; and upon that, two blue lotuses with bees—what indeed is this?
In this passage, because of the recognition of an excess of insertion at various points, this is a variety of *yonija-kāvya* (natural-born poetry) named *cūlikā*.
An example of a fragrance that corresponds only to its reflected shadow is as follows:
"O lady with thighs like plantain stalks, do you perhaps have a desire in your heart for this prince?"
“In the succession of gardens shaken by the breezes from the waves of the Siprā, [she was] intent on sporting.
And as it is said:
“In that [city], while playing the lute in connection with a festival procession, she [saw] Mahākāla, who is not subject to obstruction.”
"O slender-limbed one, may you at last obtain the fruit of your long practice of the arts in the tuning of the strings of the lute.
Here, only the shadow of the literary composition has been imitated; thus, this is the variety of *yonija* poetry named *parimala*.
Among those [varieties], the shadow of popular proverbs (*lokokti*) is as follows:
‘The end of my curse shall come when the wielder of the Śārṅga bow has risen from his serpent-bed; pass these four months with your eyes closed.
Afterwards, we two shall enjoy our respective desires, multiplied by our separation, during nights illuminated by the mature autumnal moonlight.
This [verse] is an imitation of common worldly expression, characterized by the shadow of such expression, in the phrase “with your eyes closed.”

By the phrase "closing her eyes" (*locane mīlayitvā*) in the sense of "the end of the curse," the imminent nature of the time of reunion is indicated through an imitation of common worldly expression, just as one closes one's eyes [in anticipation]. And thus, the intention of the resolve regarding the life of the exceedingly delicate beloved is revealed to one whose mind is possessed by the pangs of separation during a journey abroad (*pravāsa-vipralambha*).
And this is merely an elliptical indication; even the common worldly expression "for four months during the rainy season" is simply a reflection of poetic idiom (chekokti), as for example:
"Homage to that beast of a king who has fallen under the power of that lovely face, with its long, dark eyes and playfully arched brows!
This "homage to that beast of a king" is an imitation of the speech of the clever, possessing the luster of *chekokti* (witty or double-entendre speech).
For he who considers the face of his beloved alone to be the entirety of his life, and who possesses full confidence in it— toward such a person, the refined lover behaves like a beast;
an example of this in the form of a child’s speech is as follows:
"Is the moon some celestial tree whose flower it is?
O Mother, what kind of trees are those whose fruit is the pearl? This is an imitation of the speech of an unlearned child, possessing the shadow of a child's utterance.
"Who indeed is he?

Surely this person seen here, delighting us with his nectar-like splendor, is a single cluster from some tree such as the Pārijāta, whose fame is renowned for fulfilling the desires of all the multitudes of supplicants throughout the three worlds"— such is the shadow of the speech of a madman.
“O slender-limbed one, how was he seen? What did he do? Does he ask after us? Does he hear our news when it is being reported?
Let that be; tell me quickly—will that proud man come here, or will he not?
This is an imitation of the speech of a madwoman, possessing the shadow of a madwoman’s utterance, characterized by incoherence.

By the words "It was seen," and so forth, he reveals his single-minded absorption; by "Let it be as it may," and so forth, he expresses his sudden abandonment; and by "Tell me first," and so forth, he resumes his inquiry. This is an illustration of the style of *poṭokti* (the "sudden" or "abrupt" utterance): [The text continues: "Tell me first, O friend, what you have seen. "What did you see? "I saw a certain man. "Was he a Brahmin? "No, he was not a Brahmin. "Was he a Kṣatriya? "No, he was not a Kṣatriya. "Was he a Vaiśya? "No, he was not a Vaiśya. "Was he a Śūdra? "No, he was not a Śūdra. "Then who was he? "He was a man of great power. "Where did you see him? "In the city of Śrāvastī. "Was he there alone? "No, he was not alone. "Who were with him? "With him were many people. "Did he speak to you? "Yes, he spoke to me. "What did he say? "He said, 'I am the Blessed One. "Is that so? "Yes, that is so. "Is this true? "Yes, it is true. "Is this not false? "No, it is not false. "Is this a lie? "No, it is not a lie. "Is this a deception? "No, it is not a deception. "Is this a joke? "No, it is not a joke. "Is this a dream? "No, it is not a dream. "Is this a delusion? "No, it is not a delusion. "Is this a hallucination? "No, it is not a hallucination. "Is this a fabrication? "No, it is not a fabrication. "Is this a trick? "No, it is not a trick. "Is this a riddle? "No, it is not a riddle. "Is this a parable? "No, it is not a parable. "Is this a metaphor? "No, it is not a metaphor. "Is this a symbol? "No, it is not a symbol. "Is this a sign? "No, it is not a sign. "Is this a prophecy? "No, it is not a prophecy. "Is this a prediction? "No, it is not a prediction. "Is this a revelation? "No, it is not a revelation. "Is this a vision? "No, it is not a vision. "Is this an apparition? "No, it is not an apparition. "Is this a phantom? "No, it is not a phantom. "Is this an illusion? "No, it is not an illusion. "Is this a mirage? "No, it is not a mirage. "Is this a reflection? "No, it is not a reflection. "Is this an echo? "No, it is not an echo. "Is this a sound? "No, it is not a sound. "Is this a word? "No, it is not a word. "Is this a name? "No, it is not a name. "Is this a title? "No, it is not a title. "Is this a designation? "No, it is not a designation. "Is this a description? "No, it is not a description. "Is this a definition? "No, it is not a definition. "Is this an explanation? "No, it is not an explanation. "Is this a commentary? "No, it is not a commentary. "Is this a discourse? "No, it is not a discourse. "Is this a sermon? "No, it is not a sermon. "Is this a teaching? "No, it is not a teaching. "Is this a doctrine? "No, it is not a doctrine. "Is this a principle? "No, it is not a principle. "Is this a rule? "No, it is not a rule. "Is this a law? "No, it is not a law. "Is this a command? "No, it is not a command. "Is this an injunction? "No, it is not an injunction. "Is this an ordinance? "No, it is not an ordinance."
“I am unable to endure the *tilaka* mark; the application of camphor causes my excessive chilliness, and the saffron dye brings weakness to my limbs.
This is an imitation of the speech of a low-born young woman elevated to a high status, possessing the stylistic shadow of a *poṭā* (a courtesan).
Imitating a young woman who occupies the highest station, or as a low-born young woman elevated to that highest station might speak in the style of intoxicated speech, it is as follows: "Pi pi!
O beloved! Sa sa! Give me yourself! Mu mu! Give me the wine from your mouth! Ta ta! Abandon it! Du du! Quickly! Bha bha! [Give] the golden vessel!"
Thus, the faltering speech of the deer-eyed woman, uttered under the influence of intoxication, was studied by her companions at dawn as a cause for laughter;
this is indeed an imitation of stumbling speech, a mere shadow of intoxicated utterance, yet it is still "my dear."

Those who know the seals of poetry recognize as *mudrā* the employment of words within a sentence that possesses intentional meaning— characterized by an unmanifest mode of operation and consisting of faltering speech— that bestows delight. (40)
Regarding the term "intentional" (*sābhiprāya*):

although a complete poem as a whole is indeed a reflection of the speaker’s intention—as it has been said, "they should indicate the speaker’s intention"—nevertheless, in this [particular instance], one observes a placement in a single part that serves as a counterpart to a specific intentional meaning capable of ennobling the poem, which reveals an intention within the scope of the sentence-meaning that is not common to others;
for this very reason, it is called a "seal" (*mudrā*), just like a seal such as a signet ring.
He states the etymology: "Because it bestows joy" (*mud-pradāyitvāt*).

With *mud* as the prefix, from the root *rā* meaning "to give," the form is *mudrā*. For others, the *mudrā* itself is the ground for the linguistic usage of sounds manifested through the feet and other means.
This [arrangement] arises through the conventional application of a sixfold placement consisting of the word, the sentence, the case ending, the number, the conjunction, and the [syntactic] relation.
(41) "This in this" (sāsmin).
A *pada* is a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) consisting of a primary derivative (*kṛt*), a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), or a compound (*samāsa*).

Although case-endings (*vibhakti*) and numbers (*vacana*) stand in a relationship of general and particular, they are mentioned separately because they each manifest a distinct intention; the restriction to specific verbal forms such as *āstām* and so forth constitutes conventional usage (*saṃvṛti*).
Among those, the footprints [of excellence] are as follows:

“The blue water-lily is but the discarded remains of the beauty of her eyes; the moon is the servant of her face; the bow of the Love-god is a kinsman to her pair of eyebrows; moonlight is but the fringe of her smile; and the songs of the intoxicated cuckoo are the leftovers of her singing. Oh, how wonderful! The Creator’s masterpiece of craftsmanship, which pervades every limb, has finally come to fruition after a long time. (43)

Here, through the employment of words such as *nirmālya*, *dāsa*, *sanābhi*, *añcala*, and *ucchiṣṭa*— which yield delight by relying on figurative function (*gauṇavṛtti*) and are placed with intentional significance— this "seal of words" (*padamudrā*) is seen to rely on figurative function.

This is because, by means of indication (*lakṣaṇā*) characterized by the extreme obscuration of the literal meaning (*atyantatiraskṛtavācya*), these words such as *nirmālya* suggest a particular excellence of beauty (*lāvaṇyaviśeṣa*), thereby captivating the hearts of sensitive readers (*sahṛdaya*).
Thus:
"Only those virtues arise which are cherished by one's own kin;
like lotuses favored by the rays of the sun, they become truly lotuses."
Likewise:
"The nectar is nectar, the moon is the moon, and likewise the lotus is the lotus;
Rati is Rati, Kāma is Kāma, and the honeyed liquors are indeed honeyed liquors."

In such instances, one should recognize the presence of *dhvani* (suggested meaning) manifested through the transference (*saṃkramaṇa*) of the literal sense into another meaning, and so forth. An example of this in a sentence is as follows:
“That which, when reflected in the god who is the lord of the night—the very essence of clear water—appears in the form of nectar, is indeed said to be a distinct reality called moonlight.”
"The sharp radiance shines long in the sky; therein resides the divine Person, by knowing whom all the knots of worldly existence are severed once again.

Here, because the subsequent sentence beginning with "therein resides the divine Person" serves to assist the preceding sentence by providing a sense of joy, and is placed there intentionally, this is *vākyamudrā*, as in the example "which is clear... [from verse 43].
The traditional teaching (āgama) is that the very digits of the sun, when reflected, receive the designation "moon";
thus it is said:
"In the moon, which consists of water, the rays of the sun are concentrated, [dispelling] the darkness of night."
"They fade away within the interior of the palace as if struck against the surface of a mirror"—
thus [it is said], by way of assisting the preceding statement.

Regarding the statement, “In the sky, there shines a distinct reality in the form of nectar, a sharp radiance,” which is indicated by the word *kila* as being something conjectured due to its unfathomable nature—the phrase beginning with “there exists” (*tatrāsti*) serves to fulfill the expectation of what its connection might be.
For instance, this appears to be an intentional presentation of the meaning of the Upaniṣads, such as: “This Person who shines, pervading the path of the sun.”
By this, other modes of expression revealed by sentences should also be understood as being included;
it should be understood that duality was previously internalized within the sentence.
This is the "seal of the case-ending" (vibhaktimudrā), as follows:

‘A pure intellect indeed milks out prosperity, wards off calamities, generates fame, wipes away impurity, and purifies others through its refined purity; for a pure intellect is truly a wish-fulfilling cow.

(45) Here, in the words *pradugdhe*, *ruṇaddhi*, *sūte*, *pramārṣṭi*, and *punīte*, there is the application of the verbal suffixes (*tiṅ-vibhakti*) according to the rule: “*Duhipacyorbahulaṃ sakarmakayor upasaṃkhyānam*” (Vārttika on Pāṇini 3.1.87).
1.87 (*vārttika*), ‘*śnam* [is added] after roots beginning with *rudh*’ (Pāṇini 3.1.78).

78) Through such applications of specific grammatical characteristics (*viśeṣalakṣaṇa*), the occurrence of the *parasmaipada* and *ātmanepada* endings is observed in the case of *śrī*, *vipad*, *yaśas*, and *malinaṃ saṃskāraśaucena*. Furthermore, regarding the case-endings (*subvibhakti*), there is the rule: *aci śnudhātubhruvāṃ yvoriyaṅuvaṅau* (Pāṇini 6.4.77).

77) Thus, because words possessing such specific characteristics— whether unmodified or modified— are observed to be employed with the underlying intention (*abhiprāya*) of conveying auspicious or inauspicious meanings,
this constitutes the "seal of case endings" (*vibhaktimudrā*),
as in the word *śriyaḥ*.

When it is said that "the wish-fulfilling cow, whose form is intelligence, spreads prosperity," there is not such excellence as when it is stated [in the following way], for from that statement the poet’s specific intention is inferred.

For instance, just as in the expression "the udumbara tree bears red fruit" (*udumbaraḥ sa lohitaṃ phalaṃ pacyate*), where the agent and the object are identical, the identity of the fruit and the udumbara tree is understood; so too here, intelligence manifests itself in the form of prosperity (*śrī*).
It is precisely for this reason that the Vārttika states: "The roots *duh* and *pac* are frequently used with an object even when they are intransitive" (*duhipacyorbahulaṃ sakarmakayoḥ*).

1.87) Thus, the status of being treated like the object (*karmavadbhāva*) is prescribed only for an agent who possesses an external action, as in the rule: "The suffixes *yak* and *ciṇ* do not occur after the roots *duh*, *snu*, and *nam*" (Pāṇini 3.1.89).
Thus, even the absence of the *ya*-affix is restricted by the intention toward a specific [meaning], as in the form *ruṇaddhi* (he obstructs);
[in the case of] *sūte* (she gives birth), the [suffix] is elided.
"pramārṣṭi" is that which effects increase; "punīte" is that which purifies. Furthermore, a *vikaraṇa* (conjugational suffix) is that which is modified in its own form.
The placement of the *ātmanepada* and *parasmaipada* endings occurs at intervals of one [suffix].
In *śriyaḥ*, the substitution of *iyaṅ* in the stem portion is a modification, and it is also a modification in the case of the case-ending; however,
in *vipadaḥ*, the stem remains unmodified,
while the case-ending is modified by the substitution of *ru*.
In the case of "yaśāṃsi," both members are modified; in the optional rule for *parasavarṇa* (assimilation to the following sound) regarding the word "malinam," both are unmodified;
and in the phrase "saṃskāraśaucena," the base form (*prakṛti*) remains unmodified.
The suffix *pratyaya* is modified by the substitution [of *ya* for *i*];
likewise, "Śrī" signifies auspiciousness, while "Vipad" is its opposite. Thus, through this sequence, the pure intellect is established as the "Wish-fulfilling Cow" (*Kāmadhenu*).
By thus concluding with a series of auspicious associations, it appears as if radiant with variegated silks, manifesting an indescribable splendor like a reflected image.
"By virtue of being subsequent to words that signify auspiciousness or inauspiciousness" means by virtue of occurring after words that denote auspiciousness or inauspiciousness;
for example, the Seal of Speech (*vacanamudrā*) is as follows:

“The divine Viśvabhārā gave birth to you; your father Janaka is a king equal to Prajāpati; O daughter, you are the daughter-in-law of those kings in whose lineages both the Sun-god and we ourselves are gurus.

Here, by using the plural “we” (*vayam*) with respect to himself and the singular “the Sun-god” (*savitā*) with respect to the Sun, the speaker’s intention is to convey that he himself is highly esteemed even by the Sun; this is the *vacanamudrā* (seal of speech).
In the verse beginning with "viśvaṃbharā," it was previously stated that the quality (*guṇa*) functions as the motivator for the growth of the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*);
here, however, the distinction is that a specific intention of the poet constitutes a component of the poetic figure (*alaṃkāra*).
The *samuccaya-mudrā* (the gesture of conjunction) is as follows:
"This face of yours has appeared before us, fond of frowning; and the lineage of Vasudeva has gone to such a state that only its name remains. (47)

Here, because the treatment as a past event (*bhūtavat-bhāva*)— prescribed by the rule *āśaṃsāyāṃ bhūtavacca* (Pāṇini 3.3.132)— is introduced by way of a conjunction (*samuccaya*) to praise the extraordinary power of Hayagrīva, this is the "seal of conjunction" (*samuccayamudrā*).

Regarding the statement "here, by [the rule] *āśaṃsāyām*," since the past tense is indicated by the *niṣṭhā* suffix (*-ta*), one might ask: even if there is a perception of hope (*āśaṃsā*), how does this nourish the present context? To this it is replied: "by way of conjunction" (*samuccayadvāreṇa*).

For when equality of status is perceived through that [conjunction], the thought arises in the speaker’s mind: "If you indeed accept your anger, then what is desired is already accomplished. Thus, upon the perception of this specific determination of the speaker, the conjunction itself attains the status of a poetic figure (*mudrā*).
The rest is easily understood.
As for the seal of conventional reality (*saṃvṛtimudrā*), it is as follows: "The jewel of Maṇiratna was [stolen] by the ignoble Viṣṇu."

“By whom [the truth] has been attained through this present yoga, what is the use of that being proclaimed to you? (48). Here, because it is said, “Indeed, even a mere story is sufficient for the misfortune of the wicked,” the phrase “what is the use of that being proclaimed to you” constitutes this *saṃvṛtimudrā* (seal of concealment), which effects a concealment with a specific intention (*sābhiprāya-saṃvṛti-karaṇa*). This occurs either by way of affirmation or, alternatively, by way of negation.
When a qualified meaning is understood, that expression is here called *abhidhā* (denotation).
[The term] "vidhi" refers to the expression (*ukti*).
*Abhidhā* means denotation.

Since that [cognition] has both existence and non-existence as its objects, one might ask: "What, then, is the difference between this [cognition] and the cognition 'this is a cow's offspring' (which is expressed as) 'this is a cow'? Anticipating this objection, [the author] says "or by way of affirmation," and so forth; the cognition of existence is affirmation (*vidhi*), while the cognition of non-existence is negation (*niṣedha*).

The meaning is this: by the power of linguistic proficiency acquired in the world, speech ascends the path of the cognition of either existence or non-existence and, ultimately resolving upon the domain of poetry alone—which consists of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) and the like—becomes an ornament (*alaṃkāra*).
This very [ornament] manifests in six ways through the expansion of positive entities (*bhāva*) and so forth; thus he says:
"It may arise from affirmation, or from negation, from restriction, or from option."
"From restriction, there is enumeration; this [limiting condition] here is sixfold. Regarding "of the injunction," the limiting condition (*upādhi*) is a qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*).
The injunction and the entitlement are distinctions of pure affirmation;
the prohibition and the restrictive rule are distinctions of pure negation; and the option and the exclusive specification are distinctions of the mixed type.
In this context, an injunction (*vidhi*) is that which brings about what has not yet been attained;
a prohibition (*niṣedha*) is the negation of what is applicable;
and an entitlement (*adhikāra*) is the connection between an action and its fruit.
*Vikalpa* (option) is the connection with one of two [alternatives] of equal status through the exclusion of the other;
*niyama* (restriction) is a positive injunction whose fruit is the exclusion [of others];
and *parisaṃkhyā* (exclusive specification) consists of a particular prohibition or injunction that is inseparable from a remaining injunction or prohibition.
Regarding these, the formulation of an injunction (*vidhi*) is as follows: "Serve your elders; act with the conduct of a dear friend toward your co-wives.
Here, an injunction is a statement that brings about what has not [otherwise] been attained.
Regarding the statement that an injunction concerns what has not been attained:
since an injunction consists essentially in impelling one toward what has not yet been undertaken, how can it be consistent with dependence on anything else?
For this very reason it is said: "An injunction applies where there is absolute non-attainment."
An example of a statement of prohibition is: “Even though you have been mistreated by your husband, do not act perversely out of anger.
Here, the prohibition consists in the warding off of what has [otherwise] occurred.
"Obstructing what has been attained" means that one is restrained from acting contrary [to the goal] due to the impulse of anger; an example of a statement regarding the qualification is as follows:
"Be most generous toward your attendants, and do not be arrogant regarding enjoyments;

for young women who act thus attain the status of a true housewife, whereas those who are contrary are a source of anxiety to the family. Herein lies the qualification for [receiving] injunctions and prohibitions, based on the knowledge of what is enjoined and what is prohibited.

"From the knowledge of injunctions and prohibitions" means that eligibility (*adhikāra*) consists in the fitness for connection with the results of enjoined and prohibited actions through the knowledge of those actions;
for example, "Serve! and "Be very generous! are two enjoined [actions].
"Do not go against [his will]," and "be not arrogant regarding enjoyments"—these two are prohibitions.
Fitness for injunctions and prohibitions is the fitness for connection with the fruits of injunctions and prohibitions;
the attainment of the status of a housewife is the fruit of the enjoined action.
The statement regarding the alternative— that the abode of the family-deity (*kulādhībhavana*) is the fruit of prohibited actions— is as follows:
"Either one leader, whether a Kṣatriya or a twice-born (*dvija*), or one knowledge, whether spiritual (*adhyātmikī*) or the triple Veda (*trayī*)."
‘A single wife, whether of noble birth or beloved; a single friend, whether a king or an ascetic.
This is the fourfold conceptualization based on genus, action, quality, and substance, as expressed by the phrase ‘this is that.’
The categories such as genus (*jāti*) and so forth are the very objects [of cognition], yet they are conceptualized;
from what [source] does this determination by means of genus and so forth arise?
Or rather, the word "or" (*vā*) expresses an alternative possibility, whereby there is a confusion between existence and non-existence.
An example of a restrictive statement (niyamokti) is as follows:
“This dispute is indeed pointless; Pārtha alone is the wielder of the bow—he who is celebrated not only by his own people, but even by his enemies. (51)

Thus, this threefold restriction— characterized by the exclusion of non-connection (*ayoga*), the exclusion of connection with another (*anyayoga*), and the exclusion of absolute non-connection (*atyantāyoga*)— is indeed devoid of purpose;

for the particle *eva* attached to the qualifier, by virtue of grammatical usage, excludes the absence of that [connection] when a connection with the qualifier alone is impossible, and thus it remains fixed upon the exclusion of connection [with anything else].

In the phrase "Pārtha alone [is the archer]," the particle *eva* is connected with the qualificand (*viśeṣya*); by excluding the attribute of being an archer from anyone other than him, it serves to indicate the exclusion of connection with another (*anyayogavyavaccheda*).

However, in the word "kevalam" (alone), it does not exclude either non-connection (*nāyoga*) or connection with another (*anyayoga*) regarding the act of praising; rather, by making known that specific relation, it indicates absolute non-connection, which is termed the "exclusion of absolute non-connection" (*atyantāyogavyavaccheda*).
An example of this is the statement of exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*): [e.g., "Only grasses are eaten by the deer"].
‘Five five-nailed animals are to be eaten; he does not see with his left eye; what is there that is improper which does not please her regarding the firmness of her breasts?
This is called *parisaṃkhyā* (exclusion), which consists in the permission of the remainder through both injunction and prohibition.
Regarding the five-clawed animals, "five are to be eaten, and no others";
regarding her breasts, "hardness is not [to be found] in speech and the like"— these specific injunctions imply the prohibition of everything else.
He does not see with the left eye, yet he certainly sees with the right;

what is non-existent, and what is unseemly? If this [right eye] does not please him, then the other is indeed existent. Thus, the negation of a specific case (viśeṣa-niṣedha) and the permission regarding the remaining case (śeṣa-vidhi-abhyanujñā) concern that which is not mutually connected in terms of word or meaning. Furthermore, [this applies] to that which is not joined together.

The construction (*yojanā*) that is performed is what is called "reasoning" (*yukti*) by the wise. First, there is syntactic unity within a single word (*padaikavākyatā*); next, syntactic unity within a sentence (*vākyaikavākyatā*); and thereafter, syntactic unity within a section (*prakaraṇaikavākyatā*). This process continues until the completion of the composition; such is the function of the poet.

In this regard, although expressions such as "Bring the white cow with a stick"—which have their linguistic conventions (*vyutpatti*) already established in common worldly usage—may enter into poetry, they nonetheless occupy the path of poetry only when accompanied by a striking mode of expression (*bhaṅgībhaṇiti*). Therefore, since even well-known phrases are worthy of adoption [in poetry], where a mutual syntactic connection does not immediately appear on the surface, the poet must ensure that there is no stumbling in the comprehension of the intended sentence-meaning by introducing specific qualifiers that serve as reflections of his own intention. It is precisely because of this distinctiveness (*vaicitrya*) that these constitute figures of speech (*alaṃkāra*);
thus it has been said: "of that which is otherwise unjoined... (*ayujyamānasya*).
The word "at first glance" (*āpātataḥ*) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].

The application (*yojanā*) consists in the introduction of specific qualifiers conducive to the syntactic connection (*anvaya*); its objects are words, meanings, individual words (*pada*), sentences (*vākya*), context (*prakaraṇa*), and literary compositions (*prabandha*).

He states that meaning (artha)— whether as the meaning of a word (padārtha) or the meaning of a sentence (vākyārtha)— is sixfold according to its distinctions, and that this constitutes reasoning (yukti): "The word and the word-meaning, the sentence and the sentence-meaning."
Its subject matter, its context, and its composition are thus designated;
and therein, it is also called a "pada."

The series of states consisting of the yoga, the cause, the synonym, the member, and the whole, being well-established, serve as the basis for the application of words for the sake of establishing the word-meaning. (46) "Yoga" [etc.]...

In the passage beginning with "yoga," the word *paramparā* (succession), which follows the *dvandva* compound, is construed with each member individually: *yoga* (etymological derivation), *yogarūḍhi* (conventional-derivative meaning),
and *kāraṇa* (the causal relation).

Although words are established through their meanings for the sake of establishing the sentence— which consists of a collection of words— as a single unit, nevertheless, a specific feature conducive to that [establishment] is perceived directly in some cases within the words themselves, while in other cases it is perceived in the word-meanings; with this in mind, he says:
They know that "yukti" (reasoning) in this context is the mutual connection of contradictory categories and so forth; [this is] regarding the objects of meaning.
(47) [The phrase] "of contradictory [things]" means:

In this way, even for a sentence and its meaning, another sentence situated within the sentence that conveys a sentiment (rasa) consistent with the primary sentiment under discussion constitutes the "embryo" (*garbha*); along with the "inner embryo" (*nigarbha*), these are the "concealment" (*saṃvṛtti*) and the "conjunction" (*sasamuccaya*).
Such are the causal factors (*hetu*) of the logical connections between sentences, beginning with "let it be done thus. || 48 ||
"Garbha" refers to the womb; "nigarbha" is that which is situated as a part within that [womb] in such a manner.
"Saṃvṛtti" is the concluding statement of what has been said.

*Samuccaya* (conjunction) is the simultaneous connection of multiple elements of equal primary status with a single action; by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), *anvācaya* (incidental mention) and others are included. It involves the employment of pronouns such as *yat* and *tat*, as well as the repetition of an action and conjunction.

And the repetition of an action (kriyāsamabhihāra) is mutually connected with the sentence-meanings [of the pronouns] "yat" and "tat," and so forth. By the inclusion of the word "ādi" (and so forth) in the phrase "yat-tad-ādi," which refers to those [pronouns] residing in the subject and the predicate respectively, there is the recurrence or repetition (āvṛtti) of these actions; this is called *abhyāsa* (repetition).

The conjunction (*samuccaya*) or accumulation (*samabhihāra*)— meaning intensity or excellence (*prakarṣa*)— of heterogeneous things in a single place at one time is what serves to justify descriptions of mountains and so forth that would otherwise be incredible.
In this context, the statement is intended as a logical argument concerning the subject matter of the section.
As for the word "yat," it refers to the state of appearing in an excessive degree, which constitutes untrustworthiness.
Thus, the wise have stated that reasoning (*yukti*) also pertains to the subject matter of a literary composition (*prabandha*).
A series of examples is presented here to clarify their specific forms.
Since these reasonings are exceedingly difficult to comprehend, he says: "The example itself [is provided]. (51)
In this regard, the application of words based on etymological derivation (*yoga*), conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), and their successive combination (*paramparā*) is as follows:

"May the light of the Sun protect you—that light which, in the eastern quarter, possesses the beauty of the vermilion from the head of the elephant that conquered Indra; in the western ocean, it possesses the brilliance of the fire from the mouth of the horse-faced one (Agni) who was cast out; at dawn, it is magnificent with the pollen of lotuses blooming from intoxication; and it fills the interior of the cauldron-like expanse of the sky. (Verse 53)

In this [verse], the following series of manifestations are seen shining forth in the eastern quarter: the series of *yogarūḍhi* (etymological-conventional) compounds beginning with "Jambhajit-dvīpa" (the island that conquered Jambha); the series of synonyms (*paryāya*) beginning with "the fire from the mouth of Hayāṅganā" (the mare-headed goddess); the series of causal relations (*hetu*) beginning with "intense with the pollen-paste of lotuses blooming through the intoxication born at dawn"; and the series of part-whole relationships (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*) beginning with "the interior of the cavity of the sky-cauldron. Thus, the word "Jambhajit" is etymological (*yaugika*) because it is formed with a primary suffix (*kṛt*).

Likewise, because *jambhajit* and *dvipa* are also compounds, both of these, when employed through their etymological connection (*yoga*), are restricted by two conventional usages (*nirūḍhi*) to the intended object in the form of an elephant; similarly, *hayāṅganā* is a synonym for a mare.
"Āsya" is a synonym for "mouth," and "hutabhuj" is a synonym for "fire"; thus,
this sequence of words, through the recognition of these synonymous terms, produces the intended cognition of the submarine fire (*vaḍavāmukhānala*).
The causal sequence is as follows: the opening of the filaments of the *madana* flower is the cause of its pollen, and that [pollen] is the cause of its prominence;

furthermore, the sky-vat is the locus (*aṅgin*), its part (*aṅga*) is a single region, and its cavity is its interior—this sequence of whole and parts is the source for the syntactic unity of the intended words. This he explains with the word "here" (*atra*).

Vibrating with the power of poetic expression, it reflects in the hearts of the sensitive (sahr̥daya) as a conceptual construction of word-meanings based on the conjunction of contradictory classes and so forth, as for example:

“That body of your father, which possesses the form of both woman and man— with thighs like the trunk of a lordly elephant, arms like [elephant] trunks, and full breasts and shoulders like the heads of elephants— we behold in your face, both beautiful and terrible.”
"May he protect you—he whose face becomes playful at the thought of Vārāhī, who, looking at her face, neither praises nor scorns it while laughing, and who is then embraced by his Mother.

(54)" In this verse, the following are observed as instances of the conjunction of opposites (*viruddhayojanā*): the conjunction of contradictory species (*jāti*) in "having the forms of both woman and man"; the conjunction of contradictory actions (*kriyā*) in "neither praises nor scorns"; the conjunction of contradictory qualities (*guṇa*) in "charming yet fierce"; and the conjunction of contradictory substances (*dravya*) in "we behold the body in her face.
This is [the figure] *nāga*.

"The thighs of your father, the Lord (Ishvara), are like the trunks of the king of elephants in the portion belonging to Parvati; his arms are in the portion belonging to the Goddess (Devi); his breasts are as full as the frontal globes of an elephant in the portion belonging to the Goddess; and his shoulders and upper arms are in the portion belonging to the Goddess. Thus, we behold such a body of your father, Ishvara, in your face through the union of a male and female elephant in the form of your single tusk"—this is the humorous remark of Varahi. Varahi is a specific Mother-goddess (Matr) who is of the nature of a boar.

The leader (vināyaka) with the face of an elephant—by the negation of both praise and blame through the phrase "your father," despite the fact that even two contradictory qualities such as femininity and masculinity are perceived through mutual exclusion; and by the distribution of the parts of loveliness and terror through the similarity between the face and the body, which reflects the intended meaning on all sides—a construction has been established. Thus, the unity of the sentence (*ekavākyatā*) of those words expressing this is achieved.
This is what he says: "In this [verse]... (atra).

The logic of sentence (*vākyayukti*) concerning the internal structure of a sentence (*vākyagarbha*), etc., is as follows: “The earth, with its four boundaries demarcated by the temples of the world-elephants, is being established; and it is already established. Even as we speak of this, our hair stands on end. Behold!
It is now being bestowed upon a Brahmin. What more need be said? Salutations to that Rāma, from whom this wondrous tale emerged and into whom it has likewise vanished. (55)

In this case, while they are speaking, "Behold! We are indeed thrilled with horripilation" is the *vākyagarbha* (the embryo within a sentence); therein, the phrase "Behold! is the *bhāvāviṣkāravācānigarbha* (the disclosure of emotion through speech);
and furthermore, "Salutation to that Rāma" is the *vākyasaṃvṛtti* (the concealment of a sentence).

The collection of statements, "From where this wonderful narrative emerged, and where it has set," constitutes this very *yukti* (logical reasoning) concerning sentences, which serves as a mere indication of their arrangement.

By means of the sequence beginning with "birth" (*jāti*) and "action" (*kriyā*), the contradiction of action (*kriyāvirodha*) has been explained, bypassing the contradiction of quality (*guṇavirodha*), since the latter is well-known [as a contradiction].
*Āghāṭa* means a boundary;
*garbha* was previously explained [in that context]. In that very place, for the speaker who is seized by the sentiment of wonder, the subsequent sentence "Look! (*paśyata*) is the *nigarbha*.

When a rasa that is connected to the primary rasa being presented by the *garbha* (embryo) sentence imparts excellence to that [primary] rasa, this concealed *garbha* is called *nigarbha* (the inner embryo).
This has been stated to be expressive of the manifestation of a *bhāva* (emotional state).
For instance, when one ought to say, "It was bestowed upon the Brahmin; it was enjoyed by them," and so forth, the phrase "what else? is joined as a *saṃvṛtti* (concealment/elision).

For thus, when one considers how much of the conduct of this Greatly Powerful One (mahānubhāva) can be obtained, it is determined that silence alone is appropriate here; a great excellence is thus inferred from the conjunction of the two statements—“from whence this wonderful story emerged” and “wherein it has set”—by means of the particle *ca*, which expresses the accumulation of the logical reason contained in the preceding sentence. Such are the examples.
Namely: the thirteen components of the plot (*vīthyaṅga*) comprised within the introduction;

the sixty-four junctures (*saṃdhi*) beginning with *vilāsa* and so forth; and the five junctures (*saṃdhi*) which constitute the limbs of the drama—known as the opening (*mukha*), the counter-opening (*pratimukha*), the development (*garbha*), the pause (*vimarśa*), and the conclusion (*nirvahaṇa*)—which consist of the five stages of the fundamental sentiments (*rasa*).

The functions of the seed (*bīja*), the drop (*bindu*), the banner (*patākā*), and the series (*prakarī*) are to be understood as the application of specific portions of speech in the form of various chapters and compositions, which serve as the causes for taking up those respective [themes]. This logic of sentence-meaning is illustrated by the following example: "Stay at the door; go to the courtyard; go outside; enter the house; look at the path; enter the hall; ascend the platform; go to the turret; go to the roof-terrace; enter the mansion. In this passage, each successive phrase serves as the cause for the subsequent one, thereby establishing the logical connection between the meanings of the sentences.
"O pitiless one! 'Send the messenger! Send the messenger!'—having thus commanded her repeatedly, she remains upon the bed as if made of stone, so that the night does not reach its end.

Here, in the first quarter there is *kriyāsamuccaya* (accumulation of actions); in the second, *kriyābhyāsa* (repetition of action); in the third, the expression "send the messenger, send the messenger" constitutes *yāvat-kriyāsamabhihāra* (intensive repetition of an action);

and in the remainder, the employment of the relative and demonstrative pronouns (*yat* and *tat*) in the phrase "she remains in such a way that the night does not reach its end" is understood as the cause for the logical connection of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha-yukti*).

This aforementioned *vākyārthayukti* (logical consistency of the sentence-meaning) serves as the basis for the justification of descriptions of mountains and other things that might otherwise seem incredible; it pertains to the subject matter of a literary context (*prakaraṇa*), as in:
"For the delight of Murāri, the gods brought [the mountain] from Sumeru and piled it up with its peaks..."
"The qualities of loftiness and beauty in poets whose speech is unrestrained do not become false.
The cause for the establishment of the subject matter pervading the composition, however, is the *yukti* (logical reasoning) pertaining to the composition;
as follows:
“Where is a cloud—a mere confluence of smoke, light, water, and wind—and where are the meanings of a message, which must be delivered by living beings with functional senses?
Yet, disregarding these things out of eagerness, the Guhyaka made his request; for those afflicted by desire are naturally wretched toward both sentient and insentient things.
“Wait! he said.

When her beloved transgresses the boundary of the appointed time for her attendance, his heart becomes agitated by a longing doubled at that moment; sometimes he stands at the door of the inner chamber as before,
then, not seeing her there, he goes out into the courtyard of the house,
and after that, he departs outside the dwelling.

This very *hi* is prescribed after the imperative (*loṭ*) in all tenses when it refers to various verbal roots whose actions are of different classes, according to the rule "optionally in a collective sense" (*samuccaye 'nyatarasyām*, Pāṇini 3.4.3).

For this very reason, the verb *īkṣati* ("he sees")—which expresses generalities such as the state of abiding in the door that serves as the delimitation for the act of seeing—is employed with a restricted application, according to the grammatical rule: "In the case of a cumulative conjunction, the verb expressing the general action is used [with the specific]. Thus, it is employed in subsequent construction (*anuprayoga*).

Utterly disbelieving that the hero’s heart was completely shattered, she ascends the hall (*śālāgṛha*) desiring to look out from the street-corners at ever-increasing distances; from there, to the highest turret (*aṭṭālaka*); immediately after that, to the higher roof-ridge (*valabhī*), that is, the upper chamber (*uparitanakuṭī*).
For this very reason, the action of stretching upward is repeated here, according to the rule: *kriyāsamabhihāre loṭ loṭo hisvau vā ca tadhvamoḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.2).
2) Thus it is instructed; and for this very reason, it is stated: "In the case of the first [verb], there is the subsequent employment according to the rule" (Pāṇini 3.4.46).

4) Thus, even when that very verbal root is employed [in this way], if the hero does not come, the activity of the female messenger (*dūtī*) is the only recourse; it is therefore taught that one should either blunt [the hero's pride] oneself or go there. By this, the excellence of the message—which intensifies his various inclinations—is manifested through the repetition of the word [indicating frequency].

For this very reason, the former teachers maintain that the co-utterance with the imperative suffix (*loṭ*) is the scope [of the particle *yāvat*], and not its denotation as it is in the case of *ghañ* and other suffixes; thus, they delimit it by the word "as far as" (*yāvat*), which enters into the fourth sentence following the word "iti. The direction is: "as far as 'send, send' (*saṃdiśa saṃdiśa*). *Bhaṇiti* is a mode of expression, and it occurs both in cases of possibility and impossibility.
"And it is conceptualized among the conceptualizations of wonderful particular conventionalities.
[Regarding] "utterance" (*ukti*):

utterance is expression, the act of vocalization, or the act of definition; since that is common to all sentences, one might wonder how it can be an ornament (*alaṃkāra*). Anticipating this doubt, the word "manner" (*prakāra*) is used.

*Prakāra* is a specific mode or form, a particularity that transcends both worldly and scriptural expressions; this very thing has been described by some, who do not consider the issue of non-pervasion (*avyāpti*), as the general nature of poetic figures (*alaṃkāra*).

Since there is no difference in their being forms of speech, how can this [distinction] be consistent? Therefore, under the guise of demonstrating the division, he establishes that very nature [of each] based solely on the specific object: "Possibility," and so forth.

In that context, "possibility" (*saṃbhava*) is the cognition of something that, though impossible in the external world, appears like a horse painted by an illusionist; a statement whose essence is "conceivability" (*saṃbhāvanā*) is that which imparts such a cognition.

For that very [power], by the maxim: "But there is indeed another sequence of words in which nothing at all appears as if it were something," is skilled in the creation of various meanings; it becomes the cause of worldly transaction according to the principle: "The universe transforms exactly as it pleases him. Thus, in such a subject matter, the description of sublation (*bādha*) by way of a reversal of the methods well-known in the treatises is called "impossibility" (*asaṃbhāvanā*).
It is said:
"In this world, those poets are victorious who can transform this entire universe at will."
“Or it is seen situated in the sky like a cloud, yet it is insubstantial.

For this very reason, this [figure], being negative in form, is a specific attribute (viśeṣa) that excludes things of its own kind; by establishing that [attribute] in some instance, it conveys a particular intention of the poet. Thus, following the principle that “in the context of a negation, a statement of a specific attribute takes the form of an affirmation,” it relies upon that [affirmation] and, while producing aesthetic wonder, culminates in the specific attribute. While the description [of the moon] undergoes contraction in the context of the sprouts, it culminates in an affirmation that is negative in form.

When a wonder that arises unexpectedly and generates astonishment is to be negated, any formulation other than one characterized by the nature of a marvel is incapable of ascending to the level of poetry; therefore, in this context, the presentation of astonishment must certainly be adopted as the very essence of the work. Thus, in the occasion of a prohibition, a statement in the form of a negation constitutes a poetic conceit (*utprekṣā*) regarding a particularity that is externally impossible or non-existent.

Relying on that [general statement], having fulfilled its purpose through mere injunction and prohibition, it effects some specific detail; thus, in the context of injunction and prohibition, it prohibits in a general sense and enjoins in a specific sense. This is the poetic formulation (*bhaṇiti*) consisting of the form of a prohibition-injunction.
Herein, an example of a formulation based on possibility (*saṃbhava-bhaṇiti*) is as follows:
"Having previously possessed a beauty such that it bore the splendor of a stream from the interior petals of a freshly opened *ketaka* flower, and a luster fit for the weaving of a string of pearls—"
‘That moonlight, whose power is unclouded, must be ladled out with jars, drunk from cupped hands, and measured with lotus-stalk sprouts;

it exists [now]. Here, because the resemblance of the moonlight to a stream flowing from the freshly split inner petals of a ketakī flower is possible, this is a *saṃbhavabhaṇiti* (statement of possibility) of two forms, due to the word ‘sadyas’ (freshly).

The melting of the petals of the *ketakī* flower, followed by their assuming the form of streams; then, the sprinkling of that [liquid] which is compared to the thick outer portion of a water-jar; thereafter, the measuring of the slightly diminished middle portion with the hollows of palms and cupped hands; and finally, the drinking of the remaining essence by means of lotus-sprouts—by means of these metaphors, a wondrous poetic conceit (*saṃbhāvanā*) arises through appropriate words such as "to be sprinkled" (*utsekyā*), which possess a beauty impossible in the external world.
An example of an impossible statement (*asaṃbhavabhaṇiti*) is as follows:
"Where can this moonlight-water be drunk? How could a garment be fashioned from the fibers of lotus-stalks that serve as channels for the vine of her face?
Alas, where is the fragrance of bakula-garlands that can be measured by a vessel? How, indeed, can a dream bring that lotus-eyed woman before my very eyes?

(60) In this passage, because it is impossible for the moonlight and other things to be drunk like lotus-stalks and the like, this is an "impossible statement" (*asaṃbhavabhaṇiti*) in the form of a negation.

The capacity of a dream to directly manifest the thought "Where can this be drunk? is inconceivable; yet, when stated in such a manner, it brings forth a certain splendor. Thus, by means of the *prativastūpamā* (point-by-point comparison), this seemingly impossible statement (*asaṃbhavabhaṇiti*) expands the beauty of the passion suggested by the implied meaning, while the term *pārī* refers to a vessel.
An example of a specific statement (viśeṣabhaṇiti) is as follows:
"May Halī, intoxicated with wine, purify you—he who carries eyes whose lids are cleansed by the remnants of Revatī’s teeth from the drinking party. (51)

In this case, the fact that the eyes of Balarāma are pure even though they have tasted the remnants of Revatī’s teeth, and that Balarāma is purifying even while intoxicated by wine— this is the "particularity" (viśeṣa); thus, this statement of particularity takes the form of an affirmation within a negation,
as in the verse beginning with "Revatī."

Since it has never been observed that what is left over from the teeth of a dog or what is kissed by those who eat leftovers possesses purity or sanctity, this statement— which prescribes such acts for the plowman and his wife as a form of divine conduct— demonstrates the world-transcending nature of the gods' behavior; thus, this is a statement in the form of a prescription occurring within a context of prohibition,
an example of *saṃvṛtibhaṇiti*.
“‘An ornament for ornaments, a special mode of adornment for the act of decoration,

and even a counter-comparison for a comparison— such is her body, O friend. Here, by means of sentences such as ‘the body is an ornament for ornaments,’ which conceal the expansion of the method of describing well-known [qualities], this is *saṃvṛtibhaṇiti* (concealing speech) in the form of a negation within a positive injunction.”
Regarding the phrase "of the ornament":

here, in the context of an elaborate description well-known in poetic convention—such as "moon-faced, with eyes white as milk, lips like the *bimba* fruit, and breasts like the frontal globes of an elephant"—the restriction or prohibition of that [description] in the manner stated is an "ornament" (*alaṃkāra*) consisting of a statement of its establishment; thus, while manifesting a particular luster, it becomes a "statement of wonder" (*āścaryabhaṇiti*) in the form of a negation when an injunction would otherwise have been expected. For example:

"From lights this darkness has arisen; this fire was born from the waters; this deadly poison has emerged from nectar; and heat, born of shadow—what indeed is the logic behind this? This knot is truly firm and strong, O friends, that even through what is pleasing, this unpleasantness has been produced by your consolations.

(63) Here, because the emergence of darkness and so forth from light and so forth is of a marvelous nature, this is an "utterance of wonder" (*āścaryabhaṇiti*); in the form of a prohibition of a positive injunction, it takes the form of both injunction and prohibition.

Regarding the phrase "to the lights," the statement "for he is dear [and] does not act unkindly" indicates that while the non-practice of unkindness is established as a general rule, its occurrence toward a rogue by the turn of fate is a marvel; this [verse], by opening up such a wonder, reveals through a universal succession of experiences an inner heart permeated with love.

If there were the emergence of darkness and so forth from light and so forth, then even though it must be categorically denied that "the unpleasant arises from the pleasant," because that which is established by direct perception cannot be otherwise made, [the text] prescribes and forbids while unable to tolerate a contradiction with the object of knowledge; thus, in the context of prohibition and prescription, there occurs a statement in the form of both prescription and prohibition, which is a figurative expression based on conceptualization (*kalpanā-bhaṇiti*), as for example:
"The visible is to be perceived by thousands of eyes and to be contemplated by tens of thousands of minds."
‘The indescribable youth of the fair-browed one, which is to be enjoyed for hundreds of millions of well-performed deeds, is delightful.

Here, because the excellence of the beauty of her youth is such that it can only be beheld by those with thousands of eyes and the like, there is an attribution of such fitness; thus, this is a "statement of imagination" (*kalpanābhaṇiti*), appearing as a prohibition within an injunction, or an injunction within a prohibition.

Although the visibility, perceptibility, and enjoyability of youth—along with age itself—are brought before the consciousness through two eyes, one [eye], and even a very small amount of mental effort and good fortune, nevertheless, unable to endure the commonality of this woman—who is the very essence of his life—with other lovers, he imagines a thousandfold quality in her eyes and so forth. Thus, having ascended the path of negating common attributes, he establishes a specific distinction.
This statement, in the context of affirmation and negation, takes the form of an affirmation by means of a constituent negation; let this suffice for the detailed discussion.
In a sentence, the proper arrangement and weaving of word and meaning is known as *gumphanā* (composition);
it is produced by means of words, meanings, sequence, synonyms, phrases, and sentences.
(Verse 53) Regarding the term "in a sentence":

A sentence (*vākya*) is a collection of words delimited by the communication of a single meaning; when that [sentence] is the subject matter, its composition (*racanā*) is the arrangement according to sequence. To the question, "How can such [composition], even if it were over-extended, be an ornament (*alaṃkāra*)," he says: "Properly" (*samyak*), which means having attained the fitness (*aucitya*) characterized by the conferring of nourishment upon the subject at hand.
The status of being a sentence is established through the two terms "meaning" (*artha*) and "word" (*śabda*), acting as qualifier and qualified respectively.
With the intention that the synthesis of these two alone is completed, he said "of word and meaning.
In this context, the word is of two kinds: the expressed (*vācya*) and the qualifier (*upādhi*).
The expressive word is of two forms, distinguished as the word (*pada*) and the sentence (*vākya*).
The term *pada* is twofold: that which consists of synonyms (*paryāyabhūtarūpa*) and that which does not consist of such [synonyms] (*atathārūpa*).
Having accepted this diversity of intended meaning (*vivakṣāvaicitrya*), he analyzes it as follows: by the word "word" (*śabda*), a word that is non-expressive (*apratipādaka*) is stated.
The meaning is what is to be expressed;
the mention of "sequence" is an illustration of a limiting condition (*upādhi*).
Among these, that which is produced by words is as follows:
‘During Rāma’s consecration, the golden pitcher from the hand of a young woman, overwhelmed by intoxication,

fell and, reaching the steps, made the sound “ṭhaṃṭhaṃṭhaṭhaṃṭhaṃṭhaṭhaṭhaṃṭhaṭhaṃṭhaḥ. This verse, beginning with “ṭhaṃṭham,” is an example of *śabdaracanā* (verbal composition), because it lacks a sentence structure consistent with the meaning of such meaningless syllables.

The sound of the golden pitcher—fallen from the hand of her who was filled with joy at the festival of Rāma’s royal consecration, slipping as it descended the series of steps, and gradually reaching the ground—is imitated by the succession of words [uttered by the people]. This conforms precisely to the intended meaning;
for by thus [describing the sound], a certain excellence of intoxication is suggested, such that she does not even notice the pitcher has fallen from her hand.
An example based on meaning (arthakṛtā) is as follows:

"May those forms of the enemy of Manmatha protect you—those whose omnipresence is equal to space, time, and the self; in whom he shines; wherein the rays of that mass [of light] become nectar; who became the bile for that [fire]; who was the fuel for its oblation; who is the carrier for its life-sustenance; and whose quality this [wind] possesses. (66)

This [term] *artha-racanā* (the arrangement of objects) consists of the eight entities beginning with space (*vyoman*), which are characterized as the forms of Maheśvara; because it is constructed by the successive synthesis of these, it is called *dikka-la* (space-time).

Since all corporeal things are equal to the nature of space and time, and since all-pervasiveness is defined as being the substratum of conjunction, it belongs to space alone. When that [space] is implied by the object, the word "this" (*ayam*) applies to the subject under discussion; and depending upon that, it is proper to refer back to it with the word "that" (*tat*).

The Lord Sun shines in the sky with a specific power characterized by the ability to overpower the light of the moon, stars, and so forth; having referred to him with the word *yat* (which), the author points back to him in the subsequent sentence with the word *adaḥ*.

The rays of the sun, reflected through the path of the ears, receive the designation "nectar" (*sudhā*) only when they reach the water-like *iṣṭāśinī* (the vessel of the desired). The word *yat* is situated right there, and the subsequent word *tat* takes as its object the meaning brought forward by it—and so on: from the very mass of waters the moon was born; their bile is fire; the sacrificer [is the one] for whose morning and evening oblations [that fire exists]; he lives by means of the wind.

And since the construction of the meaning of the subsequent sentences is established through the cumulative synthesis of each preceding one—just as the quality of fragrance belonging to earth carries [the scent]—even though the arrangement of words is necessarily concomitant with the arrangement of meanings, nevertheless, because the arrangement of meanings is what must first be considered here and is thus primary, it is appropriate to designate it by that alone; with this intention, he explains: "In this context," the sense being that if this chain were not perceived, how could the eight forms of the Supreme Lord be obtained?
An example of [simile] formed by sequence is as follows:
“The length of her pair of eyes surpassed the blue lotuses; the expanse of her breasts acted as the prima facie argument against the grandeur of the jars;
the playfulness of her eyebrows emulated the grace of Cupid’s bow; and the moonlight of her face eclipsed the luster of the moon. (67)

Since the presentation of the leaf, the statement of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), the restatement, and the exposure of the refutation have been composed here according to the sequence well-known among learned people, this arrangement of the sequence suggests a competitive spirit in the offering of the leaf, as expressed by the phrase "blue-black" (*nīlābja*).
And since that [comparison] culminates in similarity, it is an implied simile (*pratīyamānopamā*);
by making the frontal lobes of an elephant the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), the status of the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is understood to belong to the expanse of the breasts,
and thus a contrast (*vyatireka*) is suggested.

The meaning of the explanatory passage on the example is as follows: even by way of a positive statement (*anuvāda*), a simile (*upamā*) is perceived, and by way of a negation (*dūṣaṇa*), a contrast (*vyatireka*) is perceived; thus, when the primary subject is concluded through *samāsokti* (condensed expression), a sequence that is not directly denoted by the words—serving as a limiting condition (*upādhi*)—is woven together, such as in the case of "giving" (*dāna*) and so forth, which are well-known in the terminology of scholars and others.
An example created by means of synonyms (*paryāya*) is as follows: "Even while merely scratching [the ground], she knows the secrets of the *kunta* bird; she converses with the parrots..."
“Release Pūṣābhāsa; indeed, I am not a brazen female parrot.
[Only a female parrot knows the prattle of a male parrot; you who speak like a parrot, release him, for I am certainly no impudent female parrot.]
