Since this was composed in accordance with the meanings of the various synonyms for the name Śuka, it is called *paryāyaracanā* (a composition of synonyms); thus, a certain libertine, imitating the speech of a parrot, began a jest toward his beloved, saying, "Kaṇailli ccia" (only [the parrot]).
Perceiving his foolishness, she gave him a fitting reply: "A female parrot indeed knows the prattle of male parrots, but no other does;
and I am not a female parrot.
Therefore, this effort of yours is in vain"—this is the meaning.
In this context, the words *kunta*, *kīra*, and *pūsa* are synonyms for the male parrot (*śuka*),
while the words *kaṇaillī* and *vāāḍī* are synonyms for the female parrot (*śukī*); furthermore, among these, the word *kīra* is a direct loanword from the source language.
Others are regional forms;

thus, the weaving together of these synonyms— which correspond to the forms already described— within a single sentence is the very domain of a poet’s creative effort, as illustrated by the following example:

By him were obtained those winds which, having reached the shore, were kin to the lotuses blooming on the high banks; winds that were agitated by clusters of piṇḍītagara flowers and caused the monkeys—swinging from the trunks of bakula trees entwined with their lolling, vine-like tails—to cry out, thereby making the echoes resound through the ancient cave-dwellings in the forest groves. (69)

In this place, where the old cave-dwellings resound with the cries of baboons entwined with *bakula* trees and their tails like creepers, the winds—kinsmen of the lotuses, tossing the tall *piṇḍītagara* flowers—have reached the shore; because these words, though redundant and even superfluous, were composed in accordance with the sense for the sake of alliteration and to fill out the meter, this poetic arrangement, beginning with "lolallāṅgūlavallī," is an example of such composition.

When the intended purpose is accomplished merely by the composition of the stated words, such as "encircled by a creeper-like tail" (*lāṅgūlavallīvalayita*), the insertion of additional words like "trembling creeper" (*loladvallī*) serves no other end than this: without it, the desired alliteration (*anuprāsa*) cannot be achieved; without that, the propriety of the meter (*vṛttaucitī*) is not fulfilled; and without it, those various specific qualities of the tail and so forth would not be perceived. For the Goddess of Speech (*sarasvatī*) wins over the connoisseurs (*sahṛdaya*) only when she is firmly established upon her foliage. Thus: "That which [occurs] among words employed solely for the sake of the comprehension of the sentence..."
They call that "pallava" (sprout) which is embellished by other words;
however, that sentence which is without such "pallava" is not pleasing to poets.
Nevertheless, such [a style] is employed by those from the North, though it is censured by poets.
This is what he says with the words beginning with "here," as stated by the author of the Vākya:
"The status of being a husband's brother-in-law [is appropriate] toward the elder brother; the status of being a husband's younger brother [is appropriate] toward the younger brother."
"And in the middle [sections], there are three [verses] for each of the three Pāñcālas.

Here, because a vast subject matter is expressed with very few words, the meaning of the sentence has been composed even by means of an inversion [of the usual order] for the sake of brevity of the text; this composition of sentences is what is called "vākya" (sentence).
The composition of sentences occurs only within a great sentence (*mahāvākya*);

for instance, for those sensitive readers who contemplate how even a very brief sentence such as "the husband, the father-in-law, etc. conveys a vast mass of meaning, their power of poetic creation shines forth without obstruction.

For this very reason, by setting aside the [literal] power [of words], the violation of sequence is also set aside when, after denoting the beginning and the end, one denotes the middle; thus he says: "In this context, they call it *śayyā* (bed) when there is a mutual arrangement of word-meanings; that occurs in some cases through what has been introduced (*prakrānta*), and in others through what has not been introduced (*aprakrānta*). (54)

"Śayyā" (the couch) refers to the act of arranging the principal subject matter after first fixing some single object in the mind; it consists of the composition of a continuous sequence based on that subject, wherein the principal element is occasionally joined with other elements,
both relevant and irrelevant, among the various objects.
And that [yojanā] is twofold, distinguished by its application to words and meanings;
therein, the yojanā of things and sentences is seen in the compositions of great poets.
As for meaning, it is twofold: that which is useful for the contextual subject matter and that which follows from it.
The second type is also "transcendent" (*atikrānta*) and "not as it is" (*atathābhūta*); the analytical statement (*vibhāgavākya*) is to be explained as before.

It is observed that the transcendent [simile] occurs in some cases between word-meanings (*padārtha*), in some between phonemes (*varṇa*), in some between sentence-meanings (*vākyārtha*), and in others between sentences (*vākya*), or even among miscellaneous elements. (55)
The word "atīti" (thus) is used for the purpose of establishing the meaning of the words; likewise, it serves to establish the meaning of the sentence.
An example of such a connection introduced therein is as follows:
"Having promised 'So be it,' and having somehow dismissed Umā, the Destroyer of Smara (Śiva) called to mind the seven sages who consist of light.
This is the very account of the arrival of the seven sages that was already under discussion.

This [verse], "seyaṃ saptarṣīṇām," is an instance of an irrelevant incident (*aprakrāntaghaṭanā*), wherein the narrative of the Seven Sages is introduced through its connection to the context of Gaurī’s marriage. For example:

"In this regard, they cite this ancient history, the dialogue between a Niṣāda and the sage Saṃvaraṇa" (72). This is an *aprakrāntaghaṭanā* (the introduction of an uninitiated matter), because it introduces the dialogue between the Niṣāda and Saṃvaraṇa, which was not previously under discussion.
This [example] concerns that which was not previously introduced;
although the conversation regarding the concealment of the sitting posture has no utility for the preceding or succeeding context, its connection is established by way of an anecdote.
An example of a past event is as follows:
“Even though the time has passed, the rows of *kadamba* groves, with their buds moistened by smiles, have caused him amazement.

This is an instance of *atikrāntaghaṭanā* (the occurrence of what has passed), because there is a connection— by means of Rāma’s memory— with the moist budding of the *kadamba* groves, which, though past, still produces amazement in the mind of the lover in separation.
Regarding the phrase "this [fear] occurs even for that which has passed":

since it is possible for the very perception of the blooming of the *kadamba* flower to cause distress to people separated from their lovers, how can it be said that the fear belongs to something past? To this it is replied, "by way of memory";
the meaning is that it occurs through the power of mental construction (*saṃkalpa*), such that the past object appears as if it were being perceived directly.
In this way, the construction of the words through future application by means of qualities and so forth should also be understood, as for example:
"By that mouth which was forcibly cast into the fire while falling [with its wings] severed..."

“Because he was addressed by Hara with the words ‘Sve ti heti,’ he became this Rāvaṇa. Since the word *svāhā* is composed of the syllables *sve ti* and *he ti*, this is an instance of *padaghaṭanā* (the construction of a word).
This is *svā*.

The *homa* consists of an offering accompanied by the utterance of *svāhā*. At that moment, when the head had been severed and only half a step remained before the completion [of the sacrifice], because the Supreme Lord’s heart was pacified by a surge of compassion for living beings, He uttered the word *hā*, expressive of his distress. By that very word being uttered incessantly, the term *svāhā* was established.
The construction of the sentence is as follows:
“O *Haṃsa*, give me back my beloved; her life has been taken away by you.”
"When one is accused of theft based on a single manifested part [of the act],"—

this is "Sentence-Composition" (*vākyaghaṭanā*), because the latter half of a verse established in a previous treatise has been joined into a single syntactical unit with a preceding half-verse that, while not following its literal meaning, is nevertheless not contradictory to the subject matter at hand.
This is what is meant by the phrase "in a previous treatise," and so forth.
An example of *sugabha* with scattered composition (*prakīrṇaghaṭanā*) is as follows:
“In one eye there is Śrāvaṇa, in the other Bhādrapada; Māgha is on the surface of the earth, and autumn is on her cheeks.”

‘In one eye is Śrāvaṇa, in the other Bhādrapada; Mādhava dwells upon the bed of the earth; on her cheek is Śarad; summer rests upon her limbs; Mārgaśīrṣa resides in the sesame grove; and the cool season (Śiśira) has taken up its abode in the lotus-pond of the lovely girl’s face. (76)

In this context, because the [meanings] beginning with "heard" (*śrāvaṇa*) do not occur simultaneously but are scattered, their unification constitutes what is called "scattered unification" (*prakīrṇaghaṭanā*).
Furthermore, this word *prakīrṇa* (scattered) signifies "the rest" (*śeṣa*);

therefore, there is room here for other types of scattered unifications as well. Consequently, those verbal functions found in the compositions of great poets—namely, the primary (*mukhya*), the secondary (*gauṇī*), the indicative (*lakṣaṇā*), the metaphorical (*tadbhāvāpatti*), the figurative (*upacaritā*), and the indicated-indicative (*lakṣitalakṣaṇā*)—are also heard in this work.
In this context, among the six initial locative expressions, the term "of the girl" (*mugdhāyāḥ*) is primary as a word denoting a relation;
in the remaining two locative expressions, it is secondary;
and in the four month-denoting words beginning with Śrāvaṇa, it is metaphorical (*lakṣaṇā*).

Furthermore, even when the six locative expressions such as "in the rainy season" (*varṣāsu*) and so forth are indicated and expressed, since they cannot occur simultaneously, the attainment of existence (*bhāvāpatti*) is obtained through the presumption based on what is heard (*śrutārthāpatti*);
moreover, the verbal form "has settled" (*āvāsita*) is understood as being merely figuratively indistinct,
and even indication-by-indication (*lakṣitalakṣaṇā*) emerges in these very cases through [grammatical] exposition.

For this term *āvāsita* has its expressive power firmly established (*nirūḍhābhidhānaśakti*) in reference to great kings and the like who have settled in a desired location with great retinues; when it is applied metaphorically (*upacāreṇa*) to things such as the *śrāvaṇa* [sacrifices], it indicates their own greatness, thereby implying a vast retinue and a grand scale of production, and thus suggests that even the undertaking at hand possesses a significant consequence.

Furthermore, these [months], whose simultaneous existence in the eyes and other [senses] is untenable, being applied here and there by the power of their own words, indicate the excellence of those respective qualities through the excellence of their own qualities.
Just as this or that [month], even while possessing separation, indicates the intensity of the pain of parting, which in turn indicates the intensity of affection for the lover;
so too, the rainy season is indicated by these two constituent parts, namely Śrāvaṇa and Bhādrapada.

And although its presence in the eyes is logically untenable, it is introduced by the force of the grammatical suffix (*vibhakti*); thus, while indicating a continuous abundance of tears proximate to its own natural quality—the flow of droplets of milk—it indicates the intensity of longing in her who yearns for union.
By the latter member of the compound, "Mādhava," the spring season is indicated.

He too, finding no place to rest upon the bed of the earth's surface, is—as before—established by the power of verbal suggestion (*śabdaśakti*). Perceiving the abundance of his own qualities in the flowers, tender shoots, lotus stalks, lotus petals, and so forth, which constitute a collection of cooling accessories, he perceives the internal fever of Kāmāvatī;
thus, by the word "autumn" (*śarat*), a specific season is denoted.

Unable to find a place on her cheeks, the word "spot" (*sthalam*), through the power of its recollection as a term of praise, draws forth the excellence of her own qualities—such as the arrival of white lotuses, the coming of swans, the clarity of the moonlight upon the lily ponds, and so forth—and by perceiving the paleness on her cheeks brought near by these, it indicates the emaciation of the deer-eyed woman caused by separation;
thus, even by this [word], a specific season is indeed expressed.

That [fever] also, being impossible in a non-limb [such as the mind], indicates the eighth stage of love (the state of madness) by attaining a wealth of its own characteristics—such as the dust heated by the harsh rays of the sun, the heat of the wind, and the impurity of forest fires—which constitute a peerless collection of symptoms for the fever of love never before seen.
By the preceding member of the compound, "Mārgaśīrṣa," winter (*hemanta*) is indicated;
and by that, it is indicated through an implied comparison—that just as a sesame field is reaped in winter, so now her ease is being reaped—thereby indicating an excessive mental anguish.
What, then, is this quality shared by sesame fields and lotus groves that constitutes such pleasantness— namely, this state of being saturated with moisture?
And it is because of this that women going to meet their lovers generally hold sesame fields and clusters of lotuses in high esteem,
as they say:
‘This cluster of lotuses, which has become the ornament of our village, is exceedingly beautiful;
it has been turned into a sesame field by the frost. (77) [Exceedingly lovely, having become the decoration of our village...]
The cluster of lotuses has been made to resemble a field of sesame plants that have been reaped by the winter cold.
For this very reason, in the subsequent sentence, he refers to the cluster of lotuses also by the term "lotus-pool," as follows:—
‘The cool [breeze] has taken up residence in the lotus-pond of the lovely one’s face.

Here, by the word *śiśira* (cool), which refers to a specific season and is applied to the lovely one’s face through the power of the word itself—just as it would be to a lotus-pond—the resulting fading of the reflected image (*chāyā*) of the well-known natural excellence of the lotus grove is observed; this fading of the reflection of the lovely one’s lotus-face, its lily-eyes, her flower-like smile, and the filaments of her teeth, indicates the intensity of the emotional state (*anubhāva*) of love-in-separation (*vipralambha*).

Furthermore, in the context of describing the beauty of the cool season (*śiśira*), by the principle that "the face is half the body" or "the face is said to be the whole body," it is also indicated here— through the characteristic of the primacy of the starting point— that among all the seasons, the cool season alone is preeminent.
In this regard, [the months] beginning with Śrāvaṇa are "scattered" (*prakīrṇa*), meaning they are dispersed and perceived in various places.
That [conjunction] is of two kinds: by way of time and by way of space.

For here, the simultaneous presence within the body of a woman separated from her lover—which is impossible for the six months and seasons beginning with Śrāvaṇa occurring all at once—is described; this, being conveyed through the words "Śrāvaṇa" and so forth by resorting to a figurative function (guṇavṛtti), makes known the intensity of the pangs of separation due to travel.
In this same manner, a conjunction of things scattered across space may also be cited as an example.

For example: "Nectar is nectar, the moon is the moon, likewise the lotus is the lotus; Rati is Rati, Kāma is Kāma, and honey is honey"—thus, for the most part, things do not undergo mutual confusion; yet how is it that this woman possesses states of being (*bhāva*) that consist of all these qualities?

As for the various distinctions such as *siddha* (perfected) and so forth described here, they do not produce such aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*), and thus we have omitted them for fear of making the work too voluminous.
Even those various unique forms that are scattered are to be understood by the term "scattered" (*prakīrṇa*);
furthermore, the inclusion [of these] is also employed because they have not been explicitly mentioned. Thus he says: "And this word 'scattered'...
He states the purpose of this alternative explanation with the words: "by that..."
The power of a word to convey a meaning is denotation (*abhidhā*); it is threefold: primary (*mukhyā*), secondary (*gauṇī*), and indicative (*lakṣaṇā*).

Among these, that in which the meaning is first perceived, as if it were before one's face, is the primary; it consists of the literal sense and the attainment of the state of being that [literal] thing.

In that regard, an example concerning the connection between intermediate meanings where the sense is exactly as it is (*tathābhūtārtha*) is as follows: “Since the entire world has been pervaded by you through these eight very bodies—your own self, the moon, fire, wind, the sun, the earth, water—who else here could be so shameless as to desire to speak otherwise? By him [it is said]...”
That very attainment of its own state— which has as its object the relationship between another meaning and its own meaning—
is indeed the bringing about of "being thus" for that which was not so;
for this reason, the Teachers maintain that the primary power is precisely the capacity for direct denotation of one's own meaning as delimited by itself or by something else.
For example: “The lotus is full of bees; the swans have been driven away;
by someone, a large umbrella has been spread over the village pond.
This is the secondary (gauṇī) [metaphorical] function, wherein the meaning is mediated by a quality (*guṇa*).
[Metaphor is] of two kinds: based on a quality (*guṇanimitta*) and based on a figurative designation (*upacāranimitta*).

Among these, that in which there occurs a relationship mediated by a quality—whether perceived or explicitly stated—due to the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the relationship of qualifier and qualified when two words denoting substances are used either in grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) or in grammatical subordination (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), is "based on a quality.
For example: "An enemy-atom-pile, a jar of loveliness, and an elephant-goad of the bodiless god (Kāma)."
"Why do you carry breasts that hang down, filled with the weight of a man?

[In this case], the application of a qualifier belonging to one thing to another—whether through a primary or a secondary sense—is indeed "metaphorical function" (*guṇavṛtti*), as it subsists upon a connection with a quality (*guṇa*).

However, there is this distinction: in the former case (metaphor), the connection with the quality belongs to the expressed object (*abhidheya*) by virtue of that quality; here, however, the connection with the quality belongs to the substantive (*viśeṣya*) which is its own expressed object.

For example: "He who experiences pain for the sake of another, who is naturally sweet, whose very transformation is indeed desired by all here—if he does not immediately attain growth when fallen upon barren soil, is it the fault of the sugar-cane, and not rather of the desert land devoid of virtue?
This is *lakṣaṇā* (indication) mediated by a connection to its own primary meaning (*svārtha*).
As it has been said: "That cognition which is inseparable from the primary meaning is called indication (lakṣaṇā);
this very function, which is the lifeblood of the clever's figurative speech (vakrokti), is held to be twofold: pure (śuddhā) and based on further indication (lakṣitalakṣaṇā)."

Among these, the *śuddhā* (pure) [indication] has as its object that which is directly related to its own meaning and is invariably concomitant (*avinābhūta*), as in: "whose face is pale like the ripening of a *tālī* leaf," and "the cheek is pale like a fresh slice of elephant tusk.
Some maintain that when that which was previously indicated itself becomes the indicator of another, it is called *lakṣitalakṣaṇā* (indication of the indicated).
For example: "The bee [drinks] honey from the single vessel of the flower," and "Bhīma [is] of terrible prowess.
For here, by means of words such as *dvirepha* (two-repha), it is only the bee and so forth that are indicated (*lakṣyate*) through indication (*lakṣita*), and not the osprey or others.
Others, however, call this "indication of the indicated" (*lakṣitalakṣaṇā*), which is an indication mediated by another indication.
For example: "Three kinds of men gather the golden flowers of the earth—the hero, the man of learning, and he who knows how to serve.

This should be explained as before: through the association with specific terms such as "attaining that state" (*tadbhāvāpatti*), words like "primary" (*mukhya*) have as their scope the exclusion of others who are not of such a nature.
But where does the repetition of a single word occur? To this he says:
"In this [verse]," namely: "In one eye, in the other, on the surface of the earth, on the cheeks, and on the limbs," and so forth.

Although the word *gaṇḍasthala* (cheeks) here is indeed secondary (*gauṇa*), nevertheless, because it has been used in such a way since time immemorial, it is considered a primary usage; thus it is said, "among the six words denoting substrates."

And since words such as "limb" (aṅga) and others are employed precisely with reference to something else as qualified by their own primary meanings, the function [of these words] is indeed primary (mukhyā).
Likewise, in the case of the possessive term "of the bewildered one" (mugdhāyāḥ), there remain two words expressing the substrata: "the lake of the mud of smiles" (suhacchitilavaṇe muhapaṅkaasari).

In this instance, the application of the terms *tilavana* (sesame field) and *saraḥ* (lake) to the face and the lotus is based solely on the qualities of being saturated with oiliness (*sneha*) and freshness (*sarasa*), respectively. Although both words in the compound *mukhapaṅkajasarasī* are secondary (*gauṇa*), the function (*vṛtti*) of the word *paṅkaja* (lotus) is equivalent to primary denotation (*abhidhā*); therefore, it is improper to treat it as a subject of the poet’s creative intent (*kavisaṃrambhagocara*).
Furthermore, the four terms *sāvaṇa*, *bhaddavaa*, *māhava*, and *maggasira* denote the four months [of the rainy season].

And those [words] indicate a collection beginning with "rain" (varṣā) which is mediated by their own meanings and their mutual relationship; according to the method to be explained, "rain" and the others denote six substrates (*ādheya*). Since these cannot simultaneously exist within the body of Virahavatī, they—being employed through the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of their respective causes for application (*pravṛttinimitta*), such as the excellence of water and so forth—attain a function (*vṛtti*) consisting in the attainment of that state [of being the body].
Six varieties of this [function], such as illusory manifestation (*vivarta*), transformation (*pariṇāma*), and superimposition (*adhyāsa*), have not been shown here for fear of prolixity.
Presumption based on what is heard (*śrutārthāpatti*) is a conceptual construction rooted in the non-occurrence of the meaning of what has been heard.

The word *āvāsita* ("caused to dwell") is conventionally established as a qualifier for a king or similar subject through its primary function (*mukhyavṛtti*). When it is employed with reference to another object—such as the spring season—which is separated from that primary sense by its own specific qualities (*svaviśeṣaguṇa*), it undergoes a secondary function (*gauṇīvṛtti*) and thereby attains the status of a qualifier even for the spring. This [secondary function] is a "metaphorical indication" (*lakṣaṇā*) mediated by another indication; it is what is termed "indication of the indicated" (*lakṣitalakṣaṇā*).
To explain how that [term] comes to be applied in the sense of "āvāsita," he says: "by way of metaphorical usage" (*upacāreṇa*).

This means that because it is used for things such as sounds (*śrāvaṇa*) through some degree of similarity, it is employed by depending on that metaphorical usage; thus, by means of indication (*lakṣaṇā*), it transfers to the subjects at hand qualities such as "greatness" (*mahattva*) which are invariably concomitant with its own primary meaning.
He states the second type of indication, which is mediated by the first, with the words: "even of the one under discussion" (*prastutāyā api*).
For even in the case of one who has encamped and possesses the aforementioned qualifications, a great consequence is observed in the seizing of an enemy's fortress and so forth;

that [consequence] is perceived here in the activity under discussion, characterized by the torment of a woman separated from her lover. Thus, this is a case of *lakṣaṇā* (indication) with the intervention of a single *lakṣaṇā*;
he states that it also occurs with the intervention of two *lakṣaṇās*: "And those... and so on.

The months of Śrāvaṇa and so forth possess an abundance of their own qualities, such as incessant rainfall; because this [rainfall] is invariably concomitant with its own purpose, it indicates a corresponding abundance of qualities in the eyes and other organs, characterized by the flow of tears and so on. This is the second type of indication (*lakṣaṇā*), which is preceded by that [first type].
He states the third type, which is preceded by these: "This very one, this very one...
Thus he says, "Another [type]... indicating that indication should be understood as being preceded by these three types of indication.
However, rasa is manifested through the *sneha* (affection) as conditioned by the *vibhāvas* and so forth; it is not, however, indicated (*lakṣyate*). This has been explained in detail elsewhere.

Now, one might ask: "Which richness of its own qualities (*svadharmasaṃpad*) is proximate [to the denoted], and which is the richness of those [seasonal] qualities? To distinguish this, he says: "In that context" (*tatra*). If there were no indication of the whole (*samudāyalakṣaṇā*) in words such as "autumn" (*śarad*), then, having begun with the months and proceeding to name the seasons, there would be a breach of the initial course (*prakramabheda*). Furthermore, the cognition of the excellence of the season (*ṛtusaṃpat*) upon the cognition of each specific season would not occur anywhere. Therefore, the indication of the whole is indeed appropriate.

The phrase "by these two" refers to each [word] individually; however, it is not possible for there to be indication (lakṣaṇā) in both words simultaneously by virtue of the direct hearing of the case-ending (vibhakti-śruti).

The relationship between locus and located is expressed by its own power through the seventh and first case endings; when that [literal expression] is untenable, indication (*lakṣaṇā*) toward another meaning arises.

Thus, since Vaiśākha is the latter constituent part of spring, which consists of the aggregate of Caitra and Vaiśākha, there occurs indication—by way of indicating the aggregate—even in the word *mādhava* (Vaiśākha) which denotes that [constituent], as well as in the case of words expressing praise.

For tigers and the like, which possess an inherent similarity (*sārūpya*), are compounded with words denoting the object of comparison; and since that similarity consists precisely in excellence, it remains focused on praise. Consequently, as long as the expressed meaning has not been perceived, it is impossible to perceive either the similarity itself or any other form [of it]. Thus, the perfection of its own qualities (*svadharmasaṃpat*)—which arises simultaneously with the perception of the expressed meaning and is akin to the resonance following a bell—is understood. Indeed, in this very sound, the autumnal sky, flowers, swans, and so forth are manifested through the expansion of its own perfection.

There is no perception of similarity between sitting at ease and cutting sesame seeds as there is between the moon and the face; nor is there anything expressed here that could constitute such a similarity. Thus he asks: "What then?
Lest it be thought that such a [literal] convention does not exist, he provides the answer: "That which is this...

[meaning] that there is no single entity called "affection" (sneha) belonging to both parties, and yet even without being explicitly expressed, a similarity rests upon the commonality of the word itself. Therefore, he states another mode: "And of the women going to meet their lovers... (abhisārikāṇām).
To the question, "How is this understood? he says: "Since it is thus.
[Objection: But surely, in this context, it is the word *kamalinī* that is presented as the object of great esteem, not the sesame grove (*tilavana*). To this he replies: "For this very reason.

The sense is that, by bestowing upon both the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*) the status of being objects of great esteem for the beloved, the poet intends to convey that even the sesame garden has now become a forest due to the winter.

By the maxim "the face is half of the body" and so forth, the word "face" (*mukha*) indicates preeminence; thus, by the metaphorical identification (*tadbhāvāpatti*) of the winter as being "cool in the lotus-pond of the face," the very preeminence of the winter season among the seasons is illuminated.

As it has been said: "The winter season, though its moon is dimmed, brings delight to young women, appearing radiant and beautiful through the application of collyrium, the sending of gifts, and the acceptance of words [of endearment]."
Recitation for the sake of specific meaning is here considered sixfold, consisting of variations in tone, division of words, distinctions, gestures, and beauty. (56)
An example by means of intonation (*kāku*) is as follows:
“If my messenger is dear to him, then I too am dear;
if his words are dear to her, then mine too are dear. (78)
In this case, injunction is perceived by one intonation (*kāku*) and prohibition by another;
*kāku* refers to that pronunciation which, having been initiated with intent toward a single meaning, is rendered otherwise through the desire to express a different meaning— this is *paṭhiti*.
And "alteration" (anyathākaraṇa) occurs through six means, beginning with *kāku*.
In this context, "a broken tone in the throat is termed *kāku* by the wise.
It is of two kinds: injunctive *kāku* (*vidhikāku*) and prohibitive *kāku* (*niṣedhakāku*).
When there is a prohibition of these two, an elliptical injunction (*vidhi-kāku*) results in a mandatory injunction by means of altering the utterance of another;
for example: "Even a dart smeared with deadly poison might be endured by the steadfast within its faltering [wounds], but not the false, bitter words of a villain provoked without cause."
Thus, by altering the intended meaning through a change in the manner of utterance according to the rules, there is the "intonation of prohibition" (*niṣedhakāku*), which manifests a negation;
he illustrates this with the verse beginning "yadi":

if, by straightforward speech such as "If the messenger is dear, then I too am dear," a feigned affection toward a deceitful lover were understood, yet through *kāku* (intonation) the sense "I am not dear to you at all" is conveyed, expressing jealousy and anger.
By tone, for example:

"O fair-browed one, you are angry; thus food has been cast aside, conversation with women abandoned, and fragrant garlands, perfumes, incense, and the like have been shunned by me from afar. O passionate one, I bow before you—cast off your resentment; be gracious now. Truly, my beloved, in your absence all the directions have become dark to me. (79)

In this context, because of the use of the protracted (pluta) accent in the word *dṛṣṭe*, even this sentence—which is primarily intended to appease an angry beloved—attains the quality of appeasing an enraged glance.
Since accents such as the protracted and the acute (*udātta*) have a much more extensive application in poetry than they do in the Veda, he cites an example: "O fair-browed one, you... and so forth.

When I have fallen at the tips of her feet and am seen by her, the mere utterance of the long vowel "pra" in the word *prasīda* (be gracious) is devoted solely to the appeasement of an angry beloved. However, when the aforementioned *pluta* (protracted) pronunciation is employed—as in calling from a distance—the cognition arises that it is an address directed toward her angry gaze, according to her instruction.
For food and such things are indeed common to both [the husband and the wife]; thus, this is simply an instance of *śleṣa* (paronomasia).
In this way, one should understand that through the transformation of a short vowel into a long one, or a long vowel into a short one, another meaning is perceived.
Just as from the words "Viśvāmitra" and "Viśvānara," two specific individuals—a sage and a royal sage—are understood, so too is there the understanding of an address as "O young woman";
in this same way, the acute accent (*udātta*) and others are also to be inferred according to what is observed.
For example, by means of word-segmentation (*padaccheda*): [text omitted].
"O Lord of all kings, I have seen a woman beautiful in every limb, separated from you in this lovely forest.

Here, if the phrase is divided as "mayā virahitā" (separated by me), it refers to Purūravas; however, if it is divided as "tvayā virahitā" (separated by you), it results in a different sentence for Parvata.
There are four types of elisions (*cheda*): *śṛṅkhalā*, *bhaṅga*, *parivartaka*, and *cūrṇa*.
Among these, *śṛṅkhalā* is the arrangement resulting from the mutual combination of preceding and following syllables;

for example, when one reads: “*kāntāratarutalāsitamṛgayuvaracitāntarā-*,” it is understood as: "the interior of which was densely covered by hunters delighted by the amorous cooing of their beloveds."
This very [structure], through the combination of various phonemes (*varṇa*), is called a "chain" (*śṛṅkhalā*).
"Breaking" (*bhaṅga*) is merely the division into two parts by means of an interruption within a single word;
he illustrates this with the example beginning with *sarva*.

In the compound expression *mayā virahitā* ("separated from me"), when it is taken as a whole, the question directed by Purūravas—who is seized by the eighth stage of love (*kāmāvasthā*)—is: "Have you seen her separated from me? However, when *mayā* is detached and connected with the preceding sentence, it becomes the reply of Parvata: "Separated [from him], she was seen by me. This shifting of syllables constitutes *parivarta*.

For example, in the phrase "kalikāmadhugarhaṇā," if one adopts the syllables exactly as they are heard, it is understood as "the censure or reproach of the honey of the bud" (*kalikāmadhuno garhaṇā nindā*). However, when there is a division through the imagination of different syllables, such as "kalikāmadhug arhaṇā," then it is indeed worship; for the analysis of the compound syllables is "the wish-fulfilling cow (*kāmadhenu*) in the Kali age. This is the "powder" (*cūrṇa*).

For example: "Behold the waters of the ocean, from which the shells and the beloveds of the fish have long since departed. Here, according to the literal reading, it is understood that [the ocean] is difficult to taste and has its edges marked by agitated oyster-shells and fish; however, when there is a division of the compound *dūrasamunmuktaśuktimīnāṅkāntam* through the process of *piṇḍacūrṇana* (breaking up the mass), then two vocatives—"O you who are possessed of extreme joy" (*atyantaharṣayuktā*) and "O you who have cast off grief" (*tyaktaśokā*)—are perceived as addressed to Kṛṣṇa through a different parsing of the words. As for example: [in the verse: "O you who are possessed of extreme joy, O you who have cast off grief, behold the waters of the ocean, from which the shells and the beloveds of the fish have long since departed. Here, the word *atyantaharṣayuktā* is a vocative addressed to Rādhā, while *tyaktaśokā* is a vocative addressed to Kṛṣṇa. Thus, the meaning is that the ocean is "difficult to taste" because it is devoid of the nectar of the lips of Śrī Rādhā, and its "edges are marked by agitated oyster-shells and fish" because it is filled with the agitation of the oyster-shells of the breasts of the gopīs and the fish-like eyes of the cowherds. Alternatively, the meaning may be that the ocean is "difficult to taste" because it is devoid of the nectar of the lips of Śrī Rādhā, and its "edges are marked by agitated oyster-shells and fish" because it is filled with the agitation of the oyster-shells of the breasts of the gopīs and the fish-like eyes of the cowherds. "May that Mādhava—who, having destroyed the Mind-born [Kāma], formerly rendered the body of Bali womanless; who bore the Gaṅgā; who brought about the destruction of Andhaka;
who is fond of peacock feathers; and whose praiseworthy name the immortals call 'the remover of the moon-bearing head'—and who wears a serpent as a necklace and bracelets, protect you at all times.
(81) In this verse, due to the difference in word-division between "yena dhvastamanobhavena" and "yena dhvastamano'bhavena," two meanings are perceived: "Mādhava" and "Umādhava."

Since both of these two are established as primary, and since they do not abide in a relationship of subordinate and principal (aṅga-aṅgin) nor in the form of the relevant and the irrelevant, this is a *śleṣa* (pun) due to their mutual lack of connection.
However, when read with a division of words (*padabheda*), because two meanings are perceived through successive turns, this is a reading with a division of words where *śleṣa* is subordinate;
[this is indicated] by the word "yena."

In the past, during the destruction of Tripura, the body of Nārāyaṇa—the conqueror of Bala—was made into a weapon by Śiva, whose mind-born passion (Manobhava) had been destroyed; it was reduced to the state of an arrow. He bore the Gaṅgā Bhāgīrathī; he brought about the end (kṣaya) of Andhaka, a particular Daitya; he has the peacock-feathered Kārttikeya as his vehicle; he possesses a head marked by the digit of the moon (śaśimat); he bears the praiseworthy name Hara, which cuts through the delusion of the universe; and his necklaces and bracelets are composed of serpents itself—at all times, throughout eternity—such is the description in the case of Umādhava (Śiva).

In the context of Mādhava (Kṛṣṇa), however: by whom the cart of the mind was destroyed—that is, annihilated; who, through non-existence (*abhavena*), meaning being free from the bonds of worldly existence, conquered Bali; whose body was formerly transformed into the form of a woman during the churning of the ocean for the purpose of deluding the demon Bhr̥tagr̥hayālu; who lifted up the mountain named Govardhana and the earth submerged in the single ocean; who is the dwelling place (*kṣaya*) of the Andhakas—a specific clan of the Yadus; and who is fond of the tail-feathers (*pattra*) of the peacock (*barhin*), as indicated by Gautama in the *Gopāla-dhyāna*: "He who wears a crest made of peacock feathers" (*barhipattrakr̥tāpīḍam*).

He who possesses the name "Śaśimad-rāhu-śirohara" (the remover of Rāhu’s head from the moon)— derived from the sense that he churns the moon— and who has as his beloved Garuḍa, the slayer of serpents; such is his praiseworthy name.
He in whom there is absorption into the Sun, which is the Word-Brahman (*śabdabrahman*); likewise, he who is "all-giving," meaning one who bestows whatever is desired.
Now, since this appears to be a *śleṣa* (pun) based on the simultaneous utterance of words of different forms, rather than a mere recitation, he says:
"And of those two"—for a *śleṣa* occurs when there is a mutual connection between the elements being joined together.

And that relation—whether characterized by a relation of identity and intentionality (*rūpatātparya*), or a relation of subordinate and principal (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*), or a relation of standard of comparison and object of comparison (*upamānopameyabhāva*)—will be explained further on.
Nor is only one of these intended here; rather, it is this very "reading" (*paṭhitir eva*), which, in a single utterance, conveys a different meaning through the differentiation of words.
By this, the distinction from both *samādhi* and *samāsokti* has also been stated.
Is it then the case that dependence on pronunciation does not exist at all? To this he says: "Subordinate to the pun" (*śleṣopasarjana*).

For where there is an intention to express something as primary, designation by that [primary element] is appropriate; therefore, even the conventional usage of "pun" (*śleṣa*) in another sense must be justified here by means of dramatic gesture (*abhinaya*), as for example:
‘With breasts of such a size, with eyelashes of such a length, in such a state, after so many days. (82) [With breasts of this very measure, with eyelashes of this very measure...]
"Only this much [of a state], in only so many days.
Here, because the words "only this much" regarding the breasts and so forth are recited along with corresponding hand gestures (*hastābhinaya*), a specific meaning of that kind is understood;
furthermore, the *apadeśa* (indication) is itself a specific type of gesture.
For example:
"Having obtained prosperity from this [source], that Daitya does not deserve destruction from this very same source"—
having thus referred to himself, he speaks.

In the expression "eddahametta" ("just so much"), since all the constituent words are common to various other meanings, the cognition of the specific intended quantity does not arise until there occurs a recognition of the accompanying gesture (*abhinaya*), which consists of the counting of fingers with both hands extended, the palms opened, and the fingers spread out.

Therefore, this is "recitation through performance" (*abhinayapaṭhitir*); it is called "performance" (*abhinaya*) because it leads toward the actualization of action, making the nature of the object itself as if directly perceived.
To this effect he says: "being thus," and so forth, including the phrase "even the designation."
The instruction on action (*kriyāpadeśa*) is a designation of the self;
although it is a specific type of dramatic representation (*abhinaya*), it is treated separately because it produces aesthetic charm (*kāntikara*).
For as long as the qualification regarding the specific utterance of its own form is not considered, the specific cause for the attainment of glory (*śrī*) and capability (*kṣama*) is not perceived.
An example by way of beauty (kānti): “The host of enemies saw that the king had lost his support; the forest, through its enjoyment of waterfalls, became devoid of strength. (83)

In this verse, regarding the support [of the meaning] as "the forest" (*vanam*)— in these two words, or rather in the second and fourth positions where the letters *va* and *ba* occur— a difference in meaning arises in a reading that possesses beauty through the semi-vowels (*antaḥstha*) and the labial class (*pavarga*), as well as the letters from the end of the labial class and the semi-vowels.

Since "beauty" (*kānti*) refers to a shadow (*chāyā*) which, being of an unimpeded nature, cannot exist in individual phonemes as it does in words, it is understood here as "auditory form" (*śrutirūpa*).

For instance, in the word *avalambanam*, when one considers the sequence of the *va* and *ba* sounds located in the second and fourth positions respectively as being [respectively] a semi-vowel (*antaḥstha*) and a labial stop (*pavarga*), the meaning understood is that he saw no cause for protection within the single word *avalambanam*. However, when there is a consideration of those same two sounds in the second position—as being a labial stop and a semi-vowel—in the phrase *abalaṃ vanam*, then through the division into two words, *balaṃ* and *vanam*, the understanding of a different meaning arises: that he went to a forest (*vana*) that was devoid of strength (*abala*).
This has been stated as follows: "In one place or in two places," meaning he saw that it was devoid of beds and food;

*śī* refers to a bed (*śayana*), and *at* refers to eating (*adana*). Because it was devoid even of the enjoyment of waterfalls—that is, the mere use of waterfall water—it was for that very reason destitute of strength.
And here, one should understand that there is a combination (*saṃsṛṣṭi*) of this [alliteration] with *yamaka*, by taking the repetition [of syllables]; otherwise, it would be merely *yamaka*.
Others, however, describe the recitation differently:
They describe that recitation of the previously mentioned *sūkta* as being performed by altering the words, quarters, halves, or phrases [of the verse]. Others, however, say... [as follows].
The word "otherwise" (anyathā) should be supplied even after this point;
for even by changing the feet and so forth, it is indeed the recitation itself that is qualified, as he says: "of the hymn previously mentioned."
For this very reason, it is not possible to recite [the verse] by altering the *śloka*;
therefore, the intended meaning is that there are twelve types of recitation when combined with the previously mentioned varieties of division.

Although altering even a single foot (*pāda*) is indeed a type of word-division (*padabheda*), nevertheless, in that case there is no abandonment of what was previously stated; however, here there is the conception of a different word through the abandonment of that [previous form]—this is the distinction.
In that regard, the alteration of words is twofold: by way of the stem (*prakṛti*) and by way of the inflection (*vibhakti*). Among these, an example by way of the stem is as follows:
"Because of her incomplete laughter, [her eyes] were as if washed away by luster; because of her half-closed eyes, they appeared like ear-lotuses."
"Let the lord of the Kuntalas, having entrusted the burden [of the kingdom] to you, drink from the honey-scented faces of his beloveds.

(84) Here, when "mayi" (in me) is read in place of "tvayi" (in you), this very sentence of entreaty becomes a sentence of permission, due to the change in case-ending—as follows: [The lord of the Kuntalas, having entrusted the burden to me, let him drink from the honey-scented faces of his beloveds. (84)
“Together with his host of servants, his kinsmen, his friends, his sons, and his younger brothers,
the son of Pāṇḍu will soon slay Suyodhana in battle by means of his own strength.

(85) In this case, when the phrase “the son of Pāṇḍu [slays] Suyodhana” is read instead as “the son of Pāṇḍu [slays] the son of Suyodhana,” then although it possesses an inauspicious meaning, it becomes auspiciously meaningful with respect to Suyodhana.

In that regard, he states that a word ending in a case-suffix is divided into two types by way of the distinction between the qualifier and the qualified: "The alteration of words is twofold. For example, through the alteration of the lines [of a verse], as in:
"In a secluded, lonely place at night, inside a house, in a rash act..."
"And in the case of denial after having deposited [the object], a divine ordeal becomes applicable.

In this verse, if the reading in place of the third quarter were "tanvaṅgī yadi labhyeta" (if a slender-limbed woman were to be found), then this, while being suitable for the investigation [of the deposit], would also be suitable for [the pursuit of] love, as it provides a secluded place.

Regarding the act of secret meeting as a form of daring, according to the maxim that "the secret is weightier than the public," the divine action— which is characterized by being akin to one's own enjoyment—
is like the alteration of half [of the original state].

“The manifestation of the moon is truly great only so long as the orb of the sun does not rise; but once that treasury of all light has risen, what difference is there between the moon and a fragment of a white cloud?
(87) Here, if instead of the middle two lines one were to read: “so long as those women do not laugh even slightly more brightly... [the defect remains].

If it is read as "tābhiḥ punarvihasitānanapaṅkajābhiḥ" (by them, whose lotus-faces were smiling), then this, although consisting of an expression of heroism (*vīra-rasa*), becomes an expression of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*). [In the case of the word *gauritarā*,] the shortening of the first member of the compound occurs by the rule "gharūpa— " and so forth.
And by altering the other three lines as follows:
“Endowed with renunciation, they fly up to heaven; bereft of renunciation, they go to hell.
There is nothing difficult for those who practice renunciation, for renunciation indeed destroys all calamities. (88)
In this context, by taking up only the fourth quarter and altering the other three quarters, the reading that is about to be stated occurs;
and while it is intended as a praise of renunciation, it also results in a censure of renunciation,
as follows:

"It is a falsehood on this earth that 'renunciation destroys all calamities,' for by the renunciation of that lovely-eyed woman, all my calamities have arisen. He further indicates that a mutual commingling of these [faults], such as the alteration of word-order and so forth, also occurs: ‘tyāgo hi sarvavyasanāni hantītyalīkametadbhuvi saṃpratīdam | jātāni sarvavyasanāni tasyāstyāgena me mugdhavilocanāyāḥ || 89 ||’ And he makes known that there is also a mutual intermingling of these [faults], such as the alteration of word-order and so forth.
By means of altering the language, for example:
“What is the use to me of that crest-jewel of kings, with his forefeet lolling as he reclines? Or what is the use to me of my father-in-law, who sits upon the throne of Indra’s laughter?
Those regions, those mountains, and those forest lands alone are dear to me—Kosalla and Tanaaya, where I may bow down and rejoice at every step. (90)
In this regard, if it is recited in another language, then this statement of Sītā in the Śaurasenī dialect was reported by Sumantu to Daśaratha in the Sanskrit language as follows:

"What use have I for my father, whose foot-tips are kissed by the crest-jewels of the foremost of kings; or what use have I for my father-in-law, who sits upon the lion-throne in the assembly hall of Vāsava?"
‘Those countries, those mountains, that forest land, and that very Kausalyā’s son who is dear to me— wherein I bow at his feet and rejoice.
(91) As for this recitation of such a kind, [the author] says— "Now, this is Śaurasenī"— to explain how the masculine and feminine genders are understood despite the difference in dialect (*bhāṣā*).

Anticipating the objection that there is a deficiency in the classification [of *yamaka*], and intending to provide a resolution according to the manner already stated, he says: "This recitation of such a kind"—that is, the occurrence of a collection of phonemes (*varṇasaṃhati*) which has a single form despite having distinct meanings, whether its parts are contiguous (*avyapeta*) or non-contiguous (*vyapeta*), is called *yamaka*. (58)
Now, the figures of speech (*alaṃkāras*) that depend on repetition (*āvṛtti*) must be defined.
Since they rely on repetition extending throughout the entire poem, *yamaka* (chiming) is the foremost among them; with this intention, he says: "vibhinna...
[and so forth]. The phrase "vibhinnārtha" (having different meanings) is intended to exclude the absence of difference in meaning (*arthābheda*).
Therefore, even if one or both [of the two words] are devoid of meaning, the *yamaka* (rhyme) is still encompassed.
However, since this would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as "saro rasaḥ" (lake, juice), it is stated: "having a single form.
Here, "form" (*rūpa*) means sequence (*ānupūrvī*). The analysis of the compound is: that which has different meanings and yet possesses a single form.

In the verse beginning with *vividhadhava*, although there is a repetition of a single syllable (*va*), it is with the intention that it is the collection of repetitions alone that evokes the sequence of *yamaka* (rhyme/alliteration) that the word "of the aggregate" (*saṃhateḥ*) is stated.
The connection with the distant term is as follows: *yamaka* is defined as the repetition of a collection of syllables that possesses a single form despite having different meanings.
This repetition is of two kinds: non-repeated and repeated with an interval (*vyavahita*).
That *yamaka* is divided into "separated" (*vyapeta*) and "unseparated" (*avyapeta*),
according to the distinction between fixed and unfixed positions, and by the division of the quarters (*pāda*).
Where the beginning, middle, and end of the quarters are designated as the positions, it is [the separated type].
That which is uninterrupted, or otherwise [interrupted], they know as *sthānayamaka*.
He classifies it generally: "uninterrupted" (*avyapeta*) means the absence of intervention (*vyavāya*), that is, non-separation (*avyavadhāna*).

Since both of these [types of *yamaka*] are threefold according to the distinction of position (*sthāna*) and so forth, the author states their intermediate subdivisions following a restatement of what was previously mentioned: "That" (*tat*).
Because there is no specific delineation of the beginning, middle, and end of the quarters (*pāda*), it is called "positionless *yamaka*" (*asthāna-yamaka*);
this too is twofold.

The variations of *yamakas* in verses with four, three, or one foot consist of those at the beginning, middle, and end; those at the middle and end; those at the middle and beginning; and those occurring everywhere.
[The author] says "four, three," etc., to explain that they differ according to their scope based on the variation of four or more feet.

The beginning, the middle, and the end—these three, namely the beginning, middle, and end, are pure. When combined as "middle-and-end," "middle-beginning," "beginning-and-end," and "beginning-middle-and-end," there are four mixed types; thus, [the suffix] *tasi* is used in the sense of all case endings (*sārvavibhaktika*).
"Their divisions and their combinations are exceedingly numerous; some of them, both easy and difficult, are shown therein.

(62) He says "exceedingly" (*atyanta*) because when the various permutations of the quarters and the permutations of the initial syllables are combined with one another, there arise many other varieties as well that would cause excessive prolixity in the text.
And he says that they are not necessarily to be mentioned because of their harshness and lack of aesthetic flavor: "They are difficult [to compose].
However, he says that some must be shown for the sake of the student's proficiency: "Among those, some...
Among those, regarding the *yamakas* consisting of four quarters, an example of the initial *yamaka* without an intervening gap (*avyapeta*) is as follows:

‘[He saw the mountain] where rows of bees were restless with longing for the rows of lotuses; where it stole away the heat of the trees by means of its clusters [of shade]; and which was borne by beautiful women of the gods with lovely tresses, and was unshaken by demons. (92) ‘Rows of lotuses’ (*rājīvarājī*) refers to a series of lotuses; ‘where the bees are restless with longing’ (*tadvaśā lolāḥ*) means they are full of desire for them. He saw that [mountain].
Because it dispelled—that is, removed—the scorching heat by means of rows of trees;
because its lovely and charming women possessed masses of curly hair (cūrṇakuntala);
and because it was unshaken—that is, not assailed—by the Rākṣasas (yasmād rakṣobhiḥ).
In this regard, in the first quarter (pāda), the former [syllable] is meaningful while the latter is meaningless;
in the second and subsequent quarters, both are meaningless.
In other cases as well, this should be understood accordingly.
That same *madhyayamaka* is as follows:

“The swift rivers, whose waters were honored by various [beings] seeking pleasure, possessed banks that were uneven yet equal in their descent, scarred by elephants with their trunks raised, and abounding in clear groves of lotuses. (93)
[He was] honored by elephants praised for their excellent origins, engaged in playful activities during their maturity,
beneficial for various desires,
and highly esteemed.
The *javana* [metre] is swift;
thus, for example, is the final *yamaka*: "By the heavy hips of the celestial damsels, which were slow with the weight of their girdles, the ocean was gradually agitated."
It is spread far and wide on all sides by the hoods of serpents, and [adorned] with clusters of beloved, beautiful *bakula* creepers.
Because their girdles— consisting of strings of small bells (*raśanā*) from which no water has escaped and which have not moved far away— are joined together,
the arrangement of gems and other materials, being uneven and rough, nourishes the distress of the ocean.
Slowly and gently,
by thick and substantial [clouds],
it is spread out on all sides and extended everywhere.
Pervaded by families of hooded serpents, it is rendered cool and fragrant by *lavaṅga*, *bakula*, and *mālatī* flowers; thus it possesses the quality of being dear to the serpent-king.
An example of the *ādimadhyayamaka* (rhyme at the beginning and middle) is as follows:

‘That city, which was like a massive mountain and served as a dwelling for those who desired homes, became the most preeminent among the cities of the earth—beloved by gods and demons alike, and dark-hued like a dense rain-cloud.
(95) *Ghanāghana* means a cloud; *tadābhaḥ* means resembling that, i.e., dark.
"Mahī" refers to the earth; on it, "mahīyān" means the one worthy of worship (the venerable one), and "dharādhara" refers to the mountain, whose houses have that same shape.
An example of initial-and-final *yamaka* is as follows:

"Quickly, quickly, the city—having met with fire, melted, and thus swiftly descended to the earth, spreading out upon the ground and illuminated by a luster no less than the earth itself—was made level on all sides and devoid of its gates by enemies who were themselves unsurpassed.

Having encountered fire, it melted; therefore, "quickly" (drutam) meaning speedily, it went to the earth, falling and spreading across the ground, beautified and adorned by a splendor that was not inferior to the earth's own radiance.

The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: that very city, which had been established with a dense arrangement, level on all sides, uniform, beautiful, and without unevenness, and which had not been overcome by enemies— whether by "enemies" (*paraiḥ*) meaning foes or by "others" (*paraiḥ*) meaning superior beings— was turned into a golden city by fire, rendered without gate-towers (*apagopura*), that is, without gates, and brought down to the earth.
An example of *madhyāntayamaka* (rhyme at the middle and end) is as follows: “O beloved, your rising, firm hips; your body, slender like that of a young maiden;
your eyes, equal to the minds of the wise; and your face—turn them all toward me, O you who dwell in the sky. (97)
Arising and emerging means possessing expansion; thus, it is joined with that which is rising,
dense, and fleshy,
yet thinned by fresh pollen from the sacred ford.
They were a sacred ford for the treatises on women and the menses; they were like a chariot for the flowers— that is, for the minds— or,
according to the reading "sumanasāṃ manasām," they were like the minds of the *sumanas* (the wise or connoisseurs), being in harmony with them.
*dyauśca kṣuca* means heaven and earth; *dyukū* refers to heaven and earth. Of these two, the salt ocean (*lavaṇākara*) is the *umā*, because it is the place where beauty (*lāvaṇya*) comes to rest.
An example of *yamaka* at the beginning, middle, and end is as follows:

“*sīmāsī mānabhūmiḥ phaṇibalabalano-dbhāvirājīvirājī hārī hārītavadbhiḥ parisarasaraṇāvastamālaistamālaiḥ*. [The mountain] is the very limit and the ground of pride, shining with rows of splendor arising from the movement of the host of serpents; it is captivating with *tamāla* trees that have spread along the paths of its slopes like dark-blue peacocks.

"O Lord, before you—the source of existence for gods, asuras, and rākṣasas—the ocean is not wretched; it is not devoid of pearls, nor is it lacking in gems, nor is it a sea of the splendor of white luster, nor is it without its own brilliance. [The compound *nadīno nadīno* means:
it does not transgress its boundary (*sīmā*); it is habituated to remaining within that limit.
*Māna* refers either to an excellence of measure or to honor; it is the ground of that."
It is characterized by a row of lines produced by the coiling of the host of serpents (phaṇibala);
it is radiant with *hārīta* birds situated along the path on its banks, which is strewn with rows of *astamāla* trees arranged in clusters.
The connection is as follows: "captivating" (*hārī*) means "charming" (*manohara*), by such *tamāla* trees that have attained a fragmented form.

"From the gods" (*devāt*) means from the gods and asuras; "one from whom protection was obtained" (*rakṣā... āptā*) refers to that which was secured through their presence and internal abiding; "thus made" (*tathā kṛtabhavaḥ*) means "produced" (*saṃpāditodbhavaḥ*).

Is the ocean, the lord of rivers, not humble before you? (The answer is: Indeed, he is humble, for he is "one from whom other clear jewels have not been released" (*amuktānya*) by means of pearls (*muktābhiḥ*). Furthermore, he is one whose "limit of increase" (*ullāsamudrā*), his state of fullness, is beautiful and captivating due to the moon (*sitarucaḥ*), which possesses white luster.
Thus, since there is *yamaka* as described in all four quarters (*pāda*) of these examples, this is an elaboration on *catuṣpādayamaka*.
As for *ādiyamaka* without interval (*avyapeta*) among the *tripādayamakas*, it is as follows:
"Viśadā viśadāmattasārase sārase jale" (The clear [night] in the water, which has clear, intoxicated cranes, O Sarasā!)... [and so forth].
"She does not do it, she does not do it; this is no female swan, but Death devouring me as her prey.
[The commentary continues: "There is no cleverness in this application," and thus the remaining varieties are not illustrated at all.
He states that a similar expansion of *yamaka* (rhyme) occurs even with three lines: "In the *tripādayamakas*..."
In that place where intoxicated cranes enter the clear, white [waters],
there is a lake belonging to the cranes (*sārasa*).
Because it produces the agitation of love, its sound is contemptible;
why then have the *tripādayamakās* (yamakas occurring at the middle, end, and beginning) not been illustrated? To this he says: "Not of this...
In the case of *dvipādayamakas*, an example of the non-intervened (*avyapeta*) initial *yamaka* is as follows:
"This sound of the intoxicated cuckoo makes my mind even more restless with longing than the bud of the mango tree;
for 'utkalikā' means longing, and 'taduttaram' means its further limit or peak."
My mind is unmanifestly sweet;
my mind is my own mind.
That very thing is the middle *yamaka*, as for example:

"The bee compared its own blackness—the quality of resembling collyrium—attained through contact with clusters of *kurabaka* flowers and enhanced by its association with a virtuous object, to the pupils of the eyes of the women of Mādhava (the Yādavas).
This is the connection: that the blackness of the bee, which has the appearance of soot, was weighed against the pupils of the eyes of the women of the Yādava clan.
An example of *antayamaka* (end-parallelism) is as follows:
“Because their hopes were shattered by her turning away from them, compassion entered that man who had made a tall monkey his banner. (102)
In this manner, the beginning and middle [of the verse] should also be understood.
Since the non-interrupted [yamaka] in *ekapādayamakas* does not mention the beginning and end, it is not cited here as it would be considered fragmentary.
Hanumān, the monkey, was made into a banner by Ketu;
Nara is Arjuna.

The term "non-mention" (*anullekha*)—meaning not being mentioned at the beginning and end—is well-known in the compositions of great poets as something that produces a particular beauty; it is thus an absence of mention, not an impossibility.
This should be understood in the same way regarding the phrase "but the middle *yamaka*," and so forth.
The *Madhyayamaka*, however, illustrates only the fourth quarter, as follows:
“Disheveling the mass of tresses and touching the sweat born on the foreheads of the deer-eyed women...”
The wind blew, fanning the rows of delicate ripples upon the lakes and rubbing away the opening blue lotuses;
"dalatkuvalayam" is an adverbial modifier describing the action of rubbing.
The nature of the bursting of full-blown blue-lotus buds [is produced] by the movement of the waves hither and thither;
likewise, examples of *avyapeta* (unseparated) repetition should be cited even when there is an increase in the number of repetitions—
as follows:

"‘The sky is filled with a succession of showers; the rows of clouds are dark with thundering; the lakes are white and full of their own essence and cranes; the assembly is devoted to the night, and the night is exceedingly long.
(104) Repetition is accomplished by a single recurrence alone. Therefore, he asks: does this not constitute *yamaka* even when there is multiple recurrence? To this, he says: ‘In this way...’"
The meaning is that both the greater and the lesser commonality of recurrence (*āvṛtti-sāmānya*) are intended by the term "recurrence" (*āvṛtti*). "Viyat" means space (*ākāśa*);
it is so called because from it the succession of rains (*vṛṣṭi-paramparā*) departs (*viyati*, *apagacchanti*).
The rows of thick clouds, most exquisitely beautiful,
remained suspended as they thundered and roared.
White and bright; and lakes, ponds, and pools;
where the *sārasa* birds—whose essence is their own natural cry and luster that blossoms at that particular time—are present. Such were they.
The *sabhās* are in the form of assembly halls or collections of water;

they possess radiance, and their "high-pitchedness" (*tāratā*)—the excellence of the stars' purity—is such that it is "slightly high-pitched" because of the presence of some slight density or obstruction. Such is the description.
Even when there is a single form through repetition,
the *ādīyamaka* (initial rhyme) occurs there as follows:
“O night, which is subject to three watches (*yāma*), I go toward death with [my] life-force (*yāma*) diminished.”
"By me, with an ever-turning intellect, that very [verse] has been churned.

The meaning is that by the term *āvṛtti* (repetition), another variety is also included: namely, that whatever kind of word is repeated in the first quarter-verse (*pāda*), that same kind of word must be repeated in the second and subsequent quarters as well, according to their respective positions.

He asks: "Why is such an inauspicious thing being wished for, namely, 'May death come during the watch'—that is, during the night which consists of three watches and lasts for as long as a rest of three *praharas*? To this he replies with the verse beginning with *yām*: "By the thought (*dhiyā*) that 'this [night] is a watch (*yāmā*)', I brought it within the scope of my pride as the very essence of my life; yet by this night—which, due to its length, seems like hundreds of millions of *kalpas*—the affliction (*ārti*) of my vital breaths (*asūn*), acting as the gateway [to death], will likely crush me. This is a statement expressing the resolve to give up the life of a most delicate beloved woman.
In this [verse], the word *yāmā* alone is repeated in all four quarters; likewise, in the following [example],
there is a middle *yamaka* as follows:

"O ascetic, you who are steadfast and have restrained your senses do not fall away from your practice; even though you have reached the state beyond deceit, it has led to your happiness, and for you, the future has come to an end.
Here, *āyati* refers to purity in the subsequent time.
With senses restrained and the collection of senses conquered— one who has become thus does not fall away from his striving; the meaning is that he becomes exactly equal to one who strives.
The word *api* (also/even) is displaced [in its syntactical order].

*Amāyatā* means the absence of illusion (*māyā-śūnyatvam*). That too belongs to you, who are immeasurable (*iyate*)—that is, impossible to be delimited—and who attain (*mayate*) destruction (*kṣayam*), that is, do not go toward ruin (*vināśam*), for the sake of bliss (*sukhāya*).
That very same internal *yamaka* is as follows:
"O Lord, those like you do not know the flavor of bowing; for indeed, there is no flavor in bowing to one who is hostile.
Only those who are wretched move about with their heads bowed before you, and they are fully possessed by that very flavor of wretchedness.
All of this constitutes an *avyapeta-yamaka* (non-intervened repetition) occurring within a continuous sequence of syllables.

The aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) of bowing—which takes the form of appeasing an angry beloved—is the even sweeter *rasa* of union (*saṃbhoga*) that follows upon the state of separation (*vipralambha*). Why, then, do they not recognize such a *rasa*?
For submissiveness (*sannatā*), which consists in being subject to another, and lordliness (*prabhu-tā*), which consists in being independent—these two opposites cannot coexist in one place;
for those who are lords do not bow.
He confirms this very point by way of contrast:

"Those who are indeed..."—meaning those who are wretched are characterized by bowed heads; for that reason, they move about and conduct themselves excessively with the flavor of wretchedness (*dainyarasa*).
He explains the meaning of the uninterrupted words as follows: "All this... and so forth.
Now, an example of *vyapetam ādimayamaka* (separated initial rhyme) in all four quarters is as follows:

“The breeze from the forest on the banks of the Kāñcī river, following that lovely woman along the streets of Kāñcī, removes the fatigue of love-play from those who have cast off their ornaments, such as the girdle. (108)

Since it is now the turn to provide an example of the *vyapeta* (separated) type, he says: "Now (*atha*)"—there is a certain city; its *pratolī* is the royal highway; along that [highway], taking it as the object, there is a flowing river whose nature is to sprinkle with water; the wind from that forest is the *ātariśvan*.

The girdles beginning with *kāñcī* and the waist-bands (*mekhalā*) and so forth—some of which bestow a languid grace upon the entire body—it is for this very reason that there is a renunciation of ornaments such as the waist-band.

Here, in each quarter-verse (*pāda*), the repetition of *kāñcī-kāñcī* and so on occurs in immediate succession (*nairantaryeṇa*); however, if there were an interval, it would merely be an initial or middle *yamaka*. Therefore, its occurrence is possible only through the distinction of the quarters.

That very same *madhyayamaka* is as follows: “Rising fierce with passion, with its crest of flame [the sun] possessing the hue of the face of a Hūṇa woman intoxicated by honey-wine, this fire of the mango grove in my heart—cruel toward young women—simultaneously consumes the quarters of the sky and my own heart. (109)
Madana himself has become a piece of wood;

from it has arisen a crest of flame-like clusters of blossoms, naturally copper-red yet twice as crimson with the intoxication of spring honey. That Hūṇa face, terrible and fearsome, has blocked all directions along with my heart.
The mango grove itself is a fire (*anala*) because it causes distress;

although here a middle *yamaka* (rhyme) could have occurred through the separation of syllables in every quarter-verse, nevertheless, since such a feature was not intended, an example similar to the preceding ones has been cited.
An example of final *yamaka* is as follows:

"O you of virtuous conduct, who are vigilant, that ornament which you wear here because of its brilliance—due to my excessive delight in the festival of love—is of no use to me by virtue of its mere beauty.
Regarding the phrase "saccaritāpramattā": [it means] "one who is vigilant in her virtuous conduct."
Two vocatives have been added:

"O you who are intoxicated by the excellence of the joy of amorous play and the height of delight in the arts of love—your beloved—this ornament, intermingled with the rays of sun-like jewels, ought to be worn by you.
(The suffix -arha is used in the sense of "fit for" or "ought to be done").

To the question, "Why do you not wear it?", he replies: "There is no fruit for me whatsoever from this splendor produced by ornaments," according to the maxim: "The beauty of the adornment of lovers indeed attains fruition through the sight of their beloved. This is an example of *ādimadhyayamaka* (alliteration at the beginning and middle): ... [text omitted] ... Thus ends the section on *yamaka*. Now, regarding *anuprāsa* (alliteration), it is defined as follows: the repetition of consonants (*vyañjana*) with the same effort of articulation (*yatna*), place of production (*sthāna*), and point of contact (*sthāna*), while the vowels (*svara*) differ, is called *anuprāsa*. It is of four kinds: *chekānuprāsa*, *vṛttyanuprāsa*, *lāṭānuprāsa*, and *śrutyanuprāsa*. Among these, *chekānuprāsa* is the repetition of consonants with different vowels, occurring in a single word or in multiple words. An example of its occurrence in a single word: *“kṛtakṛtakaruṇaiḥ kim eṣi bāṣpa-pravila-vilolair locanaiḥ paṅkajākṣi |”* An example of its occurrence in multiple words: *“mṛgamada-tilakam alikam avataṃsayati sā kusuma-samitām |”* *Vṛttyanuprāsa* is the repetition of consonants with the same effort of articulation, place, and point of contact, even when the vowels differ, occurring in multiple words. An example: *“ullāsya kālakaravālam ahobhir uccaiḥ pītvā ca raktam akhilāṃ vasudhāṃ vilopya |”* *Lāṭānuprāsa* is the repetition of words or parts of words with different meanings, provided they have the same sound, occurring in multiple words. An example: *“bhramim aratim klamam agham ca tanoti vipulam alam ilātmaje |”* *Śrutyanuprāsa* is the repetition of sounds that produce a similar auditory impression, even if the effort of articulation, place, and point of contact differ. An example: *“dāmodarakarāghāta-vidārita-tarakṣuṇā |”* Thus ends the section on *anuprāsa*. Now, *śleṣa* (paronomasia) is defined: the simultaneous application (*samāveśa*) of two or more distinct meanings (*arthāntara*) within a single sentence or word is called *śleṣa*. It is of two kinds: based on words (*śabdaśleṣa*) and based on meaning (*arthaleṣa*). An example of *śabdaśleṣa*: *“ayi rājendra! candreṇa narendreṇa sadā satā |”* An example of *arthaleṣa*: *“deva! tvam eva pātālam āśānāṃ tvaṃ nibandhanam |”* Thus ends the section on *śleṣa*. Now, *vakrokti* (indirect speech) is defined: the expression of a meaning other than what was intended, through a clever turn of phrase, is *vakrokti*. It is of two kinds: *abhidhāmūla* (rooted in denotation) and *lakṣaṇāmūla* (rooted in indication). An example of *abhidhāmūla*: *“gaccha gacchasi cet kānta! panthānaḥ santu te śivāḥ |”* An example of *lakṣaṇāmūla*: *“upakṛtaṃ bahu tatra kim ucyate sujanatā prathitā bhavatā param |”* Thus ends the section on *vakrokti*. Now, *svabhāvokti* (description of nature) is defined: the description of the natural state (*svabhāva*) of objects, whether moving or stationary, as they truly are, is *sv

‘The daughter of Janaka, possessing the luster of a lotus and with eyes like [lotuses], was seen by the forest-dwelling monkey as she lay upon a tree-stump in the woods— she who was renowned among people and who surpassed even the lord of massive mountains.
Here too, in the context of alternating and non-alternating [metres], the mixture consists precisely in the difference of the quarters (pāda).
Since mixed and unmixed [types] occur specifically at the level of each quarter-verse (*pāda*), he provides an illustration:
"Beginning with Mālyavān and extending as far as Suvela, the dense line of mountain ranges... the lotus born of the forest... and so forth.
Hanumān, the tree-dweller and branch-monkey esteemed and approved by the people,
is here the possessor of the sound "ghana" and so forth; in all four quarters, the word "girīndra" and so forth recurs between the beginning and middle without being repeated or interrupted.
An example of *ādyantayamaka* (rhyme at the beginning and end) is as follows:

"Here, birds repeatedly produce notes of various melodies, fragrant with the scent of *kadamba* flowers; and the wind, shaking the groves of fresh *nīpa* trees, approaches, repeatedly causing the clouds to wander. (112)
The clouds of the rainy season, brought by the fragrance of *kadamba* flowers, perceive the lowing of the cows and lead that lowing to a state of melodic beauty;
the interval between these acts of lowing is a single tempo consisting of fast, medium, and slow;
"cloud" (*abhra*) means a rain-cloud (*megha*).
The *nīpa* is the *kadamba*;
by the shaking of the *kadamba* grove, the manifestation of fragrance occurs everywhere.
Here, the phrase "vihagāḥ" (birds) and so forth recurs at the beginning and end of each quarter-verse (*pāda*), separated only by six non-repeated syllables.
An example of *madhyāntayamaka* (rhyme at the middle and end) is as follows:

"O Goddess, Hanumān spoke measured yet noble words with joy; 'I go into the presence of the bull of the Raghus, clearly [to report] that your sorrow is known and that all the enemies have been seen. I go to Mount Mālyavān, which eternally possesses splendor. (113)

Measured—meaning concise with few syllables—and yet exceedingly noble; expressed with few syllables and with joy (*mudā*), that is, with delight; the bull of the Raghus, Rāma, was honored by her who had made his presence her dwelling place.
Here, the word *dāra* and so forth recur at the middle and end of each quarter-verse, separated by five non-repeated syllables.
An example of *yamaka* (rhyme) at the beginning, middle, and end:

“Accompanied by his army on all sides, he of equal splendor to Indra entered the city with its lofty gate-towers; having placed that woman, languid with passion and full of joy, in a state of imperishable youth, he departed. (114)
Equally, together, equally, splendidly;
*saṃmada* means joy.
The horse fit for the Aśvamedha sacrifice went [forth];
