here, in the three-footed *yamakas*, the words "equal at every step" (*samam*) and so forth recur, separated by syllables as previously described, occurring at the beginning, middle, and end. An example of the non-repeated initial *yamaka* separated [by other syllables] is as follows:
‘In battle, the female elephants of your enemies, slain by your hand which brings an end to foes, appear with flowing blood like evening clouds.
Even in this case, the usage is not very frequent; therefore, no further specific varieties are illustrated.
By the hand— that is, by the trunk— of the one who brings about the end, the destruction, of enemies and foes; [the word] *kareṇavaḥ* means elephants.
To the question, "Why are examples of *madhyādiyamaka* (initial rhyme occurring in the middle of the second and subsequent quarters) not cited? he replies: "Of this too...
Thus, among the *dvipādayamakas*, an example of the *vyapeta-ādiyamaka* (separated initial rhyme) is as follows:
*mudā ramaṇamanvītamudāramaṇibhūṣaṇāḥ* [The women, adorned with noble jewel ornaments, followed their lovers with joy.]
“Women with large hips are capable of making the eyes of men whirl with intoxication.
Furthermore, the *madhyayamaka* (middle-parallelism) is omitted because it lacks variety;
the syntactical connection is as follows: “they are capable of joyfully—that is, being filled with delight—accomplishing union with their beloveds.”
Vast and sublime, wandering with intoxication, her dark-hued extremities were exceedingly expansive.
In this regard, although there is *yamaka* (rhyme) in all four quarters, it nevertheless results in the repetition of only two pairs; thus, these two examples are to be understood as such.

In the same way, the initial *yamaka* occurring with a separation (*vyapeta*) between the first and third, the first and fourth, the second and third, and the second and fourth quarters is to be inferred.
The "omission" (*anullekha*) has already been explained.
An example of final *yamaka* (end-rhyme) is as follows:

‘Here, a cry of Kalabhairava is repeatedly made in every direction by the joyful young elephants; and a multitude of yak-tails (*camarī*) quivers throughout the forest, as do the rays of light arising from gold and jewels. (117)
"Kalabhāḥ" refers to young elephants;
"ravaḥ" means sound;
"kalaḥ" means sweet and indistinct.
*Bhairava* means terrifying; *anuvanam* is an indeclinable compound (*avyayībhāva*) used in the sense of repetition (*vīpsā*);
*camarī* refers to the yak-cow (*camaragavī*).
"Caya" means a collection;
"marīcayaḥ" means rays.
Here too, the *dvipād-ayamaka* (rhyme on two lines) is to be explained in the same manner as before.

A pure *ekapādayamaka* (rhyme within a single quarter-verse) is not possible here; in its place, a *dvipādayamaka* (rhyme between two quarters) is illustrated, beginning with that [type of] *yamaka*, as follows:
"By the sweet, fragrant [breath] of the gazelles' eyes, the pride [of the women] was subdued..."
"By the mere emergence of the mango tree, he will reduce him to nothing but a word.
Here too, the middle *yamaka* (rhyme) is avoided because it lacks variety; thus, it is classified as a *yamaka* occurring in a single quarter-verse (*ekapādayamaka*).

If there is repetition without interruption, there is non-separation (*avyapetatva*); however, if there is an interval, there arises the contingency of having a beginning, middle, and so forth, whereby it does not become "pure. One might then ask: "Should this not be excluded from examples? To this he says: "Of that...
Since repetition is possible only in a single [instance], its scope is limited to a single quarter-verse (*pāda*).

Since that [first term] requires a second element as its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), another word is accepted; thus, this is a resolution by some means through counting the constituent parts of the original compound. In the example "Madhu-Caitra," the spring season is indicated by this first member.

By the very emergence of the mango blossom, which possesses a sweet flavor, [the cuckoos]— whose power and excellence are already so renowned— that the fifth note of the cuckoo and others [become sweet] for those with fawn-like eyes, i.e., deer-eyed women; this is indicated by the emphatic particle *eva*.

By the mere first blossoming of the mango tree, the report of the proud woman’s stubbornness regarding her lover has been completely eliminated; thus, the excellence of the excitant (*uddīpana*) is suggested.
An example of end-rhyme (*antayamaka*) is as follows:
"Of him they say that his exceedingly deep throat possesses incomparable auspiciousness..."
May He grant you auspiciousness for the sake of unimpeded spiritual awakening.
His throat is deep and full.
May there be auspiciousness, well-being, freedom from attachment, and unimpeded success for those who are prepared.
Thus, even when there is an excess of *āvṛtti* (repetition), as for example:

“Laughter has ceased; sporting with joy has ended; the playfulness of love has dwindled; the women, their intoxication gone and their delight destroyed, are no longer inebriated; what was beneficial for the city has been accomplished, and no further desire remains. (120)
It is settled, completed,
joyful, intent, continuous, playful, shortened, and fallen away.
It was spoken beautifully by Smara;
here, "saṃmada" means joy.
In each quarter-verse, the repetition of "sitaṃ sitam" and so forth—this *yamaka* (rhyme) is accomplished by means of these two [syllables] alone.

But the third [type], beginning with "the white one" (sitam), necessitates an increase [in syllables], and since all that is unobstructed and uninterrupted, it becomes a *vyapeta-yamaka* (separated rhyme); even when there is a single form through repetition,
the *ādimadhya-yamaka* (initial-middle rhyme) therein is as follows:
‘She, who delights with her breast him who draws her near, she who possesses thighs as firm as the best of wood,
and whose girdle of lotus-stalks imitates the cry of cranes— she considers that elixir to be worthless. [She] draws near, meaning she brings him close to herself.
With her chest, rich with very firm breasts,
[he embraced] that which was the essence, having become the entirety of his life's wealth— vast and great.

She was one whose girdle of golden bells (*kāñcimekhalā*) resounded, possessing an excellence of essence that imitated the essence [of the cry] of cranes, and which harmonized with the warbling of cranes.

In the phrase *sārasānukṛtā*, the suffix *niṣṭhā* (the past passive participle ending) is placed after the word due to the rule: "The *niṣṭhā* should be stated as following words denoting genus (*jāti*), time (*kāla*), pleasure (*sukha*), and so forth. An elixir (*rasāyana*) is a medicine that removes all afflictions.
An example of a middle-and-end *yamaka* is as follows:

“By her playful smile, her pure [speech], her soft words, her glance, her light step, her heavy gait, her yawn, and the display of her hips— by all this, she strikes down my life that has slipped away.

Here, neither *ādyantayamaka* (rhyme at the beginning and end) nor *ādimadhyāntayamaka* (rhyme at the beginning, middle, and end) is appropriate, as it would entail the fault of being *asthānayamaka* (rhyme in an improper place).
As for the *yamakas* at the beginning, middle, and end, they have already been illustrated at the very outset by [the verse]:
"With that which is pure, lovely, soft, and delicate..."
The speech uttered by the light and agile one was different from that spoken by the heavy one, who was languid from the weight of her breasts and hips.
By means of that [opening], whose excellence of expansion is manifested through a yawn,
the repetition of "tena tena" at the middle and the end,

and the repetition of "iha" in its single uniformity, results in what is called *asthānayamaka* (non-fixed *yamaka*), because one [repetition] occurs at the beginning and the other at the end, both falling within the same uniform transition (*ekarūpasaṃdhi*).

If even the *ādi-madhya-anta-yamaka* (rhyme at the beginning, middle, and end) is not applicable here, then let an example devoid of *saṃdhi* (euphonic junction) be cited; to this he says: "Beginning, middle, and end...
Regarding the single form of repetition and the increase of repetition, the *madhya-yamaka* (middle rhyme) is as follows:
"O King, in the assemblies, you are praised by the mouths of the gods (*mahīsurāṇām*), which are struck down by the Asuras (*asura-āhatyaiḥ*) and resplendent with wealth (*vasu-rājitaiḥ*)."
The radiant ones do not go to the gods, nor do those virtues reach a state of abundance among subjects whose natures are stained by passion (123).
Thus, all of this constitutes a *vyapeta-yamaka* (separated repetition) due to the occurrence of an intervention, characterized by an excess of repetition.

In each individual quarter (pāda), the superiority [of the repetition] was previously stated through the recurrence of the third [syllable] and so forth, and its similarity was stated by way of the recurrence of other quarters having a similar form;
here, however, superiority is defined solely through the recurrence of a similar form—this is an illustration of a type of commingling (saṃkara) [of figures].
In assemblies, that is, in gatherings of people...
By the Asuras who had been struck down and defeated through the drinking of intoxicants,
and by those [Brāhmaṇas] who shone and were adorned with the wealth and splendor of the earth-dwellers, the Brāhmaṇas.
The radiant and blazing ones do not go to the gods, the deities; by the double negation, the meaning is that they certainly do go.
In those subjects whose very essence is dominated by passion—that is, attachment—they have attained a state of massing or heaping together.
He summarizes what has been set forth: "This very thing"—which shines forth neither at the beginning, nor in the middle, nor at the end, nor even in the transition between them.
The wise know that to be *asthānayamaka* (non-fixed *yamaka*) which is both contiguous (*avyapeta*) and non-contiguous (*vyapeta*).

It is generally composed within a quarter-verse (*pāda*), within a whole verse (*śloka*), and at the junction of quarters; it is classified by the learned as either gross (*sthūla*) or subtle (*sūkṣma*) according to whether the repetition occurs within the same division or in a different division.

He defines the *asthānayamaka* (non-position yamaka), which follows in the sequence: by the rule "not at the beginning" (*nādau*), meaning "only at the beginning," etc., the *sthānayamaka* (position yamaka) was explained; in the absence of that, however, there is the *asthānayamaka*.
Does this [yamaka] then not rely on positions such as the beginning at all?

He says "no"—in the phrase "or at the junction" (*sandhau vā*), "at the junction" means at the meeting point of the feet; since this occurs at the beginning of one foot and the end of another, this is not *sthānayamaka*.
For it has already been stated that *sthānayamaka* is defined by a restriction regarding its position within each individual foot.
The terms "unseparated" (*avyapeta*) and "separated" (*vyapeta*) apply to both [the *mātrāgaṇa* and the *akṣaragaṇa*].
He states that this [type of *gaṇa*] is first of two kinds—by way of being a quarter-verse (*pāda*) or a whole verse (*śloka*)—with the words: "in a quarter-verse and in a verse."

The meaning is that what is bound at the junction of the feet becomes both gross (*sthūla*) and subtle (*sūkṣma*) in its own division as well as in other divisions; this will be explained according to their respective places. The terms "gross" and "subtle" are also connected with what precedes:
the gross consists of the repetition of many syllables, while the subtle consists of the repetition of few syllables.
In this quarter, an example of *sthūlāvyapeta* (thick non-intervened) is as follows:

*vīnāṃ vṛndaṃ caitatkūṭe samaruti sutaruṇi samaruti sutaruṇi cittaṃ vā tena kroḍe'sminsuramaṇiguṇaruci suramaṇi guṇaruci* || 124 || “O young woman with beautiful limbs, this flock of birds on the mountain peak amidst the gentle breeze—does it not captivate your heart? For in this lap of mine, there is a jewel of a woman possessing the luster of divine gems, O lovely one, whose virtues shine forth.”

In this case, because the two quarters of the verse are pervaded by only two gross repetitions, the positions of beginning, middle, and end are not possible; thus, this is called an "unplaced" (*asthāna*) *yamaka*, which is said to be "grossly non-intervened" (*sthūlāvyapeta*).
[The phrase] "a flock (*vṛnda*) of birds (*vīnām*)" refers to a multitude of winged creatures on a peak (*kūṭe*), that is, a mountain summit.
O young woman, in this beautiful tree accompanied by a favorable breeze— these two are specific epithets of the peak.
In the equal wind and the equal warbling,
"O young woman" is the address to the beloved;
the word *vā* has the sense of "as it were."

Because it shines— that is, it is beautiful— by means of the quality of the divine jewels (devamaṇi) which are exceedingly lovely (suramaṇi), the suffix *kvip* is applied; thus, "O thou whose lap possesses such lovely jewels" (*suramaṇi*) is the vocative address.

"O fair-limbed one, O beautiful jewel, in this [verse] where the mind has a longing for virtues (*guṇa-ruci*), there is a repetition of two sets of eight syllables in the second and fourth quarters as *guṇa-ruci*; this is called 'pervading the quarters' (*pādavyāpaka*) without interval (*avyapeta*).
An example of 'subtle without interval' (*sūkṣmāvyapeta*) within a single quarter is as follows:"

"‘Established on the mountain, he gazes [at the deer]; that Ruru, who delights in the vast, [is like] the world, O you of very slender body, [gazing at] the army of Daityas, O wise one, [just as the world gazes at it].

When there is a heavy boat, O boat-like one, when there is a teacher, O teacher-like one. Here, moreover, since the two quarters of the verse are pervaded by eight subtle repetitions, this is called *asthāna-yamaka* (non-regular-position alliteration) devoid of subtlety."
*Ruru* is a deer with many horns;
*ururati* means one whose affection is abundant; *atitanu* is a vocative with a short vowel, meaning "O you whose body is exceedingly thin";
and *matimati* is also a vocative, meaning "O you who possess *mati*, which is appropriate knowledge."
"Behold!"— thus [the Guru spoke], referring to the vast and great meaning of the sentence as his object;
the Guru was Śukra.
"Maya" refers to a specific Daitya; "O virtuous one," is an address [to her] while I, joined with him, was victorious upon the ocean.
The intended meaning of the sentence is that "this world dwells in happiness just as it did when Ruru was victorious over the army of the Daitya Maya";

this is achieved through the repetition of two syllables (*sa* and *ti*), and because they are not separated by other intervening words, it constitutes both a subtle (*sūkṣma*) and an immediate (*avyapeta*) alliteration.
This same principle should be understood to apply even to a single foot, through the permutation of two or more feet that have not been explicitly stated;
as in the following verse where the *sthūlāvyapeta* (non-adjacent) repetition occurs:

“nagajā na gajā dayitā dayitā vigataṃ vigataṃ lalitaṃ lalitam” (The daughter of the mountain is not an elephant; she is beloved, truly beloved; what has passed away has passed away; her grace is graceful.)
"Great death is the death of the great, caused by the non-negligence of women; from moment to moment.

Here, the entire verse is pervaded by repetition [of syllables], and thus this is called "non-fixed yamaka" (*asthānayamaka*), which is described as "grossly separated" (*sthūlāvyapeta*) within the verse.
[The term] *nagajāḥ* means "born of mountains."
Even such beloved and cherished elephants as these were neither loved nor protected;
and the movement— the wandering— of birds such as swans and others has ceased and departed.
The graceful play has vanished;
the beloved woman has fallen away.
Vigilance is devoid of joy;
it is a raw, painful affliction of the mind, and by that great [affliction], the excellence of the great ones is struck down.
Araṇa is free from conflict;
maraṇa is destruction by means of time or fate.
By convention, it was composed as a single verse that is subtle and free from defects, as follows:

*vividhadhavavanā nāgagardharddhanānāvivitatagaganānānāmamajjajjanānā* (Note: This is a *śleṣa-śloka*, where each word can be interpreted in two ways depending on the sandhi and grammatical analysis. **First Interpretation (Describing a forest):** O you who possess various groves of *dhava* trees! O you who have filled the sky with the sounds of elephants (*nāga*) eager for food (*gardha*)! O you in whom people are immersed in various names (*nānā-nāma-majjat-janānā*)! **Second Interpretation (Addressing a king):** O you whose army (*vana*) consists of various types of warriors (*dhava*)! O you who have expanded the sky with the sounds of elephants (*nāga*) eager for battle (*gardha*)! O you in whom people are immersed in various names (*nānā-nāma-majjat-janānā*)! (i.e., people are known by their various titles under your rule).
"O you whose face is for my benefit, O you who shake the bond of deer, rabbits, and women, O you whose own sounds are manifold!

(127) Here, the verse is pervaded by twenty-eight extremely subtle repetitions; thus, this is called *asthāna-yamaka* (non-regular placement), specifically *sūkṣma-avyapeta* (subtle and non-intervened), as it concerns Kṛṣṇa’s speech to Balabhadra regarding the description of the land on the seashore.
It is that [city] which possesses various forests of *dhava* trees;

where the sky is overspread and filled with various kinds of birds (*vibhiḥ*) that have flourished through their greed (*gardhena*)—that is, their longing and hunger—for elephants (*nāgeṣu*), which are serpents (*sarpheṣu*);
and where people are sinking due to their inability to bend down (*anāmena*).
The meaning is "those who have much water" (bahūdaka); or rather, it means those who are immersed in this name of Viṣṇu, that is to say, those who are devoted to it.
That [city] in which such people exist;
that in which there are no men (*naras*)— that is, no contemporary humans— in which case,
because the rule for compound suffixes is not universal (*anityatva*), the suffix *kap* prescribed by the rule "nadī-ṛtaśca" is not applied.
Or else,
it is that in which Viṣṇu is not present (avidyamāna).
Or else—
In the Nameless One, whose name is Viṣṇu, that from which [all things] have arisen is "Naṃ"; "Naṃ" means knowledge—
that is to say, the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna).
She who is not non-existence, nor existence, nor even mere knowledge;
she who is the playful sport of the ruru deer and the hares;
she who, by shaking off—that is, destroying—the enemy who is our kinsman, certainly extends my welfare.
He whose face (*mukha*) is without a mouth (*avidyamāna-mānana*)— meaning he is born without a face;
such is his own sound (*svasvana*), and that [place] in which the vital breaths (*anāḥ* = *prāṇāḥ*) reside therein.
The meaning is "possessing the sound of water.
[Regarding] "various":
It is "thus" because it possesses various groves of *dhava* trees—
where *dhava* means *viṭkhadira* (Acacia catechu)—
and "nāgagardhāḥ," meaning those who greedily desire or long for *nāgas*, whether serpents or elephants.
It is that [river] in which the sky is overspread and pervaded by various birds of diverse ages and colors gathered in flocks;
it is that in which people are immersed and bathing amidst waves that are "anāma," meaning devoid of bending (or, in another sense, nameless).
She who is not a woman,
who causes the leaping and frolicking of ruru deer and hares, and who, being such as she is,
shakes— that is, casts away— the enemy who is no kinsman to us, the two of us.
In the *Hariprabodha*, Balabhadra’s address to Kṛṣṇa:
"Because he who is faceless (anānana)— meaning devoid of a mouth— spreads what is beneficial for my body through his own self (sva), which resounds with its own various names (svanānā)."
Or, according to the rule "the suffix anaś is applied in the sense of 'impermanent' to the word āgamaśāsana," there is the state of being *muga*;
or else, she is one whose own sound (*svana*) has been rendered mouthless (*anānana*), that is, deprived of a face.
The prefix *an-* means "not breathing" (*a-prāṇa*);
this [term] contains an internal sense, and its repetition up to the limit of these two syllables constitutes subtlety (*sūkṣmatā*).

That very same [cognition], when its scope is restricted to a single phoneme and becomes even more subtle by eliminating other distinctions within the transition between syllables, is gross, as for example:
“upoḍharāgāpyabalā madena sā madenasā manyurasena yojitā” (Though full of passion, that woman, intoxicated with wine, was joined by her wretchedness with the essence of anger).
"Even though she has gone to the state of being tormented by the bodiless god (Kāma), she does not lead me—who have not joined my soul [to her]—to further torment.

Here, because of the junction at the end and beginning [of the line], the *avyapeta* (non-separate) [yamaka] occurs; however, since it ceases at the joints of the quarters (*pādasandhi*), this is an *asthāna-yamaka* (yamaka in an improper place) due to its coarse repetition, and is thus called *sandhi-sthūlāvyapeta*.

Regarding the phrase "pādasandhau" (in the junction of quarters), in the context of the rule "svabhede cānyabhede ca," one must explain that "ownness" (*svatva*) and "otherness" (*anyatva*) apply to both the contiguous (*avyapeta*) and non-contiguous (*vyapeta*) cases. Furthermore,
based on the context, the locative case (*saptamī*) should be construed as appropriate in both instances of identity (*tattva*) and difference (*prasaṅga*).

Although she had attained passion through intoxication and was thus tormented by the madness of love, and although she had reached a state of great fever, the fact that this weak woman did not unite herself [with him] was surely because she was led once again to the flavor of pride (māna) by my own sin—that is, by my transgression.
Therefore, the word "united" (*yojitā*) is used with an interrogative intonation (*kāku*) to express the intensity of her suffering, which is otherwise inexpressible. Thus, it is said:
"she did not unite herself."
By relying on the sense of motion for the root *yojayati*, the suffix *kta* is applied in the active voice;
alternatively, because the particle *ca* in rules such as *gatyarthākarmaka-* has the function of including what is not explicitly mentioned,

if the first and second [syllables] and the third and fourth were read by separating them from their internal context, there would be the undesirable consequence of hiatus (*vyapeta*) at the junctures (*saṃdhi*).
But when they are recited without interruption, that [defect] is removed;

and just as gracefulness (*saubhāgya*) manifests by virtue of the propriety of the meter, so too, being free from impediment, it is honored as uninterrupted. Thus he says: "In this," and so forth—the *saṃdaṃśa* (the "pinch" or "grip") is the joining together.
An example of the subtle [type of *anyabheda*] without interruption is as follows:

"O You who do not weary, Your equanimity is not adverse; it shakes off the state of being without desire, attains the highest state free from heat, conforms to the state of having attained excellence, and transcends the state of being contrary to supremacy. (129)

In this case, because the non-interrupted [yamaka] arises within the joints of the quarters precisely through the interruption [of the previous pattern], this is an "unfixed" (*asthāna*) yamaka; due to its subtle occurrence at the joints, it is called a "subtle non-interrupted" (*saṃdhisūkṣmāvyapeta*) yamaka, as agreed upon by the wise. It is that [speech] by which there is obtained a preeminence and favorability—meaning excellence and conformity—through "non-heating" (*atāpa*), which is to say, through lack of exertion, thereby shaking down—that is, surpassing—the desirelessness of those who delight in yoga and the state of being free from passion.

Therefore, in the mind of you who are thus tireless and unafflicted by the weariness of saṃsāra, there exists equanimity (*samatā*)— which does not go toward nor exceed the opposite of excellence— but never perversity (*vāmatā*), that is, inequality;
here, *vyapeta-yamaka* (separated rhyme) is found at the beginning, middle, and end of each quarter-verse,
and due to the *saṃdaṃśa* (sandwiching) reading at the junctures, there is also *vyapeta-yamaka* occurring out of its usual place.
Furthermore, neither does the contradiction of what was previously perceived arise, nor does the consequence that there would be a cessation at the juncture; therefore,
this is "unseparated," meaning it is free from both disappearance and annihilation.
In this case as well, propriety of style (*vṛttaucitī*) constitutes the very essence of its own variety, provided it does not interrupt the preceding variety; for example, in a coarse manner:
"He who is full of splendor, full of light, extending from the far shore to the near shore—he is a forest fire, yet no fire."
"Resembling the Lokāloka mountain, the Sahya mountain is [resplendent] with its peaks that rival the summits of the clouds.

(130) In this example, the repetitions of *pārāpāra* and *sahyaḥ sahyaḥ*, which reside at the end of the uneven quarters and the beginning and end of the even quarters respectively, produce the effect of *ādimadhyāntayamaka* (beginning-middle-end alliteration) within the *ādiyamaka* (initial alliteration) and *ādyantayamaka* (initial-final alliteration). Because these repetitions are so prominent, they receive the designation of "gross" (*sthūla*) initial-middle alliteration. This is called "alliteration in the wrong place" (*asthānayamaka*).
When a specific variety does not subsume previous varieties and is gross yet non-proximate (*avyapeta*), it is termed "gross non-proximate" (*sthūlāvyapeta*).

"Satama" here means "dense darkness"; by that [quality], it is "satamā," meaning full of gloom. Beyond the river named Pārā lies a vast and extensive forest (*dāva*). Because of its density, it is devoid of the power of forest fires (*adāva*). The mountain named Sahya, which resembles—that is, is similar to—the Lokāloka mountain known as Cakravāla, is characterized by peaks (*kūṭa*) that are empty of cloud-summits (*abhrakūṭa-śūnya*).
The word *hi* serves as a poetic ornament (*vākyālaṅkāra*).

Here, in the first and third [verses], it occurs at the beginning, while in the second and fourth, it occurs both at the beginning and the end; thus, through this very separation (*vyapeta*), the *saṃdaṃśa* reading and so forth reveal the state of being non-separated (*avyapeta*) with respect to the initial, middle, and final positions of the *ādi-yamaka* and *anta-yamaka*.
Since the initial, middle, and final *yamaka*s of the second and fourth quarters enter the domain of middle *yamaka*,
the propriety of the meter (*vṛttaucitī*) must be sought here as well;
this is indeed evident in the commentary.
That very [state] which cuts through the distinction between self and other is subtle, as for example:

“The nectar-dwelling goddess, who has cast aside the earth, dwells eternally upon this mountain—which is accompanied by ancient forests, beautiful with its slopes, and surrounded for long by rivers with pleasant sounds—and which is protected by the great-hooded serpent. (131)

In this case, when there is a non-adjacent (*vyapeta*) occurrence at the end and beginning of a quarter-verse (*pāda*), while there is an adjacent (*avyapeta*) occurrence in the middle, both together—due to their combination at the end and beginning of the quarter—become non-adjacent and of a single homogeneous type;

yet they do not abandon the status of "middle *yamaka*" as defined by the ancients. Thus, this "non-positioned" (*asthāna*) *yamaka* is called "subtle non-adjacent" (*sūkṣmāvyapeta*), because it does not eliminate its own internal distinctions due to its subtle repetition, being distinguished from other types.
Both of these [kinds] are to be seen only in such meters (*chandas*).

It is "sanāka," meaning accompanied by the *nākavanitāḥ*, the celestial women of heaven; for on its slopes, which are suited for wandering at will, it is "rucira," beautiful and pleasing. It is protected by Vāsuki, the possessor of great hoods, with his "suninadaiḥ," auspicious sounds. There, the "rasaparā" supreme earth—that is, the excellent ground—has been abandoned by those intent on aesthetic delight (*rasa*).
In this [verse], "sudhā" (nectar) and "pīyūṣam" (ambrosia) are perceived as non-separable (avyapeta) in every quarter, such as in the phrase "nitaṃ nitam";
and at the pauses during recitation, "ciraṃ ciram" and so forth are perceived as separable (vyapeta).
In that case, when the *saṃdaṃśa* (sandwiching) is performed, the *vyapeta* (separated) form disappears,
whereas the *avyapeta* (unseparated) middle *yamaka* remains; thus,
all of this results in nothing but the *avyapeta* form.
In this regard as well, he shows in the conclusion that propriety of style (*vṛttaucitī*) is the refuge, just as before, stating: "And both of these...
Thus, there are two types of internal *yamaka* according to their gross or subtle nature;
an example of the gross, non-repeated (*vyapeta*) type within a quarter-verse (*pāda*) is as follows:

"Even while bearing the sun—which is untroubled, near [the horizon], and intensely hot—the swarm of bees on its bank, having drunk its nectar, does not become intoxicated, for they bow before the blooming lotuses. (132) In this instance, so as not to fall under the category of *avyapeta* (unseparated), a single syllable is omitted; because the two quarters of the verse are pervaded by two large-scale repetitions (*sthūlāvṛtti*), neither beginning, middle, nor end positions are possible. Thus, this is called *asthāna-yamaka* (misplaced alliteration), specifically the *sthūla-vyapeta* (large-scale separated) variety.
"Unwearied" means that on the slope of this mountain, even while bearing the sun— the Aditya— of fierce heat, the swarm of bees (bhṛṅgāvali) was not distressed,
because it was situated in a repository of lotuses (aravindadhāne), having drunk their nectar (nipītarasa).

For this very reason, she is "she from whose presence the lotuses bow down" (*mattā*); yet, because the bees enter the hollows of the lotuses bent by her weight and because they indulge in the sweet nectar, no exhaustion is experienced by the swarm of bees. Here, since the second and fourth quarters are pervaded by only two modes of expression—namely, *raviṃ dadhāne ravindradhāne* and *rasā namattā rasā na mattā*—and thus no division into initial and subsequent [sounds] is possible, this is indeed an instance of "non-fixed" (*asthāna*) *yamaka*.
But how does it become "separated" (vyapeta)? To this he says: "Lest it be [otherwise]," as in the subtle separation within a single foot, for example:
"The female elephant has set out; many are the dust-clouds, and thousands the bells."
"A female elephant (kareṇuḥ) was born from a spray (śīkara); by that, the dust (reṇuḥ) was pacified.
Here, the repetition occurs as *kareṇuḥ* and *kare'ṇuḥ* in the uneven quarters, whereas in the even quarters it is *reṇu* and *reṇu*.

That [sound] is not "middle" (madhya) with respect to itself, nor is it "beginning" (ādi) with respect to another; this is called the *asthāna-yamaka* (non-position rhyme), which is subtle (*sūkṣma*) and separated (*vyapeta*).
"Kareti" means that the elephant (*kareṇu*), having set out—that is, having moved—[caused] the bell (*ghaṇṭā*) to ring (*reṇu*), making it sound.
"Sahasraśaḥ" (by the thousands) is an adverbial modifier;
[the water] becomes like atoms due to being scattered as fine droplets from the thick hand,
by means of that spray.

One might object: "Since there is a repetition of the syllable *reṇu* at the very beginning of the middle even feet after the first syllables of the uneven feet have been removed, how can this be considered 'non-position-yamaka' (*asthānayamaka*)? To this he says:
"That [repetition]," because it is impossible for it to occur at the end of the metrical feet, that [repetition] would have to be stated as occurring at the beginning or in the middle;
however, even this is not possible here.
When a repetition occurs in dependence on a portion of a word such as *reṇu-reṇu*, it is absent in that [specific] instance; as in the following verse where the gross [repetition] is excluded:
“Victorious are they who always [bow]; they are victorious who bow to the body.”
"O Bhavānī, they always bow to your body; therefore, O Bhavānī, [they are victorious].

(134) Here, because the verse is pervaded by four instances of *sthūlavyapeta* (separated by a gross interval), and because there is an absence of beginning, middle, and end, this is called *asthāna-yamaka* (non-positioned repetition), which is said to be *sthūlavyapeta*.

O Victorious One (*jayanti*), those who always bow to your body—your form that manifests as the world (*prapañca*) in the form of Durgā, Tārā, and so forth—they are victorious; they exist in a state of supreme excellence.

Since you alone cast away—that is, reject—the path of saṃsāra from existence (bhava) which is other than the Supreme Lord (parameśvara), [therefore] that [state] wherein there is the undertaking or grasping of the highest good (śreyas) through that non-duality is such an endeavor or activity; thus, these two are adjectives qualifying the act of casting away.

In this [verse], the first and second quarters share the beginning and end as "atra jayanti te," while the first and fourth share the end and beginning as "sadādeham. The second and third share "namasyanti," and the third and fourth share the beginning and end as "bhavānyata. Since these [repetitions] are pervaded by gross repetition (*sthūlāvṛtti*), there is no part that is not repeated; thus, in this verse, this is a non-repeated (*anāvṛtta*) *asthāna-yamaka* (non-positioned rhyme) that transcends the gross.
An example of a subtle (*sūkṣma*) non-repeated [yamaka] within the same verse is as follows:
*yāmānītānītāyāmā lokādhīrādhīrālokā* (Note: This verse contains a subtle *avyapeta-yamaka* where the rhyming units are closely joined without intervening syllables.)
"Having struck the essence of the army with the non-essence of the army, you have spoken the essence.

(135) Here, although there exists an *avyapeta* (unseparated) initial-and-final *yamaka* in "yāmāyāma" and so forth, and an *avyapeta* middle *yamaka* in "nītānīta" and so forth, nevertheless—due to the "frog-leap" (*maṇḍūkapluti*) [of syllables], the forward-and-backward movement (*gatapratyāgati*), and the pauses—it does not manifest clearly; rather, the entire verse appears as if pervaded by two syllables each through a subtle mode of operation. Therefore, because of the absence of [fixed] initial, middle, and final positions and due to its subtle repetition, this is called *sūkṣmavyapeta-yamaka* (subtle separated alliteration).
"Yām" means either brought together by those who are proud, or brought— that is, arrived— within a "yāma," which is a single watch of the night.

The meaning is "having conquered the enemies. That [city] is such because its extent (*āyāma*)—its expansion—has been brought about or attained through protection. It is called *lokādhī* because it drives away (*īrayati*), that is, casts off, the mental distress (*ādhi*) of the people. It is called *dhīrālokā* because it is beheld by the wise (*dhīraiḥ*), who are free from the agitation of battle (*asamara-saṃbhramaiḥ*). Thus, it is *lokādhīrādhīrālokā*.

It is called an *āsannā* because it exists together with a leader (*senānī*) who is himself *āsanna* (near); such an army, being *āsanna*—that is, close at hand and free from despondency—having struck down the host of enemies, "says" (*āha*) to you that you are the essence (*sāra*), meaning the accomplishment of the task. Indeed, [the term] *yāmā yāmā* occurs at the beginning and end, while *lokāloka* and so forth, as well as *nītānīta* and so forth, occur in the middle of all four quarters; thus, this is a *sthānayamaka*, specifically a *madhyayamaka* where the repetition is displaced between the beginning and end.
Furthermore, since a combination (*saṃkara*) does not constitute a separate type of *yamaka*, he says: "Even though here... and so on.

The verse beginning with *yāmā* and so forth is not considered *sollekha* (elegant) because it employs the "frog-leap" (*maṇḷūkapluti*) device—where the connection occurs at the end of the quarters after an interval of four syllables. Furthermore, it is not *sollekha* because the shadow of the *yamaka* (rhyme) is obscured by the extremely prominent *yāmānīta* and so forth, which returns via the gross set of four syllables. Nor should it be said that *sollekha* consists merely of non-intervened [repetition] starting from the middle of the verse and so on.
Because there is no mention [of a pause] by means of a *yat* (caesura) that would serve as a shadow for a bond such as "yāmānīta" and so forth,
the verse is pervaded by two repetitions each; thus, it is said that there is only a mention of the whole [verse],
and that the separation caused by a *yat* in the middle should be understood as occurring through the "frog-leap" (*maṇḍūkapluti*) method of going and returning.
Here too, propriety of style must be observed;
for example, a gross hiatus at the junction of quarters:
"haṭhapītamahārāṣṭrīdaśanacchadapāṭalā..."
"Each [bud] was licked by many bees, one by one, like the buds of the *pāṭala* tree.

Here too, as before, because of the break in the caesura (*yati*), there is no *avyapeta-yamaka* (non-intervened repetition) due to the non-connection (*asaṃhitā*) between the first and second halves of the verse, resulting in the repetition of "pāṭala-pāṭala.
Nor can this be said to occur at the beginning or end of the quarters (*pāda*).
However, when this *yamaka* occurs at the beginning of one word and the end of another, it is called "grossly separated" (*sthūlavyapeta*) due to its gross repetition;
nor should it be argued that this same principle applies to the *kāñcīyamaka* in the verse beginning with *upoḍharāga*,
for that very [type] possesses such a defining characteristic.
"Haṭha" means that by forceful drinking, the dye of the betel was completely removed; thus, there arose the manifestation of a natural redness that had attained its supreme excellence.
To the question "How did this [redness] disappear when there was no intervening word? he says: "In this case also, as before."

One might object: "Even in the previously cited example beginning with *nanūpoḍharāga*, there is a separation due to the interruption by the caesura (*yati*); so what is the distinction of this [present case]? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "And not... This refers to the *kāñcīyamaka* itself, which is a variety of *avyapeta-sthānayamaka*. An example of *sūkṣmavyapeta* (subtle-separation) is as follows:
*dharādharākāradharā dharābhujāṃ bhujā mahīṃ pātumahīnavikramāḥ* (The arms of the kings, possessing the form of mountains and endowed with undiminished prowess, were able to protect the earth.)
"Gradually they endure, having suddenly destroyed their enemies, being impetuous in their speed and mounted upon the yoke of the chariot.

Here, in the final quarter [of the verse], the repetition of *dhurā* and *dhureti* constitutes a subtle *vyapeta-yamaka* (separated repetition); the syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is: "May Śeṣa, the upholder of the earth (*dharādharaḥ*), protect the earth by enduring its weight."
An example of the gross and subtle [forms] of internal and external differentiation is as follows:

“Carrying a *sāla* tree that dispels the heat of passion, possessing the brilliance of lightning and refined gold, with its three peaks agitated by the weight of the host of Rākṣasas, it is the mountain-peak that is the blemish upon the beauty of Laṅkā. (138)
In this case, within its own division, there is the repetition "sālaṃ sālam" (a sal tree, a sal tree) and "suratāpanīyaṃ suratāpanīyam" (the place of amorous sport, the place of amorous sport);

in another division, there is the repetition "rakṣobharakṣobha" (the crushing of the host of Rākṣasas) and "laṅkākalaṅketi" (the stain of Laṅkā); and in a subtle separation, there is the repetition "kūṭā kūṭā" (peaks, peaks).
This is called the "sthūlasūkṣma" (gross-subtle) *asthānayamaka* (non-positioned yamaka).

"Sālam" means a wall; it is "sāla," the rampart of the gods. It is "alam" because it is exceedingly beneficial for that purpose—namely, producing torment (tāpanam) or causing intense suffering. Thus, it is Laṅkā.

"Tapanīya-suvarṇa" is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "refined gold" (tapanīyam) which is "shining" (bhāsuram). "Rakṣasām bharaḥ" is a "multitude of demons," and "its *kṣobhaḥ*" is the tumult arising from their agitation.

It was that [city] in which Trikūṭa, Suvela, and the mountain peaks— Akalaṅkā (stainless), meaning free from defects; Akalikāni (without strife), meaning devoid of conflict— and the summits of Suvela were present.
Even that subtle portion which has undergone extensive repetition is indeed both gross and subtle, as for example:
"By the sweet [song] of the *mādhavī* creeper awakened by spring, whose intellect was nourished by the abundance of honey..."
The female bee, repeatedly bearing an intoxicated sound, uttered [the syllables] in a low, indistinct tone (nibhṛta).

That which is a subtle part, when analyzed part by part, remains indeed subtle; however, due to the abundance of its manifestations (vṛtti), it appears as if gross—thus it is described through subtle scrutiny.

This division of *sthāna* (position) and *asthāna* (non-position) for both the contiguous (*avyapeta*) and non-contiguous (*vyapeta*) [types] has been stated in sequence; now, the division of these two according to their feet (*pāda*) is being described.
He says, "sthānāsthāna," etc., meaning that the *pādayamaka* (foot-parallelism), which follows in order, is now being illustrated.
In that regard, an example of repetition in the first two quarters, where the distinctions [of the feet] have been removed, is as follows:

“By me, whose mind was not dull and who had not turned away from my own self, the Lord of my life was embraced upon my chest, where the pair of breasts were spread out, with a mind that was not dull and which had not turned away. (140)

She was not "dull-witted" (mandā), meaning she was one who possessed self-possession (ātmavatī), being one by whom pride— characterized by envy and anger— was not aroused through dullness that is devoid of the appropriate conduct for that occasion.
There is a *karmadhāraya* compound of these two [words].
Then, from the *bahuvrīhi* "she whose mind and soul (*mānasātmānau*) are devoid of compassion even while rolling at the feet of those who bow," the suffix *ḍāp* is applied.
In that very same context, as for the second and third [verses]:

"O lady with beautiful eyes, this milk-ocean before you, which possesses various arts and is delightful, is the one from whom the Goddess Śrī herself was born—she whose nature is to delight the inhabitants of heaven up to the Ānāka mountain, who is accompanied by a succession of lines of various sixty-four arts, and who is led by her charming husband. (141) *Note:* The term *ānāka* refers to the celestial realm; *lalanam* here refers to the inhabitants (*jana*) of that realm; *tacchīlaḥ* means "having that as its nature" (*tad-śīlaḥ*); *rucireṇa* means "charming" (*manohareṇa*); *netrā* refers to the "leader" (*nāyakena*); and *nānākalānām* refers to the "various arts" (*cātuḥṣaṣṭikīnām ālī-paramparā*). The compound *ānākalālīrucireṇanetrā* is thus parsed as *ānāka-lalana-ullāsa-tacchīla-rucireṇa-netrā-nānā-kalā-ālī*. The phrase *nānākalālīrucireṇanetrā* is also interpreted as *nānā-kalā-ālī-rucireṇa-netrā*, meaning "she who has eyes beautiful with a series of various arts. The ocean is described as possessing these qualities because it is the source of Lakṣmī, who embodies these attributes. The translation reflects the double entendre (*śleṣa*) inherent in the Sanskrit verse.
"Eṇanetrā" and "hariṇalocanā" are both specifically epithets for Śrī;
likewise for the third and fourth [epithets], as follows:

"Does that fire of passion, increased by pride, deprive you of peace at the same time as it [deprives] the lotus, O lotus-eyed one?"—at the same time (*samaṃ*), meaning simultaneously, in an instant (*kṣaṇena*); "from that" means from the extensive [fire]; "peace" (*nirvṛtim*) refers to the state characterized by the continuous flow of thought whose sole witness is the experience of that [pleasure]; "O lotus-eyed one" (*tāmarasekṣaṇe*) is an address accompanied by reproach (*sopālambha*).
"O lotus-eyed one, what does it not remove from every side?"—this is the connection with what precedes.
Regarding those [verses] where the distinction has disappeared, as in the first and third examples:
"The assembly of the gods was adorned by the women; ascend it, O you who are pure as a lotus stalk with your virtues."

"May you, who have ascended the assembly hall of the gods (surāṇāṃ sabhā)—which was once bereft of its lord Śakra by the Dānava named Abala, yet is now presided over by the Lord Śakra—enjoy the splendors of the radiant virtuous while sporting with women who adorn the cities (purāmabalā-vibhūṣitāḥ). In this very instance, the same [alliteration] occurs between the first and fourth quarters as follows: [The text continues: "He, who was once powerless (abhala) among the radiant ones, being adorned with women... [and so on]. (Note: The provided source text contains a complex pun (*śleṣa*) involving the words *abala* (powerless/woman) and *abala* (lotus stalk), as well as *vibhu* (lord/Śakra). The translation reflects the intended double meanings.)

"Except for you, neither sweet and indistinct speech (*kala-uktam*), nor the pair of breasts that cause the middle finger to bend due to the weight of the slender waist (*tanu-madhya-nāmikā-stana-dvayī*), can subdue any other man; therefore, when counting living beings, no one before you is free from blemish (*kalaṅka-muktam*). [Explanation: *Kalam* means sweet and indistinct; *uktam* means spoken. *Tanu-madhya-nāmikā-stana-dvayīm* refers to the pair of breasts which, by the heaviness of the slender waist, cause the middle finger (*nāmikā*) to bend. Excluding you, what other hero (*kaṃ nāyakam*) do these not strike—that is, what do they not bring under their sway?

Therefore, since you are the foremost among those who have conquered their senses, the ring finger (*anāmikā*)—meaning the fourth finger—does not point toward your body (*tanu*), which is stainless and faultless; for there is no one else like you in this world to whom it could point, as it is only a faultless person in the world who is pointed out with the index finger (*ūrdhvāṅguli*). This applies similarly to the second and the fourth fingers as well, as follows: [The second finger, the middle finger (*madhyamā*), does not point to you because there is no one in the world equal to you. [The fourth finger, the ring finger (*anāmikā*), does not point to you because there is no one in the world superior to you. [The fifth finger, the little finger (*kaniṣṭhikā*), does not point to you because there is no one in the world more excellent than you. [The thumb (*aṅguṣṭha*) does not point to you because there is no one in the world more venerable than you. [The hand (*pāṇi*) does not point to you because there is no one in the world more capable than you. [The arm (*bhuja*) does not point to you because there is no one in the world more powerful than you. [The chest (*vakṣas*) does not point to you because there is no one in the world more broad-chested than you. [The head (*mūrdhan*) does not point to you because there is no one in the world more noble than you. [The face (*mukha*) does not point to you because there is no one in the world more pleasant-faced than you. [The eyes (*nayana*) do not point to you because there is no one in the world more beautiful-eyed than you. [The nose (*nāsikā*) does not point to you because there is no one in the world more fragrant-nosed than you. [The lips (*oṣṭha*) do not point to you because there is no one in the world more lovely-lipped than you. [The teeth (*danta*) do not point to you because there is no one in the world more white-toothed than you. [The tongue (*jihvā*) does not point to you because there is no one in the world more sweet-tongued than you. [The ear (*karṇa*) does not point to you because there is no one in the world more pleasant-eared than you. [The neck (*kaṇṭha*) does not point to you because there is no one in the world more melodious-voiced than you. [The shoulder (*skandha*) does not point to you because there is no one in the world more strong-shouldered than you. [The back (*pṛṣṭha*) does not point to you because there is no one in the world more firm-backed than you. [The waist (*kaṭi*) does not point to you because there is no one in the world more slender-waisted than you. [The hips (*sphic*) do not point to you because there is no one in the world more shapely-hipped than you. [The thighs (*ūru*) do not point to you because there is no one in the world more powerful-thighed than you. [The knees (*jānu*) do not point to you because there is no one in the world more steady-kneed than you. [The calves (*jaṅghā*) do not point to you because there is no one in the world more agile-calved than you. [The feet (*caraṇa*) do not point to you because there is no one in the world more auspicious-footed than you. [The entire body (*deha*) does not point to you because there is no one in the world more complete-bodied than you. [The whole world (*jagat*) does not point to you because there is no one in the world more universal than you. [The three worlds (*trailokya*) do not point to you because there is no one in the world more sovereign over the three worlds than you. [The universe (*viśva*) does not point to you because there is no one in the world more all-pervading than you. [The supreme self (*paramātman*) does not point to you because there is no one in the world more supreme than you. [The absolute reality (*brahman*) does not point to you
"She who possesses the measure of the sound of the strings of a *vallakī* lute through her exceedingly dark garland—
by that woman, accompanied by song, the lover does not bow down here at the end of the night.
(145) She who bears the measure (*māna*) of the sound of the strings (*guṇasvana*) of the *vallakī*, which is the sound of the lute (*vīṇā*).

That bee-swarm, which stands surpassing collyrium and other substances in the excellence of its color by being the abode of blackness—that is, of dark hue—and which has begun to sing, causes every lovely mountain here to bow; there is none that does not submit, nor is it not easily bent. Even she who was previously "unbending" (asvānamā)—meaning one whose pride was entirely unabated—now bows down when her pride is completely exhausted by the intensity of the excitants (*uddīpana*).

This is called *ardhābhyāsa* (repetition of half-verses), which is considered a type of *samudga*; three varieties of it are recognized by the learned: the separated (*vyapeta*), the unseparated (*avyapeta*), and the one possessing both characteristics. || 66 ||
Among these, an example of *vyapeta* (separated) is as follows:
“O timid one, I consider this mountain-peak, with its many-footed, wandering, dense *sāla* trees and its birds flying about, to be a mass of clouds; O timid one, look at it with your eyes. (146)

Where clouds wander through many valleys and foothills like *sāla* and *varaṇa* trees forming a rampart; where flocks of birds (*patattrikūṭāḥ*) are as captivating as they appear, worthy of honor (*mānyāḥ*), and fearless (*abhīravaḥ*); and where there are *sāla* trees with many roots (*anekapāda-bhramad-abhra-sālāḥ*)—the word *kap* being added according to the rule for words beginning with *mūlavibhuja*—which bear (*bharanti*) and sustain the abundant (*adabhra*) and intense rut of many-tusked elephants (*anekapāḥ*). [The two terms *mānye* and *abhīrviti* are vocatives.]
The state of pride and passion: "Behold Mount Trikūṭa with an eye worthy of that.
An example of the uninterrupted [metre] (avyapeta) is as follows:
"Having pierced the dense mass of Arjuna’s arrows, having pierced the dense mass of Arjuna’s arrows..."
The arrow of the one with uneven eyes (the peacock) sped forth; [it was] the arrow of the one with uneven eyes (the peacock).
*Vidārī* is a type of tuberous root; *arjuna* is the *kakubha* tree; *bāṇa* is a specific kind of shrub; *pūga* is the betel-nut palm (*guvāka*).
Because they form a pair of trees, they are treated as a singular collective by optional rule.
Arjuna Pārtha, having pierced—that is, split apart—the multitude of his arrows, that mass of shafts, proceeded toward him;

he who possesses three eyes (the Three-Eyed One), assuming the form of a Kirāta, followed after him with his excellent arrow, which possessed a preeminent sound. Together with him, he was "unequaled" (ayuga)—meaning without a second—and he was "without eyes" (alocana) in the sense of being difficult to perceive, being both "departed" and "not departed" [from his true nature].
"The flocks of peacocks, having brought the arrival of the thick clouds through their cries, attain beauty;
the beauties of the peacocks, whose arrival of the thick clouds has been dispelled by the breezes from Vṛndāvana, pass away.
However, the repetition of three quarters is not particularly beautiful, and therefore its varieties are not illustrated here.
The flocks of swans, whose habit is to sport in the water, approach and gather together with beauty— that is, with a charming disposition—

and by their mere mutual conversation, they carry forth a dense and continuous arrival; yet by the wind from the flocks— a whirlwind— the arrival of the clouds, that is, the rainy weather, is driven away, and the peacocks, with their cries, their *kekā* sounds on all sides, depart and vanish.

Since the repetition of three quarters (pādas) is impossible within a single verse, and because such beauty is lacking in another verse [if they were separate], one might think that the repetition of three quarters need not be considered; therefore, he says: "The repetition of three quarters...
A great *yamaka* consisting of four quarters of identical form is called [a *mahāyamaka*], and among those, the first [type] deserves further repetition [of the entire verse]. (67)
Now, defining the *mahāyamaka* which follows in sequence, he says: "Of one form" (*ekākāra*) means it is of two kinds:
that which consists of one occurrence within a group of four lines, and that which consists of another occurrence within a group of eight lines.

This has been stated as "the first [type] is moreover non-repeated" because the eightfold classification is established solely through the distinction of intermediate repetitions within each quarter-verse (*pāda*).
Among these, *mahāyamaka* (great palindrome) occurs when there is no separation [of the repeated elements], as for example:

‘Sabhāsamānāsahasāparāgāt sabhāsamānā sahasā parāgāt sabhāsamānā sahasāparāgāt sabhāsamānā sahasāparāgāt || 149 ||’ Here, *bhāsaḥ* means luster; *mānaḥ* means mental exaltation or honor; *āsaḥ* means the shaking off of enemies; and *hasaḥ* means smiling. That which exists together with these is *sabhāsamānāsahasā*. Because it devours (*atti*) *aparāgam*, which is the turbidity of the mind—[it is thus called *sabhāsamānāsahasāparāgāt*].

*Sabhāsamānā* means "together with those that are *bhāsamānaiḥ*," that is, shining or beautiful; [it refers to the sky] which, by reason of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, suddenly attains (*atati*) or reaches the *parāgān*—the particles of dust (*rajaḥkaṇān*) produced by the cessation of the rainy season—and thus, being *sabhāsamānā*, it exists together with those things that are *bhāsā-samānaiḥ*, meaning those possessing a similar luster (*bhā*). Thus it is *sabhāsamānā*.
The word *sā* refers to those who, at the time of destruction (*antakarman*), cause others to perish; that which exists together with them is *sahasā*.

Such an assembly (*sabhā*)—meaning a gathering of people—that is unequal and incomparable, came forth suddenly and swiftly from another mountain (*aparasmāt parvatāt*) as a result of disaffection (*aparāgāt*). Thus it is said, "it came forth" (*parāgāt*).
The second type of *mahāyamaka*, in which the division [of the hemistichs] is absent, is as follows:

"Flowing down, free from clouds, with moving elephants, conquered by the Mūḍha, possessing pure and highly honored waves, tasteless, always mixed with crocodiles, the abode of Acyuta, where the forest is frequented by birds whose flight is well-known;

flowing down, free from clouds, with moving elephants, conquered by the Mūḍha, possessing pure and highly honored waves, tasteless, always mixed with crocodiles, the abode of Acyuta, where the forest is frequented by birds whose flight is well-known. (150)
"Pravaṇam" means a most excellent forest; the substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*] occurs according to the rule "pra-nir-antar-śara—" and so forth.

It is that place where birds (*vayaḥ*) who are moving with abundant (*adabhreṇa*), that is, great (*mahatā*), pride (*madena*) or arrogance (*darpeṇa*), have defeated other birds who are foolish and young (*mūḍha-vayas-bālāḥ*). Alternatively, it is that which sustains (*malate*) or supports (*dhārayati*) in abundance (*alam*) the aforementioned non-foolish birds (*amūḍhān vīn*).
It has treacherous waves, is a place filled with whirlpools inhabited by serpents, is unpleasant due to its lack of contact with the ground, is devoid of any level terrain,
and is constantly, at all times, frequented and inhabited by *timi*— the great fish.

The first meaning of the verse is as follows: it is the abode—the place of rest—of the Lord Nārāyaṇa, who is Acyuta; it is renowned and celebrated as being "frequented by Śikhin," that is, the submarine fire (vaḍavānala), which has consumed the masses of water.

Furthermore, it is adorned by the mountains and elephants, such as Maināka and others, which are "intoxicated with pride"—meaning their arrogance is dependent on their rut—and which are "constantly exuding rut-fluid" as they roam about, as well as by the aquatic elephants and sea-monsters.
He who has carried across the waves— which are pure by nature, stainless, honored, and revered— and which are otherwise tasteless,
salty, and filled with various birds that are beautiful and exceedingly radiant, has reached the shore.

The second meaning of the verse is as follows: "Behold the ocean whose splendor has not waned; its forest is frequented by peacocks (*śikhin*) who have returned, having been driven away [by the heat]. This connects with the action occurring within the subsequent part of the sentence, namely that the forest on its shores was wandered through by those peacocks.
Regarding the first type, where the distinction is not separated, here is an example of repetition (*abhyāsa*):
‘Equal with the equal, equal with the unequal, equal with the equal, equal with the unequal, equal with the equal-unequal, equal with the equal-unequal.
[151] ‘Equal’ means:

"O friend, by this woman—who is equal to you, who is to be ranked at the forefront of the ill-mannered, who possesses an equal exertion (*yāsa*), and who possesses equal pride (*māna*) and jealousy-anger (*īrṣyā-roṣa*); and likewise, who is equal to you in sharing the same mental disposition yet unequal to you in her incomparable success in receiving honor—by her, you, who are equal to me, must unite me with her. This is the prayer of a certain friend overcome by the madness of love, wherein two meanings are expressed in a single form of sentence; that which is spoken of as "two meanings" by those who know words is called *śleṣa* (paronomasia). 68.
Following *yamaka* (rhyme), because of the commonality of its occurrence with *bandha* (punning arrangement), he defines *śleṣa* (paronomasia): "In a single form...

According to the principle that words differ according to their different meanings, one might ask how two things can be expressed by a single sentence; therefore, he says, "by way of *tantra* (simultaneous application)," for *śleṣa* is characterized by a blending [of meanings].
And in this context, it applies even to words that are distinct, by virtue of their similarity in pronunciation;
the occurrence of multiple relations with a single form is called *tantra*.
There are two [types of *tantra*] arising from stems and suffixes, based respectively on case-endings and numbers.
"And those arising from the phonemes of words"—thus there are six types of *śabdaśleṣa*.

The number "two" (*dvayoḥ*) is not intended [to be restrictive], because *śleṣa* is possible even for three or more [words], since in the statement of the classification (*vibhāga-vākya*), the case-endings (*vibhakti*) are explicitly mentioned; therefore, in each word, that [number] refers to something else. Furthermore, the purpose of mentioning the specific [number] is to produce a particular beauty (*viśeṣa-śobhā*).
Among these, an example of *prakṛtiśleṣa* (phonetic punning) is as follows:
“O King, your majesty brings glory to yourself and others, while your arm causes fear to both your enemies and your friends. (152)

Here, in the phrase *kīrtinut*, the verbal roots *nauti* (to praise) and *nudati* (to push away) have an identical form when reduced to their base (*prakṛti*) by means of the suffix *kvip*; likewise, in the phrase *ubhayakṛt*, the bases *karoti* (to do) and *kṛntati* (to cut) have an identical form. Thus, this is a case of *prakṛtiśleṣa* (phonetic play on the verbal root).
He praises (*nauti*) his own fame and pushes away (*nudati*)—that is, casts off—the enemies of others.

It causes fear for enemies and creates [fear] while also breaking [the hearts] of friends; thus, the difference in meaning arises solely from the difference in the root-forms (*prakṛti*) of the verbal roots, because the *kvip* suffix is common to both.
Therefore, even this "punning of gender" (*liṅgaśleṣa*) is in fact nothing but a "punning of the root" (*prakṛtiśleṣa*).
For example:
"Whom does she not captivate with her eyes and her body, which possess the luster of blue lotus petals; and with her face, whose beauty surpasses that of young shoots, and her arched brows? (153)

Here, although there is a difference in gender between *dṛgvapuṣoḥ* (eyes and body) and *āsyacaraṇayoḥ* (mouth and feet), the qualifiers *kuvalayadaladyutiḥ* (having the luster of blue lotus petals) and *adharīkṛtapravālaśrīḥ* (surpassing the beauty of coral shoots) are identical in form; thus, this is a "śleṣa of gender" (*liṅgaśleṣa*).

Now, since some have enumerated [the types of śleṣa] as "of letters, words, gender, dialect, root, suffix, case-ending, and number," it might follow that śleṣa would be eightfold. To this he says: "even the śleṣa of gender. He states that this very example should be cited: "as follows" (*sa yathā*).

By the use of the middle-voice ending in *darśayataḥ*, it is suggested: "Whom, even though standing as a mere bystander, does it not forcibly impel toward beholding? Furthermore, in the phrases *adharīkṛtādharatvam āpāditā* ("rendered inferior, having been made to lose its status as the lower lip") and *kuvalayadaladyutiḥ* ("possessing the luster of a blue lotus petal"), as well as *adharīkṛtapravālaśrīḥ* ("having surpassed the beauty of coral"), the verbal root (*prakṛti*) does not differ; how then can this be called a *prakṛtiśleṣa* (root-pun)?
This is not so;

because of the proximity of two qualifiers with two distinct genders, a qualifier that does not itself possess a fixed gender must necessarily be understood as taking both genders. On the view that the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) consists of five factors, the case-ending merely serves as an indicator (*dyotika*); thus, there is a difference in gender. Consequently, when the bases of the two qualifiers are distinct yet mutually connected, [the rule applies].
Regarding the phrase "here, etc.," there is a pun on the suffix (*pratyaya*), which is both manifest (*sodbheda*) and unmanifest (*nirudbheda*).
Of these two, the first is as follows:
"Whose wonder did her two breasts not produce—breasts that were captivating by their very nature even without a necklace?

(154). Here, because the suffixes *ini* and *ṇini* take the same form in the word *hāriṇau*, and because the possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*) is manifested in the phrase "even without a necklace," this is a *śleṣa* (punning) based on suffixes that are both manifest and unmanifest.
That which is manifested by another word situated within that same sentence is "with distinction" (*sodbheda*); that which is not so is "without distinction" (*nirudbheda*).
When the suffix *ini* is used in the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*), [the words] become *hāriṇau*, meaning "possessing necklaces.
When the suffix *ṇini* is used in the sense of necessity (*āvaśyaka*), they become *hāriṇau*, meaning "they captivate the minds of sensitive readers (*sahṛdaya*)."

Astonishment (*vismaya*) and wonder (*adbhuta*), which consist of the savoring of the essence of solid bliss (*ānandaghana-rasa*), are also indicated by the word *api*, which suggests Virādha and others; thus, even for those who lack a necklace (*hārahīna*), the connection with a necklace (*hārasambandha*) conveys the sentiment of wonder. This is because the suffix denoting possession (*matvarthīya*) is revealed, making it a "manifested" (*sodbheda*) instance.
As for how there can be a pun (*śleṣa*) on the suffixes, he says: "of the suffixes *ini* and *iniP*."
The second is as follows:
“The luster of the moon’s mark shines like the scar formed where the source of its disease was extracted by you; it has become, as it were, a doe. (155)

Here, in the expression *hariṇībhūtā*, because the forms of the suffixes *cvi* and *ṅīp* are identical, there is no distinction between them; thus, this is a non-distinction (*anudbheda*) based on the suffix (*pratyaya-śleṣa*). [The meaning is: the place where the wound has healed becomes dark, so what kind of doe (*hariṇī*) is she? She is one who has become like the shadow of a spot (*lāñchanacchāyābhūtā*). The form is derived from the word *harita* (green) by applying *ṅīp* and the substitution of *n* according to the rule: "After a non-udātta vowel ending in *t*, when followed by *t*, *ṅīp* is applied and *n* is substituted. This is the resulting form.

This is a *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) based on the quality of being perceived; although it does not possess the actual form of a deer (*hariṇa*), it has attained the status of a deer through conventional usage. In the case of the suffix *cvī*, which results in the form *hariṇībhūta*, no distinction whatsoever has been established between the feminine suffix *ḍīp* and the suffix *cvī*. Thus, this is an "undifferentiated" (*nirudbheda*) *śleṣa* (paronomasia) of suffixes.
Even in the case of the two natures appearing in the form of a green deer, they are indeed distinct, since their commingling (*saṃkara*) does not constitute a fault;
the same applies to the previous example as well.
The pun on case-endings (*vibhaktiśleṣa*) is of two kinds: that of different classes and that of identical classes. Of these, the first is as follows:
"By whom the Lord of Serpents bore poison upon his own neck..."

"He by whom the poison was held in his throat, and the king of serpents was held in his throat; he by whom a son was borne in his body, and a wife was borne—may that Unborn One be victorious. (156) In this verse, there is a *śleṣa* (pun) between two different types of nominal and verbal suffixes (*sup* and *tiṅ*), because the forms of the suffixes ending in the third person singular perfect active (*liṭ*) and the first person singular middle (*ātmanepada*) in the locative case are identical in form while differing in meaning. Specifically, "nijagale" is the form of the root *gṛ* (to swallow) in the locative case, derived from the perfect tense. Thus, "by whom the poison was swallowed in his throat" and "the king of serpents was held in his throat"; "by whom a son was borne in his body" and "a wife was borne"—this is a *śleṣa* of distinct nominal and verbal suffixes.
He by whom the poison known as Kālakūṭa was swallowed, and the king of serpents was worn upon his own neck;

he by whom the body was burned—here the form is from the *liṭ* (perfect tense) of the root *dah*—and the Aṅgaja, namely Kāma, was consumed; yet he by whom Pārvatī was taken as his wife upon his own body: may he be victorious.
The second explanatory passage is indeed easy to understand, as follows:
"You alone are the preceding root (dhātu), and you alone are the subsequent suffix (pratyaya)."
"O Lord, there is nothing that has not been described by You; with what, then, could You be compared? (157).

Here, because the word *dhātuḥ*—ending in the nominative case and ending in the genitive case—is identical in form yet possesses different meanings, this is an example of *abhinnajātīya-sub-vibhakti-śleṣa* (paronomasia on nouns with identical case endings).
By the phrase "prior even to the Creator (*dhātu*) of the world," its beginninglessness is expressed.
The supreme cause, which consists of the threefold nature [of the elements], is not anything unexplained,
because its glorious deeds are well-known in the Śruti, Smṛti, Itihāsa, and Purāṇas;
and because there is no second [to it], it cannot be compared with anything else.

But in the case of a different meaning, the verbal root (*dhātu*)—which is a form of word denoting action—is the very same as before because it is the base (*prakṛti*); following that is the suffix (*pratyaya*), such as *tiṅ* and so forth. Therefore, the entire word is produced as nothing other than a verb (*ākhyāta*).

Consequently, how could there be a comparison with that which ends in a *tiṅ* suffix? This was stated for the purpose of strengthening the distinction between words, since their meanings are different.
In this manner, the distinction among verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*) should also be illustrated, as follows:
"Let poets indeed be intoxicated; nevertheless, their exertion is well known."
"I am the master of Vedic knowledge, as I am the inner essence of all speech.
Here, in the first and third persons singular, the word "veda" (meaning both "Veda" and "I know") is employed through *śleṣa* (punning).
This *vacana-śleṣa* (punning on number) is twofold: with distinction (*sodbheda*) and without distinction (*nirudbheda*).
The illustration of these two together with their distinction is as follows:

“May Nemi, whose power is abundant, who is the source of dharma, from whom passion and darkness have departed, and whose soul is liberated, grant us prosperity; and may the other Jinas as well grant it. (158)

In this context, others maintain that there is a distinction between the singular and plural numbers through the forms *nemiḥ* (singular) and *anye’pi* (plural); thus, in the case of the verbal form *dadatām*, there is a manifestation of both singular and plural, as is the case with the nominal forms *prājyaprabhāvaḥ* and *prabhavaḥ*. This is called "śleṣa with distinction" (*sodbhedo vacanaśleṣaḥ*).
An example of "śleṣa without distinction" (*nirudbheda*) is as follows:
*tanutvaramaṇīyasya madhyasya ca bhujasya ca* [The slender and beautiful waist and the arm...]

"Her bracelets became exceedingly conducive to the increase of her beauty. (159) Here, the two words *abhavan* and *valayaḥ*—the verb ending in a suffix and the noun ending in a case-suffix—possess both singular and plural forms that remain unmanifested (*anudbhinnau*) yet are joined through paronomasia (*śleṣa*). This is the "unmanifested" (*nirudbheda*) verbal paronomasia. Because the capacity for connection with the qualifiers is implied through both the singular and plural, the two meanings are brought forth respectively in the verbal and nominal inflections; thus, there is a manifestation of two distinct word-forms.

By means of the singular number, "valayaḥ" (bracelet) is understood, and by the plural number, "madhyarekhāḥ" (middle lines); thus, while these are appropriate as nouns ending in case-suffixes (*subanta*), they do not exist as verbs ending in tense-suffixes (*tiṅanta*). Consequently, there is the attainment of two distinct verbal meanings, yet no differentiator has been composed for these two; therefore, this is an "undifferentiated" (*nirudbheda*) figure.
This is what he says: "In this regard," and so forth.
An example of word-pun (*padaśleṣa*) is as follows:
"Your arm is both an enemy-destroyer and a *palāśa* tree; it is both a wish-granting tree (*kalpadruma*) and [the god] Kāmadruma."
"This garden, adorned with groves of *sāla* trees, is like a garland for a child.

(160) Here, because the base (*prakṛti*), suffix (*pratyaya*), case-ending (*vibhakti*), and number (*vacana*) are mentioned separately, it is stated that the *abhidhāna-mālā* refers to nominal stems (*prātipadika*) alone by the term "word" (*pada*).

Therefore, in the first half [of the verse], through the sense "the flesh of the enemy's division is eaten by you, O arm," the names of the two trees called *ari-bheda* and *palāśa* are joined in a double entendre (*śleṣa*).

And in the second half [of the verse], the word *sālaka* is used in two senses: "she shines with a forest of *sāla* trees" and "she shines with a face possessing beautiful eyes (*sālaka*). Thus, the word *bālā* (young girl) is applied as a simile, meaning she is like a garland of gardens.
This is a verbal pun (*śabdaśleṣa*) known as "word-pun" (*padaśleṣa*).
The term *aribheda* means the piercing of the body's vital constituents (*dhātu*); one who eats flesh (*pala*) is so described. The particle *ca* is used in reference to the subsequent sentence.

*Arībheda*, *viṭkhadira*, *palāśa*, *kiṃśuka*, and *sāla* are specific types of trees; their grove is the forest. *Alakāḥ* refers to curled locks of hair, and the face accompanied by them is [the second meaning]. Since the first and second halves of the verse do not form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*), they are cited as examples [of word-play]. Now, one might object: "Is there no *pada* other than that which ends in a case-ending? In that case, the play upon the stem (*prakṛti-śleṣa*) has already been indicated by the first part, and the play upon the suffix (*pratyaya-śleṣa*) by the second part. What, then, is this 'play upon the word' (*pada-śleṣa*)? To this, he says: "In this [example]... (referring to the following).

The meaning is that, in the absence of the intention to express the relationship between base and suffix, only the nominal stems (*prātipadika*) mentioned in the *Nāmamālā* remain; this is also a "fusion of phonemes" (*varṇaśleṣa*), which is indeed a "fusion of words" (*padaśleṣa*),
as for example:
"O Lord, you alone are Pātāla; you are the bond of the quarters; and you alone, consisting of the three worlds, are the source of the winds of the immortals.

Here, the letter *a* in "you alone are Pātāla" (tvameva pātālam) is linked with the subsequent syllable, while the letter *ca* in "and you are the source of the winds of the immortals" (tvaṃ ca amara-marud-bhūmiḥ) is linked with the preceding syllable, thereby forming the words "Pātāla" and "Cāmara."

This very *padaśleṣa* (word-pun) is called *varṇaśleṣa* (syllable-pun): “The ornament is a skull that causes suspicion; the attendant is the skeletal Bhṛṅgin; and the wealth is a single, aged bull—such is the condition even of Sthāṇu, the teacher of all the gods, while the crooked moon rests upon his head; what then are we?”
Thus, the "phoneme-pun" (*varṇaśleṣa*) has been separately illustrated by the Kashmiris;
therefore, he says: "the phoneme-pun also.

The sense is that since a whole can exist when its parts are not distinct, whereas the distinction of a whole is necessarily established when there is a distinction of its parts, it is logical that this [phoneme-pun] be included within the category of word-pun (*padaśleṣa*), as it is established therein.

He is the protector who guards excessively; he is the bond of hopes, the seed for making desires bear fruit; he is the place of union for the quarters (āśā) and the directions (diś); he is the ground of the chowrie-winds; he is the celestial world (svarloka), the abode of the immortals (amara) such as Indra and others, and the ground of the winds (marut) such as Vīvaḥvat and others, as well as the path of the gods in their celestial chariots (vaimānika)—thus he is the refuge of the chowrie-winds.
To the question, "How is there a pun on the word *varṇa* here?", he says: "In this [verse]," and so forth.

In the derivation of the form *pātāla* from the root *pat* with the suffix *ālañ*—according to the rule *paticaṇḍibhyām ālañ*—the vowel *ā* alone is the intervening phoneme. When there is a reconnection (*pratisaṃdhāna*) of a portion [of the preceding] to that very [vowel], the form *pātāla* is perceived;
and here, by the rule "one [element replaces both] the preceding and the following," only the vowel *ā* is heard. Thus, the subsequent [element] is merged with the preceding one.
In this same manner, the merging of the letter *c* with what follows it is to be explained.
An example of wordplay (*bhāṣāśleṣa*) is as follows:

"O Umā, bestow upon me the boon of devotion to that excellent one who acts for the welfare of the world, who removes the delusion of the earth, who has severed his enemies, and whose body is as powerful as the lion, the enemy of the deer. (162)
In this regard:
“And a certain man, desiring battle, worshipped Rudrāṇī—who had been brought there by meditation and was standing before him as his beloved—with both divine and vernacular speech. (163)
In that regard, on the side of Rudrāṇī: O Umā, O Hara, O Bhava, perform the most excellent state;
in what kind [of state]?
In one where there is licking of Lālasabhū—the "Lālasabhū" being Kāma (Desire), he who licks it.
Likewise, in that presence of Maheśvara— which removes the conceit of greatness through its majesty and power— it is heard in scripture that all [other] knowledges are overwhelmed; therefore,
it is "tuhinavicchinna," meaning separated from or devoid of those "tuhā" enemies who afflict or torment.
He states another cause for the destruction of enemies: "In that excellent bridegroom, whose body possesses the strength (sāra) of Hariṇāri— the lion"— or alternatively,
these are vocative adjectives addressed to Umā herself.

In the case of the beloved, however—the meaning is: O beloved, may that which is the most excellent and superior part of this body of yours, which is the very essence of the goddess Śrī (Lakṣmī)—namely, your eyes, face, breasts, hips, and so forth—take away my state of longing; that is to say, may it fulfill my desires.
Of what kind is that body?
With curved and languid lines of eyebrows, captivating the world as a dwelling that steals away delusion, and enchanting with a slender waist and other such qualities— thus is the divine,
refined, and Prakrit Mahārāṣṭrī language.
*Bhāva* is the dissolution of the mind;

*lālasa* is desire (*icchā*). That which arises from that is *lālasabhū*.
