‘That conqueror of enemies begot upon the daughter of the lord of Niṣadha a son of no inferior strength, whom they call by the very name Niṣadha, after the king of Niṣadha.
(217) Here, in the word *niṣiddhaśatruḥ*, there is a harshness of sound due to the excessive conjunction of consonants (*saṃyoga*).

This very alliteration of words (padānuprāsa) is called "jagged" (dantura); for instance, in the verse beginning with "naiṣadha," the cluster of letters forming the word "Niṣadha" has become a part of a single word and is thus common [to both meanings].
To the question, "In what way, then, is there jaggedness here?", he says: "here, [the word] 'niṣiddha'..."
An example of the gentle [speech] is as follows: "Come here, beloved Vaidehī; give me an answer.
O lotus-eyed one, courtesy is indeed the ornament of women. (218)
Here, because it occurs together with a vowel, its smoothness constitutes this *padānuprāsa* (alliteration of words), which is called "smooth" (*ślakṣṇa*).
An example of the "box" (*saṃpuṭa*) type is as follows:
"Like Kandarpa full of pride, my mind is fickle; like this world which is essence-less, please grant me your favor.
Here, because the word "iva" functions as an exception (apavāda) and thus does not create a separation, this alliteration is called *saṃpuṭa* (the casket).

A *saṃpuṭa* is the continuous repetition of a single segment in the manner of a casket; how then is it accomplished with the word *kaṃsa* as an interval? To this he says: "In this case, of the word *iva*"—the sequence of *saṃpuṭas* is as follows:
“What does this *kiṅkirāta* do, having drawn forth its arrows (*śilīmukha*), that which the *kiṅkirāta* does by drawing forth its arrows?

(220) In this verse, there are four types of *saṃpuṭa*: first, *karoti* and *karoti*; second, *kiṃ kirātaḥ* and *kiṅkirātaḥ*; third, *samākṛṣya* and *samākṛṣya*; and fourth, *śilīmukhān* and *śilīmukhān*.

This *padānuprāsa* (alliteration of words) is called *saṃpuṭāvalī* (a series of caskets), as in the verse beginning "What does this hunter do? (*kiṃ kirāto'yam*); here, first there is the inner casket formed by "arrows" (*śilīmukhān*) within the phrase "arrows" (*śilīmukhān*), and outside that, serving as its covering, is the second casket formed by "drawing back" (*samākṛṣya*) in the phrase "having drawn back" (*samākṛṣya*).
For that [word] as well, there is a third [derivation], *kiṅkirāta* from *kiṃ kirātaḥ*;
for that too, there is a fourth, *karoti*.
Manifesting this through an inverse interpretation, he says: "In this context, 'he does' (*karoti*), etc."

He was weary, as it were: "For those who are entangled by family and caste, whose consciousness is deluded regarding the hope for pleasure amidst suffering, and who are greedy for the acquisition of worldly power and existence—may there be [this teaching] once more for the sake of shattering the bonds of existence within cyclic birth. (221)
Here, because the *rīti* (style) is not sustained, there is weariness;
this very *padānuprāsa* (alliteration of words) is called "wearied," as in the word *kula*.
In this verse, in the first quarter, the pair of syllables *kula*—whose vowels and other properties are not intended to be significant—is repeated as *kulī*, separated by four syllables.

In the second and third quarters, however, there is a repetition with a single intervening syllable: *sukhada-sukha* and *abhava-vibhava*. In the fourth quarter, the sequence *bhava-bhava* does not constitute a fault, even though it breaks the established rhythmic pattern (*rītibhaṅga*).
Just as a cluster of flowers, through its proximity,
causes the three worlds to appear within the collection of poets and others, even though it does not actually illuminate them.
"Which authors do not fall into the servitude of Kālidāsa?
(222). This very *padānuprāsa* (alliteration of words), like *varṇānuprāsa*, is called "clustered" (*stabakavat*) because it is arranged at various points;
it manifests the status of an ornament through a particular variety of charm, as in the example beginning with *bhāsayati*, where the repetition occurs between distant beginnings and ends.
However, the restriction regarding position is not intended to be significant;
this is what was stated: "in each respective place," just as in the case of the substituendum.

‘But the moonlight is hot, the essence of sandalwood is like poison, the pearl necklace is caustic to a wound, the Malaya breezes burn the body, the lotus stalks are like a forest of spears, and even the water-lily is a flame; for when that fair-faced one with eyes like lotuses was seen, she was the supreme balm for my slender frame. (223)
"The lotus-stalk, the row of arrows, and the slender body moist with water—all these burn, yet that fair-faced one with lotus-eyes, when seen, is most excellent.
This is *padānuprāsa* (alliteration of words), which is called *sthānī* (position-bound) because of the restriction of its position;
for instance, in the verse beginning "joṇhā uṇhā riso raso," there is a repetition restricted to specific positions such as the middle or the end of each quarter-verse (*pāda*).
Alkali applied to a wound;
a cloth dampened with water; a couple like [water and] a wet garment.

"First, on the shore of the near and far banks, a monastery; then a preeminent city; then the Indus; then the Indus; then the purifying forest of the Lord of Serpents; before that, a lofty mountain; and in front of that mountain, the city of Viśālā shines forth with its halls and charming women.
This is a "pair" (mithuna), due to the arrangement of two instances of alliteration (*anuprāsa*) in each successive quarter-verse.
The river named Pārā is "apārā," meaning devoid of a further shore;
the river Sindhu is the one known by the name Sindhu.

In the phrase "Viśālā Ujjayinī śālābhiḥ," the third case ending is used in the sense of a characteristic mark (itthambhūtalakṣaṇe). Here, there is an arrangement of two types of alliteration (*anuprāsa*) respectively in the first and subsequent quarters: *pārāpāra* and *sindhu*, *sindhur* and *dagra*, and *śālā* and *śāla*.
Although in the third quarter the second pair [of syllables] "girigiri" is also possible, he nevertheless disregarded it as being unremarkable due to the intervention of two other letters.

An example of a series of such pairs is as follows: "A śarabha on his head, a boar on his chest, an elephant trumpeting at his temples, a ruru deer on his breast, a deer on his vital spot, and a crow cawing at his mouth."

"The poet too is delightful in his heart; from afar, Hari, the slayer of the elephant [Gajendra], has been struck by him with his bow; the victory of this illustrious one over the target is unprecedented.
This continuous repetition of two quarters is called a "pair" (mithunāvalī), as in the example beginning with "śirasī."
The śarabha is the eight-legged beast; the kroḍa is the boar;
the ruru is the deer with many horns.

The lion-like *hari* (sound) partakes of the resonance when there is a desire to speak; a pair of consonants repeated constitutes a "pair" (*mithuna*), and that same pair, through an abundance of repetition— as in the sequences *śara-śara*, *kroḍa-kroḍa*, *kara-kara*, *dava-dava*, and so forth— is easily recognized in its proper order.
An example of that which is "released after being grasped" (gṛhītamukta) is as follows:
"Fragrant with the lingering scent of the pollen of *puṃnāga* and *nāgakesara* flowers, the breeze has arrived, sweet and beloved by the humming of six-legged bees. (226)
This very alliteration, which resembles a circular enclosure (*cakravāla*), is called "seized and released" (*gṛhītamukta*). An example of the "seized and released" is as follows:
"puṃnāgaḥ puṃgajaḥ," which is well-known [as a name for the tree].
Kesara is the Bakula flower; Bhāvanā is latent impression (vāsanā); Surabhi is the spring season.
The movement— the wandering— here of the six-legged bees, who are eager to drink various kinds of honey,
is clearly a *cakravāla* sequence;
and because there is no repetition or excess, there is the release of exactly what has been grasped.
Another example of tautology (punarukti) is as follows:

“O friend, when the sky is filled with smoke from the bow whose string is being drawn by the hand, and which roars while its peaks resound, and which is dark with smoke and ablaze with water... (227).

"The sky resounds with the bow, which smokes, being obscured by smoke; it blazes, with its flaming grip held by the living beings; it fills the quarters with echoes; and it roars, with its tips dripping with resin.
Here, because of the repetition of words such as "smoke" (*dhūma*) and so forth, this alliteration (*padānuprāsa*) is said to possess tautology (*punarukti*).

Regarding the term "possessing tautology" (*punaruktimān*): since there is no difference in the expressed meaning, "tautology" refers to that [figure] in which there is alliteration (*anuprāsa*) characterized by repetition;
yet, because there is a difference in intended meaning (*tātparya*), it is not a defect.

Because the smoke, flames, and tongues of fire pervade the expanse of space, they suggest through the excellence of the poetic figures (dhanuḥ-prakarṣa) the energy and power residing in Rāmabhadra; thus, there is a nourishment of the prevailing heroic sentiment (vīrarasa).
Here, by means of the repetition of "dhūma-dhūma" and so forth, there is a variety of the expressed meaning (vācyabheda).

Now, one might object: "The definition of alliteration (anuprāsa) as the repetition of phonemes is generally applicable, yet such repetition does not exist here in the repetition of words and so forth. To this, he says:
Alliteration (*anuprāsa*) is the repetition of phonemes both in verses (*pāda*) and in words (*pada*);
it is a distance between words that awakens the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of prior experience. (97) Regarding the phrase "repetition of phonemes":
Even occurrence in a collection is merely occurrence in individual phonemes, for there is no such thing as a "collection" distinct from the phonemes;
however, this much is the distinction: that the recollection of occurrences belonging to a preceding type constitutes the state of being an ornament.
And in that regard, it is precisely a specific proximity of convention (*samaya*) that is the operative factor, which is to be inferred from its effect; thus,
this has been stated merely as a general direction,
for as far as the scope of the category of *lāṭānuprāsa* (alliteration) is observed.
Even within the category of word-alliteration (*padānuprāsa*), only that much has been elaborated [here].
He says that other varieties of word-alliteration are also to be conceived by oneself: "The *lāṭa* manner" refers to the type or variety.

"That [repetition] which occurs by way of its inherent nature (*svabhāva*), by way of figurative usage (*gauṇī*), by way of distributive repetition (*vīpsā*), frequent occurrence (*abhīkṣṇya*), and so forth—whether through names or through double utterances within a sentence—is called *tadanuprāsa* (internal alliteration).
(99) He analyzes *nāmadviruktyanuprāsa* (alliteration consisting of the repetition of names), which follows in the sequence: "by way of its inherent nature," etc.

Although the repetition of names is overly broad as a definition for *padānuprāsa* and other such figures, it is nevertheless intended here as that which occurs in conjunction with the introduction of meaning.
Meaning (*artha*) is of two kinds: the denotative (*ābhidhānika*) and the adjectival (*upādhi*).

The former is of two types, distinguished as secondary (*gauṇa*) and primary (*mukhya*); the latter is also manifold, including varieties such as distributive repetition (*vīpsā*) and frequency (*abhīkṣṇya*).
It should be understood that there are two kinds of repetition: that which brings about a physical body and that which pertains to a name already existing.
For this very reason, it was stated that [the power of expression] belongs to what is repeated by its very nature;
as for that [repetition] by way of its own nature, it is as follows:
"Making this clamor, swaying to and fro by the wind, these clouds murmur at dawn like elephants.
Here, in the word *kalakalam* and others, natural tautology (*punarukti*) is taught.
"Kurvantaḥ" means moving or flickering; "cañcalāḥ" is derived from the root *cal* with the suffix *ac*, where the form of the reduplicated syllable is *ak*.
In the case of an imitation of an indistinct sound such as *gulu*, when the suffix *ḍāc* is applied and reduplication occurs, the name *gulugulā* is established.

In this regard, for words like *kalakala* and others, whose very form consists of a reduplication necessitated by the sense of the object, their establishment in the aforementioned form occurs by their very nature.
An example of the figurative (*gauṇī*) [usage] is as follows:
‘Nectar is nectar, the moon is the moon, likewise the lotus is the lotus; Rati is Rati, Kāma is Kāma, and honey is honey.
Thus, for the most part, an object does not possess a mutual commingling of its nature; so how is it that this woman possesses a luster that consists of all these [qualities] together?

(229) In this verse, although there is no actual difference in expressions such as “nectar is nectar” and so forth, the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣyabhāva*) arises through the metaphorical attribution (*upacāra*) of difference. This occurs because of the relationship between the general and the particular (*sāmānya-viśeṣabhāva*), yet it appears like a tautology (*punarukta*).

Regarding the term *amṛtam* (nectar) and so forth: since the repetition of these words ending in the accusative case results in the fault of tautology (*dvirukti*), their intended meaning cannot be fully realized there; thus, while it must be assumed that they refer to qualities such as nectar, because grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is untenable if they were taken to refer merely to inferior qualities, the status of being a substantive and the status of being an attribute are both established by their dependence on the general sense conveyed by the first word—namely, those [qualities] residing in the nectar and other substances, which are themselves augmented by their respective unique attributes.

Furthermore, the former teachers maintain that when these terms are employed in succession (*paryāya*), it is impossible for them to possess the quality of "transfer of denotation" (*saṃkramitavācyatā*).
This is what is called "repetition dependent on a secondary sense" (*gauṇārthaparavaśā dvirukti*), such as in the case of distributive repetition (*vīpsā*):
"Not every mountain has rubies; not every elephant has pearls."
"In every region there are no scholars; in every forest there is no sandalwood.
This is the repetition known as *dravyavīpsā* (repetition of the substance).
In the same way, it should be understood that this applies to the repetition of qualities (*guṇa*), genus (*jāti*), and actions (*kriyā*).
*Vīpsā* is the speaker’s desire to convey the pervasion of various objects simultaneously by means of a single word; it is a property of the user that is manifested through reduplication.
For this very reason, any repetition drawn by the force of the meaning is designated as a "repetition of a name," just like the case of *saptavarṇa* and others; for instance,

in the expression *śaile śailaḥ*, one who intends to speak of a certain unique object as the locus of specific qualities, being unable to tolerate the touch of those same qualities in anything else of that same class, has instead mentioned an irrelevant thing such as a mountain.
In individual objects other than those from Rohaṇa and so forth, the pervasion by qualities such as being a ruby is intended to be understood simultaneously;
a category that is established in its own nature and perceived from a word as a subordinate element is called a "quality" (guṇa).
In this same way, pervasion by action (kriyā) is also to be understood.
This is "desire for a substance" (*dravyavīpsā*);
it means the desire to pervade substances such as mountains and so forth by means of a single quality or the like. [This refers to] *Pāṇini 8.1.12*: *prakāre guṇavacanasya*.
The passage beginning with "1 12" is also a type of distributive repetition (vīpsā),
as follows:
Receiving the glances of proud women, turbid with tears heated by the heat of their indignation, the cool-rayed moon rose slowly and slowly and departed toward the sky as if trembling with fear.
[The rule *prakāre guṇavacanasya* applies here.]
The mode [of *upamā*] is similarity (*sādṛśya*). This occurs when an object with fewer qualities shares common qualities with an object possessing full qualities;
and thus there exists both the state of being denotable by the same word and pervasion (*vyāpti*).

However, this is the distinction: in one case, similarity is the reflection of what is established in one place onto another; whereas in pure distributive repetition (*vīpsā*), it is the simultaneous connection of a single thing with multiple objects.
This is the meaning of the word *vīpsā* (repetition) as a manner;
for this very reason, [it is stated] "in the sense of manner, of a word denoting a quality" (Pāṇini 8.1.12).
The intention is that while this was formulated as a separate sūtra elsewhere, here this meaning is to be understood through the very word *vīpsā* (repetition); thus,
"as if rising very slowly" is an adverbial modifier used in a comparative sense (*upamitam*).

Thus, even though "terrified, terrified" (*bhītabhīta*) is an adjective qualifying the agent, the word *iva* functions as in the case of a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) based on the quality of similarity— as in the following example of frequency (*ābhīkṣṇya*).
‘Pressing against [hers], I drank again and again from the lotus-face offered by the deer-eyed one; drinking thus, with eyes half-closed, I took my pleasure.
This is the suffix *ṇamul* used in the sense of repetition (*ābhīkṣṇya*).
The phrase "and it is applied" is a redundancy;
[the sense of] "repeatedly" is already conveyed by the rule *nityavīpsayoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.1.4).
By this [sūtra], "1.4," repetition (*ābhīkṣṇya*) is stated as constancy (*nityatva*).
Indeed, that form of repetition is when the agent desires to perform an action primarily and without interruption.

For this very reason, this reduplication of finite verbs (*tiṅ*), indeclinables (*avyaya*), and primary derivatives (*kṛt*) is unique [to these], because in both cases there is the perception of the primacy of the action.
For when a thing is already established, the perception of repetition occurs only by virtue of the action as a limiting condition (*upādhi*), and not in its own essential nature (*svarūpa*).

Now, one might object: "Since the suffix *ṇamul* itself expresses repetition (*abhīkṣṇya*), what is the purpose of the reduplication? To this he replies: "This is that [repetition]," for repetition is not the primary meaning of *ṇamul*, as it is expressed by the sense of the suffix *ktvā*.

The meaning of the term *dvirukti* (reduplication) is either a dual substitute consisting of two words that are most similar (*antaratama*) in terms of their phonetic form and meaning, or a dual utterance; for it is precisely such [a substitute or utterance] accompanied by reduplication that serves as the indicator of non-cessation (*anuparati*). However, in the case of the reduplication of a verb expressing frequency (*abhīkṣṇya*), even a repetition (*punarukti*) constitutes a reduplication (*dvirukti*).
For example:
"Victory, victory to the Lord, the blue-throated wielder of the Pināka bow; victory, victory to the Goddess, the Mother of the World, Bhavānī;
victory, victory to that blessed devotee of the two! What else can be described as blessed here? Let it be described only to that extent. (233)

It is not necessarily the case that only two words must be employed; rather, as many instances of the word *abhīkṣṇya* (repetition/frequency) should be used as are required for the intended meaning to be understood. These are not seen in the formation of indeclinables (*avyaya*), but only in verbal forms (*tiṅpada*); thus he says: "of the verb. Although, according to the connection with the sense of a single sentence, there may be only two utterances of the verb, nevertheless, from the perspective of poetry (*kāvya*), an abundance [of such usage] is to be understood.
By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), terms such as *nimūla* (rootless) and *saṃbhrama* (confusion) are included.
Among these, examples beginning with *nimūla* (root-and-all) are as follows:
“In the fever of love, he scrapes his heart root-and-branch; in his chest, the strings of pearl necklaces quickly burst like parched grain. (234)
By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (ādi), one should include under that term all modes of repetition introduced in various other contexts;
for example: "The mountain ranges nearby have knots as hard as heavy stones, while far, far away, is the jewel-peaked mountain with its girdle of gem-studded rocks."
"That this ocean is near, while the Ocean of Milk is far, far away—that is the very proof that the Primal Artisan possesses an incomparable craft.

[The commentary notes: "In this case, there is a double usage because two instances of 'near' (ārāt) occur. Intending to show that such modes of reduplication for emphasis on the primary meaning (*svārtha*) should be understood by oneself, he provides an illustration as a mere hint: "root-and-all" (*nimūlakāṣam*).

According to the rule *‘kaṣādiṣu yathāvidhyanuprayogaḥ’*, when that very [verb] has been employed, the formation of a reduplicated expression is established for the sake of agitation, as for example: “Bones, bones! A hide, a hide! Ashes, ashes! The moon, the moon! The Gaṅgā, the Gaṅgā! The serpent, the serpent!”—thus they were agitated by panic.
"May the words of the Gaṇas protect [you] when Śiva is intent on beginning a dance, while they are occupied with providing the multitude of ornaments, garments, and requisites.
Here, "agitation" (*saṃbhrama*) consists of fear, excitement, and reverence; "excitement" (*saṃvega*) is haste.
That very [state] brings about the repetition in the present example;
furthermore, joy, agitation, wonder, and so forth are also conditions of *saṃbhrama* (bewilderment).
Among these, as an example of bewilderment caused by joy:
"Then the celestial women of Amarāvatī, agitated by curiosity, blocked her path, crying out, 'Where is Arjuna? Where is Arjuna?
Indeed, the repetition of words such as "joy" (harṣa) and others is observed in the compositions of great poets.
To explain how that [confusion] is to be understood, he says: "Joy," etc.

Even joy and the other [emotions] are causes of confusion; when they are delimited by having attained a state of uniqueness, the resulting confusion becomes distinct from one another, yet it does not lose its essential nature as confusion. Thus, the meaning is that this is merely a mode of repeating the term "confusion. An example of confusion caused by agitation (*āvega*) is as follows:
"Cast off cloak after cloak! Abandon necklace after necklace! Alas, alas! The forest fire burns; remove garment after garment! (237).
Here, in the verbal forms *muñca*, *parityaja*, *dahati*, and *apākuru*, there is no repetition due to the agitation and confusion [of the speaker].

For instance, upon entering a vast forest, a certain woman, out of the frantic agitation caused by the forest fire, speaks thus to her husband who desires to conquer his enemies: "First, remove the bodice alone, for that is impossible to take off once the forest fire has arrived;
next, the necklace, which is the cause of its attachment; and finally, the two garments set ablaze by the falling forest fire."

Regarding the phrase "O you whose depth is hidden! O agitation!"—is it not the case that "cast off the bodice, cast off the bodice" and so forth arise solely from the confusion of agitation? Why, then, is it not repeated twice? To this he says:
"In this context," the cause of the confusion is the apprehension of the bodice being entangled with the necklace, and the necklace being entangled with the upper garment.
An example of [the utterance] due to astonishment and agitation is as follows:
“Oh, what beauty! Oh, what beauty! Oh, what a face! Oh, what a face! Oh, what a waist! Oh, what a waist! Of this fawn-eyed woman! (238)
In all these instances of confusion, the repetition "up to awakening" (*yāvadbodham*) occurs twice;
likewise, the triple repetition is also to be understood as follows:
"Victory! Victory! Victory! O illustrious Bhoja, the night is dawning; speak, speak, speak what is worth hearing, O learned one, for this is indeed being committed to memory."
"Listen, listen, listen! Like you, the sun becomes colored [red] in its orb; no, no, no—the sun of the earth (the king) becomes discolored in an instant.

Revealing the meaning of the word "yāvat" as it refers to the limit of awakening during moments of agitation, he says, with reference to what was stated previously: "Even this threefold repetition is merely an illustration."
The repetition of four or more [syllables], which is not prohibited by the rule against *adaṇḍa*,

as well as *kriyāsamabhihāra* (intensive action) and *kriyābhyāsa* (repetition of an action), which were previously illustrated in the discussion on *yukti*, are also desired as *nāmānuprāsa* (name-alliteration). || 100 ||
Repetition results in intensity, and the commingling of figures of speech does not constitute a fault in poetry;
even a necklace adorns the breasts and the necks of fawn-eyed women. (101)

[Objection: But surely, since the poem is already graced by the employment of the sentence-meaning itself, what is the use of alliteration? To this, he says: "It does not arise... By means of this example, it is intended that just as the commingling of the *alaṃkārya* (the subject of ornamentation) is well-known in the world, so too the commingling of *alaṃkāra*s (ornaments) is a cause of beauty.
[The verse continues: "That repetition of words here, which occurs through different applications despite the non-difference of meaning..."
That [type of] alliteration is called *lāṭīya* by the wise.
(102) He defines *lāṭānuprāsa*, which follows in the sequence: when there is no difference in meaning, the alliteration favored by the people of Lāṭa is *lāṭānuprāsa*.
To the question, "If there is a difference in meaning, how is there no fault of tautology? it is said: "By a different application," which means "by a difference in intention (tātparya).
For this very reason, there is a distinction from the figure of speech *yamaka* (rhyme).
And that [repetition] is further said to be immediate, separate, both, both [together], the circular enclosure (cakravāla), and the womb (garbha).
The word "and" (ca) in the phrase "sa ca" serves to include the unmentioned immediate repetition.

Alliteration (*lāṭānuprāsa*) is generally of two kinds: contiguous (*avyavahita*) and non-contiguous (*vyavahita*). That which is not separated by a repeated word is contiguous; that which is separated by it is non-contiguous. Of these two, the contiguous type is sixfold.
The two [types] are the separate and the combined; thus, there are four.
Among these, the "both" (ubhaya) category is of two kinds; therefore, six varieties are to be explained by way of both the general and the specific states.
Furthermore, as for "both" (punar ubhaya)...
The word "again" (punaḥ) indicates a distinction;
the meaning is that this object denoted by the word "one" (eka) is indeed different from the previous one.
The first two pairs will be explained later.

However, as for that which is called "intermediate" (*vyavahita*), it is not possible to determine its number by means of methods such as word-division (*padavṛtti*) and other such devices, starting from one and so forth.
But since the second type was stated to be "the womb and the cosmic rim" (*cakravāla*), how many varieties of the intermediate then exist? To this, he says: "As for that... and so on.
The meaning is that because it is a specific sub-variety of the *bahubhāva* (many-fold) type, this is not counted as being on an equal footing with them.
For example, among those immediate varieties, when taken individually:
“By the fame of the Ocean [of Fame], fame [is increased]; by the steadfastness of the Steadfast One, even the heavy is made more heavy.”

‘Rāma, surpassing the ocean’s fame with his own fame, its fortitude with his own fortitude, its greatness with his own greatness, and its stability even with his own stability, proclaims his own roar with a roar as he advances. (240)
In this context, because indeclinables function as indicators (*dyotaka*) and so forth, their separation by particles such as *iva* and others is not accepted;
for even in the present case, particles like *iva* do not possess the status of a separate word.
If this were the case, then the following would be a suitable example:
"O slender-waisted one, your face is like your face, your eyes are like your eyes, and your form is like your form; you are indeed like yourself.
This is certainly so.

However, just as in expressions such as "nectar, nectar" or "moon, moon," where there is repetition of a name despite the absence of actual difference due to a metaphorical attribution of distinction, so too does he imagine this here; thus,
in the case of the doubled words "teṣu" (in them), neither the preceding nor the following part is included within a compound, and so they remain separate.

By this, the qualities beginning with *samasta* (completeness) are explained. The majestic power of speech (*vāganubhāva*), which is produced simultaneously with firmness, gravity, stability, and profundity, acts as the cause for the manifestation of beauty; like the overflowing of a jar filled with nectar, it bestows its respective excellence as if directly present, while swelling forth and advancing.

One might object: "In the example *nanu jaseṇa dhīreṇa garuiāi vi i raveṇa a*, since [the particle *a*] is separated from the preceding case-ending by the word *iti* in the *apaca* group and by the two subsequent *ca*s, how can it be cited as an instance of an immediately contiguous (*avyavahita*) *bheda*? To this he replies:
"In this context, the mention of 'indeclinables' (*avyayānām*) is merely illustrative;
the reason—that they are 'indicatory' (*dyotaka*)—is common to all case-endings."
In the view that the meaning of a nominal stem consists of five factors, the suffix is merely indicative;

Śākalya, who maintains that indeclinables are denotative, also does not believe that particles such as *iva* possess denotative power independently, just like other words whose meanings are non-substantial (*asattvārtha*).

Since he did not teach that they are separate words, and because indicators (dyotaka) function through cooperation with another power and thus enter into it— according to the maxim that "one's own limb does not create an interval"—
why indeed resort to such a strained interpretation here?
He raises a doubt, thinking that there is yet another example that is not separated [by the intervening verse]: "If it is so...

He refutes this by stating, "There is," because the pair occurring in the first half-verse serves as an example for the pair occurring in the second half-verse, owing to their similarity to the former.

The mere absence of positive concomitance (*ananvaya*) is the example cited here; since a distinction must necessarily be postulated therein, a relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*) must be expressed, and thus it would constitute a "repetition" (*dvirukti*) known as the metaphorical (*gauṇī*). Only ten phonemes have been determined for the purpose of establishing the form of meter;
an example composed of syllables and consonants of that very measure is easy to understand.
An example of the manifestation of the notes ṣaḍja and so forth is as follows:
‘sā mamāridhamanī nidhāninī sāmadhāma dhanidhāmasādhinī māninī sagarimāpapāpapā sāpagā samasamāgamāsamā || 265 ||’
Regarding the phrase "beginning with ṣaḍja":

the seven notes, such as *sa*, *ri*, *ga*, *ma*, *pa*, *dha*, and *ni*, are designated by names beginning with *ṣaḍja* and so forth; they are observed by those learned in the science of music (*gāndharvaveda*).
That which consists of the manifesting sounds (vyañjana) of the mere elements (tanmātra), such as the notes beginning with *ṣaḍja*, exists together with Viṣṇu; thus she is Lakṣmī.

She "blows" (dhamati)—that is, she torments—the enemies; from the root *dhmā* with the suffix *lyuṭ*, the substitution of *dham* for *dhmā* occurs according to the rule that the *bahulavacana* applies elsewhere as well.
The ellipsis is "may I become such as this"; *nidhāninī* means possessing treasures such as the *padma* and others;
*sāmnas* means of conciliation, and *dhāma* means a home.
She who accomplishes the dwellings of the wealthy, who adorns splendor,
who is proud, who possesses worship,
who has dignity, and who is full of respect.
She is like the river *Āpagā*, which is renowned for its power as it protects (*pāti*) those who are free from sin (*apapāpa*) and devoid of impurity (*niṣkaluṣa*);
likewise, she is one whose meeting (*samāgama*) is transient and fragile, vanishing in an instant.
Unequalled and incomparable,
like the syllables and phonemes of the drum (muraja): "The one whose throat was blackened by the poison of the Kharas, who crushed the Gadās, and who brought about the death of Makaraketu— "
“Taḍit” (Lightning)—I inwardly held the terrible Hara, the destroyer of Ruru’s head.
Regarding the syllables of the reading “Muraja”: in the word *muraja*, there are the letters *la* and *ha*; likewise, *ta*, *tha*, *da*, *dha*, *accha*, *ma*, and *au*, as well as the letter *ra*.
The sixteen syllables na, ṇa, ka, kha, ga, gha, ṅa, and a, thus arranged by Bharata and others,
constitute an example of a Muraja-letter composition (*murajākṣaravyañjana*) fashioned from the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), which is easy to understand.
An example of *niṣkaṇṭhya* (the absence of difficulty) in paintings with four positions is as follows:
“May he of sharp luster and intellect gratify Viriñci—who possesses abundant prosperity, vast joy, a large form, and stands before [us]—with pure hymns of praise. (267)

Although there is a variety [of sounds] regarding the places of articulation (*sthāna*) as well, governed by rules such as the fourfold [classification], even though it is said: "The places of articulation for the phonemes (*varṇa*) are eight: the chest, the throat, the head, the root of the tongue, the teeth, the nose, the lips, and the palate," nevertheless—because the *jihvāmūlīya* (the *visarga* before *k* and *kh*) is a vowel, and because the *urasya* and *nāsikya* do not enter into poetry—the determination of the fourfold [classification] and so on is made within the five places of articulation, excluding the chest, the nose, and the root of the tongue.
He, whose intellect shines like a needle, should gladden— that is, please— the creator Brahmā, who possesses the aforementioned attributes, with pure and stainless hymns of praise;
for the letters *a*, *u*, *ha*, and the *visarjanīya* are gutturals,
while the *tālavya* (palatals) are excluded, as follows:
“Then Meghanāda, variegated by the mass of jewels from his shimmering earrings which resembled Indra’s bow, appeared in battle like the rainy season.
The Rākṣasa named Meghanāda was variegated (karbura) by that very mass of jewels from his earrings, which were like the bow of Maghavan (Indra).
The *icuyaśas* sounds are palatals (*tālavya*),
excluding the dental *y*, as for example:
"May the discus-wielder Cakrapāṇi, who removes evil, who is skilled in the art of battle, and who is accompanied by Caṇḍīśa, protect me."
"May he, who is worthy of being beheld by Śrī and Apashrama, and who is worshipped by the foremost hosts of immortals, lead us to liberation.
[Verse 269] "Caṇḍīśamiśra" refers to one who has attained a single body with the Supreme Lord;
"foremost immortals" refers to Brahmā and the others.
The letters *l*, *ṛ*, *t*, *l*, and *s* are dental (*dantya*);
they are not labial (*aniroṣṭhya*), as for example:
"producing joy for the eyes, shining with clusters of stars..."
“O fair-limbed one, let your gaze be cast even once upon the cloudless sky,” [he said].
By the phrase “cloudless” (aghane),
it is meant that [the sky] is most visible due to the beauty of the autumn season.
The *upadhmānīya* and *upadhmanīya* are labials;
the *mūrdhanya* (cerebral) is as follows—for example:
“Like locusts running, the arrows of that king [fell].”
Severed by his arrows, they fell upon the edge of the battlefield; thus,
by that King Kapila,
[the weapons] of that Lord of Kosala, Prasenajit, were struck down.
The retroflex consonants *ṛ*, *ṭu*, *ra*, and *ṣa* have the head (*mūrdhan*) as their place of articulation.
Among the variegated examples of the three places of articulation, one that does not involve the lips (*oṣṭha*) or the teeth (*danta*) is as follows:
"May he whose body is dark and tawny, whose movement is most venerable and supreme in the world, conquer by means of the radiance of his discus."
"Haris, the destroyer of Hiraṇyākṣa’s body, who dwells upon the lord of birds, whose bed is sought by Śrī.
By this very rule— "having no labials or dentals"— one should seek out the *loṣṭa* arrangement, avoiding any two consonants separated by an interval.
Likewise, in what follows as well,
there is no labial or cerebral [consonant], as for example:
“alinīlālakalataṃ kaṃ na hanti ghanastani” (O lady with thick breasts, whom does she not strike, she who has locks of hair dark as bees?).
"Your face has the luster of a lotus, and your eyes have the brilliance of the moon.
(273) Regarding the variety of [alliteration] in two positions, with dental and guttural sounds, for example:
"The beautiful woman (*sadaṅganā*), whose various anxieties (*nānātaṅkā*) were not attached due to the transgression of the bodiless one (*anaṅga*)."

"O ever sinless one, O ever blissful one, united with the embrace of a woman with curved limbs (274)!"— O sinless one, irreproachable, always filled with joy through the attainment of your beloved, you are united with the embrace of some other woman with curved limbs; your beautiful wife exists by assuming various forms through the power of desire.
Therefore, "have compassion for her"—this is the meaning of the request accompanied by reproach.
As in the following examples of alliteration (*ekasthānacitra*) involving guttural sounds (*kaṇṭhya*):
"agā gāṃ gāṅgakākāṅkagāhakāghakakākahā" [She] went to the earth, [she who is] like a crow seeking the reflection of the Ganges, [and who is] a destroyer of the darkness of sin.
"Ahāhāṅgakhagāṅkāgagakaṅkāgakhagāṅkaga || 275 ||" [The word] *gaṅgaka* refers to the water associated with the Gaṅgā; its *aka* is its crooked course,
according to the rule "the root *aka* (with prefix *aga*) means to move crookedly."
The one who plunges into the lap—that is, the middle—of that [bird] is the restless one;
he is the "aghaka," for *aghaka* means vile sin (*agham*); he alone is the crow (*kāka*), and thus he is the "aghakakrākrahā" (the destroyer of the crow-like sinner).
Others, however, read the word with a final visarga (*aghakaḥ*).

Then, in the sense of a benediction (*āśaṃsā*), the suffix of the past tense is used for the root *jahāti* (to abandon) in its injunctive form: "May you, being such as this, go to heaven (*gām*). Being of what nature? [He is one who has abandoned all attachments.]

*Hānaṃ* means abandonment (*hā*); *ahā* means non-abandonment (*na hā*). That which attains (*jihīte*) or reaches that [non-abandonment] is *ahāham*. He whose limb (*aṅga*) is such is the bird Garuḍa or the Sun; he who has such a one as his mark (*aṅka*) is the Mountain (*aga*), namely Meru. The birds called *kaṅka* that dwell upon that mountain are *agakhagāḥ*. He for whom even they are *ākākakāḥ*—desirous of following (*ākāka*) his movement—is "one whose journey is celebrated even by winged creatures. To give an example of a single short vowel among the various sounds of his own [poetic] compositions: [The verse continues: *...yadā tvamānaya mānasaṃ mama...* (When you bring my mind... (Note: This passage describes a king whose fame is so great that even the birds on Mount Meru desire to follow him, and it provides an example of a specific metrical feature.)
‘They urged on, they grew weary, they cried out, they praised, they were greatly enamored, they flourished amidst joys, and they repeatedly fainted again and again.
(276) The presentation of these [verses] in a sequence beginning with one and so forth within their own meters is for the sake of the variety of the composition.
The wide-striding one of far-reaching speech,
the teacher of the dwellers in heaven,
for the sake of battle in the combats.
According to the rule "nimittātkarmayoge," the locative case is used; thus,
the divine warriors, weeping and crying out in distress, sought refuge and for that very reason praised him profusely in many ways.
He states the purpose of the battle: "In moments of joy (*mud*), they lusted (*lulubhuḥ*) and flourished (*pupuṣuḥ*), that is, they became robust;
*nu* is used as a particle of deliberation."
"Again and again"—that is, at every single moment—why did they "faint," meaning they fell into a state of delusion?
The sense is that there was no order to their crying out and so forth.
This should be recited with a long, single tone—as follows:

By means of those various [powers] belonging to the Vedic seers (Vaidha), the Ādityas (Ānaira), the Rudras (Aiśa), Indra (Aindra), the Aja-pādas (Ai-ja), the Ailas (Aila), the Jinas (Jaina), the Siddhas (Siddha), Mitra (Maitra), and by many forms of fortitude (Dhairya), by enmities (Vaira), by the powers of the gods (Daiva) belonging to each of their own respective [spheres], [he was protected]. || 277 ||

*Vidhi* is Viriñci (Brahmā); *ī* is Lakṣmī, and her *inaḥ* (lord) is Viṣṇu; *īśaḥ* is Mahādeva; *indraḥ* is Vāsava; *ījaḥ* is Kāma, because he is the son of Lakṣmī; *ilā* is the Earth; *jinaḥ* is Buddha; *siddhāḥ* are a class of deities; *mitraḥ* is the Sun; *raidaḥ* is Dhanada Kubera; and *devāḥ* are the Maruts and others distinct from those already mentioned. With their various *dhāmnī*, *dhyaiḥ*, *dhṛtibhiḥ*, and their own manifold riches (*vittaiḥ*)—by means of these well-known forms—I am "well-wealthed" (*svairaiḥ suṣṭhu samantāt samṛddhaḥ*) on all sides; such is the prayer (*āśaṃsā*), which serves as an ornament of speech (*vākyālaṃkāre*).
An example of two short syllables is as follows:

“O Three-eyed One, who knows the rules for casting away the maintenance of worldly existence, you who possess the power of wealth; O Hara, whose skill is bowed to, O Destroyer of Smara, remember me! (278)
The earth is *kṣiti*; its maintenance is *sthiti*, its measurement is *miti*, and its destruction is *kṣipti*. He knows the method for these;
he who possesses the supernatural powers of the treasures (*nidhi-siddhi*) is called *leḍhī* [by the suffix] *kvip*; because Dakṣa’s splendor was bowed down and shattered by him.

O Smarahara, O Kāmadahana, O Tryakṣa, O Trinayana, O Hara, O Mahādeva, remember me; [here] the genitive case is used for the object in connection with a verb meaning "to remember" (adhi-gartha), according to the rule regarding long vowels and two syllables.
“Fortune and splendor, modesty and fame, wisdom and policy, speech and joy—
these two pairs flourish in him who is not among these [other] lords of gods.
Fortune and splendor refer to Lakṣmī and brilliance.
*Hrī* and *kīrti* are modesty and fame;
*dhī* and *nīti* are intellect and policy; *gīḥ* and *prīti* are speech and joy.
These two, which do not even exist among the lords of the gods, flourish and increase for you within the three vowels, just as a short vowel occurs within the three vowels—
as in: *kṣiti-vijiti-sthiti-vihiti-vrata-ratayaḥ para-gatayaḥ*.
In battle, the Kurus obstructed the broad [path] and violently shook their own enemy host.

(280) *Vijiti* means conquest; *vihiti* is the ordaining or establishment characterized by the boundaries of the castes and stages of life (*varṇāśrama-maryādā*) for the stability of the earth; those whose vow (*vrata*) is that very thing, and whose supreme (*parā*) goal (*gati*)—meaning knowledge—is such, they are described as "those who delight in that vow" (*tatra-rati*).
They are likewise [described as] those whose supreme goal is knowledge.
Such were the Kurus; they obstructed the vast and extensive lineage of their enemies, and they shook— that is, they caused to tremble— that very heavy and great [burden],
just as one inserts a long vowel among four short vowels.

"Among the scriptures, the final word—the Upaniṣad—is intent upon teaching what is beneficial and what is harmful; what does it say? [It says: 'One should desire pleasure, pain, fear, joy, worldly enjoyment, disease, delusion, and even liberation, in a place that is secure and conducive to meditation. (281) What does that final word among the scriptures—the Vedas—the Upaniṣad, which is devoted to establishing what is beneficial and what is harmful, declare?
Those which are songs are calamities and portents; those which are pleasures are fears and terrors;
that which is enjoyment is disease.

That which is joy or exhilaration is delusion; he did not say this with reference to the Supreme, but rather that one should form a desire— that is, cultivate the wish— for the object of meditation, for the state characterized by liberation, which is secure and free from afflictions.
The word "vā" is used for conjunction; others, however, read it as "ca," as in the case of a vowel placed after each consonant, for example: [omitted].

"May our body be fierce with heat toward that which is to be abandoned, for she—who is praised by those who delight in what is to be discarded, who is most dear to the virtuous, and who sprinkles nectar—has cast away beneficial advice in the presence of her husband.
(282) "In 'that which is to be abandoned' (*heye*) means in an object that ought to be relinquished; *villābha* refers to one who finds delight therein."

According to the root *vidl* meaning "to obtain," he is the one who, through the heat of his nature which censures those who are greedy and possessed by greed, is fierce by implication like the sun with its scorching rays; may he, as such, be the radiant one within my body— this is the sense.

To the question, "Why is this wished for? he says: "In the presence of the beloved who flows with nectar, the most dear to the virtuous, delay is indeed harmful; rather, immediate action is beneficial for the sake of battle.

Having thus bestowed this blessing upon himself, a certain warrior went to the battlefield to perform his duty with the bow—to engage in the self-choice marriage (*svayaṃvara*) of the Goddess of Victory over his enemies.
That very same [verse], with all vowels removed, is as follows:
‘tapana grastadahana hayavallabhanandana’ (O son of the beloved of the horse, who has swallowed the sun and fire).
Victory to you, O foremost of the Gaṇas, destroyer of the wicked, shatterer of pride!
You who have swallowed the fire and overwhelmed the god of flame—
Revaṇta, the beloved of horses, is his son.
O destroyer of the night, O remover of darkness, O creator, O you for whom the festival is esteemed; as in the case of the eight-petaled [lotus] among figures of various forms:
"Resorting to which [state] through purification, one who cuts off lowly suffering is to be entreated with a mind free from the toil of illusion; she is praised by Śrī.
Herein—
“One should place one [syllable] in the pericarp, two in each of the cardinal and intermediate directions,
and perform the entry and exit in the cardinal directions within the eight-petaled lotus.
The example beginning with “yā śritā” and so forth has already been explained previously (Paṭala 1, verse 170).
Hereafter, the commentary by Harihara is also written right here, as follows:

"The Goddess who is resorted to for purity with an unyielding (*anīcayā*) and exalted (*tuṅgyā*) intellect; she who is to be entreated and prayed to for the cessation of the exertion and exhaustion of this expansion of *māyā* and *avidyā*; she who cuts through the torment—the suffering to be experienced in hell; and she who is praised even by Śrī."
He states its ritual placement (*nyāsa*): "In the pericarp" means that the first letter, *yā*, is situated in the pericarp; then, in sequence, two letters each are placed upon the eight petals;
and in the cardinal petals, beginning with *yā śritā śriye*, there is entry and exit.
The second [circle] has eight petals, as follows:
‘carasphāravarakṣāra varakāra garajvara calasphāla valakṣālavala kālagala jvala || 286 ||’

The color of the pericarp is eightfold; likewise, there are eight others on the petals, and eight more in their joints within the eight-petalled lotus. [Regarding the mantra beginning with] *carasphāra*, etc. (287).

He whose nature is to move about extensively is *sphāraḥ*; he who pours forth—that is, bestows—boons (*varaḥ*) is so called because he scatters, hurls, or performs excellent things (*varāñ śreṣṭhān*), or else [the suffix] *aṇ* is applied in the sense of an action, as in "he harms" (*kṛṇoti hinasti*).
*Garaḥ* refers to the *kālakūṭa* poison; *jvaraḥ* is so called from the act of feverish burning (*jvaraṇāt*).

O you whose movements are vigorous at the commencement of the *tāṇḍava* dance, O you with a body white as snow, O you who have attained power over the ocean, O blue-throated one who has swallowed Time, blaze—be radiant!
Thus he states the ritual placement (*nyāsa*). It is eightfold.

Now, in the first half [of the circle], there is one *repha* (the letter *r*) alone in the pericarp (*karṇikā*); in the second half, the other eight letters, excluding *la*, are on the petals, and the remaining eight *lakāras* (the letter *l*) are at their junctions.
The third [circle] has eight petals as follows:
“O Moon-faced One, O you who have bowed to Kāma, O you whose vows are bent [in humility], I bow to you, the one who humbles pride; indeed, am I not now entreating you?

Furthermore, the wise one should proceed here from the center of the pericarp to the petal, from the petal to the tip of the petal, and from the tip of the petal back to the pericarp, for each individual petal in this eight-petaled lotus.
In this same manner, the four-petaled and sixteen-petaled lotuses are also to be understood.
Regarding the phrase "not on the moon" (na śaśīśe) and so forth: the remainder of the sense is that he is situated in devotion toward the new state, which is the moon (the Lord).
I do not bow to you; rather, by bowing, I bow indeed with a tone of irony, for my desire has been shattered because of you.
He whose vow was bowed and inclined due to his preeminence in self-restraint;
[his] honoring [of others] caused the destruction of the elevation of his enemies.
The word "nanu" is used here as a vocative of respect.
Addressing you with the word "tvā" (you), he,
practicing humility and making a request,
says: "First, to the pericarp," and so forth.

First, the initial letter *na* is to be taken at the pericarp (*karṇikā*). Then, *śa* is in the middle of the petal, and *śī* is at the tip of the petal. Having turned back, the letters *śa* and *na* are at the pericarp and the petal respectively. Furthermore, from the pericarp to the tip of the petal and back again, this same sequence applies to the four-petalled lotus;
as for those four petals, it is as follows:

"She, who possesses the *āsravas*, with a well-disposed mind, she who is bowed, with full breasts, comes to me for support by her power, O powerful one, she who is richly clothed. From the pericarp, one should lead upward the row of letters in the form of petals.
One should place this four-petaled lotus within the pericarp (karṇikā).
[Regarding] "sāsavā" and so forth:
*sāsavā* means one who has tasted liquor (*madya*).

With a full chest abounding in breasts, she is bent, possessing a firm luster and supreme beauty; suddenly, or unexpectedly, characterized by the nature of an excitant of erotic passion (*śṛṅgāra-uddīpana*) through the month of Mārgaśīrṣa and by beautiful garments—O you who act with daring, O lover of daring who approaches at the dead of night, she comes to you, she approaches you.
Thus he states the *nyāsa* [the formal arrangement of letters], saying "Karṇikā," which is easily understood.
An example of the sixteen-petaled [lotus] is as follows:
‘Obeisance to you, O Mahima-prema, O Namasyā-mati-maddama, O Kṣāma-soma, O Namat-kāma, O Dhāma-bhīma, O Sama-kṣama. (292)
By means of the *gomūtrikā* arrangement, all the syllables become equal and uniform;
through the placement of the letter *ma* in the center, this becomes a sixteen-petaled lotus.
(293) He describes the sixteen petals with the words beginning "Homage to you" (*namaste*).
Salutations to Him whose love for greatness subdues even the prideless; He who is the subduer of the prideless,
being emaciated by a mere digit of the moon resting upon His crest.
O Bhīma, terrifying by your splendor and majesty, you are one by whom Kāma has been humbled and broken,
and whose forbearance is equal to all things and common to every cause for rising up.

He states the *nyāsa* (placement) as follows: "Someone pays homage to you, who possess these specific vocatives and qualifiers"—namely, that the syllables, excluding the letter *ma*, are equal when accompanied by the letter *ma*. This is called the *gomūtrikā* (cow-urine pattern).

The repetition "samāḥ samāḥ" (equal, equal) is for the purpose of indicating that the letter *ma* is present in each syllable; this is the eight-petalled lotus (*aṣṭapattram*) itself, marked with the name of the poet, as follows:

*rātāvadyādhirājyā visarararasavivdyājavākkṣmāpakārā rākā pakṣmābhaśeṣā nayanananayanasvā [sā] khayā stavyamārā* [She who is] the sovereign queen over the night, whose speech is free from the poison of falsehood, who is the source of the science of the essence of the world, who causes the earth to be free from harm, who is the full moon when only the eyelashes remain, who is the mistress of the eyes of the eyes, she is to be praised by you.

May Rādhā—whose beauty is like that of the moon when its rays are scattered, who is a stream of camphor, and who is the incarnation of the science [of subduing] the most venomous serpents through her power over the egoless Śiva—grant me protection and auspiciousness.
(294) This lotus, marked with the name of the poet, is arranged by the devotion of half-verses placed upon eight petals, without touching the pericarp at the corners. (295)
In this regard, the mark (aṅka) is "Rājaśekharakamala"; by this, the wheel is also explained as having exactly eight petals. He states the poet's name as the mark: "rātāvadya... and so forth.

"A certain noble warrior of the gods, desiring to fight with the army of the Daityas, worshipped Māyādevī, who had manifested her presence at that time. For instance: *vyāja* is *māyā*; she whose name is *vāc* (Speech) has *vyāja* as a prefix to her name—that is, she is called *Vyājāvāc*. The connection [of the verse] is: "May she grant me protection."*”

She who bestows—that is, grants—the kingdom, which is given as a gift yet is blameworthy and full of faults; or rather, a kingdom characterized by such blameworthy anxieties (*ādhayaḥ*); she who knows or finds that essence (meaning *vīra*, the hero) which causes the dispersal of flight; and she from whom there is harm upon the earth (*kṣmāyām*) in the form of sons, wife, and so forth—this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound formed because the meaning is clearly understood.

*Rākā* is the full moon; she is in the form of a girl about twelve years of age. *Pakṣmābhaḥ* refers to the serpent Śeṣa, who is attached to her body. *Nayanam* means that which leads to policy (*nīti*); thus, *yannayanam* refers to her vision.
That which is knowledge is itself its own self (*sva-ātman*); she who goes (*yāti*) in the sky (*khe*), that is, in the void (*vyomani*), is therefore *khayā*.
She who is to be praised, or who desires the destruction of Māra,
is Rāmā; she is a delightful woman,
or one by whom stability has been shattered and destroyed.

“Tuhinana” means one who leads or brings forth frost (tuhina); from the root *nī* with the suffix *ḍa*, it refers to the Moon (*tuhinana*). Of that [Moon], which is the binder in the matted locks (*jaṭājūṭa*) of the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*), there is “Nahī”—the Goddess Śrī, whose form is Power (*śakti*).

She is so called because she binds or fastens (*nahyati*); from the root *nah* with the suffix *vic*, and then with the suffix *kvip* according to the rule “*kvip* is to be prescribed after all nominal stems,” the form of the word ending in *tṛc* is obtained. She attains praise (*stuti*), hence she is “Nahaṃ. Thus, the form is derived from the stem ending in *tṛc*.

*Kara* means that which gives (*rāti*) happiness (*kaṃ*). *Kṣāra* refers to those who are like thieves (*dasyu*); their "edge" (*dhārā*) is like the edge of a sword and so forth, and it is "cutting" (*chettrī*).
Thus, *Rādha* is a name of the Goddess according to the Purāṇas.
The indeclinable *mama* emphasizes the state of being [the possessor].

O Śivā, even for those self-controlled yogins who possess the power of *manas*— that is, those who measure and delimit reality— you cause them to descend into the science of serpents (*vyālavidyā*), which is a base science (*kṣudravidyā*).
Regarding that, he describes the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) with eight verses beginning with "niviṣṭā," forming an eight-petaled lotus with four and a half lines per verse.
Regarding the eight syllables that arise from the name, he says: "O Rājaśekhara-kamala!
Because of the attainment of the name of the poet and the poem, even the lack of case-endings is not a defect;
by this [he means]..."
By the mention of the lotus marked with a name, the discus (*cakra*) as well should be understood as being marked with a name; for example, as in the verse:

"O auspicious one, you, having seized that foremost of men in the heat of battle, have attained the purity of destroying sin before you, and with joy, you have become the ground for the most exalted *śrīvatsa* mark."
Having abandoned desire and cast off fear, that supreme hunter of deer let out a roar; with floods of arrows, he simultaneously covered the sky with his shafts.
(296) One should draw three hexagons one after another, and rotate the fourth; these two [hexagons] are marked with the name—this is the procedure for the wheel. (297)

Here is the verse: "This is the Māgha-kāvya, the *Śiśupālavadha*. [The commentary continues: "O you, who possess the Śrīvatsa mark upon your chest, with your heart uplifted by the impetuosity of battle (*ājirabhasāt*)—that is, from the joy of combat—you raised your lion-like roar (*siṃhanāda*) against Hari with your arrows (*ropaiḥ*, i.e., *bāṇaiḥ*). Having taken hold of him with pride (*mānena*), you were distinguished by that [pride]; this is the qualifying attribute (*viśeṣaṇam*)."

Having attained the destruction of his sins, the enemy—the deer-hunter—was freed from fear and, with joy and delight, then covered the sky with a lion’s roar; such is the connection [of the words] at that time.
He explains the *nyāsa*: "In front"—having written [the letters] one after another in front, one should write others in front so that six spokes are produced.
Likewise, an example of the four-limbed [puzzle] is as follows:

“O you who are pure, whose essence is the bones of bound gods, uneven, firm through the conquest of disease, having fallen from the dust of the path of dharma, with a face like a window, with trembling eyebrows, truly possessing hidden thought, having destroyed the divisions of the directions by ritual, not a wheel, of pure conduct, short-statured, cloudless, fierce-bodied, delightful, and shining with the luster of Bhavānī. (298)
Here is the verse: "With words exceedingly pure, the royal preceptor spoke respectfully, having bound the circle of my mind," as it were:

"Pure," and so forth—the circle of my speech (*gavi*) is pure and stainless; that which has strayed from *dharma* is *ud-dharma*; such is the dust (*rajaḥ*), meaning the state of passion (*rājasabhāva*), the ground or locus of which has fallen away and perished.

May that [Lord], who is free from dependence on the eight directions and their presiding deities, and whose vast, accumulated, and unassailable auspiciousness has not been bent by sorrow or grief—may He expand that welfare! [He is] formidable with garlands of skulls fashioned from the bones of the heads of the gods, such as Brahmā and others, which are adorned with prayers;
and He is exceedingly firm through His victory over diseases and afflictions.
"Characterized by a bull (vṛṣeṇa) that is unexhausted, well-nourished, with trembling horns, and full of joy"—
this is an adverbial phrase meaning "truly";
[he] by whom the protection (guptiḥ) of beings— that is, their preservation— has been contemplated.
Your conduct is delightful; you are the fierce Mahādeva, not tall, yet standing on a station higher than all.
The connection is that the body is beautiful due to the luster of Bhavānī—that is, the splendor of Pārvatī situated in the left half [of Śiva’s body].
Here, as before, is the *nyāsa*;
however, the specific difference is that there are four numerical figures (*aṅka*).
An example of *gatapratyāgata* (repetition with reversal) within various meters is as follows:

“‘vāraṇāgagabhīrā sā sārābhīgagaṇāravā kāritārivadhā senā nāsedhāvaritārikā || 299 ||’” [That army, deep like a lordly elephant, possessing a multitude of powerful warriors and a roar, having caused the slaughter of enemies, was not obstructed by those who had hindered the foe.]
Here, there is movement in the odd-numbered quarters and return in the even-numbered quarters;
now follows the discussion on various types of movement (gaticitra): "vāraṇa" and so forth—by the "vāraṇas," which are themselves mountains (agāḥ), it is deep and difficult to penetrate.
Where there is the sound of such hosts who, being most excellent and essential, experience fear; or where there is the sound of a multitude of fearsome beings.
She by whom the slaughter of enemies was caused— that is, performed—
by means of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) for her own purpose; she who is devoid of restraint, that is, the prohibition imposed by others.

That [verse] in which enemies, having been challenged for battle by excellent warriors (*subhaṭa*), are *varitaḥ* (warded off) is thus described; the form *varita* is established from the root *vṛ* (in the sense of "desiring") with the suffix *kta*.
Here, having taken the sequence of syllables in the first and third odd-numbered quarters in their natural order, the second and fourth even-numbered quarters are taken as being the reverse of that.

"Movement" (*gati*) is the transition from one phoneme to another during recitation; "wondrous movement" (*gaticitra*) is the artistic variation resulting from the regulation of that movement, and it takes the form exactly as described here.
An example occurring within the syllables is as follows:
*niśitāsirato'bhīko nyejate'maraṇā rucā*... [etc.]
"Who, being fearless, delights in the assembly of the beautiful while [the enemy] roars and devours?

(300)" Here, by means of the *gatapratyāgata* (back-and-forth) repetition, that same verse is [restated]: "O immortals (*amaraṇāḥ*), those free from death; one who delights in the sharp sword and is devoid of fear does not tremble (*nyejate*)—that is, he does not shake—due to the brilliance (*rucā*) of his splendor."
For how could one who is afraid find delight in a battle crowded with shouting rākṣasas, piśācas, and others, and with chariots, elephants, horses, and so forth?
The meaning is: "not at all.

Here, the sequence of phonemes (varṇamālā) that was taken up until the conclusion of the composition is itself completed by returning from the conclusion back to the beginning; thus, it is "in this way" by means of the half-verse [at the end].
Another verse is as follows:
“In the pride-born [elephant], from the king of elephants who was intoxicated and devoid of rut, there arose the sound of people fleeing from the heavy burden of the rutting king of elephants. (301)
In this regard, there is another verse in reverse order as follows:
"The darkness, having taken away the sound, resorted to the essence of passion."
The army,
consisting of the most excellent men and horses, was devoid of pride; immediately thereafter, the army became humble, being free from arrogance.

In that supreme battle, where the *sāra* (essence) was extracted, the intoxicated royal elephants (*rājebha*)—the lordly tuskers possessing excellent gait and bearing their masters' burden of war—were present; thus, they were endowed with appropriate movements, and "where there is the sound of those people, which is a lion’s roar" is an adverbial phrase describing the action. This is the meaning of the verse in its forward order (*anuloma*). [In the reverse order: Where the captivating elephants, trumpeting and roaring with speed and force, are present...

Then there arose a vast clamor and tumult created by the soldiers, wherein was the battle—the duel—of proud and heroic men; such an army, out of the passion for *rāga* (the desire to seize the fortune of the enemy), entered into *tamas* (darkness) and fell into anger; this is the meaning of the verse read in reverse order (*pratiloma*).
An example from another language (Prakrit) is as follows:
“O you who are full of passion here, this young woman, darkened by the eclipse of Rāhu, is intent on the playful essence of love; she is a bee at the high lotus, devoted to its beauty. (303)
In this regard, there is another Prakrit verse in reverse order as follows:
“taralā kalilā gātuṃ sālālī sarakālasā” (The row of *sāla* trees, tremulous and dense, is like a woman with trembling limbs, stained with mud, and possessing dark hair).
"The *sāmalī* (the dark-complexioned girl) with sweet speech remains as the *selālā* (the moon-like one).

(304) Here, in the context of *lāsa*—meaning dance—the girl is "thick" (*bahalā*), meaning unrestrained; she is "dark" (*śyāmā*) like Rāhu, stained by impurity; she possesses "locks" (*sālakā*), meaning she has curly hair that provides a secondary grace to her brows, ears, and other features; she possesses "play" (*līlā*) arising from the erotic sentiment (*rasa*); and she is "lofty" (*tuṅgā*), meaning her conduct is elevated. Thus, O lover of the sixty-four arts, such a young girl was cherished (*alāli*) by you—this is the meaning of the Sanskrit verse.

Kalā refers to one who is highly skilled in singing, instrumental music, and dancing, including the art of mixing [melodies]. Paṭīyasī means clever at singing. Taralā means quick. Sālālī is a row of various trees. Alasā means languid due to that *saraka*—the honey-wine. Śyāmā refers to a woman with a sweet voice. Selā is an excellent woman; as stated in the *Deśīkośa*: "Selā is an excellent woman."
Some say that [the word] *selā* occurs together with *irayā* and *madirayā*, because of the traditional rule regarding the identity of *r* and *l*; however, this is questionable,
as [the word] *alā* means "an ornament."
"Hava dhava" is an address; "rehai" means it shines,
which is the meaning of the Prakrit verse.
In this way, the process of going and returning among different languages should also be understood; as follows, in accordance with their meaning:
"O you who are known in heaven, who [are there] in the army? To him who goes, having conquered the field..."
"In *vigadaṃ gavi roddhāro yoddhā yo natim eti na* (305),
by reversing [the order], that very same meaning of the words is understood as *vidita* and so forth."

In that army where even the dwellers of heaven are well-known and by whom the battles—meaning wars—with enemies have been conquered, who indeed are those warriors (bhaṭāḥ) who, having reached such a conflict (anīke), are free from distress (vigadaṃ)—that is, devoid of the fever of the heart—in the face of the enemy's challenge (gavi), which consists of speech?
The meaning is: there are none at all. Who is he? [The answer follows: Him... [the rest of the verse].

The warrior who does not show even the slightest bowing or humility—he for whom there is this very same *pratiloma* verse (one read backward) to that effect, as follows: "That warrior who does not bow, he is a restrainer; [he is] without disease in the cow."
Having conquered the unconquered, she has gone to the army; her horse's hoofprint is known in heaven like [the tracks of] a steed:
"The young girl, with hair as dark as the black clouds, who is adorned by locks of radiant beauty—"
Sasvā, Suvati, Sārā, Darpikā, and Vratagardhitā—
when these four lines of his are written out in sequence, one by one, another verse arises through the movement of the horse’s steps (the *turaṅgapadavyatyaya*).
For example:

“The young girl, charming and intense in her own nature, skilled in the arts, satisfying with passion, possessing beautiful teeth, increasing her presence, dark-hued, and dancing upon the ground. (308)

"O young girl," and so forth: "young" (*bālā*) means about sixteen years of age; "possessing beautiful black hair" means adorned with radiant, curly locks; "endowed with her own excellence" (*sasvā*) means possessed of personal merit; "having a son" (*sutavatī*) means accompanied by a son; "possessing the passion of supreme pride" means endowed with the erotic sentiment characterized by high self-regard; and "desiring the vow of her own marriage and so forth" means longing for her desired wedding and other rites—therefore, "worship him" [is the sense], with the word "in your heart" (*hṛdaye*) being understood as the ellipsis.

He states the ritual assignment (nyāsa): "In sequence" means she who is charming, delightful, intense, and skilled, whose very self is [filled] with passion— that is, love— and who satisfies [the deity].
She who possesses beautiful teeth,
whose dwelling has increased, who has filled all places,
and who is accompanied by Kāla (Time), whose speech is false.

The meaning is that she is one who possesses such dancers and performers— that is, one who has surpassed the entire world of dancers; the sense of the sentence is that you have enjoyed such a young woman.
They say that if there is a revolving of half a verse, it is called *ardhabhrama* (half-revolution);
if there is a revolving in all directions, this is *sarvatobhadra* (auspicious in every way). Of these two, *ardhabhrama* is as follows:
‘[That voice] which always bestows joy upon all beings, which destroys fear and resentment,
and which, through its exceedingly swift resonance, draws forth the excellence of delight. (309) [The word] *sasatva*...
Where there is a clamor of those in great haste, moving here and there with cries of distress and fear,
that very sound excites the passion of the heroes.
An example of *sarvatobhadra* (the "auspicious in all directions") is as follows:
“devākānini kāvāde vāhikāsvasvakāhi vā | kākārebhabhare'kākā nisvabhavyavyabhasvani ||” [310]
‘Kan’ means to shine; that which has the nature of causing the gods to shine is *kāva*, where there is *īṣadvāda* (slight speech).
The word *vāhikā* means "that which is connected to" (*sannā*) or "that wherein there is grasping" (*ādā-grahaṇaṃ yatra*) of the head;
it denotes a "successive carrying" (*paryāya-vahana*), according to the rule: "the suffix *ṇvuc* is used in the sense of succession, honoring, and production."
"Those for whom she herself is their own wealth"—such are those who are "svakāḥ," meaning those belonging to one's own side; "ājihīte" means he approaches them.
"Kam" refers to the ichor (madajala) which he scatters; "kākāraḥ" refers to such a mass of elephants (ibhabhara), that is, a herd of elephants (*hāstikam*).
"He akākāḥ" is an address to those who are *sāttvika* (possessing the quality of goodness).
Crows, greedy for battle, may sometimes even produce the *ghañ* suffix in the word *kartari*;

yet those who are devoid of wealth (*niḥsva*), devoid of self (*nirātman*), and possessed of qualities that can be instilled (*ādheyaguṇa*)—even them they destroy and augment by their own power. Those who are thus "destroyers of the destitute and the worthy" (*nisvabhavyavyāḥ*), [behold them] in the fire that is prone to scorching.
From the root *bhās* in the sense of "threatening," the suffix *kvanip* is applied;
an example of a double-quadruple wheel-arrangement (*dvicatuṣkacakrabandha*) among various types of poetic figures (*bandhacitra*) is as follows:
"O Jayadeva, O King! O Lambodara Vināyaka!"
"The splendor of the teeth, which surpasses the moon, shines upon the face that is the wealth of the world" (311).

"In this case, one should support the series of joints of the peak with syllables resting on half [the space] in the construction of a wheel of two and four [parts], and one should rotate the other in the fashioning of the rim" (312).
"Victory-giver," and so forth: he to whom Indra and the others have bowed is such; he is the nourisher and increaser of the worlds.
He who possesses a row of teeth that surpasses the splendor of the moon and outshines the beauty of the moon is "Candrābhālaṅghinī-candrakāntivijayinī-dantaprabhāṇāmāyatiḥ.
He states the *nyāsa* (placement): "Here," one should successively bear and complete the garland of peaks and the garland of joints with the letters of the first half.
And in the construction of the *nemividhi*, one should rotate the other half of the verse so that it forms a double *śṛṅgāṭaka* (crab-claw) arrangement, as follows:
"O Lord of the World, [place] the hand; O You who possess the weight of the sky, [bestow] the essence of aesthetic flavor."
“O you whose nature is the forest, having joined the ring [of letters] with suspicion toward me, O Gaurī—[thus] from peak to knot, then from peak to peak, and from knot to peak;
in this construction of a double-peak crossroads, the rim shall consist of the remaining syllables. (313–314)
The meter here is *aṅka*: "Of Rājaśekhara"—where two *śṛṅgāṭakas* (rhombuses) are mutually inverted, it is a *dviśṛṅgāṭaka*;
that which joins with rays (*karaiḥ*) or beams (*kiraṇaiḥ*) is *karāsañja*.
He who possesses weight in the sky— that is, in the atmosphere—

and who, having established his affection for the nectar in the lunar digits which consist of water and possess the nature of the forest, has by his internal clarity drawn a circular outline like a wheel upon the rim of the visible portion of the sky; O Gaurī, dispel my dark doubt.
The word "sya" is a verb meaning "may he become complete," while "vaśeśamāyattaśaṃkaram" is an adverbial modifier of that action.
He states the ritual placement (nyāsa): "From the horn," and so on;
"with the remaining syllables" means starting from the first letter, *ka*, until the completion, [using] those remaining syllables—the placement is thus called "the rim" (*nemi*).
In this [verse], by the very syllables of the knots (*granthi*), the sequence of letters forming the name-mark "of Rājaśekhara" is obtained through a complex arrangement of the meter, as follows:
*sā satī jayatādatra sarantī yamitātrasā* (Note: This verse is constructed such that when read according to its specific metrical constraints, it reveals the author's name.)
He is the supreme essence and the victorious one who has stilled the sins of his enemies.

(315) On one half of the rim, starting from another peak, it revolves along a line at every joint; on the other half of the rim, in the construction known as the *viviḍita-cakra*, it moves in the opposite manner. (316)
But regarding the *viviḍitabandha*, the *pañcaśṛṅgacakra* has been shown in the tradition (*amnāya*) of that deity:
“Her body is as white as camphor and the *kunda* flower; she is both subtle and non-subtle, with bow-like eyebrows.”
I bow to her who has hands beautiful for granting boons, who is seated upon the various wheels,
whose majesty is renowned as "A," who is the virtuous Gaurī, who flows forth with unobstructed expansion, and who does not tremble— thus she is "Atrasā."

"By means of a steady [state] free from flowing [of the senses], she was calmed— that is, rendered free from agitation— by sin (enas) and defilement (kalmaṣa); 'śama' [is used] in the sense of agitation."
In this world, he who is the supreme essence, the Blessed One whom [the goddess] Itā has approached and united with— that victorious Maheśvara may he be victorious!
Thus he states the ritual placement (nyāsa), beginning with the words "from the peak" (śikharāt).
Regarding the reading ‘anyatamād vā’,
if one adopts the reading ‘anyatamasmāt’, the status of this as a pronoun (sarvanāman) is questionable; however,
some, having read the rule as ‘kiṃ-yad-tad-ekānyebhyaḥ’, maintain that its status as a pronoun is established through the suffix -tamap.
Furthermore, they do not recite the word "anyatara" in the list [of pronominals],
for this is merely a lack of etymological derivation; rather, the word "anyatama" is that which denotes one undetermined [member] from among many.
An example of the *śarayantrabandha* (arrow-mechanism arrangement) is as follows:
"Salutations to you, O body of the worlds! Always the destroyer of the race of Dānavas! O unborn one! O refuge of the virtuous! Behold the joy here! (317)
Moreover, when all four quarters are written here in rows, each quarter is completed by the feet [of the syllables] starting from the beginning of each respective colored section.
"Homage to you," and so forth.

O Aja Viṣṇu, who are the very body of the world’s manifold expansion of names and forms, and who are the protector of joys accompanied by the destruction of the race of Dānavas—among the virtuous in this world, there is none equal to You;
therefore, look upon me with a glance of Your eye and favor me. (This is the implied sense.)
He states the ritual placement (nyāsa): the word "even in the four" is the ellipsis; the remainder is easily understood.
As for the "bond of space" (vyomabandha), it is as follows:

"I do not for long bow to that Sun, the beginningless one of the worlds, who bears a special blossoming that captivates the rows of lotuses; whose rays do not reach the mountains, though he dwells in the sky; who is the essence of delights for those who are weary, yet not for the darkness; and who, by the power of his playful destruction of the strength of the old, is the best among the beloved of the people.
(319) One should observe this four-line verse, which moves through eighteen peaks by means of the *gomūtrikā* pattern.
That which is seen with a beginning and an end is to be known as the "Sky-Bond" (vyomabandha).

In the rows of lotuses—those excellent clusters of lilies—the bearer of that captivating and beautiful particular blossoming is praised by people; his head, marked there as a sign, does not have hands reaching down to the mountain, but rather possesses spreading rays. In the sky, along the path of the celestial chariots, he is the essence; he is not unpleasing to the aged who have reached maturity, but is indeed a source of delight.

In the waning of darkness, his continuous activity proceeds by the power of his play; therefore, he is excellent and preeminent. He is beloved by his progenitor and touches the hearts of the world. He is not the beginningless one of the worlds, but rather the very first.
