Do I not bow to such a Blessed Lord, the Sun? Indeed, I do bow to him.
He states the ritual placement (*nyāsa*): "eighteen," and so forth.
"It is seen by the first and last [letters]" means it should be understood that this is due to the identity of the letters at the beginning and end of each quarter-verse (*pāda*).
An example of the *muraja-bandha* (drum-pattern) is as follows:

‘That army, at the start of its march, was incessantly full of vigor, with people raising shrill cries, and possessing elephants that were both intoxicated and steady in their gait. (320) Here, when each of the four quarters is written out in succession:
The three lines of gods and asuras would be formed according to the sequence of the quarters of the verse.
"Anāratā" means one whose activity of striking was uninterrupted;
this is an adverbial modifier for the phrase "mattadhīranāgam."
Regarding the heroic rasa (*vīra-rasa*) which produces the sound of great vital breath (*mahāprāṇa*),
he states the placement (*nyāsa*) here: "here, in the quarter-verse" (*atra pāde*).
Here, through the arrangement of four *puṭas*, there is the unfolding of three *murajas*.
An example of the one-syllable *muraja-bandha* is as follows:
"O Surānana (Sura-face), I praise you again for the destruction of [my] non-destruction (*na-na-hānanaṣṭaye*), you whose face is a dense, priceless flood."
"In the mind, there is the shaking off of constant calamities, along with the roaring of rivers situated within the forests"—
when the four feet of this verse are written out, there shall appear a row of four single syllables on each side of the three mṛdaṅgas. (113)

"O Fire, you who are the face—the mouth—of the Suras, the gods; for the sake of that [face's] non-destruction—that is, for the destruction of its loss—I do not *not* praise you, but rather I praise you indeed.
This is used either to exclude other deities or to indicate the repetition of the act of praise.
Because it is priceless and provides abundant life—

following the root *ana* in the sense of "breathing" (*prāṇana*)— it thoroughly shakes off (*pradhūnana*), that is, rejects, the deficiency in the minds of those who bow before it: the suffering that has persisted through the beginningless succession of births.

Regarding the compound *nadīnasya payorāśer iva nardanaṃ kolāhalo yasya* ("one whose clamor is like the roaring of the ocean in its forested groves and dense thickets"), he explains the *nyāsa* (grammatical analysis) of this verse:

starting from the syllable in the first quarter and proceeding to the syllable in the fourth quarter, one takes a series of four syllables of the same type; then, having reversed them, another set of four of that same type is taken.
Thus, by this very same method, there is the manifestation of one *muraja* even elsewhere; in this illustration, there are three *ekākṣara-murajas*. This is the meaning of the *nyāsa*.
The expansion of the *muraja* is as follows:
*tālasāraprabhā rākā tārakāpatidaṃśitā*
Having mastered the abode of Māra, she caused the ocean to circle.
As his four feet gradually extended, this verse was produced through the path of the fourth muraja-drum. 114.

"She who possesses a radiance as pure as the essence—the edible portion—of the palmyra tree; she who bestows boons, who is steadfast, whose splendor is transcendent, who is peerless, who is adorned with a garland of creepers, and who has attained an exceeding sweetness like the light of the stars. (323) [Note: The compound *tālataroryatsāraṃ khādyabhāgastatprabhevāvadātā prabhā yasyāḥ* is analyzed as follows: She whose luster is as white as the luster of that which is the essence (*sāra*) of the palmyra tree (*tālataru*), namely its edible portion (*khādyabhāga*). The term *sāra* here refers to the heartwood or the most substantial part. The phrase *atirasāgatā* means "one who has arrived at [or attained] extreme sweetness (*atirasa*). The epithet *amāsikā* implies she is without measure or peer (*amā*). The term *tāradhāmā* indicates one whose majesty (*dhāman*) is far-reaching or piercing (*tāra*). The name *Tārā* is also suggested by the word *tārābhā*. The phrase *latāmālayā'mā* suggests she is not measured (*amā*) by a garland (*mālā*) of creepers (*latā*), or she is measured by such a garland. The entire verse thus describes the goddess Tārā through a series of poetic epithets.
The full moon night (rākā) was bitten— that is, swallowed— by the lord of stars, the moon,
at that place which is the abode of Māra, the god of love.
The meaning is that she, being endowed with *lakṣmī*— that is, having mastered and practiced the *ramā* [the goddess of speech]—
encircled it, or caused it to move, or made it powerful.
According to the grammatical rule *vin-mator-luk*,
by following the sequence starting from the first syllable of the fourth quarter, this other verse is obtained through whichever path yields the form of a *muraja* drum.
That heroine— whose radiance (*dhāma*) was bright (*tāra*) and bestowed the cause (*kāra*) of the desired object,
and whose stay (*āsikā*) was peerless (*asamā*), being shared by no other— attained, together with the *latāmālā* (the bower of the appointed creeper),
that which is *tārā* (the star Rohiṇī and so forth, or that which shines with *tāra* [pure pearls]), having that as her very self.
Filled with an extraordinary aesthetic flavor (rasa), approached and joined together,
within the present example, the specific type that falls within the eight-syllable prosodic scheme is obtained through the syllables of the *muraja* meter;
this is merely an illustration, for by this means other varieties of poetic figures (*citraprakāra*) such as *gativicitrā* and *gomūtrikā* also come into being.
Where the movement of the urine is up and down like that of a cow, those who know the art of *citra* call that the *gomūtrikā*; it is considered difficult to perform.
Among these, the *pāda-gomūtrikā* is as follows:

"May he who strikes down Namuci protect you from the fear of hell— he who, casting aside his illusory power, spreads forth like a cloud, longing for the pressure of the breasts of Puloman’s daughter and the pressure of the stretching caused by the speed arising from his chest.
This is the *gomūtrikā* pattern with an odd number of feet.

Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that only what has been cited constitutes the variety [of *citra*]? If that were so, would there not be a disruption of the distinct division of parts in the *gomūtrikā* and other such figures? To this he says: "And this is merely an illustration.

The connection is as follows: *gati* is the movement or transition of syllables; having cast off the *māyā*—the worldly bondage consisting of high and low [syllables] proceeding in alternating vertical and horizontal order—one should protect [us] from the fear of suffering.

As for *nyāsa* (the layout): beginning from the first and third quarters of the odd-numbered lines, by means of the "cow's urine" (*gomūtrikā*) pattern through the intervals of the second and fourth quarters, there is a mutual unfolding between the first and second, and the third and fourth; this is the *ayukpādagomūtrikā*.
As for the even-numbered lines:
"The Lord, adorned with the crescent moon, wielder of the Pināka bow, accompanied by his serpent, is to be sought; he who is the sole refuge for those devoid of tranquility."

"May the mind perform auspicious deeds within the heart of the great host of Asuras; may the mind [of him] whose bow is bent by the submission of the great host of Asuras—Brahmā and the others—be such that he has rendered the elephant-riders powerless through his singular tranquility, having defeated the fierce battle of the elephants. (325) [The meaning is: By the great host of Asuras, beginning with Brahmā, [the mind] should be bestowed and held in the heart; [he is one] who, by means of his singular peace, has disarmed the enemy, having won a great battle against the elephants.
May [the Lord] establish a pure mind free from defilement for all transmigrating beings alike.

Here, having begun with a uniform line as before, the conclusion is reached through the interlocking of dissimilar lines; this specific feature constitutes a *yukpādagomūtrikā* (half-verse *gomūtrikā*), as follows:

"May the Lord—who shatters the circle of the *skandilī* darkness with the luster of the crescent moon fixed upon his crest; who brings joy to the people through his noble tranquility; whose radiance is peerless; who playfully casts down the splendor of Śiva’s consort; who cuts short the extension of the celestial abode with his brow; who is the Goddess herself, difficult to subdue; who delights the immortals; and whose abode is not to be envied—grant us sublime peace.
(326) The 'portion' (*bhāga*) of the moon is a fragment (*khaṇḍa*)."
Śam means auspiciousness; amarajanatā refers to the host of gods;
he whose other abode or place does not exist is "ananyadhāmā" (one who has no other abode).
The meaning is that he delights in his own self;

not only that, but may the Lord and the Goddess, by the movement of their eyebrows—that is, by a mere glance—drive far away [our afflictions] and grant us self-restraint (dama) within our bodies; such is the connection [of the words].
The wives of the lords of the quarters, having had their anger toward the Supreme Lord removed by his affection—
according to the root *bhāma* meaning "anger"—
are the gods who dwell in heaven (*dyusadana*).
Uma, who is bowed to by Nandin, whose [abode] is unsurpassed splendor and energy, and who is ever-active and never-resting; regarding her,
the first verse of the *gomūtrikā* arrangement is as follows:

"May Śaṅkara—who bears the moon; whose lotus-feet are licked by the crowns of all the gods; whose body is embraced by the Goddess; who is the cause of the solidification of consciousness during the forest-fire of the city-demon (Tripura); who reduced Kāmadeva to ashes; who possesses the pride of being sung of by the circles of the wives of the gods; whose toe-nails were bowed to by Andhaka, the lord of the Daityas; and who is the object of contemplation for the fortunate—protect us!
(327)" An example of the second [type] is as follows:

May He—whose splendor is fierce, whose hand holds the water-vessel, whose lotus-feet have taken root; who possesses a body marked by the colors of the breaking of disease; who is the repository of renunciation that subdues gods and men; who brings auspiciousness; whose glory causes the quarters to tremble; who is inaccessible to the words of the female serpents who bite the virtuous and the wicked; whose nectar-like policy descends to destroy the bonds of the Daityas; who is the supreme giver of peace and worthy of divine service—[may He grant us bliss].
He is the forest fire for the ancient Dānava, and the source of dense, solid consciousness.
He whose feet were bowed to by Andhaka, the lord of the Daityas, who is to be meditated upon and contemplated by the noble and the excellent,
from whom the lotuses of the other [sages] have their roots firmly established.
He whose passion for the suffering of those who bow before him subdues the pride of both gods and men;
he is the treasury of the perfection of renunciation and their refuge.
He whose presence brings prosperity that causes the very quarters of the sky to tremble,

and for whom even his own wife in the inner garden was filled with fear and distress— may He, who is not the progenitor of Daityas and upon whom no thought is fixed on the Daityas, protect us from the words of reproach and the censuring speech of those who would break Him.

The meaning is: may the Sun of fierce radiance— who is the "Śampara" (the one who bestows *śam*, or happiness) because he fulfills (*piparti*) happiness, whose method possesses far-reaching momentum for severing the bonds of *saṃsāra*, and who is divine and worthy of service— grant us welfare (*bhandam*) and auspiciousness within our bodies.
In the *viparītagomūtrikā* (reverse cow’s urine) pattern, the first verse is as follows:

“I bow to Vināyaka, whose face is fragrant with the scent of rut-fluid (*dāna*), whose countenance is smiling, who moves slowly in discourse, who is the essence that destroys the multitude of obstacles, the son of Satī, and the beloved of Śaṅkara. (329)
An example of an inverted verse (*viparītaśloka*) is as follows:

“I bow to the moon, the maker of nectar, who has attained tranquility through the beginning of a trembling creeper, who possesses beautiful luster, who is the destroyer of worldly existence, who is honored by many sages, whose interior is of the same color [as its rays], and who is enriched by nine conch shells. (330)
Moving slowly with a gentle gait, his face was radiant with smiles due to his noble-mindedness during conversations and inquiries concerning the devotees of the gods;
he was the supreme essence of those who dispel a succession of obstacles.
He who, because he bore the crest-jewel of the king of birds, had begun to console the swaying creepers— many of whom were greatly distressed—
by moving among those of his own kind.
Below the first verse, one should write the second verse in reverse order, enriched with a new *kambu* [ornament] and filled out;
thereafter, there should be a mutual interlacing by means of the *gomūtrikā* pattern in sequence.
In the *Bhinnacchandogomūtrikā*, the first verse is as follows:

"Pay homage to Hara, whose ornament consists of the crescent moon, whose neck is embraced by the arms of the Daughter of the Mountain, who bestows fortune, who is intent on praise, and whose prowess lies in the destruction of Rāvaṇa’s assembly. (331)
The second verse is as follows:

“I bow to the incomparable, playful manifestation of Nārāyaṇa, which grants desires, is fiercely beautiful, crushes the intoxicated, is invincible with its ivory tusks, is variegated by its mace, and has cast down the demon Kaṃsa through the weight of its profound splendor. (332)

He by whom [Rāvaṇa’s] command and prowess— his authority and manliness, which were shattered when his power failed upon lifting Mount Kailāsa in battle— were rendered instruments of misfortune, scratching, and destruction, that is to say, in the assembly and in combat.
It is the bestower of desires,
fierce and formidable, yet charming and desirable;

it is invincible— that is, impossible to conquer— in the battle fought with the fangs of the serpent named Kāliya, whose nature is to crush the pride of others, or with the tusks of the elephant named Kuvalayāpīḍa.
With a mace inlaid with various gems— meaning variegated or wonderful—
the Sanskrit verse in the *saṃskṛta-prākṛta gomūtrikā* (the "cow's urine" pattern of Sanskrit and Prakrit) is as follows:

"May Skanda, who possesses desired supernatural powers, who is straightforward and has torn apart the host of his enemies, who is ever-active and ready with a gentle touch, who sports in the midst of the clamor of worldly fear, who dances with great joy, who is the destroyer of offerings here, who is not diminished by fierce heat, and who is devoted to the majesty of the body of the King of Divine Splendor through the display of his valor— may he grant [blessings]. (333) Skanda is Kārttikeya.

When the multitude of enemies is torn asunder, he is expansive and vast; he is active, manifesting a throbbing form, yet slow and tranquil in mind. In this world of mortals, he is one who, through his abundant capacity for dispelling the perception of the fear of existence—the terror of *saṃsāra*—is radiant with health and vigor, and is the slayer of the powerful.

He was devoted to a greatness characterized by a fierce and sharp nature, possessing a vast and unyielding foundation that stood above all others, wherein his efforts were such as to shatter the divine power of kings.
An example of a Prakrit verse is as follows:

“The moon—friend of Kandarpa, companion in his wanderings, who has captivated the host of stars, self-willed, worthy of homage, the delighter of the blue water-lily, the bringer of union in the midst of the crowd, the dancer of the throbbing buds, the ornament upon the crest of Śiva, whose rays are drenched in the water of nectar, who brings joy to the world by the power of his play—victorious! (334)

Victorious is the moon—the friend of Kandarpa, fruitful in its wandering, having eclipsed the splendor of the stars, acting according to its own will, worthy of adoration, the destroyer of the night-lotus, the bringer of union with Śaṅkara, dancing with the thrill of the lunar digits, serving as the ornament upon the crest of Śiva, pouring forth floods of nectar-like moonlight, and bestowing its own delight through the power of its charms.
[In this verse, "viharaṇe saṃcaraṇe saphalaḥ" means: fruitful in its wandering and movement.]
It is "arisen" because it indicates both the auspicious and the inauspicious;
it is "melikārī" (the uniter) because it brings about conjunction, or "aikyakārī" (the maker of unity) because it is the crest-jewel [of all], or because it is their very embodiment.
"Kandoda" here is intended to mean the white water-lily (*kumuda*); he is one who shines by its blooming,
bestowing floods of moonlight-water,
and who has established delight within his own self through the power of his playful charms.
An example of the *pāda-gomūtrikā* using entirely *saṃskṛta* (Sanskrit) is as follows:

“*bālā vilāsāvalihārihāsā lolāmalā bhāvasahā sahāvā dehaṃ harantī sahasā surāmā gehaṃ carantī sahasābhirāmā* || 335 ||” [The maiden (*bālā*), whose laughter is captivating with its series of playful charms (*vilāsāvalihārihāsā*), who is restless (*lolā*) yet pure (*amalā*), who possesses natural emotion (*bhāvasahā*) and spontaneity (*sahāvā*), who suddenly steals away the body (*dehaṃ harantī sahasā*), who is intoxicated by wine (*surāmā*), and who moves about the house (*gehaṃ carantī*) while being exceedingly delightful (*abhirāmā*).]
She whose laughter is captivating amidst her graceful gestures, and whose flickering glance is unsteady,
pure, and stainless.
She who endures various kinds of states is "bhāvasahā";

*hāva* is a particular kind of play, as in the arrangement of the half-*gomūtrikā* pattern: [The verse follows: *“yathā nātha tathā nātho yathā dāsas tathā hy aham | yathā lakṣmīs tathā tvaṃ me yathāhaṃ tvaṃ tathā mama ||”* [This is followed by: *“yathāhaṃ tvaṃ tathā me tvaṃ yathā tvaṃ tvaṃ tathā mama | yathā tvaṃ tvaṃ tathā tvaṃ me yathā me tvaṃ tathā mama ||”* [And finally: *“yathā me tvaṃ tathā me tvaṃ yathā me tvaṃ tathā mama | yathā me tvaṃ tathā me tvaṃ yathā me tvaṃ tathā mama ||”* [This concludes the half-*gomūtrikā* arrangement.]
‘Homage to Divasapūra, who speaks with the voice of a celestial being, who destroys the enemies of the bowing devotees, and who proclaims the essence of the true core.
(336) He is called Divasapūra because he fulfills the days; to him [homage].
To him who is radiant upon the lotuses, to whom the fortunate bow down—
he who tears asunder his enemies is called Aridāra.
Then there is a *karmadhāraya* compound:
"the destroyer of enemies for those who are bowed [in devotion] and worthy," or "he in whom the worthy are bowed and enemies are destroyed.
Or, it refers to him who contemplates that which is the abiding in the excellent essence (*sāra*), the dissolution (*laya*) therein—that is, the act of dissolving (*layana*). To him [be salutation].
In this regard, the following *gomūtrikā* verse arises:

"Salutation to Him who is not easily accessible even to the gods, who possesses a beautiful assembly of pure and gentle qualities, who is a flood of worldly existence, and who brings about the swift crossing [of that flood]. (337)
The divine gods bowed to him for whom the wheel of existence was non-existent; [this is] a *karmadhāraya* compound consisting of "for whom" (*yasmai*) and "non-existent" (*avidyamāna*).
To him who is radiant by virtue of the shining of beautiful *sāman* chants;
to him whose nature is to cover the *bhāni*, the stars or constellations; to him who fills and pervades the sky (*bhavāri*);
and to him who is destined for suchness through his excellent, lofty, and swift speed of motion.
An example of the *gomūtrikā-dhenu* (cow-patterned verse) is as follows:

"May Hara, together with the gods, manifest within my consciousness—he who possesses a mind constantly intent on providing protection, whose splendor is praised by all the various [deities], who brings security from the god of love, who delights in prosperity, who has warded off the diseases of passion through his diverse acts, and whose radiant smile is marked by salutations. (338)
This *gomūtrikā* cow consists of all four quarters arranged in direct order, reverse order, and by way of inversion;
may it flash forth within me. (116)

May Hara, together with the Maruts and the gods, who has ascended my consciousness and entered my awareness, manifest eternally within my object of meditation— He whose splendor and beauty are depicted, praised, and extolled by all twelve suns, the Ādityas, as if they were a protective amulet.
The word *sama* is recited in the Gaṇapāṭha as a synonym for *sarva* (all), meaning that which cuts or destroys the welfare and well-being of Smara; it was intensely meditated upon— that is,
forcefully contemplated— by those who delight in all the supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), such as *aṇimā*.
He by whom the various maladies of passion arising from separation from his wife were rendered [tranquil] through salutation;

he whose radiance of smiles, born of grace, was marked by inquiries of greeting accompanied by prostrations— of him [the author] states the placement [of the letters] with the words "of the four," etc.

In sequence, by means of the uninterrupted combination of the first and second, the second and third, the first and fourth, and the second and fourth—these are three variations through transposition; and by reversing this order, starting from the fourth down to the first, there are likewise six modes through both sequential and reverse orders.
These twelve variations are the pure ones.
Furthermore, those arising from the intermingling of these produce another twenty-four variations.
It should be understood as follows: by means of the first and third, the first and second, the first and fourth, the second and third, the first and fourth, and the third and fourth;
thus, this single *gomūtrikā* verse, according to the stated method, gives birth to thirty-six *gomūtrikā* calves. This *gomūtrikā* cow is like a "hundred-cow" cow (*śatadhenu*).

‘The Goddess, daughter of the mountain, whose lotus-face is eternally sweet as honey, the presiding deity of women, praised by the gods, sung of by the Kinnaras, who out of devotion crushes the buffalo-demon Mahiṣa of wicked deeds, the sovereign of the three worlds,

meditated upon by the Siddhas, mounted upon a lion, desirable, whose heart delights in the four sentiments of battle, the beloved of the Three-eyed Lord, worshipped by the steadfast, mirror in hand— she is surely the most graceful abode of virtues, the leader among virtuous women.
Indeed, this unsurpassed cow of poetry (Ślokadhenu) provides the milk of verses even for those who have broken their poetic discipline.
Through the excellence of her poetic meter, she brings forth a hundred young calves of verses (śloka).
She is one whose flow of virtues is unrestrained by the grace of the deity [Vandyā], and who possesses a charming, delightful, and graceful elegance.
Regarding the phrase "breaking the pause" (yativicchedinī), the method is as follows: "One should cast [the sequence] in reverse order and cast it in forward order below;
one should multiply the adventitious [number] by the established [number] and divide by the desired [number]."

The inverse [arrangement] is established as adventitious, while the desired [result] is placed in regular order; for the fruit of the inverse is obtained through its sequence, and likewise, multiplication is the direct order while division is the inverse.
By this method, there are seven verses when one pause (*yati*) is added at each step, and twenty-one verses when two pauses are added.
In the arrangement of three pauses, there are thirty-five; in the arrangement of four pauses as well, there are exactly that many;
and in the arrangement of five pauses, there are twenty-one.
There are seven [mountains] at sixty yojanas [apart],
and one at seventy yojanas; by adding them all together, there are one hundred and twenty-seven.

In this regard, having set aside twenty-six meaningless [syllables]— by virtue of being devoid of action, devoid of grammatical case-role (kāraka), and by being merely parts of words or mere fragments of words— the "Cow of Verses" (Ślokadhenu) gives birth to exactly one hundred "Calf-verses" (Ślokatarṇaka) through various metrical varieties;
for instance,
with pauses at the first, second, and fourth [syllables], the *atyuktā* genus is produced.
By the third and fifth [verses] it is Supratiṣṭhā; by the sixth, Gāyatrī;
and by the seventh, Uṣṇih.
In counting by ones, there is a break in the sequence;
likewise, this should be investigated for counting by twos and so forth, as in the example of "a thousand cows": [sahasra-dhenu].

“By her nails, face, hands, neck, and hair; by her gait, sudden smiles, and graceful glances; by her jewels, moon-like countenance, lotus-face, conch-shell neck, and chowrie-like hair—this fair-limbed woman has surpassed the gems, the moon, the lotus, the conch, the yak-tail, the elephants, the nectar, the deer, the serpents, the hosts of *siddhas*, and the beloveds of the *sādhyas*.
She is not equal to any of these, for she has utterly eclipsed them with her beauty, the pride of her strength, and her long-enduring, clever deeds.
For this is indeed the unsurpassed “Cow of Verses” (*ślokadhenu*), which provides the division of the words.

Through the variation of meters, it produces a thousand verses like young calves; "O Nakhī, O Lalitā, O Gaurī, by your beautiful glance, [behold] the fair-bodied one of beautiful form. (118) "Nakha" means O Lalitā, O Gaurī; [this refers to] your beautiful gaze upon the fair-bodied one of beautiful limbs.

The *sādhya*s are specific classes of deities; those dwelling in the sky are the planets, stars, and so forth (*rāpya* means that which is nourished or protected—according to the rule *āsuvapirapitrapicamaśca*, it is stated that the root *rāp* is used;
alternatively, it may be construed with the reading *darya*).
Regarding the term *padavicchedinī*:

although in this meter named *Sudhākalaśa* six words are divided per line—even though there is an excess of words in the second and third lines due to two *ca*s, and in the fourth line due to the word *tava*—nevertheless, because they serve to color the meanings of the things being conjoined or negated in accordance with the meaning of the first word, and because they follow the meaning of the vocative, the *ca*s, the *na*s, and *tava* are merely constituent parts of those respective lines; thus, [the objection] is essentially invalid.

And likewise, when three quarters are taken from six [metres] within a *jāti* consisting of seventeen syllables, there are ten variations in the first half according to the sequence of the arrangement of the *prastāra*; and in the third and fourth quarters, there are exactly that many [ten] for each. Thus, by ten multiplied by ten, one hundred;
and by one hundred multiplied by ten, one thousand verses (*śloka*) arise as "calves" (*tarṇaka*). This is the "thousand-cow" [type];
the "ten-thousand-cow" type is as follows:

‘Thou art active, thou triumphest, thou expandest, thou createst, thou art born, thou protectest, thou art praised, thou forgivest, thou art patient, thou rejoicest, thou art reviled, thou art pleased,

thou art praised, thou forgivest, thou art impudent, thou art crooked, thou art bold, thou art effeminate, thou art abashed, thou takest away, thou art impassioned, thou art colored, thou shinest, thou art radiant.
(341) This, however, is indeed a cow that yields milk only when its words are analyzed, by means of its verbal forms.
"We have seen her, the mother of ten thousand verses, by those foremost of the awakened ones;
thus, O Kriyā, I shall act.
(119) O Kriyā, [this refers to] action.

The roots *miṣ* in the sense of rivalry, *pīṅ* in the sense of drinking, and *mṛḍ* in the sense of happiness (belonging to the *tudādigaṇa*); *hoḍṛ* in the sense of disregard, and *kuḍa* in the sense of destruction; you are attached, you are intent, you are colored with passion, you are envious, and you shine.

"You shine, you blaze intensely"—in this meter named *Pṛthvī*, when four feet are employed following six vocatives, within the eleven-syllable class (*jāti*), because of the smallness of its arrangement (*prastāra*) or because the difference between the meters is not explicitly stated by word, that distinction should also be illustrated. In that very meter called *Rathoddhatā*, among the ten variations occurring per foot, there arise ten thousand verses (*śloka*)—ten times one hundred, one hundred times one thousand, and one thousand times ten thousand—like young calves; thus, this is the "Ten-Thousand-Cow" (*Ayutadhenu*).
An example of *lakṣadhenū* (the hundred-thousand-cow [verse]) is as follows:

“O Durgā, Bhadrā, Īpsubhadrā, Aditi, Surabhi, Diti, Saiṃhikā, Gaurī, Padmā, Nityā, Hṛdyā, Vareṇyā, Kalikamalikalā, Kālikā, Caṇḍī, Caṇḍā, Dhanyā, Puṇyā, Śaraṇyā, Śacī, Śabarī, Śivā, Bhairavī, Rājñī, Sandhyā, Chāyā, Māyā, Manojñā, Avani, Janani, Jayā, Maṅgalā—grant us peace! (342)
This cow, composed of vocatives and single verbs,
gives birth to three hundred and sixty thousand verses;
it does so through variations in the final words and through repetitions such as those caused by agitation.
Furthermore, until enlightenment is attained, she gives birth to the calves of verses for those who are self-restrained;
thus [it is said] with the vocative "O Durgā. (121)

For here, in the meter named *sragdharā*, according to the requirement of three feet [of the first type], one must arrange each single foot within the final two feet; thus, when nine feet are established in all cases—whether four or five feet are taken—there arise twenty-five variations in the first case, the *āpātalikā*; twenty-four in the second case, the *vaitālīya*, with either one *prācyavṛtti* or five *prācyavṛttis*; twenty-four in the third case, the *aupacchandasika*, which is the same as the *vaitālīya*; and twenty-four in the fourth foot, with two *prācyavṛttis*, sixteen *āpātalikās*, one *prācyavṛtti*, six *vaitālīyas* along with one *prācyavṛtti* and one *vaitālīya-prācyavṛtti*, and likewise two [of the latter] in the *aupacchandasika*. When these twenty-four variations are multiplied by twenty-five, there are six hundred in the twenty-fourth [set].
When struck by six hundred [verses], twenty-five thousand [verses] arise;

when struck by fifteen [hundred], twenty-four [thousand]; and when struck by three hundred and sixty [thousand], one hundred thousand verses arise—thus, this is the "Cow of a Hundred Thousand" (Lakṣadhenu).

For in this case, when three feet are taken in the first [meter], nine in the fourth, and ten in the third; or when four feet are taken in one and five feet in another; then in the first *aupacchandasika*, there are twenty by the repetition of one foot; or in the *āpātalikā*, ten;

or in the *vaitālīya*, fifteen; or in the *aupacchandasika* with two *udīcyavṛtti*s, nineteen; or equally in the *vaitālīya* with four *udīcyavṛtti*s, nineteen; and in the twenty-fifth [meter], in the third *aupacchandasika*, there are eleven together with five *prācyavṛtti*s.

Likewise, there are fourteen in the Vetālīya; in the Aupacchandasika, there are six including the three Prācyavṛtti meters, making twenty in total. In this third [meter], the Aupacchandasika, there are five in the twenty when combined with the three Udīcyavṛtti meters. However, in the fourth, the Āpātalikā, there is only one.

When the eighty possible combinations arise through the sixteen traditional methods beginning with repetition (*dvirukti*), and when these are multiplied by twenty-five (the product being one thousand two hundred and fifty), and again multiplied by twenty-two (the product being twenty-seven thousand five hundred), and finally multiplied by eighty (the product being two million two hundred), there arise *tarṇaka* verses numbering ten lakhs; thus, this is the "million-cow" (*prayutadhenu*) [of metrics], just as the "ten-million-cow" (*koṭidhenu*) is described.

‘You give what is gross; you hold what is subtle; you exist upon the earth; you are impetuous; you sport; you take delight in heaven; you cut asunder; you break thoroughly; you roar fiercely; you glance at the bow; you think of victory; you expand within the city; you remain for a moment; you command for an eon; you move in the unconscious; you strive for glory; you are bold in battle; you speak what is pleasing; you hear the desire; you enter the heart; you accompany the word; you shine with splendor; you blaze in sight. [This is expressed] by means of vocatives ending in the second case and verbs ending in the seventh case.
This cow gives birth to three and a half crores of verses.
However, when repetitions of these occur due to confusion and other causes, she then gives birth to ten crores by means of such [repetitions] as "sthūla" and so forth.
"Sthūlam" (the gross),

"preṣa" (impulsion)— this [latter] being from the root *iṣ* meaning "to go"— "citi" (consciousness), "caitanya" (sentience), "gṛdhu" (greed/longing), "gārghya" (pride/arrogance), "sacase" (thou dost accompany), "vacase" (speech), "rame" (delight), "jaye" (victory), "cale" (movement), and "ruce" (splendor)— these are the vocative terms for the Goddess.
Regarding the term "with vocatives" (*saṃbodhanaiḥ*):

here, in the *bhujaṅgavijṛmbhita* meter, when five or six feet are taken from among eleven feet, it is the *navamālinī* meter, brilliant with well-known syllables within the *jagatī* class, according to the *Chandaḥsaptati*.

In the second [section], there are one hundred [varieties] arising from the *candravartman*, *druta*, and *vilambita* meters; in this third [section], fifty [varieties] arise like those of the first quarter-meter; and in the fourth quarter-meter, there are hundreds of varieties arising like those of the second quarter-meter. When these hundreds are multiplied by seventy, they become seven million; when multiplied by seventy thousand, they become five million three thousand; and when the hundred [varieties] are multiplied by five hundred, they result in thirty-five million verses (*śloka*). Thus, this is the "Cow of a Hundred Million" (*koṭidhenu*).
"But when," however.

For instance, when three, four, or five *padas* are employed, within the very same original genus (*jāti*), by repeating one or two of the meters—namely *jaladharamālā*, *prabhā*, and *chandas*—respectively in the first, second, and fourth quarters, and likewise in the third quarter of the hundred variations among the meters *maṇimālā*, *ujjvalā*, *anavamālinī*, and *tāmarasa*, there arise one hundred options. When that hundred is multiplied by itself, there are ten thousand; when multiplied by those, there are one million; and when multiplied by those again, there are ten million verses (*ślokas*) produced. Thus, this very [genus] is a "cow of ten million" (*daśakoṭidhenu*).
As in the *Kāmadhenu*:

“Speech (yā), prosperity (śī), fortune (śrī), intellect (dhī), woman (strī), modesty (hrī), fear (bhī), speed (jū), earth (mū), praise (tū), progeny (sū), a woman (strū), smoke (dhū), a city (pū), the earth (bhū), a sacrificial ladle (sruc), a garland (sraj), a pair (yug), one who eats (bhuj), a cry (ruk), light (śuk), thirst (tṛṣ), hatred (dviṣ), union (yut), anger (kruddha), consciousness (cit), knowledge (vid), a face (mukha), the quarters (diś), and heaven (dyu). (344)

The *ṛk* (verse), the *dṛk* (vision), the lovely one (*vāmā*), the maker of clay (*mṛtkṛt*), the radiant one (*bhāmā*), the one desiring liberation (*mut*), the one desiring food (*kṣut*), the desire (*kāmā*), the door (*dvār*), the sky (*dyauḥ*), the cow (*gauḥ*), the *sāman* chant, the extent (*āyāmā*), the act of piercing (*vedhā*), the piercing ones (*vedhāḥ*), the non-harming one (*anāghā*), you (*tvam*), by whom (*yena*), the ship (*auḥ*), the vehicle (*yānam*), she who goes (*yāti*) is "she who goes" (*yā*), and whatever else is "she who goes" (*yā*).
*Giraṇam* (swallowing) and *girati* (he swallows) give rise to *vāk* (speech) and *gīḥ* (speech);
*śaraṇam* (refuge) and *śṛṇāti* (he destroys) give rise to *śīḥ* (destruction); and *śrayati* (he rests upon) gives rise to *śobhā* (beauty) and *lakṣmī* (fortune), which is *śrīḥ*.
The intellect (*dhī*) is like a woman who meditates upon meditation; the mantra-syllable is spread by her.
Māyā desires modesty (*hrī*); thus, *hrī* is both shame and modesty.
*bhī* means "he fears," thus it denotes fear (*bhaya*) and dread (*bhī*);
*jū* means fever (*jvara*), movement (*gati*), and old age (*jarā*);
and *mū* means fainting (*mūrchā*), delusion (*moha*), swelling (*samucchrāya*), and bondage (*bandhana*).

*Tvarā* means haste; *hiṃsā* means injury. *Tūḥ* is that which hastens. *Savana* is that which is well-pressed (*suṣṭhu sūyate*). *Uśca sūḥ* refers to the one who impels. *Dhūḥ* is that which bears the burden (*bhāra*) or the yoke (*dhura*) at the front part (*agre bhāge*).
*Pūḥ* means protection, filling, and the city;
*bhūḥ* means the earth, the dwelling, and the world;
*sravaṇam* is that which flows, namely the sacrificial vessel *sruk*.
*srak* means a garland of flowers; *yoga* means a row; *samādhi* means that which is produced; *sama* means even; *yuk* means joined;
*bhuj* means eating, protecting, and crookedness; *ruk* means disease, radiance, and breaking.
*Śuka* denotes sorrow, purity, and radiance;
*tṛṣ* denotes desire, thirst, and violence.
Hatred (*dveṣaḥ*), the strength of the enemy, and desire (*abhilāṣaḥ*); the enemy (*dviṭ*), purity, mixing, and non-mixing; conjunction (*yuk*);
anger (*krodhaḥ*), "he becomes angry" (*krudhyati*), and the power of Rudra (*rudraśaktiḥ*)—these are *krut*.

Cetanā is that which accumulates; caya is the accumulation; cit is knowledge; sattā is existence; vit is the attainment of power; mokṣa is liberation; moha is delusion; and muñcati means "it releases."
Hope, relinquishment, instruction, direction, play, the desire for victory, legal procedure, gambling,
scriptural statement, discernment, and violence— these are the *ṛc*.
Vision is knowledge; it sees, thus it is "dṛk.
Movement is smelling, or rather, it is conceptualization, fortune, measurement, and the constituent part of sound.
*Mṛttikā* (clay/earth) is so called because it "dies" (*mṛdnāti*). *Mṛt* means it cuts or makes (*kṛntati*, *karoti*); the act of making is *kṛt*.
*Bhā* is radiance or shining, for it shines (*bhāti*).
Sound and the components of sound, negation,
joy, delight, exhilaration, and gladness; hunger, the gnawing of hunger, and the act of eating.
"Question," "happiness," and "forest"—what is that which cannot be surpassed?

The word *alakṣmī* (misfortune) has the sense of "affliction" (*pīḍā*), and its component parts are "measure" (*amā*), "door" (*dvāra*), "gatekeeper" (*dvāḥstha*), and "means" (*upāya*). "Door" (*dvāḥ*) [is also a part].
Heaven, space, and the gods are *dyau*;
speech, the earth, and the cow are *gau*.
Because she exists together with that *akāra* and with Viṣṇu, she is Lakṣmī.
She is pride,
she is form,
she is the counter-gift, she is a component of sound, and she is a pronoun.
The word *iṣṭā* (desired) and *ayata* (unrestrained) are components of a name;
*yā* refers to a digit of the moon (*candrakalā*) and the Great Reality (*mahadartha*); and *mā* is an address to Lakṣmī in both the dative and genitive cases.
The root *dhṛ* means "to hold" and "to nourish," and it is a component of the word *dhātrī*.
*Dhātrī* means "nourisher," and it is a component of the word *dhā*. The syllable *dhā* is a component of the word, signifying "me" (the speaker) and serving as an address to Lakṣmī.
The negation (*pratiṣedhaḥ*), the word denoting a person (*puruṣavācī*), and the verbal root *mā* (as in "he measures," *mimīte*);

the verbal root *mā* (as in "she measures," *mātā*) and its meaning; the referent of the pronoun *yuṣmad* (the second person), and the address to Lakṣmī (*lakṣmīsaṃbodhana*)—these are [the components]. *Te*.

The abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) has "you" as its referent (*yuṣmad-artha*), and "you" (*tvam*) is a constituent of the word; likewise, "we" (*asmat*) and its referent are constituents of the word "me.
There is no boat for me (*me jalayānaṃ na vidyate*). That which possesses the dual ending (*aurdvivacanam*) is "without a second" (*advitīyā*); and "boat" (*nauḥ*) is a constituent of the word.

This cow of plenty for us, however, yields not only as much milk as desired from the grasping of single words, but produces millions upon millions of verses as her calves, distinguished by meters such as *ekākṣara* and by variations in rhythm and composition.
124. Through the diversity of meters beginning with the one-syllable verse, and through differences in movement and structure.
She gives birth to all things, both those already mentioned and those yet unmentioned, in their manifold variety.
In a single utterance of her, one *vināḍikā* passes;
sixty of those make a *nāḍikā*, and sixty of those constitute a day and night (*ahorātra*).
For those who recite her words, beginning with the syllable *praṇava* and ending with *namaḥ*,
in all languages, their speech proceeds without interruption.
Having examined the scriptures, she was composed by means of perfected mantra-words.
To those who recite [mantras] and offer oblations, the Goddess grants all desires. One should distribute the guest [offering] and so forth according to what is desired;
thus do its divisions come to be, and one should apply this principle to other cases as well.

"Because it is difficult, because it is harsh, because it is hard to understand, and because there is no limit, only a mere indication has been shown here; the remainder should be inferred by the great-souled ones.
This is what is meant by "the song."
Regarding the phrase "from the seizing of words" (*padagrahāt*):

for instance, when one accepts the combination of nine or more words from fifteen words through both regular and inverted sequences, there arise, starting from the *bṛhatī* meter, various permutations for each meter and each quarter-verse (*pāda*). As these permutations strike one after another, or alternatively, when twenty-four, twenty-eight, or more words are joined from the sixty words of an entire verse, there arise, starting from the *gāyatrī* meter, various permutations for each meter and each quarter-verse. By these means, verses (*ślokas*) are produced that are like calves compared to the supreme numbers (*parārdha*). Thus, this is the "cow of the supreme number of supreme numbers" (*parārdhaparārdhadhenu*), which consists of a single syllable (*ekākṣara*).

The meaning is that when three words are conceived for each quarter-verse (*pāda*) by way of conveying three distinct meanings, this very [composition] gives birth at will to all varieties of poetic figures (*citra*), both those explicitly mentioned—such as the four-syllable patterns (*caturvyañjana*) and others expressed through various meters—and those not mentioned, such as the sword-pattern (*khaḍga*). Scholars know *vākovākya* to be speech consisting of question and answer; they maintain that it occurs between two speakers, or even in the assembly of many. (131)

Direct speech (*ṛjūkti*), indirect speech (*vakrokti*), bold speech (*vaiyātyokti*), as well as hidden question-and-answer speech (*gūḍhapraśnottarokti*), and figurative speech (*citrokti*)— these are its divisions.
Among these, direct speech is of two kinds.
The *grāmya* (vulgar) style is both rustic (*grāmya*) and refined (*upanāgarika*).
An example of the rustic is as follows:
"O you who go about, restrain your desire; O you with a beak as hot as fire, I am one who causes destruction."
“O Bhāruṇḍa bird, sell me this straight arrow for a small price; tell the truth, O Bhāruṇḍa!
(345) ‘The arrow is straight, it has a fine point, and its feathers are soft; even when struck, it does not waver from its aim.
But the crooked fish, facing its enemy, brings suffering upon itself by approaching young women. (346)”

Thus, when both the statement and the reply proceed with equal directness along a straightforward path, this is the *vākovākya* known as *ṛjūkti* (straightforward speech), which is itself the *upanāgarikā* style, as in the following example:
“O girl! O lord! O proud one, abandon your anger. What have I done out of wrath? The distress is mine; you are not at fault, for all the offenses are mine.”

"So why do you weep with a faltering voice? Before whom are you weeping? Is it not before me? 'Are you my beloved? 'I am not,' and for this reason one weeps. This is *vākovākya* (dialogue) called "straightforward speech" (*ṛjūkti*), which is crooked and extremely difficult due to its intonation on one side; such *vakrokti* (paronomastic speech) is of two kinds.
There is that which is fully developed (*nirvyūḍhā*) and that which is not fully developed (*anirvyūḍhā*).
Of these two, the fully developed is as follows:
"O Gaurī, why are you angry with me? But I am indeed fair (Gaura); at whom could I be angry? 'In me'—by such inference [I understand your intent]."
"I know the truth by means of inference alone; yet such are the crooked words of the Mountain-Daughter that they triumph.
This is *vakrokti* (paronomastic speech) as *vākovākya* (dialogue) because it is carried through to its conclusion with the completion of the sentence.
An example of it being *anirvyūḍha* (not carried through) is as follows:

"Whence is this darkness upon my head? And whence, O fair-browed one, is this dimness here when the moon is so lovely? Is the beloved also right here, O lover? "Indeed, I have asked only this much; I do not engage in a debate. Remove this [darkness] from your head immediately! May the Enemy of Manmatha (Śiva), who was thus addressed by Bhavānī and rendered speechless by her reply, protect you all. (349) This is a dialogue known as *vakrokti* (circuitous speech), which is termed *anirvyūḍhā* (unresolved) because it remains inconclusive.
Both of these are dialogues known as *śleṣavakrokti* (equivocal indirect speech); *vaiyātyokti* (impudent speech) is of two kinds: natural and incidental.

An example of the natural (*svābhāvikī*) form of these two is as follows: “Is this water in the jar not from the river? It is said to be ‘from the river’ alone. True; indeed I am drinking it. But how many thirsts have been quenched by the mere name? Do even letters exist within a name? Is it devoid of them? Enough with that! Why do you trouble me? Because you are my sister, for that very reason you afflict me. (350)

In this context, the following is an example of *vākovākya* (dialogue) called "Natural Boldness," which arises from the innate audacity of a wanton woman: "Are you well, Rādhā? Are you happy, Kaṃsa? Where indeed is that Kaṃsa? And where is that Rādhā? The following is an example of "Occasional Boldness": "Are you well, Rādhā? Are you happy, Kaṃsa? Where indeed is that Kaṃsa? [Since the source text repeats the same dialogue twice, the translation reflects the literal repetition. "Are you well, Rādhā? Are you happy, Kaṃsa? Where indeed is that Kaṃsa? And where is that Rādhā? "Are you well, Rādhā? Are you happy, Kaṃsa? Where indeed is that Kaṃsa? And where is that Rādhā?"

"Thus, with these retorts, Hari triumphs with an embarrassed smile. (351) Here, because an answer was given through impudence by using the very name of the rival upon the slip of the tongue regarding the lineage (*gotraskhalita*), this is an occasional expression of impudence (*naimittikī vaiyātyoktiḥ*). *Vākovākya* and *gūḍhokti* are each of two kinds.
The [meaning] is primary (mukhyā) and secondary (gauṇī); of these two, the primary is as follows:
"O Keśava, who was it that spoke to the female swan at dawn on the bank of the Yamunā today?"
"O beloved, with a heart distressed by the fear of separation from my wife, I am indeed that [Haṃsa].

(352) Here, in the phrase "priye haṃsa," when the letter *a* is elided, the meaning "O beloved, I am he" is conveyed through the primary function (*mukhyā vṛtti*) itself; because this is hidden, it is called "Primary Hidden Speech" (*mukhyā gūḍhokti*), a form of witty dialogue (*vākovākya*).
An example of the secondary function (*gauṇī*) is as follows:
“‘The birth of the lotus was in vain, for she did not behold the orb of the cool-rayed moon;
likewise, the birth of the moon was rendered fruitless by him who did not awaken the sleeping lotus.

These two [verses], through the mutual address of the first and second halves, constitute a *gūḍhakāmalekhā* (a hidden exchange of words); this is the secondary type of *vākovākya* known as *gūḍhokti* (hidden speech).”
The expression of questions and answers is twofold:
that which is charming through being explicitly stated (*avidhīyamāna-hṛdyā*) and that which is charming through being implied (*pratīyamāna-hṛdyā*).
Of these two, the first is as follows:
“O girl with thighs like the trunk of an elephant, where are you going in the thick of this night, to where my life’s lord, my beloved, dwells?

Tell me, O young girl, how is it that you are not afraid being all alone? “Is there not the god of love, with his feathered arrows, as your companion? This is an example of *praśnokti-vākovākya* (dialogue in the form of a question) called *abhidhīyamānahṛdyā*, because it explicitly states the very thing that was intended to be asked within the heart.
The second type is as follows:
“O Brahmin, how much water is there? It reaches only up to the knees, O lord of men;
yet such is your condition. Indeed, not all are like you. (355)

This is *vākovākya* (dialogue), because it consists of the expression of questions and answers that are perceived as charming due to the manifestation of proficiency in the science of grammar (*śabdavidyā*).
*Citrokti* (wondrous speech) is twofold: *citrā* (variegated) and *vicitrā* (extraordinary).
An example of the *citra* (variegated) type of these two is as follows:

“O Lord, if desired objects are obtained at the confluence of the Yamunā and the Bhāgīrathī, then this servant desires to be maintained by you. Is this indeed death? No, for death is the departure of the mind from the body. Live long! Your mind remains in the lotus of your feet; here, it is only the body that stays. (356)

This is a marvelous dialogue consisting of wondrous statements and counter-statements (*citrā nāma citroktipratyukti-vākovākya*), which serves as a cause for wonder by establishing the attainment of another birth even while one is still living, through a series of imagined questions and answers.
An example of the second [type] is as follows:

"O beautiful woman, what is this ornament of yours, you rogue? Why is it red? "Because of the saffron. "But it is covered by your bodice; tell me, my dear, where else is there a replacement for it? "I see, where else could it be?"
"Having said, 'I see,' Hara, his hair standing on end with thrill, laughing as he rubs Mṛḍānī’s breasts with his hand—which has surpassed the moon—let him descend [to you] in the game of dice.

(357) In this instance, because the dialogue reaches its conclusion through the marvelousness of the breast-massaging following the statement and the reply, this exchange of words (*vākovākya*) is termed "Variegated" (*vicitra*).
A riddle (*prahelikā*) is a single question; it is also of six kinds, beginning with the "cyutākṣarā" (the one where a syllable is dropped).
The *dattākṣara*, *ubhaya*, *muṣṭi*, *bindumatī*, and *arthavatī*—
these riddles (*prahelikā*) are useful for playful gatherings, for secret consultations among those who know them, and for bewildering others. (133–134)
Among those, an example of one with dropped syllables (*cyutākṣarā*) is as follows:
“If she were not adorned with a necklace, who would not falter by even a single step, bending down at every pace under the weight of her breasts? (358)
In this case, although it should have been said that "Vihangikā does not go because she is deprived of her necklace (kāhāra)," it was stated that she is "deprived of her garland (hāra)";
thus, because of the dropping of the syllable *kā*, this is an example of *cyutākṣara* (dropped syllable).
An example of *dattākṣara* (added syllable) is as follows:
"Who is this, followed by his beloved, with thick shoulders and arrogant with pride, who goes behind the deer—a Śambara in the full bloom of youth?
(359). Here, because the syllable 'ra' has been added to the word *śabara* to form *śambara*, this is an example of *dattākṣara* (the addition of a syllable).
An example where syllables have been dropped (*cyutadattākṣara*) is as follows:
“Who is this clever, passionate, and charming rogue who, perched upon the hips of a slender-limbed woman and embraced by her at the neck, warbles sweetly? (360)

In this instance, when the letter *i* is dropped from the word *viṭa* and the letter *gha* is added, a second meaning arises: "the jar (*ghaṭaḥ*) is creaking. This is the "cipher of syllables" (*akṣaramuṣṭikā*) consisting of letters that are dropped and added, as in:
"atiḥ atiḥ anmaalaṃ prīdya radya jadya phadya."
"melā melā melaṃ melaṃ phasa phasa phasa phasa" (361). This is the "fist of syllables," known as *akṣaramuṣṭikā*;
here, a verse arises through four *murajabandha* (drum-pattern) arrangements written in four lines per quarter-verse (*pāda*).
Namely:
“Today my joy is fruitful; today my delight is fruitful;
today my birth is fruitful; today my fruit is fruitful. (362)
An example of *bindumatī* is as follows:
“Your instruction is [ever] present at every year, your banner at every battle, your fruit at every marvelous means, and your glories—at no place are they not [present]. (363)

By this verse, the method of indicating the meaning as it stands—including the vowels, *anusvāra*s, *visarga*s, and conjuncts (*saṃyoga*)—by means of *bindu*s in the subsequent verse is as follows: *bindumatī*.
For example: u·āu·āāā ṃue ṃue ·ḥ.
Ā e ā e iiḥ ॰॰॰ ॰॰ īḥ || The undivided [state]: "In every ocean, there is the command; in every battle, there is victory."
In every daring act you achieve success; everywhere are your glories.
(364) An example of a riddle concerning meaning (*arthaprahelikā*) is as follows: "Possessing the luster of refined gold, with his lips bitten [by his teeth]..."
"What is it, so full of flavor, that even joyful elders kiss so brightly?
This is an *arthaprahelikā* (semantic riddle), because although the object "ripe mango fruit" was already indicated, its comprehension occurs through the use of a redundant expression;
it functions through the action, the agent, the relation, the words, the intended meaning, and the underlying reality.
Those who know the hidden meaning declare that there are six types of concealed [expressions] among those [six types of *śleṣa*].
Among them, an example of the concealment of action (*kriyāgupta*) is as follows:
"This slow gait, charming due to the weight of her breasts and hips, belongs to her whose eyes are reddened by wine..."
"How is it that you young men, beholding [her], are not shattered by the fever of the arrows of Love?

(366) In this verse, the meaning is: "O young men, as you behold the slow gait of the intoxicating-eyed woman, which is charming due to the weight of her hips, how is it that you are not shattered by the fever of the arrows of Love? This is an example of *kriyāgūḍha* (concealment of the verb), where the verb is hidden by its proximity to the word "breasts" (*stana*) instead of "hips" (*jaghana*).
An example of *kārakagupta* (concealment of the grammatical factor) is as follows:
"By what wicked person have these two been placed in your heart while you were drinking water cooled by white lotuses from a shallow dish?
(367). Here, because the object-agent (*karmakāraka*) "from a shallow dish" (*śarāv*) is concealed, this is an example of *kārakagūḍha* (concealed agent).
An example of that which is hidden by its connection (*saṃbandhagūḍha*) is as follows:
“My heart is not unacquainted with the products of the cow (milk); why then do you become angry? Enough of these misplaced weeping, O lady with blood-red eyes! (368)

In this case, because the word *mayā* (by me), which is a term of relation, has been concealed by the delusion that it is the instrumental case of *mama* (of me)—as in the phrase "here my mind is not skilled in the art of theft"—this is a "concealed relation" (*saṃbandhagūḍha*).
An example of a "concealed quarter-verse" (*pādagūḍha*) is as follows:
"Moving through the sky, its ears struck by loud cries..."
"A garland of gold shone like a mass of lightning" (369).
Here, the fourth quarter, hidden by the second, first, seventh, fifth, eleventh, ninth, thirteenth, and sixteenth syllables located in the first half, is to be elicited as follows:
"like a mass of lightning."
This is an example of concealment of the feet and concealment of the intention:
"If you are told by your elder brother, 'Take up the sword and go to the royal palace'..."
“If the brother-in-law said, ‘Take Khadge and go to the royal palace,’ then why did the servant’s wife laugh and look toward the bed? (370)
Here, [the husband] has observed here the marks of a man’s posture, such as red lac from his feet; with the intention that "he therefore does not employ me in my duties," the wife gazes at the bed.
This is an example of *abhiprāyagūḍha* (concealed intention), which is like *vastugūḍha* (concealed fact): "O lotus-eyed one, I wish to drink water from you."
‘If you will give [it], I do not desire it; if you will not give [it], I shall drink it.

(371) Here, because the object characterized as a maidservant (*dāsī*) is concealed by the word *dāsyasi* (“you will give”), this is *vastugūḍha* (concealed object); furthermore, the breaking down of the inquiry is effected by means of the words.
In a refined assembly, they indeed know that [type of discourse] to be *praśnottara* (question-and-answer) through speech.
It is of six kinds, categorized by internal questions, external questions, external-internal challenges, and those known as *jāti*, *pṛṣṭa*, and *uttara*. || 136–137 ||
Among them, an internal question is as follows: “‘Who am I? the Cave speaks; what is the answer to this question?
Why do you not understand how it was stated? You are merely wasting your effort, O friend! (372)

In this context, how is the word *kadarthayasi* used with the letters *repha* (r) and *yakāra* (y), as in *darthayasi*? Because a question and answer have been stated in another sentence, this is an internal question (*antaḥpraśna*).
An external question (*bahiḥpraśna*) is, for example:
"My dear boy, tell me, what kind of man is your father?"
"And what is the great ocean like, with its waves tossed by the tide?
(373). Here, because the answer "with submerged crocodiles" was stated outside of the question, this is an example of an external question (*bahiḥpraśna*).
An example of both an external and internal question (*bahir-antaḥpraśna*) is as follows:

“Who married Subhadrā? What is the answer to this question? Of what nature is he whom one calls a monkey? Why does he have a full presence in the sky? (374) In this case, by the answer “From Vāyu,” which is stated outside the scope of the questions, it is implied that from Vāyu a man becomes a monkey (*vānara*), and thus the one who married Subhadrā is also indicated.
Therefore, this becomes an inquiry concerning the exterior and interior, an inquiry concerning the genus— as for example:
"By what kind of footprint on the ground is it inferred that the king has bathed?"
When they were told, "Prepare the courtyard," what did those who were unwilling say?

With the two responses, "'With golden bars and lattice-work' and 'We shall not prepare the courtyard,'" a variety of question-and-answer (*praśnottara-jāti*) consisting of a "go-and-return" (*gatapratyāgata*) structure is expressed;
therefore, this is a question of the *jāti* type.
An example of a question asked in response is as follows: “What is that which measures a league? What are the two thousand [fingers] of the staffs?
Who is Kālī? Who is Madhurā? What is the shade of the grove of parrots and young grain? (376)

In this regard, whatever questions there may be—such as "What is that quarter of a *yojana*? or "What is that which consists of two thousand *daṇḍas*? and so forth—the answers are precisely those: "A *krośa* is a quarter of a *yojana*" or "Two thousand *kodaṇḍas*," and so on. Likewise, regarding the question, "What is *Kālī*? What is *Madhurā*? What has the shade of a parrot’s broad face?", the answer is: "What remains to be asked after [the statement] has been expressed? This is the "question within a question" (*pṛṣṭapraśna*), such as the following question-and-answer exchange:
[Example omitted for brevity] Thus ends the discussion of the question within a question.

(2) Now begins the third chapter for the purpose of defining the figures of speech (*alaṃkāra*) pertaining to meaning (*artha*), which follows in the sequence;
therein, he states the general definition useful for its classification:

Wise men should understand that universals (*jāti*) and the like are to be known by the name of "figure of sense" (*arthālaṅkāra*), when they serve to embellish the sense through the path of word-derivation (*vyutpatti*) and so forth. [Verse 1] Regarding the phrase "to embellish the sense": *alam artham alaṃkartum* (to embellish the sense sufficiently). *alam* here functions as a prefix (*upasarga*) meaning "sufficiently" (*paryāpta*). It is not used in the sense of prohibition (*pratiṣedha*), because the suffix *tumun* is attached to a verb preceded by an *upasarga*. Nor does it mean "capability" (*śakti*), because that would result in a tautology (*punarukti*) with the word *alaṃkartum* (to embellish). Nor does it mean "cessation" (*nivṛtti*), because that would contradict the intended meaning. Therefore, it is understood in the sense of "sufficiency. Thus, the compound *alam-artha* means "that which is sufficient for the sense," i.e., the "sense itself" (*artha eva*). The term *alaṃkāra* (ornament) is derived from the root *kṛ* ("to do") with the suffix *ghañ*, signifying the instrument (*karaṇa*) or the location (*adhikaraṇa*). Consequently, *arthālaṃkāra* means "that which serves as the instrument or locus for the ornamentation of the sense. Since the word *alaṃkāra* is a common noun (*jātiśabda*), it denotes its own form; therefore, it is not necessary to apply the feminine suffix *ṭāp* (as one might expect in a tatpuruṣa compound ending in *alam*). Thus, the term *arthālaṃkāra* is established as a masculine noun. Alternatively, one may interpret it as follows: the word *alam* is used in the sense of "capable" (*śakta*). In this case, the compound *alam-artha* is a *tatpuruṣa* consisting of two words in apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*), where both members denote the same object. The suffix *ṭāp* is then added according to Pāṇini’s rule *ajādyataṣṭāp* (4.1.4), resulting in the feminine form *arthālaṃkāra*. This interpretation is supported by the fact that the word *alam* is frequently used in the sense of "capability" in various grammatical treatises (*śāstra*). For example: *alam atyartham uddhataiḥ* ("sufficiently" or "excessively" arrogant), *alam asthānanirbandhena* ("enough with this misplaced persistence"), *alam ātmaparikleśena* ("enough with self-torment"). In these instances, the word *alam* is used in the sense of "capability" (*śakti*). Furthermore, the word *alam* is also employed in the sense of "cessation" (*nivṛtti*), as in: *alam anyathā gṛhītena* ("enough with this misunderstanding"). However, in the present context, the sense of "cessation" is not applicable. Therefore, the word *alam* is taken in the sense of "capability," and the compound is analyzed as a *tatpuruṣa* of two words in apposition. In this view, the word *alam* is understood as synonymous with *śakta* ("capable"). Thus, *arthālaṃkāra* is explained as "that which is capable of being an ornament to the sense. In this analysis, the word *alam* is a synonym for "capability," and the compound is a *tatpuruṣa* of two words in apposition. The feminine suffix *ṭāp* is applied according to the rule *ajādyataṣṭāp*. This interpretation is consistent with the usage of the word *alam* in various *śāstras*. "Distinctive production" (*viśiṣṭotpatti*) refers to *vyutpatti* (derivation); "the mode that delimits the genus" (*jāter avacchedakaḥ prakāraḥ*);

and by the word "etc. (*ādiśabdāt*), the twenty-three [types] such as the obstruction of various powers (*vividhaśaktipratibandha*) and the delimitations of *vibhāvanā* and so forth are included under the designation of "figure of sense" (*arthālaṃkāra*).

"Distinction (vicchitti) is an ornament of meaning (arthālaṃkāra) whose purpose is the cessation of the mere beauty of the literal sense"—this is the clear definition. [The following are its varieties:

Jāti (Natural Description), Vibhāvanā (Poetic Causation), Hetu (Cause), Ahetu (Non-Cause), Sūkṣma (The Subtle), Uttara (The Reply), Virodha (Contradiction), Saṃbhava (Possibility), Anyonya (Mutuality), Parivṛtti (Exchange), and Nidarśanā (Illustrative Comparison). || 2 ||

He shows the divisions: "Genus, difference, the collective, error, deliberation, the closed-eye illusion, memory, emotion, and the means of valid cognition preceded by perception [are the subjects] according to Jaimini. (3)
Jaimini’s means of valid cognition (pramāṇas) are six— namely perception, inference, comparison, verbal testimony, presumption, and non-existence—
and it was stated that they are "preceded by perception" in order to explain their definitions in that very sequence.
Since the Sāhitya [tradition] is present in all assemblies, it is entirely appropriate for it to rely upon the methods of various philosophical systems.
There is indeed no meaning-ornament that does not depend upon its own form; therefore, he states that primacy belongs to the genus alone:
"Among those—in various states—those forms of an object which are produced..."
They declare those [qualities] to be "birth" (jāti) according to their respective inherent natures.
Among these,
"state" (avasthā) is the distinction produced by time.
With reference to her, [cognitions] arise—indeed, they are produced as deviating from the actual nature of things.
For instance: "O, those sacrificers of celebrated luster, those kings, these fawn-eyed women—enough with further talk of the cycle of rebirth;

To the objection that [the term] "jāti" would also apply to such cases as these, he says: "From their own respective [parts]" means those which have become its very nature;
the definition of *jāti* is the delineation of a form that is to be manifested solely through the poet's creative intuition (*pratibhā*).
Even that which is the object of worldly conceptualization appears through *pratibhā* (creative intuition),

as it has been said: "For the poet whose mind is momentarily stunned by reflection upon words and meanings that accord with aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), *pratibhā* is indeed a discernment arising from the touch of a particular excellence."
"For he is indeed celebrated as the third eye of the Blessed One,

Intending to refer to this very distinction already mentioned, he says: "This [speech] conveys a certain degree of differentiation from the manifestation of the object; it expresses that which is pleasant as it arises, yet its form is eternal. (5)

Regarding "the manifestation of meaning" (*arthavyakti*): the manifestation of meaning, which consists in the delineation of the essential nature of the thing (*vastu*), has been described among the qualities of meaning (*arthaguṇa*).
In that context, its "ever-present form" (*sārvakālikam rūpam*) means that it pervades the interval between its arising and its passing away.
In this context, however, the meaning is that [the figure] which arises from adventitious causes and originates from their conjunction is "deviant" (*vyabhicarita*).

Because there is no confusion between the two modes of interruption (*vicchitti*) and because each confers a distinct beauty, the distinction between them is justified. Therefore, the claim made by some that "Svabhāvokti (Natural Description) itself is Arthavyakti (Explicitness of Meaning)" is refuted.

For this very reason, it is not correct to argue that other varieties belonging to different classes should also be treated as separate ornaments, as this would result in a contradiction with one's own intermediate statements.

For there is no distinction between the universal and the particular such that [the former] is the essential nature, the substratum, or the cause; rather, it is their causes of differentiation— namely,
configuration and so forth— in which that [universal] shines forth preeminently.

"Own-nature" (*svarūpa*) refers to a mode of delimitation that is distinct from both the specific substratum and the specific cause; he analyzes this very point by stating: "those [factors] such as configuration (*saṃsthāna*), etc."
Now, one might object: "What is the use of this elaborate discussion, since only that which possesses the nature previously described constitutes a *jāti*? To this he replies:

"Among those [cases], it (the *jāti*) is a cause of excellence by virtue of its specific distinction; for indeed, an ornament (*alaṃkāra*) is precisely that which causes excellence, and such a state exists here. This is the intended meaning.

In that regard, intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) is twofold: characterized by the arrangement of the limbs of the body and its opposite; the former is also twofold: produced by intelligence (*buddhi*) and not so produced.
This is what he says:

"In that regard, [the form] exists in many ways through various distinctions such as essential nature (svarūpa), configuration (saṃsthāna), state (avasthāna), as well as dress (veṣa), activity (vyāpāra), and so forth. (7)

In that context, by the phrase "its own nature" (*svarūpa*) and so forth, the inclusion of the nature of trees and other such things is intended; and the substrata (*āśraya*) are the bewildered woman, the child, the animal, and the actor.
Place, time, capacity, and the means are the causes.
