"For whose sake, daughter Cūtamañjarī, has the village been adorned by you?

Here, at the spring festival (*vasantotsava*), this attire of the village young women serves to delight the minds of the people; thus, "attire" (*veṣa*) is a specific variety of *jāti* (conventional type).
In this context, it is the spring festival.

Even if the time and the recipient are appropriate here, there is nevertheless no *saṃkara* (commixture) in such instances as: "The ear, its lobe hanging loose, catches the mango juice dripping from the opening of the crest-jewel of the *saṃvāraṇa* [head-ornament]. This occasional occurrence is indeed a merit (*guṇa*). What remains to be considered is: how does this attire possess such a power to delight?

Regarding this, he says: "For the delight of the minds of people" means that the inclination and desire for the arising of those things opposed [to the goal] remain unimpaired; such is the sense. An example of the operation [of this] is as follows:

"Having first occupied a delightful dwelling, [the leader] became preoccupied with repelling the attacking soldiers; as his own followers were fleeing elsewhere, he quickly called out from afar with a raised arm and a faltering voice. (4) Here, because such a specific nature arises for those engaged in such an activity, this is a variety of *jāti* (universal) named *vyāpāra* (activity).

Regarding the basis [of the joke], as in the case of an innocent young woman: “O friend, while she is being teased by her companions, the simple bride laughs as she shakes out the *kusumbha* flowers clinging to her breasts, thinking they are moths. (5)

"In this verse, 'The young bride, being praised by her friends, smiles as she wipes away the nail-marks while the safflower clinging to her breasts [is revealed],' this is a *jāti* (a universal poetic figure) based on a beautiful woman (*mugdhāṅganā*), because it describes the nature of the action performed by that charming maiden."
An example based on a child is as follows:
“Cursing others, calling out to them, running in circles, and weeping, the boy drives the cows that have descended upon the crops with a staff. (6)
Since this describes the nature of the operation based on a child, it is a "child-based" (arbhakāśritā) genus;
for although there is a standing [of the action] as expressed by "having gone forward" and "having raised his arms," nevertheless, by excluding that, the example remains unconfused.

In the verse: "‘O friends, as she was wandering about, the foolish young bride, shaking off the safflower blossom that had stuck to her breast, laughs at the nail-marks [on her body]’"—here, while this statement might occasionally arise as a conjecture for a single person, it does not do so for many; such is the natural force of the plural number.
"She enters the field again and again to gather the saffron filaments of the safflower"—this is the suspicion [of the husband].

The innocent bride, who has not yet experienced the pleasures of pride, does not retreat even though you are shaking her; "oh, what delicacy you possess!"—thus he laughs, his words laced with endearment.

For this very reason, her state as the most beloved is manifested by the use of the present tense; thus, in the explanation of the subsequent example, the mention of "the operation of action" (*kriyāvyāpāra*) is intended as an illustration, and there is no confusion of operations.
Others, however, say that here the cause of distinction is the externalization [of the object] through the delimitation of its locus (*āśrayāvacchedena*).
An example of one resting on the side is as follows:

"Having placed his face—which has its forepart licked and made pale by the rubbing of his tusks and which is split open to the ears—between the tips of his two front feet, Hari sleeps in the forest thickets upon a recently slain elephant; the elephant's temples are scented with rut, and bees hover restlessly, shaken off by the blows from the tips of his trunk as it flicks sideways with disdain. (7)
Here, because of the description of the lion's true nature, this is a *jāti* (conventional) figure based on an animal;
the term *līḍha* means "devoured," that is, stripped of its blood.
The connection is that they were struck by those two corners of the mouth (*sṛkkaṇī*) as she turned her face askance with contempt;
the secret of the plural number is that their appearance was the same elsewhere as it was while sleeping in one bower,
and for this very reason, there is no suspicion regarding the cause being the location.
The meaning here is that she is distinguished by the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of intoxication, as indicated by the word "lioness" (*siṃhī*).
An example of one who resorts to the base is as follows:

"‘Blessings upon you! It is fitting that your fame is proclaimed by hundreds of travelers; it is no wonder that your form is unsurpassed, for Karna was surpassed by the gift of one who has performed such good deeds.
Having reflected thus for a long time, a traveler—afflicted by the cold and longing for a single handful of straw—praises [the field]; yet the plowman merely basks in pride.
Here, this description of the nature of the lowly character, the plowman, is *jāti* (a figure of speech) based on an inferior subject.
With the words "May it be well with you," which possess a particular quality expressive of compassionate humility,
he who is truly free from pride becomes one who possesses pride.

Because in cases such as *bhṛśa* and so forth, there is a possessive indication (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*) of the sense of "being characterized by" (*lakṣatva*) and so on; now, as for the causes [of doubt], among them, place (*deśa*) is as follows:
"These are those regions of the Vindhya mountains, dense with bamboo groves green as parrots, where the rustling sounds are broken by the tusks of elephants restless in play;
from whose creeper-bowers the winds blow, dispelling the sweat upon the cheeks of Śabara women exhausted by lovemaking through their whistling.
Here, because it is stated as a reason that such winds blow in such regions of the Vindhya mountains, this is a *jāti* (universal) that serves as a cause for the description of a place (*deśahetu*).
By specifying the particular location with the words "these are they," the rule regarding the winds is established, and this serves as the reason for the subject of the injunction.

Because the bamboo forests are difficult to penetrate, the winds become sluggish; however, when elephants gain entry by breaking the trees, the winds become bold. Thus, he states that these winds possess the capacity to remove fatigue and sweat—all of which is expressed here by the phrase "of the Vindhya mountain."
An example of time as a cause (*kālahetu*) is as follows:

“The monkeys tremble violently; the cattle, goats, and sheep wither away due to the cold water; and the dog, though cast for even a moment into the hollow of the hearth, does not leave it, being afflicted by the misery of suffering from the cold.
Furthermore, this wretched person, like a tortoise, desires to hide his own limbs within his very own body. (10)
In this case, because the nature of the activity of the substrata—such as animals—is stated to be caused by winter, this is the fallacy known as *kālahetu* (the reason of time).
[The example] "cattle, goats, and sheep" is according to *Pāṇini* 2.4.12: *vibhāṣāvṛkṣamṛga...*.
By the rule beginning with "4.1.12," there is optional singular collective treatment (*ekavadbhāva*) here for the term *hemanta*.
Although this genus has animals as its substratum, nevertheless, due to the inclusion of an additional cause, it exists as a distinct category;
yet, this commingling (saṃkara) does not constitute a fault, just as in the case of potency (śakti).
"Causing horripilation to arise on the limbs, producing bliss in the mind, and causing the eyes to close— this touch of the beloved proceeds.

Here, because the cause for the occurrence of the touch of the beloved is stated in relation to the arising of horripilation and so forth, this is the *jāti* (class) known as *śaktihetu* (the cause being power).

In the phrase "in the binding of horripilation" (*romāñcabandhādiṣu*) and so forth, the agent is denoted by the present participle suffix (*śatṛ*) in "binding" (*badhnan*); and because of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), that agent is none other than the touch itself.
The meaning is that, although there is no difference in the nature of touch, it is indeed the specific capacity (*śakti*) that must be stated as the cause of the proof (*sādhana*). For example:
"The door, barred by the yokes of plows placed nearby, with vessels moved close at hand by the womenfolk who were startled from afar..."
"Catching the streams of water blowing crosswise due to the force of the wind, the bull enters the cowherd’s hut with its horns turned.

Here, because of the description of the nature of the agent and the object— the two factors (sādhana) that serve as the causes for the action taking place— this variety of *jāti* (class) called "cause based on the means" (*sādhanahetu*) is presented.
Because the door of the house was blocked by a plowshare, it was difficult to enter; for this very reason, there was a long delay outside while waiting for permission to leave or to enter.
This is an illustrative instance (upalakṣaṇa), and by extension, examples such as "instrumentality" (karaṇa) and so forth should also be cited.

Since there is a conclusion regarding the essential nature (*svabhāva*) within the category [of poetic figures], he says the following in order to illustrate a particular, slightly inferior form of *vibhāvanā*:
"When some other cause, or even an inherent nature (*svābhāvika*), is portrayed by the exclusion of a well-known cause, that is *vibhāvanā*. (9)
It is described as being pure (*śuddhā*), variegated (*citrā*), diverse (*vicitrā*), and manifold (*vividhā*).
Pure [negation] is that wherein, with reference to a single [object], a single cause is negated.
It is known as "established" (*prasiddhā*).

The inclusion of the word "well-known" (*prasiddha*) is because the cause of the [perceived] touch is something to be mentally constructed; furthermore, this [superimposition] is rooted in the necessary attainment of that state, and thus there is a contradiction.

For instance, in the verse beginning with *ṇamaha avaṭṭhiatuṅga* ("Bow to the one whose height is fixed..."), the height produced by growth is one thing, while the innate height belonging to the Supreme Lord is another; yet there is an identification of these two.
It is with this very intention that the Kashmiris have stated that the root of this [figure] is hyperbole (*atiśayokti*).
The particle *yat* is used in the sense of "wherein" (*yatra*).

Although its definition is simply that the effect arises even in the absence of a cause, nevertheless, in response to the doubt as to what the purpose of employing such a grand technical term (*mahāsaṃjñā*) might be, he states that two things are to be discerned.
This is the summary here: first, there is the *vibhāvanā* (poetic conceit) as previously described.
That twofold [classification] is concluded by way of external causes and by way of intrinsic nature;
and each of these becomes sixfold through the distinctions of purity and so forth. By this much alone, the body of the meditative cultivation (*vibhāvanā*) is fully established.
Just as a color mixed with another color is variegated, so too is *vibhāvanā* variegated when combined with another *vibhāvanā*; thus he says:

"Where there is more than one [cause], that is *citrā* (variegated); where it is manifold (*vicitrā*), some particularity is expressed regarding it by means of that [other] or another turn of phrase. (11)

The word "aneka" (many) shows that just as garlands, wreaths, and so forth are variegated due to the inclusion of specific elements distinct from those that constitute their essential nature, so too is this [vibhāvanā]. Thus, he indicates it by the phrase "wherein it is variegated," referring to that *vibhāvanā*.
By that other [type of] *vibhāvanā*, meaning by way of another poetic figure (*alaṃkāra*), in that case of the *vibhāvanā* of another cause, the "pure" (*śuddhā*) form is as follows:
“The world was enchanting: the geese were not intoxicated, the sky was unstained by impurity, and the subtle waters were not turbid.
Here, with respect to each individual element such as the geese, a single well-known cause for intoxication and so forth—namely, their being drunk—is excluded.
And another cause, the power of autumn, is perceived;
this is the "pure" (śuddhā) form of vibhāvanā within the context of the manifestation of causes, as in the case of "the drink has been drunk."
It is subtle and stainless,
manifested through its autumnal splendor by virtue of both the context and propriety.
An example of the pure [type] in the manifestation of naturalness is as follows:
“O beautiful one, your gaze is black without being anointed; your brow is curved without being bent; and this lower lip of yours is red without being stained. (14)

In this case, with respect to each individual factor such as vision (*dṛṣṭi*), one by one the reasons—such as being unstained (*asitatva*) or being unadorned (*anañjitatva*)—are excluded; and the inherent nature (*svābhāvikatva*) of the vision and so forth, characterized by being unstained and so on, is brought to light.
This is what is called "pure" (*śuddhā*) in the context of the poetic figure of "bringing to light the inherent nature" (*svābhāvikavibhāvanā*).
An example of variety in the manifestation of other causes is as follows:
“Then she reached that age beyond childhood, which was an unadorned decoration for her slender body, a cause of intoxication known as no wine, and a weapon of Love other than flowers. (15)
Here, with reference to a single object characterized by youth, many well-known causes such as adornment and the like are excluded— such as being "well-nourished" (saṃbhṛtatva)—
and other causes, such as the budding of breasts, the increase of bodily constituents, beauty, and the attainment of splendor, are brought to light;
this is the variety known as *kāraṇāntaravibhāvanā* (the Poetic Fancy of another cause).

One might argue that since "unprepared" (asaṃbhṛta) is well-known as being preceded by the act of preparation (saṃbharaṇa), let it be considered a *vibhāvanā* (causation without a cause). But how can this apply in the following case: "The intoxicant called wine is not the cause of intoxication; the flower is not the weapon of Love"? How can this be?

For instance, regarding the term "instrument" (*karaṇa*): if the suffix *lyuṭ* is applied in the sense of an instrument (the *karaṇa-kāraka*), then in the first case, liquor (*āsava*) would be the instrument of intoxication (*mada*), whereas youth (*vayas*) is distinct from that; thus, there might occasionally be a relation of difference (*vyatireka*), but not the figure of speech known as *vibhāvanā*.
In the second case as well, it is not at all consistent to claim that the activity of intoxication does not possess the name "flowing" (āsava);
likewise, regarding the statement that the weapon is distinct from flowers, one should state the refutation by applying the same alternatives as appropriate—
so how can this be?

It is said that the instrument (karaṇa) is the action; because it causes the influx (āsrava), it is called "influx" (āsravākhya). This is a rule for the application of suffixes, similar to the formation of words denoting feminine gender.
That which is called "untainted" (anāsava) is not such [as it appears],
for as a cause it is nowhere capable of producing taints;
thus, the negation of its causality is shown by way of this indirect method.

Even the *astra* (missile), which is of the nature of an action, is distinct from the flower; it is "fallen from the flowers" (*puṣpacyutam*), meaning "without the flowers," as should be inferred from the previous examples.
In cases such as *stanodbheda*, there is no doubt regarding the meaning.
That same [concealment] occurs in the manifestation of naturalness (*svābhāvikatva-vibhāvanā*), as for example:
‘Bow down to the slayer of Madhu, whose height is firmly established, who is neither spread out nor expanded,
who is not bent down yet is profound, who is neither light nor harsh, and whose feet are the supreme reality unknown to others. (16)
[The Lord] who is neither light nor smooth, and who has not reached the further shore of ultimate reality— [this refers to] Madhumathana.
Here, with reference to the single Madhumathana, several well-known causes such as "tallness" and "grown largeness" are excluded,
and their inherent nature (*svābhāvikatva*) with respect to him is contemplated.

This is the figure called *citrā* (the variegated), which is a form of *vibhāvanā* (poetic causation) intended to manifest the quality of being natural; it is rendered variegated by a particular turn of phrase, as follows: “His face is naturally fragrant; his body is beautiful without artifice.”
"Her enemy is one without cause, and my friend is one without motive.

Here, in the latter two [verses], there is a distinction from the previous two *vibhāvanās*—which consist of the imaginative representation (*vibhāvanā*) of other causes such as separation and reunion—by means of the former two *vibhāvanās* which are natural (*svābhāvikī*).
This is called "the wonderful" (*vicitrā*) *vibhāvanā*, occurring within a *vibhāvanā* by means of *vibhāvanā* itself, and within a *viśeṣokti* by means of that very same verbal artifice.

Regarding the statement "her face is naturally fragrant," since the intended meaning is understood through the connection that her face— which possesses a curved form— is both my causeless enemy and my causeless friend, there is no fault characterized by the expression of a single word having multiple meanings (*arthāntaraikavācakatva*).
This is according to the rule of *yathāsaṃkhya* (correspondence in order).
Because each of those two is also capable of imparting a specific distinction characterized by its own accomplishment,
that very same [quality] is expressed through another turn of phrase, as follows:
“The splendors of those forest-dwellers accompanied by their wives, resting within the interior of cave-dwellings...”
"In which [place] there exist medicinal herbs that serve as lamps for lovemaking at night, filled not with oil.

Here, in the *vibhāvanā* (poetic conceit of cause) regarding the natural state of "lamps for lovemaking filled not with oil," a specific distinction is expressed through the remaining words—which themselves take the form of *avibhāvanā* (non-conceits). Thus, this is the variety of *vibhāvanā* known as *vicitrā* (the variegated), occurring through a different turn of speech.
By the remaining categories— such as being accompanied by a woman and so forth, which facilitate sexual union and the like—
the cause (hetu) of the action is both the producer (kāraka) and the indicator (jñāpaka).
"Non-existence and the manifold cause are held here to be fourfold.

[Verse 12] Since the negation of the cause was stated in the context of "contemplative cultivation" (*vibhāvanā*), one might ask: "What, then, is the cause itself? In response to this expectation, he states the definition of a cause: "The cause is the instrument of action" (*kriyāyāḥ kāraṇaṃ hetuḥ*).

Some explain that the phrase "of action" (*kriyāyāḥ*) was stated with the intention that, in the case of a logical proof, the status of being a causal condition for everything is determined only in relation to an action.
That is incorrect;

for while the *hetu* (cause) has substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), and action (*kriyā*) as its scope, the *kāraka* (participant in an action) has action alone as its scope. Since this distinction is made in the context of miscellaneous operations, the explicit mention of "action" (*kriyā*) here would be fruitless. Therefore, wherever the status of being a limit (*avadhi-bhāva*) relative to an action is determined, there are two possible interpretations: either a desire to express mere causality (*nimittatva-mātra*), or a desire to express unreality (*avastu*). Even in the second case, there is either a desire to express the status of a *kāraka*.

In the first case as well, there is the intention to express either that [the entity] which has the status of being dependent on a limit is the cause of another distinct thing, or the intention to express its non-substantiality (*avastutva*).
In the second case as well, it is the state of having an operation (*vyāpāra*) connected to the action of being an agent (*kārakatva*),
which is to say, the inclusion of another action conducive to the primary action.
That [object] is of two kinds: that which is denoted by a word as it truly is, and that which is not so;
the former is the domain of the case-ending of the agent (kāraka-vibhakti), while the latter is the domain of the instrumental case-ending (hetu-vibhakti);
yet both have action (kriyā) alone as their objective.
Since all six factors of action (kārakas) have their very forms constituted by action, the cause— which is non-substantial— cannot undergo modification because it is of the nature of non-existence;
and due to the absence of modification, it is not qualified by action, as it does not possess such a state.

Nor is it a *kāraka* (grammatical cause); thus, this is the third variety. When a reason (*hetu*) is presented by inverting the well-known relationship between cause and effect, it becomes a "wonderful" (*citra*) cause due to its capacity to produce astonishment; this constitutes the fourth variety. Furthermore, even though the status of being a cause is merely superimposed, it remains truly a cause, as it is brought forth by the force of the poet’s creative intuition (*pratibhā*). Since it bestows a particular aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*) even when such a thing is impossible in the external world, its status as an ornament (*alaṃkāratā*) remains unimpaired. As it has been said: "For who would concern himself with the actual state of things in poetry, which consists merely of mental apprehension?"*10* *10. Kāvyaprakāśa 2.234. This verse is cited in the Dhvanyāloka (pp. 175–76) and the Locana (p. 189). It is also quoted in the Alaṃkārasarvasva (p. 104), where it is attributed to Ānandavardhana.*
Having considered all this, he states the classification: "The agent," and so forth.
"That which, entering between activity, cessation, and instigation, may act even while remaining indifferent—that they call the agent. (13)
The existence of what was non-existent is "occurrence" (pravṛtti); the departure of what was existent is "cessation" (nivṛtti);
and the impelling of that which is currently occurring is "instigation" (prayukti).
Entering between [the object and the result], possessing a means of apprehension,
being indifferent, and not being otherwise—
by these, there are six types of the agent (kāraka).
Among these, the *pravartaka* (instigator) is that which is permeated by action, as for example:
"This Malaya breeze, shaking the sprouts of the full-grown sandalwood trees, produces joy in everyone. (19)
This aforementioned Malaya breeze, by virtue of its engagement in the act of generating delight, is called the "instigator" (pravartaka), a specific type of efficient cause (kārakahetu).
That same [cause], when not engaged in the act, is as follows:
"By the power of that king, those gardens came into being."
"The abode of divine trees with sprouts like moist garments.

(20) Here, the *prabhāva* (power/agency), not being involved in the action itself, brings about the third case (*tṛtīyā*) in the sense of a cause (*hetu*), but not in the sense of an agent (*kartṛ*). Thus, this is a distinct type of causal factor that does not enter into the action.

In the expression "by the power of that king" (*tasya rājñaḥ prabhāvena*), although agency (*kartṛtva*) is present, it is not intended to be expressed; therefore, when only the causality is intended, the third case occurs optionally. This is what he means by saying, "the third case in the sense of a cause."

But the state of being an instrument is indeed impossible for that which is mere power (*prabhāvamātra*), because of its deviation [from the effect]; it is a remover when engaged in action, as for example:
"Having shaken the sandalwood forest and touched the mountain torrents of Malaya..."
‘This wind has arrived to afflict the travelers.

Here, because this kind of wind enters into the action of being the instrument for the affliction of travelers as its agent, it is the causal factor known as ‘the one with an entered action’ (*āviṣṭakriya*).
The sense is that it is designated by the past passive participle suffix (*niṣṭhā-pratyaya*) as being the agent in the action of being the instrument for the affliction.
That very same [state] when not permeated by action is as follows:
“Her reunion in a dream has been rendered impossible by her waking; yet tears do not permit her even to see him depicted in a painting. (22)
In this case, wakefulness (*prajāgara*), not entering into the cessation of coming together, causes the use of the ablative case in the sense of the third [case];

furthermore, tears (*bāṣpa*), not entering into the act of seeing due to their immersion in the act of giving, take up that [act] through its connection with the object and by way of being subordinate. This is the variety of causal factor known as the "non-entering agent" (*anāviṣṭakriya*), whose function is to cause cessation;
cessation (*nivṛtti*) is the state of becoming barren or obstructed (*khilībhāva*).

Regarding the meaning of the third case: since it is not perceived as a cause (*hetu*) or a limit (*avadhi*), it is considered to function as an ablative (*apādāna*) in relation to the act of giving (*dānakriyā*).
The implication here is that the integration of the act of seeing could occur if there were an integration of the act of giving;
however, that very thing does not exist because it is negated by the particle *nañ*. Thus, the meaning is that the instigator is one who is engaged in an action, as for example:
"While that invincible one lives, even though our army is slain, it is as if not slain; but now that Hanumān has given up his life, though we live, we are dead.

(23) Here, because Hanumān enters [the scene] by virtue of being the causal factor (*nimitta*) expressed by the locative case—the locus (*adhikaraṇa-kāraka*) for the two actions of the army’s revival and death—he becomes the instigator (*prayojaka*). Thus, this is the variety of causal factor known as the "instigator" (*prayojaka*), which is characterized by action (*kriyāviṣṭa*).

The phrase "he lives in him" (*tasmin jīvati*) indicates that Hanumān exercises his own independence regarding both life and death; furthermore, his status as the instigator (*prayojakatā*) is conveyed by the two words "he lives" (*jīvati*) and "when life has been abandoned" (*ujjhitaprāṇe*).
He says that this [locative] becomes a *kāraka*: "expressed by the seventh case-ending" (*saptamīvācyā*).

Now, one might object: since the seventh case is found even in imaginary cases such as "the rogue, as if showing a jar of wine on the tip of his finger," how can it be a *kāraka*? To this he replies: "as a conditional cause" (*naimittika*), the sense being that no other [type of relationship] is possible.

That same [emotion], when not manifested through action, is as follows: “Thinking, ‘I shall show her honor,’ the young girl, her eyes askance with a frown of the brows and her lower lip quivering, gazes at her friend who stands in the presence of her beloved. (24)

In this context, because the practice of the act of pride (*mānābhyāsakriyā*)—consisting of the knitting of eyebrows, sidelong glances, and so forth—does not result in the self becoming fully absorbed in itself, there exists a specific causal factor known as the "instigator" (*prayojaka*), which is designated by the term "this person is not possessed by the action.

Thus, even in the practice of the act of pride—characterized by the knitting of eyebrows, sidelong glances, the quivering of the lower lip, and so on—the young girl possesses autonomy; yet it is a particular intention, expressible through words such as "such a one indeed she is," that instigates her toward that [action].
However, no other action is attributed to it; moreover, it is logically impossible for the act of measuring, which has already been undertaken, to be contained within itself,
for even intention is included within another action consisting of a series of operations.
As the author of the Mahābhāṣya has stated: "Whatever there is that is preceded by an intention, whether it be a command or a request, all that is the meaning of the root *pac*";
and since activities such as recollection are possible for this [agent], its status as a non-agent (akāraka) must not be asserted.
Having this in mind, he says: "In the self alone, by the self."

The second, third, fourth, and seventh [cases], which express that which is not entered into by the action— that is, the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) and the indicator (*jñāpaka*)— are expressed by the second case.
An example of what is expressed by the second case is as follows:
Various amorous gestures of the kings, whose desires were made manifest toward her, arose like the beauty of young shoots on trees, acting as the foremost messengers of their affection.
Here, the amorous gestures of the kings toward Indumatī are perceived precisely through their lack of verbal expression.
This very [word] *lakṣaṇahetu* (the cause as a characteristic), when used in conjunction with *prati*, generates the second case ending (*dvitīyā*).
Here, only five case endings are prescribed for expressing a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), namely: [the first, second, third, fifth, and seventh].
‘anurlakṣaṇe’ (Pāṇini 1.4.84),
‘lakṣaṇetthaṃbhūtākhyāna... (Pāṇini 1.4.90).
Having prescribed the technical designation *karman* by means of [the sūtra] beginning with "4.1.90," [the sūtra] states: "When joined with a *karmapravacanīya*... (Pāṇini 2.3.8).
8. Thus, the second [rule]: "When there is a modification of a limb, [the seventh case ending is used]. (Pāṇini 2.3.21)
The third case ending [is used] by these two rules: Pāṇini 2.3.21, *itthaṃbhūtalakṣaṇe*.
The fourth case ending is used when something is indicated by a portentous phenomenon (utpāta). (Pāṇini 2.3.44)
The locative case ending is used according to the rule: "And [the locative is used] when the state [of one thing] indicates the state [of another]. (Pāṇini 2.3.37)
The genitive case is used here according to the rule: “And the sixth [case] is used in the sense of disregard” (Pāṇini 2.3.38).
This is what he says: "And the second [case]," and he will explain the sixth case later in the rule:
"The sixth case is also used in the sense of disregard. (Pāṇini 2.3.38)
In the sūtra "3.3.8," because of the particle *ca* (and), [the action] is not primary; thus, it is not reckoned here as being of equal status.
That which is engaged while remaining inactive—devoid of its own operation and merely bystander—is distinct from a *kāraka*.

For here, the amorous gestures (*śṛṅgāraceṣṭā*) being enjoined for one who is not yet engaged in action, having made Indumatī the objective excitant (*ālambana-vibhāva*), are delimited by her alone; they are perceived as being in that very state. Consequently, she possesses the status of cause (*hetutva*), characteristic (*lakṣaṇatva*), and limit (*avadhitva*).
Now, one might ask: "How can the accusative case (*dvitīyā*) be used here, since because of her being the cause, the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) ought to occur? To this he replies:
"The accusative"—the meaning is that since the instrumental has not [otherwise] been established, this [accusative] being prescribed is powerful and sublates it.
An example of the third case, expressing a characteristic mark (itthaṃbhūtalakṣaṇa), is as follows:
“The bull-bannered Lord appeared with the moon upon his crest, with a skull held in his hand, and with matted locks that were glossy and copper-colored. (26)

In this context, expressions such as *kaṇṭhekāla* ("the one with Kāla on his neck") inform us of the bearer of the bull-banner (*vṛṣadhvaja*) even without entering into the verbal action, just as in the case of "an ascetic by means of matted locks" (*jaṭābhis tāpasaḥ*).

Although examples such as *kapālena* or *jaṭābhiḥ* are the primary illustrations, the explanation of the others is provided here incidentally; this constitutes their status as indicators (*jñāpakatva*).
However, there is a distinction in that both cases involve being expressed by a case-ending in grammatical apposition;

thus, it is implied that other similar types of defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) should be inferred by oneself. This is what he will state with the words, "And this is merely an illustration," etc.
He confirms what has already been said by means of a well-known example: "as in 'by means of matted locks,'" and so forth.

The sense is that, just as for one who possesses a certain state, the characteristic of that state is indicated by that very state—as in "his matted locks [indicate his asceticism]"—so too here, the skull and so forth [indicate his nature].

The characteristic of a bodily modification is indeed expressed by the instrumental case, as in: "He was a child, with a body like that of the four-armed [Viṣṇu], a face resembling the full moon, and three eyes."
"A youth who has firmly grasped the mountains with his hands is undoubtedly the sun now by virtue of his splendor.

(27) Here, through the modifications of the parts—namely, "with a body [like that of] Viṣṇu," "with a face [like that of] Śiva," and "by splendor [like that of] the sun"—the modification of the whole is indicated, just as one is called "one-eyed" because of the eye; thus, this is expressed solely by means of the instrumental case.

In the Sūtra, by the word *aṅga* (limb/member), the possessor of the limb (*aṅgin*) is indicated; and because there is a rule regarding its relationship, the third case ending occurs for that which denotes the limb.

Furthermore, the limb is of two kinds: primary (*ājānika*) and figurative (*aupacārika*), and both are intended here. Moreover, this [usage] involving modifications and so forth is precisely a characteristic of "being in such a state" (*itthambhūtalakṣaṇa*).

For this very reason, intending to show that the sequence of the Sūtra has not been adopted [here], he explains: "In this context, by the word *vapuṣā* (by the body), modification (*vikṛti*) is meant the attainment of another state;
the meaning expressed by the instrumental case is characterized by production, as for example—"

"May the Daughter of the Mountain protect you—she who, at the time of her marriage, was both joyful and fearful; she who applied medicinal powder against the serpent [Gonāsā] and wore herbs around her neck; she who bore potent gems in her hand against the poison residing there; and she who, directed by the elderly women of her lineage, uttered the syllables of mantras against the host of spirits surrounding her husband.

(28) In this verse, because the auspiciousness of Gaurī’s wedding is inappropriate for the context, the serpent Gonāsā and other elements associated with the Lord are indicated as portents through the application of medicinal powder and so forth, just as in the expression: "The lightning is tawny for the wind."

Then, because the connection [implied by] "announced by the omen" (*utpātena jñāpite*) is established between two bases, the dative case occurs after the word expressing the *lakṣya* (the object characterized) as if it were for its sake (*tādarthya*), and not after the word expressing the *lakṣaṇa* (the characteristic).

Since the scope of the instrumental case is thereby precluded, and since the relationship existing between both members is expressed by that single case-ending—just as in the expression "the king’s man" (*rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*)—the instrumental case also does not occur; hence, [it is said] "for the snake" (*gonāsāya*).
Now, it may seem that the definition of this [dative] should be stated as: "that which is indicated by something possessed of an omen (*utpāta*) is the fourth case. This is not so;
for what is being expressed here is the relationship between the indicator (*lakṣaṇa*) and the indicated (*lakṣya*), but not [the dative] in relation to the indicated object itself.

Thus, the question remains: "How can things such as *agadarajas* (antidote-powder) be of an inauspicious nature?
To this, he says: "In this context, of Gaurī... and so forth.
[Objection: Even so, how is it determined that the dative case occurs only after a word expressing the *lakṣaṇa* (the defining characteristic)? To this he says: "And therefore...

The meaning is as follows: just as in the expression "gold for a bracelet" (*kaṅkaṇāya kanakam*), although the state of being for the sake of something (*tādarthya*) resides in both [the cause and the effect], the dative occurs only after the word expressing the effect (*kārya*) and not after the word expressing the cause (*kāraṇa*); likewise here too, although the relation (*saṃbandha*) rests upon both [terms], the dative occurs only after the word expressing the *lakṣya* (the object characterized) and not after the word expressing the *lakṣaṇa*.
[Question: If that is so, why does the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) not occur? To this he says: "And by one alone... and so forth.

Since the two relata themselves constitute the distinction of the relation, the indication (*lakṣaṇa*) is also expressed by the dative alone; therefore he asks: "Since the meaning has already been stated, why is the instrumental not used? The intention is that the nominative is used when there is an expression of the mere meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*).
An example of indication expressed by the locative is as follows:
*iti śāsati senānyāṃ gacchatastānanekadhā*. (While the commander was thus instructing them, they departed in various ways.)
"Having laughed slightly and rebuked him, Andhaka stood there.

Here, by the act of instructing the fleeing hosts, the commander-in-chief’s own act of revealing himself is indicated; this is just as [the phrase] "He went while the cows were being milked" serves as an indirect indication (*upalakṣaṇa*).
And this is merely an illustration.

By this, another characteristic of an action (*bhāvalakṣaṇa*) denoted by the suffix *śatṛ* and others is also indicated; for example, in this very same context: *hasatā tasthe* ("he stood while laughing"), according to Pāṇini 3.2.126:
*yasya ca bhāvena bhāvalakṣaṇam*.

The meaning of this sūtra (Pāṇini 3.2.126) is as follows: when the existence or action of one thing is characterized by the existence or action of another thing, the seventh case ending is used after the word expressing that [characterizing factor]. Therefore, he says: here, in the phrase *senānyā hasati tasthuḥ*, the suffix *śatṛ* is prescribed for the purpose of characterization according to Pāṇini 3.2.126 (*lakṣaṇahetvoḥ kriyāyāḥ*).
126. Because of this formulation [in the Sūtra], or for example—as it is said:
"He [accepts] the oblation prepared by the sacrificers in the extended sacrifices..."
"The illusory one snatches [our wealth] from the mouth of Jātavedas while we look on.
Thus, even the genitive case occurs when the characteristic of a state (bhāvalakṣaṇa) is conditioned by disregard (anādaropādhika).
Furthermore, non-existence (abhāva) here is fourfold, distinguished as prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) and so forth.
However, due to the distinctions such as the absence of a jar and so forth, no numerical count of that [absence] exists.

Regarding the general category of absence (*abhāvasāmānya*), he will state it in the section defining the means of knowledge of absence (*abhāvapramāṇa*) by the words "of the non-existence of categories" (*asattāyāḥ padārthānām*);
therefore, he did not provide a definition of its general characteristics here.
It is of two kinds: that which has identity as its counter-correlate (*tādātmya-pratiyogika*) and that which has relation as its counter-correlate (*saṃsarga-pratiyogika*).
The second is threefold, distinguished as prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), emergent non-existence (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*), and absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*).
Thus he says: "from prior non-existence," and so forth.

Now, one might object that there is no single entity such as prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) and the rest, because they differ according to their counter-correlates (pratiyogin). To this he says: "of the non-existence of a jar, etc.
In this form, there is indeed no numerical plurality;
rather, the fourfold nature is based upon the general properties (sāmānya) such as "prior-non-existence-ness" (prāgabhāvatva) and so forth. This is the meaning of the word "but" (tu).
Among these, antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) is as follows:
“Through the lack of practice in the sciences, through lack of association with the wise, and through the failure to restrain the senses, vice arises in men. (31)
In this context, the antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of the practice of knowledge and so forth serves as a cause for addiction and the like;
as for the non-existence by destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*), it is as follows:
"The intoxication of talk about desire has passed away; the fever of youth has subsided."
“Delusion has departed, craving has fallen away, and my mind is fixed upon the holy hermitage.

Here, the non-existence of the destruction of passion, talk of desire, intoxication, wandering, and so forth, serves as the cause for the mental pursuit of the holy hermitage through non-habituation (*anabhyāsa*).
As long as they do not practice knowledge, they are not associated with the wise; and as long as they do not restrain their senses, that is called calamity—this is what is intended to be said.
Therefore, there is no confusion with absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*).
The venerable teachers, however, have said: "Since this verse is also intended for another purpose—that of one intent on training (*śikṣā*)—there is no confusion with absolute non-existence."
Mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*) is as follows: “These are forests, not houses; these are rivers, not women;
these are deer, not kinsmen; therefore my mind rejoices. (33)
In this context, the fact that these are forests and not houses, and so forth, serves as a cause for mental delight;
for mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) is indeed attested by the cognition "these are forests" in the form "this is not that."

However, *vaidharmya* (dissimilarity), known as a distinct figure of speech (*alaṃkāra*), involves the inclusion of some attribute; for even the distinction of essential nature (*svarūpa*) becomes an object of the convention of "difference" [only] by means of such an attribute.
An example of absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) is as follows: "The conduct of the noble is absolutely non-existent [in others], being unobserved."
"Therefore, in those [virtues], the supernatural powers (vibhūtayaḥ) increase without obstruction.
Here, the absolute absence of unconsidered action is the cause for the unimpeded growth of the powers;
by this, the absence of an absence is also explained.

In this regard, the absence of antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāvābhāva*) is as follows: “The mango blossoms in the garden have not yet burst forth; therefore, let no handful of water mixed with sesame seeds be offered by the wives of travelers. (35)
In this context, the "arising" (*utpāda*) of an entity is said to be the absence of its prior non-existence (*prāgabhāvābhāva*); therefore,
here, the emergence of the mango blossom is the cause of the death of the wives of travelers,
which constitutes the arising of an entity.
Existence itself is the ground for the linguistic usage of "non-existence," and the division made regarding the mere objects of the linguistic usage of non-existence—

such as prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) and so forth— is simply that they take the form of destruction (pradhvaṃsa) and so on; thus, one should not suspect any deficiency in the statement of this division.
The word "tena" (by that) refers to the conjunction of the past and the future;

according to the maxim *bhūtaṃ bhavyāya* (the accomplished serves the to-be-accomplished), it attains the status of being the agent (*kāraka*) for the blossoming of the clusters of flowers. Otherwise, if there were a split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*), nothing would follow because of the absence of a prior state (*prāgabhāva*).

Furthermore, by means of the negation of that absence of prior state, the full blossoming of all the clusters suggests the intensity of spring, thereby nourishing the *vipralambha* (love-in-separation) under discussion.
An example of the absence of the absence of destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāvābhāva*) is as follows:

"May the Creator—the dweller in the lotus at the navel of Acyuta—grant you auspiciousness; he whose mind was satisfied by the thought that his own abode had not been destroyed, and who at that moment closed his eyes, meditated upon the lovely body of the Daughter of the Ocean embraced by her beloved—a body with full hips, a deep navel, a slender waist, and very high breasts. (Verse 36)

Here, this non-destruction of the Creator’s residence in the navel-lotus even during the act of embracing— by means of her body as described— is said to be the very persistence of the thing-in-itself, which is the absence of an absence of destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāvābhāva*).
And that [persistence] here becomes the cause of the Creator’s mental bliss, who dwells in the navel-lotus of Acyuta,
because of her "full-hipped" form.

That even the Daughter of the Ocean desires a secret, imperceptible embrace covering all her limbs, and that the Blessed One likewise desires it— this is what is manifested by the words "by the beloved" and "the beloved";
and this is merely an illustration.

The absence of absolute non-existence of identity (*tādātmyātyantābhāvābhāva*) should also be illustrated as follows: "Earth, water, fire, air, ether, the moon, the sun, and the Puruṣa— whatever some call distinct bodies,
O Sinless One, they merely create for you, who are free from all veils, a resemblance to a false mirage appearing amidst a flood of water through the variety of their words."

Here, having introduced "mutual non-existence" (*anyonyābhāva*) by the word "distinct" (*bhinna*), there is a negation by the two terms "unobscured" (*nirāvaraṇa*) and "false" (*mṛṣā*). And as it is said: "Even if that wondrous intuition, which follows upon all latent impressions and qualities, does not exist, the speech [of the Guru], when worshipped with learning and effort, certainly bestows some grace."
Having introduced absolute non-existence by stating "it is not found here," the negation is effected through the expression of its appearance as "some [thing]";
thus there are innumerable diverse causes, such as those that are remote from their effect, innate, immediate to the effect, or likewise, those that are logical and illogical. || 16 ||
These [figures], relying upon secondary (gauṇa) functions within the paths of poetic application, are to be employed in poems; for in this way, they are capable of producing aesthetic variety.
Among these, an example of one whose effect is remote is as follows:
"Even though he had not yet reached manhood, lacked the calluses from the bowstring as his mark,
and had never touched the hilt of a sword, the earth was protected by his arm.
This is the "Paradoxical Cause" (citrahetu), wherein even in childhood he performed the deeds of fresh youth, making his purpose far-reaching.

Regarding the term *vidūrakārya* (remote effect): it refers to a case where an effect, which is to be accomplished through a state existing at a later time, is said to arise from that very thing which possessed the prior state; and since that effect depends upon a specific potency (*śaktiviśeṟṣa*), the protection was performed by the arm alone even during childhood, as evidenced by the observation of an extraordinary power (*prabhāvātiśaya*). This is because the state of being a lotus (*padmatva*) is the primary quality of the effect, while the state of being a face (*mukhatva*) is the primary quality of the cause. Since the effect is superimposed upon the cause, the word *padma* is employed in a figurative sense. Thus, the recourse to figurative function is established. Furthermore, in the case of that which arises immediately after the effect: [Example: "The lotus has become the moon. (The meaning is: "The lotus has become the moon. Here, the word *candra* ("moon") is used figuratively for *indumukhi* ("moon-faced woman"), because the former is proximate to the latter. This is because the state of being the moon (*candratva*) is the primary quality of the effect,
‘Only after the rays have spread does the orb of the moon rise; yet for the fawn-eyed women, the ocean of passion has already surged.

Here, because of the cause characterized by the rising of the moon, the effect—the surging of the ocean of passion—is shown to have occurred at an even earlier time; thus, there is the attainment of the precedence of the effect.
In this case, he nourishes an excellence by resorting to a figurative function (*guṇavṛtti*) as the cause; thus, this is the *citrahētu* (wondrous cause) known as "born immediately after the effect.
An example is as follows: "By your fame, which spreads forth mixed with affection for your virtues..."
"Suddenly, half-saffron has appeared upon the faces of the brides of the quarters.

Here, the passion for his virtues is the saffron on the faces of the brides of the quarters, while his fame is the sandalwood paste; this is a "proper" cause of wonder based on figurative function (*gauṇavṛtti*).
An "improper" example is as follows:
‘The moon of your face does not cause the lotuses to close, nor does it plunge into the sky; it exerts itself solely for the purpose of stealing away my life-breaths.
(41) Here, the closing of the lotuses and so forth by the moon of the face is not logically consistent; thus, this is the variety of *citra* (poetic figure) called *ayukta* (the inconsistent).

Now, if it is intended that the reason (hetu) is innumerable even when there is a difference in individuals, what is the purpose of using the word "evam" (thus) as something additional? To this he says:
because the word "evam" signifies "manner" (prakāra), terms such as "vyadhikaraṇa" are employed;
for example, "vyadhikaraṇa" [is used] as follows:

"She is a young girl while we are of unsteady age; she is a woman while we are timid; she possesses a pair of full and elevated breasts while we are burdened with distress; she is overcome by her heavy hips while we are unable to walk; and we have become incompetent through faults that belong to another person—how wonderful! (42).

Here, the discrepancy between the locus of the cause and the locus of the effect is clearly perceived; thus, this is the "discrepant" (*vyadhikaraṇa*) variety of the figure of speech known as *citrahetu* (the marvelous cause).

The meaning is that, in the phrase "of the word" (*śabdasya*), what is intended to be expressed is the distinction of the *prakāra*— that is, the qualifier (*upādhi*)— and not merely the individual instance (*vyakti*).
That [word] is feminine.

The causal relationship between childhood and so forth, on the one hand, and boldness and so forth, on the other, is perceived only when they reside in the same substratum (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). When this relationship is expressed here by resorting to figurative usage (*gauṇavṛtti*), it brings about aesthetic charm (*kānti*).

For instance, the boldness of a young girl is of one kind, characterized by an inability to engage in straightforward glances or conversation; whereas the boldness of a preeminent hero is of another kind, characterized by indecision as to how he might restrain them.
And in these two cases, the attainment of that state is clearly evident;
this should be understood to apply to cowardice and so forth as well.
By the inclusion of the term "and so forth" (ādi), that which is depicted by way of its own cause and by way of its effect is thereby subsumed.

Immediately after [the definition of] a cause, he states the definition of its opposite, the non-cause (ahetu): "That which, either by the nature of the thing itself or due to a cause for the loss of its capacity, has not performed its own effect, or that which is obstructed, is a non-cause. (18)
Regarding the object (*vastu*),
that which is perceived as a cause but is said not to produce its effect is called a "non-cause" (*ahetu*);
it is of two kinds.

Whether by its own nature it deviates from the effect, or whether, despite being such [as capable], it does not produce the effect due to a contradiction in its operation— in both cases there is a twofold basis: either the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of that entity in which the effect is to be produced, or the loss of power (*śaktihāni*) in that which is intended to be the cause.

That [non-existence] is also twofold: absolute non-existence (*ātyantikābhāva*) or mere obstruction (*pratibandhamātra*). Regarding these, it is stated by the phrase "having made its own nature non-deviating from two forms" through the [absence of] power due to the nature of the thing (*vastusvabhāva*) and the absolute non-existence [of the effect]. Furthermore, by the phrase "the operation, though of two kinds—due to the nature of the thing and the obstruction of power—is non-deviating and unimpeded," although there can be no causal status at all when power is absolutely non-existent, nevertheless, one must understand that there is a superimposition of causal status by way of figurative application (*guṇavṛtti*). And that figurative application, being supported by wordplay (*śleṣa*), becomes of a different kind.
Now, one might object: "Since the third case-ending here conveys that the gesture (*ceṣṭā*) is the cause, it would be more appropriate to state it as such. To this he says:
"In that regard, by the very nature of things, when no effect has been produced, as for example:
'No frown was fashioned upon the surface of her forehead to perform a dance; nor was her sweet smile interrupted by a harsh *huṃ* sound.'"

“O Blessed One, your lotus-face has not been clouded even by your fierce action resulting from the agitation caused by Niśumbha. (43) In this instance, regarding the incapacity of the cause—the agitation caused by Niśumbha—to produce the clouding of the Blessed One’s lotus-face through the medium of fierce actions such as the knitting of eyebrows, the cause is the inherent nature (*svabhāva*) of the object known as her face. Thus, this is an *ahetu* (non-cause) figure where the effect is not produced due to the inherent nature [of the object].
Here, the word “Niśumbha”...
The sense is that [the action occurs] by way of fierce gestures such as frowning;
otherwise, the fifth case-ending (ablative) in the phrase "due to the agitation caused by Niśumbha" would be inappropriate. That very [agitation] is the cause of the loss of power, as follows:
"The twilight is full of passion, and the day is its forerunner;
oh, how strange is the course of fate, that even so there is no union!

(44) Here, although the state of being "full of passion" and "having it as a forerunner" are the causes for a union, their capacity is obstructed by the course of fate, which acts as the cause. Thus, this is the figure *ahetu* ("non-cause"), wherein the power [of the causes] is destroyed by a cause that prevents the accomplishment of their own effect.
*Anurāga* means redness as well as affection;
*puraḥsara* means that which has the habit of going before, and that which stands in close proximity to an object by its very nature— as obstructed [in the following example]:—

"Where, when their lovers—hands unsteady with passion—seize the silken garments of the Yakṣa women, loosened by the slackening of the waist-knots, the handful of scented powder becomes futile for those women bewildered by shame, as it strikes the lofty jewel-lamps that stand before them.

(45) In this case, regarding the extinguishing of the jewel-lamps, although the nature of the handful of powder remains unchanged even when its function is thwarted, the very nature of the object called the "jewel-lamp" acts as the cause. Thus, this is an instance of the figure *vyāhata* ("thwarted"), where the cause is non-causal (*ahetubhūta*) because it is obstructed by the inherent nature of the object.
What is the reason for the obstruction of the skeleton’s desire for life through the sprinkling of nectar? To this he says:

"By that very [power], as it were, through the cause of the loss of power—as when, during Śambhu’s intense dance, the primordial skeleton in his hand was restored to life by the nectar flowing from the lunar orb split open by the friction [of his foot]."
"May he protect you—he who, seeing the new enemy of Mura (Viṣṇu) prostrate at that moment and displaying the grace of Śrī, made false leaps with a mind reddened by anger.

Here, although his mind was reddened by anger and thus capable of making those leaps, they are designated by the word "false" (*mithyā*) because of the grasping of the hand of the Lord (Śiva). Thus, the perceived contradiction (*vyāghāta*) is a specific type of cause called "contradiction" (*vyāhata*), which is caused by the loss of power (*śaktihāni*), arising from the grasping of the hand of the Lord.
Now, one might object: "How can that which has already produced its effect—the mind being stained by anger—be said to be 'acting otherwise'? To this, he says: "In the case of *mithyāpada*," etc.
Here, some have stated that *kāraṇamālā* (the chain of causes) is a distinct figure of speech; its definition is the statement of a preceding element as the cause for each subsequent one.
It is declared to be of two kinds: either explicitly expressed (*abhidhīyamāna*) or implied (*pratīyamāna*).
In either case, it does not differ from the "causeless"; thus he says:
"But that which is called a 'series of causes' (hetusaṃtāna), consisting of a garland of causes, because each individual [cause] lacks capacity, even that does not differ from the causeless. (19)
"One [type of cause] occurs among those causes that are explicitly stated, while another arises among those causal factors that are merely implied.
(Verse 20) "As for that which... [is as follows].

Although the causal status of the first [link] with respect to the first [moment] has indeed ceased, nevertheless, the causal status of the subsequent [link]—which is engaged in looking toward the face of the preceding one—is stated with respect to what follows it;
for the "garland of causes" (kāraṇamālā) does not appear when there is a causal status belonging solely to something independent.
Manifesting this by way of a single part, he says:
Of these two, the first is as follows:
"Control over the senses is the cause of discipline; excellence of virtue is attained through discipline;
people are attracted to a man who abounds in virtues; and prosperity arises from the affection of the people. (47)

In this context, although qualities such as mastery over the senses (*jitendriyatva*) serve as causes for each subsequent quality, when their production depends upon the preceding ones, it is the collective state of these combined factors that is designated by terms such as "means" (*sādhana*). Thus, this is the second variety of the "causeless" (*ahetu*), known as the "chain of causes" (*hetumālikā*) being expressed; for example:
"By him who, having fattened his belly—which was difficult to fill and held fast by a cruel nature..."
"Riṣṭa’s neck, thick and difficult to grasp, held fast within by his cruel arms and twisted unevenly, has passed away with its life in great suffering. (48)

In this case, regarding the overcoming of the suffering of life, the throat's contraction is the cause; the firm grasping of that contraction is the cause; and the difficulty of grasping it due to its thickness is also a cause—thus, there is a "chain of causes" (*kāraṇamālā*), which is a variety of the *ahetu* (non-reason) figure where the cause is implied.
[The phrase] "here, of self-control and so forth" refers to [the causes], while "here, the overcoming of the suffering of life" refers to [the result].

If there were no chain of reasons (*hetumāla*) here, then even the enrichment of the sentence-meaning would not occur when they are presented without mutual dependence; therefore, immediately after [the figure of] *sādharmya*, which is a specific type of reason characterized by definition, he defines *sūkṣma* as follows:
"The meaning that is to be inferred from gestures and facial expressions is *sūkṣma*; however, it arises from a subtle quality."
The subtle is distinguished as being perceptible or imperceptible;
here, the subtle is considered to be of two kinds: the expressed and the implied.
The characteristic common to both of these is that they are to be inferred from gestures and facial expressions.

Among these, that which is indicated by a gesture (*iṅgita*) while being explicitly stated (*abhidhīyamāna*) is subtle (*sūkṣma*), as for example: “toward her, whose desires were made manifest” (*tāṃ pratyabhivyaktamanorathānām*). Here, the desire characterized by the attainment [of the princess] on the part of the kings assembled at the *svayaṃvara* is explicitly stated; however, because it is suggested (*vyaṅgyatvāt*) by a gesture consisting of an erotic action (*śṛṅgāraceṣṭā*), this explicit variety is called "indicated by a gesture" (*iṅgitalakṣya*). This is the subtle type. Regarding "gesture": [it refers to] a sign (*cihna*) consisting of a change in appearance (*ākāraviśeṣa*). It is said: "A change in appearance is called a 'gesture' (*iṅgita*); it is a sign consisting of a particular state of the body, face, eyes, and speech. For example: “O friend, why do you look at me with such a gaze? Why do you speak so much? Why do you embrace me? Why do you laugh? I am not one who can be won over by mere words; I am won over by the very gestures of love. In this verse, the king’s desire to win the princess is indicated by his gestures, such as his gaze. This is the variety of the explicit-suggestive (*abhidhīyamāna-vyaṅgya*) where the suggestion is based on a gesture. Thus ends the section on the subtle type indicated by a gesture. As for the term "explicit" (*abhidhīyamāna*): it means that which is directly expressed by the power of denotation (*abhidhāśakti*). It is said: "That which is directly expressed by the power of denotation is called 'explicit' (*abhidhīyamāna*). For example: “O friend, why do you look at me with such a gaze? Why do you speak so much? Why do you embrace me? Why do you laugh? I am not one who can be won over by mere words; I am won over by the very gestures of love. In this verse, the king’s desire to win the princess is indicated by his gestures, such as his gaze. This is the variety of the explicit-suggestive where the suggestion is based on a gesture. Thus ends the section on the subtle type indicated by a gesture. As for the term "explicit" (*abhidhīyamāna*): it means that which is directly expressed by the power of denotation (*abhidhāśakti*). It is said: "That which is directly expressed by the power of denotation is called 'explicit' (*abhidhīyamāna*). For example: “O friend, why do you look at me with such a gaze? Why do you speak so much? Why do you embrace me? Why do you laugh? I am not one who can be won over by mere words; I am won over by the very gestures of love. In this verse, the king’s desire to win the princess is indicated by his gestures, such as his gaze. This is the variety of the explicit-suggestive where the suggestion is based on a gesture. Thus ends the section on the subtle type indicated by a gesture. As for the term "explicit" (*abhidhīyamāna*): it means that which is directly expressed by the power of denotation (*abhidhāśakti*). It is said: "That which is directly expressed by the power of denotation is called 'explicit' (*abhidhīyamāna*). For example: “O friend, why do you look at me with such a gaze? Why do you speak so much? Why do you embrace me? Why do you laugh? I am not one who can be won over by mere words; I am won over by the very gestures of love. In this verse, the king’s desire to win the princess is indicated by his gestures, such as his gaze. This is the variety of the explicit-suggestive where the suggestion is based on a gesture. Thus ends the section on the subtle type indicated by a gesture. As for the term "explicit" (*abhidhīyamāna*): it means that which is directly expressed by the power of denotation (*abhidhāśakti*). It is said: "That which is directly expressed by the power of denotation is called 'explicit' (*abhidhīyam
The meaning is that "iṅgita" and "ākāra" refer to gestures and appearances; "iṅgita" is the movement of the limbs of the body,
while "ākāra" is the alteration of form and so forth.

Fearing that there might be a redundancy since "subtle" (*sūkṣma*) was already mentioned among the qualities of the object as "perception of subtle objects," he says: "But it [the aesthetic flavor] is [subtle] because of its subtle quality.
This refers to that which is experienced by the hearts of three or four people who share a resonance of heart;
for this very reason, because such an extremely subtle object appears as if directly perceived, it is called the "subtle" quality of the object.
For just as a poet’s intuition (*pratibhā*) delineates subtle distinctions, so too does the word rooted in it; thus, through its vividness, a cognition of an object of perception arises.

Indeed, in such cases as "intermingled with one another," it is established by experience that even a love characterized by mutual remembrance between a husband and wife—which is perceptible only to a few—is rendered as if directly perceived (*pratyakṣāyamāṇatva*) by the power of the word.
This is what he says: "from the subtle, [it becomes] perceptible."

In the case of subtle ornament (*sūkṣmālaṃkāra*), however, because it pertains to the domain of the poet’s creative intuition (*pratibhā*), the word also pertains to that very same domain. Furthermore, the cognition arising from a gender marker (*liṅga*) proceeds by way of a universal (*sāmānya*) and is not capable of delineating its specific particulars like direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); thus, it possesses a dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) with subtle qualities (*sūkṣmaguṇa*).
This is what has been stated: "The subtle is imperceptible."

Regarding this, some have assigned the name "bhāva" (state) to the subtle suggested meaning and proposed it as a distinct figure of speech; that is incorrect, because it is already encompassed by the general definition of the *sūkṣma* (subtle). Thus he says: "being indicated through gestures and appearance.
By this, the objection regarding the redundancy of the term "indicated" (*lakṣyatva*) is removed.
Here, [the context is] "at the self-choice marriage" (*svayaṃvare*).

Nor should it be argued that the meaning conveyed by the word *manoratha* (desire) when presented through the gestures of love (*śṛṅgāraceṣṭā*) is redundant; for we shall explain at length and in detail how mental states are not presented as clearly by their own words as they are by the manifestations of passion (*anurāgānubhāva*). What remains to be addressed is the purpose of using the word itself; regarding this, we say:

For those whose general longing had already entered the path of perception through such events as entering the assembly of the *svayaṃvara*, that very longing—possessing countless subtle distinctions—was manifested in the presence of Indumatī by the power of her influence; thus, it nourishes the highest pinnacle of love characterized by firm attachment.
This same principle, observable through its outward form, applies elsewhere as well, for example:
"Because of her modesty, she was unable to express her bond of longing for that youth;
yet, through the visible sign of horripilation, it emerged, piercing the slender body of the dark-haired maiden.

(59) Here, by the statement "the bond of longing emerged, piercing the slender body through the visible sign of horripilation," the subtle variety (*sūkṣma-bheda*) characterized by outward appearance (*ākāra-lakṣya*) is expressed.
An example of that which is characterized by both [the speaker and the listener] is as follows:
“In the musical assembly, a certain radiance, betraying unrestrained passion, grew upon the lotus-face of her whose gaze was fixed upon you. (50)

In this instance, the phrase "with your gaze fixed upon him" refers to a certain shade of gesture (*iṅgita*), while the phrase "upon his lotus-face" refers to its form; since the passion of the face, which is expressed by these two, is perceived in a subtle manner as indicated by the words "betraying unrestrained love," this is a "subtle variety" (*sūkṣma-bheda*) where both the expressed and the indicated are the objects of perception. Immediately after [the discussion of] the specific cause consisting of indication (*lakṣaṇā*), he defines the "subtle" (*sūkṣma*) through its similarity: An example of the indicated being the object of a gesture (*iṅgita-lakṣya*) that is implied (*pratīyamāna*): [Example omitted in source] ...is an example of the indicated being the object of a gesture that is implied.
"Addressed, she gives no reply; she grows angry with each one individually, as the noble lady stands watching along the riverbank for no reason at all. (51)
"O noble lady, [you are standing] on the riverbank which is ablaze without any apparent cause.

Here, by the statement "on the riverbank which is ablaze," the mental anguish of the woman born from the wall at the rendezvous—being made known through the reason of the retinue's provocation—is characterized as the sentence-meaning. Thus, this is the subtle variety of the suggested meaning (*pratīyamāna*) where the suggestion is based on a gesture (*iṅgitalakṣya*).
In this context, the phrase "by the taking of a reply" refers to the aforementioned.

It is not merely the absence of giving a reply that is striking here, for that could occur in other ways as well; therefore, by the phrase "non-giving of a reply," what is intended is a certain action—characterized by moving away to a nearby spot and so forth—which reveals a specific contrary state of mind underlying the intention to give a reply.

Furthermore, even anger, unless it attains the status of a perceptible form, does not reach the state of being relishable; thus, the author, intending to convey that even in that case, it is surely a physical action such as the knitting of eyebrows that is meant, has stated: "by gestures" (*iṅgitābhyām*).
If this is so, then since that [intended meaning] is already achieved through the perfection of the poetic beauty (*kāvyaśobhā*), what is the use of another [meaning] being indicated?
No; for no intended purpose is gained by the aforementioned giving of a reply or the display of anger.
The sense is that it is the *pratīyamāna* (the implied) alone which is characterized as the form, as in the following example:

‘The beauty of the face of the dark-complexioned girl, who casts sidelong glances, is enhanced as she turns her head, adorned with earrings fashioned from jambu leaves, toward the wandering young son of a farmer.
(52) ‘Because of the dark complexion of the dark-complexioned girl, the splendor of her face is revealed by her sidelong glance— ’
"While the son of the plowman wanders about with an ear-ornament made from a *jambū* leaf," [it is said].

Here, through the two physical traits of half-closed eyes and a darkened face, the distress arising from the failure of her secret tryst—communicated by the phrase "with an ear-ornament made from a *jambū* leaf"—is perceived in the case of Śyāmā. Thus, this is a subtle variety of the suggested (*pratīyamāna*) where the suggestion is based on physical appearance (*ākāra-lakṣya*).
An example of that same type where the suggestion is based on both [physical appearance and speech] is as follows:
‘When the proud woman was offered flowers by her lover, who had addressed her by the name of her rival, she said nothing; with eyes clouded by tears, she merely scratched the ground with her foot.

(53) Here, the scratching of the ground with the foot is a gesture (*iṅgita*), and the clouding of the eyes with tears is an expression (*ākāra*); through these two, the mental anguish of the proud woman arising from the slip of the name is perceived. Thus, this is the variety of *sūkṣma* (the subtle) characterized by gestures and expressions.
Since that which is being analyzed possesses a similar nature [to its constituents], he states the subsequent definition immediately after the subtle:
"That which is the essence of categories (padārtha) is here called the subsequent; it is distinct from both the property (dharma) and the substratum (dharmin) due to its difference from them. (23)
The meaning of "of the categories" (*padārthānām*) is as follows:
the genitive case is used here in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*), referring to that which constitutes the essence, which possesses excellence, and which serves as the very soul of all things.

"Uttara" is a name whose meaning corresponds to its etymology (*anvartha*): the sense of *uda* is "excellence" (*utkṛṣṭatva*), while *tarap* denotes the superlative degree (*prakarṣa*) in that very excellence;
[this applies] by way of both the property (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmī*).
Whether considered individually or collectively,
that which is perceived through its inclination toward another is a thing in which the property (dharma) is subordinate;
however, that which does not possess such [inclination] is the nature of the substrate (dharmirūpa).

This is the meaning: the subsequent [type of] determination (*nirdhāraṇa*) is the selection of one thing from among well-known objects by virtue of its excellence; that determination has three forms: the property (*dharma*), the substratum (*dharmin*), and both.

For each of the first two, two types are to be determined: the apprehension of that which is being isolated as pure, or [the apprehension] by virtue of its possessing a property distinct from that which is to be isolated. This is what he expresses by saying "and because of distinction."
Since even the last [element] possesses the nature of "form" by way of being both a universal and a particular, the response is sixfold.
Among those, the essential nature of dharma is as follows:
"Generosity from wealth, truthfulness from speech, and likewise fame and dharma from life."
“One should extract the essence from this essenceless body by means of benefiting others.

(54) Here, since giving, truthfulness, fame, and so forth are the essential qualities (*dharma*) of material things such as wealth, this extraction of them constitutes the essence that is the nature of *dharma*.
Thus, it is said: “of material things such as wealth.”

The separation [of the gift] is conveyed by the fifth case-ending, and since that is necessarily preceded by conjunction, there is the cognition of the subordinate status of the giving and so forth; for example, in the form of the substratum (dharmin):
‘The palace roof adorned with honey and blossoming white lotuses, sprouting from the rays of the moon;
and the beloved woman whose amorous grace is born of passion—these are the true riches of the wealthy; all other prosperities are [mere] others.
Here, because the essence of honey and the rest has been extracted from among the various prosperities, this is *sāra* (essence) in the form of the substratum (*dharmirūpa*).
Regarding the phrase "from the manifestations" (*vibhūtibhyaḥ*):

since the manifestations (*vibhūtayaḥ*) are mentioned in the nominative case, as before there is no appearance of them as the substratum (*dharmibhāva*). Thus, a specific form such as the road and so forth is understood as a subordinate factor (*aṅgabhāva*) of the object.
Now, as for the form of the attribute (*dharma*) by way of distinction, it is as follows:
‘Whatever is well-learned by mature women brings pleasure in lovemaking; whatever is unlearned by young brides gives rise to various forms of passion. (56)
"Whatever is unpracticed by young brides, each such thing bestows pleasure.

Here, while the sexual act is well-practiced for mature women, it is the unpracticed act that brings happiness to immature women. Thus, the attributes characterized by well-practiced and unpracticed sexual acts are presented as non-different from the attributes of the women themselves, in contrast to other attributes that define the acts. Therefore, this is the figure of speech *sāra* (the essence) in the form of "attribute-exclusion" (*dharmavyatireka*), as indicated by the phrase "of immature women."
If the relationship between the quality (dharma) and the possessor of the quality (dharmī) is expressed by the genitive case, then why is there a selection (*nirdhāraṇa*)? To this he says:

because of the general mention [of "delight"] by the word *rata* ("delighting"), a specific contrast is presented; namely, having taken as the specific attribute the "well-trained" nature of the grace belonging to mature women, the "untrained" nature belonging to innocent girls is presented as the contrasting particularity.
An example of the nature of the substratum (dharmin) by way of exclusion (vyatireka): “In the kingdom, the essence is the earth; in the earth, the city; in the city, the palace;
in the palace, the couch; on the couch, the beautiful woman—the very all-in-all of Love. (57)

In this case, the subjects (*dharmin*), such as the earth and so forth, are distinguished from each preceding one in a successive order; thus, this is the "essence" (*sāra*) consisting of the distinction of attributes (*dharmavyatireka*).
Here, in the phrase "the earth and so forth," the earth possessing cities is distinguished from the earth as determined merely as "earth."
Just as a city is like the earth, a palace is like a city, a bed is like a palace, and a beautiful woman is like a bed— thus it has been stated "in a sequence of successive stages.
By this, the nature of both the property (*dharma*) and the possessor of the property (*dharmin*) is also explained.
It is twofold: by way of generality and by way of particularity.
Therein, by way of generality, it is as follows:
"By means of song, the moon, betel, camphor, women, and so forth,
this essence-less cycle of existence (saṃsāra) appears as if it were possessed of essence.

Here, because all things such as song— which are the very essence of the world— are mentioned without distinction, and because they function as subordinate factors (aṅga) through their status as instrumental causes expressed by the third case ending, this "essence" (sāra) consists generally of both the attribute (dharma) and the substratum (dharmin).
Regarding the phrase "of the song and so forth" (*gītādīnām*) here:

since no specific distinction has been stated regarding the song and so forth, and for that very reason the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) [is used], nevertheless, the status of being an auxiliary (*aṅgabhāva*) is perceived for curd and the like; therefore, he says: "and by virtue of ending in the third case."
