For by the third [case], the status of being a *kāraka* (participant in an action) is expressed; and the meaning is that the status of being a *kāraka* consists in having the form of a subordinate element to an action.
For example, specifically:
"O best of the twice-born, I consider myself purified by two things alone."
"And by the descent of the Gaṅgā upon your head, and by the water from the feet of the Seven Sages [washing] your feet" (59).

Here, because the descent of the Gaṅgā and the water from the feet of the Seven Sages—which are specifically the essential elements—are mentioned, and because they constitute the constituent parts of the Himalaya’s purity, this is a "sāra" (essential element) consisting of both the attribute (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*).
In this context, the phrase "descent of the Gaṅgā" [is the specific attribute].

He establishes the status of being a subsidiary (*aṅga*) by specifying that the Ganges possesses both the water at its source and the water at its confluence, as well as being distinguished by the Seven Sages (*saptarṣis*). Regarding the phrase "and in the purity of the Himavat," he states the definition of contradiction (*virodha*) because there is an imposition of contradictory attributes (*viruddhadharmākrānti*) within the subsequent counter-argument (*vyatirekottara*), providing the logical connection:
"Contradiction, however, is the mutual inconsistency of things."
"Inconsistency (asaṅgati), the contrary (pratyanīka), the excessive (adhika), and the incongruous (viṣama)— these are contradictions.
(24) "Contradiction," however, refers to mutual inconsistency or lack of connection, which is to say, the impossibility of coexistence.
The concise meaning is this: the statement that two things which are necessarily incapable of coexistence cannot exist together constitutes a contradiction;
furthermore, that [contradiction] is of two kinds: the fully developed fault and the un-developed.
Through the application of *śleṣa* (paronomasia), there is a threefold transformation [of meaning].

The superimposition of necessity (*naiyatyāropa*) based merely on frequent observation of two things that cannot coexist is seen, for example, in such verses as "Where is the softness of a young woman? and so forth; or else, it is the well-known status of the subject of a statement regarding contradictory attributes as possessing an inconceivable excellence of power.
Just as in examples such as “*digvāsā yadi...*” and so forth, there is merely a cognition of contradiction through its imposition (*āropa*),
or as in “*sā uppaḍī...*” and so forth;
and all this contradiction, whether expressed (*abhidhīyamāna*) or implied (*pratīyamāna*).

Now, that which is denoted by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) is indeed being denoted, yet when it is perceived, it is devoid of that [explicit mention], as in Bhaṭṭabāṇa’s verse: “Where there are women who walk like elephants, yet are virtuous; who are fair-complexioned, yet devoted to wealth; who are dark, yet possess ruby-like [lips]; whose faces are pure with white teeth, and whose breath is fragrant with wine.
Here, other authors of alaṃkāra treatises have separately defined four figures—*asaṃgati*, *pratyanīka*, *adhika*, and *viṣama*—as distinct from *virodha*.
The tallakṣaṇas: "The occurrence of a contradictory effect by that very same cause, while [the entity] has attained a fixed state through its connection with dimensions and so forth—
that which is designated as 'lack of fixedness' (avyavasthā) is declared to be *adhika*."
"Those whose intellects are conversant with words declare that an effect which is dissimilar to its cause, as described above, and which produces wonder, is called *viṣama* (the incongruous)."

Since these [two] do not differ in their defining characteristics, they are indeed included within *virodha* (contradiction); for it is not the case that inclusion under a general category ceases merely because of a difference in intermediate modes of expression. With this intention, he says: "Inconsistency (*asaṅgati*) and the adversary (*pratyanīka*) are [types of] contradiction among those [figures]. Of these two, the first is both pure and composed; of these, the first is as follows:
‘Where is the softness of a young woman, and where the ferocity of a great battle? Where is the hand adorned with bracelets, and where the sword with its hilt made of elephant tusks?
Where is fresh youth, and where this indifference toward the flower-armed god [Kāma] in your feminine behavior? This is *lalita* (graceful charm).

Here, because there is a mutual incompatibility between the purely distinct qualities of “the softness of a young woman” and so forth, and “the ferocity of a great battle” and so forth, this is *śuddhavirōdha* (pure contradiction).
"Of pure [entities] alone"—
since contradiction is resolved by stating the non-coexistence with only a single counter-positive,
the second [example] is as follows:
“If he is naked, what need has he for a bow? What need has a weapon for ashes? And if he has ashes, why does he have a woman? If he has her, why does he hate desire?
Seeing this mutually contradictory behavior of his own master, Bhṛṅgin maintains a body reduced to mere bones, coarse and covered with a dense network of veins.

(51) In this passage, because the qualities such as nakedness and the rest are linked in a successive sequence, yet remain mutually inconsistent, this is a variety of *virodha* (contradiction) named *grathita* (the interwoven).
Regarding the phrase "due to successive stringing together" (*uttarottaragrathanāt*):

although a thing may be strung together even when mentioned alongside one contradictory element while still attaining that same state with another contradictory element as well, the intention is that it bestows a particular beauty by virtue of being strung together in successive order. An example of "inconsistency" (*asaṅgati*) is as follows:
‘That has arisen in the cow-pen as some entirely new kind of poisonous knot; he dies who does not have it stuck in his throat.
(62) [That has arisen in the cow-pen as some entirely new kind of poisonous knot...]
On the contrary, he for whom this knot of poison does not stick in the throat perishes.

Here, because there is no mutual connection between these two statements— that "this is a knot of poison" and "he for whom it does not stick in the throat perishes"— this is the contradiction known as *asaṅgati* (inconsistency),
as in the case of the term *goṭhṭhauhī*.
In the cow-pen,
there is some unprecedented [creature], some kind of poison-knot.
The feminine gender [of the word *romāñca*] is established by the rule "‘romāñcādayas triyām’" (Amarakośa 1.7.28);
moreover, its lethal nature is understood through its connection with the neck of one who has swallowed poison.
There is a manifest contradiction in describing a form as being exactly as it is; for example, as an opposing [sentiment]:
“Longing, feverish distress, restless yearning, sleeplessness, and emaciation of the body...”
"Aha! This fruit has been obtained by me for my happiness, having seen the fawn-eyed one.

(63) Here, although the sight of the fawn-eyed one is indeed said to have contentment as its fruit, I, having seen her, have instead obtained internal torment and the like; because this is a contrary fruit, this is the contradiction known as "contrary" (*pratyanīka*).

In this context, although it is not contradictory for a single thing to perform two opposing actions—as in the case of "the very sight of the deer-eyed woman"—nevertheless, one does not perform that which is opposed by the same activity with which one was intent upon performing a certain effect; this is what is illuminated by the dative case as being "for the sake of pleasure" (*sukhāya*).
An example of the "additional" (*adhika*) [type of *śleṣa*] is as follows:
‘The son of Daśaratha was alone, while the Yātudhānas were by the thousands; yet he appeared to them in battle as many as they were.

Here, regarding the act of combat between the single son of Daśaratha and the Yātudhānas who numbered in the thousands, his being seen by them as being equal in number to them conveys an excess that contradicts his singular number; thus, this is the figure of speech called *adhika* (excess), a type of contradiction (*virodha*).
An example of the uneven (viṣama) is as follows:

“The mass of sacrificial smoke, which had assumed the appearance of a false lock of hair on the quarters of the sky and served as a tamāla sprout upon the ear of the Goddess Trayī, made your already exceedingly white fame even whiter. (65)

In this case, regarding the whitening of fame by a mass of smoke from soiled sacrificial rites: since there is a well-known rule that "whatever kind of cause produces an effect, the effect must be of that same kind," there is a disparity between them; thus, because they are mutually incompatible, this is the figure of speech called *viṣama* (the Uneven).

Since the existence of the effect is established here merely through the presence of a portion of its causal complex, it possesses the character of a semblance of contradiction (*virodhacchāyā*). Therefore, immediately following that, the occasion for *saṃbhava* (Possibility) arises; hence he says: "It might be so from the light of abundant causes"—this is *saṃbhava*.
Whether in the case of affirmation, negation, both, or neither,
having observed many causes— such as "it will arise as an effect" or "it might not arise at some point due to fate"— the possibility of such knowledge arises. (25)

And this is not doubt (*saṃśaya*), for it does not waver as "it might be so" or "it might not be so"; nor is it a conceptual construction (*vitarka*), because there is an absence of the superimposition of a pervader (*vyāpyāropa*).

Where, then, is it included? Nowhere, because it is described as being a distinct type of cognition; for if it were included merely by virtue of its indeterminate nature, it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Nor is it an error (*bhrānti*), because it is preceded by a subordinated sublation (*nyagbhūtabādha*).
It will be stated that "only when error is established does sublation arise" (in the verse beginning) "Whether in an injunction or a prohibition.
The possible object, determined by its specific domain, is fourfold— consisting of injunction, prohibition, both, or neither—
and the instigation of one who has not yet acted is of two forms.

The first [type of negation], pertaining to the instigator (*prayojaka*) and the one being instigated (*prayojya*), was stated by the phrase "by way of a positive injunction" (*vidhidvāreṇa*) in the verbal ornament (*śabdālaṃkāra*) called *pratyukti*; however, the second, characterized by the occurrence of what has already happened, is here described as "negation" (*niṣedha*), which is the absence of that which is currently engaged.
By this, those of both forms and neither form are explained.
Among these, an example of the scope of affirmation (*vidhi*) is as follows:
"O thief of the color of the peacock-bannered god (Kṛṣṇa), when you bent down to take water from her, the stream of that river—though broad—appeared thin due to its distance."
"Those moving through the sky will surely cast their gaze downward and behold [the river] like a single string of pearls from the earth, with a large sapphire at its center.

(66) Here, when you have bent down to take water, the current of that river—with a sapphire situated in its midst—will become visible to those traveling in the sky as if it were a string of pearls; because this is a possibility being conceived regarding a future action, this is a *saṃbhava* (possibility) concerning a future event (*vidhi*). [The phrase "here, when you... refers to the present situation.
The positive injunction (*vidhi*) consists in making that which is not worth seeing appear worthy of being seen;
an example of the scope of a prohibition (*niṣedha*) is as follows:
"Excessive exertion in seeking the vulnerabilities of another, while forcibly guarding one's own weak points..."

"Even in Bhīṣma or in the Preceptor (Droṇa), this is not conceivable; it is simply impossible among forest-dwellers. Here, the "possibility" (*saṃbhava*) which is the object of negation is the skill in the science of archery—unconceivable in Bhīṣma and Droṇa—which is said to be impossible in this forest-dweller, as expressed by the phrase "in this forest-dweller."
Because there is the perception of many reasons for guarding one's own weak points when attacking the weak points of others, the negation "this is not a forest-dweller" is what is actually possible;
this is an instance of the scope of affirmation and negation, as in:
"O friend, though you wish to go quickly for the sake of my beloved, I foresee that you will experience delay on every mountain fragrant with *kakubha* flowers."
"Having welcomed you with cries of joy (*kekā*) from eyes moist with tears and glances cast from the corners, you have been met; therefore, you should somehow resolve to depart quickly.

(68) In this case, [the statement] "I perceive a delay for you even though you desire to go swiftly" takes the form of an injunction (*vidhi*), while "you should somehow resolve not to depart quickly" takes the form of a prohibition (*niṣedha*). Thus, because both the injunction and the prohibition are impossible [to be taken literally], this is a "possibility" (*saṃbhava*) pertaining to both.
"I perceive a delay on your part"—
I perceive, that is, I consider,
that for one who is not subject to delay, the occurrence of delay is a violation of the proper rule.
The phrase "somehow" (kathamapi), established through a suggestive intonation (kākūpasthita), indicates the negation of going;
nor should it be said that there are two possibilities here, such that not even one would apply to both objects.

Since the very same collection of conditions that causes a delay in time, when conjoined with auxiliary causes such as "those with white outer corners [of the eyes]," etc., also takes negation as its object,
therefore, due to the difference in possibility, there is a certain means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) whose object is neither [the positive nor the negative]. For example:

“If you, hanging from the upper half of the sky like a celestial elephant, were to gaze askance at her water as clear as pure crystal while she glides through the assembly hall, she would become beautiful through a union with the Yamunā reached out of place, reflected in your stream.
Here, since there is no comprehension of either an injunction or a prohibition— namely, “if you were to do this, then it would be so”— this is a *saṃbhava* (possibility) that pertains to neither.
In this case, since the non-existence [of the action] is not perceived in the sense that "if you were to do it thus," negation is not possible;
nor is affirmation possible.

For when the occurrence of a specific entity is established through the observation of a fixed cause, that is designated by the term "positive possibility" (*vidhisambhava*); however, it is not so here, as it has been stated: "because of non-comprehension.
By this, the case of alternatives (*vikalpa*) regarding both affirmation and negation is also explained.
For example:

"O lotus-faced one, even if there were a thousand mouths capable of eloquent speech, incomparable attentiveness, and an exceedingly long life, would it still be possible to perform a full investigation of all the virtues of that king? (70)
This has been explained by the very word *nigadenaiva*;
the meaning is that there is an option (*vikalpa*) regarding the individual, because two things that are mutually exclusive are both possible in a single instance.
Having set forth the definition of origination according to the former [view], he refutes it:
"Just as the production of a *droṇa* from a *khārī* is like that of fifty from a hundred, others have described origination in such a way; this does not differ from inference. (26)
However, if there were uncertainty, [the cognition] would be split; thus,
the view of the Easterners is that from the cognition of the whole (the aggregate), the cognition of a part arises.
And thus, because a collection is pervaded by its constituents, the inference—"This khārī contains a droṇa, because it is a khārī"—is easily established;
the meaning is that its inclusion is within inference itself.

[Objection: "In that case, how is your 'possibility' (sambhava) distinct? Since the causal totality (sāmagrī) is pervaded by the effect, there too it will simply be inference. To this he says: "It is distinct."

For the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is not perceived from which the effect could be inferred; rather, it must be said that through the perception of numerous causes, a distinct cognition of the effect arises. Thus, the separate existence [of the cause and effect] is logical in our view.
To instruct one who does not connect the specific instance [with the general rule], he states another example:
For example:

"With the movement of its outer corners obstructed by tears, devoid of the luster of collyrium, and having forgotten the play of its eyebrows due to the rejection of even honey-wine—when you draw near, I suspect the eye of that deer-eyed woman, twitching upward, will attain the beauty of a blue lotus agitated by the disturbance of fish. (71)

In this regard, just as there is a fixed rule that one *droṇa* is contained in a *khārī* or fifty in a hundred, such a rule does not apply here. For in the case of *vipralambha* (love-in-separation), there is no necessity for the presence of *alakās* (curls of hair), nor is there a prohibition against collyrium for the eyes or honey; nor do the throbbing of the eyes necessarily occur at the start of receiving news from a friend. Furthermore, these things are possible because they are observed in the world through many causes. Thus, this *saṃbhava* (possibility) is also of a positive nature (*vidhirūpa*).
In the verse beginning with "ruddhāpāṅga" and so forth, it is shown how she, emaciated by the pain of separation, appears to have produced compassion even in the insentient *alakās*.
Therefore, lest she should suddenly behold the cloud, they restrain the movement of her naturally fickle sidelong glances;
by this act of affectionately applying collyrium to her eyes, an unblemished bond is revealed, which manifests their mutual fitness for friendship.

It suggests that because the collyrium does not attain its beauty when applied elsewhere than to her eyes, there is a certain excellence of loveliness such that even when the collyrium is removed, she is unable—even with single-minded focus—to perceive herself. In this way, the natural inclination (*svarasa*) should be inferred in other instances of excellence as well. Furthermore, he clarifies through the following commentary that two possibilities exist here, based on the observation of the cause in the form of separation (*vipralambha*): "the trembling of the eyes is expected," as in the example: "Just as in the case of the *khārī*... (etc.).

Since one can perceive the specific quality of one among two things that mutually assist each other, and thereby know the specific quality of the other, the author states the definition of mutual relation immediately following [the section on] "possibility" (saṃbhava), due to their similarity:
"That which is a mutual assistance is 'mutual' (anyonya). It is threefold:
it may be expressed (vācya), it may be implied (pratīyamāna), and thirdly, it may consist of both. (27)
Mutual crowning, mutual delusion, and mutual unity—
these three are intended here as the internal ornaments of mutual [beauty].
(28) "Mutually" means...

The "bestowal of excellence" (*viśeṣārpaṇa*) constitutes the benefit (*upakāra*), yet this is not a case of exchange (*parivṛtti*), because there is no removal of what is already present and no giving back of what was received.

However, the excellence—which is manifold in form—is inferred in various instances through its conformity with the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) that constitutes the meaning of those respective sentences;
he demonstrates this division as being threefold.

That which is being denoted is twofold in nature: it is grasped by the word in a general sense and made an object of the word in a general sense, yet it is perceived specifically; thus it possesses both aspects.
The author himself will clarify how it is not perceived as anything other than these two, through the characteristics of the various *cūlikās* and so forth.

Among these, as it is stated here regarding one another: “Between his neck, which was beautiful with its breasts, and his flat necklace of pearls, there arose a mutual relationship of the ornamented and the ornament, through the production of reciprocal beauty. (72)

Since the relationship of mutual benefit between the two has been stated here by the phrase "producing mutual beauty" and so forth, this [beauty] is expressed as being mutual; thus, "the neck... is elegant and graceful.
It is perceived as flat or circular,
as for example: "The traveler drinks water with his fingers spread wide for a long time, raising them higher and higher."
‘The traveler, with his fingers spread apart, drinks the water for as long as he can; and the girl at the water-station likewise makes the stream, though already thin, even thinner. (73)

In this passage, regarding the mutual passion between the traveler and the woman at the water-stall, the fact that one drinks water with a hand whose fingers are spread apart while the other excessively thins the stream of water— through this mutual relationship of benefactor and beneficiary, this "mutuality" (anyonya) is implied.

Here, by the phrases "the traveler" and "mutual passion," the intended view is that the specific contribution (*viśeṣārpaṇa*) in this context consists precisely in the intensification of their reciprocal affection.
For instance, when the hand is made with fingers spread apart, the very intention of the water-drawer woman—“How might I behold her for a long time?”—is further enhanced;
this should be understood to apply likewise to the thinning of the stream of water.

Moreover, since such a meaning is not expressed by any word at all, it possesses the status of being "suggested" (pratīyamānatā); it emerges as a suggestion (dhvanana) precisely through the consideration of specific factors such as the speaker and the person addressed.
An example of that which is both implied and explicitly stated is as follows:
“Under the pretext of being joined with the Godāvarī, he placed himself upon her breast;
by him also, she was firmly embraced, free from the reproach of pity. (74)
"Under the pretext of descending into the uneven waters of the Godāvarī, she cast herself upon his chest;
he too, out of compassion, embraced her firmly and without reproach.

Here, by stating that she threw herself upon his chest under the guise of stepping into the treacherous waters of the Godāvarī, and that he, out of pity, embraced her closely and faultlessly, a mutual relationship of benefactor and beneficiary arising from reciprocal passion is perceived; thus, this is "mutual" (*anyonya*) in its dual nature.

Here, although the mutual assistance between the two is already suggested as before by the word "Godāvarī," it is touched upon through direct denotation (*abhidhā*) by means of the words "compassion" (*anukampā*) and "faultless" (*nirdoṣa*); thus, it possesses both forms [of suggestion].
Nor should it be argued: "What is the use of suggestion (*dhvani*) for that which is already conveyed by the words?"
Because their objects are distinct, they are mutually subordinate, as for example:
"The night by means of the moon, and the moon by means of the night; and by means of the moon and the night, the sky."

"And by you, the assembly is possessed of fear; and by the assembly, you are possessed of fear; and likewise by you, the world [is possessed of fear]. (75) Here, while the night and the moon, as well as the assembly and the lord, stand in a relationship of mutual benefit, this sky and this earth—which are already well-known—are obtained one above the other like crowns (*cūḍikā*) that provide such benefit; this is "mutual crowning" (*anyonyacūḍikā*), as exemplified here by the night and the moon.

Just as a crest or tuft of hair is perceived as distinct from the body and its limbs, so too here, having intended the mutual assistance between the night and the moon within the assembly hall, a further reciprocal assistance between the two pairs— the sky and the earth— is described as something entirely different. And it is not by this much distinction alone that there is a state of separateness, because such [separateness] is possible only when [the elements] have been swallowed up by the figure of *anyonyālaṃkāra* (mutual ornamentation).
An example of mutual delusion is as follows:
“The parrots, having begun a festival of drinking the fresh honey amidst a heap of *jambu* blossoms, peck at and release the female bees, mistaking them for ripe fruit;
likewise, the female bees suddenly fly toward the beaks of these very parrots, which possess a luster similar to the petals of the blue *kiṃśuka*, due to their own confusion regarding flowers. (76)

Here, the delusion of parrot-birds regarding female bees situated in a grove of *jambu* flowers as being ripe *jambu* fruits, and the delusion of the female bees regarding the parrots' beaks as being *kiṃśuka* flowers— this is a mutual delusion (*anyonyabhrama*) that is indeed non-different from each other.

In this context, the phrase "grove of *jambu* flowers" [is used] because a delusion does not possess the status of an ornament (alaṃkāra) merely by virtue of being a delusion, such as the perception of hair by one suffering from ophthalmia (*taimirika*), but only when it is rooted in a real similarity (*tadbhūtasādṛśya*).

And thus, since it culminates in a comparison with another striking object, the very connection of the illusion (*bhrānti-saṃsarga*) is the service rendered by the bestowal of distinction; and since its mutual reciprocity has been shown by that very expression "mutual" (*anyonya*), how could it be distinct from the definition of *anyonyālaṅkāra* (reciprocal ornament) due to its connection with it?
By this, the identity of *anyonya* [with *anyonyālaṅkāra*] is explained.
The state of mutual identity is as follows:

“With their pure complexions mutually smeared by the auspicious rays of the sun, which resembled blossoming *tāpiccha* flowers, and by the dust of the *saptacchada* tree, white as powder, those two became as if they were of one single color. (77)

Here, because the dark and pale colors are made into a single color through their mutual exclusion, there is a variety of illusion called "mutual identity" (*anyonyaikatā*), which is indeed distinct from "mutual [identity]"; now, by virtue of the similarity in being defined by one another, he describes the figure of speech "Exchange" (*parivṛtti*) which follows in order: "That which is the transposition of things, or that which is a mutual barter."
This is called *parivṛtti* (exchange) in the definition of poetic ornaments (*kāvyālaṃkāra*).
The term "reversal" (*vyatyaya*) is a statement regarding the inversion of the state of affairs; thus, "exchange" (*parivṛtti*) is indeed its clear definition.

That [exchange] is described by the masters of poetry as being threefold: that which possesses transposition (*vyatyayavatī*), that which consists of a reciprocal exchange (*vinimayātmikā*), and the third, which possesses both characteristics (*ubhayavatī*).
It is threefold: by means of stating the arrival of an object situated in one place at another location, by means of stating a giving and a counter-giving, or by means of stating both.

Thus he says: "It is threefold"—this shows that in every case there is a sixfold nature, as such a state of being is expressed either through primary function (*mukhyavṛtti*) or by resorting to secondary function (*gauṇavṛtti*).
Furthermore, even this threefold [state] becomes twofold through the distinction between primary and secondary, and thus results in six modes.
Among these, the primary type is that characterized by transposition, as for example:

“The lily grove has lost its splendor; the glorious cluster of lotuses is abandoned; the owl is devoid of joy while the cakravāka bird is full of delight; the sun rises and the moon sets. Alas! How strange is the ripening of the playful workings of fate! (78)

In this context, that which is primarily perceived in the morning— the lack of splendor and so forth in the groves of night-lotuses (*kumuda*), and the possession of splendor and so forth in the clusters of day-lotuses (*ambhoja*)— is this "reversal" (*parivṛtti*) known as "primary" (*mukhyā*),
which is threefold; thus,
[the example] begins with "the grove of night-lotuses."

From the lily grove, the owl; from the moon, beauty; from the lotus cluster, the female ruddy goose; and from the female ruddy goose, joy; and from the moon, rising—all these have departed and reached one another. Thus, a clear transposition (*vyatyaya*) occurs. Primacy (*mukhyatva*) is evident in the very text itself.
An example of that which possesses transposition but is not primary (*amukhya*) is as follows:
‘That very redness of her lower lip which was extinguished by her beloved during the night is now seen at dawn, having transferred itself into the eyes of her rival wives. (79)

That very [lip-stain] is seen in the morning, transferred to the eyes of her co-wives. Here, this transfer of the lip-stain— which was removed by the beloved during the night— to the eyes of the co-wives occurs because of the beloved.

The redness of the lower lip caused by betel and such is one thing, while the bitterness characterized by a reddish-brown hue reaching the eyes caused by jealousy is another; yet, the identification of these two as non-different is what is understood through those two words. Thus, the secondary (gauṇī) function of the word manifests, and the attainment of the eyes by that which resides in the place of the lower lip is evident through the verbal operation itself; by this much alone, the completion of the figure of speech is achieved.
An example of the primary function involving exchange is as follows:

"Playing in the waters of the river, which were fragrant with trickling ichor, the lordly elephants emerged with their cheeks— scented like lotuses and marked by streaks of copper-red hue veiled by filaments.

(80) In this verse, there is a primary form of *parivṛtti* (exchange) called *mukhyā* (primary), wherein the fragrance of the ichor on the elephants' cheeks and the scent of the pollen of the lotuses act as mutual auxiliaries to one another through the medium of the river water and the elephants' cheeks respectively.

In this context, "the transfer of the frontal globes (*karika-pola*) of lordly elephants"— referring to the ichor and the moon-like spots on their temples— to rivers where they have taken refuge, and the taking up by those situated in the rivers of the filaments and the fragrance of the lotuses, constitutes an exchange characterized by giving and receiving in return.
An example of exchange (*vinimaya*) as a secondary figure of speech (*amukhya*) is as follows:
"And why is that aged Jaṭāyu, who has now ascended to heaven, to be lamented here?
For by the sacrifice of his worn-out body, he purchased a fame as radiant as the rays of the moon.

(81) In this case, because it is stated through the non-primary mode (*amukhyā vṛtti*) of exchange—that fame white as the moon's rays was purchased by giving up a worn-out body—this is a "substitution involving exchange" (*vinimayavatī parivṛtti*) by way of non-primary function.

In this case, since there is an evident contradiction regarding the offering and purchasing of the price in the word *jarjarā*, there is clearly a metaphorical usage (*upacāra*); however, as before, the primary function of the word (*śabdavṛtti*) remains blunt, and thus it constitutes a "double-meaning" (*ubhayavatī*) primary [metaphor]. For example:

‘The wine, having taken away the passion from the lower lip and placed it in the eyes, and having perfumed the mouth with its own special fragrance, brought about both the transposition and the exchange of the qualities of the other and of itself.

(82) Here, because the wine removed the redness from the lower lip and deposited it in the two eyes, it is *vyatyayavatī* (possessing transposition); and because the fragrance of the mouth was distinguished by its own scent through the perfuming of the mouth, it is *vinimayavatī* (possessing exchange).
Thus, since this has been stated in both ways through its primary sense (*mukhyavṛtti*), this is a "primary exchange possessing both" (*mukhyobhayavatī parivṛtti*).

In the phrase *locanādhare*, because the redness (*rāga*) has been transferred to the eyes and taken away from the lips respectively, there is a transposition (*vyatyaya*) such that what was on the eyes is now on the lips, and what was removed from the lips [is elsewhere].
She whose specific fragrance was infused into her mouth by him,
and by whom his mouth was likewise perfumed; thus there occurs an exchange of one's own qualities for the qualities of another.

Regarding "of others' virtues," the connection is that there is an exchange of others' virtues and a barter of one's own virtues; agency is thus poetically imagined (utprekṣita). He demonstrates this with the word "here" (atra), as in the following secondary example involving both [the giver and the receiver]: [Example: *paraguṇān svaguṇīkaroti yaḥ svaguṇāṃs tyajati ca pareṣu yaḥ | sa eva dhanyaḥ sa ca pūjyate janaiḥ śeṣāstu bhāravahatāṃ bhajante ||* "He who makes others' virtues his own virtues, and he who casts off his own virtues upon others—he alone is fortunate and is honored by people; the rest merely endure the burden. In this case, the agency is figurative (amukhyā) because it pertains to both parties.
"What is the point of tribute if the kings have been made tributary by Your Majesty? Has Your Majesty not also been made to pay tribute by them in turn, from behind? (83)

In this context, the giving of tribute by kings who pay taxes, and the placing of a hand upon the back of one who desires victory—this very thing constitutes a "exchange" (*parivṛtti*) in the case of the transposition of substances, qualities, and so forth, based on their respective positions. Furthermore, that the King made the kings his tributaries, and that the King was likewise made to place his hand on their backs by them—this is an exchange characterized by the act of giving and receiving. Since both of these are expressed here through words with double meanings (*śliṣṭapada*), they are perceived as being stated only in a non-primary sense; thus, this is a "non-primary exchange" (*amukhyā parivṛttiḥ*) possessing both characteristics.

When that which is perceived in one place is understood in another through a transposition, it is likewise in the case of the *nidarśana*. Therefore, immediately following that, he defines the *nidarśana*:
"The *dṛṣṭānta* (exemplification) is stated for the sake of establishing [the point]; that which [occurs] when the matter is already established is the *nidarśana*.
When there is equality between the preceding and the succeeding, it is called *ṛju* (straight) and *vakra* (crooked). (31)
"Example" (dṛṣṭānta) is defined as the establishment—that is, the ascertainment—of that which is under discussion and has been previously mentioned.

Now, one might object: "Should not the statement of an example, even when it serves as a member of an inference, be a separate figure of speech? To this, he says: "When the matter is already established."

The distinction is as follows: when the matter is already established, the statement of an example (*nidarśana*) is made to communicate some specific detail; however, when the matter is yet to be proven, it is an inference (*anumāna*).
First, there is the case where the statement of the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*) is completed first, followed by the statement of the example;
second, there is the case where both the example and the subject of the illustration are conveyed by a single statement; and third, [the case where they are presented sequentially].

Regarding this, he says: "In the case of equality between the prior and the subsequent"—where the similarity of the historical events (*itivṛttatā*) of the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) and the object of comparison (*dārṣṭāntika*) is understood through the words alone, that is *ṛju-nidarśana* (straightforward illustration);
but where, once the statement has reached its conclusion, it is [understood] through the deliberation of a sensitive reader (*sahṛdaya*), that is *vakra* (crooked).
This is what he says: "Straight and crooked"—by this, there are six varieties of illustration; among them, first, the straight, as follows:

"‘As soon as he rises, the sun bestows beauty upon the lotuses; [likewise], the favor of a friend manifests the fruit of prosperity. Here, by means of a straightforward statement, the illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*) is presented first and the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*) afterwards. Thus, this is an illustration preceded by a straightforward statement (*ṛjupūrva-nidarśana*), which, through the example of the sun, makes known that the fruit of prosperities is the favor of a friend."

By means of the analogy of the sun, it is established that [the Buddha] favors his friends through supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*); however, the presentation of the solar analogy is intended to state a specific distinction, namely that this very [favoring] is the fruit of those powers.

Here, the fact that the fruit of prosperity consists of friendship and the quality of favoring is understood from the words themselves within the sun and so forth, which are accepted as the analogies (*dṛṣṭānta*) and the subjects of the analogy (*dārṣṭāntika*). This is the meaning of "straightforwardness" (*ṛjutva*).

Thus, an example of the crooked [vakram] is as follows: “Even if the fire in his hand has been extinguished, the sacrificial fire still burns; therefore, men who are situated in precarious conditions must not be shunned. (85)
"Even after setting fire to the liquor shop, the fire blazes; it does not spare even the sacrificial ground—indeed, you must not abandon men who are situated in adverse circumstances.
Here too, the simile comes first, followed by the subject of comparison.

However, whereas in the previous example the similarity of events—namely, that "the rising sun bestows beauty upon his friend, the lotuses"—is expressed directly by the word itself through straightforward statement (*ṛjuktyā*), it is not so here. Rather, the similarity with the event of "flaming" is understood through the cleverness of reasoning (*yukticāturyāt*) as being the event of those [lotuses] who are servants (*tatpuruṣāṇām*), even though it is not expressed by words (*aśābdam*). This and the preceding case are examples of *vakrokti* (oblique expression).
Furthermore, in the word *pāṇauḍī*, the term *pāṇa* is a regional dialect form (*mlecchadeśīya*).
Regarding "a hut for drinking" or "a tavern," here too— in this illustrative example— the qualifying attributes such as the burning of the drinking-hut and so forth have been employed.

And that [literal meaning] is neither possible in the context of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*) nor is it conveyed by the word; rather, it occurs here according to the analogy of the original object and its reflection (*bimbapratibimba*).

For instance, just as there is the blazing of fire in a tavern (*pānakuṭī*) and likewise in a sacrificial enclosure (*yajñavāṭa*), so too, one who—due to an unsettled mind—having become attached to an unrefined village girl, subsequently becomes enamored with sophisticated city women, is told: "Even she should not be abandoned. Through this cleverness of expression, a similarity of events (*tulyetivṛttatā*) is understood; therefore, he says it is "curvature" (*vakratva*)—namely, "but just as," which is the straightforward answer.
“O traveler, in the heart of her who has cast a sidelong glance,
met face-to-face, and then turned her gaze away, there is now only a single cowrie-shell remaining, as it were, at the crossroads. (83)
"Indeed, for a traveler at a crossroads, there is but one [path] that is more difficult.

Here, by means of a straightforward statement, the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*)—which possesses a similarity expressed through words—is first stated, and subsequently the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is presented; therefore, this is "straightforward subsequent illustration" (*uttara-ṛju-nidarśana*). Thus it is said.

That woman who was desired by the traveler as he passed by is the one alone who has become fixed in his heart; thus she remains clinging to him. For this reason, she acts like a transverse thorn (*tiracchīyai*), piercing him from the side because he has turned away from her face; furthermore, she has caught his sidelong glance, for he has been struck with wonder as he took her glance from behind.
The word *ekkejjā* means "only one" (*ekaiva*), with the particle *ṇam* used for emphasis.

Indeed, among four [directions], one assumes the state of being facing forward, another the state of being transverse, and another the state of being behind; but for the traveler, the Gaurī alone is thus.

Here, by the "straightforward" (*ṛjūkti*) manner, it is "by the word alone" (*śabdata eva*), because animals and so forth—which belong to both [categories]—are apprehended through the mere perception of their inclusion by the word; thus, the sustenance of the figure of speech is achieved.
An example of that same [figure] in the "crooked" (*vakra*) manner is as follows:
"Above, a dense mass of clouds; far away, my beloved—what has befallen me?
On the Himalayas are divine herbs, and upon his head is a serpent overcome with rage.

(7.87) Here too, having first stated the subject of comparison (*dārṣṭāntika*), the illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*) is provided only afterwards; thus, this is "Direct Illustration" (*ṛju-nidarśanā*). However, whereas in the previous example [the verse on] the heart, the similarity was expressed directly through words such as *tiryak* and so forth, it is not so here. Rather, through the artfulness of the expression "What has befallen me? and by means of inversion, there is a correspondence of gender, number, and sequence (*liṅga-saṃkhyā-yathāsaṃkhya*).
This very example is both superior and crooked;
however, it is "crooked" by means of the skillful phrasing, "But what has happened here?

For, one might object: since the word "above" (upari) conveys a sense of separation, and in the illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*) it is the word itself that reflects back, how can there be crookedness? To this he says: "by way of reversal" (*viparyayeṇa*).

The term *ghanapaṭalam* (mass of clouds) is neuter, while *phaṇī* (serpent) is masculine; *dayitā* (beloved wife) takes the singular number, whereas *oṣadhayaḥ* (medicinal herbs) takes the plural. Having first introduced the *ghanapaṭalam* as the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*), the serpent (*phaṇī*) is not mentioned first when stating the illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*). Consequently, there is a reversal of gender and number, whereby both the semantic meaning and the verbal expression convey a sense of distance between the two illustrations; this is because they are perceived in a different form by means of the words *śirasi* and *himavati*.
But since the resulting meaning is indeed the same, it is merely a matter of indirectness; this is equal to the direct form, as for example:
“The mass of darkness, touched by the moonbeams, goes to its destruction.”
"Immediately showing the miserable end of those who oppose the king" (verse 88).

Here, because the word *rājaviruddhānām* ("those who oppose the king") is a pun (*śliṣṭapada*), because the verb *darśayantī* ("showing") indicates the present tense, and because the particle *sadyaḥ* ("immediately") is a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) and the subject of the example (*dārṣṭāntika*) are stated verbally in a straightforward manner at one and the same time; thus, this is a simile (*nidarśana*) that is both "straightforward" (*ṛju*) and "balanced" (*sama*).
The word *rājā* (king) applies to both the moon and the monarch; because it functions as a pun (*śliṣṭokti*), their sequential relationship is not clearly perceived.

By using the suffix *-śatṛ* in the words *candrāṃśuparābhūtadhvāntarājī* (the mass of darkness overcome by the moon’s rays) and *nṛpativiruddhadurantayoḥ* (of those who are difficult to endure for the king’s enemies), and by using the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) *sadyaḥ* (immediately), [the poet] demonstrates the equality between the two.

However, when the statement of the example—"the mass of darkness goes to its destruction"—has been made, and the corresponding instance (*dārṣṭāntika*) "those who are enemies of the king" has been stated in between, it is said that they [the poets] again demonstrate a qualification of the example.

Therefore, with the intention that the equality of the example and the instance arises because they are both swallowed up by the statement, he explains: here, "of those who are enemies of the king"—that very same [instance] is indirect (*vakram*), as follows:
"But, daughter, even among men who possess excellent bows, such a twanging sound does not arise in one who is likewise devoid of virtue, even if he is born of a noble lineage. (89)
"Even for one born of a noble lineage (*vaṃśa*), if devoid of merit (*guṇa*), there arises only a clanging sound (*ṭaṅkāra*).

Here, it is not only in the case of the staff of a bow that this is so, but it is exactly the same even for a human being; thus, by expressing both simultaneously through a form of *vakratā* (poetic curvature) as if they were coordinate members of a compound, and by means of the word-play (*śliṣṭapadatva*) and the function of secondary meaning (*guṇavṛtti*) via the method of contrast (*vyatireka*), one understands the similarity (*sādharmya*) through this indirect expression (*vakrokti*) that, just as with a bow, only in a human being who possesses merit does a great sound arise. This is an illustration (*nidarśana*) that differs from the previous one due to its lack of explicit verbal statement (*aśabdatva*) and other features, being both similar and curved.

However, the word *guṇa* does not denote both "virtue" and "the string of a lute"; *vaṃśa* does not denote both "lineage" and "bamboo"; and *ṭaṅkāra* does not denote both "an indistinct imitation of sound" and "fame," as these do not function through mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*).

To explain: in the example "Your face and the lotus are both blooming" (*tvanmukhaṃ puṇḍarīkaṃ ca phulle*), the word *phulle* (blooming) is connected to both [the face and the lotus] by means of a single expression through the rule of *itaretarayoga* (mutual conjunction) and *ekaśeṣa* (single remainder). Similarly, even without *ekaśeṣa*, in the phrase *guṇavajjieṇa vaṃsuppaṇṇe ṭaṅkāra* ("a sharp sound produced from a bamboo rich in qualities"), the two [words] are connected simultaneously. Now, one might object: "Just as in the case of 'those who are enemies of the king,' where straightness is implied by the remainder (*śeṣa*), so too will it be here. To this, he replies: "Even though the words are *śliṣṭa* (double-meaning/pun-based)."

The intended meaning is that even in the case of a human being, a great sound arises as if from a bow; yet this meaning is not understood from the word through the method of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) in the application (*upanaya*). Since the meaning is nevertheless perceived, it is appropriate to call this "curvature" (*vakratva*). Now, one might ask: why is similarity of function (*tulyavṛttitā*) not accepted precisely through negative concomitance? To this he says: "And by means of figurative function (*guṇavṛtti*)."
This is true; nevertheless, one must state that there is an identification (adhyavasāya) between the two subjects of description based on their common qualities and so forth.
Likewise, it is precisely by resorting to figurative function (gauṇavṛtti) that there is "curvature" (vakratva).
This very point has been stated by way of contrast as: "and by means of figurative function."
Since the relationship between the exemplum (*dṛṣṭānta*) and the subject of comparison (*dārṣṭāntika*) cannot exist without contrast (*vyatireka*), he states its definition by means of that contrast:

"When the similarity between two things is either expressed through words or understood [implicitly], the statement of their difference and the difference itself are called *vyatireka* (contrast). (32)
The phrase "expressed by the word" (*śabdopātta*) is a statement of distinction intended precisely to state a difference in nature.

If this were the case, then the expression of similarity even between Mount Meru and a mustard seed would constitute an *alaṃkāra*; therefore, it is said: "when there is similarity between two things" (*sādṛśye vastunoḥ*).
The meaning is "of the standard of comparison and the object of comparison";
similarity is twofold: that expressed by words and that which is understood [through implication].

Even though it is not explicitly conveyed by words, it is understood through suggestion (*dhvani*), inference (*anumāna*), and so forth; thus there is no contradiction. This is what was stated: "Or [it is understood] upon being perceived.

The meaning of this is as follows: *vyatireka* (contrast) is the expression of the lack of aesthetic charm (*vairasya*) between two things that possess manifest charm and similarity; however, it has been stated that there is no separate category called "essential nature" (*svarūpa*).
He demonstrates the classification:
Through the limiting adjuncts of its own genus and individuality, it is divided into one and both;
and through similarity and dissimilarity, it arises as sixfold, being distinct in each case.
(33) "Through its own genus," etc.

The first variety of "exclusion of its own class" (*svajātivyatireka*) is as follows: having conceptually constructed a counter-correlative of exclusion (*vyatireka-pratiyogin*) possessing that specific form by which the exclusion is apprehended, one then establishes the exclusion from that [counter-correlative].
The second variety, however, is that very same individual being "dissimilar" (*vidharma*).

These two varieties correspond respectively to the "similarity" (*sādṛśya*) and "likeness" (*sadṛśya*) being expressed. Just as this constitutes the primary twofold division, there is likewise another twofold division characterized by "oneness" and "manyness. Within that same context, there is another pair consisting of "similarity" (*sādṛśya*) and "dissimilarity" (*vaisādṛśya*). Thus, a sixfold division is intended in this sequence.
Furthermore, it will be explained later on how it is impossible for the perceived or expressed similarity to extend to the exclusion of one's own class (*svajātivyatireka*);
therein, regarding the similarity conveyed by the word, the exclusion of one's own class is as follows:
"That which cannot be removed even by the light of jewels, yet cannot be dispelled by the rays of the sun..."
"The darkness born of youth, which obstructs the vision of the young.

(90) Here, having stated the similarity between the "darkness born of youth" and the genus "darkness" by means of the phrase "which obstructs vision," the contrast (*vyatireka*) is established through the attributes "not removable by the light of gems" and "unobstructable by the rays of the sun. This is "contrast with its own genus" (*svajātivyatireka*), as indicated here by the words "born of youth."

The darkness characterized by the ignorance produced by youth is one thing, while the form of physical gloom is another; this very attainment of their respective states is what we have called "imagination" (*kalpanā*).
By this method, the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) flourishes, and thus it is counted among the figures of speech (*alaṅkāra*).
An example of the distinction from its own manifestation when there is an implied similarity is as follows:
‘By hundreds of mutual good deeds performed day after day, their pride increases; yet neither for me nor for you is it equal to that of the Self. (91)
"Indeed, even for him, there is no one equal to himself, even though he be great.

Here, because the similarity with the implied object of comparison (*upamāna*) is treated as a figurative distinction, a difference from his own manifestation (*svavyakti*) is expressed through various other hundreds of good deeds;
this is what is meant by "distinction from his own manifestation."

When two things, which are presented as having distinct bases through imagined differences and are perceived from the word as possessing contradictory attributes, are understood to have qualities such as unrestrainedness (*niryantraṇatva*) and so forth, a similarity (*sādṛśya*) becomes manifest. An example of this, where the similarity is expressed by the word and there is a single negative concomitance (*ekavyatireka*), is as follows: *anyonyair mānaḥ...* [The pride or honor of each other... [In this case, the similarity is directly stated, and the comparison is established through a single point of exclusion.]
"Your bull is indeed ever dear to you, your prosperity is also firm, and the hand of Durgā, the daughter of the mountain, has been properly grasped by you as well.
By this much, you do not allow people to speak of your supreme lordship without artifice, since you are clearly dejected when the ocean was churned up in sport.

In this verse, between the standard of comparison (upamāna) and the object of comparison (upameya)—both of whom possess stated similarities such as having a "dear bull" and so forth—it is more appropriate for the object of comparison alone to feel dejection regarding the aforementioned similarity; thus, this is a case of *ekavyatireka* (the single-sided contrast).
The bull is indeed the beloved;
it is the bull, dharma, prosperity, wealth, and the sacred ash.
Durgā, Gaurī, Viṣamā, Bhūdharabhūḥ, Girijā, Parvatabhūmi,
Kara, Hasta, and Rājadaṇḍa.
The ocean is the lord of rivers (vāhinīśa), and the commander-in-chief is one who is dejected (viṣādī) and a consumer of poison (viṣabhakṣaka);
although there is no corresponding similarity here, nevertheless, a simile does indeed proceed even through similarity of sound.
For example: "This city has now become possessed of a stain, like the orb of the moon.
For this very reason, simile possesses the nature of being both a figure of speech (śabdālaṃkāra) and a figure of meaning (arthālaṃkāra).
That same [simile] where similarity is implied (*pratīyamāna*) is as follows:
"‘What kind of similarity can there be between you, a mine of virtues, and the moon, which is both stained and dull?

O one who is not a libertine (abhujaṅga), how can you, whose eyes are even, be compared to Śiva? Here, in the first half-verse, the quality of being stained and so forth—which belongs to the moon as the standard of comparison—is stated in the second half-verse as a distinguishing attribute of the subject of description (the upameya) itself, namely its not being a libertine (abhujaṅgatva) and so on; this too is indeed a single *vyatireka* (contrast)."
By "sakalaṅkena" (with stain):
*kalaṅka* means both censure and a physical mark;
*jaḍa* means both a fool and something cold.

He is not a lover of unchaste women (*abhujaṅgaḥ*), yet he is not one whose wife is a courtesan; he is without snakes (*avidyamānasarpaḥ*), yet he possesses two eyes (*yuganayanaḥ*); and because he leads all equally (*sarvān samaṃ nayati*), his similarity to the moon is perceived through qualities such as being delightful, while his similarity to the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*) is perceived through the possession of unobstructed sovereignty (*aniruddhaiśvarya*).
When similarity is expressed by the word itself, there is *ubhayavyatireka* (double contrast), as in:
“The ocean and you both have unchanging shores and are deep; yet he is like black collyrium, while you possess the luster of gold. (94)

In this case, there is a double vyatireka (contrast) regarding the two similarities being expressed: "abhinna" means both "the limit" (*velā*) in the sense of a boundary (*maryādā*) and "the shore" (*tīra*).
It is profound, bottomless, and characterized by an unwavering state of mind;
this very [state] is illustrated by the following example where similarity is perceived: "Between your face and the white lotus, there is a difference between these two."
"The lotus grows in water, while your face has you as its support.
This has been explained by the very words [of the verse];
thus, this is the *vyatireka* (distinction) between both [the lotus and the face] whose similarity is being implied.
An example of the exclusion of the similar (*sadṛśavyatireka*) between the expressed object and the similarity is as follows:
“Your face and the white lotus are both blooming and fragrant; the lotus has hovering bees, while your face has darting glances. (96)

Here, regarding the two lotus-faces, for which similarity is expressed by the words "blooming" and "fragrant," the common properties of having wandering bees and having restless glances are presented as the points of distinction; thus, this is the *vyatireka* (distinguishing feature) of the similar, where the similarity is directly expressed by words. The same [type] occurs when the similarity is only implied, as in: "This moon is the crest-jewel of the sky; this swan is the ornament of the water."
"This sky is garlanded with stars; this water is filled with blooming lilies.

(97) Here, in the first half-verse, the sky and the moon, whose similarity is implied, possess respectively the qualities of being the "crest-jewel of the heavens" and the "ornament of the waters. In the second half-verse, however, the sky and the water possess as their differentiators the qualities of being "garlanded with stars" and "filled with blooming lilies," which are themselves similar.
This is "dissimilitude based on similarity" (*sadṛśavyatireka*) between two things whose similarity is implied.

The *asadṛśavyatireka* (dissimilarity based on non-similarity) regarding both the expressed and the similar [objects] is as follows: “The rain from the clouds ceased upon the slope of that mountain, but the continuous stream of tears from Rāma did not cease. (98)

Here, by the word *bhūbhṛtaḥ* ("of the mountain"), Rāma and Mālyavat are directly presented as possessing similarity. That which is the falling of the entire torrent of tears upon the lap—wherein there is an absence of the rain from clouds—is a distinguishing feature that makes these two indeed dissimilar.
This is called "the contrast of dissimilarity" (*asadṛśavyatireka*) between two things whose similarity is being expressed, as indicated by the words "the rain ceased."
And regarding the mountain and the king, where the similarity is implied, as in:
“The deer-eyed [face], devoid of the play of eyebrows and untouched by the flush of intoxication...”
"But these two eyes of yours are adorned with those very qualities.

(99) Here, between the beautiful deer-eyed woman and [the goddess], whose similarity is implied, the playfulness of the eyebrows and the flush of intoxication are present, while their absence is present in the other; thus, these dissimilarities serve as the differentiators. This, then, is the "dissimilarity of the implied similar" (*pratīyamānasādṛśyāsadr̥śavyatireka*).
By means of these two types—similarity-dissimilarity and dissimilarity-dissimilarity—the "dissimilarity of both" (*tadubhayavyatireka*) has also been explained.
For example:
"The sky shone with the stainless moon; the lake gleamed with blooming lotuses; yet both brothers, their faces bathed in tears, grew utterly pale. (100)

Here, in the case of the sky and the lake whose similarity is implied, "the state of being a spotless moon" and "the state of being a blooming lotus" serve as the differentiators of the similar objects, just as before. Through these two—the face-moon and the face-lotus—and through the qualities of being heart-stealing and refreshing (which imply their own similarity), the tear-staining on the faces and the pallor on the bodies of Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa—whose similarity is likewise implied—are shown to be dissimilar to those [qualities]. Thus, this is a *vyatireka* (poetic contrast) based precisely on the distinction between the differentiator of the similar and the differentiator of the dissimilar.
And by means of those two—the face-moon...
The state of the face being like the moon or a lotus is established through beginningless conceptual construction; therefore, it is said that there is a perceived similarity even in that form.
Now, one might object: "Is it not illogical to calculate the varieties of mutual exclusion (vyatireka), since the exclusion of the similar and the dissimilar is also possible? To this, he says:
"By this, the combination of single exclusions and so forth is also explained."
For example:

"O King, it is false that the wish-granting tree (kalpadruma), possessing little power, vies with your arm; for your sword—which is a great sacrificial feast of fearlessness for the three worlds—does not approach it.

In this regard, your majesty is equal to the sacred fig tree at Prayāga, within whose trunk Hari places the entire universe and sleeps upon its branches during the single ocean [of dissolution]. (101)

Here, there is a single *vyatireka* (distinguishing figure) based on the fact that the sword (*kṛpāṇa*) serves as the differentiator between the arm of the subject and the wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpadruma*), both of which possess a well-known similarity through their capacity to grant desired fruits and so forth;

for while the sword bestows fearlessness upon the three worlds, it rests upon the branches of the arm of the subject, whereas Vaikuṇṭha—having withdrawn the entire universe into his own body at the time of the great dissolution—is the one who provides the great sacrifice of fearlessness to the three worlds for the other [the tree], namely the *prayāgavaṭa*, whose similarity [to the arm] is likewise understood as before.

These two [qualities] are indeed the differentiators of those two, just as darkness and other such traits are the differentiators of a lion and a sword when their similarity is perceived; these very qualities serve as the differentiators. This type of "commingling of contrast" (*vyatireka-saṃkara*) is to be understood as follows:

where there is a perception of similarity despite the difference between members of the same genus (*svajāti-vyatireka*), and where there is an expression of similarity despite the difference between individual instances (*svavyakti-vyatireka*). If an example of this is seen or if it is possible, then that too should be cited by this method.
"Exactly as before" means by way of [the mantras'] bestowing the desired fruits and so forth;
"of such a kind" refers to this manner.

For it does not produce such aesthetic wonder merely by being situated within a single sentence as it does through mutual interconnection— such as the relationship between primary and subordinate members (aṅga-aṅgin);
that very [interconnection] is what is expressed by the word "manner" (prakāra),
provided that an example is seen or is possible.

For, unless there is similarity, the determination of non-difference between two things—given that they are distinct from their own respective classes—does not bestow any aesthetic charm (camatkāra); thus, one must admit that [the object] is merely imagined (*kalpita*). Yet, without the word "imagined," the perceived similarity cannot possibly exist, because similarity has difference as its locus and is impossible even when referring to one's own individual instances. It might be argued that such [an object] is indeed conveyed by the word; therefore, it was said: "if it is seen."
Since the state of being a cooperative cause (*sahakāritva*) is to be determined through negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), he states the definition of *samāhita* immediately after *vyatireka*:
"Whatever attainment of assistance in the commencement of an effect occurs here—whether produced by fate or human effort, accidental or intentional, or both—that is *samāhita*. (34)

Among these, that which is accidental and caused by fate is as follows: “To dispel her pride, I was about to fall at her feet; by good fortune, this thundering of clouds has arisen for my benefit. (102)

Here, at the commencement of the refutation of pride (*māna*), the sudden, dense thunder that arises in time acts as a cooperative factor (*sahakārin*) in the destruction of that pride; thus, this "attainment of assistance" (*sahāyasampatti*)—which is accidental and brought about by fate—is the "commencement of the task" (*kāryārambha*).

Therefore, "assistance" (*sahāya*) is that which cooperates with the cause of the matter at hand. By means of this, it constitutes an ornament (*alaṅkāratā*); for it is accidental, not previously conceived, and the opposite of that which is preceded by deliberate intent (*buddhipūrva*).

It is stated by implication that for each of the categories beginning with "accidental" (*ākasmikī*), when combined with the distinctions of being caused by fate (*daiva*) or not caused by fate (*adaiva*), there are six types established. An example of that which is both accidental and not caused by fate is as follows: "Thus instructing his elder brother Arjuna, who was unagitated yet whose path of policy was perplexed... (*Anuśāsatam ity anākulaṃ nayavartmākulaṃ arjunāgrajam*)... [and so forth].
"the son of Parāśara approached him like a desired object that had come of its own accord.
Here, because Vyāsa’s arrival at the very commencement of Bhīma’s instruction serves as an aid to it, this acquisition of assistance is both sudden and not brought about by fate.
This refers to Vyāsa’s arrival.
Regarding that which is being accomplished by Vyāsa, [the distinction is made] between that which is intentionally done and that which is done by fate—as follows:
...is not caused by fate.
As for that which is caused by fate: [it is] intentional, as for example—

"May the Great Bhairava—who at the end of the aeon becomes a fisherman, dragging along both the Fish and the Tortoise who rejoice in the singular state of the universal ocean; who has the carcass of the Three-Strider (Viṣṇu) as his great fishing pole, extinguished at its tip; and upon whom the flesh of the Primeval Boar is impaled by the claws of the Man-Lion’s gaping mouth, which are joined together by the serpent Śeṣa—may he destroy the delusion of the world. (104)

In this context, regarding the manner in which Trivikrama and others—whose destruction had been commenced by Maheśvara at the time of the dissolution of the world—were dragged out from their respective abodes by means of hooks and other tools fashioned from those very materials, it occurs that this process is intentionally devised by the Lord Bhairava and, by chance (*daiva*), is accomplished through those very things already existing. Thus, this is an instance of "attaining assistance brought about by destiny" (*daivakṛtā sahāyāptiḥ*) which is nonetheless intentional.

The phrase "by chance, through those very things already existing" indicates that for the claws of Narasiṃha and so forth—which possess forms suited to hooks and the like—destiny alone is the instrumental cause (*nimitta*); yet, because the thought of using hooks and such is made the object of his intention, it is characterized as being intentional.
An example of that which is preceded by intelligence and not caused by fate is as follows:

"Who has not heard of Rāvaṇa—he who, delighting solely in extraordinary audacity, offered worship to Śambhu with flower-garlands arranged such that there were five at the base and four thereafter, using blood from his own head as seen in the various positions of the flowers; and while touching the Lord’s head with his hand, he placed his own tenth head upon it? (105)

In this regard, concerning the manner in which the ten-faced one himself commenced the worship of the Lord Śambhu with his own severed heads—the elaborate arrangement of those heads, consisting first of five at the base and then four above, was a conscious act not performed by fate; yet, as it was being performed, it served as a contributory cause for the completion of this ritual. This conscious, non-fatalistic act is distinguished by its systematic order: "five at the base" refers to the arrangement of larger flowers placed lower down, while "four above" refers to smaller ones, which is the well-known method of worshipping with *dūrvā* grass.
In this context, the means of worship well-known in the world— consisting of superimposed signs such as various visual objects— is the causal factor (*kārya*),
while the successive production of a subtle arrangement [of the deity] upon [the visualization] is the auxiliary condition (*sahakārin*).

And since this was accomplished through the exertion of Rāvaṇa, it was not the work of fate (adaivakṛta) but rather an act of deliberate intent; thus, the placing of one head upon another did not continue until the ninth decapitation.

For [the Lord] is pleased by the very nature of the worship itself, and not merely by its being known as such—this is the intention of one whose devotion is waveless. Therefore, the wonderfulness of that rash act is such that it is both spontaneous and deliberate, brought about by fate—as for example: [The verse follows: *“O Lord, you who are the cause of the world’s creation, preservation, and destruction, and who are the supreme goal of those seeking liberation, how could you be satisfied by my offering of a handful of water?”* In this case, the offering of a handful of water is not something produced by fate, nor is it an act of deliberate intent; rather, it is a spontaneous act arising from the power of devotion. Thus, the offering of a handful of water is a form of worship, and the Lord is pleased by that very act of worship. It is not the case that he is pleased simply by the knowledge that "this is an act of worship. This is the underlying meaning. Consequently, the devotion is "waveless" (*nistaraṅga*). By that, the wonderfulness of the rash act is established. It is both accidental (*ākasmikī*) and deliberate (*buddhipūrvā*), brought about by fate (*daivakṛtā*). As for example: [The verse follows: *“O Lord, you who are the cause of the world’s creation, preservation, and destruction, and who are the supreme goal of those seeking liberation, how could you be satisfied by my offering of a handful of water?”* In this instance, the offering of a handful of water is neither produced by fate nor performed with prior deliberation; rather, it is an act arising spontaneously from the force of devotion. Thus, the offering of a handful of water constitutes the nature of worship, and the Lord is pleased by that very act of worship. It is not that he is pleased merely by the cognition that "this is an act of worship. This is the intended sense. Therefore, the devotion is "waveless. By that, the marvelous nature of the rash act is explained. It is both sudden and intentional, brought about by destiny. As for example: [The verse follows: *“O Lord, you who are the cause of the world’s creation, preservation, and destruction, and who are the supreme goal of those seeking liberation, how could you be satisfied by my offering of a handful of water?”* In this case, the offering of a handful of water is not something produced by destiny, nor is it an act of conscious design; rather, it is a spontaneous action arising from the power of devotion. Thus, the offering of a handful of water is a form of worship, and the Lord is pleased by that very act of worship. It is not the case that he is pleased merely by the knowledge that "this is an act of worship. This is the underlying intention. Consequently, the devotion is "waveless. By that, the marvelous nature of the rash act is established. It is both accidental and deliberate, brought about by fate. As for example: [The verse follows: *“O Lord, you who are the cause of the world’s creation, preservation, and destruction, and who are the supreme goal of those seeking liberation, how could you be satisfied by my offering of a handful of water?”* In this instance, the offering of a handful of water is neither produced by fate nor performed with prior deliberation; rather, it is an act arising spontaneously from the force of devotion. Thus, the offering of a handful of water constitutes the nature of worship, and the Lord is pleased by that very act of worship. It is not the case that he is pleased merely by the cognition that "this is an act of worship. This is the intended sense. Therefore, the devotion is "waveless. By that, the marvelous nature of the rash act is explained. It is both sudden and intentional, brought about by destiny. As for example: [The verse follows: *“O Lord, you who are the cause of the world’s creation, preservation, and destruction, and who are the supreme goal of those seeking liberation, how could you be satisfied by my offering of a handful of water?”* In this case, the offering of a handful of water is not something produced by fate, nor is it an act of deliberate intent; rather, it is a spontaneous act arising from the power of devotion. Thus, the offering of a handful of water is a form of worship, and the Lord is pleased by that very act of worship
“That Kaumudī is a noble birth for your eyes, and you too are the kinsman bound by her heart’s desire;

O friend, there is no doubt regarding their union, for both Fate and Love have exerted themselves toward it. (106) Here, this longing of Mādhava for union with Mālatī, and Mālatī’s corresponding engagement—whether spontaneous or intentional—is both a "fortuitous acquisition of assistance" (*daivakṛtā sahāyāptiḥ*) and a "resolution of a complication" (*samāhitabhedaḥ*).
In this context, by the statement "this [plan] of Mādhava" and "Madana and [Mādhava], having undertaken their efforts," the prior conditions (*pūrvānubhāva*) of Mālatī are described;
and since these are of two kinds, there is a sudden attainment of assistance (*sahāyasampatti*) brought about by destiny.
It is both accidental and intentional, not brought about by fate, as in:
“The glance is a garland of *vandanā* flowers; the pair of breasts are two jars filled with loveliness; the smile is a heap of white blossoms; the radiance of her face is a mirror;

the emergence of horripilation is indeed a grain of mustard seed; and the hands are two tender sprouts. By her very limbs, the slender maiden has performed the auspicious rites for the beloved entering her home. (107)

This auspicious rite, such as the offering of a garland of salutation, performed for the sake of the beloved who is arriving here, is a cause for the satisfaction of her mind; yet, that his turning back occurs solely through the gestures and expressions of that slender-limbed woman—this very event is both sudden and intentional, and because it serves as a cooperative cause for that [turning back], it is non-fated (*adaivakṛta*). This constitutes a variety of *samāhita*. The phrase "for the sake of the beloved who is arriving here" refers merely to the auspicious rite and is not itself the locus of aesthetic wonder; therefore, it is specified as "a cause for the satisfaction of the mind."
A smile is preceded by conscious intent, whereas the bristling of body hair is not;
in this same manner, it should be understood accordingly for the gaze and other such expressions.
Since there is sometimes even error in the acquisition of an assistant through deliberate intelligence, he defines it immediately thereafter:
"Error is contrary cognition; it is applied in two ways: that which takes the form of reality regarding what is not real, and that which takes the form of unreality regarding what is real. (35)

That which appears as the nature of reality in what is not reality is also taught to be threefold: the uncontradicted, the contradicted, and likewise that which is contradicted by its cause; this is called "error. (36)
The determination that "this is that" with respect to what is not that is error; that alone is misconception.
It has been stated previously that doubt and the like are not of this nature.

That [superimposition] is of two kinds: the attribution of existence to that which is non-existent in a certain place, or the attribution of non-existence to that which is existent in a certain place.

This restriction based on presence and absence occurs even within the restrictive rule of sublation (*bādha*) regarding error; in some cases there is the presentation of an example, while in others there is not.
This presentation is of two forms: by means of direct denotation (*abhidhā*) and by means of another function [of language].

The meaning is that when there is either the presentation of a sublation (*bādha*) or the non-presentation of a sublated [object], that very statement is "one whose sublation is unknown" (*avijñātabādha*). This is because, in a manner other than its presentation, the sublated is known to be sublated, since the speaker’s intention regarding the statement of the cause of sublation culminates in the sublation itself. He demonstrates this by saying: "both un-sublated and sublated."

In that regard, an instance where the nature of reality is uncontradicted despite being applied to what is not reality is as follows: “By him, upon the cessation of delusion, his gaze—full of passion—was fixed upon the orb of the full breasts of the celestial nymphs, such that they were perceived as being like the frontal globes of elephants. (108)

[In the verse: "Upon the broad orb of the breasts of the celestial nymphs, which were swelling with passion, he fixed his gaze—out of delusion—with the perception that they were the frontal globes of elephants.

Here, when the orbs of the celestial nymphs' breasts are apprehended as being the frontal globes of elephants—which are not their true nature—there occurs a false superimposition of reality upon what is unreal; and since no subsequent sublation is presented, this is an uncontradicted error consisting in perceiving reality in what is unreal.
The term *mohavirama* is established with its etymological suffix (*sapallava*),
because it is well-known that the root *sthā* (to stand) is used there in its completed form (*paripūrva*).
The term "with anger" (*saroṣam*) is an attribute of the constituent elements (*samavāyin*); and since there is no existence of an action without such attributes,
it is thereby suggested that even in the state of delusion (*moha*), the essential nature of the experience of the rasa under discussion was not lost.

And thus, this rasa possesses such firm continuity that even upon contact with a more powerful opposing element, it did not succumb to harshness; this is made manifest by the words "the celestial damsels of the broad orb" (*sthūlamaṇḍalasuravadhūpadaiḥ*) through poetic probability (*saṃbhāvanā*), but not by a previously arisen cognition, because the frontal globes of elephants possess a much stronger latent impression (*vāsanā*).
