He demonstrates how the term "unsublated" (*abādhitā*) is intended here in its literal sense in the phrase "the presentation of a sublater" (*bādhakopanyāsa*).

An example of that which appears in the form of reality when it is not reality, yet is sublated, is as follows: “Travelers, having approached a hollow tree trunk, laughed with hand-clapping; for the woodpecker had flown away, [leaving behind] what resembled the fruit of a leaf. (109)
"When this flock of parrots, resembling leaves and fruit, has flown away, the travelers who have approached the withered banyan tree laugh with clapping hands.

Here, when the cognition of reality has arisen regarding that which is not real— namely, "This is a banyan tree bearing leaves and fruit"— the subsequent realization of its leaflessness and fruitlessness sublates this error, which is the attribution of the nature of reality to what is not real.
"Pūṣan, laugh!
Śuka,
salute Vṛnda after Vṛnda!"

Although no contradiction is explicitly stated here regarding the similarity between the parrot’s beak and tail and a ripe *nyagrodha* fruit or a fresh *palāśa* leaf, nevertheless, by the word "having flown away" (*uḍḍīṇa*), a cognition concerning the absence of the object is produced;
otherwise, how could there be the presentation of the effect consisting of laughter, hand-clapping, and mimicry?
An example of that which appears in the form of reality despite being unreal, and which is sublated by its cause, is as follows:

“Hari, laughing with the bashful smile produced by his beloved, repeatedly wipes away his own dark luster—which is reflected in the circle of Rādhā’s breasts, clear as golden jars—as he mistakes it for the edge of her dark garment; thus he is made to laugh by his dear one. (110)

In this instance, regarding the dark-complexioned woman who possesses the luster of her own body, the cognition that the edge of her garment is black—which takes a non-reality for its object—is sublated by the cause that is the beloved’s laughter; thus, this is an error where a non-reality is taken as a reality, sublated by a cause.

Here, in the phrase "regarding the dark-complexioned woman," there is no absence of the object made the focus through any verbal function (*vṛtti*) as was the case in the previous example; rather, it is inferred through another means.

For instance, even when the hero performs the playful act of snatching away her garment, Rādhā’s movement of limbs to conceal her cloth, the knitting of her brows, and so forth—which contradict the graceful charms (vibhrama) appropriate for a charming young woman—constitute the cause of a "laughter that obstructs" (bādha-hāsya).

This laughter, though its nature is unreal (atattva-rūpa) with respect to the true state of affairs, arises as the cause for the threefold process of abandonment, acquisition, and indifference regarding the truth. || 37 ||
In that regard, an instance where that which is not the reality serves as a cause for rejection within the context of reality is as follows:
“O fool, you have been so tormented by my expectations—which are like mirages in the desert—that even a river consisting of mere imagination has not turned its back on me. (111)

"That bewildered deer, tormented by the mirages of your hopes, has become averse even to rivers consisting of real water; for here, being deceived by a mirage, the deer does not proceed to drink the water even when it is present in reality, but rather abandons it. Thus, this is an error that consists of non-reality even regarding reality, serving as a cause for loss."

He clarifies through his commentary that "abandonment" (hāna) is intended here in two ways— as the absence of engagement and as a contrary effort— by stating: "he does not merely fail to grasp [it], but rather he abandons it."
An example of taking that which is unreal as the material cause for what is real is as follows:

“Whatever I first resolve regarding my beloved, in an instant it turns out otherwise for me; therefore, while my eyes are wide awake, I shall not suddenly touch her, lest she become displeased by the contact. (113)

In this context, I maintain that the reading *vibhāvitāpriya* is appropriate; for it refers to Purūravas, whose eyes were closed by the bliss of embracing Urvaśī in her assumed form as a creeper, and who—despite her having appeared in her true form at the end of the curse—possesses the notion of not opening his eyes because of the expectation of various kinds of separation such as he had previously experienced. This is an error (*bhrānti*) where, even though the reality (*tattva*) is present, the cause for perceiving non-reality (*atattvarūpa*) is taken up. This is so because [the compound] is a prohibition of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva-pratiṣedha*) when applied to words such as *priyā*.

Since it is not clearly understood here that there is a superimposition of non-existence, he explains this by taking up the context: "It should not be said that 'this cognition is of the nature of doubt because of its oscillating state,' for although the beloved is indeed not present here, nevertheless, for Purūravas—who knows that the alleviation of mental anguish is appropriate through the superimposition of her presence—the intensity of his persistent longing is nourished, and not otherwise; this is witnessed by the hearts of those with aesthetic sensitivity."

He clarifies this point slightly: even when a thing is in its true state, the perception that "it was previously experienced as being such-and-such" is a cause for indifference toward its actual nature—for example:
"With the desire to build [a nest], upon the pigeon-perches of the dwellings, amidst the rows of artificial birds..."

"In this [verse], 'Even a cat with limbs stretched out and motionless was regarded by the people as if it were artificial,' although the cat is in its true state, the thought 'this is artificial' arises; since that [thought] is the cause for the neglect [of the cat's true nature], this is the error (bhrānti) which, being the cause of neglect, consists in regarding even the real as unreal.
This is what is meant by "neglect due to [the presence of] a cause."

That which does not produce either engagement or withdrawal, or the cognition of relative expectation— delusion, a series of delusions, the intensification of delusion, and the non-determination of delusion— all these, in my view, are indeed delusion itself. (38)
In the word *bhrāntimān*, the suffix *matup* is used in the sense of abundance (*bhūman*).
This sense of abundance is twofold: either the multiplicity of many errors having a single object, or the commonality of agency among errors that have different objects.
The first is the object of a single error; the second is the object of a series of errors.
For there is no fixed order of succession in a series within a single error, since [the objects] may arise simultaneously even when produced by different agents.

An "excess" (*atiśaya*) of error is an error whose excellence is brought about by words; it is perceived as taking up a *vitarka* (discursive thought) that is its own effect, and being the cause of a misconception, it is followed by further delusions.

Among these, an example of Illusion (*bhrāntimān*) is as follows: “A cat licks its paws on the cheek [of the moon], thinking, ‘It is milk’; an elephant gathers the lotus stalks threaded through the gaps in the tree-trunks, thinking, ‘It is lotus fiber’; and even a beloved woman, at the end of lovemaking, takes up the garment lying on the bed, thinking, ‘It is her own. Oh, how the moon, intoxicated by its own radiance, causes this entire world to wander in delusion! (114)
In this context, due to the abundance of errors such as perceiving water in the rays of the sun, there is a variety of error called *bhrāntimān* (the state of being mistaken).
An example of a "garland of errors" (*bhrāntimālā*) is as follows:

"With the suspicion that [her eyes] were blue lotuses, with the thought that her lower lip was a bandhūka flower, with the notion that her hand was a lotus, and likewise with the delusion that her cheeks were madhūka blossoms..."

“O young woman, how many places will you protect from the bees, who—driven by a longing born of their delusion regarding your kinswomen—cling to your braided hair? Their resistance is difficult to overcome.

(115) In this verse, the perception of blue lotuses and the like that arises toward the eyes and other limbs of the young woman with respect to the bees—which occurs in a serial manner—is a "garland of error" (*bhrāntimālā*). This is a variety of error itself.
Excess of error (*bhrāntyatiśaya*) is twofold: that caused by doubt (*vitarkahetu*) and that caused by misconception (*viparyayahetu*).
Of these two, they call the first "simile-confusion" (*upamā-bhrānti*), while the second is simply "excessive confusion.
Therein, simile-confusion is as follows:
"Marked by the falling drops of water from her eyes, which had stolen the redness of her lips, as she was submerged at the navel..."
"Without doubt, this breast-cloth, dark as the belly of a parrot, has fallen [here] due to her movement being interrupted by anger.

Here, Purūravas—who has conceived the delusion that the breast-cloth has appeared even upon the grassy meadow—possesses this conjecture (*vitarka*) which exceeds mere similarity; this is *upamābhrānti* (delusion of comparison), as it occurs prior to those two [the actual comparison and the delusion].

The sense is that when something is perceived as identical in reality, yet a slight distinction from it is delineated in the interim, a resemblance certainly arises in the mind due to the equality of difference and non-difference.
By the word "asaṃśayam" (without doubt), excellence and deliberation are conveyed.
An example of the heightening of delusion is as follows:

May the digit of the moon, shining like a fragment of moonlight upon the river that is the crest-tuft of Śiva, grant you joy—a digit that vanishes as soon as it is seen due to its reflection in the water;
and at which the serpent, mistaking it for a darting fish, repeatedly closes his row of hoods in delusion and strives intensely to seize his mark with repeated contractions and expansions.

In this context, for Vāsuki, who was beholding the digit of the moon reflected in the waters of the Gaṅgā, there arose this erroneous cognition (*viparyaya-buddhi*)—the thought "this is a fish"—which caused him to contract his row of hoods in the delusion that it was a fish. This is what is called "excessive error" (*bhrāntyatiśaya*), which is indeed a specific variety of error itself.

[The phrase] "desiring most intensely to seize" (*jighṛkṣatitamām*) [is derived from the root *grah* with the desiderative suffix *san*, followed by the superlative suffix *tamap* and the primary suffix *tumun*].
"From verbal roots ending in *tiṅ*" (Pāṇini 5.3.56).
Regarding that [suffix] as well, [the rule] "kimettiṅavyayaghādāmvadravyaprakarṣe" (Pāṇini 5.4.11) applies.
Thus, this error, as well as non-determination (*anadhyavasāya*), is also twofold: with an objective basis (*sālambana*) and without an objective basis (*nirālambana*).
Of these, that which has an objective basis is, for example:

‘The mango grove is instantly judged by the hearts of women separated from their lovers to be the God of Death; yet it is immediately concealed by Caitra with swarms of bees, so that neither the *kalamba*, nor the *āmra*, nor the *jambū* can be distinguished by its blossoms.

(118) The mango grove is instantly determined by the hearts of women separated from their lovers to be the God of Death; it is then covered by Caitra with throngs of bees, so that neither the *kalamba*, nor the *āmra*, nor the *jambū* can be recognized. (118)

Now, even among those [trees], one is struck by their blossoms such that it is not known whether it is a *kadamba*, a *nāra*, or a *jambū*. Because these three serve as the basis for the cognition, this type of error is called "with a basis" (*sālambana*); it is a variety of error consisting of non-determination (*anadhyavasāya*), which is the state of having an object that cannot be definitively ascertained.
In the phrase *virahiṇījanana*,
[the word] *virahiṇījana* [is used in the sense of] "one who feels for" (*adhīgartha*)— according to Pāṇini 2.3.52.
By [the rule] beginning with "3.52," the genitive case is used in the sense of the object (*karman*).
By means of his teeth, acting with compassion and protecting [her],
it appears as if [he did so] at that very moment.
The mango grove (*cūtavanī*) is being covered by the agent Caitra (*caitrena*), using as the instrument the swarms of bees (*alinivahaiḥ*).
In that same way, even among those [other women], he (the husband) is likewise bound and fettered by her as well.

Since the object has not yet been determined, how can there be a distinction between that which has an objective support (*sālambana*) and that which lacks one (*nirālambana*)? To this he says: "Because [the other] three alone serve as the objective support.
This means that the object is specified by way of this phrasing.
As for that which lacks an objective support (*nirālamba*): [text follows].

"Two plantain-stems inverted above two lotuses, and above those a slab of jeweled stone—something utterly inscrutable; then two jars, followed by two sprouts of lotus-fibers, and upon them a blue water-lily with bees: what indeed is this? (119) In this case, regarding the limbs of a young woman [mistaken for] objects such as the earth and so forth, there arises a delusion of plantain-stems. This state of non-determination (*anadhyavasāya*)—the thought "What is this? directed toward that entire collection—is produced without a supporting basis (*ālambana*). This is the variety of delusive non-determination called "unsupported" (*nirālambana*), which is a specific subtype of delusion itself.
"Without an object" means that the non-determination of the sense-object has been made manifest;
"ūha" (reasoning) is *vitarka* (investigation), which is established within the interval between doubt and certainty.
This [vitarka] is declared to be of two kinds: that which ends in a definitive conclusion (nirṇayānta) and that which does not end in a definitive conclusion (anirṇayānta).
Following the general category of false cognition (mithyāpratīti), the definition of vitarka is given—the meaning is that its common designation is "ūha" (speculative inquiry).
A definition is indeed established even by means of a synonym;

for example, consider one who is doubtful regarding the referent of the word "jar" (ghaṭa) but certain regarding the referent of the word "kalaśa. To the question, "How is this [definition] distinguished from doubt and error, given that 'whatever is a kalaśa is a jar'? he says: "Because of doubt... and so forth.

Doubt, consisting of multiple alternatives, gives rise to an inquiry of that very nature; whereas reasoning (*tarka*), occurring immediately thereafter, consists of a single fixed alternative and is of that same nature.
Thus, there is a distinction between doubt and [reasoning] due to differences in time, essential form, and function;
the same applies to error (*viparyaya*) as well.
For that [tarka] consists of a certainty arising from another form of reasoning and serves as a cause for purposeful activity and so forth;

thus, this distinction of objects has been made regarding the fallacy of tarka (*tarkābhāsa*), which does not culminate in a definitive conclusion. However, the distinction of objects for valid *tarka* itself is quite clear, as it occupies the intermediate position between doubt (*saṃdeha*) and certainty (*nirṇaya*). He states that distinction as it exists therein: "It is of two kinds."

Intending to show that the final determination (*nirṇaya*)— which is presented as the result [of inquiry] and consists of a certainty— is of two kinds, namely, one that conforms to reality and one that does not conform to reality, because it takes the form of either valid cognition or its opposite, he divides it for the sake of defining *nirṇaya*:
"That which conforms to reality, that which does not conform to reality, and that which possesses the nature of both."
That [cognition] which ends in a definitive conclusion is [valid], while the other is of the nature of both false and non-false;
this has been explained by the very word "conforming to reality" (tattvānupātī).
Among these, that which conforms to the reality and concludes with a definitive resolution is as follows:
“Is this Maināka obstructing my unimpeded path through the sky? Whence could he have such power? He is surely afraid of Indra due to the fall of the thunderbolt;
even Tārkṣya knows me to be Rāvaṇa along with his own Lord. Ah, now I know! This is Jaṭāyu, distressed by old age, who desires death. (120)

In this context, regarding the *vitarka* (speculative inquiry) whose definition has been established, there is the *vitarka* culminating in a definitive conclusion (*nirṇayānta*) that conforms to reality, such as "This is Jaṭāyu.

For one whose mind was previously wavering with the thought "Is this Maināka? Is this [Maināka]?"—expressed through an interrogative intonation (*kāku*)—there is presented a specific cognition that touches upon a determined alternative; that itself is *tarka*.
Likewise, in other cases as well, that very same [superimposition] follows from non-reality, as for example:

"In the creation of this [woman], was the Creator Prajāpati? Or was it the moon, the bestower of luster? Or was it Love himself, whose sole essence is passion? Or was it the month, the source of flowers?"
"How indeed could the ancient sage, dulled by the study of the Vedas and with his curiosity turned away from sense-objects, be capable of creating this heart-stealing form? (121).

Here, the thought—"How could such an ancient sage be capable of creating this form as described? Therefore, it must have been created by one of the Prajāpatis, such as the Moon"—is a *vitarka* (speculative inquiry) that does not conform to reality (*atattvānupātī*) because it ends in a definitive conclusion (*nirṇayānta*).
That same [type of *vitarka*] is of a dual nature (*ubhayātmaka*), as for example:

"Having fixed my mind upon her, that creation of a jewel-like woman appears to me as if fashioned by the mind through an accumulation of exquisite forms, joined with the imagined union of a living being; this is so when I reflect upon the sovereign power of the Creator and her physical form.
This is a *vitarka* (speculative inquiry) that concludes in a definitive judgment, possessing a dual nature because it both conforms to reality and does not conform to reality.

By the phrase "the creation of the jewel of a woman" (*strīratnasṛṣṭi*), that which conforms to reality (*tattvānupātī*) is indicated; by the word "another" (*apara*), that which does not conform to reality (*atattvānupātī*) is revealed as being of a false nature (*mithyārūpa*), ending in uncertainty—as for example: [the following].
"‘Is the wind carrying away the peak of the mountain?’—thus gazed upon with wide-eyed alarm by the innocent wives of the Siddhas looking upwards;
fly up from this place of lush *nicula* trees toward the sky, facing north, avoiding on your path the arrogant thrusts of the trunks of the world-elephants.

Here, the thought directed toward the cloud—"Is this the wind carrying away the mountain peak?"—is a false form of deliberation (*vitarka*) ending in uncertainty, because it is a fabrication regarding the cloud and because the actual object remains undetermined.
The false and the non-false forms consist of sublated and unsublated objects;
for even a reasoning that is unsublated exists, such as: "If this has a blue form, it is a blue lotus."
That very same [cognition] is of an unmistakable form, as for example:

"Is this the Blessed One, or is it the Pāṇḍava? Is the Moon-crested Lord standing there, or has he been mounted by Brahmā, or perhaps by Arjuna? Thus the attendants were bewildered by the force of his speed. (124)

In this case, because the forms of both the Blessed One and Pārtha are non-illusory and possess momentum, there is a non-illusory doubt (*vitarka*) ending in indecision regarding which one [is the Blessed One].

Now, regarding "of the Blessed One and Pārtha," there is no sublation whatsoever of the visual cognition that perceives the specificities of the two states of the Blessed One and Pārtha, as well as their simultaneous mounting and dismounting; thus it is through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
The double-natured [sandeha] ends in indecision, as for example: “Is this an illusion, or a delusion of my mind? Has my prowess been destroyed, or am I another person?
For the arrows released from the *gāṇḍīva* no longer strike their mark against the Kirāta as they did before. (125)

In this context, because the conceptualizations of "illusion" (*māyā*) and so forth are false in nature, my arrows do not operate against Kirāta; since this [statement] is false in nature and ends in non-determination, this is a *vitarka* (speculative inquiry) of the "doubtful" type ending in non-determination (*anirṇayānta*). Here, the phrase "of illusion and so forth" does not refer to the Lord’s illusion as a deception, nor to a delusion of the intellect regarding Śakti, nor to the destruction of his prowess, nor to Arjuna being someone other than Arjuna—because such objects are sublated by reality.
Since there is a delusion when [an object] is closed [to view], he states the definition of *mīlita* immediately after [the discussion of] delusion:
"The concealment of one thing by another thing is known as *mīlita*;
it also consists of the covered and the uncovered, as well as that which possesses its qualities and that which does not. (41)
In the phrase "vastvantareti," the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used in a double sense (*śliṣṭa*): [it means] "of things" (*vastūnām*),
and in the phrase "tiraskāre," it is used in the objective sense (*karmaṇi*), meaning "by another thing."
The "obscuration of another object" (vastvantarasya tiraskāraḥ) is, in effect, the same meaning when expressed in the active voice;
thus, the definition means that the obscuration or subordination of an inferior quality by a superior quality is what constitutes [the figure].
The attainment of a single form through the concealment of distinct forms is called *mīlita* (the hidden).
Thus states the *Kātantra*: "The *mīlita* is said to be that which is joined.

Concealment preceded by intention is of two kinds: that which results in a realized intention and that which results in an unrealized intention; these correspond respectively to *pihita* (concealed) and *apihita* (unconcealed).

Nor does this much distinction constitute a separate category [of poetic figure], because intermediate varieties are pervaded by the general definition (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) and because they are infinite in number. It is clear that "the concealment of its own quality by a similar quality" (*tadguṇa*) and "the non-concealment of its own quality by a dissimilar quality" (*atadguṇa*) are merely specific types of *mīlita*.

In this context, *mīlita* (the concealment of one thing by another) occurs through a primary object characterized either by an expressed quality (*abhidhīyamāna-guṇa*) or an implied quality (*pratīyamāna-guṇa*).
Of these two, the first (that characterized by an expressed quality) is as follows:
"Even though he entered at dawn, his complexion, red like a spreading sprout, was not noticed."
‘Even as he approached, he was not seen; for at dawn, intoxication was upon his cheeks, which were red like spreading sprouts, and indignation was in his eyes, which were copper-red with wine. (126)

Here, the redness of intoxication in the eyes—which are already reddened by their immersion [in water]—and the passion of anger in those [eyes] which are already reddened by intoxication, are shown to be eclipsed by the very quality being directly expressed; thus, this is *mīlita* (concealment) by means of a thing whose quality is being expressed.
He states the classification: "In this case, it is *mīlita*," as in the verse beginning with *entovī*.
The truth-teller saw her bathing— that is, performing her ritual immersion— in the morning at dawn.
In this instance, a quality (*guṇa*) is expressed by the words "copper" (*tāmra*) and "redness" (*aruṇarāga*),
which is understood through the implied quality (*pratīyamānaguṇa*), as in:
"O you who are not seen, my eyes do not become closed from the pleasure of bliss."
‘If her eyes were not blooming with the essence of bliss due to the sight of her beloved, by whom could that blue lotus placed upon her ear be noticed? (127)

In this case, the *karṇakuvalaya* (ear-lotus) of the woman is perceived only while her eyes are closed due to the pleasure of seeing her beloved; it is not perceived when the eyes are open. Thus, the concealment of one thing by another is established as having the nature of a suggested quality (*pratīyamānaguṇatayā*). Therefore, this is *mīlita* (concealment) by means of a thing possessing a suggested quality. Now, one might ask: how can "piadaṃsaṇeṇa" (*priyadarśanena*) and so forth be considered *mīlita*, since no word here explicitly conveys the act of concealment? To this, he replies: "but not when [the eyes] are open."
The sense is that this results in the dismissal of the argument, "If they were not closed, how could the blue lotus (kuvalaya) be perceived?"—
as in the following example where a quality such as form or appearance, though being perceived, is concealed:
‘Just as you were seen by her while she was occupied with concealment, through the display of manifest affection, true feeling, and amorous playfulness, so too was another person. (128)

"Even another person [would act] in exactly the same way while occupied with concealment. Here, because her amorous confusion (*vibhrama*) is manifest as she gazes at you, she thinks, "Let no other person know this," and thus, by casting a tender glance everywhere, she conceals it; yet even though it is covered, this is merely a variety of *mīlita* (the concealed), as in the following example of *apahnuti* (the veiled): [Example omitted per instructions] [End of example] In this case, although the [feeling] is hidden by the casting of a tender glance everywhere, thinking "let no other person know this" upon seeing you with manifest amorous confusion, it is still merely a form of *mīlita*. ‘He who was not seen even when looked at, nor addressed even when spoken to, nor to whom a courtesy was shown— he has been treated with contempt by the clever ones. (129)

"Because she did not look [at him] when looked at, nor speak when spoken to, nor perform the hospitable reception for a guest, her passion was not merely concealed by those clever people; on the contrary, through that very concealment, it was made manifest. This is the variety of *mīlita* called *apahnuti* (concealment). Now, one might ask: "How can this be an ornament (*alaṃkāra*) when it is said that she was not even seen by one who was looking? [The answer follows: It is an ornament because the very fact that she was not seen despite being looked at, and so forth, serves to reveal her intense passion through the cleverness of the concealment. Thus, it is a specific type of *mīlita*.
For there is no power [of suggestion] here; therefore, he says "on the contrary" (*pratyuta*).
The meaning is that because it is being relished by those who are clever and discerning (*cheka-vidagdha*), poetry possesses the quality of attractiveness (*āvarjakatva*).
An example of that quality is as follows:

‘Fair-limbed young women, veiled in white attire and bound by passion for their beloveds, hasten forth to meet them under the moonlight; yet, with their dark bodies, Love likewise advances, as it were, concealing himself behind their shadows. (130)
Furthermore, Madana, with his dark limbs, moved there among the shadows; thus he became invisible.

Here, the fair-limbed young women, dressed in white attire, move in the moonlight, while he, dressed in blue attire, moves in her shadows. Because of the merging [of the two] through the assumption of each other's qualities (*tadguṇa*), this is the figure of speech called *mīlita* (concealment), as expressed by the words "fair-limbed" (*gauraṅgau*).
The fair-limbed Johna [is] in the moonlight;
*ṇevaccha* means attire, that is, the assumption of garments, cosmetics, and so forth.
Having waited and taken [it], he takes delight as if in a beloved;
in the shade of those fair-limbed women.

An example of "motion" (*calita*) where the quality of the object does not transfer [to the subject] is as follows: "A Śabara woman, longing for pearls, picks the *karkandhū* fruit; even a crow, in the presence of a flock of angry owls, acts like a swan."
"O Protector of the Earth, when the three worlds have been whitened by your fame, Lakṣmī, seeing Kṛṣṇa before her, slowly speaks with suppressed shame, thinking, 'This is Bala'.
Here, because the *karkandhū* fruits have lost their own specific quality, this is the figure of speech called *mīlita*, specifically the variety known as *atadguṇa*.
This refers to "the *karkandhū* fruits."
The meaning is "of qualities that are dissimilar.
Recollection is the cognition of an experienced object arising from similarity, unseen perception, reflection, and so forth; recognition, dreams, and the like are also not outside of that. (42)
Since knowledge exists even when [the senses] are closed, he next defines recollection (*smṛti*) by virtue of its similarity [to perception]:

"From a similar object" means from a perceived similarity; "recollection born of effort" refers to *cintā* (reflection) and so forth, which he will explain later. Recollection is the cognition of an experienced object, consisting of a specific type of knowledge restricted to an experience of a similar object.
Recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) likewise has as its object only that which was previously experienced.
In this way, even a dream is similar to that; as it is said:
"Before him were seen rows of sporting wagtails."
"they remembered, sighing deeply, the playful movements of their beloved’s eyes.

Here, due to the sight of the row of *khañjana* birds, there arises a recollection of the playful movements of the beloved’s eyes—which are similar to them; this is the type of recollection born from seeing something similar.
In this instance, the word "khañjana" [is used].

By the word "atra" (here), it is understood that there is a causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*)—namely, that immediately after the row of wagtails was observed, the recollection of the beloved occurred;
and since this causality exists in the cognition of the wagtails without being included within "similarity" (*sādṛśya*), the sense is that similarity is what is perceived [as the basis].
As for "the unseen" (*adṛṣṭa*), for example:

"O friend, my mind, separated from the darkness that obstructed the memory of my love for the daughter of the sage, has had a mango-arrow placed upon its bow by the Mind-born [God of Love] as he prepares to strike.

(133) Here, the statement "my mind was separated from the darkness that obstructed the memory of my love for the daughter of the sage" constitutes this recollection brought about by an unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*).
In this context,
the meaning is that when the obstacle characterized by darkness has been removed, the effect in the form of recollection necessarily occurs;
as for instance, in the case of *cintā* (reflection):
"Where there was once a stream, there now is a sandbank; where there were rivers, there is now a reversal; the density and sparseness of the trees have changed.
Having been seen for a long time, this forest appears as if born anew; yet the fact that it is the dwelling of these same mountains solidifies the recognition that 'this is indeed that very place.
Here, although the stream, trees, and forest are perceived directly, because the recollection is produced by anxiety (*cintā*), this is "recollection arising from anxiety."
By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (ādi), there is also the effort of another, as for example:

"The beloved, having come within the range of vision, has been depicted once more by you in a painting—with a heart made of her very essence through memory—as if she were present before my eyes. (135)
In this case, because the thought has been set in motion by a specific effort made by another, this too is indeed a memory,
just like a dream— for example:
"I know that during my sleep today, there appeared before me at dawn a mass of light rivaling the moonlight, capable of being held in the hollow of a cup, like a halo of light."
"By her limbs, which possess the luster of the autumnal moon polished by her inner nails, some extraordinary woman has forcibly made even the God of Love [Manmatha] subject to love.
Here, since a dream is produced by reflection (*cintā*) and other such factors, the "recollection of a dream" (*svapnasmṛti*) is also indeed a form of recollection (*smaraṇa*).

If the recollection of a dream is also indeed recollection, then what among the causes such as similarity (*sādṛśya*) and so forth is present here? To this it is said: "reflection and so forth" (*cintādīti*).
Recognition is as follows:

"This very hand of hers—beautiful like a tender sprout of the lovely *lavalī* creeper, which was once grasped during the marriage ceremony, which was familiarized by the nectar-cool feet of the embodiment of ambrosia (the Moon), and which possesses the grace of being compared to her other hand—has now been found by me. (137)

In this regard, even the recognition—"This very hand of hers which was previously grasped is this one"—is indeed nothing but memory; it demonstrates the essential nature of recognition by means of the form "That which was before is this very same [thing].
Now, one might object: since recognition prior to dreaming was indicated in the Sūtra first, why is it being illustrated here afterwards?
Regarding this sequence of examples, the venerable teachers maintain that this is merely a scribal error;
for "state" (bhāva) is defined as activity in accordance with one's intention, and it is said to be either manifest or unmanifest, occurring either on one side or all around. || 43 ||
Immediately following the rule of contemplating desired objects such as pearls and the like, there is the definition of the state (*bhāva*);
he states this: "the intention" (*abhiprāya*), meaning the contemplation of the desired object.
Activity characterized by action is an absence [of the self] due to its conformity with that [intention];
for this very reason, it differs from the subtle [intention].

Intention, which is manifested through the disclosure of its own object by means of an expression of activity, is manifested in some cases by a word accompanied by the operation of another word, and in other cases by a word alone.
These two— manifested (sodbheda) and unmanifested (nirudbheda)— delight in their mutual connection; and by this [treatment],
the engagement with them is described, whether it belongs to that [connection] or to those two.

This is what he says: [the word] "ekataśca" and "abhitaśca" is established at the stage of manifesting the intended meaning; having reached the path of aesthetic relish (*svāda*), it brings about a sense of wonder (*camatkāra*).
For this very reason, since its two effects consist of the nature of the transitory moods (*anubhāva*), the heart's conviction is that it remains unimpeded for as long as those [moods] persist.
Among these, an example of the *sodbheda* (with disclosure) variety on one side is as follows: “‘Take it! Look at this!
O lady with blossoming eyes, the mistress of the house offers to her dear son the *bora* fruit, marked by the pair of teeth that have just emerged. (138)
"Take it! Look at this!"—with these words, the mistress hands to her beloved a jujube fruit marked by the pair of newly erupted teeth of their son.

Here, through the eyes wide with intense joy, the mistress's intention—that she herself has now become fit for enjoyment because of the son's eruption of teeth—is revealed; yet it is not the husband's intention that is thus disclosed. Thus, this emotion (bhāva) is manifested in one direction only.
An example of *abhitaḥ-sodbheda* (manifested on both sides) is as follows:
“Even while the sun is still above the horizon, the housewife, having taken hold of her husband’s feet, washes them with a smile—even though he does not wish it—as he himself smiles. (139)
"While the sun is still shining, the housewife, laughing, takes hold of her husband's feet—even though he is unwilling—and washes them as he laughs.
Here, the sense is that since the master of the house has arrived home while the sun is still out and the wife is washing his feet, the implication is: "We two must not leave the house today."

And since that emotion is manifested on both sides by laughter, it is "on all sides" (*abhittaḥ*) with its disclosure; whereas this emotion is "on one side" (*ekataḥ*) without disclosure, as for example:
"The drops of dew flying up from the cowherd's wife in the rice field..."
"Even though she is beautiful in every limb, when the cowherd girl of the rice field is scaring away the flocks of parrots, the travelers look only at her eyes. (140)

In this context, regarding the intention of travelers who, due to her extreme beauty, mistake her for a goddess while gazing upon the cowherd girl in the rice field, their observation of her eyes is as follows: "Because she eclipses the rice field, the distinction between a god and a human—namely, whether her feet touch the ground or do not touch it—is not perceived; therefore, we shall observe only her eyes: if she blinks, she is a human woman; if she does not blink, she is a goddess."

Thus, even though this emotion arises only in travelers despite her being beautiful in every limb, it is not manifested here by any action; therefore, on one hand, this emotion is "unmanifested" (*nirudbheda*), and because it is "not manifested here by anything," the meaning is that there is no operation of another word here.
An example of a *nirudbheda* (uninterrupted) *abhitaḥ* (on both sides) [simile] is as follows:
“Having seen the son of Gaṅgā’s husband (Bhīṣma) stationed on the Gomatī river, the wives of the farmers began to cross by a path that was difficult to traverse.
[Seeing the householder’s son standing on the bank of the Godāvarī, the farmer’s daughter began to descend by a path difficult to traverse.

Here, seeing the farmer’s daughter approaching, the householder’s son remained on the bank of the Godāvarī; and upon beholding him, she began her descent by that path so hard to cross. In this regard, their intention was: "By lending us a hand, may our physical union be accomplished."
And since that [state] arises on both sides, it is not pierced here by any action; thus, this state is "unpierced on both sides" (abhito-nirudbheda).
It might be pierced as something "heart-like" (hṛdya) or "subtle" (sūkṣma), but it cannot be pierced in any way from its essential nature (bhāva).
In this regard, they establish this through the following illustrative example concerning the heart (hṛdya): || 44 ||

‘In her heart, she wept bitterly as he, with his head bowed, begged for a kick from her foot; yet he was not struck by her. Here, the underlying meaning (*bhāva*) is that because he requested a kick from her foot with his head while it was whirled about in anger, and because he was not struck by her, [the poet implies] that his beloved dwells within her heart.
And that state of being, which is emerging through longing and weeping, is called "heart-rending" (*sodbheda*);
for the term "heart-rending" (*hṛdyam*) refers to an activity undertaken after one has perceived the presence of a desired object within the confines of the heart.

In that regard, although there is a distinction, nevertheless, being pervaded by the general characteristic of existence (*bhāva-sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), it will be included within that very category; however, that state which is devoid of differentiation is called "subtle" (*sūkṣma*) by them, and from that subtle state, discernible through gestures and physical expressions, another stage (*bhūmikāntara*) arises. (45)
For example:
"Perceiving that her lover was unable to say, 'When shall our union take place? because the place was crowded, the frail woman closed her play-lotus. (143)
Since neither gestures (*iṅgita*) nor facial expressions (*ākāra*) are perceived here due to an inability to speak, this constitutes another stage in the apprehension of emotion (*bhāva*).
Now, one might ask: how does this "subtle" (*sūkṣma*) differ from the previously mentioned "subtle"? To this he says: "not characterized by gestures or expressions.

No gesture or physical change of the lover has been presented that reveals the intention, "When will our union take place? Nor is there any action that corresponds to the intention manifested by the words beginning with "having understood," and so forth.
Otherwise, how could the closing of the play-lotus with reference to him be consistent?
Therefore, this is indeed something else— a subtle state characterized by a specific condition—
suggested here by the closing of the lotus, indicating a union during the night.
"Desiring to console her beloved who was tormented by love.

(144) Here, even though there is both the object of imitation and the imitation itself, they occur only when separated by a role (*bhūmikā*); thus, this very emotion (*bhāva*), being without outward manifestation, is called "subtle" (*sūkṣma*).
He explains the example for the second half [of the verse]: "In this case, because of the closing of the lotuses... and so forth.
If it were thus, then the state of being indicated by a gesture (*iṅgita*) would be established; therefore, he says: "In that case" (*tatra ca*).

The closing of the lotus is the *anukārya* (the original action), while that produced by the fingers of the beloved's hand is the *anukaraṇa* (the imitation). The intention residing in the beloved is: "A meeting will take place at night.
However, the meaning is that the closing [of the lotus] is not an *anukārya* [in this context], for it does not invariably indicate this specific matter.
Perception (*pratyakṣa*) is defined as knowledge born of the senses (*akṣaja*), as well as mental (*mānasa*) knowledge;
likewise, that which arises from self-experience (*svānubhūti*) is spoken of by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*).

(46) Following the discussion on the connection between types of knowledge, there now begins the section on the ornaments (*alaṃkāra*) consisting of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Since other means of valid cognition are rooted in perception, he first states the definition of perception: "Perception," etc.

Direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) is well known as *pratyakṣa*; he states its classification: "born of the sense-organ" (*akṣaja*) means born from the external sense-organ (*akṣa*); "mental" (*mānasa*) means produced by the mind independently of the external senses;
and "self-experience" (*svānubhūti*) refers to that which has arisen from the innate power of consciousness (*cicchakti*).

When the mind is overcome by bodily injury and the like, or when it is set aside by withdrawal (pratyāhāra), a certain knowledge arises that is at times extremely vivid; it cannot be asserted that this has the mind as its basis, but rather it rests upon the power of consciousness (cicchakti) itself. [Objection: But since in the world "directness" (sākṣātkāritā) is well-known only as being produced by the senses, how can that which arises from experience (anubhūti) be so? To this he says: "by way of metaphor" (upacāreṇa).
If directness were restricted to what is produced by the senses, then this would be a mere figurative enumeration.

Now, if the position is that [cognition] occurs even without the sense organ through the power of cultivation (*bhāvanā*) and so forth, then the meaning is that it is indeed primary [in that case]. In that regard, cognition born of the senses (*akṣaja*) is of two kinds:
simultaneous and successive.
An example of their simultaneous occurrence is as follows:

“The group of senses found rest in the honey—which reflected the face of the beloved, was fragrant with the scent of young mango blossoms submerged within it, was delicious, resounded with bees, and was cool. (145)

Here, the simultaneous perception by the sense organs of sight, smell, taste, hearing, and touch—namely, the fragrance, sweetness, pleasantness to the ear, and coolness of the reflections on the surface of the wine—is conveyed.

Since this describes the simultaneous operation of all five senses (smell, taste, sight, touch, and hearing) within a single sentence, simultaneity (*yaugapadya*) brings about aesthetic wonder through its harmony with the sentiment (*rasa*). Thus, it is appropriate to include this as a distinct figure of speech in the section on *alaṃkāra*, as it functions in two ways.
An example of each is as follows:
"With her face cast downward, the young bride gazed slowly at the face of her lover, her modesty melting away very gently as she raised her eyes with lashes slightly trembling. (146)
This is indeed visual;
in the same way, auditory and other types [of perception] should also be cited as examples, and mental perception is likewise twofold.
Regarding their objects, such as pleasure and so forth, and their objects which are previously experienced things— for instance, that which has pleasure and so forth as its object:
"Our [minds] are filled with no small wonder, have not forgotten past events, and are shattered by the fever of a newly arisen fear."
"In a single moment, the mind undergoes a variegation of joy, bliss, and sorrow, broken and joined together.
This has already been explained by that very statement;
thus, the mental [body] is also twofold.

One [instance of recognition] is governed by conjunction-inherence (*saṃyuktasamavāya*), while the other is governed by mental impression (*saṃskāra*); for, through the proximity characterized by mental impression, just as recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) is distinct from memory (*smaraṇa*), so too is this case— therefore, nothing is untenable,
as it is evident even from the mere statement.
The meaning is: if he had not directly perceived [objects such as] wonder and the like, how then could he describe their overflowing intensity?
An example concerning an object experienced through direct perception is as follows:
"In a bedchamber closed off and shrouded in darkness so dense that it could only be pierced by the tip of the point of a needle..."
"And even when my eyes were closed, the beloved's face was clearly manifest.
This too is not difficult to understand, and thus it has not been explained.
By the word "manifest" (vyakta), direct perception is indicated;
for manifestation does not occur through memory, but rather it abides in the self alone,
meaning it relies upon one's own experience.
That which arises from one's own experience is twofold:
false in nature and non-false in nature.
Of these two, that which is false in nature is as follows:
‘Then, about to enter a much deeper darkness, his momentum suddenly broken, he thought with agitation that the sun was falling to the earth and that the ground was covered in a ring of trees.
This [state], not remaining in the senses or in the mind, abides in the Self alone.

An example of that which is not of a false nature (amithyātmaka) is as follows: “O Self, when the yogis—having fixed their minds within the inner consciousness, having restrained their breath, with hair standing on end from joy, and with eyes bathed in tears of rapture—behold You and experience an indescribable bliss, as if plunging into a lake of nectar, they perceive an ineffable reality within; surely that is You. (150)
The fact that this [knowledge] has the self as its object is clearly proclaimed by yogis;

the meaning is that because the knowledge of the self— attained through the power of *nididhyāsana*— has an object well-known only to yogis, people such as ourselves do not perceive it in the same way that yogis do.

He states the definition of inference: "That cognition of the possessor of a mark (liṅgin) which arises from a mark (liṅga) is called inference; it is [of three kinds]: that which is 'prior' (pūrvavat), that which is 'residual' (śeṣavat), and that which is 'seen through generality' (sāmānyatodṛṣṭa). (47)

"From the mark" (*liṅgāt*): when the pervasion (*vyāpti*), characterized by the inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) between that which [is the mark] and that [which is to be proven], as well as the property-of-the-subject (*pakṣadharmatā*)—consisting in its occurrence within the subject (*pakṣa*), which is the locus of the doubtful property to be proven—are apprehended, then the cognition of that [probandum] arising therefrom is inference (*anumāna*). For example, fire from smoke; for that [smoke], having been established as being of such a kind, indicates the presence of fire of that same kind.
In this context, that from which cognition arises is the *liṅga* (logical mark) or sign;
the meaning is that it indicates the property (*dharma*) in the subject (*pakṣa*) as qualified by pervasion (*vyāpti*).
It is so called because it possesses another *liṅga* as its indicator.

Inference is threefold—based on what has been previously perceived (*pūrvavat*), based on what remains (*śeṣavat*), and based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*)—and since this has already been explained by the author himself later in the text, it is not elaborated here.
This [inference] is divided into two types according to the difference between its result and its causal complex; separate examples will serve to clarify their specific forms. || 48 ||
Regarding the phrase "by the totality of the result" (*phalasāmagryā*):

although it has been stated that "cognition is inference," nevertheless, its common [definition] must be expressed as being primarily concerned with non-statement in some cases, and in others, primarily concerned with the statement of the consideration of the inferential mark (*liṅgaparāmarśa*) which functions as the instrument. Thus, the aforementioned distinction arises; for the word *anumāna* is derived either from the suffix *lyuṭ* in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*), or from the suffix *lyuṭ* in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe*).

The meaning is that in the first case there is the result, while in the second there is the non-production of the causal complex; since the predominance of the introductory formulation is difficult to grasp, he says: "It is simply an example.
Among those [types of inference], where one infers the effect after having perceived the cause, that is *pūrvavat* (inference based on the prior), as for example:
“With clouds scattered and trembling, and forest breezes fragrant with *kuṭaja*, *arjuna*, and *nīpa* flowers—alas, this season has arrived; woe, the wives of travelers are destroyed!
Here, from the rainy season as the cause, the death of the separated women, which is the effect, is inferred.

Therefore, because this cause exists here previously, it is described as "as before" (*pūrvavat*); the meaning of the sentence is that the tenth stage— characterized by the absence of the effect— is known [to exist] in the case of the wives of travelers.

Therefore, the intention is that this poem places its entire burden upon the presentation of the result (*phala*). By using the suffix of completion (*niṣṭhā-pratyaya*), it is illuminated that if the arrival of the clouds occurs, then the destruction of the traveler’s wife—which had already begun—is perceived as if it were already accomplished.
That in which the cause is inferred by seeing the effect is called *śeṣavat* (inference from the remainder), as for example: [the inference of rain from the rising of clouds].
"Surely you have come with contempt and fallen at her feet;
otherwise, how could there be this row of tilaka-marks made with lac-dye upon your forehead? (152).
Here, the falling at the feet, which is the cause, is inferred from the row of tilaka-marks made with lac-dye, which is the effect.
Therefore, because there is a remaining effect here, it is called "residual" (*śeṣavat*);

otherwise, how could this not be a case of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*)? Rather, such a specific row of lac-dye dots on the hero's forehead is necessarily connected to the falling of a woman's foot.

Furthermore, the knowledge of a row of dots of liquid lac does not taste as sweet as the knowledge—which is the resulting fruit—of the inferred bowing of the feet of a rival woman; for that [latter] nourishes the height of deception by manifesting the envy directed toward the rival.
That in which neither the effect nor the cause is perceived, but only the mere inseparable relation (*avinābhāva*) is understood, is "inference from general observation" (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*), as in:
"The clouds thunder in the sky, the barley has blossomed, and the peacocks have begun to dance."
"The clouds thunder in the sky, the *nīpa* trees are in full bloom, and the peacocks have begun their dance; the moonlight has vanished, O friend—the rainy season has arrived. (153)

In this case, the rainy season is inferred in a general manner through the thundering of clouds and other such phenomena that are invariably concomitant with it; thus, this is an inference based on general observation (*sāmānyato-dṛṣṭa*).
These examples pertain to the view that the word "inference" (*anumāna*) denotes the result (*phala*) when used as a bhāva-sādhana, namely: "they are thundering."

In this case, there is an inference based on temporal conditions such as the thundering of clouds; through this, the relationship of cause and effect is established. For here, the cognition of the thundering clouds and so forth does not produce aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*) in the same way when it is independent, as it does when it is bound to the cognition of a rainy night. Indeed, when that [night] is known, it generates either the eagerness to don elegant attire—such as the *ketakī* flower used as an ear-ornament—or the longing for the arrival of a traveler who is the hero of the story; thus, the emphasis lies entirely upon the result.

Furthermore, when the word *anumāna* has the sense of an instrument (*karaṇasādhana*), then by the word *anumāna*— meaning "that by which something is inferred"— the aforementioned logical mark (*liṅga*) is expressed, as it has been said:
"That which is connected with the object to be inferred (*anumeya*) and is well-known (*prasiddha*) in what is similar to it..."
And in the absence of that [subject], whatever does not exist cannot be a logical mark (*liṅga*) that brings about inference.
[The phrase] "by means of the inferable" means by means of the subject (*pakṣa*), because it is precisely that which is to be inferred as possessing the property to be proven (*sādhya*).

As it has been said: "This very same thing, being of a dual nature, is held to be both the object of inference and the means of inference; it is the object of inference by way of its well-known part, and the indicator by way of its established part."
"Established in that which is associated with it"— that is, established pre-eminently (prasiddha) in what is associated with the probandum (sādhyānvita),
meaning it has been cognized as being pervaded (vyāpyatayādhigata).
In the absence of that [the probandum], because it leads to the inference of the non-existence of the probandum, it is therefore a *liṅga* (logical mark);
this is as in the case of *pūrvavat*. For example:
“O friend, with your crooked words and with a sidelong glance cast by your powerful, playful smile, you will cover the head of the family in ashes. (155)

"By her smile, which casts a lingering glance and is turned slightly aside"—here, by means of such indirect speech (*vakrokti*) characterized by this kind of smile, one infers the cause from the effect, namely: "You are defiling my family right before my eyes. This is what is called *pūrvavat* (the "as-before" type) in the context of the *sāmagrī* (causal complex) category.
It is so called because it is "possessing the prior" (*pūrvavat*).

That which possesses a prior cause as its inferential indicator is a "pūrvavat" mark; indeed, when that [object] is to be inferred, it is called "pūrvavat" because it relies upon the prior cause by virtue of being the object of the cognition of the mark—
the meaning of this being expressed by the locative case.
Regarding the phrase "by way of cause":

for instance, just as a crooked speech or a laugh arising from the natural propriety of a charming woman imparts beauty by virtue of its power of suggestion (*dhvanana*) through its subject matter, it is not so with a breach of character expressed in words; this is perfectly clear to those who know the seal of literary aesthetics (*sāhitya-mudrā-vid*), as in the following example: [Example omitted in source] In the remaining cases, it is as follows: [Example omitted in source] Thus, the meaning is that while a transgression of conduct may be suggested through the power of resonance, it does not possess the same aesthetic splendor when it is explicitly stated in words. This is a well-known principle among connoisseurs of literature.
‘The mango bud is not seen today, nor does the wind carrying the fragrance of the Malaya mountains blow; O friend, this is the month of spring, yet it causes such longing. (156)
"O friend, it is the month of spring that has arrived, since my heart is filled with longing.
Here, because the cause, spring, is inferred from the effect, characterized by longing, this is called *śeṣavat* (inference from the remainder) within the category of *sāmagrī* (causal complex).
Thus it is said.
In this context, the longing for the mango blossom and the Malaya breeze is a source of wonder;
for it is a matter witnessed by those of sensitive heart that the extraordinary pride established in the expectation of a beloved’s imminent arrival is not matched by the arrival itself.
Thus, it should be understood in the case of the example of *sāmānyato dṛṣṭa* (inference based on general observation).
An example of *sāmānyato dṛṣṭa* is as follows:
"Appearing first, [the sight] causes the heart of the beloved to breathe with relief within."

"Like a flash of lightning appearing before rain to a young peacock scorched by the summer heat—so too, this Kāmandakī, being perceived for the first time like lightning, leads one to infer Mālatī’s arrival through their inseparable connection. This is an instance of *sāmānyato dṛṣṭa* (inference based on general observation) within the category of *sāmagrī* (the collection of causes).
Furthermore, that which is the word of a reliable person (*āptavacana*) is to be known by the designation of *āgama* (scriptural authority).
That [verbal testimony] is threefold: superior, middling, and inferior.
Regarding the phrase "the word of a reliable person" (āptavacana), a reliable person (āpta) is one who speaks words that correspond to reality.
The highest [type of dharma] has its root in the sacred revelation (śruti);
for that very reason, it is declared to be necessarily to be performed.
The intermediate [type] has its root in beginningless worldly convention (lokavyavahāra); this will be clarified by the statement that such [dharma] is not necessarily to be performed.
Among those that accord with external results of both kinds, the inferior is [the former],
while the superior is of two types:
that which has the form of an injunction and that which has the form of a prohibition.
The positive form of these two is as follows:
"Learn self-restraint, charity, and compassion; this thundering cloud says, 'Give!'—the divine voice declares: 'Be compassionate, give, and restrain yourselves. (158)

And here, this divine voice follows after it: "O you who thunder, bestow [dayadhvam]! meaning "be compassionate (dayadhvam), give (datta), and be self-controlled (damyata). According to the Śruti, "One should learn these three: self-control (dama), charity (dāna), and compassion (dayā)," this authoritative statement in the form of an injunction is expressed through the thundering of the clouds as an imitation of various sounds with the word "dadadhva. Thus, under the guise of those three qualities, the cloud speaks.

"Be compassionate, give, and be self-controlled"— this divine voice from the Veda culminates in the injunction that self-control, charity, and compassion must be practiced; here, "self-control" (dama) refers to the restraint of the cognitive senses,
while "charity" (dāna) and "compassion" (dayā) are well known.
He shows the foundational scripture (*śruti*) here with this negation-form:
"O friend, let this young brahmin be stopped; he wishes to say something more, his upper lip quivering."

"Not only he who speaks ill of the great, but even he who hears it from him shares in that sin. (159) Here, because the friend’s proficiency has been increased by the restatement of the prohibition stated in the second half of the verse, this instruction for warding off the censuring boy—whose purport lies in the sentence-meaning "one must not speak ill of the great"—is an *āgama* (scriptural authority) in the form of a prohibition.
Both of these [the *arthāpatti* and the *āgama*] are "superior" (*uttama*) because they must necessarily be put into practice.

Now, one might object: "Since [the verse] beginning with 'Not only he who speaks ill of the great' is a statement of a present fact (*vartamānāpadeśa*), how can it have the nature of an injunction? To this he replies: "In this case, by means of the second half-verse, which is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) censuring slanderous speech, an injunction of prohibition is inferred; thus, the verbal formulation 'The great should not be spoken ill of' is derived.
This constitutes the middle [section], which is twofold.
[There are two types: that with a specified speaker and that with an unspecified speaker.
Of these, the first is as follows:
"Ah, this worldly verse appears to me as auspicious."
"Joy comes to a living man even after a hundred years.

(160) Here, the meaning "a living man beholds what is auspicious" is indicated by the speaker himself; thus, since all sentences ultimately resolve into injunctions and prohibitions, this authoritative statement—"here, a living man"—takes the form of an injunction that one should strive for the preservation of life.
This is an ancient worldly verse;

because the scripture beginning with "eti jīvantaṃ" (he follows the living one) is rooted in this, here too— as previously explained— a mandatory injunction is inferred through a commendatory explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) that one should strive for life.
This is what was stated regarding "all sentences," as in the second example:
"A *piśāca* dwells in the die, the Sun-god in the *picumanda* tree, and a *yakṣa* in the banyan tree."
“Fortune rests upon the lotus; Gaurī dwells on the Madhūka tree.
(161) This is an *aitihya* (traditional lore), handed down through an unbroken succession of worldly renown from time immemorial, whose speaker is not specified.

Here too, since all statements ultimately resolve into injunctions or prohibitions, there occurs an ellipsis [of a prohibition] such as: “Therefore, one should not resort to the *akṣa* tree; one should not cut the *picumanda*; one should not fell the *vaṭa*; one should not wear a lotus on the head; one should not touch the *madhūka* with the foot.”
This scripture, which takes the form of a prohibition—
that neither of these two must necessarily be performed— is intermediate;
thus, it is one whose speaker is not specified.
By this it is shown that *aitihya* (tradition) is included within *āgama* (testimony) itself, because it is well known as such specifically as testimony whose speaker is unknown. Here too,
as before, injunctions are inferred from reports such as "dwelling of *piśācas*" and so forth.
The inferior [action] is of two kinds:
that which is motivated by desire and that which is prohibited.
Of these, the motivated is as follows:
“Oil prepared with the powder and decoction of *muṇḍitikā*, when administered as a drink or an errhine (*nāvana*), makes even the breasts of women with drooping bosoms full and uplifted. (162)
"Even for those whose breasts have fallen, oil makes the breasts full and elevated.

This is the aforementioned authoritative statement (āptavacana) regarding a desired result (kāmya), which takes the form of an injunction (vidhi); [it is stated thus: "By means of a shaven head... and so forth.
The decoction (kaṣāya) or infusion (kvātha) of Muṇḍitikā and Alambuṣā, used as water for nasal administration (nāvana),
serves as a snuff (nasya).
It is called "kāmya" (desirable) because it is performed only by those who possess the desire for full and elevated breasts;
as for what is prohibited, for example:
"In childhood we desire children, in youth we desire young men, and even in old age we desire the aged for the rite of marriage; such is our custom.
You have begun to destroy this lineage by an untimely decree; O daughter, in our family there has never been anyone stained by the mark of unchastity.
This is authoritative speech in the form of a prohibition, which is indeed prohibited [by the context].
"Both of these [options] should not be practiced due to faults such as being mixed with those who commit root sins; thus, what you have begun is base.

In this passage, the explicit prohibitive injunction—"a courtesan must not be one who possesses the character of a virtuous woman"—explains the state of being base (*jaghanyatva*). "Both of these [options] should be [avoided] by those who commit root sins"—here, analogy (*upamāna*) is of two kinds: the cognition of the similar from the similar.
The first [type of recollection] would occur regarding an object already experienced, while the second occurs regarding an object not yet experienced;
thus do the Mīmāṃsakas describe it here, [stating] "from a similar [object]."
Comparison (*upamāna*) also produces a cognition regarding an object not present [to the senses] through similarity; its meaning is that "similarity" refers to the knowledge of similarity.
That is to say, the similarity that is being cognized is itself the means of comparison (*upamāna*). Why is this so? To this he says:

because it produces a cognition regarding an object that is not present (*asaṃnikṛṣṭa*) and which consists of another similar thing, therefore the apprehension of the similar from the similar is *upamāna*.
Knowledge does not arise from a similar object that has not been previously experienced, because that would lead to an over-extension of the principle;
therefore, for the Naiyāyikas, this [knowledge] has only an experienced object as its domain, whereas for them, comparison (*upamāna*) has only an unexperienced object as its domain.

To explain: when a forest-dweller is asked by a city-dweller and replies, "As is a cow, so is a gavaya," then for that city-dweller—who recollects the meaning of the statement of analogy (*atideśavākya*) and knows the cow as the counter-correlate of similarity—the cognition of the similarity of the cow in the gavaya is the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) known as comparison (*upamāna*). Subsequently, the knowledge of the relationship between a name and the object named, namely "this [animal] is denoted by the word *gavaya*," arises; this is comparison (*upamiti*). In this context, the meaning is that from the cognition of similarity—which exists in the mind as revolving around the similar object—there arises the knowledge of the relationship between the name and the named with respect to the similar gavaya.
The examples and so forth have been explained by the very words [of the commentary].
Of those two, that which has for its object what has been previously experienced is as follows:
"Striking his chest, which was surrendered by all his vital breaths, the fiercely radiant one (the sun) shattered it into a massive fragment through that impact."

"Thus, with thousands of lightnings, he quickly turned the sky into a thunderbolt, and those loud laughs of his master, tawny with the glow of the vajra-fire, [were likewise]. (164) In this passage, the Mīmāṃsakas describe *upamāna* (analogy) as having an object that has been previously experienced, such as the perception of a Rāvaṇa messenger—who beholds the sky filled with thousands of flashes of light released from the bow of Dhūrjaṭi when it was drawn and broken by Rāma's hand—as having a cognition of similarity toward the master’s own loud laughs, which were witnessed by him as they rent the chest of the Lord like the crashing of vajra-shards and pervaded the firmament.
An example of *upamāna* having an object not previously experienced is as follows:

“Know that Rohiṇī is that cluster of stars within this circle of luminaries which has assumed the shape of a cart. In this case, for one who has received the authoritative instruction that the form of the cluster of Rohiṇī stars is exactly like the form of a cart, the realization of the relationship between the name and the named— namely, “This is that cart of Rohiṇī”— upon seeing the circle of stars in that shape, is what the Naiyāyikas propose as *upamāna* (analogy), even though its object has not been previously experienced [through perception].
Therefore, by the reason of being generators of cognition of unreal objects,
dramatic gesture (*abhinaya*), painting, seals, images, and so forth, are not distinct from this [category]. Among these, dramatic gesture is as follows:
‘The castor-oil plant, its leaves protruding through the gap in the fence, seems to announce to the young men that in this house lives a farmer’s wife with breasts of such-and-such a size. (166)

"In this house lives the wife of a plowman with breasts of such size. Here, although the fullness of the plowman’s wife's breasts is directly indicated by the arrangement of the lotus petals—which resembles a mimetic gesture (*abhinaya*) of hands with fingers extended upward to suggest the great expanse of her bosom—the cognition of a connection to the fullness of breasts experienced in the past arises even when the object itself is not present. Therefore, this mimetic gesture is conceived as a *upamāna* (means of knowledge through comparison) whose object is a previously experienced thing;
thus it is called *vaivivara*.

The fullness of the breasts of a farmer’s wife, repeatedly experienced by village youths whose internal organs were bound to no other object during the raising of the pestle and so forth, ascends to the intellect upon the mere sight of castor-leaf petals bearing holes of a corresponding shape; yet that cognition resides in the middle of the Mīmāṃsaka’s definition of analogy.
For how can the arrangement of the castor-leaf petals be the "representation" (abhineyatā)?
For representation is indeed imitation (anukāra).
And since that [shadow] cannot exist there, he says: "resembling a hand-gesture" (*hastābhinayasaṃnibhā*).

The meaning is this: the reflection of the extension of another object by means of the configuration of a hand with fingers extended upward is well-known in the world; here too, because the expansion of the castor-oil leaf is seen, it arises as if intercepted by that very [leaf].
An example of painting is as follows:
“In a portrait drawn by a slender woman trembling with curiosity, one girl, having first depicted a discus below, draws the son of Suparṇa;
then another, her hand perspiring, quickly wipes this away and draws a flowery bow and a sea-monster above it. (167)

In this context, when for one who has previously experienced the sight of the hero, a cognition arises that "he is such-and-such" merely from the display of a painted image of his form, and when—by way of concealment—there occurs a recognition of two figures exactly like him, such as Viṣṇu and Kāma seen in a temple or similar place, then this [recognition] has as its object a thing already experienced.
However, when for one who has not previously experienced the sight of the hero and so forth, there is an instruction from a reliable authority in this manner:

In this way, Viṣṇu becomes one who has Garuḍa as his banner and holds the discus in his hand; in this way, Kāma becomes one who has the Makara as his emblem and the flower-bow. Just as these two are, so too is the object of your desire. However, since he lacks [the symbols] such as Garuḍa, at a later time, upon seeing the forms of those very things depicted in a painting, someone like me might paint him, thinking, "This is my beloved. Thinking, "I shall conceal him by means of the emblems of Viṣṇu," she places the Garuḍa and the discus in the hands at the lower part of the picture, which serve as the banner-hands.

Then another woman, desiring to understand [his form], both concealing and revealing it, wishing to describe his appearance which resembled that of the God of Love, drew a flowery bow in her hand and a sea-monster above it.

Regarding this form and its object, the cognitions of the people concerning the relationship between name and named—such as "this is Viṣṇu" or "this is Kāma"—are what is called a "picture" (*ālekhyam*), an analogy whose object is a previously experienced thing; thus she says, "This is your picture."

The word *tanvī* (emaciated) suggests that she sustains herself with great difficulty by diverting her mind through the contemplation of painted images and the like, being distressed by the failure to attain him;

yet it is not that she merely seeks to preserve her life, but rather, being agitated by the curiosity to behold your form, she reveals even her hidden intention through the creation of this portrait— this is what is suggested by the words *kautūhala-taraṅgita* (agitated by curiosity) and *ekā* (alone).

She, who has heard in the scriptures in many ways of the son of Devakī—the object of Rādhā’s affection, the subduer of the three worlds, and one naturally delicate—now perceives his divine nature as being inconsistent with such unrestrained suppliability; for by her, the bow and the makara, which are the emblems of the flower-arrowed god whose excellence of fortune surpasses the three worlds, have been drawn. This is suggested by the words "then," "with perspiring hands," and "quickly."
In this example, he demonstrates both types of comparison (*upamāna*).

First, according to the Mīmāṃsaka position: having seen a slender woman’s portrait that has been defaced, a certain woman recognizes the hero she previously experienced; and because the similarity is indistinguishable, she also realizes that Kṛṣṇa and Kāma [are similar]. In that case, cognition derived from a similar object constitutes *upamāna*.

In the view of the Naiyāyikas, when a woman has previously experienced passion for a hero in general, yet does not know his specific physical beauty, she hears the instruction of a reliable person (*āpta*) stating, "Your beloved is exactly like Kṛṣṇa and Kāma in such-and-such a form. Subsequently, having apprehended the form in a painting, she acquires the cognition that it is denoted by those respective words; this is *upamāna*.

To the question of how words such as "Kāma" can be applied to a painting, he says: "In the form"—the meaning is that it is through the arrangement of lines and strokes, according to the analogy of a "painted horse" (*citraturaganyāya*).
An example of *mudrā* (a seal or impression):

“With eyes wide with wonder as if startled, those women beheld upon the pure sands superhuman footprints on the ground, marked by the signs of the banner and the wheel belonging to the victorious one. (168)

In this case, because one perceives the footprints of Arjuna (Jiṣṇu) marked with the discus and banner, the cognition of the relationship between the name and the named— namely, "these are non-human footprints"— is simply called "comparison" (*upamāna*), even though its object is a thing not previously experienced;
and even that inferential knowledge which arises when Arjuna’s feet are not seen, such as "that [man] of the deer-eyed women was like this," is likewise based solely on the meaning of comparison,
as he said:
"Moreover, there is also similarity between the mark (liṅga) and the possessor of the mark (liṅgin) even in inference, as when a hunchbacked foot is inferred by the word 'hunchback'.
[Thus ends] "Sacakitā" (The Startled).
[Objection: Is it not the case that here there appears to be an inference of Viṣṇu’s feet based on the foot-print? How, then, can this be included within analogy (*upamāna*)? To this he says:

"And even though... The meaning is that although there is no specific connection between the general term "foot" and the specific foot [of Viṣṇu], a cognition of the similar arises from the similar, and by means of that [cognition], such a designation occurs.
He confirms this very point with the agreement of the Master Dārḍhya: "And also..."
An example of a reflection is as follows: “Beholding her lover seated behind her in the mirror as she looked upon her own reflection, she performed various actions out of bashfulness. (170)

In this regard, when the apprehension of the relationship occurs in this manner—namely, that one's own face is of such-and-such a nature as the reflection seen in a mirror—and consequently, even though one's own face is not directly perceived, there arises the cognition "my face is like this," this [cognition] has for its object a thing already experienced. Furthermore, when, through the instruction of a reliable person, it is understood that a reflection in a mirror or similar medium is exactly like the object itself, and then, upon seeing the reflection of a beloved, there arises the designation "this is the reflection of my beloved"—this apprehension of the relationship between a name and the named object likewise has for its object a thing not previously experienced.

However, when one who has previously experienced seeing her own face in paintings and the like perceives a reflection and recognizes, "My face is similar to this," or when one who has seen the form of a beloved recognizes, upon seeing the form of a reflection, "This form is dear to me," and perceives that since the arising of a reflection was observed in the presence of a reflection, "Therefore, it must exist here in its proximity"— that which consists of such a transformation of shame is what they call the "reflection" (*pratibimba*) as an object of comparison (*upamāna*) for what was previously experienced,
[as stated in the phrase] "in the presence of a reflection."
He shows the purpose for which inference was explained as a consequence: "the transformation of shame" (*vrīḍāvikāra*).
For this very reason, there is a summary of the primary [subject] alone:
"an object perceived through perception and other means which is not so established."
They call that *arthāpatti* (presumption) which makes known another meaning.

He defines *arthāpatti*: *arthāpatti* is the knowledge produced by the cognition of the impossibility of accounting for a fact established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) such as perception in any other way.

And since a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that makes known an object not [otherwise] established consists of six types—namely, the divisions beginning with perception (*pratyakṣa*)—presumption (*arthāpatti*), which is preceded by those [six], likewise becomes sixfold.
