They call that "presumption" which makes known another object;
thus it is clear that presumption is simply the comprehension of another object.
Because it is preceded by all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is declared to be sixfold through its divisions, such as "preceded by perception" (*pratyakṣapūrvikā*)—both singly and manifold.
Regarding the term "singly": [it refers to each individual means of valid cognition].
How is it that [the lineage] is sixfold— being sometimes preceded by a single authority and sometimes preceded by multiple authorities?
Therefore it was said: "by means of the distinctions such as 'preceded by perception' and so forth.
This has been explained.
Among those [types of inference], that which is preceded by perception is as follows:
"O slender-waisted one, it can be determined that a waist exists for you, solely because of the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the presence of the weight of your breasts.

Here, no waist is perceived between the weight of the breasts and the hips, yet the presence of the weight of the breasts is observed; thus, this presence of the weight of the breasts, being otherwise inexplicable, makes known the supporting waist which is not perceived.
This presumption based on perception (*pratyakṣapūrvikārthāpatti*) is what is intended here as a single category;

for this too occurs frequently in the following manner: that middle term which is obtained through presumption is itself incapable of performing its function without the power of retention (*dhāraṇaśakti*); thus, the power of that [middle term] is also postulated.
This is "presumption based on presumption" (*arthāpattipūrvikārthāpatti*).

Furthermore, this absence of perception in the case of the neutral conceptualization of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti-vikalpa*), being impossible through any other means, expresses the excellence of [the subject's] plumpness and emaciation;
and this is an "inconsistency preceded by non-existence" (*abhāvapūrvikānupapatti*).
Moreover, this is not derived from the words themselves here, but is understood through the force of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha-sāmarthya*).

In this context, "the weight of the breasts" refers to the state of the breasts' heaviness, which is apprehended through direct perception. Since that state is logically untenable without a supporting substrate, it leads to the postulation of a waist;
and that postulation is presumptive testimony (arthāpatti).

Regarding the phrase "not being perceived," [the author] says "this too" (iyam api), meaning that otherwise, when an object has already been grasped by perception, for what purpose would there be presumptive testimony (arthāpatti)?
In this very example, it can be explained in many ways. Thus he says: "this too."

In the Mīmāṃsaka system, potency (*śakti*) is eternal and beyond the senses; furthermore, since non-existence (*abhāva*) is apprehended only through non-existence, the perception of the middle is preceded by the means of knowledge that is non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*).
The point is that the eye, being overwhelmed by extraordinary power (*adbhutaprabhāva*), is incapable of perceiving the middle even when it is nearby.
That which is preceded by perception and other means occurs many times, as for example:
“Having beheld this incomparable form of yours, O tremulous-eyed one, we imagine you to be the primordial Creator, the teacher of the principles of the arts. (172)

In this regard, the statements "this form of yours is peerless" clearly manifest both a basis in direct perception (*pratyakṣapūrvatā*) and a basis in non-existence (*abhāvapūrvatā*). Therefore, this [inference] occurs many times; here too, this peerlessness of form—which is otherwise inexplicable—establishes for oneself the fact of being created by a teacher who knows the principles of time (*kālātattvaguru*). That knowledge of comparison (*upamāna*) regarding forms such as Urvaśī or Ahalyā, which serves as the premise for that, is preceded by it; and that status of being a teacher who knows the principles of time, which is postulated for the creator through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), is itself preceded by the postulation of such a power. Thus, this is an instance of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) preceded by presumptive testimony based on comparison (*upamāna*).

That [agency] too—whether it be the status of being the teacher of the *kalā*-tattva or the state of being the substratum for such power—belongs to the Creator (*vedhas*) who performs that [action]; and since this is postulated by an ignorant person through either inference or scripture, this presumption (*arthāpatti*) is preceded by inference.
Furthermore, these four [factors] are not merely verbal here, but are understood through the force of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha-sāmarthya*) as being "unparalleled."

Form devoid of the image is indeed distinguished; therein, the function of negation pertains to the qualifying aspect (*viśeṣaṇāṃśa*), while perception pertains to the qualified aspect (*viśeṣyāṃśa*).

He provides the explanation here as well, as before: "In this case too," the cognition of the absence of the image is preceded by the cognition of the image. And the image is similarity (*sādṛśya*); and that [similarity] is to be known through the perception of two similar words. Thus, there is first the means of knowledge called comparison (*upamāna*).
An example of that which is preceded by inference taken individually is as follows:
“The fever of love has been indicated by the bristling of her cheeks; O friends, it tells me that her mind is incessantly attached to her beloved. (173)

In this context, the fever of love inferred from the horripilation on her cheeks is logically untenable (anupapanna) without constant attachment to the beloved; thus, this is an *arthāpatti* preceded by inference (*anumāna*).
There are many instances of [this type] preceded by comparison (*upamāna*) and so forth, such as:
"Having seen that your face and the moon are equal, we conceive this [similarity]."
"The mutual exchange of beauty belongs to these two alone.

(174) Here, the fact that the moon of your face and [the real] moon are equal is understood through the very words as being preceded by both an implied comparison (*arthāpatti*) and direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Furthermore, the mutual transfer of beauty—which is obtained through the impossibility of their similarity [otherwise]—is likewise not possible without a Creator of such a kind; thus, here too, this must be understood from the power of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha-sāmarthya*), as in the previous case.
An example of that which is preceded by the absence of one [of the two] is as follows:
“This face of the fair-browed woman, bereft of its smile, reveals that her mind has become a vessel for the punishment of her lover’s offense. (175)
In this context, by the phrase "of the fair-browed one" (*subhruvaḥ*), the possession of all auspicious marks by Vilāsavatī is indicated.

Since the absence of such a woman’s curved, playful smile is logically untenable, it necessitates the postulation of a cause other than grief; thus, this is an instance of presumption based on negation (*abhāvapūrvikārthāpatti*). To the objection—"How can this be presumption, given that the state of smiling can be accounted for otherwise?"—the author replies: "In this context, 'of the fair-browed one'."
In many cases, it is preceded by presumption (*arthāpatti*) and other means of cognition, as for example:
"Having seen this woman who is so full of grace, we know that Love is her teacher in play; and we know that Love has taken up residence in the mind of this deer-eyed girl. (176)

Here, in the word *vibhramiṇīm*, the suffix denoting possession (*matvarthīya*) is used in the sense of praise; by this, the excellence of her amorous gestures (*vibhramas*) is indicated. Since such gestures are impossible [for others] except through instruction from another, they inform the Teacher, Manmatha.
This indicates that he resides either in front of her or at her side, even though he is not perceived there.
This [first] is presumption based on perception (*pratyakṣapūrvikā arthāpatti*), and this second is presumption based on presumption (*arthāpattipūrvikā arthāpatti*).

Furthermore, because it is known from the instruction of a reliable authority (*āpta-upadeśa*) that such a state occurs in the minds of amorous women, this very [presumption] is also one based on scripture (*āgamapūrvikā*).
Having raised the doubt that it might be explained otherwise, he explains it further below with the words: "In this case, she is deluded."
He states the meaning of the possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*): "In the sense of praise.

Non-existence (*asattā*), which is the absence of things, is what is denoted; it is accepted here as being sixfold, according to the divisions of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and the rest. || 54 ||
He defines non-existence (abhāva):

"Non-existence" refers to prior non-existence and subsequent non-existence; thus, antecedent non-existence and the others are established precisely in the form of non-existence. Even in mutual non-existence (itaretarābhāva), the non-existence of one thing in the form of another consists in its being of the nature of non-existence.
Antecedent non-existence and the others are the four previously mentioned.
Together with absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) and mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*), there are six types of non-existence;
we shall explain the distinction between those two later.
Among them, antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) is as follows:

‘I remember the heaven without the *pārijāta* tree, the chest of the Slayer of Madhu bereft of the splendor of the *kaustubha* gem, and the slope of Mount Harajaṭā with its moon no longer eclipsed. (177)

I remember the moon, not yet deluded by its fullness, at the time of the churning of the ocean, and the mass of Shiva’s matted hair; [and I remember] heaven as being without the *pārijāta* tree— this explains prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) through the very words used.

Just as in the case of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) preceded by non-existence, the instrument was stated to be the inference of difference (*bhedānumāna*), so it should be understood here as well;
for the prior non-existence of the *pārijāta* tree is clearly of the nature of an object of cognition (*prameya*),
since non-existence is cognized only through non-existence itself.
In the case of perception, even though sound is not mentioned as its instrument, its status as a suitable means of valid cognition is understood;
likewise, this should be inferred by oneself for the subsequent cases as well.
For example, regarding non-existence through destruction (pradhvaṃsābhāva):
“Fortitude has set, movement has ceased, song is gone, the season is without festival; the purpose of ornaments is past, and my bed is utterly empty today.
(178) An example of mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*) is as follows:

‘Even though a person knows that the lotus on the ear is not his eye, nor is the eye the lotus on the ear, he nevertheless perceives the length of his eyes. An example of absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) is as follows:

‘Whatever is one’s own essence, that he gives away—what is there to marvel at in this? Yet even that which was previously non-existent, namely the misfortune of your co-wives, has been given by you. (180)
Indeed, misfortune was bestowed by her even upon her co-wives.
Others, however, explain it differently as absolute non-existence, as follows:—
"Be gracious; O fierce one, immediately release this anger residing in your mind.
Even toward one who has merely been seen by you, your wrath there becomes like a flower in the sky.

Relying on the view that absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) is a specific kind of non-existence characterized by the absence [of an object] at all three times (past, present, and future) in a location other than where it is perceived, absolute non-existence is thus illustrated as falling within the fourfold classification [of non-existence].
Now, he demonstrates absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*), which is the specific type appropriate to the fifth absence— introducing it with "others, however":
other [schools], such as the Saugatas and others,
hold that absolute non-existence is an absence whose counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) is absolutely non-existent.
Just as "the non-existence of a sky-flower" is a clear example,
so too is the absence of capacity— for instance:
"How could the birth of such beauty possibly occur among human women?"
‘No light flickering with radiance arises upon the surface of the earth.
These six [factors] have already been explained by their very names:
the absence of capacity (sāmarthya) and the absence of fitness (yogyatā).
In this very form, having attained the state of being a flavor (rasa), it is apprehended;
even the absence of an absence is indeed an absence, as for example, prior non-existence and destruction.
‘The mango blossoms of the garden have not yet burst open;
let a libation of water with sesame seeds be offered to the wives of travelers.
This refers to their non-existence.

It has been stated previously that being the very object of the conventional usage of "non-existence" is the defining characteristic of such a thing, just as in the case of the prior non-existence of destruction:
"The mortal world would not be deprived of heaven, nor would its beloved people die beforehand, if..."
An example of the negation of destruction (*pradhvaṃsadhvaṃsa*) is as follows:
"The purpose of heaven has indeed ceased; yet if he is dead, he lives only while alive.
Here, the death of a beloved person is a case of destruction, which is negated by the particle *nañ*; however, that negation itself consists essentially in prior non-existence (*prāgasattva*).

"If he were dead"—meaning that after death there would be non-existence, which is his *pradhvaṃsa* (posterior negation); and although this is impossible, it is suggested by the word "api" (even/if) as a cause for [the king's] longing, thereby ascending to the rank of a poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*).
An example of the *pradhvaṃsa* of a *prāgabhāva* (prior negation) is as follows:
"O Lord, there is nothing whatsoever of the Kāñcī region that has not been obtained by you in every way..."
"Let this hand of yours extend even to her waist, though it is naturally slender.

By the term "destruction of prior non-existence" (*pradhvaṃsa-prāgabhāva*), the destruction [of the body] by death is indicated; the absence of that [destruction] is expressed by the whole [phrase], while the absence of even one who has been born is expressed by the distinct [term].
An example of the non-existence of destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*) is as follows:

“Having somehow returned from her journey abroad, she has once again fallen into doubt; for who indeed is able to shut the doors of fate against a living being that is facing its final ripening? (186)
By the phrase "how could there be the destruction of destruction," the tenth stage during exile is indicated; by the phrase "the passing away of that [destruction] is the destruction of destruction,
which is reunion," its own destruction is further indicated.
The rest is easy to understand.
The absence of mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*) is as follows:
"Even though the teaching is weighty, appoint me as you wish to a task that must be performed."
"Do not think of me as being other than Dhanañjaya, for this wealth is the wealth of your purpose.
As for the negation of absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) and the negation of incapacity (*sāmarthyābhāva*), the negation of destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*) is illustrated thus:
"Unattainable by those who have not accumulated merit, difficult to reach, the mother of fruit whose dust has been shaken away..."
"This attainment of the sight of you is equal to a rain from a cloudless sky.
These [examples] were not explained because they are not difficult to understand.
Now he states the number of the figures of speech (alaṃkāra) whose meanings have been discussed:

These figures of sense (arthālaṃkāras) are also said to be twenty-four in number for the sake of gladdening the hearts of those who possess knowledge of poetry. [Verse 55] "The figures of sense" (ity arthālaṃkṛtayaḥ).
Clearly.

Having received the command of His Majesty Śrī Rāmasiṃha Deva, this work titled *Darpaṇa* (The Mirror) has been composed by me; may the illustrious Sarasvatī be forever pleased thereby. This lord of poets named Ratneśvara shines with the consecrations of the nectar of poetry, incessantly causing the earth—struck by the crookedness of fallacious arguments and afflicted by the wicked—to blossom anew. May the Goddess of Speech today take delight in the ornament of my throat, as I, whose mental faculty is fixed on Brahman, fashion this mirror of gems. Thus ends the third chapter, concerning the Figures of Sense (*arthālaṃkāra*), in the *Darpaṇa*, a commentary on the *Sarasvatīkaṇṭhābharaṇa*, composed and published by the Great Mahāmahopādhyāya Manīṣī Ratneśvara under the patronage of the illustrious Mahārāja Śrī Rāmasiṃha.

Thus ends the third chapter, on Figures of Sense, in the treatise on poetics titled *Sarasvatīkaṇṭhābharaṇa*, composed by the illustrious King Bhoja, the supreme sovereign of great kings. Now begins the fourth chapter for the purpose of analyzing the figures of both word and sense: [The Fourth Chapter] Now he begins the chapter for the analysis of the figures of both [word and sense]:
That distinguished meaning which is perceived from words and objects as simile and so forth— those are the two-fold ornaments dear to poets.
Simile, metaphor, equality, poetic doubt, and concealment;
Samādhyukti, Samāsokti, Utprekṣā, Prastutastuti;
|| 2 || Tulyayogitā, Ullekha, Sahokti, Samuccaya, Sākṣepa, Arthāntaranyāsa, and Saviśeṣa Pariṣkṛti. || 3 ||
The *dīpaka*, *krama*, *paryāya*, *atiśaya*, *śleṣa*, and *bhāvika*—these twenty-four have been designated as *saṃsṛṣṭi* (conjunction) by the wise, [arising] from words. 4.
From words.

Among those "double ornaments" (*ubhayālaṃkriyā*), those from which a specific meaning in the form of a simile (*upamā*) or the like is understood through words such as *iva* and so forth would be "double ornaments.
Of what nature are they?
They are dear to poets, being the objects of their affection, because similes and the like constitute the very essence of poetry.
Since both the word and the meaning exist together with equal application, this is "Equal Application" (*tulyayogitā*);
the same applies to the other [figures] as well.

*Pariṣkṛtiḥ* (ornamentation) is *parikara* (the poetic elaboration); the third case ending in *bhāvikaiḥ* is used in the sense of accompaniment (*sahārthe*). Now follows the definition of the figure of speech known as *upamā* (simile).
"That which is a frequent conjunction of common parts between two objects, in accordance with established convention, is considered here to be simile (upamā).
He states the definition of simile: "In accordance with established convention," and so forth.

The connection—that is, the relation—between the two things, the object of comparison (*upameya*) and the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), consisting for the most part in the conjunction of numerous common features or partial similarities of their parts; that, in this treatise (this work), is considered *upamā* (simile).

If that were so, then as in "the face is like a lotus," one might also say "like a water-lily"; therefore, he says: "by virtue of convention" (*prasiddheḥ*), meaning by following or prioritizing worldly convention (*lokaprasiddhi*).

And likewise, the defect that the simile between the *kumuda* (white water-lily) and the face is not established in common worldly usage would apply if only one [similarity] were expressed; however, when two similar attributes of two things are perceived—even if only implied—that simile is of two kinds, and each of those is further divided into three types. || 6 ||
These twenty-four [types of simile] are further established as eightfold through the distinctions known as *pada*, *vākya*, and *prapañca*.
Here, simile is twofold, according to whether its object is a directly expressed meaning (*abhidhīyamāna-artha*) or an implied meaning (*pratīyamāna-artha*).
That [simile] is also threefold due to the distinction between word-simile (*pada-upamā*), sentence-simile (*vākya-upamā*), and elaborate simile (*prapañca-upamā*).
He states that these three types, being each further divided into eight kinds, constitute twenty-four varieties, beginning with the words "pada" and so forth;
he first explains the eightfold nature of the word-simile.
Metaphor (*padopamā*) is of two kinds: by means of compound (*samāsa*) and by means of suffix (*pratyaya*).
Among these, the metaphor by compound is understood to be fourfold:
one [type] arises from the inclusion of the sense of "like" (*iva*), and another from the inclusion of a common property (*sāmānya*).
That [simile] in which both meanings are included is another; it possesses all types of compounds.
Thus, based on the compound, there are four kinds [of simile], beginning with that whose meaning is "like" (ivārtha).
The meanings included within those [figures] are as follows:
"O beautiful one, your face is as lovely as the moon; your two vine-like arms are as tender as lotus stalks; and this region of your hips is as broad as a mountain rock. (1)

In this context, the meaning of "indusundara" (moon-beautiful) is "as beautiful as the moon," according to Pāṇini 2.1.55: "Words denoting the standard of comparison [are compounded] with words expressing common properties."
Thus it has been stated in brief:
"In this way, [the comparison] 'tender as a lotus sprout' and 'vast as a mountain crag'—
this is indeed the division of word-comparison (*padopamā*) within the category of compound comparisons (*samāsopamā*), wherein the object of comparison is contained within the compound."
"Your face," and so forth:

O beautiful one, your face is as lovely as the moon; your vine-like arms are as tender as the young shoots of a lotus stalk (*bisakisalaya*); and your hip-region is, in comparison to the former [the face], as long as a mountain rock. At the conclusion of the sentence, the particle *iva* carries the sense of similarity (*tulyatā*).
*Bhakti* means division;
as Medinīkāra states, "Bhakti [is used] in the sense of division and service.
An example where the general category is included within [the specific term] is as follows:
‘Her face is like the moon, and the flavor of her mouth is like nectar; to whom can her kiss, radiant with the joy of her own spontaneous grasp, be compared? (2)
"To whom is that passionate kiss, radiant with the seizing of the hair, comparable?

Here, "moon-like" (*candrasadṛśa*) refers to a face similar to the moon, and "nectar-like" (*amṛtasadṛkṣa*) refers to the flavor of the mouth similar to nectar. In this compound, the use of general terms such as "beautiful" (*sundara*) or "sweet" (*madhura*) is not heard [explicitly], yet it is understood because of the indicator (*dyotaka*) such as *sadṛśa*. Since the common property—beauty, sweetness, and so forth—which is well-known in the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), is conveyed by the compound itself within the object of comparison (*upameya*), this is the variety of *padopamā* (word-simile) called "the one where the common property is internalized" (*antarbhūtasāmānyā*) among the types of simile based on compounds. [The word] "moon" (*candra*)... (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the grammatical and rhetorical analysis up to that point.)

"Her face is like the moon, and the flavor of her mouth is like nectar; to whom is a passionate kiss, brilliant with the sudden seizing of her hair, comparable? Thus, someone speaks of the excellence of his beloved to a friend for the sake of diverting the mind—beginning with "Her face is like the moon."

In the phrase "by the seizing of the hair" (*kacagrahe*), which refers to the grasping of the mass of hair, the passionate intensity (*rabhasa*) with which it is accompanied makes the kiss brilliant and charming;
this is understood here through the compound as an implicit common property, such as delicacy (*saukumārya*) and so forth.
Since it is not explicitly heard, one might wonder whether it exists at all; therefore, he says: "it is perceived."

The phrase "dyotakāditīti" means that since similarity (*sādṛśya*) possesses a counter-correlate (*sapratiyogika*), its very function as a communicator of that [similarity] constitutes its status as a *dyotaka* (indicator); this refers to the term "upamāna" (standard of comparison).
The meaning of "standard of comparison" (*upamāna*) is that by which something else is compared— that is, brought into a state of similarity— on account of its superior qualities.
The meaning of "the object of comparison" (*upameya*) is that which is compared, being inferior in its qualities.
An example where both meanings are included within [the single expression]:
“How indeed can she, who has lotus-hands, plantain-stalk thighs, blue-lotus eyes, moon-face, fresh-campaka limbs, and lotus-stalk arms—that beloved of yours—cause you distress? (3)

How indeed does that beloved— whose hands are like lotuses, whose thighs are like plantain stalks, whose eyes are like blue water-lilies, whose face is like the moon, whose limbs are like fresh campaka flowers, and whose arms are like lotus stalks— endure the heat?

In this verse, she is described as one whose hands are like lotuses—copper-red; whose thighs are like plantain stalks—plump; whose eyes are like blue water-lilies—dark; who is as beautiful to behold as the moon; who is fair as a fresh campaka flower; and whose arms, thighs, face, limbs, and hands are as tender as lotus stalks. Since the general quality of comparison has already been expressed by the compound itself through its constituent members (the *anyapadārtha*), this is a case of "internalized" (*antarbhūtā*) *samāsopamā* known as *sāmānya*, which functions as a type of *padopamā*. Thus, the phrase beginning with "lotus-hands" results in: "She whose hands are like lotuses, whose thighs are like plantain stalks, whose eyes are like blue water-lilies, and whose face is like the moon."

"How indeed does my beloved, whose limbs are like fresh campaka flowers and whose arms are like lotus stalks, burn me?"—how could such a lovely woman not burn? Indeed, she burns; she surely causes torment.

She whose thighs are like two plantain trees (*rambhā* or *kadalī*)—that is, like two banana stems—and she whose hands are copper-colored like a fresh *campaka* flower (a *campaka* bud) or like a lotus; here, in such instances, the word "like" (*iva*) is an indicator (*dyotaka*). Since the common quality (*sāmānya*), such as the copper color and so forth, is already expressed by the compound itself, this [type of compound] contains both meanings within it.
Examples of all types of compounds are as follows:

“She, whose face is as beautiful as the autumn moon, whose eyes are long like blue lotus stalks, and whose thighs are as lovely as the interior of a plantain tree, burns my mind incessantly—how so? (4)

In this case, the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), the object of comparison (*upameya*), and their common attribute (*dharmas*) are expressed through compounds alone—such as the words *indusundara* ("moon-beautiful") and so forth—wherein everything is contained within the compound; thus, this is the "compound simile" (*samāsopamā*) among the varieties of compound similes, which is a sub-type of the "word-simile" (*padopamā*).
[An example is: "How does such a woman as autumn (*śarat*) and so forth incessantly burn my mind?"
"What kind [of woman] is she,
whose face is as delightful as the autumn moon, whose long eyes are like the petals of a blue lotus, and whose thighs are as beautiful as the trunk of a plantain tree?
Here, the moon is the *upamāna* (standard of comparison), the face is the *upameya* (the object compared), and beauty is the common property (*tulyadharma*)."

Likewise, in other cases as well, such as "she whose face is beautiful like the autumn moon," even the sense of comparison (iva) is expressed by the compound; however, in analyses such as "that in which every compound [is present]," the intended meaning is not obtained. Therefore, he says: "all."
He states that even the simile based on suffixes (*pratyayopamā*) is merely a sub-variety of the simile based on words (*padopamā*) and not something additional:

"That which is called *pratyayopamā* by those learned in poetics—that simile based on words (*padopamā*)—is also divided into four types according to the distinctions in the meaning of the suffixes. (10)
Furthermore, since the cognition of the word and its meaning depend upon one another, the same applies to the simile; thus, there is no difference,
for the cognition must exist in the object of comparison (upameya) as well as in the standard of comparison (upamāna).
In that case, some [similarity] might exist in the general category (*sāmānya*); however, it is intended here as being like something else.
By virtue of those [qualities], there arises a comparison (*upamā*) which receives that designation.
An example is shown for this very purpose, in order to clarify its specific form.

In that regard, an example for the meaning of the object of comparison (*upameya*) as a condition (*pratyaya*) is as follows: “O eloquent woman, if you speak [thus], then the swan would be the cawing of a crow, the cuckoo the braying of a camel, and even the peacock the braying of a donkey. (5)

In this context, by the rule *kartary upamāne* (Pāṇini 3.2.79), when the suffix occurs in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*) itself through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)— as in "he cries like a crow" (*dhvāṅkṣa iva virauti*) with the word for the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) as the attendant word (*upapada*)— then the suffix expresses the meaning of the object of comparison (*upameya*).
In the same way, this should also be understood for the two cases of *uṣṭrakrośī* and *kharanādī*.

Thus, this is the function of the nominal suffix (*pratyaya*) within the category of word-similes (*padopamā*) among the similes based on suffixes (*pratyayopamā*), which brings about the cognition of the object of comparison (*upameya*).
The meaning is "due to the difference between the meanings of the suffixes"; he says "an example" (*udāharaṇam*) for the sake of clarifying the form, that is,
for the sake of knowing its essential nature.
"Haṃsa," and so forth: O eloquent one, if you speak words that are praiseworthy, then the swan cries out like a crow, the cuckoo shrieks like a camel, and the peacock brays like a donkey.
"‘Dhvāṅkṣa,’ ‘ātmaghoṣa,’ ‘paramṛd,’ and ‘balibhuk’ are synonyms for a crow,” according to Amara;
and “rāsabha,” “gardabha,” and “khara” [are synonyms for a donkey].

In examples such as *iha dhvāṅkṣa iva virauti* ("he cries here like a crow"), the suffix *ṇini* is applied by the rule *kartary upamāne* (Pāṇini 3.2.79). Since this suffix is prescribed when the agent is the object of comparison (*upamāna*), it occurs in the sense of the object being compared (*upameya*), in accordance with the requirement for grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
An example of the comparative sense of the particle *pratyaya* (as in *kalpa*, *deśya*, etc.
is as follows: “She, whose face resembles the full moon, whose vine-like arms are like lotus stalks, and whose hips resemble a discus—even in heaven she is not seen. (6)

In this context, although words such as *pūrṇendu* ("full moon")—functioning through metaphorical application (*upacāra-vṛtti*) like the phrase "like the full moon"—refer to the objects of comparison (*upameya*) such as the face, and although secondary suffixes (*svārthika*) such as *-kalpa* arise from them with their own primary meaning, nevertheless, by the very nature of the power of words, they express only the quality of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) as a subordinate element. This is just as the suffixes *-tara* and so on function when applied to words like *śukla* ("white").
For instance, when it is said, "This one is white, and this one is whiter of the two," what is understood is the excellence of the whiteness itself, not the possessor of whiteness.

This division of word-similes (*padopamā*) within similes based on cognition (*pratyayopamā*), such as "complete" (*pūrṇā*) and so forth— which involve the cognition of the meaning of the standard of comparison—
is not seen even in dreams.
Of what kind is she?
She whose face is slightly incomplete [in comparison] to the full moon,
and she whose vine-like arm is slightly incomplete [in comparison] to a lotus stalk.

She whose hips are slightly incomplete in their circularity and so forth is "kalpā" here; regarding this slight incompleteness, the rule states: *īṣadasamāptau kalpab-deśya-deśīyaraḥ* (Pāṇini 5.3.67).

67. Thus, [in expressions such as] *kalpa* and so forth, here words like *pūrṇendu* (full moon) function as the object of comparison (*upameya*) by way of metaphorical application (*upacāra*). Through the word *kalpa* and others occurring in conjunction with them, and through a suffix having its own meaning (*svārthika*), it is precisely the excellence of the meaning of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) that is expressed. Therefore, the suffix has the meaning of the standard of comparison.
This very point he states with the words "śabda... and so forth.
The meaning of "being subordinate" (*guṇabhūta*) is that since the suffix denotes excellence (*atiśaya*), being its qualifier is precisely what constitutes subordination;
this is as in the case of a suffix having a general sense.
‘The moon acts like the sun; Love acts like Death; even heaven acts like hell for one who has died through separation from his beloved.

(6) In this instance, by means of the suffix *kyac* and others applied to the standard of comparison (*upamāna*)—such as the sun and so forth—through the sense of "acting like" (*ācāra*), etc., specific actions characterized by such conduct arise. These [suffixes] arise precisely in the commonality (*sāmānya*) between the standard of comparison and the object of comparison (*upameya*). Thus, this is the category of "word-simile" (*padopamā*) within the "similes involving suffixes" (*pratyayopamā*), wherein the suffixes convey a common meaning.
By means of the cognition of the sense of "as it were" (ivārtha), for example:
"The single Self of all beings, though established in every being, is seen as one and as many, like the moon in water. (8)

In this context, by the rule *tena tulyaṃ kriyā ced vatiḥ* (Pāṇini 5.1.115), the suffix *vati* is applied after the word *candra* in the sense of "like" (*iva*)— as in "it is seen as equal to the moon"— and not in the sense of an identical action; otherwise, just as there is the sense of "like" (*iva*) in the expression "it is seen," there would likewise be no employment of the identical action.
Furthermore, even in the absence of that [suffix], the suffix *vati* would result in cases such as "the gavaya is like a cow";

thus, this is the application of the category of word-based simile (*padopamā*) within similes based on cognition (*pratyayopamā*), which involve the cognition of the meaning of the particle *iva*, as seen in examples such as *sūryīyati*.

The moon acts like the sun (*sūryīyati*), meaning it behaves like the sun; love acts like one who has transcended death (*atimṛtāyate*), meaning it becomes like that which has passed beyond death. In separation from the beloved, even heaven acts like hell (*narakaīyati*), meaning it behaves like hell.
Regarding the form *sūryīyati*, [the rule] "upamānād ācāre" (Pāṇini 3.1.10) applies.
Thus, by the rule *kyac*, as in *atimṛdāyate*, the suffix *kyac* is applied in the sense of habitual action (*ācāra*).
By the rule *akartuḥ kyaṅ salopaśca* (Pāṇini 3.1.11), the suffix *kyaṅ* is applied [after a verbal root] when not denoting the agent, and there is elision of the *s*.
Thus, regarding the form *narakīyati* [derived from *naraka*], [the suffix] *kyaN* is applied by virtue of Pāṇini 3.1.94 (*adhikaraṇācca*). 2664. Sūtra.
Regarding the suffix *kyac* [in the sense of] "acting like" (*vā*):

here, "conduct" (*ācāra*) refers to the act of performing; and since that act is common to both the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*), the suffixes expressing the commonality are identical, as in "one," and so forth.
The single one, the self of beings, the Supreme Self, residing in every body, is seen as one and as many—in manifold ways, like the moon in water.

Regarding the phrase "is seen here like the moon in water," the suffix *vat* is used in the sense of similarity (*ivārthe sādṛśye*), and not for the purpose of making [the moon] equal [to the Self]. For if it were made equal, there would be tautology due to the semantic overlap between the word *dṛśyate* ("is seen") and the suffix *vat*. [Objection: Let there be no employment of the word "equal" (*tulya*). [Response: What undesirable consequence follows from that? To this, he says: "That... (*tad*...).
The meaning is that in examples such as "a cow is like a gavaya," because there is no employment of an action, there is an absence of the employment of a common action (*tulyakriyā*).
He states that sentence-simile (*vākyopamā*) is of eight kinds:
"As for that which is sentence-simile therein, it also undergoes a twofold division."
One [type of simile] occurs when there is similarity between two word-meanings (*padārtha*), while the other occurs when there is mutual similarity between two sentence-meanings (*vākyārtha*).

The former is declared by the foremost of poets to be fourfold: complete (*pūrṇā*), elliptical (*luptā*), that which has lost its letters (*luptavarṇā*), and likewise the complete-elliptical (*pūrṇaluptā*). || 13–14 ||

The *pūrṇā* [simile] occurs when there is the employment of the common property (*sāmānyadharma*), the indicator (*dyotaka*), the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), and indeed the object of comparison (*upameya*). This is called the *vākya* [type]. (15)
In that context, regarding the simile (*upamā*), "mutually" (*mithas*) means "reciprocal similarity";
as the author of the *Medinīkośa* states: "The words *mithas*, *anyonya*, and *rahas* are used in the sense of secrecy, and *mithas* and *anyonya* are also used in the sense of conjunction."

The first type, the *padārthopamā*, is "complete" (*pūrṇā*) because it possesses the entirety [of the elements] such as the common attribute (*sāmānyadharma*); this applies to every instance of its usage,
as follows:

“‘O lady with intoxicating eyes, your face is as beautiful as a lotus, your pair of arms is as tender as a lotus stalk, and likewise your braid of hair is as dark as a swarm of bees. (9) Here, because the similarity between the two things is expressed through the separate employment of all four words— the indicators of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), the common attribute (*tulyadharma*), and the designators of the object of comparison (*upameya*)— this is called *pūrṇā* (complete) sentence-simile (*vākyopamā*) among the types of simile based on word-meanings (*padārthopamā*).”

When there is an elision of both the common attribute (*sāmānyadharma*) and the indicator (*dyotaka*), and the simile is one where similarity is only implied (*pratīyamānasādṛśya*), they know that as the "elided in both" (*dvayor luptā*).
(Verse 16) [Example: *kamalam* etc.
O lady with intoxicating eyes and reddish pupils, your face is as beautiful as a lotus,
your two arms are as soft as lotus stalks,
and your braided hair is as dark as a row of bees.
"She whose eyes (īkṣaṇa) are red like wine"—according to Amara, "kabara" means "an arrangement of hair.

Here, the lotus is the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), the word "like" (*iva*) is the indicator (*dyotaka*), the word "beautiful" (*cāru*) presents the common property (*tulyadharma*), and the face is the object of comparison (*upameya*); thus, there is completeness (*pūrṇatā*). The meaning of the sentence is the similarity between the two things. If [the simile] were deficient due to the absence of the common property and so forth, it would be an "elliptical" (*luptā*) simile; however, if everything were omitted, there would be no simile at all. Therefore, he says: "it is understood" (*pratīyamāna*).
The sense is that even in such a case, the perception of common attributes such as beauty and so forth is indeed well-established—as for example:
"This is not a lotus; this is the face itself. These are not two bees; these are the eyes."
‘These are not the filaments of a lotus; these are the rows of teeth of my beloved.

Here, although there is an absence of words such as ‘iva’ (like) and others—since the cognition of the reversal of the lotus and so on with respect to the object of comparison, namely the face of the beloved, is itself a rejection [of that identity]—there is still the perception of the omitted attribute such as ‘loveliness. Thus, among the varieties of *padārthopamā* (simile based on the meaning of words), this belongs to the category of *vākyopamā* (sentence simile). When the common attribute (*sāmānyadharma*) is omitted, it is called *luptapūrṇā* (the complete simile with omission).
"No," and so forth:
this is not a lotus, but rather the face of the beloved;
these are not two bees, but rather her eyes.
These are not filaments, but rather these well-known rows of teeth;
and these two are eyes— according to the rule "the dual endings ī, ū, e, o, ai, and au are *pragṛhya*."
11. Thus, there is the status of being a *pragṛhya* [vowel];
"this lotus is the face of the beloved" is a false cognition (*mithyājñāna*), and its rejection or negation is "it is not a lotus.
In this way, even in the absence of words such as *eva*, because the beauty and other qualities are understood through their very well-known nature, this is an elided (*luptā*) [metaphor].
For example:
"Your face is like a lotus, your eyes like blue water-lilies, your thighs like plantain trunks, and your breasts like the frontal globes of an elephant. (11)

Here, when the common property (*sāmānyadharma*) is elided, the relationship of subject and object of comparison (*upamānopameyabhāva*) between two things is complete by virtue of the similarity being implied; this is the variety of *padārthopamā* known as *luptapūrṇā*, which is a sub-type of sentence-simile (*vākyopamā*). For example, in the verse beginning with *rājīvam*:
"O beloved, your face is like a lotus, your eyes are like blue lotuses, your thighs are like plantain trunks, and your breasts are like the frontal globes of elephants."
In the expression "utpale iva," the term *pragṛhya* is applied by the rule "īdūded dvivacanaṃ pragṛhyam" (Pāṇini 1.1.11).
In this case, there is the elision of common attributes such as "beauty" and so forth, while the others remain complete; thus it is called *luptapūrṇā* (the complete-with-elision).
However, when the indicator (*dyotaka*) is elided, that which remains is known as *pūrṇaluptā* (the elided-with-complete). || 17 ||
For example:
"O slender one, your face and the lotus are both in full bloom and fragrant; your tender, slightly pink lips and the young shoots are alike. (12)

In this treatise, because similarity is not explicitly stated when two similar things are mentioned by a single term (*tantra*), and because similarity is intended through the relationship of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*), and because—given that they are distinct due to *śleṣa* (paronomasia)—the standard and object of comparison are expressed together in a copulative compound (*itaretarayoga*), while their respective qualifiers are expressed by a single remainder (*ekaśeṣa*), all four elements, beginning with the standard of comparison, are complete even without an explicit word for "like" (*iva*). Consequently, since the meaning has already been conveyed, words such as "like" are elided; thus, this variety of *pūrṇaluptā* (complete-elided) belongs to the category of sentence-simile (*vākyopamā*) within the scope of word-meaning similes (*padārthopamā*).
This has been explained in the section on "Distinction from the Similar" (*sadṛśavyatireka*), starting with the verse beginning "tvad... and so forth.
By "tantra" is meant primarily [the primary element], according to Medinīkāra, who states: "tantra means the principal or the established doctrine.

Alternatively, by "tantra" is meant that which brings about a single purpose; here, it refers to the designation of two similar lotus-faces as being in a relationship of primary and subordinate, and their equality is the meaning of the word.

And thus, by mutual connection, there is the designation of the object of comparison and the standard of comparison; the two qualifiers "in full bloom" (phulle) function as a *ekaśeṣa* compound, indicating the cause, the standard of comparison, the object of comparison, and the common attribute, thereby manifesting completeness (*pūrṇatā*).
The elision of *iva* and other particles occurs because their meaning has already been expressed; therefore, this is a case of "complete elision" (*pūrṇaluptā*).

Since there would be over-extension (applying the definition too broadly) to cases where two things are mentioned with equal status—wherein it is simply *śleṣa* (paronomasia)—the author says: "Because of *śleṣa*" (*śleṣataḥ*), for the meaning of a sentence depends upon the sentence itself, and thus it constitutes a distinct variety of that [metaphor].

That [simile] which pertains to both the sentence and its meaning is also fourfold: that containing the word *eva*, that not containing the word *eva*, that devoid of words such as *iva* and the like, and that characterized by contrast (*vaidharmya*).
Among these, examples of those containing the word *eva* are as follows:

‘This Pāṇḍya king, with long necklaces resting upon his shoulders and his body anointed with yellow sandalwood paste, shines like the king of mountains, whose peaks are reddened by the morning sun and from which mountain torrents burst forth.

(13) Here, when there is an intended mutual relationship of standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and object of comparison (*upameya*) between Himavat and Pāṇḍya, and between the mountain torrent and the necklace, as well as between the morning sunlight and the yellow sandalwood paste—by means of the conceptualization of the relationship between the qualifiers and the qualified—the two sentence-meanings (*vākyārtha*) are both constructed. Thus, through a single word *iva*, their mutual relationship as standard and object of comparison is expressed; this is the variety of sentence-simile (*vākyopamā*) within the similes of sentence-meaning (*vākyārthopamā*) characterized by a single *iva*.
That [region] in which there is only one word,
"Pāṇḍya"—
this Pāṇḍya, a particular king, shines.
With a long necklace placed upon his shoulder— meaning bestowed thereon—

and with his body anointed with *haricandana*, a variety of sandalwood, he shines like the Himalayas, which possess peaks red with the rays of the newly risen sun and from which mountain torrents flow.

In this case, the relationship of simile between two sentence-meanings is expressed by a single *iva* word; thus, there is one object of comparison (*upameya*) and multiple *iva* words, as for example:
“Day by day she grew, having attained her rise like the digit of the moon.”
"She nourished special qualities consisting of loveliness, like other digits of the moonlight.

(14) Here, because the verb—which is the cause for the unification of the two sentence-meanings—is transitive, the word *iva* is employed separately for both the agent and the object, each of which serves as a point of comparison. Thus, this is an "expressed similarity" (*abhidhīyamāna-sādṛśya*) among the various types of sentence-similes (*vākyārthopamā*) involving multiple instances of *iva*; it belongs to the category of sentence-similes (*vākyopamā*).
As for the word *dina*, [it is used]... [the rest of the commentary follows].
That Gaurī, growing day by day— that is, increasing daily— nurtured, or rather continued to nourish, specific excellences consisting primarily of loveliness and radiance;
she was one by whom an "udaya," meaning growth or increase, had been attained.
The meaning is as follows: just as the digit of the moon, having attained its emergence and increasing day by day, assumes other successive digits and other forms of moonlight;
in that same way—wherein beauty (*lāvaṇya*) corresponds to the moonlight and the particular excellence (*viśeṣa*) corresponds to the digit—or rather, what kind of "other digits" are they?
Those in which there is moonlight within the interior,
or those in which there is an interval or space for the moonlight;
"lekha" means both writing and a digit, according to the Viśvakośa.
This [belonging] to the moon is "cāndramasī"; [this is an example of the suffix *cha* applied by Pāṇini 4.3.120:
*tasyedam*.]
120. Thus, Śāśvata states: "Lāvaṇya is considered to be beauty (cārutā)";
and [the word] *antara* is used in the sense of specific internal spaces within the womb, like a word whose gender is determined by its referent (*vācyaliṅgavat*).
Thus says Medinīkāra.

Here, there is a syntactic unity between the two sentence-meanings through the action in the form of nourishing (*poṣaṇa*); and since that [action] is transitive (*sakarmaka*), because the agent and the object are expressed by separate words such as *iva*, there are multiple objects of comparison (*upameya*), as in the following examples: [text follows].
"‘The enemy of Puloma (Indra) awakens for the protection of heaven; you, O Lord, [awaken] for the protection of the earth.
By him the Asuras are slain; by you arrogant kings are destroyed.

Here, through the convergence of identical actions between the two—the sky and the earth, described as the enemies of Puloma, and the arrogant kings—there is understood a mutual relationship of standard of comparison and object of comparison (*upamānopameyabhāva*) among the sentence-meanings even without the use of words such as *iva*. Thus, this is a case of *vākyopamā* (sentence-simile) within the category of *vākyārthopamā* (simile of sentence-meaning) that lacks explicit comparative words."
"O Bhūmi, as Pulomāri Indra remains awake for the protection of heaven— meaning the celestial realm—
the Asuras are slain by that Indra; likewise, kings are slain by you."
"Sāvalepāḥ" means "possessing pride," which is an epithet for kings;
Puloman was a specific type of Daitya who was slain by Indra, and his daughter, Indrāṇī (Pulomajā), was taken [by him]—so it is in the Purāṇas.

Here, the action is identical (*tulyā*), consisting of both the act of keeping watch and the act of slaying; thus, the relationship between the object of comparison and the subject of comparison (*upamānopameyabhāvaḥ*) is constituted by those two [actions].
An example of the *vaidharmyavatī* (negative) [type of syllogism] is as follows:
“I have been sent by the King to summon Mādhava for battle;
for those of great prowess do not harm their enemies through deceit, unlike common thieves. (16)

In this case, although there is a standard of comparison (*upamāna*), an object of comparison (*upameya*), and even the word *iva*, that property of things known as "the performance of deception" belonging to both the highly powerful ones and the thieves is restricted by the negative particle (*na*) to the standard of comparison alone; thus, this is a variety of *vaidharmyavatī* (based on contrast) among the *vākyārthopamā*s (sentence-level similes), specifically a division of *vākyopamā*.

In examples such as *prahita* and so forth, where various dissimilar qualities are mentioned, even though there is similarity in other respects, the expressed property is restricted to the standard of comparison alone by means of negation; this constitutes the contrast (*vaidharmya*).
This is that [type of] simile;
he now states the eightfold nature of the *prapañcopamā* (elaborated simile):
"Where similarity is understood through a particular turn of expression within the meaning of a sentence."

That [simile] will be explained in detail as *prapañcopamā*, wherein the similarity between two sentence-meanings is understood through a particular turn of phrase in the expansion of those sentence-meanings.
(19) That is to say, *prapañcopamā* is that wherein the similarity between two sentence-meanings is known in detail by means of a specific verbal formulation within the sentence-meaning.
He states its classification: "But that [speech] may be of a natural form or likewise of a modified form; of these two, it should be understood that the one of natural form is fourfold. (20)
There may be the complete simile (*samastopamā*); likewise, another is the partial simile (*ekadeśopamā*);
the third may be the garland simile (*mālopamā*), and the fourth is the aesthetic-savor simile (*rasanopamā*). (21) This refers to [the aforementioned].
The natural form is innate (*sāhajika*), while the modified form is adventitious (*aupādhika*). Among these, a complete simile (*samastopamā*) is as follows:
"In spring, with swarms of bees like curls of hair, and with clusters of blossoms like breasts..."
"The creepers shine even more like women with their hands, as it were, with their sprouts.

(17) Here, when there is an intention to express the relationship of standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and object of comparison (*upameya*) between the creepers adorned by the splendor of spring and women—whose similarity is already implied—the use of the word *iva* ("as it were") separately for each part, such as the bees (as curls) and so forth, despite their similarity being already implied, constitutes a stylistic mode of expressing the simile between the whole sentence-meanings through both the wholes and their parts.
This is the variety of "Extended Simile" (*prapañcopamā*) among the types of "Complete Simile" (*samastopamā*) within the category of "Similes based on the Form of the Subject" (*prakṛtarūpopamā*).
"Alītyādi":
creepers in spring shine exceedingly like women— like female beings— with what?

With swarms of bees as if they were curls of hair, with clusters of flowers as if they were breasts, and with sprouts as if they were hands— in this case, because there is a relationship of comparison between the whole parts (the individual components) of the two wholes (the creeper and the woman), namely the bees, the bracelets, the curls, and so forth, it is a *samastopamā* (a complete simile).
And their status as the subjects of description (*prakṛtatva*) is well-established.
An example of partial simile (*ekadeśopamā*) is as follows:
“The lotus ponds shine with their lotuses—as if they were faces—with their petals like lips, their filaments like teeth, and their swarms of bees like locks of hair. (18)

Here, while it would have been appropriate to state a mutual relationship of comparison (*upamānopameyabhāva*) between the lotuses (*nalinī*) and the playful women (*vilāsinī*), the characteristic features of the playful women are presented for the sake of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*). Thus, having set aside the other body parts such as the breasts which serve as the objects of comparison (*upameya*), the lotus alone is compared in detail with its own parts—such as the petals—and with the [woman's] lips and so forth, which serve as the standards of comparison, through their separate and distinct application. Therefore, this is called "Partial Comparison" (*ekadeśopamā*), a variety of the "Extended Comparison" (*prapañcopamā*) among the types of formal comparison; thus, the lotus-ponds shine.
With what [features]?
With lotus petals as if they were lips, with filaments as if they were teeth, with swarms of bees as if they were curls of hair, and with lotuses as if they were faces;

here, through this extensive series of similes, there is a "proliferated simile" (*prapañcopamā*), and because the single part [the face] is compared to the lotus petals and so forth along with the lips and other parts, it is also a "partial simile" (*ekadeśopamā*) due to the exclusion of the swan and the breasts.
The *mālopamā* (string simile) is as follows:
“Her gaze clings to Lakṣmaṇa’s face like a necklace, to the broad chest of the Lord of the Monkeys like a forest garland, to Hanumān like his fame, and to the armies like his command. (19)
"His gaze clings to Lakṣmaṇa’s face like beauty, to the formidable chest of the Lord of Monkeys like a forest garland, to the Son of the Wind like fame, and to his armies like a command.

Here, because the gaze of Rāma—which rests upon Lakṣmaṇa’s face and so forth—is compared through a series of metaphors such as "beauty," wherein the similarity is implied, this is called *mālopamā* (garland simile) due to its extensive comparison; it is a sub-variety of *prapañcopamā* (extended simile) within the category of *prakṛtarūpopamā* (simile based on the nature of the subject).

His gaze clings to Lakṣmaṇa’s face as a garland of forest flowers adorns it, to the broad chest of the Lord of Monkeys like a wild woodland wreath, to the Son of the Wind like his own fame, and to his forces like a royal command.

This gaze of Rāma lingers upon and fixes itself on the face of Lakṣmaṇa, like a beauty [that follows] immediately after the sight [of it], due to the serenity of his countenance; that same gaze lingers upon the broad chest of Sugrīva, the lord of monkeys, like a forest garland [offered] on account of his manly resolve. The sense is that, because he beheld his entire chest, this gaze—white and dark—was like a forest garland bestowed as a favor by the Lord upon Sugrīva at the opportune moment.

The sense is that he gazed with a gaze that was blossomed and white-washed the sky, as if his fame were clinging to Hanumān, the son of the Wind, whose prowess was already known; his armies clung to him like his command, for immediately thereafter those exceedingly powerful ones made preparations to depart— [the poet] knows that garland which slopes down from his feet is called a "forest-garland" (vanamālā).
Thus, according to Śāśvata,
the mouth and other such substrates themselves possess the status of the object (*karman*);
or else, "by means of a prefix, the meaning of a verbal root is forcibly led elsewhere."
By this etymology, the root *vi-lag* is transitive here;

the stringing together of Rāma’s glances with a garland consisting of similes such as "beauty" and so forth is precisely what constitutes the composition. This is a *mālopamā* (garland simile) due to the extensive application of comparison, and it is not a *bahūpamā* (multiple simile), because a single attribute is not presented by multiple [similes].
An example of the *rasanopamā* (taste-like simile) is as follows:

“The swan acts like the moon with its white luster; the beloved acts like a swan with her graceful gait; the water acts like the beloved with the pleasure of its touch; and the sky acts like water through its transparency. (20)

Here, through the series of *pratyayopamā*s (similes based on verbal suffixes)—beginning with the moon and others, expressed by means of similarity such as whiteness and so forth, and involving swans and other objects—which unfolds like the process of *rasanā* (tasting) through subsequent reversals, being both extensive and causal; and which, by forming a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*), describes the loveliness of the autumnal waters—this is what is called *rasanopamā*. Among the varieties of *prakṛtarūpopamā*, it belongs to the sub-class of *prapañcopamā*. [The verse begins: "The moon...
Now, the swan acts like the moon (*candrāyate*) due to its white luster; that is, it behaves like the moon.
By her lovely and charming gait, she behaves like a swan;
by the pleasantness of her touch, she behaves like water;
by her purity, she behaves like the sky; and by her clarity, she behaves like water.
According to Amara, "vārvāri jalam" (water is vār, vāri, etc.
and "puṃsyākāśavihāyasī" (the sky is ākāśa, vihāya, etc.).

Here, the subsequent turning back in relation to what precedes it, the sequence of small bells, the state of being manifold like the phenomenal world (prapañca), the possession of causes such as taste (ruci), and the abundance of perceived similes are all clearly evident.
In that case, how can there be the nature of the subject at hand (*prakṛtarūpatā*)? To this he says: "Thus" (*tathā*).

The sense is that by establishing a single syntactical unity through the series of similes and the description of the autumn season, the nature of the subject at hand is maintained. [The word *turīyā* means "the fourth," derived with the suffix *cha* according to the rule: "After *turaṇa*, *matta*, etc., there is elision of the initial syllable."]
Thus, these four [types of simile] are explained according to their natural form; we shall now describe four other types of similes according to their modified forms.
Among them, the first is the simile of inversion (viparyāsopamā), and the next is the simile of both (ubhayopamā).
Now, the fourth type is called *utpādyopamā* (imaginative simile), which is a *ananvayopamā* (simile of non-comparison).
Among these, the *viparyāsopamā* (reversal simile) is as follows:
"O beloved, that blue lotus which was submerged in the water and possessed a luster equal to your eyes is now hidden by clouds; and the moon, which imitates the beauty of your face, is obscured."
"Even those royal swans who followed in your footsteps have departed; yet fate does not permit me even the slightest diversion from the thought of your likeness. (21)

In this case, while it is well known that the eyes and so forth are the objects of comparison (*upameya*) and the blue lotuses and so forth are the standards of comparison (*upamāna*), because of excessive passion there arises in the eyes and so forth a perception of superiority, and because of a lack of such passion there arises in the blue lotuses and so forth a perception of imitation thereof. Thus, by Rāma, who is separated from his beloved, a mutual relationship of standard and object of comparison is imagined among these things—which possess similarity—by reversing their conventional status; this is therefore called "Inverted Simile" (*viparyāsopamā*), which belongs to the category of "Elaborated Simile" (*prapañcopamā*) among the varieties of distorted similes.
As for the words:
"O beloved, even the mere joy of seeing your likeness is not permitted by fate."
For that blue lotus submerged in the water— of what nature could its beauty possibly be equal to yours?
The moon, obscured and covered by clouds, is like what?
It is like the reflection of your face.

Even those royal swans have gone, whose gait was equal to yours; here, by the reversal of conventional renown, there is a "reversal simile" (*viparyāsopamā*), which is a "mutual simile" (*ubhayopamā*), as follows:
"Your face is like a lotus, and a lotus is like your face;
how indeed shall we find you, who are hidden within a cluster of lotuses? (22).

Here too, due to extreme similarity, there is a reversal of what is well-known regarding one side [of the comparison]. Thus, this is the variety of *prapañcopamā* (extended simile) among the sub-types of *vikṛtarūpopamā* (modified similes), known as *ubhayopamā* (mutual simile) where the similarity is implied (*pratīyamāna*).
"O beloved, how indeed might we obtain you? Of what sort are you?"
He says that there is no gain even by looking at her face as she stands hidden among the clusters of lotuses: "Your face is like a lotus, and a lotus is like your face.
In the first case, this is a reversal (viparyāsa); however, because both possess the status of being the object of comparison and the subject of comparison, it is a mutual simile (ubhayopamā).
An example of a produced simile (*utpādyopamā*) is as follows:

“If two separate streams of the waters of the celestial Gaṅgā were to fall from the sky, then [the chest] of this [hero], dark as a tamāla tree and adorned with a string of pearls, might be compared to it. (23)

Here, having produced a standard of comparison (*upamāna*) for the sake of illustration, the similarity—whether implied or explicitly stated—is expressed by means of the object of comparison (*upameya*). Thus, this is the variety known as *utpādyopamā* (produced comparison) among the types of non-altered form comparisons (*avikṛtarūpopamā*), which is a sub-species of the *prapañcopamā*. This [comparison] beginning with "both" (*ubhau*) has been explained under the quality of *śleṣa* (paronomasia).

Here, if the state of being a standard of comparison (*upamāna*) for these [two] is produced by the thought "they might fall," this is *utpādyopamā* (the produced simile). Regarding the elaboration (*prapañca*) of similes involving many objects of comparison,
there is *ananvayopamā* (the simile of non-connection), as follows:

"O slender-waisted one, your face is like your face, your eyes are like your eyes, your form is like your form; you are like yourself—there is no other like you. Here, although there is *ananvaya* (non-repetition), because the intention is to express the relationship between the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*), a distinction is imagined even for a single entity. Thus, the perceived similarity is expressed through a metaphorical comparison (*aupamya*). This is therefore called *ananvayopamā*, which is a variety of the *prapañcopamā* (extended metaphor) among the types of non-altered metaphors (*avikṛtarūpopamā*).
This passage beginning with "tvad" has been explained under *lāṭānuprāsa*.
Here, however, the absence of connection with any other object of comparison— namely, that there is no one else like you— is *ananvaya* (non-comparison).
How can there be a comparison (upamiti) of that [self] with itself, since comparison involves a distinction? To this he says: "Even of one" (*ekasyāpi*).
Thus, even though there is no actual difference, there is no fault because a distinction is conceptually constructed;
for comparison (*upamā*) is by means of a likeness (*aupamya*), where the suffix *ka* is used in its own sense (*svārthe*) and then replaced by *ṣyañ*.
Thus concludes the examination of the poetic figure of Simile (Upamā). Now follows the examination of the poetic figure of Metaphor (Rūpaka); he states the definition of Metaphor:

When words denoting the standard of comparison (upamāna) function by resorting to a figurative sense (gauṇavṛtti) with respect to the object of comparison (upameya), then the wise know that as *rūpaka* (metaphor). (24) "When" (yadā)—

If the occurrence—that is, the capacity for signification—of the words denoting the standards of comparison (*upamāna*), such as "lotus" and so forth, were to reside in the objects of comparison (*upameya*), such as the "face" and so forth, then how could there be *rūpaka*?
For otherwise, there would be the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of one thing signifying another.
To this, he replies: "By means of secondary [signification] (*gauṇa*)."
The secondary function (*gauṇavṛtti*) is "secondary" (*gauṇī*) because it relies upon that [quality]; thus, the secondary function is simply the capacity of one thing to convey another.

Consequently, where non-difference between the word for the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*) is conveyed by means of qualities and so forth, there is a metaphor (*rūpaka*); where only similarity is conveyed, there is a simile (*upamā*). This is the distinction between the two.
He states the classification:
"It is said to be threefold due to the distinctions of being predominant in word, meaning, or both;
among these, that which is predominant in word is likewise [divided into] the original (prakṛta) and the modified (vikṛta). (25)
They say that even when the meaning (artha) predominates, there are two types based on the distinction between the suggested (vyaṅgya) and the expressed (vācya);
likewise, when both [word and meaning] predominate, there are two types each, according to the distinction between pure (śuddha) and mixed (saṃkīrṇa).
26. [The term] "in word" (śabde) [is used].
First, *rūpaka* (metaphor) is of three kinds: distinguished as predominant in sound (*śabdabhūyiṣṭha*), predominant in meaning (*arthabhūyiṣṭha*), and predominant in both (*tadubhayabhūyiṣṭha*).

Among these, that predominant in sound is twofold through the distinction between the original (*prakṛta*) and the modified (*vikṛta*); that predominant in meaning is twofold through the distinction between the primary and the subordinate; and that predominant in both is also twofold through the distinction between the pure (*śuddha*) and the mixed (*saṃkīrṇa*). This is the classification.
Now, he states the classification for that which is predominant in sound regarding the original:
Among those, the primary [type] is said to be fourfold:
the compound, the non-compound, both, and that which includes a qualifier. (27) Among these, the compound is as follows: [Example: *yena dhvastamanobhavena*... [etc.]
“The rays of the moon-like nails of your feet, pure as jasmine, are able to cause the lotus-hands of kings to close.

Here, [the figure of speech is] *upamita* (simile), according to the rule: “That which is compared with words such as *vyāghra* (tiger) when the common property (*sāmānya*) is not expressed. (Pāṇini 2.1.56).

56. Thus, in the compound *padmāni* (lotuses), [the term is applied] through metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*) based on the produced similarity—such as "lotuses" being like actual lotuses and "moons" being like actual moons—in the designation of hands and nails by means of "lotus," "moon," and so forth; because words such as "like" (*iva*) are not employed, the meaning of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) is obscured. This, therefore, is the variety called "compound-formed" (*samastarūpa*), which relies upon figurative language (*gauṇaśabdavyapāśraya*) and is caused by a compound; it is one of the four types of verbal metaphor (*śabdabhūyiṣṭharūpaka*) among the varieties of metaphor in the present context.
The rays— meaning the splendors— of the moon-like nails of your feet are able, that is, capable, of causing the lotus-hands of kings to close;
how are these rays?
"Stainless like *kundapuṣpa* flowers"—according to Amara, "flame, weapon, and crest are feminine (*arcir-heti-śikhā striyām*).

Regarding the expressions "the hand is like a lotus" and "the nail is like the moon," [this refers to] Pāṇini’s rule: "That which is compared [to something else] is a *karmadhāraya* compound when followed by words such as *vyāghra*, provided that a common quality is not explicitly stated. (Pāṇini 2.1.56).
1.56 Thus is the compound.

Here, because words such as "iva" (like) are not employed, the meaning of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) is obscured through the metaphorical treatment (*upacāra*) of non-difference; hence, there is a prioritization of the secondary sense (*gauṇī*).

And as for the state of being concealed (*tirobhūtatva*), although difference exists in the ultimate sense, it does not manifest; that, however, has been treated in brief. For this very reason, due to the abundance of words, there is a preponderance of verbal expression, as in the following expanded example:
"The fingers were the young shoots, and the radiance of the nails was the flowers."
"Your arms are like creepers, you are the beauty of spring, appearing visibly before us.

(26) Here too, as in the previous case, because the words *pallava* (sprout), *kusuma* (flower), *latā* (creeper), *vasantaśrī* (beauty of spring), and so on—relying on metaphorical functions (*guṇavṛtti*)—stand in grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the fingers, nails, rays, arms, and the name of the woman being described, and because generalizing terms such as "like" (*iva*) are not employed, the referent of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) remains concealed even though the compound has not been formed; thus, this is called the "uncompounded form" (*asamastarūpa*), which is a variety of "verbal predominance" (*śabdabhūyiṣṭha*) among the types of *rūpaka* based on the subject matter, beginning with the word "fingers" (*aṅgulyaḥ*).
O beautiful one, you are the very personification of the splendor of spring, moving visibly before our eyes, whether within the range of our vision or treading upon our feet.
He states the basis for this metaphorical identification of non-difference: "Your fingers were the young shoots, and the luster of your nails was the flowers."
The two arms are like two creepers;
regarding the term *pallava*, Amara states: "It is not feminine; it means a sprout.
He explains the distinction between the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object compared (*upameya*) by using the word "common" (*sāmānya*).
In this case, due to the absence of a compound, there is a state of being both combined and separate; for example:
"A smile is the moonlight upon your moon-like face, and your luster is the water within your jar-like breasts."

"O friend, on the hand that is a sprout upon the creeper-arms, the rays of the nails are the flower. (27) Here, the smile itself is the moonlight of the face-moon; the luster alone is the water of the jar-like breasts; and on the hands, which have become sprouts upon the creeper-arms, the rays of the nails alone are the flower. Because all these—both those expressed as compounds and those not—are presented by means of figurative words while setting aside direct comparison (*upamā*), this is the variety called "compound-and-non-compound" among the types of *prakṛta-rūpaka* (inherent metaphor), specifically the type where the verbal element predominates, beginning with the word "smile."
O friend, in the moon of your face there is the moonlight of a slight smile;
in your jar-like breasts there is the radiance of luster, which is the water;
on the jewel that serves as the sprout of your vine-like arms, the glints of your fingernails are the flowers.
According to Amara, "nīrakṣīrāmbuśambaram" [is a compound]; here, because of the exclusion of the opponent, there is a sublation of the simile.
This consists of both compounded and uncompounded forms, first being compounded and then uncompounded; thus, it is "compounded-and-uncompounded" (samastavyastatā).
An example with a qualifying attribute (saviśeṣaṇa) is as follows:

“Victorious is the foot of Hari, which has the water of the daughter of Jahnu clinging to its crest like a silken cloth, and which is the banner for the festival of joy of the gods who are free from fear of the demons. (28)

In this context, there is the foot of Hari, characterized by the aforementioned attributes, and the banner during the festival of joy for the gods—who are free from fear because the Asuras have been slain by Hari. Between these two, which possess their respective qualifiers and whose similarity is implied, there exists a mutual relationship of object compared (upameya) and object comparing (upamāna). This is called "with qualifiers" (*saviśeṣaṇa*), a variety of verbal *rūpaka* among the types of *rūpaka* based on the subject matter (*prakṛta*).

Since all four of these [types of *rūpaka*] are composed using words such as the compound *prakṛta-samāsa* and so forth, they are termed "subject matter" (*prakṛta*); thus, the word "Hari" and so on is used.

Victorious is the foot of Hari in his Vāmana form—fixed upon the head of Bali during the Trivikrama incarnation when he reached the cosmic egg—which is like a silken cloth (*aṃśuka*) consisting of the water of the Gaṅgā, the daughter of Jahnu, offered by Brahmā for the purpose of washing the feet; this very foot served as a banner during the festival of joy of the gods who were freed from fear after the victory over Bali. For this reason, the water of the Jāhnavī is metaphorically described as a silken cloth, since a banner would otherwise be impossible without it. As Medinīkāra states: "The word *śira* means both 'the top' and 'the head.'"

In this case, because the metaphorical identification (*rūpaṇa*) occurs only between the two subjects—the feet and the banners—along with their respective qualifiers, it is a "metaphor with qualifiers" (*saviśeṣaṇarūpaka*).
"Prakṛtatva" (the state of being the subject) means the state of being under discussion;
and since that [subjectivity] is established precisely through compounds and other such devices, it constitutes a "metaphor of the subject" (*prakṛtarūpaka*).
He analyzes that which abounds in distorted words; he announces four further subdivisions of the distorted [type]:
the series (paramparā), the girdle (raśanā), the garland (mālā), and the metaphor upon metaphor (rūpaka-rūpaka). || 28 ||
"Four":
the wise (the remainder of the sentence being "so it is understood") acknowledge— that is, accept— the four varieties of even the *vikṛta* [drama].
The sequence among them is as follows:

"The rainy season has somehow passed for the descendant of Daśaratha—a season that was a shower of obstacles to his resolve, a firm chain for the elephant of his anger, and a cage for the lion that is his fame. (29)

The rainy season has somehow or other passed for the son of Daśaratha— a cage for the lion of victory— acting as a sun to the darkness of his resolve and a firm chain to restrain the lordly elephant of his wrath.

Here, by conceiving a relationship of simile and object of comparison between the resolve of the son of Daśaratha and the sun, his wrath and the lordly elephant, and his victory and the lion—there is one metaphorical identification (*rūpaṇa*). Then, there is a second [identification] based on their connection with evening, the iron chain, and the cage. Therein, all three are further identified with the rainy season; thus, this is a *paramparita-rūpaka* (chain metaphor), which among the varieties of modified metaphors (*vikṛta-rūpaka*) is a type where the verbal element predominates.
In the passage beginning with *vavasāa*, etc., [the meaning is]:
"The resolve is the sun, and the wrath is the firm binding of the iron chain of the lordly elephant."
"In some way or another, the rainy season has passed for the lion of victory that is the son of Daśaratha.
Here, the rainy season—the monsoon—has somehow or other, through a painful process, elapsed for Rāma, the son of Daśaratha;
of what nature was it?
Determination is the exertion toward action; that itself is the sun because it consists of splendor, and its "dusk" is the time of its setting.
Fault itself is a lordly elephant because it is difficult to restrain, and the firm chain binding it acts as a restraint.
Victory itself is a lion, and its cage is the breaking of the home because it serves as a controller.
The author of the *Bhedinī* states: "The word *śṛṅkhalā* [is used] in three genders for 'fetters'.
Here, because there is a metaphorical identification (*rūpaṇā*) of that which is related to the one related to Rāma, it is a "successive metaphor" (*paramparārūpaka*).
It is considered "modified" (*vikṛta*) precisely because of this relationship between the related and the related-to-the-related.
An example of *raśanā* (chain):
