“Madana conquers the world with the sprout-like hands of creepers, the lotus-like hands of deer-eyed women, the lotus-faces of water-lilies, and the moon-like faces of young women. (30)

Here, the composition of words in the sequence of a *raśanā* (girdle)—"with sprout-hands," "with lotus-hands," "with lotus-faces," and "with moon-faces"—is perceived; this leads one to infer that the meanings of those words function as instruments (*karaṇa*) in the victory over the world by the Mind-born God (Cupid) through their connection with creepers and so forth. Thus, among the varieties of *vikṛta-rūpaka* (modified metaphors), this *raśanā* is a type of metaphor consisting primarily of words, such as "sprout-hands" and so on, wherein the Mind-born Cupid conquers the world using the lotus-hands of fawn-eyed women as the sprout-hands of creepers.

The world is conquered here by the moon-like faces of women and the lotus-faces of lotuses; in this case, the girdle (*raśanā*) is understood through the sequence of its sound as it moves backward, turning, and unfolding one by one— thus, this is a *raśanā-rūpaka* (girdle-metaphor), such as in the following *mālā* (garland):
“He is my master in the encounter with rogue elephants, a teacher in the instruction of valor, a heart in times of confidence, a servant at the time of command, and a refuge in fear;
he is the giver of the earth girdled by the seven oceans as its sash—oh, in every respect, who is not Karna my friend in this self-choice ceremony?

(31) Here, because the roles of master and so forth are described in the sequence of a string of similes (*mālopamā*), it is called *mālārūpaka* (garland-metaphor), a variety of figurative metaphor (*vikṛtarūpaka*) that is preponderant in terms of verbal expression (*śabdabhūyiṣṭha*).
"Who indeed is not a master? and so forth; rather, it is everyone.
He states that very point: "In the warding off—that is, the prevention—of wrong reasoning (durnaya), there is an involvement or attachment; therein, he is the master, the lord."
The meaning is "one who wards off misconduct";
he is a teacher and instructor in the matter of valor, and a heart— that is, a vessel of trust— in matters of confidence.
He is the command and the authority; at that time, he is the servant and the refuge in fear;
he is the giver of the earth bounded by the seven oceans, which is marked by the girdle and the cord.

Oh, what a wonder! In every respect, he is both a friend from a self-choice marriage (*svayaṃvara*) and an innate companion; the meaning of the word *svayaṃvara* is "being without conditions" (*nirupadhitva*).
The connection [of the word] with "heart" (*hṛdayam*) occurs through its non-abandonment of its gender.
According to Amarasimha: "Command, injunction, and direction are synonyms."
Because it is elaborated here in detail, this is a "garland metaphor" (*mālārūpaka*).
An example of a "metaphor upon a metaphor" (*rūpakarūpaka*) is as follows:
"On this stage of your lotus-face, the creeper of your eyebrow is a dancer..."
"O friend, the nectar of playful dance pours into the eyes of young men.

Here, the face itself is the lotus, that very [face] is the stage; the eyebrow itself is the creeper, that very [eyebrow] is the dancer; playfulness itself is the dance, and that very [playfulness] is the nectar. Since there is a superimposition (*rūpaṇa*) even upon those things already superimposed through compounds, this is called "Metaphor upon Metaphor" (*rūpakarūpaka*). This is a variety of verbal metaphor among the types of modified metaphors (*vikṛtarūpaka*). All four of these are termed "modified" (*vikṛta*) because they are composed using words such as compounds that are modified by means of "succession" (*paramparā*) and so forth.
"O friend," and so forth: upon this stage-paint of your lotus-face, your creeper-like eyebrows are a dancer who sprinkles the nectar of playful drama upon the eyes of young men;
"playful drama" refers to the very essence of graceful sport, which is itself the dance, and that is the nectar.
Here, the face is compared to a lotus, and [the face] is further compared to a stage; likewise, the eyebrows are compared to creepers, and [the eyebrows] are further compared to dancers.
Since playfulness itself is the dance, and that very [dance] is the nectar, this is a "metaphor of metaphors" (*rūpakarūpaka*) due to the superimposition of one metaphor upon another.
Among the types of metaphor rich in meaning (*arthabhūyiṣṭharūpaka*), he now distinguishes that in which the principal element (*aṅgin*) is predominant:
The *aṅgī-rūpaka* (principal metaphor), which is rich in meaning, may be of four kinds: combined (*samasta*), uncombined (*asamasta*), appropriate (*yukta*), and inappropriate (*ayukta*).
Among these, an example of the combined (*samasta*) is as follows: [29]
"The lotus of your feet, with its rows of copper-colored petal-like fingers and the filaments of the luster of the nails, is borne upon the heads of kings. (33)

Here, in this *samastopamā* (complete simile), the two wholes known as "feet" and "lotuses" are perceived as being mutually related as the object of comparison (*upameya*) and the standard of comparison (*upamāna*). These are represented in their entirety through the fingers, rows of toes, and the luster of the nails—which are the implied points of similarity—and through the rows of petals and filaments—which are the expressed points of similarity. Because they are arranged in their appropriate positions, the primacy of the subject matter (*artha*) is asserted; thus, this is called a *samasta-rūpaka* (composite metaphor). Among the types of *aṅgi-pradhāna-rūpaka* (metaphors where the whole is primary), this is a variety of *arthabhūyiṣṭha-rūpaka* (metaphor rich in meaning). Nor should it be argued that this does not differ from examples such as "the lotus-hands of the kings."
For in that case, primacy is understood to belong to the action through its integration with the rays of the nails, and not to the "moon-nails"; therefore, it is not a *rūpaka*.

As for the expression "lotus-hands," although there is an integration of the action of closing, those [hands] are nevertheless not presented as the objects of description; rather, they are introduced as a subordinate element in the description of the state of desiring victory.
Thus, because only the integration is mentioned, neither the "lotus-hands" nor the "moon-nails" possess primacy in meaning (*artha*), but only primacy in word (*śabda*).

In this case, however, the preeminence of that which is distinguished by such attributes as the row of petals consisting of the copper-colored toes of the lotus-feet is perceived through their placement upon the crowns of kings; thus, both [theories] are faultless, and the entire compound is valid,
beginning with the word *tāmra*.
How is it that Your lotus feet are borne upon the heads of kings?
It is such that the copper-colored fingers are its rows of petals and its lines of leaves.
The meaning is that where the rays of the nails are the filaments,
it is a "complete" (samasta) [metaphor];

just as in a complete simile (samastopamā), there is a comparison between two wholes in their entirety, so too here there is a metaphor between two wholes in their entirety, with the wholes being the primary focus.

If it were merely the state of being perceived in the finger and so forth, or the state of being denoted in the petals and so forth, then there would be a preponderance of words; therefore, he says: "suitable for that" (*tadyogyā*).

The meaning is that because the objects presented by words are here arranged in their proper places, there is a predominance of meaning, and thus it is said to have a preponderance of sense (*arthabhūyiṣṭhatva*).
Fearing that there might be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to all varieties of metaphor (*rūpaka*) where words predominate, he raises an objection with "And not...

He refutes this with "For in that case... with the underlying intention that even there, among the objects presented by various words, the two constituent parts (*avayavin*) alone possess primacy; therefore, there is no distinction between these two [types of metaphor].

In this context, the primary status of the flames (*arciṣ*) is due to their connection with the direct realization (*sākṣātkriyā*); whereas the primary status belongs only to the two constituent parts when they are capable [of such realization]. Therefore, the intention is that there is a distinction between these two.

If it is argued that the moon-nails (*nakhacandra*) are connected as subordinate members (*aṅga*) to those [flames], and thus let the metaphorical nature (*rūpaka*) belong to the flames alone—even so, that defect remains exactly as it was. To this, he says: "And those... (*tāśca*).
Regarding the phrase "those rays [are] lotus-hands," since the defect remains even if it is taken as a metaphor (*rūpaka*), he says:

"In the description of the state of desiring victory (*jigīṣubhāva*), the connection with 'lotus-hands' and so forth is subordinate (*aṅgatayā*) to the primary element; thus, there is indeed primacy of the word (*śabdaprādhānyam*)."
In the present case, however, the distinction is that the whole, such as the feet and so forth, is connected with the principal action; thus, there is a predominance of meaning.
An example of the uncompounded form is:
"O fierce one, your sprout-like lower lip quivers all of a sudden..."
‘The face bears clusters of drops of perspiration, possessing the luster of pearls.

Here too, because the description begins with a single part—the clusters of sweat-drops on the sprout-like lower lip—which are both innate and adventitious parts, and because the whole object of comparison (the face) is not explicitly mentioned, this is a type of *rūpaka* called ‘Non-composite’ (*asamasta*). Among the varieties of *rūpaka* where the primary object is predominant and rich in meaning, this establishes the predominance of the principal subject—the face as qualified by the attribute ‘trembling with sprout-like lips’—through its engagement in the action of bearing clusters of sweat-drops.
"Without cause," and so forth:
O wrathful one (caṇḍi), your face—the agent—possessing throbbing sprout-like lips, suddenly and without any reason at all, bears clusters of drops of perspiration with the luster of pearls;
"even here" [is the meaning].

Just as in a partial simile (*ekadeśopamā*) there is a predominance of the parts, so too here, because of the predominance of the parts alone, it is precisely a non-composite metaphor (*asamasta-rūpaka*). Thus, since there is an absence of metaphor for the face as a whole (*avayavin*), the sense is that this is a "metaphor of the parts" (*avayava-rūpaka*). [The distinction is: the lip possesses innate parts (*sahajā-vayavatā*); the tear-drop possesses figurative parts (*aupacārikī-vayavatā*) by virtue of being a borrowed part (*āhārya-vayavatā*), since it rests upon the parts [of the face].

He states the distinction between this [type of simile] and the "complete metaphor" (*asamasta-rūpaka*), which is a variety of metaphor consisting predominantly of words where the whole of the object of comparison is called a "creeper": "In this case too," etc.
The distinction here is that, by the reasoning stated previously, the meaning (the object) is predominant.
An example of the appropriate [use of the simile] is as follows:
"O fair-browed one, to whom would this face not be a source of delight—a face radiant with the flowers of smiles, with its hovering bee-like eyes, and fragrant with the breeze of her breath? (35)

In this case, "Whose Nandana grove is your face not to [the bees], radiant with the flowers of your smile, possessing the bees of your flickering eyes, and fragrant with the breeze of your breath?"—since this is logically established through the mutual connection of the flowers, bees, and so forth, it is rightly called a type of metaphor (*rūpaka*) rich in meaning (*arthabhūyiṣṭha*), characterized by the relationship between the primary and subordinate members (*aṅga-aṅgin*).

In this context, although the word *nandana*—derived through secondary metaphorical application (*gauṇavṛtti*) as "like the Nandana [garden]"—is embellished by all the qualifying attributes, nevertheless, when the action is expressed by a *kṛt*-suffix as "that which delights" (*nandayati*), the primacy of the actual entity known as the "face" is understood; yet that primacy is here set aside. Thus, this verse beginning with "smile" (*smita*) and so forth is primarily concerned with the meaning: O fair-browed one, to whom is this face of yours not a source of delight (*nandana*), for it brings joy to everyone indeed?
Our head-shaking consists of what kind of smile? It is indeed a flower; by that, it is radiant and luminous.
That which possesses bees in the form of her rolling eyes, and that which possesses fragrant breath as its breeze— here,
both "yukti" (logical connection) and "upapatti" (justification) are intended.
For instance, the "fitness" (*yukti*) or connection between the flower and the bee is the relationship among bees with flowers, consisting in the drinking of nectar;

it is for this very reason that the coexistence of the flower and the bee in one place is logical, since flowers do not shine without bees. With the intention of showing that this constitutes a "fitting metaphor" (*yuktarūpakatā*), he says "mutually" (*parasparam*).

Although in the word *nandana* there is primacy of the verbal root (as in "that which causes joy"), according to the rule that "the state expressed by a *kṛt*-suffix appears like a substance," the primacy of the object (the garden) is indeed intended. This is established through the presentation of an objection and its resolution.
An example of the improper is as follows:
“How can this face—the moon for the eyes of the world, with its moonlight of moist smiles and its lotuses of affectionate eyes—be a source of torment for us? (36)

Here, because of the impossibility of the moonlight and the night-lotuses [existing together], this cause of distress for the world’s eyes—the moon—is inappropriate; thus, among the varieties of *pradhānarūpaka* (primary metaphor), this is the variety characterized by an abundance of meaning (*arthabhūyiṣṭharūpakabheda*).
As before, since the object called "the face" is embellished by its qualifiers, its very primacy is understood through the words "this" (*idam*) and so forth.
O beloved, how is it that this face of yours, which is a moon to the eyes of the world, can cause distress to us? How is it possible?
It is a face where there is a soft smile—a gentle, moist laugh—which serves as its own moonlight.

Where the lotus of the eye is glossy, that glossiness is perceived as being produced by affection due to the moisture of her smile; however, because the smile of anger is subtle, there is here a lack of coexistence between the moonlight and the lotus, and since these two stand in a relationship of mutual non-benefit, this constitutes an inconsistency in the metaphorical identification (*rūpaka*).
He states that the primacy of the meaning (artha) applies here as well, by means of the reasoning previously mentioned: "here too.
He distinguishes the primary and subordinate members within the *rūpaka* that abounds in meaning:
"the fourfold divisions of the primary and subordinate [members] based on the limbs."
They are described by way of being innate (*sahaja*), unremovable (*ahārya*), their conjunction (*tadyoga*), and their disparity (*tadvaiṣamya*).
Among these, an example of the innate part (*sahajāvayava*) is as follows:
“With its petal-like lips quivering, and a profusion of honey-like blood instantly flowing forth...”
‘The lotus-face has fallen, its petal-like lips quivering, vomiting forth the honey of blood that flowed at that moment, its stalk-like throat severed, and its filament-like teeth laid bare. (37)

Here, in the case of the face-lotus, the parts such as the lips and so forth, and in the case of the lotus, the parts such as the petals and so forth—characterized by qualifiers such as "quivering," "drooping," "torn," and "distinctly manifest," and constituted by a mutual relationship of object of comparison (*upamāna*) and subject of comparison (*upameya*)—are understood to be innate. Thus, this is the variety called "Innate Parts" (*sahajāṅgava*), which is a type of metaphor rich in meaning (*arthabhūyiṣṭha-rūpaka*) among the metaphors where the parts are predominant.
It should not be argued that this does not differ from the variety where the meaning is predominant, such as "the row of petals of the copper-colored fingers."

For in that case (the *sahaja-vaiṣamya*), the predominance of the whole (*avayavin*) is intended through its absorption in the act of being borne upon the crowns of the kings; but here, however, because the parts (*avayava*) are predominant in the act of falling, they are distinguished by qualifiers such as "quivering" and so forth.
Thus, the "union" (*yoga*) is the conjunction of those two—the innate and the acquired—and their "disparity" (*vaiṣamya*) is the unevenness of the parts.
"Papphuria" means here that the lotus is the mouth itself; what kind [of thing] has fallen upon it?
That [face] wherein the quivering lip itself was the petal,
and wherein the flow of blood dripping at that very moment was the stream of honey;
"viccharda" means a stream or flow.
That in which the stalk is indeed a severed throat,
and in which the filaments are indeed blooming teeth—
here, the lips and so forth of the face are the petals and so forth of the lotus; since these are innate [to both], this is a *sahajāṅgarūpaka* (metaphor of innate parts) due to their predominance.

Nor should it be argued that there is no difference between this [type of metaphor] and one where the whole (the subject) is predominant, such as *na ca tāmrāṅgulī*; for in that case the predominance of the whole is intended, whereas here the predominance of the parts is intended. Thus he says: "Nor...
An example of a metaphor with superimposed parts (*āhāryāvayava*) is as follows:
"His anger, like a serpent whose fierce venom is stirred by the staff-like reply of Kumbhakarṇa..."
‘Then,
his anger aroused by Kumbhakarṇa’s reply and struck by the staff-like iron club,
the ten-headed Rāvaṇa became like a terrifying serpent whose sloughing skin had fallen away. (38)

Here, in the case of the ten-faced one (Rāvaṇa), the parts [of the body] are "Kumbhakarṇa’s reply," "impatience," and "swift action"; in the case of the serpent, they are "the terrible poison" and "the sloughed skin. Since these parts are superimposed [upon the subject], this is the figure of speech called *āhāryāvayava* (superimposed-limbed metaphor), which is a variety of *arthabhūyiṣṭha-rūpaka* (metaphor rich in meaning) among the types of *aṅga-pradhāna-rūpaka* (metaphors where the subordinate and the principal are combined).

Furthermore, in this instance, it is understood that the very parts—specifically those characterized by being struck and loosened through contact with Kumbhakarṇa—are primary in the act of making the ten-faced one more terrifying than a serpent.
Thus, etc.
"Then, struck by the staff-like mace of Kumbhakarṇa’s retort,
the ten-headed Rāvaṇa— whose terrible venom was his wrath and whose sloughed-off skin was his falling garment— became a fearsome serpent.
Immediately thereafter, the ten-headed one himself became a serpent, a most terrifying creature."
What kind [of being was he]?
He was one whose terrible poison was his indignation, which had been stirred up—raised up—as a staff by the very reply of Kumbhakarṇa;
and he was one whose slough was his garment, which had slipped off and fallen away.
According to Amarasimha, "The two sleeves are like the sloughed skin of a snake.

Here, because the replies and so forth lack the status of being [natural] limbs, they possess the quality of being superimposed limbs (*āhāryāvayavatā*). Since these alone constitute the primary elements, this is a case of "superimposed-limb metaphor" (*āhāryāvayavarūpaka*).
An example of a "metaphor with both types of limbs" (*ubhayāvayava*) is as follows:

“May that creeper of craving—whose seed is egoism, whose heavy root is the grasping ‘mine,’ whose sprout is the memory of permanence, whose shoots are children, friends, servants, and the like, whose trunk is the acquisition of a wife, whose flower is humiliation, and whose fruit is an evil rebirth—be cut down by me with the axe of worship at your feet. (39)

In this case, regarding the creeper, the seed, root, sprout, flower, and fruit are innate parts; whereas in the case of craving (*tṛṣṇā*), egoism (*ahaṃkāra*) and the rest are acquired parts. Thus, by means of the mutual relationship of standard of comparison and object of comparison among these innate and acquired parts, this is the figure of speech called "Metaphor with Both Parts" (*ubhayāvayava-rūpaka*), which is a variety of "Metaphor Abounding in Meaning" (*arthabhūyiṣṭha-rūpaka*) among the types of metaphors based on primary and subordinate elements.

Here too, the predominance of the act of prayer is understood through its immersion in the thought: "May the creeper of craving (tṛṣṇā-latā) be cut down by the axe of the worship of the Blessed One. This is because the constituent parts—egoism, possessiveness, persistence, recollection, the acquisition of sons, wives, and so forth, as well as humiliation and miserable rebirths—are themselves metaphorically represented as the seed and other components of that creeper.
The phrase "of which...

and so on refers to this very creeper of my craving, O Kṛṣṇa; may it be cut, may it be severed, by the axe of the worship of Your feet. Indeed, the axe or hatchet is nothing other than the adoration of Your feet.

The construction of the sentence is as follows: for that creeper of craving (*tṛṣṇā-latā*), egoism (*ahaṃkṛti*)—that is, the very sense of "I"—is the seed, the primary cause; the weightier grasping at "mine," the determination of possessiveness (*mamatva*), is the root; the constant memory that "this is permanent" is the sprout; sons, friends, servants, and so forth are the shoots; the acquisition of wives and the attachment to them is the trunk (*skandha*); humiliation and defeat are the flower; and miserable rebirths and hell are the fruit. Regarding the term *skandha*, the *Viśva-kośa* states: "In the context of a tree's trunk, *skandha* is masculine."
According to Amarasimha, "naraka, niraya, and durgati" are synonyms for hell (used in the feminine).

Here, the seeds and so forth possess innate constituent parts (*sahaja-avayava*), while the ego-sense (*ahaṃkṛti*) and so forth possess acquired constituent parts (*āhārya-avayava*); since the predominance of these very parts is intended to be expressed, this permanence (*dhrauvya*)—meaning eternality—is one in which both types of constituent parts are predominant.
An example of uneven parts is as follows:
“With your moon-like face, whose cheeks are flushed with intoxication and whose creeper-like brows are dancing, Love is fully able to crush the three worlds. (40)

Here, the face as a whole is described by means of the moon; the two eyebrows are described by means of the two creepers which are its parts; however, the cheeks, though red with intoxication, are not described by anything. Thus, due to this total disparity, this is the figure of speech called *viṣamāvayava* (uneven constituent), which is a variety of *arthabhūyiṣṭha-rūpaka* (predominantly objective metaphor) among the types of *aṅgapradhāna-rūpaka* (metaphors where the parts and the whole are primary).

Here too, from the words "intoxicated," etc., it is understood that the cheeks and eyebrows—specifically those "intoxicated" and "dancing"—possess the status of the most effective instrument (*sādhakatamatva*) and primacy in the act of crushing the three worlds by the God of Love.
"Intoxicated," etc. [is the relevant portion].
O beloved, with your moon-like face— specifically one whose cheeks are flushed with intoxication— the god of love is capable and able to crush and conquer the three worlds.

In this [verse], the face as a whole is metaphorically identified with the moon by that which causes the creeper-like eyebrows to dance; the two eyebrows are metaphorically identified with creepers, but the cheek is not identified by anything. Thus, there is an inequality (vaiṣamya), and since primacy belongs only to the parts, this constitutes an "unequal partial metaphor" (*viṣamāvayavarūpaka*).
Now, he analyzes the "pure metaphor" (*śuddharūpaka*) within the category of metaphors abounding in both word and meaning:
"With support," "without support," "pure," and "exclusive"—they say that the pure [simile] is of four kinds, consisting primarily of the meanings of words.
Among these, the one "with support" is as follows: [31] In those [four types], the one "with support" is as follows:

‘The moon, with its pure rays, shines like a pearl-oyster in the ocean of the sky; it is attached to the shore of night, a treasury of pearls that has been released from the shell-like folds of the clouds that have clearly parted. (41)
"A shower of pearls released by Tārā, fallen from the opened shells of clouds that have burst asunder.

Here, the sky is conceptualized as the substratum (*ādhāra*) by means of its metaphorical identification with the ocean; then, the night, the clouds, and the multitude of stars are respectively perceived and explicitly stated to possess a similarity to the shore, the pearl-oyster shells, and the heaps of pearls. Thus, a metaphor (*rūpaka*) is constructed based on both the primacy of the word and the primacy of the meaning. This is called "the metaphor possessing a substratum" (*ādhāravad-rūpaka*), and among the varieties of pure metaphors (*śuddha-rūpaka*), it is a type characterized by an abundance of both word and meaning. It is thus termed *ādhāravad*.
"Shines," and so forth.
Here, the sky itself is the ocean; therein, the stars are the pearls, and their *prakara*—the multitude—is shining.
Of what kind?
With its rays exceptionally and intensely pure,
it clung to the shore— the boundary land—
as if to the night itself; and it was released from the oyster-shell caskets that were the clouds, which had burst open clearly, having become manifest.

Here, in the case of similarity, there is the implied nature of the night and so forth, while the time and so forth are explicitly stated; this constitutes pure metaphor (*śuddharūpaka*) because it is unmixed with simile (*upamā*) and other figures.
This is a metaphor where the sky is the substratum (*ādhāra*), making it a "metaphor possessing a substratum" (*ādhāravadrūpaka*);
an example of one "without a substratum" (*nirādhāra*) is as follows:

‘With the rows of forest trees as their hands of hair, with the fragrant-moving clouds for the banners of the flower-armed god, and with the moonbeams for momentary clouds, they dispel the mass of darkness like a thick cloud of smoke.
(42) [With the rows of forest trees as their hands of hair, with the fragrant-moving clouds for the banners of the flower-armed god...]
"Clouds that are moments of moonbeams, shadows that are counter-hands, and smokes that are oppressive masses [are perceived].

Here, the "smoke-oppressions" (dhūmotpīḍāḥ) are metaphorically represented as the "hair-hands" of the forest-rows, as the "fragrant moving silk-cloths" of the flower-armed god (Kusumāyudha), as "cloud-moments of moonbeams," and as "shadows that are counter-hands. Since these are represented as being without a physical support (nirādhāra), their status as either word-predominant or meaning-predominant is determined; thus, this is the figure of speech called *nirādhāra-rūpaka* (unsupported metaphor), which is a variety of *śuddharūpaka* (pure metaphor) characterized by an abundance of both word and meaning.
[The verse begins with] "vaṇa... etc.

In this context, such masses of smoke are recognized as being like the tresses—the clusters of hair—of the forest-line (*vanarājī*); for it is said: "The words *pāśa*, *pakṣa*, *hasta*, and *kalāpa* have the meaning of 'cluster' (*kalāpa*) when they follow the word *kaca* (hair)."
Thus, according to Amara, the fragrant, fluttering banners of the flower-armed god Kāma are like momentary clouds for the rays of the moon, and they serve as proxies for the darkness;
for the Viśva lexicon states: "pratihastaḥ" means a representative.

In this case, since it is impossible for a mass of smoke to possess a forest line or a tress of hair as its substratum, this is a "substratum-less" metaphor (*nirādhāra-rūpaka*), as in the following example:
"With arched brows, with sweat trickling down, and with eyes reddened..."
"This lotus-face reveals its state of intoxication.

(43) Here, because there is a metaphorical identification (*rūpaṇā*) of the face alone as a "lotus"—the whole (*avayavin*) itself—the predominance of the word is observed; yet, due to the employment of qualifiers such as "arched eyebrows" and so forth, the predominance of the meaning is likewise indicated. Therefore, this is the type of metaphor known as "simple" (*kevala*), which is a sub-variety of "pure" metaphors characterized by an abundance of both [word and meaning].
[The word] "arched" (*vellita*)...
This lotus-face of yours, acting as the agent, reveals—that is, makes manifest—the state of intoxication born from drinking wine;
for what kind [of face]?
That wherein the two eyebrows are arched and dancing.
Where the eyes are blood-red and excessively inflamed,
this is an example of a *kevalarūpaka* (simple metaphor), because it consists of the metaphorical representation of the whole subject— the lotus-like face— alone;
it possesses the quality of *vyatireka* (distinction), as follows:

‘An unsmelled flower, a sprout untouched by fingernails, an unpierced gem, fresh honey whose flavor has not yet been tasted, and like the unbroken fruit of merits—this faultless form, I know not what enjoyer Fate will present here. (44)

Here, because the specific qualities such as "un-scented" and so forth—which establish a contrast with flowers, sprouts, jewels, honey, and meritorious fruits—result in a metaphorical identification (*rūpaṇā*) with Śakuntalā through an implied similarity, it is determined that she is the primary subject both in meaning and in word. Thus, this is a "Metaphor with Contrast" (*vyatirekarūpaka*), a variety of the "Predominant Metaphor" (*ubhayabhūyiṣṭharūpaka*) among the pure metaphors.
Regarding the phrase "un-scented" and so forth: her form is "un-sullied" (*anagha*), meaning faultless; I do not know what enjoyer (*bhoktāra*) present here on earth will come to possess it.
What kind [of thing] is it?
It is a flower whose fragrance has not been smelled and which has not yet had its scent grasped; it is a sprout that has not been plucked—that is, not cut—by fingernails.

Fresh honey that has not been poured out nor drunk from, its flavor untouched and its taste unappropriated, and even the entire, unbroken fruit of merits— regarding the phrase "āmuktaḥ parihite śubhre" (Viśvakośa),

since here there is a metaphorical identification (*rūpaka*) of flowers and so forth through their possession of contraries such as being "un-scented," this is a *rūpaka* with a contrast (*vyatireka-vat-rūpaka*).
In the section on *rūpaka* where both word and meaning predominate, the mixed variety (*saṃkīrṇarūpaka*) is now divided:
"Now, the fourfold division of the mixed variety is stated here; it may be the mixed with parts (*sāvayava-saṃkīrṇa*) as well as that called without parts (*anavayava*). (32)
Likewise, there is that which is "mixed with both" and also "infused with paronomasia.
Thus, this is the twenty-fourfold variety of *rūpaka* (metaphor).
Among these, an example of the "mixed with parts" (*sāvayava-saṃkīrṇa*) is as follows:

“The sky shines like the lotus from which the Grandfather [Brahmā] was born—surrounded by thousands of petals of white clouds and possessing a mass of filaments in the form of the sun’s rays; it is fit for the sight of the God of Love. (45)
"The sky, fit for the gaze of the Destroyer of Madhu, shines like the lotus from which the Grandfather (Brahmā) was born.

Here, because of the relationship of object of comparison and subject of comparison—expressed as "the sky shines like the lotus from which the Grandfather was born"—there is no intention to convey the non-difference between the part and the whole; thus, this is merely a simile (*upamā*), not a metaphor (*rūpaka*).

The metaphorical identification (*rūpaṇa*) occurs through the superimposition of non-difference between two things—the thousand petals of a cloud white as the rays of the sun and the thousand petals of a cluster of filaments—wherein similarity is both perceived and expressed, and which possess innate and acquired parts respectively. Because this metaphor is thus intertwined with a metaphor possessing parts (*sāvayava*), it is called "intertwined-with-parts" (*sāvayavasaṃkīrṇa*); among the types of intertwined metaphors, this is the variety where both [elements] predominate.
Now, the name is *āhvaya*.
Having unified everything, he counts it: "That is this" means twenty-four; thus [the sequence] beginning with *rai*, *ara*, and so forth.
Here, the vault of the sky shines like the birth-lotus of the Grandfather Brahmā, for he is born from a lotus;
it is such that the rays of the sun are its mass of filaments.
It is surrounded by and accompanied by thousands of petals that are white clouds;

it is fit for the vision of Madhumatha (Viṣṇu), because of his keeping a vigil during the autumn and because of its own loveliness. In the case of the lotus as well, it is fit for the vision of the Enemy of Madhu (Madhuripu) by virtue of being a navel-lotus;
or else, it is fit for the biting—that is, the devouring—of Madhumatha, the bee.
"Madhumatha" means "the churner of honey"; the suffix *ka* is applied according to the rule for words beginning with *mūlavibhuja*.
As Śāśvata states: "Madhumatha refers to Hari and the bee.

Here, because the two thousand clouds—white as the sun's rays—which possess both innate and acquired parts, are figuratively represented as a mass of filaments and a thousand petals, and because the two whole entities, the sky and the lotus pond, stand in the relationship of the object of comparison (*upamāna*) and the subject of comparison (*upameya*), this is a *sāvayava-saṃkīrṇa-rūpaka* (an integrated metaphor with constituent parts).

An example of the indivisible (niravayava) type is as follows: “The long serpent of day, expanding its hood—the orb of the sun—and emitting a mass of heat like a sloughed skin, has reached the western ocean. (46)
The long serpent of the day, its hood-jewel radiating light from the orb of the sun,
has reached the western ocean, shedding its mass of heat as if casting off its slough.

Here, there is a metaphorical identification (*rūpaṇa*) through the superimposition of non-difference between the expressed and implied attributes of length and cruelty belonging respectively to the day (the whole) and the serpent (the whole). Although the four parts—the sun’s orb, the heat, the hood-jewel, and the slough—are equally capable of being treated as non-different, because two *iva* words are employed, they result in a simile (*upamā*). Even though both [the day and the serpent] are metaphorically identified, their relationship as part and whole is not perceived due to the lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*asāmānādhikaraṇya*). Thus, since this is a case of a non-literal (*niravayava*) simile that is intermingled with metaphor, it is called "Intermingled Non-Literal" (*niravayava-saṃkīrṇa*), which is a variety of "Intermingled Metaphor" (*saṃkīrṇa-rūpaka*) where both [simile and metaphor] predominate.
Regarding the verse beginning with "dīrgha" (long) and so forth:
here, the day itself is like a serpent or snake that has gone to the "other ocean," the western sea;
of what nature is it?
Long and of great magnitude,
the solar orb itself— causing the luster of the jewels on the hoods to expand and casting off the mass of heat like a cloak—

is described here; since the relationship between part and whole is not understood through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), but rather an analogy is understood through the use of the particle *iva*, this is a "metaphor mixed with the non-figurative" (*niravayava-saṃkīrṇa-rūpaka*).
An example of the mixed type is as follows:
“The quarters of the sky, their bees—the smoke-colored clouds—driven away by the onset of the rainy season, have returned to their own places, like the branches of a tree in the firmament. (47)

"The quarters of the sky—[the *dhuta* trees], like bees drawn from the clouds during the rainy season and released as they bend down, have returned to their own places, as if to the branches of the tree that is the sky.

Here, the sky is metaphorically represented as a tree, and the quarters are represented as its branches; furthermore, the clouds are represented as a swarm of bees. Both of these [representations]—whether expressed through a genitive compound with an external referent (*anyapadārtha-ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*) or a possessive compound (*sāvayava*)—are combined with a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*). Thus, this receives the designation of a "metaphor mixed with both" (*ubhaya-saṃkīrṇa-rūpaka*).
This is the variety of metaphor (rūpaka) characterized by an abundance of both [types] among the mixed metaphors;
in the verse beginning with "dhua," here the directions have, as it were, returned to their own place, their respective positions.
The word *iva* is used in the sense of poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*).
Of what kind [are they]?
They are those in which clouds shaken off are like bees (*madhukara*).

By the rainy season (*ghanasamaya*), that is, the monsoon time, [the clouds] were drawn down from their dense covering and brought near; they became lowered, touching the ground, and were subsequently released or cast off.
They became like the branches of a tree whose very trunk was the sky.
Here, in the compound *dhutameghapada*, a *bahuvrīhi* is employed.
In the expression *nabhaḥpādapapade*, it is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*); by these two terms, "possessing parts" and "partless" are stated respectively.
For this very reason, this is a *saṃkīrṇarūpaka* (blended metaphor) in the *skandhaka*.
As for *dhvani*, the word *diśaḥ* means "directions," but here it refers to "experienced heroines" (*prauḍhanāyikāḥ*).
The other quarters also seem to go to their own places; how so? They are those who hold in their hands *madhu*—wine—that has shaken off its clarity (*dhuta-medha*);

or, they are those who hold in their hands such *madhu* as has shaken off the intellect (*medhā*) by which it was perceived; or, they are those whose bees (*madhukara*) are clever (*vidagdha*) in such a way that their intelligence (*medhā*) has been shaken off.
They were drawn by a man through a thick, firm agreement or oath, and having been struck down, humbled, and brought under his control—
that is, enjoyed—
they were subsequently released or abandoned; or alternatively, "vimuktāḥ" means those from whom pearl necklaces have departed, which is a subsequent *karmadhāraya* compound.
According to the *Viśvakośa*, "samaya" means both "oath" and "time.
Those women for whom the scratching of the nails—the wound itself—is the ornament (*prasādhana*); this is expressed through paronomasia (*śleṣa*). As it is said:
‘The fresh rainbow, clinging to the full breasts of the quarters and bestowed by the departing rainy season, fades away like a fresh nail-mark— the first token of good fortune. (48)
The rainbow of fresh nail-marks, the first sign of her good fortune, is fading away.

Here, because the rainbow—which has the form of a fresh nail-mark—possesses a produced similarity [to that mark], there is a metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*) based on its form. Through this, by means of a punning form derived from the etymology "that which has its foot (or presence) in the moist sky" (*sarase nabhasi padam asya*), and through the relationship between the qualifier and the qualified—such as "it is fixed upon the plump cloud" (*pīnapayodhare*) or "upon the breast" (*stane*)—which is the foremost sign of beauty and the first mark of good fortune (*saubhāgya*)—this [figure] is supported by *śleṣa* (paronomasia). Thus, it is called *śleṣopahita* (supported by paronomasia), a variety of the mixed metaphors (*saṃkīrṇarūpaka*) in which both [elements] predominate, beginning with the word *pīṇa*.
What kind of rainbow does Indra manifest here,
or what does it embrace?
The first and foremost sign of good fortune was bestowed upon the plump clouds by the departing rainy season— that is, by the passing monsoon— as it moved away from them.
In the moist and glistening sky— that is, in the atmosphere— his place or station is such that,
in the other sense, the fresh nail-mark gradually fades away;
of what nature is it?

The clouds belong to that season whose conduct consists of giving—that is, bestowing—water upon the full, fleshy breasts (*payodhara*) of the mature women of the quarters, or of beautiful women; it is a season (*samaya*) characterized by such a practice (*ācāra*). It is called *jalada* because it tears apart (*dyati*) or shatters the "fools" (*mūrkha*), which is to say, the waters. Thus, the season has been bestowed by the traveling hero, the cloud, upon those breasts.
The first sign of good fortune is shaped like a rainbow; according to Śāśvata’s lexicon, "samaya" means both time and conduct.
Therefore, for the sake of remembrance during a journey abroad, a clever man should leave a nail-mark.
As it is said in the *Madrasikasarvasva*: "Nails that bear the traces of affection should be given at the time of departure on a journey;
for when passions have long since been abandoned, love would suffer defeat if there were no nail-marks to remind one of the locus of passion."

In the verse, "Three lines and four [lines], the curved nail is curved in shape," the figure of speech is a mixed metaphor (*saṃkīrṇarūpaka*) precisely because it is supported by the ornament of paronomasia (*śleṣa*).
Thus concludes the examination of the figure of speech *rūpaka* (metaphor).
Now follows the examination of the figure of speech *sāmya* (simile); he states its definition:
Where the sense of comparison is understood through the skillful expression of two things,
distinct from simile (upamā) and metaphor (rūpaka), they call that "Sāmya" (Equivalence). Because its varieties are infinite, its expressions are indeed innumerable.
The statement of an illustration (dṛṣṭāntokti), the statement of elaboration (prapañcokti), and the statement of correspondence (prativastūkti).

Among these, the wise declare that when words such as *iva* are employed, it is the statement of an illustration; when words such as *iva* are not employed, it is the statement of elaboration. || 35–36 ||

Having introduced some subject matter (*vastu*), the presentation of another thing possessing similar properties (*sadharman*) such that a perception of similarity arises is called *prativastūkti* (the "corresponding statement").
In this regard, it is based on causes such as the connection with action, genus, quality, or substance.
When there is equality [between the subject and the object of comparison], an illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*) is prescribed according to the distinctions of "prior" and so forth.

That illustration of equality, based on the connection with action, is generally "prior" (*pūrva*), as for example: "Standing when she stood, moving when she moved, and sitting firm in the posture of meditation when she sat... (Raghuvamśa 1.82)
"The king followed her, who was taking water while longing for water, just as a shadow follows one," (59).

Here, because the exemplar (*dṛṣṭānta*) and the subject of the comparison (*dārṣṭāntika*) do not possess identical genders and because [the action] must necessarily be expressed, there is no fault of gender difference in words such as *sthitaḥ* ("standing").

The similarity produced by the connection with the action of "standing" and so forth is present in its entirety, and the example of the shadow was already established as common to all embodied beings.
This is the general "prior" (pūrva) type of statement of illustration based on the similarity of the cause of action-yoga; it is a variety of similarity.

Regarding the phrase "of the two," they declare—that is, they explain—that *sāmya* (similarity) is that wherein the equality of the intended comparison is understood through a difference in the verbal construction of the two, namely, the object of comparison (*upamāna*) and the subject of comparison (*upameya*).
In that case, there would be over-extension to the figures of speech *upamā* (simile) and *rūpaka* (metaphor);
therefore it was said: "Although similarity exists in all three, nevertheless there is a distinction based on their specific modes"—this is the intended meaning.
He analyzes that [point] with the words "But of that... (tasya tu).

Although that similarity is innumerable because individual instances (*bheda*) are infinite, nevertheless, there are three modes of expression (*ukti*) therein that follow the general types; such is the meaning.
[The word] "entity" (*vastu*)... [is used].

The meaning is as follows: having introduced some subject matter (*vastu*) that is to be expressed, the "statement of the counterpart" (*prativastūkti*) consists of the presentation of something possessing similar properties—that is, possessing equal qualities—thereby producing a cognition of similarity through an illustration (*udāharaṇa*).

By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "the former and so forth," the latter is included; it is established [as such] because the cause is precisely the connection with an action, due to the similarity produced thereby.
Thus ends [the section on] *sthiti* and so forth.
That king Dilīpa followed after that Surabhi; he pursued her.
To describe the very act of following, [the poet asks]: what was he like?
He was standing when she stood, moving forward when she set out, seated when she sat down, and full of longing for water when she desired water.

In the reading *jalābhilāyī*, [the root] *lā* means "to give"; with the suffix *ṇini* used in the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlika*), and the augment *yuk* applied by the rule *āto yuk ciṇ-kṛtoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.33), the meaning is "one whose habit is the drinking of water."
In what state was she? Whether standing, or having set out on her journey, or seated, or taking up water—she followed her just as a shadow follows someone; such is the meaning.
It is said that he is "steadfast" (dhīra) for the purpose of following these actions with a single-minded focus.
Now, one might object: "But since he is 'like a shadow' (chāyeva saḥ), this [comparison] is marred by the fault of a difference in gender;
therefore, how can it be an ornament? To this, it is replied: "unmanifested" (anāviṣṭa).
Because the gender is not intended to be significant— for there is no purpose here in intending a specific gender—
this comparison is of a worldly nature.
And since in the world it is a fixed rule that a shadow follows its obstructor and nothing else, only that much is intended here; thus there is no fault.
This is what was stated: because it is "inevitable," this [shadow] is prior to all action, due to its being simultaneous from the very beginning.

In a simile (*upamā*), there is only a single sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*); here, however, there is a distinction between two sentence-meanings, and thus it is a distinct figure of speech (*alaṃkāra*).
That same [figure] is specifically the former [type], based on the connection with action (*kriyā*) and quality (*guṇa*), as for example:
"O you who have illuminated the entire earth and whose majesty spreads through the whole world of living beings..."

"O you who have illuminated the entire earth and whose majesty spreads throughout the whole world of living beings, even a state of impurity, though brought about by fate, does not endure for long in a virtuous man, just as darkness does not persist for long in the sun. (50)

Here, because the act of illuminating the world and the connection with the quality of majesty share a common cause, and because the sun serves as a unique example, this is specifically a statement of a simile based on the connection of both action and quality; it is a variety of similarity known as "the former" (pūrva). In this case, regarding the virtuous person, impurity does not remain for long.
In what kind of person is there blackness—

that person by whom the entire earth has been illuminated, and whose majesty is spreading throughout the whole world of living beings, the realm of mortals? In such a one, what kind of impurity could possibly exist?
The meaning is that, by means of the ritual procedure (*vidhāna*), the manner of performance (*itikartavyatā*), or the injunction (*vidhi*), [the impurity] was produced such that,
just as in the case of the sun (*ravau*), a state of defilement does not remain for long;
in what kind [of person]?
In him whose majesty— his scorching heat— is spreading throughout the entire earth and the whole world of living beings,
what kind of darkness could there be?
Even though it has fallen from the dawn (vihāṇa).

Here, the distinction lies solely in its uniqueness (*asādhāraṇya*); its priority (*pūrvatā*) is also established through the entirety of the action, being first by way of equality and subsequently by way of a general similarity based on the connection with qualities, as for example:
“That same form is powerful; that same vigor; that same innate loftiness.”
"The prince did not waver from his own nature, even when urged by an opposing lamp" (51).

Here, there is a similarity produced by birth through the connection with qualities such as form (*rūpa*), which takes the form of a general likeness (*sāmānya-rūpa*); subsequently, the example of the lamp is given. Thus, this is a statement of an "uttara" type of simile based on the connection with qualities in a general sense; it is a variety of similarity known as *rūpa*.

The prince was a child, unborn [of worldly nature], and he did not differ from his own cause, his father; he did not undergo any separation. He states the reason for this non-difference: that form was radiant and powerful, its very tenderness was such, and its vigor and splendor were likewise so; and its innate, natural loftiness and height were such that a lamp lit and produced from another lamp does not become distinct from its cause, the original lamp.
In this case as well, form and so forth are exactly the same; for when the meaning of the primary sentence has been established through the illustration, the subsequent connection occurs later.
Thus, that very [distinction] is specifically caused by the association with action, quality, or substance, as follows:

‘The enthusiasm of the great warriors, spreading without interruption and casting the radiance of flashing heroism, surges even more intensely, like a great river whose flow has been obstructed by uneven rocks. (52)
"The enthusiasm of the great warriors, though stumbling on uneven ground, is like the current of great rivers.

Here, the similarity (*sāmya*) is based on the connection with an action in the phrase "uninterruptedly spreading forth" (*avyavacchinna-prasṛta*); it is based on the connection with a quality (*guṇa*) in the phrase "shining with the luster of valor" (*sphurita-śaurya-cchāya*); and it is based on the connection with a substance (*dravya*) in the phrase "shining with the luster of the sun" (*sphurita-sūrya-cchāya*). Furthermore, the simile of "the current of great rivers stumbling on uneven ground" takes the form of both a general and a particular instance. Thus, this specific type of statement of a simile (*dṛṣṭāntokti*), which is based on the connection with action and so forth, is called *uttara*; it is a variety of similarity characterized by the word "uninterrupted" (*avvocchiṇṇa*).

Here, the enthusiasm of brave warriors, though difficult to maintain in adversity, when it falters, surges forth and shines even more intensely; how so? It is such that it spreads continuously and without interruption, wherein the shadow—meaning the fame or the splendor—of the heroism of the brave warrior quivers.

Just as the current of great rivers, having been obstructed in uneven terrain, surges and rises up with great force, and that [surge] spreads continuously— wherein there is the shimmering shadow, radiance, or reflection of the sun (the Medinīkara states: "The word *chāyā* is known to mean reflection and radiance, as well as the wife of the Sun")— so too [is this].
"Exertion in the commencement of undertakings is called steadfast enthusiasm," says Bharata; here,
there is the specific manifestation of such a river current.

The first type of general simile (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭānta*) is stated based on the similarity of substance, genus, and cause, as follows: “Like a spreading forest fire, whatever thick mass of smoke it envelops, that very thing turns dark blue, like the coral-reef of the ocean’s blood. (53)
"Just as a spreading mass of thick smoke, like a creeping poison, darkens whatever it settles upon, so too does it darken each and every coral pedestal [of the ocean], like its own blood.

Here, there is a similarity based on the connection between the substances of smoke and poison with coral and blood, which is implied; and there is a similarity in the form of a common property expressed by the phrase "it darkens," which arises from the connection between the substances of smoke and poison.

This is the first type of statement regarding an illustration (*dṛṣṭāntokti*), known as "General" (*sāmānyataḥ pūrvā*), because it was introduced earlier and because it establishes a similarity based on the excessive application of a substance. This particular variety of similarity is called "Expansion" (*visarpa*). Here, the mass of thick smoke—the great cloud of smoke—spreads like the force of a poison; whatever coral pedestal it envelops or seizes, that coral pedestal of the great ocean turns dark, becoming like collyrium.
Of what sort?
Like blood; "this eastern direction is being swallowed" (*abhilīyate*)—the root *lī* preceded by *abhi*, meaning "to cling to" or "to dissolve into," belongs to the *divādi* class.
The *Ratnakoṣa* states: "The word *utpīḍa* may also [denote] a multitude.

Here, the similarity between the genus (*jāti*) and the substance (*dravya*) is seen as being general in nature; furthermore, because it was mentioned first, the example possesses the quality of being "prior" (*pūrvatā*).
That very same [similarity], however, is specific when based on the commonality arising from connection with a substance, as for example:

"Like a moving flame of a lamp at night, whichever king she passed by on her way to choose a husband, that very ruler of the earth fell into a state of pallor, like a turret on a royal highway [when the light passes].

(54)" Here, the similarity produced by the connection with substances such as the lamp-flame is a *sāmānya* (general) form; furthermore, the two similes—namely "the moving lamp-flame" and "the turret on the royal road"—have already been presented previously.
This is a specific instance of the previously mentioned type of simile based on the cause of material application; it is a variety of similarity known as "the moving" (saṃcāriṇī) and so forth.
That bride-chooser Indumatī, whichever king she passed by, each of those kings attained a state of paleness—indeed, they became pale.
The meaning is as follows: just as a lamp-flame moving at night causes whichever royal road-tower (*rājamārgāṭṭa*) it passes by to lose its color (become dim), so too [did he].
The form *vyatīyāya* is the perfect (*liṭ*) form of the root *iṇ* in the sense of "going," preceded by the prefix *vi-ati-*.
*Aṭṭa* is well known as *aṭārī*.
According to Amara, "aṭṭaḥ kṣaumam astriyām" (an *aṭṭa* is a silken garment, used in the masculine).

Here, there is a state of generality due to the connection with the common property of being a place for movement (*saṃcaraṇatva*), while there is a state of particularity in the form "the royal road *aṭṭa*" (*rājamārgāṭṭa*). Subsequent examples of generality based on similarity caused by the connection with a substance are as follows:
"Abandoned by you, who possess a radiant luster and are affectionate, she does not shine with her face soiled, just as a wick does not shine when abandoned by the flame of a lamp.
Here, the similarity is produced by the conjunction of substances; the lamp is the general form, while subsequently the lamp’s flame and wick serve as the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
This is the variety of simile called *yathoktarūpottara* (superiority by the nature of what has been stated), which is a distinction within the category of similarity;
it consists of the husband’s words to his beloved’s friend: "This bright [friend] of yours, having been abandoned, does not shine like a glossy, affectionate companion."
By you, who are such that your vision is radiant and stainless— by you, who are so affectionate, of what kind?
The meaning is that she whose face is soiled and withered does not shine, just as a wick abandoned by the flame of a lamp does not shine;
[the question is] "by what kind of flame of the lamp?"
By that [lamp] which has a brilliant, radiant light, what kind of wick is there?
It is smooth (*snigdha*), meaning oily; "oil" (*sneha*) refers to sesame oil.
And *malānamukhī*;
according to Amara, "that which is not *malīmasa* is *malina*.
Here, there is a conjunction (*yoga*) of two substances: the heroine and the crest-lock.

The universal nature of the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) and its subsequent presentation are indeed evident; that very [nature] consists in a similarity based on the connection with action and quality, specifically as follows:
"Therefore, having seen the face of those [women], whose eyes were fixed [on him] and whose husbands were away..."
"Then, their own natural fickleness also vanished— like painted lamps— their luster destroyed, the flicker of their eyes motionless, and their majesty departed. (56)

Here, because terms such as *hatacchāyam* (deprived of luster) function as adverbs (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*) by virtue of having an internal quality, both his own natural fickleness—which is caused by the connection with action—and [his fickleness] caused by the connection with qualities have vanished. Thus, there is a similarity based on the connection with qualities, consisting of both a general and a specific form, illustrated by the example of the painting and the lamp. Therefore, this is a specific instance of the figure of speech called *uttara*, which is a statement of an illustration (*dṛṣṭāntokti*) based on the connection with action and quality; it is a variety of *sāmya* (similarity).
Now, what is the distinction between the statement of an illustration (*dṛṣṭāntokti*) and the poetic figure of illustration (*dṛṣṭāntālaṃkāra*)? It is said:
"The meaning is: 'That object regarding which there is a consensus of understanding among worldly investigators is an example (dṛṣṭānta). However, there is no difference regarding this meaning;

rather, many distinctions exist regarding the expression itself, as follows: the mention of both the example and the subject of the example in two separate sentences constitutes the figure of speech known as *dṛṣṭāntālaṃkāra*."

The mention of an example within a single sentence for the sake of establishing the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is the figure of speech *dṛṣṭānta* (illustration); when an example is stated for the sake of establishing [the proof] through similarity (*sādharmya*), it is the figure of speech *dṛṣṭānta* even without the employment of words such as *iva*; however, when words such as *iva* are employed, it is merely the statement of an example.
For this very reason, this is a double ornament (*ubhayālaṃkāra*), yet it is specifically an ornament of meaning (*arthālaṃkāra*).
Thus, in the passage beginning with *to tāṇa*,
here— *tataḥ* (thereupon)— the natural fickleness (*prakṛticañcalatva*) of those monkeys, which was like that of lamps in a painting, has also dissolved and departed.
That in which the shadow, the foundation, or the luster has been destroyed; on that side,
where the shadow in the form of the absence of sunlight has been destroyed,
that very motionless eye is the crest-lock (śikhā).
"Proṣita" means gone abroad; "antargataḥ" means internal; and "pratāpa-pauruṣa-pratapanaṃ" refers to the blazing of prowess and majesty—these three are adverbs (kriyāviśeṣaṇa).
According to the Viśva lexicon, the word "nija" is used in the senses of "one's own" (ātmīya) and "eternal" (nitya).
The suffix *kan* here is used in its primary sense (*svārthika*).

The distinction is that while a quality such as "shadow" functions as an adverbial modifier of an action, an action cannot be conjoined with a quality; the lamp serves as the illustrative example for this point.
And the subsequent [statement] is clearly [an objection];
the sense is that the word "atha" (then) is used because it relies merely upon the similarity in both cases.
"Laypeople" are those known in the world; "investigators" are those who conduct transactions by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Since the equality of intellect (*buddhisāmya*) is the same in both cases, he says: "No one [distinguishes between them]," meaning that there is indeed no difference.
In that case, would there not be non-difference? No, he says:
"by the formulation of the statement" (*uktimiti vacanaracanayā*), the meaning is that there are many differences between those two;
"the property to be proven" (*sādhyeti*) means the property (*dharma*) which is intended to be established.
Regarding the term *sādharmyeṇa*:

*sādharmya* means the state of having common properties (*samānadharmatā*); the "cause" (*nimitta*) of that is qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth; the meaning is the establishment of those two [similarity and difference].

He states that it is both a verbal and a semantic ornament by saying "therefore," explaining that it is a verbal ornament when preceded by the use of words such as *iva*, and a semantic ornament when preceded by similarity (*sāmya*) and so forth.
He defines *prapañcokti* (elaborative expression):

"When there is a statement regarding the equality, superiority, or inferiority of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object compared (*upameya*), whether they are both contextual (*prakṛta*) or one is non-contextual (*vikṛta*), it is demonstrated as *prapañcokti*. (39)
An example of the subject matter being established through the similarity between the standard of comparison and the object of comparison is as follows:
“And the deer, cherished by her offering handfuls of forest seeds, placed such trust in her that she, out of curiosity, would measure her own eyes against theirs before her friends. (57)
Here, the similarity between those things compared to deer-eyes and their counterparts— the eyes being compared— is perceived as existing in their very unmodified states;
this is the variety of similarity known as "similarity in general" (*sāmānyena*), which is a detailed description (*prapañcokti*) of what is under discussion (*prakṛta*).
The elaborate description (*prapañca*) of the comparison between the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object compared (*upameya*)— by way of their similarity, excellence, or inferiority—
is sometimes established by nature as something contextual (*prakṛta*), and sometimes it is produced through external conditions (*vikṛtaupādhikī*),
as in the verse beginning with "araṇye... and so forth.
And upon that cow, Gaurī, they likewise placed their trust in Hari in such a manner;
for she had been cherished and fondled by him with handfuls of forest seeds known as *aṇḍorī*.
The meaning is that they were eaters of wild rice (nīvāra) held in their joined palms;
just as that Gaurī, out of curiosity, measured the eyes of her friends with her own eyes belonging to the deer,
[the word] *araṇyabīja* refers to that which has its seeds in the forest.

The form *viśaśvasuḥ* is derived from the root *śvas* (meaning "to breathe") preceded by the prefix *vi*, in the periphrastic perfect (*liṭ*) with the suffix *us*. The form *amimīta* is derived from the root *māṅ* (meaning "to measure") with the causative suffix (*ṇic*), in the aorist (*luṅ*) with the reduplication (*caṅ*).
Here, the lack of alteration [in the eyes] of the fawn-eyed women is due to their innate ease.

For this very reason, because there is no employment of words such as *iva* or *yathā*, the comparison (*upamā*) is understood as being the subject at hand through its excellence, just as in the following example:
“O charming girl, why do you carry this unbearable pride with your pair of eyes?”
"Indeed, there are such blue lotuses in the lakes in every direction.
Here, the excellence of the standard of comparison is perceived as being inherent in the subject itself—namely, that "you have only two lotus-eyes, whereas the lakes have many blue lotuses.
This is the variety of *sāmyabheda* known as *prakṛtā*, which is an elaborate statement (*prapañcokti*) based on the excellence of the standard of comparison.
Regarding the verse beginning with "garvam" and so forth:
O heroine, why do you carry this pride that cannot be borne by your two eyes?
The meaning is that you ought not to bear it.
In every direction and in every quarter, in the lakes and ponds, there are large blue lotuses equal to your eyes;
for this very reason, their pride is humbled.
Regarding the word *mardana*, Amara states: "It means crushing or pressing."

In this case, the excellence of the blue lotuses is indeed inherent due to their great number in comparison to the two eyes; that very [excellence] constitutes a disparagement of the standard of comparison, as follows:
"O simple one, turn your face away for a moment; this moon, composed of digits, might at some point transfer its stain onto your cheeks and thereby bring them to equality.
Here, the inferiority of the object of comparison (the moon) caused by its impurity is understood as being inherent in the subject itself.

This is the figure of speech known as *prapañcokti*, which consists of a description of the subject through the depreciation of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*); it is a variety of *sāmyabheda*. [The words] "O straight one" (*hesarale*) mean O you of upright nature; "lead the face" (*ānanaṃ muhūrtaṃ anyataḥ*) means lead the face elsewhere for a moment.
The reason here is as follows:

this moon, consisting of digits (*kalāmaya*), might at some time transfer its impurity onto my two cheeks and, having joined it there, bring about or attain equality with them; for the fact that it consists of digits is the reason for its being transferred from one place to another.
The suffix *tasi* is used here in the sense of the locative case (*anyataḥ*).
In this context, the inferiority of the moon—the object of comparison—is understood as being inherent, caused by its connection with the stain in the form of a spot.
That same [inferiority] may be shown through some slight superiority of the object of comparison, as follows:

"O you who delight only in the momentary taste [of beauty], why do you wish to sow the seed of a lotus in a pond? O ignorant one, this Kali age will take away the very splendor of your face, for this world is ungrateful.
Here, the slight superiority of the object of comparison (the lotus) over the subject of comparison (the face) is perceived as being entirely relevant to the context.
This is indeed what is called "elaboration" (*prapañcokti*), which consists of a slight exaggeration of the subject at hand; it is a variety of "simile" (*sāmyabheda*). [The verse says:
"O lady who delights only in the superficial, O mistress who is under the sway of a flavor that lasts but this single moment, do you wish to cast—the seed of the lotus—into the pond to sow it?"
However, the meaning is that this is not appropriate;
the reason for this is that this time is known as the Kali Yuga, and for that very reason, this world is ungrateful and lacks restraint.
Therefore, O ignorant one, after some time has passed, this lotus will stand and seize—that is to say, take away or surpass—the beauty and prosperity of your very face;
for the lexicographer Medinīkara states: "The word *āpāta* [is used] in the masculine sense of 'that moment'."

In the phrase "one who observes the bounds of propriety and is grateful," a certain natural superiority of the object of comparison (the face) over the standard of comparison (the lotus) is intended here; however,
when the similarity between the standard and the object of comparison results in a distortion, it is as follows:
‘The husband smiles at his wife’s face, which has been smeared by her hand— soiled by the soot clinging from her work in the kitchen— and which has thus acquired the appearance of the moon. (61)
"The face, touched by her husband who had reached the state of the moon, is laughed at.
Here, the excellence of the object of comparison (the face) is perceived as attaining equality with the standard of comparison (the moon) through the deformity of its blackness like ink;

this is the variety of *sāmyabheda* known as "distorted" (*vikṛtā*), which is an elaborate statement (*prapañcokti*) consisting in the attainment of equality between the standard and the object of comparison.

Regarding the passage beginning with "ghariṇī" and so forth: the housewives laugh at their husbands when their faces— touched by hands stained with soot from the work in the kitchen— have reached the state of the moon.

In this context, a certain heroine, vying with the moon and absorbed in cooking, touches her face with a hand blackened [by soot]; when this occurs, the hero, indicating that her face is equal to the moon, mocks her. One woman tells another: "By the housewife"—meaning, by the hand of the housewife which has become dark from being occupied with the act of cooking, her face was touched; for that very reason, having attained the state of the moon, she is laughed at by her husband.
(The Amarakośa states: *pākasthāna* means *mahānasa*, or kitchen.)

In this case, the state of being darkened by soot is a deformity; from that very fact, the attainment of equality with the moon-like faces is itself a deformity, since it results in the excellence of the object of comparison (the face) being diminished—as for example:
"The beauty of her lotus-petal eyes, even in her sleep, [is surpassed] by the wine-filled goblets fragrant with liquor."
‘The beauty of the red lotus petals in his goblet, filled with fragrant wine, was surpassed by his eyes, which were lovely and copper-red with intoxication as they fell upon her reflection. (62)
Here, the excellence of the object of comparison (the face) is perceived through its transformation caused by the redness of intoxication;

this is the variety of *sāmyabheda* known as *vikṛtā*, a detailed description (*prapañcokti*) based on the excellence of the object of comparison, beginning with the words "raktotpala... and so forth.

In this context, even the beauty of the lovely red lotus petal was rendered insignificant— that is, surpassed— by the reflection of the heroine’s eyes, which had fallen into the cup filled with fragrant wine; for that very reason, the eyes were slightly copper-red due to intoxication.
"Caṣaka is a drinking vessel," according to the *Hārāvalī*;
"Surā... [is] the daughter of Varuṇa," according to Amara; and regarding the form *bharita*, the optional insertion of the augment *iṭ* occurs by virtue of the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*).
Alternatively, *bharita* means "one who has acquired a burden" (*saṃjātabhara*), derived from the root with the suffix *-itac* according to the rule for the *tārakādi* group;
as Amarasimha states: "a reflection is a *pratimā*."

In this case, the excellence of the eyes—the objects of comparison—in their being copper-red with intoxication is quite evident; yet that very same excellence results in the inferiority of the object compared, as in the following example:
"The deer always bears the full moon upon its chest, but her face bears it only occasionally."
"O friend moon, remove from its cheek that deer-mark painted with musk; for such is the inferiority of that face [compared to yours].

Here, the moon always bears the entire deer upon its mark, whereas this face possesses at best only a leaf-design made of musk; thus, an explicit inferiority of the object of comparison (*upameya*) is perceived.

This is the variety of *sāmyabheda* (dissimilarity of similarity) known as *vikṛta* (the distorted), which consists of a statement of expansion (*prapañcokti*) resulting in the attribution of inferiority to the object of comparison.
"Like a deer," and so forth:
O friend, such is the excellence of that face over the moon and other [objects];
he explains that very point as follows.
The moon, Mṛgāṅka, always bears a complete deer upon its lap;
yet her face, for its part, sometimes bears a decorative design (*patrāvalī*) of musk (*mṛganābhi*) on the region of its cheeks.
Here, there is a verbal depreciation (*vācanikī apakarṣāpatti*) of the face, which is the object of comparison (*upameya*), resulting from the intended meaning of the statement.
For the statement that "the excellence of these two is but slight when compared with the spotted one" is indeed indicative of inferiority (*apasarṣa*);
and there is also "distortion" (*vikṛtatā*) due to the application of musk-designs.
That very [distortion] occurs through the attainment of equality by the object of comparison (*upameya*), and by means of the excellence of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*). As for example:
“The mortal world does not appear equal to the third heaven [the realm of the gods], provided that one’s beloved person does not die before one;
for if he has died, the purpose of the third heaven is already lost, whereas if he lives, he truly lives even while one is still alive.

Here, while the subject of comparison possesses the aforementioned attributes, there is equality with the object of comparison in the first half-verse, but in the second half-verse, there is a slight degree of superiority.
This aforementioned distorted discourse on conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), which constitutes a deviation from equanimity,
begins with the words "not mortal," and so forth.
This has been explained under the figure of speech *abhāva* (negation).

Here, when the object of comparison (*upameya*), the mortal world, is joined with the aforementioned attribute—the absence of death before one's beloved—its equality with the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), heaven, is understood as being actually a superiority, because it is subsequently stated that the purpose of heaven is absent [here]. Furthermore, by the expression of the hope for the absence of death before the beloved, there is no deformity.
He states the different varieties of *prativastūkti*: "In this context, *prativastūkti* is said to be both direct and indirect; it partakes of the shadow of *dṛṣṭāntokti* and of *prapañcokti*. (40)
That [type of *pūrvā*] which is straightforward in its positive formulation (*vidhi*) by way of the shadow of an illustrative statement (*dṛṣṭāntokti-cchāyayā*) is as follows:
"I think the splendor of the moon is to be eclipsed by the cluster of stars, if this face of hers (or of her) were to conquer the faces of young women. (55)

In this case, the statement "the splendor of that moon is to be eclipsed by the multitude of stars" is first presented as an illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*) through direct expression (*ṛjuktyā*). Subsequently, the statement "this face conquers the faces of young women" is presented as the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*) through direct expression alone. Thus, this is a *prativastūkti* (parallel instance) which, by virtue of the shadow of an illustrative statement, is both affirmative and direct in its prior form.

It is called *prativastūkti* because it enters into, or bears, the shadow—that is, the common property (*dharma*)—of both the illustrative statement (*dṛṣṭāntokti*) and the elaborated statement (*prapañcokti*); the meaning is that it carries the shadow of those two.
"I think so," and so forth:

if the faces of young women (*kartṛṇi*) conquer this face of hers, then I think that the splendor of the moon, the bearer of cold rays, would be eclipsed by the multitude of stars; here, an inference based on the object (*karmānumiti*) is to be supplied.
In the case of *vijayanta*, [the suffix *ātmanepada* is applied] by Pāṇini 1.3.19: *viparābhyāṃ jeḥ*.

Thus, here first there is the illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*) expressed with direct statement (*ṛjuktyā*), followed by the application to the subject (*prativastūpanyāsa*)— the thing illustrated (*dārṣṭāntika*)— expressed with direct statement alone; and so the shadow of the illustrative expression is clearly evident, as is its positive formulation (*vidhimukhatā*).
That same [type] is the *uttarā-vakrā*, as for example:
“If this body, difficult to find even within the inner apartments, belongs to people dwelling in a hermitage, then surely garden creepers have been surpassed by forest creepers in their virtues. (66)

Here, having first presented the subject matter (*dārṣṭāntika*) in the form of an illustration by means of the indirect expression "difficult to obtain in the inner apartments" (*śuddhāntadurlabha*), the author subsequently presents the corresponding object (*prativastu*) in the form of an illustration by the very same indirect expression "certainly surpassed by virtues" (*dūrīkṛtāḥ khalu guṇaiḥ*). Thus, this is a case of "corresponding statement" (*prativastūkti*) characterized by an indirect answer (*vakrottara*) regarding an injunction (*vidhi*) through the shadow of an illustrative statement (*dṛṣṭāntokti*); it is a variety of "pure similarity" (*sāmyabheda*) and so forth. [The meaning is: if this body of the people dwelling in the hermitage is indeed difficult to find even in the inner apartments (*śuddhānta*), then certainly the garden creepers have been surpassed by the forest creepers in their virtues.
According to Amara, "śuddhānta" means "avarodha" (the inner apartments).

Here, by the phrase "unattainable even in the *śuddhānta*," it was previously established through *vakrokti* (indirect speech) that such beauty does not exist even within the harem; thus, in the second half of the verse, the illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*) is likewise stated through *vakrokti* regarding the subject of comparison (*dārṣṭāntika*). Therefore, the presence of the shadow of an illustrative statement (*dṛṣṭāntokti-cchāyatva*) is indeed manifest.
An example of the first type, the straightforward (*ṛju*) negation by way of the shadow of a simile, is as follows:

"A garland of *mālatī* flowers is not fit for crushing; fresh love does not tolerate offenses. A wreath of *kesara* flowers does not wither even when faded; likewise, the Queen, whose affection is never broken, does not wither under any circumstances. (67)
