In this passage, by means of two direct statements—"A garland of *mālatī* flowers is not fit for crushing" and "Even when withered, a wreath of *kesara* does not fade"—two objects in the form of examples (*dṛṣṭānta*) are first negated; subsequently, by means of direct statements regarding the corresponding subjects (*prativastu*) in the form of illustrations—"Love does not tolerate fresh offenses" and "The Queen’s affection is never in any way broken"—the two corresponding subjects are likewise negated. This is "Direct Negation" (*niṣedhe ṛjvī*), and since it follows the shadow of the previous example-statement, it is a "Corresponding Statement" (*prativastūkti*). The verse beginning with "na mālatī... is an instance of this variety of similarity (*sāmyabheda*).
A garland of *mālatī* flowers is not fit for crushing because of its extreme delicacy;
likewise, fresh, newly blossomed love cannot endure offenses.

Just as a garland of *kesara* flowers or a wreath of *bakula* does not wither even when it has faded, nor does it become excessively soiled, in the same way, the Queen never becomes one whose affection is broken or whose courtesy is impaired.
According to Amara, "navya," "navīna," "nūtana," and "nava" all mean "new.
Here, by means of the shadow of a simile (*dṛṣṭānta*), a negation is expressed.
Its forwardness and straightness are quite evident;
and it is both upward-turned and curved, as in:
"How could the birth of such beauty occur among mortal women?"
"A light shimmering with radiance does not rise from the surface of the earth.

(68) Here, having first stated the subject of comparison (*dārṣṭāntika*) through an indirect negation—namely, "How could it be otherwise?"—and subsequently stating the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) through an indirect negation expressed as a grammatical mismatch (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), namely, "A light shimmering with radiance does not rise from the surface of the earth," this is a *prativastūkti* (parallel statement) under the guise of an illustrative example, characterized by an indirect answer in the form of a negation. This is a variety of *sāmya* (similarity).
The passage beginning with "among human women" (*mānuṣīṣu*) and so forth has already been explained under the figure of speech *Abhāva* (Negation).

Here, the form of negation is a *vakrokti* (paradoxical expression) arising from the doubt, "How could this possibly be? In the second half of the verse, since such a light is impossible on earth, the impossibility of [the woman] being exceedingly beautiful on earth is stated; thus, there is both a disparity of substrates (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) and a form of *vakratā* (poetic curvature).
An example of a straightforward injunction through the shadow of figurative expression (*prapañcokti*) is as follows:

“O lady, cause your eyes to ripple; let the wonderful blue lotus fall [before them]. Make your lip manifest; let the coral turn white for a moment. Reveal your body; let gold take on a dark hue. Raise your face slightly; let the sky become possessed of two moons. (69)

Here, in the first and fourth quarters, the similarity between the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*) is transformed; in the second and third quarters, the inferiority of the standard of comparison is the intended subject. Thus, this is the variety of *prativastūkti* called *vidhāvṛjvī*, appearing under the guise of elaborate description (*prapañcokti*), as in the verse beginning with "taraṅgaya" and so forth.
O beautiful lady, cause your eyes to ripple— that is, make them tremble—
and then let the blue lotus fall,
breaking apart; reveal your lip, the coverer of the teeth— that is, make it clearly manifest.
Then let coral, the *pravāla* tree, turn white;
for a moment, for just a brief instant, let it reveal its body— make it uncovered—
and then let gold, the *kāñcana*, touch upon a dark tint.
"Turn your face upward, raise it just slightly so that the sky may become possessed of two moons;
'taraṅgaya' is the form in the imperative (loṭ) of the causative (ṇic) derived from the root *taraṅga* according to the rule 'tat karoti'."

"Oṣṭha and adhara are synonyms for radanacchada," according to Amara; "vidruma is also used for pravāla," according to Medinīkāra; and "kālikā refers to the dark complexion of Caṇḍī," according to Śāśvata.
Where there are two moons, that is "two-mooned";
here, by way of the unnatural and the natural, there is the shadow of an elaborate description (*prapañcokti*): the unnatural is the non-innate, and the natural is the innate.
But that [curvedness] which is indeed manifest in the injunction is curved in the injunction as follows:
"O gazelle-eyed one, when your face— with its slightly bent eyebrows, spotless cheeks, and sidelong glances— is turned toward me..."

“O deer-eyed one, upon your face—with its single raised eyebrow and stainless cheeks—this lunar orb, the abode of the spot, has been cast upward; having been whirled about, it is now a pale vessel for wiping away [the darkness]. (70)

Here, the excellence of the object compared (*upameya*) is "modified" (*vaikṛta*), while the inferiority of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) is "natural" (*prākṛta*) and is indeed manifest. However, this [inferiority] which is expressed through the second half-verse by means of a metaphor (*rūpaka*)—as a gesture of speech—is a variety of *prativastūkti* called "crooked" (*vakrā*) in the context of an injunction, appearing under the guise of an elaborate statement (*prapañcokti*).
This is the distinction of similarity in the verse beginning with *ekko*, etc.
“O deer-eyed one, when you raise a single eyebrow and turn your face with its stainless cheeks and sidelong glances toward me,
this lunar orb— this white vessel of the stain— is lifted up and whirled above like a polishing bowl.
Here, O deer-eyed one, this lunar orb in your face is lifted up and whirled above like a polishing bowl.
On what kind of face? On that one where a single raised or uplifted knitting of the eyebrows is present,
and where the two cheeks are stainless.
In that [mirror] which has horizontal lines, such wiping away is indeed appropriate;
he describes the quality of being a wiping bowl in the lunar disc: that which has a dark spot as its charcoal is pale and white.
According to Amarasimha, "aṅgāra" means a charcoal, a firebrand, or a burning stick; and according to Medinīkāra, "karpara" is used for a skull as well as a bowl.
Here, in the object of comparison—the face—the manifestation of its deformity due to the knitting of the eyebrows and so forth is clearly evident.
The very same stylistic device of stating that "the best is being rejected" is straightforwardly used as a negation, as in:

"If there are givers, enough with the wish-fulfilling trees; if there are supplicants, what need for grass? If there are the virtuous, what need for nectar; if there are the wicked, what need for the *kālakūṭa* poison?"

‘What is the use of a camphor-twig if the beloved comes within the path of one’s sight? Even in this world of transmigration (saṃsāra), if there were any other kind of illusion (indrajāla), what would be the use of that either? (71) Here, the excellence of the object of comparison (upameya) is established by straightforward expression alone; thus, this is the variety of *prativastūkti* called ‘straightforward’ (*ṛju*) within the context of negation through the shadow of elaborate speech (*prapañcokti*), as seen in the verse beginning with ‘dātāraḥ’.
If there are donors, then enough with the five types of wish-fulfilling trees;
the act of giving is accomplished by the donors themselves.
If there are supplicants, those who seek wealth, then what is the use of grass?
Since even beggars act like grass [in their lack of power],
if this is so elsewhere as well,
then what is the use of nectar, O virtuous ones?
If there are wicked people, then what is the use of the *kālakūṭa* poison?
If the beloved comes into the path of one's sight, then what is the use of a camphor-pencil— that is, a stick fashioned from camphor?
Or what is the use of camphor and añjanī?

Even while this cycle of existence (saṃsāra) persists, is there any other illusion (indrajāla) greater than it? And what is the use of that [other illusion], since the greatness of the cycle of existence exceeds all illusions?
The author of the *Medinī* states: “*Śalākā* refers to the stick [used for applying] collyrium from the moonstone and so forth.

Here, the excellence of the donor and others is expressed through straightforward speech (*ṛjuktyā*), while the negation regarding the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) constitutes that very same [figure] when expressed in an indirect manner (*vakrā*). For example:

“If her face were that, the talk of the moon would be silenced; if her smile were that, what would nectar be? If her eyes were those, blue water-lilies would be surpassed; if her words were such, fie on honey and fie on Cupid’s bow!

And if those eyebrows are hers, what more need we say? Truly, the Creator’s process of creation has become tasteless through its repetitive nature. Here, there is a disparagement of the standards of comparison (upamāna) and a negation expressed through a clever turn of phrase (vakrokti).

The remainder is as before; these two [verses] also, preceded by an elaborate statement (*prapañcokti*), should be understood as being through the shadow of a string-of-pearls simile (*mālopamācchāyā*)— namely,
"that face" (*tadvakram*) and so forth.
If her well-known face exists, then talk of the moon is sealed and eclipsed,
because that very face is itself the moon;
so it is in other cases as well.
If that word "that" is used everywhere to denote what is well-known, then if her smile is but a slight laugh, what is the nectar? What is the ambrosia?
And if that is her eye, then the blue lotuses have been surpassed.
If those [other] voices are merely speech, then fie on honey;
if those [other] eyebrows are merely eyebrows, then fie on the bow of Kandarpa.

Or rather, what more need we say? We declare the truth: it is certain that the Creator’s method of creation is simply averse to repeating things—that is, to producing objects that have already been made.
And thus, the sense is that if those [curves] and so forth were present, the creation of the moon and such would not occur;
"the eyebrows are above the eyes in women," according to Amara.
Here, by means of the sealing of the narrative and so forth, there is a negation of the moon and so on itself; this is *vakrokti* (paronomastic speech).
The remainder—the quality of being a "shadow of elaborate description" (prapañcokticchāyā) and so forth—is as before, like the "straightforward parallel description" (ṛjuprativastūkti).
To the question, "How is there a shadow of elaborate description in these two? he says:
"Like a garland" (mālā)—the meaning is that just as in a "garland simile" (mālopamā) there is a comparison in detail, so too here there is an elaborate description in detail.

The meaning is that just as in the case of *utpādyopamā* (produced simile), where similarity—whether implied or explicitly stated—is expressed for the sake of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) by means of the produced object of comparison (*upameya*), so it is with the two preceding types as well; thus, they possess the character of being elaborated expressions (*prapañcokticchāyatva*).
This concludes the definition of the general figures of speech (*sāmānyālaṅkāra*).
The definition of the figure of speech *saṃśaya* (doubt):
He states the definition of doubt:
"Where the mind wavers due to the extreme similarity between two objects..."
Poets know that doubt (*saṃśaya*) has two types of objects: single and multiple.
Among these, that which is suspected as many in a single place has a single object; that in which a single thing is suspected in many places is remembered as having multiple objects. (41–42)
Regarding the phrase "of two objects":
when, due to the extreme similarity between two expressed meanings, the mind wavers and does not remain steady on one side, thinking "is this it? or "is that it?", they call that *saṃśaya* (doubt).
And that [doubt] has either a single object or multiple objects.
That in which multiple [alternatives] are suspected regarding a single subject is one with a single object;
that in which a single [alternative] is suspected regarding multiple subjects is one with multiple objects.
Of these two, the first is that where the similarity is expressed, as for example:

“‘Abstention from food, supreme withdrawal from the entire range of sense objects, fixing the gaze upon the tip of the nose, that which is one-pointedness of mind, this silence, and this entire void that appears as the universe—if you possess all this, friend, tell me: are you a yoginī, or are you a woman separated from her beloved?

Here, regarding a single object, there is a deliberation arising from the perception of two things through their perceived commonality and the recollection of their respective specificities; this is doubt (*saṃśaya*) having a single object.”
"Food," and so forth:
O friend, you should say this—speak! Are you a yoginī, possessed of yoga; or are you a viyoginī, possessed of separation?
He states the common characteristics of both: "abstinence from food," meaning a lack of desire for all objects of sense, such as garlands and the like; "cessation" in the highest degree;
"fixing the gaze on the tip of the nose," which means looking at the tip of the nose;
and that other [characteristic], which is the mind being one-pointed and unwavering upon the object of meditation or the Lord.
And this silence is non-speaking;
this entire universe which appears as empty everywhere is yours— this is how it should be construed.
"Lightness of diet, silence, gazing at the tip of the nose, steadiness of mind, self-mastery, and the voiding of the universe— these are the [marks] of yogins," so says the Yogaśāstra.

"Bharata says: 'Aversion to food, gazing at the tip of the nose, silence, steadiness of mind, self-mastery, and the contemplation of the emptiness of the universe— these, the sages declare, are the duties of one separated from a lover.'"

In this case, regarding a single object— the friend— there is a similarity being expressed between two things consisting of union and separation; because that similarity is perceived directly— that is to say, through the perception of common attributes— and because the specific qualities are not perceived— that is to say, through the non-perception of the specific qualities— there arises a deliberation (*vimarśa*), which is doubt (*saṃśaya*), due to the recollection of both specific qualities, namely union and separation.

In this context, the cause of doubt has been stated as the perception of a common property combined with the non-perception of distinguishing features, which serves as the cause for recollecting two alternatives;
that very same [cause] is exemplified by a perceived similarity, as in:
"Is it a lotus with bees wandering within, or is it your face with its tremulous eyes?"
"O lady with thick breasts, as I gaze upon you, my mind wavers.

Here, regarding the single object characterized by the face and the eyes, another object characterized by the lotus and the bees is apprehended through a perceived similarity; this too is a doubt concerning a single subject, such as "Is it...? and so forth.

O you with thick-set breasts and firm bosom, as I gaze upon you, my mind wavers and becomes steeped in doubt; he explains that very point: does this face of yours—with eyes like trembling lotuses—possess a lotus in its center where a bee has wandered and settled? Thus my mind wavers, acting like a swing.
Furthermore, here the similarity perceived through direct perception consists in the commonality of both extremes— namely, the mind and the swing— possessing the quality of oscillation.
The rest is easy to understand.
That which has multiple objects as its domain is twofold: pure (*śuddha*) and mixed (*miśra*).
Of these two, the pure is that in which the similarity is implied (*pratīyamāna-sādṛśya*), as for example:

The young girl, foolish and bewildered, her garment disarrayed, fled upon hearing the capture; benumbed by sleep, she gazes again and again at Rāvaṇa’s face, yet, utterly deluded, she does not even perceive the moon in the forest. (75)
Rāhu too gazes at her face again and again, wandering in the sky; he truly does not know which of the two is the moon.

Here, between the girl’s face and the moon—two things whose similarity is implied—one is suspected to be the actual moon alone. Thus, this is a pure *saṃśaya* (doubt) with multiple objects, beginning with the word "bālī" [the girl].

The young girl Bhumbhurabholī, her garment slipping as she heard the summons, rushed out in a daze of sleep; even Rāhu gazes at her face again and again, wandering in the sky and truly not knowing which of the two is the moon. Here, the girl Bhumbhurabholī is ignorant.
She whose garment was displaced and fluttered over her hips—
“over” being understood here as appropriate—
is a woman agitated by sleeplessness; having heard that the moon was eclipsed, she went out to witness it.
That is to say,

even Rāhu, wandering in the sky from his own abode, gazes at her face again and again; yet, being filled with doubt, he does not know which of the two— the beloved’s face or the moon— is the true moon.
Indeed, in this context, that which is expressed as similarity through the non-mixture of doubt and purity is "mixed," as for example:
"Both of these are abodes of the luster of fresh *japā* flowers; at the end of both, they remain within the circle of the sky during the twilight.
Who sets and who rises? Which is the sun and which is the moon? And what here is the east? We do not know which is the west.

(76) In this instance, between the two—either the sun and the moon whose similarity is being expressed, or the east and the west—one or the other single object is suspected in turn; thus, this is a "mixed" (*miśra*) doubt involving multiple objects.
This is an elliptical indication;

therefore, the mention of "vitarka" (initial inquiry) and so forth should also be understood as occurring only within the context of the mention of "saṃśaya" (doubt), as in the passage beginning with "the two," and so on.
Both of these, the sun and the moon, are the abodes of the splendors of fresh hibiscus flowers;
at twilight, near the junction of day and night, both forms—the sun and the moon—stand at the end, the conclusion, of the celestial sphere, the mandala of the sky.
Therefore, in this case, which one sets, and which one rises?
"We do not know which is the sun, which is the moon, which is the eastern direction, or which is the western direction";
here, the similarity expressed through the red color and the movement to the ends of the sky is a state of mingling precisely because it pertains to multiple objects.
If that is so, why is the mention of *vitarka* (initial thought) not stated separately? To this he says: "It is an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*).
The meaning is that because it is already included within the mention of *saṃśaya* (doubt), it is not stated separately.
For example:
“Are these the two large eyes of a wide-eyed woman, with bees clinging to the lotus petals?
Or is this a swarm of bees, silent and motionless, upon a mass of eyelashes moist with perspiration?
(77) Is this a face with its filaments blooming in an unrestrained smile, or is it a full-blown lotus?”
Thus, after a long time, the women discovered their friend hidden within the lotus grove.
(A yugma. Beginning with "saroja... and so forth.
Are these two lotus petals, upon which bees are settled and clinging,
perhaps the eyes of this large-eyed heroine?
In the state of discursive thought (*vitarka*),
the hair on the head is present; that [face] whose row of eyelashes is bent [is the face of one in the state of *vicāra*].
Is this face, silent, devoid of sound, motionless, and steady, perhaps a swarm of bees? Or is it "not hidden," and so forth? Thus [the doubt].
What is this? It is like a full-blown lotus, its filaments being the teeth made manifest and distinct by an unrestrained, radiant smile.

In this manner, after a long time, the women—the ladies—came to know (*vidāmbabhūvuḥ*), that is, they became aware, that their friend was lying hidden, situated in the midst of the lotuses in the *nalinī* grove.
Regarding the form *vidāmbabhūvuḥ*, [the rule] "uṣavida... [applies].
38. Thus, as it is in the *liṭ* (perfect tense) feminine:
"With her talk faltering from intoxication, her hair disheveled by bathing, the braid the only ornament on her body, and a pearl necklace upon her chest—"

"In the course of time, Love manifests in the tremulous eyes; in the month of Māgha, however, he is not known to dwell anywhere—whether in the mouth with its speech faltering from intoxication, or in the hair disheveled by bathing, or in the chest which is the essence of the garment of the braid and has stolen the pearls. (79)
What, then, is the distinction between *vitarka* (initial inquiry) and *saṃśaya* (doubt)?
It is said:
*vitarka* is proximate to a definitive conclusion (*nirṇaya*), whereas *saṃśaya* is proximate to *vitarka*.
For one who is in doubt, having ascended to the pinnacle of deliberation and then fallen from it, either enters into a realization of reality—
as in the previous sentence, "they came to know"—
or else plunges into doubt itself, as in: "But she does not know where he dwells in the hollows of her breasts."
Furthermore, since particles such as *kiṃsvit* and others are identical in form to those used in doubt and error, their specific distinction is difficult to discern;
[one might object: "In that case, would not *vitarka* (speculation) and the rest also be ornaments common to both?"
However, in the case of verbal expression (*ukti*), it is like inference for others (*parārthānumāna*); in the case of its own nature (*svarūpa*), it is like inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*).

This indeed is the meaning of the word "expression" (*ukti*); therefore, when there is the expression of the mere nature [of the object], doubt, conjecture, and so forth are also figures of sense (*arthālaṃkāra*).
When the emphasis is on the expression, however, there are ornaments of both types,
as in the verse beginning with *muhe*:
"Upon the face where words falter from intoxication, upon the locks of hair wet from bathing, upon the braid which is the essence of her garment, and upon the breast adorned with a pearl necklace..."
At other times—during periods other than Māgha—the god of love shines forth upon her tremulous eyes; yet in the month of Māgha, it is not known where he dwells, whether in the house of her breasts.

At other times, he shines and blazes in her face with its playful, intoxicated speech, in her hair still damp from bathing, in her braid, in her garment, in her bodice, in her chest adorned with a string of pearls, and in her tremulous eyes;
but in Māgha, he is found only in the house of her breasts, and it is not known where exactly he resides there.

Having raised a doubt regarding both cases as having two contradictory alternatives as their objects, he asks: "Which? That which is near to a definitive conclusion (*nirṇaya*) is that which immediately precedes it; that which is near to a preliminary deliberation (*vitarka*) is that which immediately precedes it, since a definitive conclusion follows upon deliberation.
Immediately after doubt, from the stage of discursive thought (vitarka),
he says this very thing: "doubting," meaning one who, while doubting, relies on the alternative of discursive thought, knows exactly what was stated immediately after the discursive thought.
For this very reason, the doubt "they came to know" was expressed;
likewise, even in cases such as *māhahu* and so forth, he states that the distinction between these two is caused by the word itself—namely, "and the words.
Then, having raised the objection that "in that case, [figures] such as *vitarka* would be ornaments of both [types]," he provides the resolution: "the statement," and so on.

Just as there is a distinction caused by the employment of words in inference for others (*parārthānumāna*), so too, in the case of "verbal" [figures], the word itself is the form (*svarūpa*) while the meaning is the object; in that case, the operation is like inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*).
Regarding the statement "as stated in the *Sāmya* [chapter] and elsewhere," this is precisely the meaning of the word "statement" (*ukti*): namely, that which is based on a statement.

Thus, when there is a statement or definition consisting of the mere form, it is a figure of meaning (*arthālaṃkāra*); however, when there is a predominance of the statement—as in the case of doubt (*saṃśaya*), deliberation (*tarka*), and so forth—it is a figure of both (*ubhayālaṃkāra*).
Thus concludes the exposition of the figure of speech *saṃśaya* (doubt). Now follows the exposition of the figure of speech *apahnuti* (concealment); he states its definition:
Apahnuti (concealment) consists in denying something while presenting another meaning;
it is said to be of two kinds: that involving a comparison and that not involving a comparison.
Of these two, the first occurs when the similarity is either expressed or implied.
Likewise, when an object is to be denied, there may be a second [type of simile];
furthermore, it is described as being "without comparison" (anaupamyavatī) and "never before seen" (pūrvāpūrvā).
Their forms will become manifest through their very illustrations.

Apahnuti (concealment) is the manifestation or disclosure of another well-known object— such as a property (*dharma*) or a substratum (*dharmin*)— by means of concealing or denying a certain [well-known] substratum or property;
nor should it be said that this figure is non-different from Ākṣepa (paralipsis).

For in that [negation], the meaning is mere negation, whereas here, the meaning is the statement of another object preceded by negation; this is the distinction. When it is stated that "a simile (aupamya) is that which possesses comparison (upamā)," [it refers to] the object to be denied and the thing that serves as the basis for the denial.
Among these, an example of that which possesses a comparison being explicitly stated is as follows:
“In summer, the peaks of the Vindhya mountains, soiled with the smoke of forest fires, are seen;
O wife whose husband has gone abroad, do not hope for fresh rain-clouds. (80)
"In summer, the peaks of the Vindhya mountains appear soiled with the soot of forest fires;
take heart, O woman whose husband is away—what are these but the clouds of the new monsoon?

Here, because the clouds of the new monsoon have their expressed similarity denied by the peaks of the Vindhya mountains, this is an *apahnuti* (concealment) characterized by an expressed simile (*abhidhīyamānaupamya*).
"In summer," and so forth: "The peaks of the Vindhya mountains are seen stained with the soot of forest fires;
take heart, O wife whose husband is away, for these are not the clouds of the new monsoon."

Here, a woman separated from her lover, distressed by the sight of the Vindhya mountains blackened by a forest fire, is consoled by her friend through the delusion that they are clouds: "O lady separated from her lover, these peaks of the Vindhya are seen darkened by the forest fire in summer;
do not think these are the fresh clouds of the rainy season—take heart."

Here, the similarity between the dark spots and the fresh clouds on the peak of the Vindhya mountains is expressed; therefore, this is an *aupamyavatī* (possessing a simile), specifically an *pratīyamāna-aupamyavatī* (one where the comparison is implied), as in:
"The needle-like filaments of the *ketakī* do not bloom; alas, Fate laughs at those away from home!"
"This flickering streak of lightning does not shine before me; rather, this light of Love expands.

(81) Here, because the similarity of the *ketakī* needles with the streak of lightning is implied through the "laughter of Fate," and the streak of lightning is negated by the "light of Love," this is an *apahnuti* (concealment) possessing an implied comparison (*pratīyamānaupamya*), beginning with the word "not" (*na*).
Alas, the needle-like tips of the *ketakī* flowers do not merely shine;
this Creator, in his malice, mocks and ridicules the traveling wayfarers.
In the form of a *ketakī* bud,
this flickering, restless streak of lightning does not shine before me; rather, it is the radiance of Love that expands and manifests here.
According to the *Viśvakośa*, "the tip of a *ketakī* needle" refers to a substance with a boundary;
here, through a certain degree of light, there is a perception of similarity between the *ketakī* needle and a smile, and likewise elsewhere—
the comparison is clearly evident in both cases.
The first type, in which an object being described as incomparable must be denied, is as follows:
“The guards might perceive my passion for the princess by the bristling of my hair; alas, I have found a cool and dark forest! (82)

Here, there is a concealment (*apahnava*) of the previously mentioned cause—the thrill of horripilation characterized by the princess’s passion, which was the reason for the guards’ discovery—by means of another cause characterized by the coolness of the forest breeze;

yet there is no similarity between these two. This is called *anaupamya* (non-comparative) because the object to be concealed is [concealed] through the presentation of a cause prior to its effect; thus it is termed *pūrva* (prior).
"O King," and so forth:

"The guards who observe me might perceive—that is, come to know—that I am enamored of the princess, being one who loves the king's daughter, by means of the breaking forth of my hair, i.e., horripilation.
"Ām" is used for recollection; it means "I have understood."
"Oh, what a cool breeze in the forest!
Hence this horripilation.
Thus says Medinīkāra: "The word *ām* is used for knowledge, certainty, and memory."

In this case, although both [the subject and the object] are designated as "prior," they lack similarity due to their dissimilarity, and thus there is no simile; that very [figure] is "unprecedented" (*apūrva*), as in:
"How is it that tears of joy have welled up in me merely upon seeing the girl?"
"My eye has been filled with flower-pollen wafted by the wind" (83).
Here, the effect— namely, the flow of tears of joy— is mentioned first, followed by the cause— "having seen the maiden"—
while the rest remains as before.
This very figure, being expressed as a denial of a thing that ought not to be denied, is called the unprecedented *anaupamya-apahnuti* (denial through non-comparison),
as in the verse beginning with "O Ānanda":
"Having seen only this maiden, how is it that tears of joy have flowed from me?"
My eye has been filled with dust (*rajas*) raised by the wind—that is, dust set in motion by the breeze;
the rest, such as the concealment (*apahnava*), is as before, following the pattern of the previous *apahnuti*.
The description, though lacking a formal comparison, is likewise as before; its "novelty" (*apūrvatva*) arises from the fact that no prior cause was previously adduced.
The first type, which is incomparable and consists of a matter that is being perceived yet denied, is as follows:
“O you who are distressed by your lover, lift up your breasts, which have been scratched by thorns and are devoid of their natural luster;
now, O you with full and high breasts, rise up! (84)
"O you who are so fond of your lover, as you gather the *karavella* fruits from the vine pushed against your chest,
with your full and elevated breasts scratched by thorns— now you must endure this exhaustion!
Here, the implied matter— that the nail-marks on her breasts were not made by a paramour, but rather by thorns— is revealed as something that ought to be denied.

Just as before, in the first half [of the verse] there is the presentation of the cause, while in the second half the instruction regarding the effect is seen; thus, this is the first type of *apahnuti* (concealment), which is incomparable and consists of a perceived object that must be concealed—arising from the application of the definition: "Concealment (*apahnuti*) is the showing of another meaning after having concealed something," as in the verse beginning with "the chest" (*uraḥ*).

"O you who are devoted to your beloved, you are now gathering the kāravelī fruits from the vine supported by your chest; O you whose full and high breasts are scratched by thorns, now grow weary [with agitation].
Here, "O you who are devoted to your beloved" means "O you who possess love for your lover"; "O you whose full and high breasts are scratched by thorns," now "grow weary" means "become agitated."
Having done what? You pluck—that is, you snap off—the *kāravellī* fruits from that enclosure (*vṛti*), which is a fence, pushed forward by your chest (*uras*).
*Kāravellī* is the same as *karavellī*.

In this case, because the cause is stated in the first half-verse, the priority [of the negation] is expressed; indeed, the lack of similarity between the two things already mentioned is quite evident.
Now, one might ask: "Is there not here a natural denial (sāhajika-apahnava)? How then can this be called *apahnuti*? To this, he says: "by means of a denial" (*apahnutya*).
The meaning is that it is called *apahnuti* (concealment) because it is characterized by the combination of superimposition (*āropa*) and denial (*apahnava*).
An example of this same [type] as something unprecedented (*apūrva*) is as follows:
“Whose anger would not arise upon seeing the bitten lower lip of his beloved?”
“Whose anger would not arise upon seeing the wounded lip of his beloved? O you who smell the lotus with its bee, you who are perverse despite being forbidden—bear this now! (85)
Here too, while the fact that her lower lip was wounded by a lover is to be denied— since it is understood that it was actually by a bee—
the first half of the verse presents the effect, namely, "the wounded lower lip," and the second half presents the cause, namely, "she who is smelling the lotus with the bee.
This is an unprecedented *pratīyamānāpahnuti* (denial of the suggested), devoid of comparison, which arises through the application of the aforementioned definition.
"Or whose anger would not arise," and so forth:
"Whose anger would not arise upon seeing the wounded lower lip of his beloved, now that she has smelled a lotus with bees and has been turned away despite being forbidden? Endure this now."

"Seeing the wounded lower lip of my beloved here, whose anger would not arise? Therefore, O you who cause the smelling of a lotus accompanied by bees, O you who have restrained your perversity and are full of courtesy, endure now; be patient.
In this latter half [of the verse], there is a sense of novelty due to the presentation of a causal argument (*kāraṇopanyāsa*).

As before, he states the doubt and its resolution with the words "yathokta" (as stated). This concludes the definition of the figure of speech *apahnuti* (concealment) and begins the definition of the figure of speech *samādhi* (resolution).
He states the definition of concentration (samādhi):
"The wise know concentration as the superimposition of other qualities onto something else; it is taught to be of two kinds: without distinction and with distinction. (44)
"Samādhi" refers to the superimposition of a specific quality of one thing onto another;
it is unmanifest when undifferentiated, and manifest when differentiated.
The absence of distinction between those two is as follows:

"When the sun has descended, its passion for the distant [western] quarter being firmly bound, the splendor of the day, unable to bear the western direction, languishes as if it were a direct reproach from her beloved. (86)
"While the sun, its passion bound at a distance, embraces the western quarter, the Fortune of Day, unable to endure it as if it were a direct insult from her beloved, languishes.

Here, the sun, the Fortune of Day, and the western quarter possess the attributes of the hero, the heroine, and the rival wife respectively; these are not disclosed through the use of punning words such as "dūrapratibaddharāga" (passion bound at a distance).
Thus, through the superimposition of other qualities and so forth, this classification of meditative absorption is without distinction;
as in the passage beginning with "far":
"While the sun was still concealing itself in the western quarter, though its rays were bound far away by passion..."
"The splendor of the day languishes as if unable to endure the manifest reproach of her beloved.

Here, while the sun—the lover—is excessively red and intensely impassioned, and while he embraces and clings to the western quarter—the other woman or rival mistress—the beauty of the day languishes and withers as if unable to endure the manifest reproach of her beloved. In this passage, the superimposition of the roles of hero and so forth is achieved through the double-meaning (śleṣa) of words such as *rāga* (redness/passion), and thus it possesses the quality of being "unmanifest" (*nirudbheda*).
The illustration is as follows:

“O beloved, depart quickly; let this [time] pass, for I shall perform many acts of worship so that your anger toward the lotus remains firm, until such time that no person speaks anything at all. Meanwhile, she has suddenly burst into tears, her body drenched by the frost. (87)
"O lotus-lake, while your lover departs quickly and returns again with many offerings, you must perform a rite against your enduring anger so that people may speak freely;
before they can say anything, your body has suddenly been shattered by frost and consumed by fire.

Here too, a certain passionate woman, unable to endure the infidelity of her beloved, perceives the lotus-pond as scorched by frost and superimposes her own attributes upon it, while attributing the attributes of the sun to her beloved.
And these [poetic figures], being manifested here by such words as "I am to be made an offering for your wrath," are perceived as this *sodbheda* (manifested) variety of *samādhi*.

Furthermore, based on the etymological derivation *anyaś cānyadharmāś cānyadharmāḥ* ("the other and the qualities of another are the qualities of another"), *samādhi* is also intended when there is a superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of the substratum itself, as in the example beginning with *vallahe*.

"O beloved, he departs quickly and returns after a long time; O lotus-eyed one, let an offering be made for your enduring anger, so that while people speak of it without agitation, his body may suddenly be shattered by frost before he has even finished saying something."

"O lotus-pond, O beloved Padminī, while the sun, your lover, departs swiftly and soon returns only after a long time due to the length of the nights in this winter season, I shall offer myself as a sacrifice for your enduring anger. Thus speaks a certain woman who has been spurned, addressing the lotus-pond; for by that very reason, before a person can speak anything at all without agitation, you—already withered by the frost—are suddenly reduced to a scorched body through this unpleasant betrayal.
‘Himānī means a mass of snow,’ according to Amara; those virtues were scorched, that is, burnt away.
Because there would be a lack of pervasion regarding the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) whose nature is the superimposition of a property (*dharma*), he says "another":
here, "another" refers to the substratum (*dharmin*) intended by virtue of its proximity to the word "property" (*dharma*); for example, as in the case of substrata that possess properties.
"On this sandy bank of the Sarayū, its sands brightened by the moonlight, a debate on non-duality (advaita) took place for a long time between two perfected youths (*siddha-yuvānau*).
One says, 'It was Keśin whom [Viṣṇu] first slew'; the other says, 'It was Kaṃsa'. Tell me the truth: which of those two was slain by you first?

In this verse, since the subject (*dharmin*)—the nature of Viṣṇu—and his attributes (*dharmas*) are superimposed upon the person being addressed who is the object of description, this is *samādhi* consisting of the superimposition of both the substrate and its attributes (*dharmidharmādhyāsa*).
"Candra," and so forth:
for some two accomplished youths, on this sandy bank of the Sarayū—a specific river—there occurred for a long time a debate on non-duality (*vādadvaitam*), that is, a verbal dispute;
in the reading "vādadyūtam," the meaning is that the debate itself was a game of dice.
On what kind of sandy bank?
It is one where the sandbank—the portion of land emerged from the water—is bright and clear with moonlight;
by this, its loveliness is expressed.
He states the nature of the debate: one person says that Keśin was the first to be slain, while another says that Kaṃsa was the first to be slain.
"O Blessed One, you who are renowned, tell us the truth as it is:
between those two, Keśin and Kaṃsa, which one was killed first by you?"
And those two youths who were perfected were "perfected youths";
Keśin was a type of asura,
and Kaṃsa also was a type of asura.

In this case, the superimposition (*āropa*) of Viṣṇu and his attributes, such as being the wielder of the discus (*cakradhara*), is quite evident; it is precisely the superimposition of the substratum (*dharmin*) itself, as in:

"Having already attained prosperity, why would he subject me again to that same exhaustion of churning? Moreover, I do not even imagine that sleep—which was previously his—could possibly occur for one whose mind is so restless."

‘Why does he build a bridge? Why, now that you have arrived, does he harbor such doubts regarding the lords of all the islands?’—thus it appears as if the ocean itself is trembling. Here, because qualities such as the exhaustion from churning are set aside by phrases like ‘having attained prosperity,’ and because terms such as ‘having attained prosperity’ are expressed through *śleṣa* (paronomasia) alone, there is an identification (*adhyāsa*) of the subject (*dharmī*)—Viṣṇu himself—with the word ‘you’ (*tvayi*), which refers to the subject of description; yet his specific qualities are not identified. Thus, this is *samādhi* in the form of the identification of the substratum (*dharmy-adhyāsa*), beginning with the words ‘having attained prosperity.’”
O Lord Rāma, the trembling of the ocean appears as if it were harboring doubts, wondering what kind of obstacle it might be to itself.

Who is this person who, having already attained sovereign fortune, would again cause distress by churning—using the churning-stick—in my domain? I do not even conceive of sleep for him, whose mind is like fire and who is devoid of all laziness.
For what reason has Rāvaṇa, the lord of all the islands, departed and now returned to build a bridge, aiming his efforts toward him?
"Mantha" is that by which something is churned; this is formed with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of the instrument, according to Pāṇini 3.3.121 (*halaś ca*).

12. Thus, by the use of words such as *prāptaśrīḥ* (one who has attained fortune), which possess double meanings (*śliṣṭa*), there is here a superimposition (*āropa*) of the substratum itself—which is Viṣṇu—not, however, of its attributes such as being a slayer of demons (*asuraghātaka*).
He states the non-difference between the resolution (*samādhi*) and the fusion (*melita*):
They consider concentration itself to be "closed," and that too is twofold:

either through the superimposition of attributes (*dharma*) or through the superimposition of the substratum (*dharmin*) upon another object. In both cases, concentration is indeed "closed" due to the superimposition of attributes.
In this case, because the attributes of one thing are superimposed upon another object, there is a blending, as for example:
“The lady’s loveliness has, as it were, put forth sprouts with her sprout-like hands, blossomed with her eyes, and borne fruit with her full breasts. (90)
"The beauty of the noble lady has, as it were, put forth sprouts through her two sprout-like hands, blossomed through her two eyes, and borne fruit through her two full breasts.

Here, by means of the poetic conceit (*utprekṣā*) expressed as "as if sprouted," "as if blossomed," and "as if fruited," the attributes of a creeper are superimposed upon the subject, which is beauty.

Furthermore, the predominance of the sprout-like hands and other such members is perceived either by virtue of their being the cause of an unappropriated activity or by virtue of their being the most effective means (*sādhakatama*).
This [figure], which consists in the superimposition of the attributes of one thing onto another object, is a specific variety of *samādhi* (poetic concentration) known as *melita*.
That it is indeed a type of *samādhi* is understood from the inclusion of the term "expression" (*ukti*) in the statement: "In its definition, it is called *samādhi*."
"Pallavitam" and so forth:
"The beauty of the noble lady has put forth sprouts as it were by her two sprout-like hands, blossomed as it were by her two eyes, and borne fruit as it were by her two full breasts."

Here, the beauty and tenderness of the noble daughter of the householder, the heroine, exists as if sprouted by her two bud-like hands, blossomed by her two eyes, and fructified by her two full breasts. He states the seed for this superimposition (adhyāropa) with the words "by means of poetic fancy" (utprekṣayā). One might then ask: if there is such a superimposition upon the bud-like hands and so forth, would they not thereby exist only externally? To this he replies: "upon the hand... (kareti).

The meaning is that those [factors] whose activity (*vyāpāra*)—which has superimposition (*adhyāsa*) as its object—is not mentioned (*anupātta*), not stated (*anukta*), and which serves as the cause for its presentation, or rather as the instrument (*karana*) for it;

for this very reason, they are construed with independence (*svātantrya*) as being primary (*pradhānatayā*) in relation to the agent (*kartṛ*). If that is so, then why is there no mention of them in the summary statement (*samādhy-uddeśa*)? To this he says: "But that... (*sa tu*).

Regarding the phrase "samādhyukti" (the expression of *samādhi*): the inclusion of the word "ukti" (expression) where one might simply have said "samādhi" indicates an additional meaning; thus, the intended sense is that the enumeration (*uddeśa*) has been made by means of the word "ukti" itself.
This is illustrated with respect to both the properties (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*), as in:
"The day falls like a body; it becomes red like a severed throat; passion... [and so forth].
‘The day falls like a body; the sun becomes red like the severing of a throat; the twilight drips like blood; and the darkness, black as hair, whirls like a head. (91)

In this context, the body and other [limbs], possessing the aforementioned actions, are bound to the act of killing a living being; they are compared to the days and so forth, and then merged with the action of the day’s end. This is called *melita* (merging), which occurs when substances possessing qualities and actions have the primary action superimposed upon them through the transference of the properties of the substratum (*dharmī*) onto the properties (*dharma*). It is indeed a variety of *samādhi* (poetic identification), as in "the day falls like a body," and so on: "The day falls like a body; the sun becomes red like the severing of a throat."
The twilight flows like blood; the darkness, black as hair, whirls like a head;
here the day falls like a severed limb; the sun becomes red like a decapitated throat; the twilight flows like blood; the darkness, dark as hair, whirls and moves hither and thither like a head.

Here, "falling" and other such actions are the verbs; "redness" and other such qualities are the attributes; the primary actions are "falls" and so forth; the superimposition of these [actions and qualities] upon the day and other objects constitutes the metaphorical identification.
Thus concludes the examination of the figure of speech Samādhi.
Now, the examination of the figure of speech Samāsokti: he defines Samāsokti as follows—
Where the object of comparison is understood solely from the standard of comparison due to its extreme renown, the wise call that *samāsokti* (abbreviated expression).
It arises when similarity is either expressed or implied.

Praise, censure, both, and neither— these they declare to have their respective conditions (upādhi). Although distinguished merely by the substantive (viśeṣya), there is one where the qualifiers (viśeṣaṇa) are similar in form,
and there is another where the qualifiers are both similar and dissimilar.

Because it is stated concisely, this is called *samāsokti* (abbreviated expression); therefore, it is described as *anyokti* (expression of something else), *ananyokti* (expression of nothing else), and *ubhayokti* (expression of both).

Where the cognition of this subject of comparison (*upameya*) arises from the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) alone due to its extreme familiarity, that is *samāsokti* (speech of abbreviation). "Abbreviation" (*samāsa*) means contraction; it is so called because it is an expression of that [contraction]. This etymological derivation is also applicable when the similarity is either implied (*pratīyamāna*) or explicitly stated (*abhidhīyamāna*).
They say that in *samāsokti* (synecdoche), these factors—the instigators—namely praise (*ślāghā*), censure (*garhā*), both praise and censure, and neither praise nor censure—are the causes.

Even though it is distinct from the two [types] based on whether the subject (*viśeṣya*) is appropriate or inappropriate, it possesses a distinction based on the two types of qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*): one has similar qualifiers (*tulyākāraviśeṣaṇā*), while the other has both similar and dissimilar qualifiers (*tulyātulyaviśeṣaṇā*).
When expressed in brief, there are two types; he states them with the words beginning "anyā" (the other).
Among these, that which possesses praise through an implied similarity is as follows:
"What need is there for words to fully express the praise of that banyan tree (*nyagrodha*) which has taken refuge on a lofty mountain peak strewn with jagged rocks?"
"Is he perhaps a kinsman from a former life, or is he the accumulation of meritorious deeds, that person by whom one finds rest upon this path of rough, leafless, and gnarled branches?

(92) In this verse, because the object of description—the generous man (*upameya*)—is described through the very simile of the *nyagrodha* tree, which conveys the implied similarity (*pratīyamāna-sādṛśya*), the praise of that [man] is understood precisely through the praise of that [tree]. Thus, this is a "Samāsokti with implied similarity and praise" (*pratīyamāna-sādṛśyā ślāghāvatī samāsoktiḥ*), beginning with the words "uttuṅge" and so forth.
Can the praise of that banyan tree (*nyagrodha-vaṭavṛkṣa*)— that is, its self-praise through its own speech— ever be completed? Rather, the meaning is that its praise cannot be fully expressed.
"O dear one" (*aṅga*) is used as a polite form of address;
"of what kind?"—
[on] the lofty, that is, the elevated.

He states the reason for the praise of one who has made his dwelling on a mountain peak characterized by high and low, uneven rocks and stones: "That banyan tree was formerly made a relative or a friend by people. (This implies it was so made) by the people.
Or rather, for what purpose is the accumulation— that is, the gathering— of good deeds, the most excellent activities,
on that path where the trees are harsh, unyielding, and leafless, such that people find rest only upon reaching this banyan tree?

Regarding the term *uccāvacaiḥ*, one should not fall into the error of thinking that the suffix *matup* follows immediately after the *bahuvrīhi* compound. This is because the possessive relation (*matvartha-sambandha*) pertains specifically to the qualified whole—as in the expression *bisakisalayacchedapātheyavantaḥ*—since the simple [constituent] and the qualified [whole] are objects of distinct cognitions. For this very reason, forms such as *adaṇḍī* and others are flawless usages; this is how it should be understood.
According to Amarasimha, "grāva," "upala," and "aśman" [mean stone].

Here, the similarity between the *nyagrodha* tree and the generous man (*vadānya*) is perceived through their common quality of benefiting others; consequently, the praise of both is itself equivalent to censure, as in the following example:

"O noble tree! Why were you born at a crossroads? If you have dense shade, what is the use of that shade? If you are laden with fruit, what is the use of that? And if you are full of fruit, why are you bent low?
O good tree, endure now the pulling of your crown and hundreds of branches, the shaking, crushing, and breaking [caused] by people—[all] due to your own wicked deeds.

In this passage, by means of the censuring of the "good tree," which serves as the point of comparison (*upamāna*), a certain virtuous person (*satpuruṣa*) who is its counterpart (*upameya*) is censured. Thus, this is the figure of speech called *samāsokti* (Concise Expression), characterized by implied similarity (*pratīyamāna-sādṛśya*) and containing censure (*garhāvatī*).
"Kimiti," etc.: O good tree, for what purpose have you been born—that is, produced—at a crossroads?
If you possess such dense and thick shade, then what is the use of that shade in vain?
If you are prosperous, flourishing, and have borne fruit, then what use are those burdens of fruit to you?
But if you possess nothing and are truly great, then why do you bow so deeply?

Now, at this very moment, because of your own wicked deeds, you must endure from the people—the pulling of the hundred branches to the very tip [of the tree], their agitation, shaking, crushing, and breaking;

"endure" (*sahasva*) is the second person singular imperative form of the root *ṣaha* (meaning "to endure") according to the rule for the present tense. (The word *ibhya* means "wealthy" or "great," according to the *Viśva* lexicon.)
‘The *śikhā* [meter] is considered to consist of one *agrapāda* [line]’—thus says Dharaṇi.

The suffix *tasi* is used here after a word ending in the fifth case (*pañcamyanta*), meaning ‘from among. ‘Censuring under a pretext’ (*vyājagarhaṇā*) refers to hypocritical censure; for, by making the censure of the banyan tree a pretext, he begins with the censure of virtuous men.

That same [type of figure] is possessed of both [the expressed and the suggested], as for example: “The female boar gives birth to other offspring in order to turn the pond into a land with its lotus-stalks uprooted, its surface uneven, and its water turbid with mud; yet while the waves of the four oceans flood her tusks, this Earth remains in calamity for that very child. Blessed is she, the mother of such a son! (94)
In this verse, censure is understood in the first half and praise in the second half; this is therefore a *samāsokti* (condensed expression) possessing both [aspects] with similarity being implied.
In the phrase beginning with "niṣkandām," another [type of] *anyokti* (indirect expression) is shown: the female boar (*varāhī*) gives birth to her offspring, the young boars.
What was she to do?

To render the lotus-pond rootless and uprooted; to turn the ground into a rugged terrain with uneven elevations and depressions; and to make the water in the small pond turbid and untransparent with mud—such was that female boar, who possessed excellent offspring.

This earth stands upon the fang of that very infant, that very child; upon what kind of fang? Upon one that is flooded—that is, filled—by the masses of waves from the crests of the four oceans during the calamity of universal dissolution.
"In the case of *vyāptāyām* (when pervaded)";
as for *jambāla*, Amara states, "mud (*paṅka*) is *jambāla*, not feminine"; and regarding *varāhī*, [it is formed] by *Puṃyogād ākhyāyām* (Pāṇini 4.1.48).
1.48 Thus, by the rule *ṅīṣ*, [the form] *putriṇī* is derived; [the suffix] *ini* is used here in the sense of praise (*praśaṃsā*).
"Varāha, sūkara, gṛṣṭi, kola, and potrī [are synonyms for] boar," according to Amara.
Here, the similarity between the two is perceived through their commonality as boars and so forth.
An example of that which possesses neither [of the two] is as follows:

"Here sleeps Keśava; here his enemies; here rest the winged mountains seeking refuge; and here too is the submarine fire along with all the clouds of universal destruction—oh, how vast, powerful, and capable of bearing the weight is the body of the ocean!
In this instance, whether there is censure or praise, it culminates in an expression of wonder.
This is the figure of speech known as *samāsokti* (synecdoche) characterized by both [the expressed and the implied] and based on perceived similarity; thus,

from this point onward, the "body" (*vapuḥ*)— meaning the interior or expanse— of the ocean (*sindhuḥ*) is described as "extended" (*vitataṃ*), meaning vast, "mighty" (*ūrjitaṃ*), meaning powerful, and capable of bearing a great burden.
In this very place lies a wonder:
here Hari dwells; here stands the city of the Asuras, the enemies of Keśava;
and here, having found refuge among the mountains, the winged birds such as Maināka and others lie down and sleep.
Nor should it be argued that in the phrase *śikharipakṣiṇām*, there is a prohibition of the genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) by the rule *na nirdhāraṇe* (Pāṇini 2.2.10).

This is because the negation of that [distinction] is non-eternal, or because the specific determination (*nirdhāraṇa*) is not intended to be expressed; thus, it is inferred through the absence of the genus (*jāti*) and other markers that indicate such a determination. Alternatively, it may be a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*)—“those who are both peaks (*śikhariṇaḥ*) and birds (*pakṣiṇaḥ”)”;
for the rule regarding the placement of the first member applies when there is a restriction among many to a single [category].
In this very place, the submarine fire (*vaḍavānala*) exists together with all the clouds.
"The lineage of clouds is proclaimed to be fourfold: the Puṣkarāvarta, the Saṃvartaka, the Ālaka, and the Antika," so says the Purāṇa.
In this case, because praise and censure have both ceased, this [figure] is called "possessing neither" (*anubhayavatī*).
When there is expressed similarity, it is "possessing praise" (*ślāghāvatī*) with identical adjectives, as in:
"No spreading in the waters even though dwelling within them; a delight in the sheath, harshness in the stalk, extreme softness in the mouth, and great humility toward a friend."

"From its very root, there is a passion for gathering virtues and an aversion toward that which is a mine of defects; since such is the nature of the lotus, it is only fitting that the Goddess of Fortune should dwell therein.

Here, because the relationship of mutual comparison between the lotus and the virtuous man is so well-established, the similarity expressed through words of common attributes by means of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) itself—possessing *śleṣa* (paronomasia)—is understood to apply to the object of comparison (*upameya*) as well.
This is therefore called *samāsokti* (speech of compression) characterized by praise, possessing common attributes, and having a similarity explicitly stated.
Regarding the passage beginning with "nālasya" and so forth:

for that lotus (*ambuja*) which stands or remains in such a manner, it is indeed fitting that the abode of Śrī, Lakṣmī, should be there. Thus he says: "the expansion (*prasara*), that is, the extension, of the stalk (*nāla*); and furthermore, the absence of the expansion, that is, the excess, of indolence (*ālasya*)."
Though he has made his dwelling in the waters—that is, in the liquid—and yet has also made his dwelling among fools;
though he possesses a luster and beauty (*ruci*) in his bud-like sheath (*koṣa*), and yet possesses a delight (*prīti*) in his treasury (*koṣa*), in his vessel, or in a multitude of riches;
though he possesses hardness (*karkaśatā*) in his stalk (*daṇḍa*), and yet possesses severity (*kārkaśya*) in his punishment (*daṇḍa*).
Gentleness at the beginning—meaning softness in the mouth, yet also sweetness of speech in the face; great humility toward the sun—the friend, yet also great affection for a true friend;

and devotion to the gathering of threads from the very root—meaning attachment to the collection of fibers from the base, yet also the effort in the cultivation of virtues such as character from the very root—meaning from the primordial ancestor.

There is malice and envy toward the moon, which is a mine of defects (*doṣākara*); furthermore, there is hatred—that is, displeasure—toward a person who is a source (*ākara*) or place of origin of faults.
Regarding this, Amara states: "The word *nāla* is used for a lotus stalk and is not feminine," and Viśva states: "'Jala' refers to water and also to a fool."
The author of the Medinī lexicon states: "The word *kośa*—which is not feminine—is used for a bud, a vessel, a collection of wealth, and a divine treasure";
and [he also states]: "*Daṇḍa* is used for a trunk and for a rule."
"Face" (*mukha*) is used in the sense of "mouth" (*āsya*) and "beginning" (*prārambha*);
"friend" (*mitra*) is used in the sense of "well-wisher" (*suhṛd*) and "sun" (*arka*);
"root" (*mūla*) is used in the sense of "fibrous root" (*śiphā*) and "cause" (*kāraṇa*).
"Guṇa refers to a thread, virtue, and so forth," and "Doṣa is said to mean a fault, the night, and the arm."
"‘Vasatiḥ’ means ‘in a dwelling,’ according to the Viśva lexicon.

Here, the relationship between the object of comparison (*upamāna*) and the subject of comparison (*upameya*)—namely, the lotus and the virtuous person—is established by conventional usage; therefore, through the use of adjectives that possess double meanings (*śliṣṭa*), a resemblance is expressed as if it were a pun (*śleṣa*).
Furthermore, because the intent is praise, there is the quality of being commendable (*ślāghāvat*)."
An example of [the figure *Vyatireka*] where the similarity is both implied and expressed, possessing praise and censure, and characterized by both common and uncommon attributes, is as follows:
"O travelers, come back once more to that lake, the ornament of the road, reaching which you may sport at will, your burden of fatigue dissolved!
But from this salt ocean, whose waters were cast out by the aged tortoise, retreat is auspicious; an entry [again] is not possible by any means. (97)

Here, in the first half-verse, praise is understood for the two things whose similarity is explicitly stated, whereas in the second half-verse, censure is perceived for the two things whose similarity is implied. This is the *samāsokti* (speech of abbreviation) characterized by both [praise and censure], where the similarity is expressed in one case and implied in the other, with dissimilar qualifiers;
as in "upādhvam" and so forth:
"O travelers, resort to—that is, frequent—that lake."
Of what nature is this lake, which has become the tilaka-mark and the ornament of the path,
having reached which you, with the burden of your fatigue dispelled, sport at your own pleasure and play as you desire?
Turning back from this salt ocean is indeed auspicious and bestows welfare, whereas entering it in any way whatsoever does not bestow welfare;
the sense is that one must not descend into it.
From what kind of salt ocean?
From that [lake] whose water (*payaḥ*) was churned by a hard, aged tortoise (*kamaṭhaḥ*);

[the form] *upādhvam* is derived from the root *ās* preceded by the prefix *upa* in the sense of "sitting down" (*upaveśane*), in the second person plural middle voice, according to Pāṇini 8.2.35 (*dhi ca*).
25. Thus there is the elision of the letter *s* [in *kalyāṇīsutaḥ*];
[the term] *kamaṭha-kacchapau* is according to Amarasimha;
[the form] *kalyāṇī* is derived by adding the suffix *ṅīṣ* because it belongs to the *gaurādi* group.

In the first half of this verse, the similarity between the lake and the virtuous person is expressed through their equal possession of qualities such as benefiting others, and praise is clearly evident. In the second half, however, because the salt ocean does not provide such benefit, censure is clearly perceived; here, although the reproach directed at the wicked person is also understood, it is not so by means of the adjectives themselves—thus, there is "unequal adjectivality" (atulyaviśeṣaṇatā).
Anyokti is of two kinds: within its own genus (svajāti) and in another genus (jātyantara). Of these, an example within its own genus is as follows:
"Stained red by the saffron from the bosom of Lakṣmī’s breasts..."
"This is Bali, by whom his hand was made into an alms-bowl.

Here, by the word *hari* or the word *bali*, a certain specific male figure from a shared past narrative is expressed. This is an *anyokti* (indirect expression) concerning its own class (*svajātiviṣaya*), which, because it takes the form of a concise statement (*saṃkṣepokti*), is indeed *samāsokti* (speech of abbreviation), as in the case of "Lakṣmī" and so forth.
That Bali alone is truly generous,
by whom— by that powerful one— the hand of this Hari-Viṣṇu was turned into an alms-bowl, brought to the state of being a begging vessel; what kind of hand was it?
"Reddened"— meaning made crimson— by the saffron from the bosom of Lakṣmī's breasts;
here, "belonging to its own kind" refers to having similar conduct,
while there is also a sense of "otherness" in relation to Hari and Bali.

If so, how can it be considered *samāsokti* (synecdoche)? To this he says: "By way of brevity" (*saṃkṣepa*); the meaning is that it is called *samāsokti* precisely because of its presentation in a concise manner.
An example from a different class [of poetry] is as follows:
"Behold, a bee, drinking honey at will from a blossomed lotus, kisses even a bud that has not yet unfolded its fragrance.

(99) Here, by the word "bee" (*bhramara*), a certain lover is denoted; by the word "blossomed lotus" (*phullapaṅkaja*), a certain mature woman; and by the word "bud" (*kuḍmala*), a certain innocent maiden. This *anyokti* concerning another species is indeed nothing other than *samāsokti*.
"Drinking," and so forth:

Behold how a bee, while drinking honey from a full-blown lotus according to its desire— that is, according to its wish— also kisses a bud that has not yet attained fragrance, even though it possesses no developed scent.
In this case, it is the meaning of the sentence itself that constitutes the object;

here, by the term "expression of non-difference" (*ananyokti*), the attainment of that state— referring to the locus of superimposition— is expressed as a distinct genus, being a genus different from [the literal] distinct genera.
Just as in the case of "this is Brahmadatta," that [naming] is twofold: pure and variegated; of these two, the pure is as follows:—

"Cast your eyes toward the top of the rampart, where the cakora birds of the garden, their beaks smeared with plaster, follow the pure moonlight that resembles the ripening of fresh *lavalī* fruit; consider for a moment—what is this cool-rayed one in the sky whose deer has vanished?
Here, someone, having superimposed the moon upon the face of a certain woman, speaks thus.

This very [figure] is one where the qualifying attributes are identical in the first half, but in the second half—in the verse "anākāśe ko 'yaṃ galitahariṇaḥ" (Who is this in the sky, from which the moon has fallen?)—it is *samāsokti* (speech of compression) with identical qualifiers; this is called *ananyokti* (speech of non-otherness).
Because the superimposition occurs upon a single object alone, it is termed "pure" (*śuddhā*); it is called *ananyokti* because there is no mention of another [object].
And thus, by the term "non-different expression," it is stated that the attainment of its state— that is, having that very thing as its object—
is of the form "this is that"; [the objection that] this is futile, and so forth.
O friend, direct your two eyes toward the top of the wall— that is, near the edge of the rampart— and consider for a moment:
what is this cool-rayed moon, devoid of its deer-mark and having abandoned its spot, appearing in a place that is not the sky— a region beyond the firmament?
Of what kind [is he] who is scattering, that is, spreading, the moonlight? Of what kind [is it]?
Followed by those cakora birds dwelling in the grove who had vainly and falsely swallowed their food— meaning they were preoccupied with devouring mouthfuls— and who thus pursued her,
she was radiant and fresh like a newly blossomed variety of lavalī creeper, and full of affection for its ripening fruit.

The *Viśvaprakāśa* states, "‘Lavalī’ is a variety of creeper (*latābhidā*). Furthermore, the word *lavalī* denoting the same object is also recorded as *lavali* in the *Śabdabhedaprakāśa*, which notes: "‘Lavali’ is [the same as] *śvetapārthapī*."
In the expression *upaprākārāgram*, there is an *avyayībhāva* compound in the sense of proximity (*sāmīpye*).

Here, in the first half [of the verse], it is stated that there is a commonality of attributes (*tulyaviśeṣaṇatva*) between the two things being seated or placed; in the second half, however, there is a lack of such commonality of attributes (*atulyaviśeṣaṇatva*).

The description of that very thing alone, the statement of nothing else, and the purity resulting from the description of only one thing, constitute the variegated [type of *citram*], as for example: "The lotus is not in water; the two blue lotuses are in the lotus; and those [lotuses] are upon a golden creeper."
"And yet she is so delicate and lovely—what is this succession of portents?
(101). Here, the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) and the variety (*vaicitrya*) are explained by the literal reading itself, as before.
This is *ananyokti* (the "non-other" expression), which is said to be a variety of *samāsokti* (synecdoche) due to the manifoldness of its superimpositions.
"A lotus," and so forth:

there is a lotus in a place devoid of water; moreover, upon that lotus are two *kuvalayas*, two blue water-lilies; and those lotuses and water-lilies are upon a golden creeper (*kanakalatikā*); and that golden creeper, being delicate and tender, is beautiful and lovely—in this manner, what is this succession of portents, this series of ill omens?
According to Amara’s lexicon, "utpāta" also means "ariṣṭa" (an omen or portent).

The phrase "as before" refers to the superimposition of a lotus and so forth upon the face and other features of a certain woman. Furthermore, the "wonderfulness" (vicitratā) consists in the expression of a lotus and the like by using the term "blue water-lily" (kuvalaya) and so on; this is stated as being non-different from that very [superimposition] because of its designation.
An example of the expression of both [the object and the subject] is as follows:

“Who indeed is this other ocean of loveliness here, wherein lotuses float together with the moon; wherein the temples of elephants emerge, and wherein there are other plantain stalks and lotus stems? (102)

Here, "this is a new ocean of loveliness" is an *anyokti* (indirect expression), while "where the blue lotuses mingle with the moon," and so forth, is a *nānyokti* (non-indirect expression). Because it possesses both of these, it is designated as *ubhayokti* (dual expression);

and this is merely an illustration, for any other concise statement regarding the relationship between the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*) is likewise *samāsokti* (speech of abbreviation).
"O Lāvaṇya," and so forth.
In this place, who is this unprecedented and extraordinary ocean of loveliness, this river of tenderness,
wherein lotuses mingle and meet with the moon?
Where the slopes of the frontal globes of elephants emerge and rise up,
and where there are other plantain trunks and lotus stalks—
Medinīkāra states that the word *sindhu* denotes a male when referring to an ocean and a female when referring to a river.

And here, by the mention of the "ocean" (*sindhu*), there is *anyokti* (indirect description); yet, by the phrase beginning with "where," the ocean itself is described, resulting in *ananyokti* (non-indirect description).
This captures the *samāsokti* (condensed metaphor) which is distinct from both *anyokti* and *ananyokti*. It is an "indicatory mark" (*upalakṣaṇa*).

For example: “The moon seems smeared with collyrium; the gaze of the deer is as if dulled; the coral leaf has lost its ruddy glow; the luster of gold is turned dark; and alas, even a slight harshness has begun to manifest in the throats of the female cuckoos and upon the plumage of the peacocks before Sītā. (10.3)

In this instance, by means of a brief statement (*saṃkṣepokti*) regarding the moon—which is the locus of the collection of parts such as the face denoted by the word "Sītā"—it is said that the moon is as if smeared with collyrium, the gaze of deer is as if dulled, the redness of coral is as if faded, the luster of gold is as if darkened, the warbling of cuckoos is as if harsh, and the plumage of peacocks is as if contemptible. Through this poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*), even though they are not explicitly mentioned, the objects of comparison—the face and so forth—are understood. This too is a brief statement, and thus it is indeed *samāsokti* (speech of abbreviation). But what is the distinction between *samāsokti* and *samādhyukti* (speech of resolution)? It is said: [the former consists in the understanding of unstated objects through the description of another].

Where a non-contextual attribute is superimposed upon the contextual subject, that is *samādhyukti* (the figure of "resolution"), as in: "The beauty of the day surely suffers, unable to endure the reproach of her beloved.
On the other hand, where a contextual attribute is [superimposed] upon the non-contextual, that is *samāsokti* (the figure of "condensed expression").
For example: "The bee drinks honey at will from the blooming lotus.
If it is argued that this is the same as [the case of] superimposition upon a substratum (dharmin), we reply: no.

In such instances as "Are you not that person? Tell me the truth; who was killed there by you previously? and so forth, and in such instances as "What is this moon with its deer vanished in a skyless space? and so forth, a specific type of superimposition (*adhyāsa*) is clearly seen;
in one case it is evident through the mind, while in the other it is through speech. This, then, is the distinction between *samādhi* (concealment) and *samāsokti* (abbreviated expression).
"Indu... and so forth: before Sītā, the moon appears as if smeared with *añjana* (collyrium);
the gaze of the does has become as if dulled, indeed rendered motionless.
The sprout, with its crimson hue as if faded,
and the harshness in the throats of the female cuckoos— alas, whether in joy or in sorrow, an offensive word has been uttered and set in motion!
The plumage of the crested peacocks has become as if censurable;
according to Amara, "harshness is excessive speech.

Here, by the word *sītā* (the furrow), the collection of facial features and other limbs is expressed. Since the various perceptions of the objects of comparison are described immediately following that, the objects of comparison—such as the face and so forth—are understood even though they are not explicitly stated. Thus, this is a concise expression regarding the objects of comparison and the things compared.
Considering there to be no difference between *samādhyukti* (synthetic expression) and *samāsokti* (elliptical expression), he asks what distinguishes them. The answer is:

*yatra* (wherein); wherein, with respect to a subject already present in the context (*prakaraṇa-pariprāpta*), there is the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of a quality not present in that context—that is *samādhyukti*.
[For example: "She languishes as if unable to endure [him]," and so forth.

Here, the superimposition of a reproach witnessed by the beloved is extraneous to the context; where there is a superimposition of the attributes of the subject at hand upon something not under discussion, that is *samāsokti* (speech of brevity).

For example, in the phrase "drinking honey as he pleases," there is a superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of the relevant lover (*kāmin*) upon the irrelevant bee; if one then objects that this case is identical to the superimposition of the substratum (*dharmy-adhyāsa*), [the author] says "nanu" (but surely) to show that the distinction between those two lies precisely in their being contextual (*prākaraṇika*) or non-contextual (*aprākaraṇika*). He then says "no" to show that there is no fault even in the case of the superimposition of the substratum.

The meaning is that there is a distinction: in cases such as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*), there is a superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of both the subject (*dharmin*) and the attribute (*dharma*), whereas in cases such as "not space" (*anākāśa*), there is a superimposition of the subject alone.
Furthermore, in "That thou art" and so forth, the superimposition occurs through the mind, while in "not space" and so forth, it occurs through speech;
this constitutes the definition of the poetic figure *samāsokti* (elliptical expression).
The Definition of the Figure of Speech *Utprekṣā*:
When an object existing in one way is imagined as being otherwise—whether it be a substance (*dravya*), a quality (*guṇa*), or an action (*kriyā*)—that is declared to be *utprekṣā*. (50)
He states the definition of *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy): "In another way" (*anyathā*) means that an object existing in one manner is there imagined or conceived in another manner; this is *utprekṣā*.
The definition is: *utprekṣā* is the attribution of what is non-existent.
In response to the inquiry as to what kind of entity it is, he says: "Substance.
Substance refers to earth and so forth; quality refers to color and so forth; and action refers to cooking and so forth.
Among these, the poetic conceit (utprekṣā) regarding substance is as follows:
"Umā sees her own reflection in the mirror, residing within her body, as if it were another form of Ardhanārīśvara produced from half of the other half.

Here, there is a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) consisting in the imagining of a substance—characterized by the form of Ardhanārīśvara which exists in a different state in the mirror as a reflected image—as being another substance in the form of a different Ardhanārīśvara produced from the other half; thus, this becomes a "poetic fancy of a substance" (*dravyotprekṣā*).
Regarding the passage beginning with "dehastha" (situated in the body):

he sees the image—the reflection—of Gaurī situated in his own body within a mirror; it is as if another Ardhanārīśvara were produced from the other half [of himself]. Here, the word "iva" (as if) serves to indicate a poetic conceit (*utprekṣā*).

The poetic conceit (*utprekṣā*) that a substance here is imagined as having the internal form of Ardhanārīśvara is an instance of a conceit regarding a quality residing in a substance (*guṇotprekṣā*). For example:
"It is as if put forth buds by her sprout-like hands, and as if blossomed by her eyes..."
