‘The beauty of the noble lady has, as it were, put forth sprouts through her sprout-like hands, blossomed through her eyes, and borne fruit through her full breasts. (105)

Here, the imaginative conceiving (*utprekṣā*) of that which exists in one form— as the beauty of the limbs— otherwise, namely as hands, sprouts, and so forth, in another form, such as being "sprouted" and so on, constitutes this *guṇotprekṣā* (quality-based imaginative conceit).
This is explained under the figure of speech *samādhi* in the verse beginning with *pallaviaṃ*.
Here, the poetic fancy (utprekṣā) regarding the quality of beauty consists in imagining it as being "sprouted" and so forth.
An example of the poetic fancy regarding an action is as follows:
"The elephants of the army, repeatedly taking up the ink of rut from their temples with the pens of their own trunks..."
"O Lord of Men, I believe that [your elephants] are inscribing garlands of praise for your victory upon the inner surfaces of the palm leaves on the shore of the ocean.

Here, the taking up of the ink-like ichor-fluid by the trunks of the army's elephants—which resemble pens—from their temples, and its deposition upon the inner surfaces of the palm leaves on the shore in the form of great letters, is imagined otherwise in the manner described; thus, this is a *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy), specifically a *kriyotprekṣā* (fancy regarding action), beginning with the words "senā" and so forth.
O Lord of Men, I believe that the elephants of your army are inscribing garlands of praise for your victory;
for what kind [of scribes] are they?
With their own trunks—their "hands"—which serve as pens known as *kāpas*, they repeatedly take up the very ink of rut from their temples.
To the question "Where do they write?", he says: "In the midst of palm leaves on the seashore.
The word *manye* indicates a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*).
According to the *Viśva* lexicon, "the term *puṣkara* refers to the tip of an elephant's trunk."
Nor should it be argued that because the root *likh* is listed among the *ku*-class roots, it would lack *guṇa* due to its *ṅit*-status and thus form *likhanī*;
for by the citation of the rule "rada vilekhane," it is understood that the prescription of *ṅit*-status is not universally obligatory (*anitya*).
Precisely for this reason, one should not trust a scribe whose ears have been marked with a stylus (*lekhanī*).
Such are the usages; "the pen is that which accomplishes writing," according to the *Ratnakośa*;
"the post for binding elephants is called *ālāna*," according to the *Amara-kośa*.
And regarding the statement, "The body (śarīra), the stature (varṣma),
the form (vigraha)," here the poetic fancy (utprekṣā) consists in imagining the lotus and so forth as being a pen and so forth;
it should not be said that this is merely a fancy of substance (dravyotprekṣā), because the intent of all [the words] lies precisely in the act of writing.

Since all [these varieties] are subsumed under that very [figure of speech], according to the maxim that "the meaning of a word is that which the word aims at," the components of *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy),
as well as what is considered *utprekṣā* and *upamā* (simile), do not differ from one another in their essential nature as *utprekṣā*. 51.
He states that there is no difference between the "parts of a poetic fancy" (*utprekṣāvayava*) and other such figures and the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) itself: "The poetic fancy...
In this regard, an example of the "part of a poetic fancy" (*utprekṣāvayava*) is as follows: "Having, as it were, seized the mass of hair—the darkness—with her rays, as if with fingers..."
"The moon, as if kissing the face of the night, has its lotus-eyes closed in buds.
(107) Here, it is a common saying that when one seizes a beloved’s hair with the fingers and kisses her face, she closes her eyes;

in this context, the action of kissing the face and so forth is perceived as the primary element (*aṅgin*), while the seizing of the hair and the closing of the eyes are subordinate elements (*aṅga*) and thus secondary.
In that case, by the poetic fancy (*utprekṣaṇa*) of the principal action, the action constituting its constituent part becomes fancied.

For just as there is no word expressing poetic fancy in the phrase "having made the lotus-eyes into buds," so too it would not apply here in the phrase "having seized the mass of darkness-hair with the rays of her fingers"; rather, it should have been stated as "the mass of darkness-hair seized by the rays of her fingers."

In this regard, that which—though occurring within a subordinate action—is, through its usage, as if distinct from the second subordinate action mentioned in the compound meaning, and which is thus structured as a separate word within the sentence, is called by poets an *utprekṣāvayava* (a part of a poetic fancy) even when it is being questioned for the sake of further explanation. Others, however, describe an *utprekṣāvayava* as that case where the principal action is not fancied, but rather a subordinate action is fancied; such is the example beginning with "aṅgulībhiḥ" (with fingers).
The moon seems to kiss the faces of the night,
as if they were lotuses bent down like eyes; having done what, so that this kissing might occur?
Having seized the mass of darkness with rays as if with fingers—as if grasping a cluster of hair—this is a figurative expression (prāyovāda) seen in the *Mahābhārata* and other texts.

Here, by means of the second occurrence of the word "iva" (*iva*), the sentence is construed with separate words; thus, even the other word and even the word devoid of that [particle] take on that same sense, which constitutes the nature of a "limb of poetic fancy" (*utprekṣāvayava*).

For this very reason, it constitutes a variety of *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy), because there is a relation of part and whole (*avayava-avayavibhāva*) based on the fancying of the action of the whole from the mere action of the parts; in that case, there is indeed a relation of subordinate and principal (*aṅga-aṅgibhāva*).
Alternatively, he states that the very imagination of the action of the parts alone constitutes the imagination of the whole,
as in the following example:
“As if dissolved, as if reflected, as if painted, as if carved in form, as if inlaid, as if fashioned from adamantine cement, and as if engraved within.”
‘That beloved is fixed in our minds as if nailed there by the five arrows of the Mind-born God, or as if tightly sewn by the web of threads consisting of a continuous succession of thoughts.
In their view, the previous example— “as if dissolved” (līneva), etc.— is not a constituent part of a poetic fancy (utprekṣāvayava).
This has been explained regarding alliteration (*anuprāsa*) according to this view;
however, he states that the previous example, beginning with “*aṅgulībhiriva-*,” is included within *utprekṣopamā* (poetic fancy-cum-simile), saying: "of these... (*teṣām iti*).
An example of *utprekṣopamā* (simile with poetic fancy) is as follows:
“Under the guise of the *kiṃśuka* tree, the fire, having climbed the tree, seems to gaze all around at the forest, half-burnt and half-undestroyed. (109)

Here, by means of the word "designation" (*vyapadeśa*), the similarity of the *kiṃśuka* flowers to fire is expressed, and the act of seeing is then imagined; thus, this is an "imagined simile" (*utprekṣopamā*).

In the previous example as well—in "having seized the darkness with rays as if with fingers, like a mass of hair"—the inclusion of the object of comparison within the imagination must be understood. This, being both a part of an imagination (*utprekṣāvayava*) and an imagined simile (*utprekṣopamā*), is indeed nothing but imagination itself.

Having done what, does the fire (*vibhāvasu*)— the *kiṃśuka* tree and so forth— seem to behold the burnt and unburnt portions of the great forest (*araṇyānī*), both those already consumed and those yet to be consumed?
Under the pretext of the *kiṃśuka* tree— that is, by means of the *kiṃśuka* flower— he climbed every tree;
for Amara states, "The great forest is *araṇyānī*," and "The fire is *citrabhānu* and *vibhāvasu*."

Here, by the word *vyāja* (guise), the similarity between the *kiṃśuka* flower and fire is intended; therefore, this is a *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) containing an *upamā* (simile). As it is said: "When that [moon] displays the grace of a water-lily within the moon, the world calls it a 'hare' (*śaśaka*), but not so for me."
"O Moon, I consider your body marked by the scar of a wound from the falling meteor-like glances of young women overcome by separation from their lovers.

(110) Here, by the statement "I consider the moon to have a body marked by the scar of a wound from the falling meteor-like glances," the justification for the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) is effected through the medium of one's own opinion; thus, this is a variety of the *utprekṣā* called "the expression of an opinion" (*matābhidhāna*), as indicated by the words "that which is this," and so forth.
When people perceive what appears like the play of a speck of cloud within the center of the moon, they call it a "hare";
but such is not my view,
for I consider this to be the moon itself.
"Of what sort is he?
His body is marked by a scar—the very wound caused by the falling meteor that was the side-glance of a young woman seized by the pangs of separation from your enemy.
(Amara states: "Lava, leśa, kaṇa, and aṇu are synonyms for a minute particle.")

And since the author here presents his own view by stating, "The words *ama*, *na*, and *no* are expressions of negation," this is a justification of the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) based on that view; thus, this is a "fancy based on a view" (*matotprekṣā*),
which constitutes the definition of the figure of speech *utprekṣā*.
In the examination of the figure of speech *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (Indirect Description),
he states the definition of the praise of what is not the subject at hand: "Indirect Description (*aprastutapraśaṃsā*) is the praise of that which is not intended to be praised."
For some reason or other, it is said that this [speech] must both be expressed and understood.
However, it is observed here in this world as arising generally through the obstruction of one among the goals of dharma, artha, and kāma, and through the fulfillment of one's own intention. (52–53)

*Aprastutastuti* (Indirect Praise) is the praise or eulogy of that which is unworthy of praise or even censurable, for some reason or other. For this very reason, it differs from *Samāsokti* (Periphrasis);

for in the latter, there is a relationship of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object compared (*upameya*), whereas here, there is the praise of one thing while another, censurable matter, is [implicitly] indicated.
He states that it is both expressed and implied; thus he says, "the expressed" (*vācyā*).
Therein, he also states a division based on the means (cause): "But that...

The meaning is as follows: through the predominance—that is, the frequent occurrence—of the obstruction of any one among those [three], namely virtue (*dharma*), wealth (*artha*), and pleasure (*kāma*), she is perceived as arising through the preeminent fulfillment of her own intention in every respect.
Regarding those [objections], she should be addressed with a refutation of the argument as follows:
“A body that has its belly thinned by the reduction of fat becomes light and fit for exertion; even the minds of living beings are observed to undergo a transformation in the face of fear and anger.
Furthermore, that is the excellence of archers when their arrows strike a moving target. They speak falsely of hunting as a vice; from where could such a diversion come? (111)

Here, by means of establishing his own intention through the aforementioned reasons—namely, "whence comes such sport? which is a direct expression of delight in hunting—this is what is called *aprastutastuti* (indirect praise) of the expressed meaning (*vācyā*). It subverts the doctrine that "non-violence is the supreme duty" by asserting that "harm is a distinction [of virtue]," and so forth; thus, the virtuous say that hunting, the chase, is a vice and should not be practiced, and that [the king's claim] is false.
From where and where could such enthusiasm for diversion arise?
Indeed, it arises from nowhere at all,
for the body becomes light and as if censured.
Of what kind is it?
It is that in which the abdomen has become emaciated through the cutting away—that is, the reduction—of fat;
whereas through the persistence of fat, corpulence occurs.
By virtue of having a slender belly alone, one is fit for exertion;
for this very reason, there is no lack of vigor in those with large bellies.
Furthermore, the minds of sentient beings—living creatures—are observed to be susceptible to the transformations of fear and anger.
Such is the mind in fear, and such is it in anger;
and that is the excellence of archers, of those who wield the bow, that their arrows hit a moving target and become piercers.
Regarding the word *medas*, Amara states: "Vapā and vasā [are synonyms for] medas."

Here, because his own intention is accomplished through the means of the stated reasons, the praising of hunting—which is being described as a violation of dharma—is therefore an *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise).
He states the violation of dharma: "Non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) [is dharma], for hunting is a cause of violence."

Therefore, the meaning is that it is solely by the sublation of the property (*dharma-bādha*) that [the cognition] is to be understood as invalid; for example: “O boy, ill-taught in the arts of love, you have clung to my neck! [where the lover’s statement is sublated by the fact that he is not actually on her neck.]
"O child ill-taught by the letters of Death, cling to my neck!
If the dwelling in hell for both of us occurs at the same time, then so be it. (112)

In this context, by the phrase "one who is ill-trained in the syllables of time," there is a certain boy—having studied the Dharmaśāstras through knowledge of scripts and so forth—who is fond of beautiful forms, being addressed with reproach by a certain ill-behaved woman: "Come here, you! Clasp my neck! In that situation, your view is as follows: if hell were to result from such an act, then if that hell were to be shared by both of us, it would not be hell; rather, it would be heaven.

Thus, because it accomplishes one's own desire, this is an instance of *niyoga* (a command) toward a great act of daring; and here, the praise of that which is not to be praised is perceived through the direct praise of that which is to be praised.

This should be understood as *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise), for it subverts the moral law that "one should not even mentally desire another's wife" by means of such words as "O black-eyed one, poorly trained child, you rogue! Cling to my neck! and so forth.
"If the dwelling in hell is equal for both of us, then let it be so!"—
O boy, poorly trained and ill-advised in these fatal words, sixteen years of age, "climb onto my neck," meaning: embrace me!
If, that being so, our dwelling in hell is equal—that is, identical—for both of us, then let it be; for even there, we are exactly alike. Thus, even hell becomes heaven;
such is the worldly designation known as "Kālākṣara."
*Re* is a term of address for one of low status;
*bāla ā ṣoḍaśād varṣāt* (a child until sixteen years of age) is from Manu; *samaka* [is formed] with the suffix *kan* in the sense of the base word itself (*svārthe*).
A *pogaṇḍa* is one who is ignorant of legal transactions;
however, beyond that age, he is a *pogaṇḍa* who knows legal transactions— so says Manu.
"Adhīta" means one by whom the Dharmaśāstra— the Smṛtis of Manu and others— has been studied;
"abhimatarūpa" means one whose beauty or loveliness is desired or longed for.
The term *rūpaka* is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "such a one" (*tādṛśa*) and "a youth" (*pogaṇḍa*). In this case, the rule *śeṣādvibhāṣā* (Pāṇini 5.4.154) applies.

154. Thus, in this case, the unrefined courtesan (*avinayavatī*)— through the accomplishment of her own desire by means of a great act of daring in the form of sexual union— engages in the praise of the subject at hand (*prastutastuti*), whether directly expressed or implied, because she does not explicitly state her commission.
He states the obstruction of Dharma: "Of another," meaning the wife;
it is to be spoken of as an obstruction of wealth, for example:—

"O cripple, you are worthy of homage, for you do not go to the houses of others as a petitioner; O blind one, you are blessed, for you do not gaze upon the faces of those intoxicated by wealth; O mute one, you too are praiseworthy, for you do not praise the miser out of a desire for gain; O deaf one, you are to be praised, for you do not listen to the words of the wicked. (113) In this instance, the direct expression of praise through the words "worthy of homage," "blessed," "praiseworthy," and "to be praised" applied to the lame, the blind, the mute, and the deaf—who are themselves objects of praise—constitutes what is called *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise). However, because the speaker takes pride in this [literal] indirect praise, it obstructs the accomplishment of the intended meaning.
"O cripple," and so forth: "O lame one, you are to be honored, for being a seeker of wealth, you do not go to the houses of others.
O blind one, devoid of sight, you are fortunate, for you do not look upon—the faces of those who are proud of their riches."
O mute one, you are praiseworthy, for you do not praise base people out of a desire for wealth.
O deaf one, void of hearing, you are to be commended, for you do not listen to the speech—the voice—of the wicked and the evil.
As the *Hārāvalī* states: "One who is lame is known as *khañja*."
Regarding the statement "the mute is addressed," Amara [states this].
Here, because the lame and others are directly praised by words such as "vandyah" (to be honored), the expressed meaning constitutes a contradiction; thus, he says "abhīti."
By this, the very subversion of the purpose of those who possess pride has been stated;
it is to be understood precisely through the subversion of the purpose, as for example:
"Let the deer in the forests eat grasses that are easily obtained without effort."
"They do not display wretchedness before the wealthy; they say, 'They are indeed beasts, and we are the wise ones.

(114) Here, the phrase "they are indeed beasts, and we are the wise ones" constitutes an indirect praise of deer; because this praise of those who ought not to be praised is perceived as the meaning of the sentence, this is to be understood as *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise). [An example of] *arthāpatti* (presumption) is: "It obstructs the attainment of the goal of the high-minded," and so forth.
The deer live quite contentedly on grass that is easily obtained in the forests without effort;
they do not display wretchedness toward the wealthy or the moneylenders.
Nevertheless, those deer are merely beasts, whereas we, on the other hand, are wise and learned men.
The word *kila* signifies either renown or certainty;
according to the *Viśvakośa*, it also means "excessively" or "consent.
Here, there is no direct expression of joy on the part of the deer, but rather it is implied; thus, this [joy] is to be inferred.
In this case as well, the contradiction of the meaning should be stated as belonging only to a wise woman due to the frustration of her desires, as for example:
“They do not let out long sighs, they do not weep, nor have they become emaciated by separation.”
“Blessed are those women whose beloved has many favorites, and not you.
(115) [They do not heave long sighs, they do not weep, and they do not become emaciated by separation;
blessed are those whose beloved has many favorites, and not you.]

In this context, the statement "Blessed are those for whom you are not a beloved"—which is a direct praise of those who ought to be praised by one who is intensely enamored—is a case of *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise) expressed through the literal meaning (*vācyā*). This very [praise] obstructs the fulfillment of her desire, as indicated by the words beginning with "not," such as:
"They do not let out long sighs, they do not weep, nor do they become emaciated by separation."
"Blessed are those women whose beloved has many favorites.

Having seen the heroine who possesses a particularly distinguished lover, her friend approaches the lover and speaks of her passion and condition: "O you who have many favorites, those heroines are blessed; they do not release their long sighs born of separation, they do not weep, and they do not become emaciated by the pangs of parting."

By the words "Among those women you are not the beloved, yet they are fortunate," and so forth, the direct praise of the enamored woman is expressed; however, that very praise should be understood as an obstacle to the fulfillment of her desire, through the very fact of her being obstructed in love— as for example:

"O benefactor, by bringing from afar to us this person who inquires after our welfare— even though such a person is difficult to find— you have committed no offense, even if you were to take away our very life. (116)
"O fever, you have been helpful to us even while taking away our life; thus, you have not committed an offense.

Here, because the previously mentioned intention of ours has been fulfilled, you have indeed rendered us a service such that even by snatching away our life, you do not incur guilt. This statement addressed to the fever with such excessive affection is understood here as a praise of the fever, who is otherwise fit only for censure. This is what is called *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise), where the praise of the subject itself is perceived through its affliction of the body, which in turn afflicts all desires, and so forth.

"O helpful fever, you have committed no offense even while seizing my very life, for you have brought here from afar even a rare person who comes to inquire after my welfare. Thus, a certain woman of excessive passion speaks with words full of censure to the hero, even though he has gone to converse with another woman to whom he is attached. "Sukha... [etc.]

O fever, you who bring even a person difficult to find—one who inquires after your well-being and asks, "Is there comfort in your body now?"—to me from a distant land; you who are thus a benefactor, and who seize even my very life, you have not committed an offense.

[The word] *sukhapṛcchakaḥ* means one who inquires thoroughly after one's welfare (*sukham suṣṭhu pṛcchati*). The suffix *vun* is applied here by the rule of splitting the sūtra *kriyāsamabhihāre vun*.

Here, by the words "inquirer after her welfare" and so forth, she utters a statement regarding the fever for the sake of accomplishing her own desire toward the one who is enamored; thus, there arises *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise), but it is not what is being directly expressed.
She describes the affliction of passion as follows: "The body... and so on.
Thus concludes the exposition of the figure of speech Aprastutapraśaṃsā (Indirect Description). Now follows the exposition of the figure Tulyayogitā (Equal Pairing); he states its definition:
When something is described by equating it with others that possess superior qualities intended [by the speaker],
for the purpose of praise or censure, that is considered *tulyayogitā* (Equal Pairing). [Verse 54] "Intended," etc.

Tulyayogitā (Equal Pairing) is the mention or description of something praiseworthy or blameworthy by equating it with another thing—whether praiseworthy or blameworthy—that is superior to it by means of a specific quality intended for expression (vivakṣita), that is, a quality desired to be spoken of.
Here, "quality" (guṇa) refers to a property (dharma), whether virtuous or non-virtuous;
and in this context, there may be either praise or blame.
That [praise] which has qualities equal to those being described is for the purpose of eulogy, as in:
“Śeṣa, the Himālaya, and you are all great, venerable, and steadfast; you uphold this earth when it wavers, having transgressed its bounds. (117)

Here, because the king is described through a common association (*tulyayoga*) with Śeṣa and the Himālaya—both of whom are preeminent due to qualities such as greatness being attributed to them—for the purpose of praise, this is "Equal Pairing for the Purpose of Praise" (*stutyarthā tulyayogitā*).
The word "Śeṣa" and so forth means:
Śeṣa [the serpent], the Himālaya the mountain, and you—all of you together uphold (*bibhṛtha*), that is, support, this earth.
What kind of things are "great" (mahāntaḥ)— possessing greatness— and what kind are "heavy" (guravaḥ)— the substrata of heaviness— and what kind are "stable" (sthirāḥ)— possessing stability?
Of what kind [is the earth]?
She by whom the boundaries have been leaped over—that is, transgressed—and for that very reason is moving here and there;
herein, greatness and other qualities are expressed.
And because the excellence [of the king] is described through the statement of his equality with Śeṣa and the Himālaya mountains, this constitutes a form of praise (stuti-yoga).
The purpose of censure lies precisely in the equality of qualities between that which is being described and the object of comparison; for example:
"The associations of fawn-eyed women, like flashes of lightning, do not endure even for two moments, though initiated by the clouds themselves. (118)

Here, because the conjunction of the gazelle-eyed women and the flashes of lightning—both of which are described as possessing equal qualities through phrases such as "even though begun by clouds"—is stated for the purpose of censure, this is *nindārthā tulyayogitā* (conjunction for the purpose of censure).

The phrase "the conjunctions" (*saṃgatāni*) and so forth means that the unions of the gazelle-eyed women, even though they were "begun by clouds" (*ghanaṃ nirantaram ārabdhāni*)—that is, performed continuously—and likewise the flashes (*vilasitāni*) of the lightnings (*taḍitām*), even though "begun by clouds" (*ghanair medhair ārabdhāni*), do not remain for even a second moment beyond the moment of their commencement; how much less for a long duration?
Here, by means of lightning—which is well-known for its flickering nature—the fickleness of union with women is stated as being equalized; thus, this is a *nindātulyayogitā* (simile of censure).
An example of this same figure used for the purpose of praise (*stutyarthā*), where the equality of qualities is implied, is as follows:
“Yama, Kubera, Varuṇa, the thousand-eyed Indra, and you too...”
"bearing the title 'Lokapāla' (Guardian of the World) which has no other referent.

Here, although it is not explicitly stated that "the five, beginning with Yama, are the Guardians of the World," their mutual similarity is understood through the very fact of their connection to an identical object for the sake of praise. This is the figure of speech *tulyayogitā* (Equal Pairing), where the equality of qualities is implied for the purpose of praise, as in the verse beginning with "Yama... and so forth.

O venerable ones, Yama and the others bear and maintain the renown and fame of being "World-Guardians" (lokapāla) in this sense—that their domain is not shared by others and that they do not go elsewhere;
and Indra, the thousand-eyed one, [is so called].
According to the *Viśvaprakāśa* lexicon: "The word *śruti* denotes fame and the Veda."

Here, there are four world-protectors beginning with Yama; now you, sir, are the fifth to be designated by the term "world-protector. This is praise of the king through the statement of his excellence, by declaring his equality with Yama and the others.
However, that [praise] serves as a censure precisely when the equality of qualities is merely implied—as in the following example:
“They serve even a king, they consume even poison, and they dally with the wives of others; indeed, human beings are fickle.

Here, this connection of men with kings and women—characterized by a similarity in the cause of their fickleness regarding service and the like—or rather, the inclusion of those actions within the category of [objects such as] kings and so forth, brings about a mutual resemblance among them. This leads one to understand that serving a king and dallying with another’s wife are equivalent to consuming poison; thus, this is *tulyayogitā* (Equal Pairing) based on implied similarity of qualities (*pratīyamānatulyaguṇatva*), intended for censure (*nindārthā*).
"Even kings," and so forth;
they serve even a monarch, they consume and eat even poison, and they dally and sport with the wives of others;
therefore, humans are fickle and reckless.

Indeed, here, either in the sense of the causal particle *khalu* or through the application of similarity (*tulyayoga*) by virtue of being the object of those actions, it makes known the equality between serving a king and dalliance with another's wife and the consumption of poison; and that [equality],
being merely implied, expresses "Equal Pairing" (*tulyayogitā*) according to another school of thought.

"Others," [the author] says, refer to those who state that *tulyayogitā* occurs when there is equality between an object that is a cause of pleasure and one that is a cause of suffering, even when they are expressed for the purpose of praise and blame respectively.
// 55 // "Others" [is the term].

Some maintain that *tulyayogitā* (equal pairing) occurs when there is parity between two things—one a cause of happiness and the other a cause of suffering—for the purpose of either praise or censure.
That [type] for the purpose of praise is as follows:
“[The king] who was summoned for consecration and sent away to the forest...”
"I did not perceive even the slightest change in his expression" (121).

Here, through the words beginning with "having been summoned," there is perceived praise for Rāma’s going to the forest and his consecration to the kingdom as being equal in nature due to his father’s command.

Of that Rāma—who had been summoned for his consecration (*abhiṣeka*), that is, his royal coronation, and who had been sent away to go to the forest—I did not perceive even the slightest change in his facial expression (*ākāra-vibhrama*), that is, any alteration in his countenance; for according to the *Dharani* lexicon, "even in the case of a different state, there is no confusion.

Here, the royal consecration is a cause of happiness, while going to the forest is a cause of sorrow; yet, because both are equal due to his devotion to his father, they are praised as being equivalent.

Examples of those intended for censure: “Whether one cuts the neem tree with an axe, or treats it with honey and ghee, or honors it with perfumes and garlands, it remains bitter in every respect. (122)

In this context, by means of the *samāsokti* (synecdoche) that "the bitterness of the neem tree remains exactly the same toward him who cuts it with an axe, him who sprinkles it with honey and ghee, or him who honors it with perfumes and garlands," the censure of the object of comparison is perceived. As for the phrase beginning with "he who," etc.: he who cuts the neem tree with an axe (*kuṭhāra*), he who sprinkles this neem with honey and ghee (*madhu-sarpiṣā*)—that is, with clarified butter mixed with honey—and he who honors it with perfumes and garlands; for all of them, that neem remains simply bitter, that is, pungent.
According to Amara, "puṣpapuṣpasrajormālyam" [means a garland made of flowers];
here, by means of *samāsokti*— that is, by the process of condensation (*samasanena*), which results in the establishment of a similarity (*sāmyāpādanena*).
The definition of the figure of speech *tulyayogitā* as the cognition of a censure regarding the object of comparison; the definition of the figure of speech *leśa*.
He states the definition of *leśa*:

"That which is the subordination of a fault (*doṣa*) or the appearance of a fault in what is actually a quality (*guṇa*) is *leśa*; nothing other than this is accepted as *vyājastuti* (indirect praise). (56)
Regarding the phrase "of the defect":
that very fact that a defect possesses the nature of a merit, and a merit possesses the nature of a defect, is the definition of *leśa*.
If so, would it not then also apply in the case of *vyājastuti* (ironical praise)?
In that case, there would be over-extension;
therefore it was said— "from that"—
meaning that the praise under the guise of a slight [criticism] is indeed non-different from it.
The meaning is that there is no over-extension [of the definition].
In that regard, the subordination of a defect to a quality is "the slight" (leśa), as for example:
"This king is young, virtuous, and powerful; he is a worthy husband for you."

"Whose mind is attached to the festival of battle even more than to the festival of love. (123) Here, this praise of the excellence of the king’s valor expressed in the second half-verse will appear as a defect to one who wishes to enter into the continuous enjoyments of the maiden. With this in mind, this friend—being clever and desiring to avoid provoking the king—describes what is actually a defect as a virtue. This "transformation of a defect into a virtue" is called *leśa* (the slight), because it is stated subtly, slightly, and gradually, without being noticed by others, as in the verse beginning with "yuvā... and so forth.
At a certain *svayaṃvara*, a certain woman, under the pretext of praise, censures a king in order to turn back her friend who has set her heart upon him:
"This man is a worthy husband for you, given your youth, your virtues, your royalty, and your strength—
[a man] whose mind, even more than during festivals of love, remains fixed and attached to the festival of battle, disregarding the pleasures of the senses."
Regarding the girl who desires to enter [the palace] and wishes to enjoy [itself], Amara states: "Nirveśa means enjoyment.

Here, by a clever friend, for the sake of pacifying the king's anger, even though the praise consisting of the excellence of his prowess is a defect with respect to one who desires enjoyment, it is presented as a merit because of its insignificance; thus, this is "Leśa" (The Slight), characterized by the transformation of a defect into a merit.
In this case, the quality becomes a defect merely by its smallness, as for example:
"That person is fickle and merciless; what have I to do with him, my friend?"
"By whom flatteries were learned solely for the purpose of wiping away offenses.

(124) Here, having first made a public declaration before her friends in accordance with her acceptance of pride, she—fearing its failure and wishing to avoid their ridicule—describes what appears to be a fault as a collection of virtues: "By whom flatteries were learned solely for the purpose of wiping away offenses. This is the figure of speech called *leśa* (the semblance of a fault), which consists in the transformation of a virtue into a fault. Others, however, state that the entire definition of *leśa* is: where a fault becomes a virtue and a virtue becomes a fault.
That [capala] is also twofold—by way of *samāsokti* (elliptical metaphor) and by way of *asamāsokti* (non-elliptical expression). Thus:
"O friend, let that person be fickle (*capala*) and fearless; what does that matter to me?"

But there was no person by whom any supreme flatteries— sweet words for the sake of wiping away an offense (*āgas*) or erasing a transgression (*aparādha*)— "for *āgas*, *aparādha*, and *mantu* all mean 'offense'," according to Amara;— were learned.
Here, "doṣābhāsa" means that which appears or seems like a fault; however, this is not a fault in the ultimate sense.
For flattery is actually a virtue, since even one who has committed an offense wins over my favor and causes the breaking of my pride;
for this very reason, there is attachment toward it.

And thus, by means of the verse beginning with "capala" (O fickle one), the young girl—being unable to carry out the indignation (māna) directed toward her friend due to her passion—demonstrates a certain quality in the form of a semblance of a fault, namely, her flattery. Regarding this, he states the view that "the quality's status as a fault" constitutes *leśa* (a slight/trace), provided that both quality and fault are combined; for "others" hold that *samāsokti* (synthetic expression) is speech through concealment, whereas *asamāsokti* (analytic expression) is speech that is explicit.
An example of these two [types of suggestion] through *samāsokti* (synecdoche) is as follows:
“By the very wickedness of his qualities, the beast of burden is yoked to the pole; yet the bull with a dewlap, whose shoulders lack scars, sleeps in comfort. (125)
This too is called *leśa* (the "hint") because it is stated only slightly out of fear of provoking anger.
Regarding the phrase "of the qualities" and so forth:

due to the "wickedness"—that is, the fault—of qualities such as the capacity for bearing burdens, the draft-ox (*dhurya*), the bull capable of carrying the yoke, is yoked to the "yoke" (*dhuri*), that is, to the burden.

Furthermore, when the shoulder-blade (skandha) is such that it has become calloused (*kali*), meaning it is not tender, being a mass of dead blood and flesh where a scar (*kiṇa*) has formed, he sleeps comfortably; thus,
one who carries a burden is called *dhurya* ("one who bears the yoke"), according to the rule "from *dhur*, *yaṅ* and *ḍhak*" (Pāṇini 4.4.77).
4.77 Thus, as for the statement "kiṇaḥ syān mṛtaśoṇite," this is from the Ratnakoṣa.

Even in the case of the phrase "galistu vahanāśakte" ("the camel is incapable of carrying [the load]"), there is *leśa* (a subtle hint) because the merits and defects are expressed through a compound solely out of anger and fear;
as for example, in *asamāsokti* (speech without compounds):
“Virtuous people, who suffer from the rise of their own good conduct, who experience constant constraints, and who are everywhere terrified of public scandal, always live in misery;

whereas the common person of unrefined intellect—who is neither distressed by what he has done right nor by what he has done wrong, whose heart is devoid of the discrimination between what is proper and improper—is truly blessed.
Here too, as before, there is the fear of provoking anger and so forth.
Now, why is this not called *leśa* (the "hint") when its characteristics are presented separately?

It is because the subordination of faults to virtues is subsumed under *aprastutastuti* (indirect praise), while the subordination of virtues to faults is subsumed under *vyājastuti* (disguised praise); thus [begins the verse] with the words "O virtuous ones... and so forth.
How do the virtuous live so as to always experience suffering? They are those who are devotedly attached to the arising of noble conduct and righteous activity.
For those for whom constraints— which are non-offenses— manifest and become apparent,
they are everywhere apprehensive and vigilant regarding the slander or disparaging remarks of people;
it is for this very reason that their state is one of suffering.
What kind of person is the common, undiscriminating folk called fortunate? It is one whose intellect is unrefined and devoid of discernment.
He is not agitated by a deed done that is good and right, nor indeed by a deed that is bad and wrong;
the meaning is that he is devoid of such deeds, whether good or bad,
and for that very reason, his heart is free from the deliberation of "this is to be done" and "this is not to be done."
In this case as well, the mention is made only briefly out of fear of prolixity;

[the author] asks—"Now then?"—in response to the question: "How is it that 'leśa' (hint) is not included here separately, given that the subordination of defects to virtues and the subordination of virtues to defects [are already mentioned]? This is the answer.

The meaning is that because the first [type] is made the subject matter in *aprastutastuti* (indirect praise) and the latter in *vyājastuti* (disguised praise), they are included within those two alone.
*Vyājastuti* is also twofold: pure (*śuddhā*) and mixed (*miśrā*).
An example of the pure form of these two is as follows:
“O King, having been snatched away from the Ancient Person (Viṣṇu), Fortune is now enjoyed by you; O scion of the Ikṣvāku dynasty, how can this be appropriate for you? (127)

In this case, because praise is expressed under the guise of censure characterized by the abduction of another's wife, this is a "pure" (*śuddhā*) instance of *avyājastuti*. It is not distinct from *leśa*, which is characterized by the appearance of a quality as a defect or vice versa; for it is said in the Purāṇa: "Having seized and taken away Śrī Kamalā from the Purāṇa-puruṣa, Viṣṇu, she is enjoyed—that is, served—by you."
"O King, for one such as you, whose lineage is that of Ikṣvāku—a distinguished monarch—is this appropriate? Rather, it is not fitting. This appears to be a censure;
however, the underlying meaning is: "Having snatched away prosperity from an ancient man—an elder person—you are now enjoying it."
In this context, within the venerable state (śrīpada), there is that very artifice, and by means of it, purity alone is attained here.
He states the distinction regarding the "traces" (leśa) with the word "guṇa," as in this mixed example:
“O Lord of the Earth, you are beloved, you are wise, you are powerful, and you are of noble birth; you are young—how many young women do not choose you as their husband?”
Therefore, you, who have attained wisdom, ought not to touch this ancient fame— the supreme consort of Raghu, Nahuṣa, and Māndhātṛ.
Here, because praise is intermingled with words of censure, this is the variety of *vyājastuti* (disguised praise) known as "mixed," beginning with the word *priya*.
O King, you are dear, you are pleased, you are wise, you possess superior intelligence, and you are a lord.
You are of pure lineage and you are young;
such being the case, how many young women do not choose you as their husband, that is, do not accept you?
Therefore, for this reason, you ought not to touch or assail her fame—
she who is the chief queen, the great sovereign lady, of such distinguished kings as Raghu, Nahuṣa, and Māndhātṛ, and who is likewise aged and advanced in years.
According to Amara, "mahiṣī" means "one who has been consecrated as a queen.
Here, through the pretext of the words "mahiṣī" and "vṛddhā," there is praise by way of censure; because this occurs only in a subtle manner, it is defined as the poetic figure *leśa* (the subtle).
The definition of the figure of speech *sahokti* (simultaneous mention) is stated as follows:
"The simultaneous occurrence (*samāveśa*) of agents and other factors together with others in respect of actions and so forth [is *sahokti*]."
That [metaphor] is said to be "expressed together" when it is both distinct and non-distinct.

When this is being described by the wise as possessing dissimilarity (*vaisādṛśyavatī*) in constructions such as *saha* (together with), it is also seen to possess similarity (*sasādṛśyā*). (Verses 57–58)
*Sahokti* (conjoined expression) is the co-occurrence or simultaneous presence of the agent and so forth with others in relation to actions and the like;
by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the object (*karman*) and other grammatical factors are included.
That immersion (*samāveśa*) is either distinct and pure (*vivikta-kevala*) or non-distinct and mixed (*avivikta-miśra*).
Regarding the immersion in an action that is distinct from the agent, it is as follows:
"The forest breezes, sweet with the warbling of cuckoos and fragrant..."
"The days of spring (surabhivāsarāḥ) attain growth along with the joys of the people.

Here, the subject "days of spring" is joined solely with the "joys of the people" in the action of attaining growth; thus, this is the figure of speech called *sahokti* (concomitance), characterized by dissimilarity (*vaisādṛśyavatī*), because it involves the joining of a distinct agent with the action, as in the verse beginning with "the cuckoo" (*kokila*).
The days of spring, fragrant with the scent of blossoms, increase along with the joy of the people;
they are such that in them the warbling of the cuckoos is sweet and captivating, and the forest breezes— the Malaya winds— are full of exquisite fragrance.
Here, there is a convergence of the action of increase upon the solitary agent, the spring day, together with the joy of people; yet this is indeed dissimilar,
because the increase of the day consists in the lengthening of its duration (daṇḍa), whereas the increase of joy consists in the nature of extreme bliss.
An example of the integration of distinct actions within a single action is as follows:
“Though you abandon your beloved at the same time [as your body], why indeed, O fool, do you say, ‘I am emaciated’?
Even a bull sheds its limbs when burdened by a load. (130)
"Even though you are being carried by your beloved in a state of intoxication, why indeed do you say, 'O, am I thin?'?
And yet, O ignorant one, even a bull drops its limbs under a heavy burden!

Here, the referent of the addressive *yuṣmad* (you), having become the object (*karman*) in the sense "you are being carried," is joined with the meaning of the verbal root alone in the action expressed by the verb *uhyase*. This is the figure of speech known as *sahokti* (conjoined expression) characterized by dissimilarity (*vaisādṛśyavatī*), due to the distinct joining of the object and the action.
"Ujjhasi" and so forth:
"Even though you are carried away in intoxication by your beloved, why indeed do you say, 'O, I am emaciated'?
And yet, O ignorant one, the bull [of your body] lets its limbs droop under the heavy burden."
A certain offender, having been asked by a weak woman, "Why are you so thin?",
said to her regarding him: "By your beloved, with intoxication and pride, you are carried away— that is, you are supported."

Nevertheless, O fool, devoid of knowledge, why do you say, "Why are you so emaciated? Even a bull sheds its limbs—that is, casts them off—due to an excessive burden such as the weight of a sack and the like; how much more so, then, for one who is weak? This is the intended meaning.
In the word *uhyasa*, the root *vah* in the sense of "carrying" (*prāpaṇe*) takes the *lakāra* (verbal suffix) in the passive voice;
*vaillo* means "bull";
and the sound *re* is used for addressing with reproach.

In this instance, regarding the action of "carrying," the meaning to be understood as "you" is the object of the action (*karman*), yet it is joined solely with the referent of the word *priyā* (the beloved); and the dissimilarity between these two is quite evident.
He states another definition for *vivikta* (distinct/separated):
where even though there are multiple factors such as the agent (*kartṛ*) and so forth, they are [distinguished] by distinct actions and so forth.
It attains a state of isolation; it is also called "isolated.
Wherever multiple factors, such as agents and so forth, attain distinction through distinct actions and so forth, that is called "isolated."
An example of that [simile] involving the simultaneous occurrence of two distinct actions upon a single agent is as follows:
“The mango blossom swells along with the fainting of the travelers, and the Malaya breezes blow together with their tears. (131)

In this instance, the mango blossom (*cūtamañjarī*) is associated with the act of increasing along with fainting, and the Malaya breezes are associated with the act of blowing along with tears; thus, the agents are presented as distinct from one another. This, too, is a case of *sahokti* (concomitance) characterized by dissimilarity (*vaisādṛśya*), involving the association of distinct agents and actions.
The same should be observed regarding the distinction of the object (*karman*), as in "it increases" and so forth.

The mango blossom (*cūtamañjarī*) grows along with the fainting of travelers; the Malaya breezes blow, waft, and fall away along with the tears of those travelers—*pathika* and *pāntha* being synonyms according to Amara.
Here, the mango blossom and the other elements are introduced as agents through their very distinction (*viveka*) in the performance of those respective actions.
The dissimilarity is indeed manifest when the actions of the agents do not coincide, as for example:
"Counsel was not followed by the heart, just as it was by the steadfast mind."
Her vigils pass away along with her fortitude; her unfulfilled instructions vanish with her heart;
her arms droop together with her energy; and her cries of lamentation fall away with her tears. (132)

In this case, many factors such as the watches of the night (*yāma*) and others are seen to be indistinctly merged (*avivikta*) with qualities such as fortitude (*dhairya*) within a single act of melting away; this is the figure of speech called *sahokti* (concomitance) characterized by dissimilarity (*vaisādṛśyavatī*), consisting in the indistinct merging of agent and action, as in the verse beginning with "by fortitude" (*dhīreṇa*), which states: "The watches of the night have melted away along with fortitude; the instructions have ceased along with the heart."
Her arms waste away along with her vigor; her lamentations dissolve along with her tears;
the watches of the night pass away along with this Rāma’s fortitude;
and unaccomplished, unfulfilled, or uncertain instructions vanish along with his heart.
Along with his enthusiasm, his arms and limbs fail; along with his tears, his outpourings, conversations, and words vanish;
and the persistence in virtuous instruction, which was never before inconsistent with his fortitude, now falters.

Then there is emptiness of mind, then the abandonment of enthusiasm (*utsāha*), then the faltering of the arms, and finally speech accompanied by tears; thus, the intensification of the stages of love (*manmatha-daśā*) has been described in this sequence.
Here, *utsāha* refers to resolve (*adhyavasāya*);
in this context, due to the singularity of the act of melting away, there is no distinction [between the stages].

And the dissimilarity (*vaisādṛśya*) of actions is indeed evident when there is an inclusion of undifferentiated activities, as in the case of using the word *sa-* (with) in place of *iva* (like) to express similarity— for example:
“He [saw] the steady mass of water like a multitude of whales, together with the mountains on its flanks.”
‘...carrying a mass of water like fortitude, a multitude of whales like the world of winged mountains, waves like the currents of rivers, and hundreds of great virtues like jewels. (133)

Here, through the power of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārthasāmarthya*), the similarity (*sādṛśya*) between the mass of water and fortitude, between the multitude of whales and the world of winged mountains, between the river-currents and the waves, and between the jewels and hundreds of great virtues, is manifested as if by the particle *iva*;

and the sense of "together" (*saha-artha*) is obtained [by implication]. Thus, this is the figure of speech called *Sahokti* (Concomitance) with similarity, wherein many things—such as fortitude and the rest—are presented as the objects (*karman*) of a single action of carrying (*vahana-kriyā*) without distinction, due to their non-differentiation.
This is illustrated in the verse beginning with *dhīraṃ vā...* and so forth.
"Carrying a mass of water like fortitude, a multitude of whales like a world of winged mountains, waves like the currents of rivers, and hundreds of great virtues like jewels—
in this context, what kind of ocean is it?"

Carrying a mass of water like fortitude; carrying a multitude of *timi* fish—like a collection of a specific kind of fish—as if they possessed wings (*sapakṣa*), or as if carrying his own winged kin (*svapakṣa*) or his own friends, namely the mountain-dwellers such as Maināka and others; carrying waves like the currents of rivers; and carrying hundreds of great qualities such as magnanimity and so forth, like jewels.
As stated in the *Rāmāyaṇa*: "There is a fish named *timira*, a hundred *yojanas* in extent."
The *Ratnakośa* states: "The word *loka* is also considered to mean a 'collection' (*samūha*). Here, the suffix *-ka* is used in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*).

The mutual similarity between the collection of the waters of fortitude and so forth is clearly perceived as if being manifested by the word *iva*; furthermore, since this association (*sāhitya*) is understood as the meaning of the sentence, this is a case of *sahokti* (concomitance) characterized by similarity.
He states the purpose of including the word "etc. (*ādi*): even when qualities (*guṇa*) are combined, the possessor of the qualities (*guṇin*) may possess similarity, as in:
"Now these nights have become long along with my sighs."

"And those moon-adorned nights, pale-white, [are] together with my very limbs. (134) Here, because of the non-discrimination between the two qualities of length and paleness—expressed as "the nights are long" and "pale-white"—there is seen a coalescence (*samāveśa*) of the nights and of those two qualities respectively with the breaths and the limbs. This is *sahokti* (concomitance), which consists in the coalescence of undiscriminated qualities even when there is no initial mention of similarity (*sādṛśya*).
The word "initially" (*ādau*)... [is used].
"Along with," and so forth:
these nights are now long for me in this state of separation; those nights, adorned by the moon—that is, having the moon as their ornament—are pale along with my very limbs.
The fact that the nights are adorned by the moon is the cause of their paleness.
In the state of separation, due to distress, there occurs the lengthening of sighs, the paleness of the limbs, and the lengthening of the nights;

here, the coalescence of the two qualities of length and paleness is rooted in similarity. Thus, this is "Sahokti" (Conjoined Description) based on similarity—this concludes the definition of the figure Sahokti.
Regarding the definition of the figure of speech *samuccaya* (accumulation), he states its characteristic: [It consists in] the connection of substances,
actions, qualities, and so forth, with actions, substances, qualities, and so forth.
The combination of many things into one would be *samuccaya* (aggregation). That which is called *itaretarayoga* (mutual conjunction) and that which is called *samāhāra* (collective aggregate)—
and even that other [category] here, *anvācaya* (concessive conjunction)— is not different from *samuccaya*.

He may be one who relies on bipeds, or he may be one who relies on many-footed beings; he may be one who relies on both, or he may be one who relies on neither. (62) Or there may be three [options] for each step, either with the indicators [occurring] subsequently or otherwise.
These [types of *samuccaya*] are pure (*śuddha*) or mixed (*miśra*), with the fourth being that which lacks an explicit indicator (*dyotaka*).
Regarding the term "substance" (*dravya*),
*samuccaya* is the co-occurrence of substance and so forth within a single action or other category.
He states the non-difference between *itaretarayoga* and *samuccaya* through the word "itara":
*itaretarayoga* is a *samuccaya* (conjunction) characterized by distinct parts that are mutually dependent;

*samāhāra* is a *samuccaya* itself in which the distinction between parts is obscured and the aggregate is predominant; and *anvācaya* is that where one thing is primary while another is secondary and is subordinated to it.
He analyzes the collection: "two-footed" refers to both two-footed and many-footed;
"neither" refers to neither two-footed nor many-footed.

Among these, he states that the first three occur either with each individual word (*pratipadam*) or later with words that illuminate [the meaning], saying: "The three"—meaning only those three—are both pure and mixed;
whereas the fourth, which rests on neither, is a conjunction (*samuccaya*) that occurs even without an illuminating particle such as *ca* (and).
Among these, the conjunction of two substances based on a biped (*dvipadāśraya*) by virtue of illuminating what is based on the path (*pratipadāśrita*) is as follows:
“Awakened by his retinue departing, with his radiant luster flashing and his eyes gleaming, the lamp and Love, both thickened by their arrival at the door, shone forth intensely. (135)

Here, the two substances—the lamp (*dīpaka*) and *madana*—are placed in each word by means of the conjunction *ca* within the single verb *didyute*; therefore, there is no need for the dual ending in *didyute*, nor does the copulative compound (*dvandva*) *dīpakamadanau* occur in the sense of "and. Thus, the lamp—the excellent light—and *madana*—Kāma—shone forth (*didyute*) exceedingly, that is, they became radiant.
Of what kind was he? He was one whose radiant, throbbing luster— meaning both light and affection— was awakened, revealed, and made manifest by a departing servant or friend who had alerted him.

The wick (*varti*) is that which shines forth; its state (*daśā*) is its condition. At the door—meaning at the house-door and in the state of awakening passion—the meeting (*saṃvalana*) or union occurs; by means of that, it is "plump" (*māṃsala*), meaning expanded.
It is called a "lamp" (*dīpaka*), with the suffix *kan* used in the sense of praise.
The form *didyute* is the perfect (*liṭ*) form of the root *dyut* (meaning "to shine").

Here, because two substances are introduced into a single action by means of the two *ca*s, there is a conjunction (*samuccaya*). He states the fault that would arise if there were no introduction [of the substances] by way of conjunction: "by that... (*tena*).
The meaning is that because they are mutually independent, there would be both dual number and a copulative compound (*dvandva*).
It is precisely when based on two words that there is a conjunction of substances (*dravyasamuccaya*) expressed by a suffix attached to the latter word, as in:
“Her limbs are exceedingly emaciated, yet she is as beautiful as the core of a fresh plantain tree; like the form of the moon with but a single digit remaining, she brings a festival to the eyes.”
"Having fallen into this state, distressed by the intense burning of the fire of love, this auspicious lady delights our minds and makes them tremble.

(136) Here, the two actions expressed by "delights" (*ramayati*) and "makes tremble" (*kampayati*) are placed simultaneously upon the single substance—the mind—as their object, through the conjunction (*ca*) occurring in the subsequent word; therefore, this is not a case of *anvācaya* (conjunction where one element is subordinate), as seen in examples such as "at will" (*nikāmam*).
This Mālatī delights and yet agitates our minds;
for she has fallen into a state of extreme distress, overwhelmed by the intense burning arising from the fire of love itself.
Therefore, her limbs are exceedingly emaciated;
she is as beautiful and captivating as the core—the inner pith—of a plantain tree.
By this, both her paleness and her sharpness [of features] are expressed.
Like the form of the moon remaining as a mere fraction, consisting of nothing but its measurement, she is auspicious, bringing joy to the eyes, and virtuous;
through the term "interior of a plantain tree" (*kadalī-garbha*), her extreme paleness and tenderness are suggested,
and she delights by accomplishing the intended purpose.
The intention here is that the mind trembles because of the fear of impending death (ariṣṭa) due to excessive suffering.

In this context, the word "ca" (and), situated in the latter part of the compound "kampayati ca," indicates *samuccaya* (conjunction), as two actions are established within a single substance characterized as the mind.
He states the fault [that would arise] if there were no such establishment by way of conjunction: "by that... (tena).

The meaning is that if there were mutual independence [of the qualities], it would result in the application of *anvācaya* (conjunction as a secondary addition) by means of the particle *ca* situated in the subsequent word.
When multiple words are involved, the conjunction of qualities (*guṇasamuccaya*) occurs through their being illuminators based on each individual word (*pratipada*), as for example:
"How could he not be a cause for wonder—he who was no ordinary man, and in whom both compassion and gratitude resided?"
“Fortune, splendor blazing with the quality of *sattva*, righteousness, human victory, and prowess [reside in him].

(137) Here, qualities such as compassion and gratitude are each introduced through a series of words (*cāreṇa*) and placed in a single action—“resides” (*uvāsa*)—by means of a conjunction (*samuccaya*).

Consequently, the plural number is not used for the qualities, nor is there a *dvandva* compound for “compassion, gratitude, and so forth. When the requirement for the locative case [in the phrase] “in whom” (*yasmin*) arises, this very collection of qualities constitutes a collection of substances (*dravya-samuccaya*).
How could that king— who is extraordinary and so forth— not be a source of wonder? Of what nature is he?
"Aprākṛta" means not lowly;
that is to say, a great person (mahājana).
As Amarasimha states: "The lowly and the common person is the *pṛthagjana*."

In him— this compassionate one— resided compassion (*karuṇā*), pity (*dayā*), gratitude (*kṛtajñatā*), discernment (*vijñatā*), fortune (*lakṣmī*) as prosperity, a splendor blazing with the quality of goodness (*sāttvika-guṇa*), righteousness (*dharma*) as virtuous conduct, pride as humility (*vinaya*), and prowess.
Since gratitude is naturally absent in one who acts solely out of compassion,
the fact that both [compassion and gratitude] reside in him indicates his status as a great personage (*mahājana*).
Nevertheless, since one who lacks fortune (*alakṣmīka*) has nothing whatsoever that is worthy of praise, "possessing fortune" (*salakṣmīka*) was stated;
yet, since one who lacks courage (*niḥsāttvika*) cannot possess the status of a great person (*mahājana*), the preponderance of the quality of courage (*sāttvika-guṇa*) was stated;
and since for one who lacks majesty (*niṣpratāpa*) everything mentioned would merely serve as a source of beauty through its characteristics, the preponderance of splendor (*tejas*) was stated.

Granted that there may be a perfection of qualities as described, yet all qualities become defective in one who is unrighteous; therefore, he says "and dharma"— meaning that morality, modesty, discipline, and prowess are each special qualities in a great man, and thus they too have been mentioned.
Here, by means of the particle *ca* (and) attached to multiple words, various qualities are placed together in a single action through conjunction (*samuccaya*).

He states the fault that would arise in the absence of such conjunction: "By that [conjunction]," meaning that if they were not placed in conjunction, it would follow that "compassion and the other qualities have departed."
Regarding the phrase "in which":
if the intention here is to express a collection of qualities within a single substance by means of the word "in which," then the meaning is that this [collection] also occurs.

Indeed, it is only when there is a basis in multiple words that there is a collection of qualities—by virtue of their being indicative based on the final member of the compound—as in the case of a collection of actions, for example:

"‘Their form, unperceived [by others], their endearing affection, their disregard for what ought to be done, their expansive flattery, and their feigned agitation—all these became a magical spell (*kārmaṇatva*) over their lovers.

(138) Here, the many qualities—form, affection, and flattery—are introduced by means of the conjunction *ca* as depending on the subsequent word, and are thus placed in a collective compound (*samuccaya*) within the single verb *āgamat*. Consequently, there would be neither the plural form *āgaman* nor a copulative compound (*dvandva*).”
In response to the inquiry as to what constitutes their "capacity for action" (*kārmaṇatva*), this very collection of the qualities of the [eight] classes—

beginning with "form" (*rūpa*) and so forth— is what constitutes that capacity for action regarding the pleasure of these women; it became, and has gone toward, the state of being a root-rite (*mūlakarma*) for subjugation.
By "without penetration" and "without insistence," it means spontaneously; that is to say,

regardless of whether the desired object is pleasing or not, there is an expanding love possessing innate radiance, as well as such artfulness of endearment characterized by unartificial, natural, and respectful zeal.
According to Amarasimha, "mūlakarma" means "kārmaṇa" (the act of moving).
Here, qualities such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth are joined by the conjunction (*ca*) at the end of the compound to the action of going; thus, this is a case of *samuccaya* (conjunction).
He states the fault that would arise in the absence of that [conjunction]: "they went" (*agaman*).
The meaning is that there would be a plural number and a *dvandva* compound even when there is no conjunction (*asamuccaya*).

This itself is the "action-nature" (*kārmaṇatva*) of the universals; he states this by saying "action-nature," implying that there is also a "conjunction of universals" (*jātisamuccaya*) through the conjunction of their classes.
The compound based on both members (*ubhayapadāśraya*) functions as an illuminator dependent on the latter member, expressing the conjunction of substances and qualities with actions, as in:
“In this world, these things shine forth—though difficult for embodied beings to obtain even when contemplated by the mind:
the night with its moon, wine with its lotuses, the affection of a beloved, and fresh youth.”

In this instance, night and wine are substances (*dravya*); passion and youth are qualities (*guṇa*). Although there are multiple words and a *dvandva* compound exists, by means of the particle *ca* residing in the final member of the compound, they are all brought into a single action through the verb *cakāsati*. Consequently, the plural form *cakāsati* and the compound itself would not be possible [if they were not unified]; and this very [unification] constitutes the "conjunction of qualities" (*guṇasamuccaya*) among substances and qualities when there is an expectation such as "this is difficult to obtain. These three types are also pure (*śuddha*).
"Having reflected," and so forth:

among these worlds, that is, among the realms of existence, this which is being contemplated by embodied beings—that is, by living creatures—is indeed difficult to obtain even by means of the mind; the particle *hi* is used for emphasis.
What is that?

It is the night with the moon, wine with lotuses, the lover’s passion—that is, affection—and fresh youth; here, by means of the final *ca* (and) situated at the end of the compound, these pairs are joined as dyads and placed within a single action.
He states the fault in its absence with the words "by that" (*tena*),
intending to show its rarity; and he speaks of the accumulation of qualities even in its state of being full of suffering with the word "this" (*ayam*),
which is mixed, depending on both terms as well as on many terms.
As it is said:
"The sun, the moon, the wind, and fire; heaven, earth, water, and the heart; Yama, day and night, both twilights, and Dharma—these know the conduct of a man. (140)

Here, specific substances such as the sun, the moon, and so forth, by means of the particle *ca* placed both after the subsequent member and after each individual member, are brought together within a single action expressed by the verb "he knows.
Consequently, in the absence of the plural number and in the absence of a compound, this constitutes a mixed variety of conjunction (*samuccaya*),
beginning with "the sun," and so on.

The wind (anila) is the air, the fire (anala) is the flame, the sky (dyau) is the ether, the waters (āpaḥ) are the water, the heart, Yama, and day (ahaḥ)—both morning and evening—the Dharma and the Ordainer (Vidhātṛ): these know the conduct and character of people.
The connection [of the sentence] is made by changing the case endings: "the Sun and the Moon know.
According to the *Ratnakoṣa*, "Dharma" refers to quality (*guṇa*) and so forth, as well as the Lord of the World (*lokeśa*).
In this context, since the Sun and others are introduced into a single action by means of the particle *ca* placed within the latter member of the compound, there is a state of mixture (*miśratā*).
He states the fault that arises in the absence of such [mixture] with the words "by that":
conjunction (*samuccaya*) and subsequent mention (*anvācaya*) do not occur when they are not based on both [the particle and the compound].

Because both [types of compound] are illuminated by the illuminator (*dīpaka*) through the removal of their respective objects, that [type of *dīpaka*] is illustrated by means of both the *itaretarayoga* (copulative) and the *samāhāra* (collective) compounds. Among these, the *itaretarayoga* is as follows:
"With words left unfinished, with indifference toward her garlands, garments, and ornaments cast aside..."
"Even rising up to go [home] without cause, they manifested the playful intoxication of these women.

(141) Here it is said: *upekṣā* (neglect), *utthitam* (having risen)—these qualifiers of action and substance—are placed within the act of manifesting intoxicated play (*madavilāsa*) through mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*). Therefore, the plural number in *dyotayanti* and the copulative compound (*dvandva-samāsa*) would occur only if that were intended; however, since neither the connective particle *ca* nor its equivalent is found here either in the subsequent word or after each individual term, this is a variety of *samuccaya* (cumulative conjunction) that relies on neither [of those conditions].

The term *anubhaya* (neither-nor) refers to cases where there is neither a conjunction (*samuccaya*) nor a sequential addition (*anvācaya*) because the particle *ca* is absent in either two-word or multi-word sentences;

for it is the very definition of *dīpaka* that it serves as an illuminator by means of a single word denoting an action or other element residing in one place, thereby benefiting the entire sentence, and since such conjunction and sequential addition would require its presence, this is the intended meaning.
Regarding the phrase "with remnants" (*sāvaśeṣa*) and so forth:
these [actions] manifested the intoxicating confusion—the playful charm of being drunk—of these women;

he describes them as follows: "with remnants" means that which exists together with remaining portions (*avaśiṣṭa-bhāga*); such was the speech uttered, characterized by words that were broken or incomplete.
The meaning is that "broken syllables" refers to speech;

"neglect" regarding those garlands, garments, and ornaments that have become disheveled or fallen means not securing them; and "rising" refers to the act of rising up to go away without cause—that is, without any reason.
In the word *uktam*, the suffix *kta* denotes the abstract state (*bhāve*); likewise, in *utthitam*, the suffix *kta* also denotes the abstract state.
In the expression *akāraṇataḥ*, the suffix *tasi* is used from the ablative case (*pañcamī*).

Here, through the mutual conjunction of the verbal action (vacanādi) consisting of what has been stated and so forth, with the substance (dravya) that serves as its substratum, there is an entry into the principal action;
for this very reason, the plural number is used in the phrase "they indicate" (dyotayanti).
He states the fault in accepting [the view of] conjunction (samuccaya) with the words "in a dvandva," etc.
An example of collective inclusion (*samāhāra*) is as follows:

"O fawn-eyed one, among the boons [sought], there is that which is sought even in the Three-Eyed One (Śiva)—a body like Virūpākṣa, a birth unperceived, and wealth indicated by nakedness—is all this found even when taken individually? (142)
In this context, by stating, "Is that which is sought among boons even partially present in the Three-eyed One?", [the author] intends the entire aggregate of body, age, and wealth;

and since that aggregate has its constituent parts manifested, it is expressed as a *itaretarayoga* (mutual conjunction), whereas when its constituent parts are unmanifested, it is a *samāhāra* (collective compound).
This [aggregate] is here expressed by the neuter singular pronoun *yat*.
And since there is no word "ca" (and) anywhere here, this too is a variety of conjunction based on neither [of the two]. Regarding the verse beginning with "vapuḥ":
O Bālamṛgākṣi—O you with eyes like those of a young deer—O Gaurī, is that which is sought and searched for among excellent things present even individually, one by one, in the three-eyed Śiva?

However, he says that such a thing does not exist at all: "The body" (vapuḥ) means the physical frame; "wherein the eyes are deformed" (virūpakṣi) refers to such a deformed state, meaning a contradictory nature, because while the connection with duality is not contradictory regarding the eyes, the connection with triplicity is contradictory.
"Alakṣyajanmatā" means the state of having an untraceable birth— where "birth" (janma) refers to origin or family lineage— and thus signifies being of unknown parentage.
The directions themselves are his garment; by virtue of that state, his wealth (vasu) is said to have been offered or described—Amara states, "One who is naked and without clothes is 'digambara'.
[The word] *mṛga* is derived from the root *mṛg* meaning "to search," used in the passive voice (*lakāra*).
In this context, regarding the collection (samuccaya) of the body and so forth: when there is a distinctness of manifest parts, it is an "mutual conjunction" (itaretarayoga);
but when the distinction of parts is concealed, it is a "composite whole" (samāhāra).
By the use of the singular number and the neuter gender here, only the composite whole (samāhāra) is expressed.
He states that even when joined with the particle *ca*, there is mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*): "And not" (*na ca*)—
even in this conjunction, there is mutual conjunction, as it is also when joined with a subsequent word (*uttarapada*).
"At that moment, she of the beautiful face became subject to both the trident-bearer [Śiva] and Intoxication (mada), who had cast aside their shame and desired her bed.

Here, if the two specific substances— the trident-bearer and Intoxication— were placed in a copulative compound (*itaretarayoga*) with the particle *ca* based on the final member (*uttarapada*), as in "the trident-bearer and Intoxication," then the dual number and the *ekaśeṣa* [retention of one term] in the subsequent phrases ending with "of the two" (*dvyoḥ*)— such as "who had cast aside their shame"— would not be possible, because the word "subject" (*vaśavartinī*) is a quality-word (*guṇapada*).
This too is a variety of conjunction (*samuccaya*), resting upon two words and indicating that which depends on the subsequent word;
thus, in the phrase "at that moment" and so forth,
that fair-faced Gaurī became subject to— and dependent upon— both the intoxication and the passion of Śūlin, Hara.
Of what two such [beings]? Of those two at that time whose shame and modesty had vanished due to being overturned,
and in whom passion was kindled and intensified.

For this very reason, regarding the two who desire to go to bed but do not wish for a bed—Śūlin and Madaya—he states the fault in their arrangement through mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*) while remaining under [their] control: "At that time," etc.
He explains that when there is a recourse to multiple words, mutual conjunction occurs by means of the *ca* (and) which depends on the final word: "In this way," etc.
Regarding the verse "samāhāram iti vicintyamānam," the meaning is that by the use of the singular number and the neuter gender in the word *idam*, the collective aggregate (*samāhāra*) is expressed.

Since the mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*) and the collective aggregate both exist when the subject matter concerns substances (*dravya*) and so forth, he states another subject matter for the case of sequential mention (*anvācaya*)— namely, "action" (*kriyā*).
In this way, other examples of *itaretara-yoga* (mutual conjunction) and *caya-yoga* (cumulative conjunction) may also be cited.

However, *samāhāra* (collective conjunction), being a domain of *caya-yoga*, has already been explained by the very example beginning with "vicintyamānam. As for *anvācaya* (conjunction with a secondary element), it is appropriate only when referring to an action (*kriyā*), and in that case, the particle *ca* must depend upon the subsequent word.
For example:

"As the women go at night toward their lovers' dwellings along the royal road, where the light is obstructed by darkness thick enough to be pierced by a needle, show them the path with a flash of lightning as smooth as gold on a touchstone; but do not be loud with the release of water and thunder, lest they become terrified. (144)

In this case, having first introduced the action with the object "the earth" (*urvī*) in the sense of "show [it]," the sentence continues by adding another intransitive action to that same agent (*dharmī*), namely, "and do not be noisy with the discharge of water and thundering. This *anvācaya* (conjunction of a subordinate with a principal) differs from *samuccaya* (simple conjunction) because of the difference in time and the difference in objects.
Now, if in *samuccaya* as well two actions with different objects were employed at the same time, what fault would there be? None at all.
However, because its subject matter has been superseded by the "Samuccaya" (conjunction) meter, it is not cited;
in the verse beginning with "gacchantīnām," you should show the earth— the ground— to the women along with the lightning, Saudāminī.
Of what kind of women, going to their husbands' homes at night during the dark of the night, and under what circumstances?
When the royal road is such that its sight is obstructed by darkness capable of piercing the tip of a needle, what kind of lightning—
beautiful and as lustrous as a streak of gold upon a touchstone— should you not become? Do not let yourself be characterized merely by the shedding of water and thundering.
For they would be helpless, distressed, and overwhelmed;
as Medinīkāra states: "Nikaṣa refers to a streak on a touchstone, a slab, or the act of rubbing," and Amara states: "Stanita is the thundering of clouds."
In the word *mābhūḥ*, there is a prohibition of the augment *aṭ* by the rule *na māṅyoge* (Pāṇini 6.4.74).

Having stated the first action here, he explains the distinction between the second action and conjunction (*samuccaya*) by means of the term "distinct" (*bhinna*): in conjunction, there is a connection [of actions] that occurs simultaneously and within a single object; here, however, because there is a difference in time and a difference in object within the connection, it is distinct—this is the meaning.
Having raised the objection that existence (*sattva*) might be suspected in the conjunction of the two stated dissimilarities, he refutes it with the words "But rather" (*kiṃtu*).
