The intention is this: in a conjunction (*samuccaya*), even if both properties are present, the exclusion of the object occurs precisely by virtue of being a conjunction; however, in this case, the determination is made solely by the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*).
Even in a compound (*samāsa*), there is a distinct type of conjunction not based on either [of the two members] due to mutual connection (*itaretarayoga*), as for example:
“I salute Pārvatī and Parameśvara, the parents of the world, who are joined together for the sake of the comprehension of word and meaning, like word and meaning themselves.

(145) Here, in the phrase “like word and meaning,” there is the taking of the gender of the subsequent term; and in the phrase “the parents joined together,” this [rule] applies: “When a masculine and a feminine [are in apposition], [the masculine remains]. 1.2.67.
2 67’, ‘The father [is equal] to the mother 1 2’

And by the rule of *ekaśeṣa* (retaining one of two similar terms), because this [pair] possesses the characteristic of distinction (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*), it attains the status of an ornament (*alaṃkāra*) while being a form of *vakrokti* (indirect or figurative speech). Thus, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to cases such as "the Dhava and Khadira trees. This too is a variety of *samuccaya* (conjunction).
[The verse beginning with] "Speech and Meaning" and so forth means:
"I worship and bow down to Gaurī and Hara."
For what purpose do speech and meaning exist? For the sake of their comprehension and ascertainment,
what are they like?
"Joined together like word and meaning"—that is, like the word and its denoted object;

just as the word and its signified meaning are eternally connected by the relationship of the signifier and the signified, so too are these two eternally joined. They are the parents—the mother and father—of the world, that is, of all living beings.

In the case of the dvandva compound *pitā ca mātā ca* ("father and mother"), by applying the rule *pitā mātrā* (Pāṇini 1.2.70) for the retention of only one term (*ekaśeṣa*), the form *pitarau* is obtained.
Because Pārvatī is her mother and because a mother is most highly honored due to her extreme gravity, she is placed first [in the compound];
for the Smṛti states: "A mother exceeds a father a thousandfold in gravity."
By this, Ardhanārīśvara is described;
or alternatively, Hara is the protector (pa) of Pārvatī, thus he is Pārvatīpa, and Hari is the lord (īśvara) of Ramā (Lakṣmī); I bow to those two.
Or again, Hara is one who is devoted to (para) Pārvatī, and Hari is the lord of Māyā (Lakṣmī); I bow to Hara and Hari.
Of what nature are the two parents, the progenitors of the world?
The rest is exactly the same.

By this, the interpretation that the form of Hari-Hara is expressed is refuted; for the *Viśvaprakāśa* states, "The word *aramā* is also desired in the sense of Lakṣmī," and the *Ekākṣarakośa* states, "And *mā* is said to be Lakṣmī."
The taking of another's gender, the gender of the meaning or the word,
and the case of the combined [term] are illustrated here in the examples *saṃpṛktā* and *saṃpṛktaḥ*, according to the rule *pumān striyā*.
67. Thus, there is a *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one from a group).

For this very reason, because of the curvature (*vakratā*) of the expression, it constitutes a figure of speech (*alaṃkāra*) here; however, in cases such as "the *dhava* and *khadira* trees," there is no such curvature, and therefore it does not constitute a figure of speech.

Also by way of combination, as for example: "When the Mind-born [Cupid] had accomplished his purpose through the gestures of the women, he placed his bow and arrows upon their faces, which were like their eyes and eyebrows. (146)
In this case as well, regarding these two terms, *akṣibhruvam* and *śarakārmukam*, [the application of] Pāṇini’s rule 2.4.2, *dvandvaśca prāṇitūryasenāṅganām*,
and [the subsequent rule] *vāṅmanasākṣibhruvaḥ...* [is invoked].
And because of this connection with specific characteristics (*viśeṣalakṣaṇa*), there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as "dhava, khadira,
and palāśa," nor in [the case of] "women" and so forth.
In that city, the Mind-born Kāma placed upon the faces of women—acting as his bow—the arrows and bow in the guise of their eyes and eyebrows;

and when their own purpose, such as mental restlessness, was accomplished through the *hāvas* (coquettish gestures) of the women—that is, the actions born of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-bhāva*)—as Amara states: "The *hāvas* are actions arising from the erotic sentiment."
Here too, since the quality of *vakrokti* (paronomasia/indirect expression) arises precisely through both the general and specific characteristics,
this concludes the definition of the figure of speech *samuccaya* (accumulation) and the definition of the figure of speech *ākṣepa* (paraleipsis).
He defines *ākṣepa* (the objection):
"Where there is a statement of negation, whether by way of affirmation or negation, it is either pure or mixed; that is *ākṣepa*. Obstruction (*rodha*) is not distinct from *ākṣepa*. (64)

Regarding the phrase "by means of a method" (*vidhinā*): whether by way of affirmation as a reason or by way of negation as a reason, that statement or definition of a negation is *ākṣepa* (paralipsis).
He states that "obstruction" (*rodha*) is likewise indeed *ākṣepa* itself, saying: "obstruction."
The meaning is that since it is already apprehended by the very definition of *ākṣepa* (implication), *rodha* (obstruction) is not distinct from it.
Among these, an example of pure *vidhyākṣepa* (implication of a command) is as follows:
"Go, if you must go, my beloved; may your paths be auspicious."
"May my birth also occur in that very place where you have gone.

Here, because the command "Go"—which is a prescriptive statement—is countered by the benediction "May my birth also occur in that very place," which indicates death, a prohibition is being made; thus, this is a pure *vidhyākṣepa* (rejection of a prescription), beginning with "Go," and so forth.
O beloved, O dear one, if you go— then go to a foreign land; this is the ellipsis—
no obstruction shall be placed by me.
However, the remainder of the meaning is that I say only this: "Wherever you go, may my birth also be there.

Here, although the act of going is expressed in the form of an injunction, by saying "may my birth be there," she indicates her own death—implying, "If you go, I must die"—and thus expresses a prohibition of the departure through an injunction. Furthermore, its purity is maintained by not being mixed with other figures of speech.
An example of the mixed type (*miśra*) is as follows:
“Enough with this dispute; let him remain exactly as you have heard him to be, in every respect.
My mind, however, is fixed here upon him alone as its singular essence; the course of passion does not regard what is said. (148)

Here, having established his position through the prohibition "enough with this dispute" and the injunction "let him be such as he is," she then challenges it again by means of an injunction—"my mind remains here, its sole essence being devotion"—and a prohibition—"one who acts out of passion does not heed censure. This is an *ākṣepa* (challenge) mixed with an injunction, consisting of both injunction and prohibition.
As for the words "enough," etc., [the sense is]: "Enough with the dispute regarding that which you have heard; it is fruitless."
"May he remain exactly as he is, entirely and in his full integrity;
for my mind remains fixed here, its sole essence being devotion and subject to his will.
Even though the qualities you mentioned, such as having three eyes and so forth, exist in him within this world, nevertheless, my mind is intent upon him alone—this is the meaning."
The reason here is that the "functioning of desire" (*kāmavṛtti*), which is the operation of longing, does not perceive what is "to be said" (*vacanīya*), that is, what ought to be spoken;
the meaning is that desire cannot be directed toward the welfare of others.

Here, through both prohibition and injunction, there is an implication (*ākṣepa*) of an injunction in the form of establishing that [other's] opinion by means of both injunction and prohibition; thus, this is a mixed type of "implication of an injunction" (*vidhyākṣepa*).
An example of pure prohibition by objection (*śuddha-niṣedhākṣepa*) is as follows:
"O sweet-voiced one, why do you place a blue lotus upon your ear?
Do you consider your side-glance insufficient for this task? (149)

Here, the negative statement “Why do you place a blue lotus on your ear? is supported by the sentence beginning with “Is it the corner of your eye...,” which, though phrased as a question, results in a negation; thus, this is a pure *niṣedhākṣepa* (rejection of a negation). [The commentary explains: “O sweet-voiced one (*kalabhāṣiṇi*), why (*kutaḥ*) do you place the blue water-lily (*nīlotpala*) on your ear?”

He states the reason for the prohibition with the word "whence" (*kutaḥ*): "In this rite, such as the subjugation of a lover through desire, do you consider even a side-glance from the corner of the eye to be insufficient or incapable? Here, because the prohibition is cast aside by a statement that results in its own negation, it is a "prohibition-cast-aside" (*niṣedhākṣepa*), and its purity (*śuddhatā*) consists in its absolute singleness (*kaivalyena*).
An example of the mixed type is as follows:
“Truly, who says that mountains are heavy and that reservoirs of water are not deep?
Nevertheless, though I am compared by the wise to [the ocean], I simply lack the courage. (150)
"Truly, mountains are heavy; who says that reservoirs of water are not deep?
Nevertheless, I have no enthusiasm to compare them with the wise.

Here, "truly, mountains are heavy" is an affirmation (*vidhi*), while "who says that reservoirs of water are not deep? is a challenge to another's opinion (*paramatākṣepa*). Through these two, the heaviness of the mountains and the depth of the oceans—which the latter half of the verse negates from the perspective of the wise, yet affirms for others—is established. This is a mixed form of *niṣedhākṣepa* (negation-cum-challenge).
"Truth," and so forth: "The teachers are indeed mountains; who says that reservoirs of water are not deep?
Nevertheless, I have no enthusiasm to compare them with the wise."
"Here, mountains are certainly the support of weight;

who says that the oceans, the reservoirs of water, are not deep? Indeed, they are deep. Nevertheless, though it is possible for the wise to compare and equate these two—the mountain and the ocean—nevertheless, I have no enthusiasm [to do so], because of the superiority of those wise ones over them."

Although the word *jalāśaya* means merely a "reservoir of water" according to lexicons—as in the definition "a reservoir (*jalāśaya*) is a receptacle of water (*jalādhāra*)"—nevertheless, due to its suitability for extreme depth, it refers here specifically to the ocean.

Thus, there is a mixture of elements: by way of both injunction and prohibition, there is a negation of weight and depth relative to others, while there is an injunction [of these qualities] in comparison to them.
Regarding what was stated—that "an obstacle (*rodha*) is not distinct from implication (*ākṣepa*)"—the distinction here is as follows:
When there is a prevention of one who is about to engage in an action by means of a reason, or a restraint through speech and logic, that is called *ākṣepa* (paralipsis).
In the case of an injunction (*vidhi*), restraint is said to be both adverse (*pratikūla*) and favorable (*anukūla*). || 65 ||

Even in the case of prohibition (niṣedha), it is said to be of two kinds, by way of both speech and reasoning. Regarding the specific nature of obstruction (rodha), he says: "In actions" (kriyāsu)—that which is the warding off of those intent on actions through the means of both speech and reasoning is obstruction (rodha).
And that which has become the remainder is indeed the implication (ākṣepa) itself;
this is the commonality of implication with both affirmation and negation.
An example of one who is adverse toward an injunction through speech:
"O Ten-faced One, what is the use of speaking? For you, who cannot sustain the burden, speaking is like [speaking] yourself."
"O Ten-faced One, what is the use of further talk?
Even others have met their end under the stroke of the thunderbolt for failing to carry out the burden of what they had promised; the essence of such talk is this much. [151]

Here, because the word *kim* signifies opposition (*pratikūla*), Daśānana is obstructed by Citraratha through his very mode of speech as he speaks; and the cause is presented as opposition by means of the proclamation of Vajraprabhā’s power. This is called *rodha* (obstruction), which is a form of *vidhyākṣepa* (negation of an injunction) that is both expressed and opposed, beginning with the words "What [is the use]..."—[the sense being]: "O Ten-faced One, what is the use of this speech that is like mere babbling, failing to carry its own burden?"
"Even others have met their end by merely uttering such words as these against the thunderbolts [of my power].
O ten-faced Rāvaṇa, what is the use of this prattling?
Indeed, it amounts to nothing at all."

For a man who fails to carry out the burden commensurate with his own words, what is the best or most essential essence of his speech? It is this very resolve regarding the burden that others too— those warriors who have met their destruction at the edge of the thunderbolt— have attained.
"‘The best extract the essence which is meaningful,’ so says Śāśvata.

Here, while Rāvaṇa is speaking, he is obstructed by Citraratha with a contrary statement consisting of the proclamation of Vajraprabhā’s fame; thus, there is a contradiction involving the prohibition of an injunction (*vidhyākṣepavirodha*). An example of a favorable [statement] through speech alone is as follows:
“Seeking to kill him,
and yourself hastening to kill the Ten-faced One— what do you wish to do, you who have been told by the Lord of Chariots that the Lord of Monkeys is dear to him? (152)
"O Lord of Monkeys, what do you wish to do that is pleasing [to me], yet displeasing to the Lord of the Raghus?

Here too, because the word *kim* (what) implies prohibition, Sugrīva—who was rising up for the sake of slaying the Ten-faced One—is restrained by Jāmbavān. Furthermore, the reason is stated with favor: "Why have you undertaken this act which, though appearing pleasing, is actually harmful to the Lord of the Raghus?
This very form of prohibition, being both expressed and favorable, is called *rodha* (restraint).
"‘To slay,’ and so forth:
‘Seeking to slay the ten-faced one, you yourself hasten to kill him;
O Lord of Monkeys, what do you wish to do that is pleasing to him, which is actually displeasing to the Lord of the Raghus?’"

"O Sugrīva, Lord of Monkeys, seeking to kill the Ten-faced one and begging [for help], how is it that you, considering what might be pleasing to Rāma, the Lord of the Raghus, desire to do him an unpleasant and undesirable thing? To explain why this is disagreeable: for one who is himself in haste to kill the Ten-faced one—who, as a master, desires to slay him—is not the killing of an offender considered a crime? Therefore, let that Supreme Person (Puruṣottama) himself cause him to be slain."
The intention is: "Let assistance be rendered by you and others who have assembled.
The word *yat* (or *je*), being an indeclinable with multiple meanings, is used here for the purpose of address;
alternatively, the word *je* serves as a verse-filler (*pādapūraṇa*).
In this case, the phrase "the ten-faced one" (*daśavadana-pada*) is connected to two acts of killing through repetition according to the sequence of desire;

here, the effort to slay Rāvaṇa—which was stated as a command—is obstructed by Jāmbavān, who presents a favorable reason. Thus, this is an instance of "obstruction" (*rodha*), which is a subordinate form of the "negation of a command" (*vidhy-ākṣepa*).
An example of both the favorable and unfavorable [reasons] being applicable to the command itself is as follows:
“I wish to say ‘Go,’ for I desire your welfare;
yet the words ‘Do not go’ issue from my mouth—what can I do?
Here, having spoken as stated, she says “What can I do” in a manner that is actually favorable [to his departure].

In this case, although the interrogative *kimaḥ* has the sense of inquiry, its meaning as a negation is understood through reasoning; this is called *rodha*, which is an implied prohibition (*vidhyākṣepa*) that is both logical and favorable.

Furthermore, in the view that this is an expression of boldness (*vaiyātya*), this very same thing becomes an implied prohibition that is logical yet unfavorable (*pratikūla-vidhyākṣepa*), as in "go," and so forth.

"O friend, I wish to say to you, 'Go to your beloved,' yet because I am a woman seeking your welfare, and because women are naturally fond of [their lovers], the words 'Do not go' escape from my mouth. What can I do?

In the reading "matpriyaṃ tvatpriyaiṣiṇī," however, the construction should be understood as follows: "Desiring your welfare, I wish to say, 'Go'; yet, so that it may be for my own benefit, the words 'Do not go' issue forth."
In this context, through reasoning—that is, by means of the logical consistency of the matter at hand—the sense of prohibition is understood from the phrase "what can I do?

If, out of impudence or boldness, one speaks the opposite, then while the intention is to say "do not go," the words that actually issue forth are "go. In such a case, the phrase "what can I do? logically establishes a prohibition; for example, when it is contrary to the intended prohibition: [Example: *“kiṃ karomi tavāṅgeṣu yad dṛṣṭir na nivartate |” (What can I do, since my gaze does not turn away from your limbs? Here, although the speaker intends to express a prohibition, the statement is made in a manner that appears to grant permission.* *Note: The provided text fragment contains the opening of a verse where the speaker’s intent is to forbid the listener from looking at her limbs, yet the phrasing suggests the opposite.*

‘The village abounds in young men, it is the month of Madhu, youth is his age, and the husband is an old man; there is wine available at will—let not the unchaste woman perish! || 184 || [The village has many youths, it is the month of spring, he is in his prime, and the husband is an elder.]
"Old wine is available; let it not be unfaithful—why should it die?

Here, he who utters the prohibition "let it not be unfaithful" states the reason—"the village is full of young men"—and then, by way of opposition, restrains it with "why should it die? In this case, through the force of the interrogative particle *kim* used in the sense of an envious question, its meaning as a prohibition is understood. This is called *rodha*, the "obstruction" which is a prohibition of opposition based on reasoning (*yaukta-pratikūla-niṣedhākṣepa*).

"O townsfolk," and so forth: "The village is abundant in provisions, the month is Madhava, the husband is young, and the wine is aged; the unchaste woman is under her own control—let her be, why should she die?"
A certain woman, having learned that the husband of another woman was of a fickle mind, told this to someone;
she, however, gave the following reply: "Abounding" (*pracura*) means where there are many (*pracurāḥ*), numerous young men (*taruṇāḥ*).
The suffix *ka* is applied [to form a bahuvrīhi compound] optionally after a word other than those already mentioned, according to Pāṇini 5.4.154: *śeṣād vibhāṣā*.

It is the month of Madhu, the spring; there is youth, and the master is an old man, aged and decrepit; the wine is old, yet it is under one’s own control and at one’s disposal. Therefore, let her not be unchaste—what, would she die? The meaning is that if she were not fickle during this year, she would surely have died.

"Old liquor is pleasing"—this is well known among drunkards. Here, by the presence of an interrogative intonation (*kāku*) in the word "kiṃ" (what?), the sense of an envious question is understood through reasoning as being directed toward a prohibition; thus, this is an *rodha* (obstruction) that is favorable to the prohibition through reasoning alone. For example:
‘How can her waist not wither away, when it cannot be seen through these eyes resembling blue lotus petals, their range obstructed by the weight of her firm breasts? (155)
“He is not seen by her eyes, whose expansion is obstructed by the weight of her thick breasts.
Here, one who speaks a prohibition—thinking, “May even her waist not waste away like her breasts”—is countered by someone’s favor with the question, “How so? Why should it not waste away?”

That which is not seen by her eyes, which resemble the petals of a blue lotus and whose expansion is obstructed by her firm breasts—since she, while looking at another through these very eyes, does not see that [other], it appears as if even her waist is wasting away, just like me. In this context, when the interrogative pronoun *kim* has the sense of inquiry, its negative sense is understood; this is called *rodha* (obstruction), a logical and favorable form of *niṣedhākṣepa* (negation by objection), as in the verse beginning with *kaham*.
"How might her waist not diminish—that waist which is not seen by her eyes, which resemble the petals of a blue lotus, as their expansion is obstructed by the weight of her firm breasts?
Here, [the meaning is]: how might the waist of this heroine not diminish, that is, not become emaciated?

"He who is not seen by her eyes, which resemble blue lotus petals and whose movement is obstructed by the weight of her firm breasts— since she, while looking at another with these eyes, did not see me, it is observed that just as I am emaciated, so too has her waist become emaciated by that very same [lack of being seen].
Here also, the negative sense of *kim* is understood through reasoning alone.
An example of both the adverse and the favorable [types of prohibition] through direct statement is as follows:
“A frown was fashioned, the forward gaze was withdrawn, and an unkind word was spoken; for even a person who is not angry acts with such excessive force when he is provoked. (156)

In this context, regarding the reproach in the form of a prohibition and an objection—namely, "even though he is not angry, he is made angry"—the speaker, by means of audacity (*vaiyātya*) presenting a contrary cause such as "she has knit her brows," expresses through intonation (*kakvā*) that the reproach is merely verbal, saying, "This is her excessive power; this is her forcefulness. Therefore, this is called *rodha* (obstruction), which is a prohibition-objection that is both unspoken and contrary.

Furthermore, according to the view that this is spoken without audacity (*avaiyātya*), when there is a description of her true nature (*svarūpākhyāna*) and so forth, this becomes a prohibition-objection that is favorable (*anukūla-niṣedhākṣepa*), as in the case of "she has knit her brows" and so on.
This excessive abundance is indeed compulsion (*balātkāra*), since even a person who is not angry is made angry by compulsion;
thus he says: "By you, a frown—the knitting of the eyebrows—was fashioned."
Having gone before me,
you immediately kissed my face; thus, what was ill-spoken has been taken away by your embrace.
The word *vā* has the sense of *ca* (and).
Here, having adduced a contrary reason out of boldness (*dhārṣṭya*), the censure is merely verbal through the use of intonation (*kāku*).

Alternatively, in the case where there is no boldness, he says "this" (*ayam*), meaning that this [statement] is intended solely to describe her true nature; thus, he states that this is also a contradiction consisting of an implied prohibition of what was previously stated.
But when, even after adducing a reason, one who is about to engage in an action is not restrained, that is merely an objection (*ākṣepa*) and not a prohibition (*rodha*).
For example:
"The breezes from the *kalamba* trees have passed; I have seen the sky covered by clouds."
‘The Kadamba-scented breezes have passed, the sky has been seen shrouded in the darkness of clouds,
and the sound of thunder has been endured; yet, alas, there is still no resolve for life in him.’

In this case, although causes for the determination to live—such as the blowing of the *kadamba* winds—are introduced, the action that is about to arise is not obstructed by the thought, "How can he not live? Rather, it is the cause itself that is sublated: "Even so, there is no determination to live on his part.
Thus, this is indeed a sublation (*ākṣepa*), not an obstruction (*rodha*).
"Gamitā" and so forth:
"The kadamba-scented breezes have passed; the expanse of the sky, darkened by clouds, has been seen;
the sound of thunder has been endured; yet, alas, there is still no attachment to life in him."

Even so, there is indeed no attachment—that is, no resolve or determination—on the part of this Rāma toward life or the maintenance of his vital breaths; this is certain, or rather, it serves as an ornament of speech.

For although winds carrying the scent of *kadamba* flowers have been experienced, the expanse of the sky filled with the darkness of clouds has been seen, and the sound in the form of thunder has been endured and heard.
Here, even though [the pain] is unbearable, the cause for not resolving to live is the intensity of love;
or rather, it is the thought that "if there were no departure even in autumn—the season appropriate for the journey—then I would never have union with my beloved";
or else, it is the resolve regarding the difficulty of the days and nights because of the severity of the time yet to be spent traveling.
Or rather, there is indecision due to deliberation: "The winds from the *kadamba* trees have already passed; how shall I endure the winds from the blooming white lotuses?

The sky was seen shrouded in futile darkness; how shall I behold it whitened by the autumnal moonlight? The sound of thunder was endured; how shall I endure the sweet warbling of the swans? Thus, through such reflection, there arises a state of indecision.

Alternatively, if Sītā were sustained by these very misfortunes—which have rendered her hopes futile and her efforts vain—then my own hope would surely perish; it is with this thought that there is indecision (*anadhyavasāya*).
Here, there is no obstruction to the action of living already present, but rather a "rejection" (*ākṣepa*) of the cause. Thus, it is a case of *ākṣepa* (poetic objection).
When there is a prevention of even one intent upon an action, if the causes are directed toward another purpose, no obstruction occurs.
For example:
"Much wealth will be obtained, and there is happiness and safety on the road; nor is there any danger to my life. Nevertheless, my dear, do not go. (158)

In this context, although the beloved has set out and is being restrained for reasons such as the acquisition of abundant wealth, the intent is solely toward departure and not toward prevention; therefore, this is not "obstruction" (rodha), but rather it is simply "objection" (ākṣepa),
as in the verse beginning with "wealth," and so forth.
My dear, although you have abundant wealth that is easily obtainable, and the path is comfortable— neither difficult nor dangerous—
and secure against harm from thieves and the like;
There is no danger to my life;
nevertheless, you must not go—do not depart.
According to Amara, "kuśalam" means welfare or safety.
Here, because the causes for obtaining abundant wealth and so forth are implied by the intent of departure, this is the definition of the figure of speech *ākṣepa* (paralipsis),
which is followed by the figure of speech *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration).

He defines *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a general truth): "That should be known as *arthāntaranyāsa* when, having introduced a certain subject matter (*vastu*), there is the presentation of another matter capable of establishing it. (67)

That [subject] is described by the learned through the similarity (sādharmya) and dissimilarity (vaidharmya) of the presented objects; in some cases, it is stated by way of inversion (vaiparītya). This is to be understood. (68)

Having introduced or commenced with some particular object (*vastu*) as the subject to be expressed, the presentation or introduction of another object capable of establishing that [first] object through the logic of the sentence-meaning is *arthāntaranyāsa*.
Its opposite is *viparyaya*.
Among these, by way of similarity (*sādharmyeṇa*), for example:
‘These rain-clouds remove the distress of embodied beings;
surely the very attainment of greatness is for the sake of allaying the suffering of others.

Here, having introduced the great object called the cloud—which is capable of removing distress—and then introducing another object characterized as a great person who is likewise capable of that same means, by means of a commonality of purpose, this is *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration) based on similarity (*sādharmya*).
"Payomucaḥ" and so forth:
these clouds, indeed— certainly— remove the distress of embodied beings.
The attainment of self and the continued existence of the great is for the sake of pacifying the suffering of others;
here, the presentation of the second half-verse by way of similarity (sādharmya) is clearly intended to establish the meaning set forth in the first half-verse.
An example by way of dissimilarity (vaidharmya) is as follows:

“No woman discarded the garland—though soiled by water—that her beloved had woven and placed upon her full-breasted chest in the presence of a rival; for virtues reside in affection, not in the physical object. (160) Here too, having presented affection as the cause for the beloved’s own placing of the garland upon the heart of his mistress, the reason for not discarding the garland despite its defect of being water-soiled is established here by way of contrast (*vaidharmya*). Therefore, this is an *arthāntaranyāsa* based on contrast.
Out of love, a certain woman did not abandon, nor did she cast off, even a garland or wreath that was soiled by water;
of what sort was it?
O lady with fleshy breasts, having woven it with love, wear it upon your heart; it has been placed and offered near your rival wife.

Here he states the justification for this: "For virtues reside in affection, not in the physical object"—this is stated by way of contrast (*vaidharmya*), showing that even a garland soiled by water is not abandoned because the cause for its retention resides in love.
By way of contrast, for example:
“He who is the beloved of her heart gives her happiness even while causing pain;
though scorched by the nails of her lover, the horripilation on her breasts increases. (161)
"Whoever is dear to one's heart gives happiness even while causing pain;
on breasts that are slightly wounded by the nails of a lover, horripilation increases.

Here, having first presented the fact capable of serving as the proof (*sādhana*), the thing to be proven (*sādhya*) is stated afterwards; thus, due to this inversion, it is the figure of speech called *arthāntaranyāsa* known as "inversion" (*viparyaya*).
"Whoever," and so forth:
"Whoever is one's heart-beloved, even when causing pain, he is likewise dear; thus, even upon breasts distressed by the pain of his beloved nails, horripilation increases."

"In this world, whoever is dear to someone's heart remains dear to them even while causing them pain; this is the reason why, even though her breasts were pained by the nail of her beloved, the thrill of horripilation increased upon them.
Regarding the word *dadat* (causing), [the rule] "not after a reduplicated stem ending in *śatṛ*" applies.
1.78: Thus, regarding this prohibition, the cause is stated first and then its effect is stated; hence there is a reversal of the natural order.
He states that there is no difference between *ubhayanyāsa* and *arthāntaranyāsa*:
"That which is called *ubhayanyāsa* is indeed *arthāntaranyāsa*; it is also *pratyanīkanyāsa* and likewise *pratīkanyāsa*. (69)
The word "prokta" (stated) refers to an adversary or opponent; it means a counterpart, a limb, or a part—as Amarasimha states: "Aṅga, pratīka, and avayava [are synonyms for limb]."
The placement of both [types of figures] in them is as follows:
“Those are rare virtuous men who accomplish their tasks without speaking;
and those trees are even rarer which yield fruit without the appearance of flowers being known.”
"Rare are those virtuous men who, even when unasked, apply themselves to the discussion of what ought to be done;
very few indeed are those trees that bear fruit without the emergence of their flowers being known.

Here, although the relationship of the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*) exists, it is not explicitly stated; rather, there is the presentation of two things (*vastu*), which constitutes this figure of speech called *ubhayanyāsa* (the double presentation).
“They are rare,” and so forth:
“Those good men who engage in conversation about their duties even when not being addressed are rare;
they are like those trees that bear fruit even though the emergence of their flowers remains unknown.”
"In this world, those virtuous people are rare, limited,
and few— meaning,

those who, even when not commanded with words for the sake of a task, apply themselves and become engaged in the work; and even among them, those trees are very few and indeed scarce that bear fruit while their blossoms remain unnoticed."

"Abhaṇyamānāḥ" (not being told) possesses a double object due to the inclusion of the causative suffix (*ṇic*); or else, they apply themselves to the performance of their duties when there is no talk of their duties—
of what sort [are they]?
"Abhaṇyamānā" means "unspoken";
according to Śāśvata, "ālāpa" refers to speech or utterance.
Here, both terms are presented by way of establishing the relationship between cause and effect.
The arrangement of opposites (*pratyanīkanyāsa*) is as follows:
“Rare indeed are those who remain indifferent like clouds; they diminish in their absence like the flow of rivers. (163)
"Rare indeed are those who, having rendered assistance, remain indifferent like rain-clouds;
they wither away in separation from them, like the currents of rivers.

Here, both the departure of those who have rendered help without expecting a return favor, and the wasting away in their absence of those who have not received such a return, are presented as mutually surpassing one another through the comparison with rain-clouds and river-currents; this constitutes the figure of speech known as *pratyanīka* (the counter-argument).
"Rare," and so forth:
"Rare indeed are those who, like clouds, exist without expectation even after having performed a service;
they diminish in their absence, just like the rare currents of rivers."
"In this world, those who, having rendered assistance and performed a favor, remain indifferent— disregarding any return favor— are rare and few;
the meaning is that they are like clouds, which, having provided benefit, remain free from desire for any recompense."
In the absence of those benefactors, they become rare indeed; they wither and become sorrowful, just like river currents.
The meaning is that they become diminished in the absence of benefactors such as clouds, just as river currents are diminished when separated from their benefactors, the clouds.
The term "kṣīyante" (they perish) is used in the sense of the object acting as its own agent (*karmakartṛ*), because the root *kṣi* does not take the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) in that sense;
"depression" (*avasāda*) means sinking down or despondency.
The suffix *ghañ* is used here in the sense of the action itself (*bhāve*).
Here, between the cloud and the river-current, which are mutually capable, there is a state of opposition (*pratyanīkabhāva*), that is, antagonism (*pratipakṣatā*).
One whose army (*anīka*)—meaning a host (*sainya*)—acts as a counter-force (*pratinidhi*) is a "counter-array" (*pratyanīka*), that is, an adversary (*paripanthin*).
The author of the Medinīkośa states: "prati [is used] in the sense of a representative (pratinidhi) and a mark (cihna)," and "anīka [is used] in the sense of battle (raṇa) and an army (sainya).
An example of the application of the term *pratīka* is as follows:
"What need is there to speak of the aiming of arrows? By the sound of the bowstring alone, from afar, he dispels obstacles as if by the *huṃ* sound of the bow.

Here, having introduced the sound of the bowstring—which is a constituent part of the action characterized by the discharge of arrows and is capable of driving away obstacles—by means of the comparison "like the *huṃ* sound of the bow," the author expresses an *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration) known as *pratīkanyāsa*.
"What talk," and so forth;
what need is there to mention his fixing an arrow upon the bow— that is, his placing the arrow on the string— since by that alone all accomplishments are achieved?
For that king dispels and wards off obstacles from afar by the sound of his bowstring alone; by what kind of sound? By the sound of the bowstring, as if by the *huṃ* utterance of a bow.
The meaning is "by that which is equal to the *huṃ* sound of the bow.
In the word *dūrāt*, the suffix *tasi* is used in the sense of the ablative case (*pañcamī*).
[The word is] *vighnān*.

Although the word *vighna* is masculine according to Amara’s lexicon—given that "obstacle" (*vighna*), "impediment" (*antarāya*), and "hindrance" (*pratyūha*) are synonyms—nevertheless, because "gender is not prescribed [by grammar] since it depends on common usage," it may also be neuter.

For this very reason, even the usage in the *Raghuvamśa*, "May there be no obstacle for you; may you remain like a father at the head of those who have sons," should be read as "sa hi vighnānapohati" (for he dispels obstacles).
Here, because a portion of the bow is placed [in the hand] by means of the word "bowstring" (*jyā*), there is the figure of speech *pratīkanyāsa* (the placement of a representative part);
this constitutes the definition of the figure of speech *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration),
followed by the definition of the figure of speech *viśeṣa* (particularization).
He states the definition of *viśeṣokti* (peculiar assertion):
"Where there is an observation of the deficiency of qualities, genus, actions, and so forth, for the very purpose of showing a distinction, that is intended as *viśeṣokti*. (70)

In the case of that which is to be understood and that which is to be expressed, it [the cognition] also occurs in some instances even through the non-perception of a deficiency in the cause of the particularity; thus [it is said],
"by means of the quality."

Viśeṣokti (the description of distinction) is that which, for the purpose of showing excellence or superiority, presents a deficiency among qualities and so forth—that is, the designation of their "defectiveness.
The definition is: Viśeṣokti is the strengthening of the remaining qualities through the conceptualization of the loss of one quality.
Thus, by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the inclusion of genus (*jāti*) and other categories is intended, with substance (*dravya*) being included as well.
By the phrase "for the sake of perceiving excellence," its distinction from *vibhāvanā* (poetic fancy) is stated;
for in that [figure], no excellence is to be expressed, but rather another cause,
whereas here, through the negation of qualities and so forth, there is an excellence of the objects themselves.
He says that it occurs even when there is no observation of a deficiency in the qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth: "By way of deficiency"—that is, by a deficiency of qualities—as for example:
"The weapon of the Flower-Bowed One is neither hard nor sharp."
"Nevertheless, by him the three worlds were indeed conquered.

(165) Here, because the flower-bowed god conquers the three worlds with a weapon that is both sharp and yet not harsh, his extraordinary power is perceived. This is a *viśeṣokti* (poetic figure of specific assertion) in which a specific cause is implied, yet it is devoid of the [expected] quality, as indicated by the words "not harsh," and so forth.
The weapon of desire is neither hard nor sharp;
nevertheless, by this very desire—the one whose bow is flowers—the three worlds were indeed conquered. By this, its lack of hardness and lack of sharpness are demonstrated.
Since the flower itself does not exist,

this statement was made to demonstrate the deficiency of qualities such as hardness and the excellence of its victory; thus, this [example] possesses a deficiency of qualities due to a deficiency of the genus (*jāti*), as follows:
"She is neither a celestial maiden (devakanyā) nor born of the Gandharva race;
nevertheless, she is capable of disrupting even the penance of the Creator.

Here, despite the absence of being a celestial maiden, the description that "she is capable of disrupting even the Creator's penance" conveys the excellence of the beauty of the subject. This is the figure of speech *viśeṣokti* (causation by exclusion), characterized by a deficiency in genus (*jāti*), wherein the cause of a specific effect is implied.
"Not a goddess," and so forth:

she is neither a daughter of the gods nor born of the lineage of the Gandharvas; nevertheless, she is capable—indeed, able—to cause the interruption of the ascetic penance even of the Creator, Brahmā.
Here, there is a negation of her belonging to the classes such as "goddess" and so on, yet the distinction lies in her being human and thus performing that specific task.
By way of deficiency in action, for example:
“No frown was knit, nor did the lip quiver, nor did the gaze become blood-red, and yet the host of enemies was conquered. (167)

Here, even in the absence of frowning eyebrows and the like, the extraordinary majesty of the subject being described is perceived through this victory over enemies; this is "Poetic Exclusion" (*viśeṣokti*) characterized by a deficiency in action, wherein a specific cause is implied.

[The verse begins: "No frown was knit," and so forth—"no frown was knit, nor did the lower lip quiver, nor did the gaze become red and rolling; nevertheless, O Hero, the host of your enemies has been conquered by you."
Here, because of the prohibition of actions such as frowning, there is a deficiency of action;
however, the excellence consists in the victory over the enemy through mere play.
By the inclusion of the word "etcetera," there is also [an example of] deficiency of substance, as follows:
‘Neither chariots nor elephants, neither horses nor foot-soldiers—by the mere side-long glance of women, the three worlds are conquered.

Here, even in the absence of chariots and the like, the side-long glance of women is stated as the cause for the conquest of the three worlds; this is therefore a *viśeṣokti* (causal anomaly) characterized by a deficiency of substance (*dravya*), wherein a specific cause is asserted despite the absence of the expected means.
"There are no chariots," and so forth:

there are no chariots, nor elephants, nor horses, nor even foot-soldiers; nevertheless, by the mere side-long glances—the sidelong looks—of women, the three worlds are conquered. (For it is said: "The army consists of four components: elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry."
Thus says Amara;

therefore, here, due to the prohibition of the constituent parts of an army, there is a deficiency of substance (*dravya-vaikalya*). However, the excellence (*atiśaya*) lies in the conquest of the three worlds even in the absence of those [parts]; furthermore, this is another instance of *viśeṣokti* (poetic figure of specific mention), characterized by a partial deficiency due to the lack of even that substance.
The distinction is that the first [type of sacrifice] possesses a deficiency of the substance as a whole, whereas this one possesses a deficiency of only a portion of the substance;
for example, regarding the deficiency of the substance:
"The chariot has but one wheel, the driver is deficient, and the horses are uneven."
"Nevertheless, the radiant one, the Sun, traverses the three worlds.

(169) Here, although the substances such as the chariot and so forth are deficient—possessing only a single wheel and the like—the fact that the Lord Bhāskara traverses the three worlds is stated here to have "radiance" (*tejasvitā*) as its cause. This is another type of *viśeṣokti* (peculiar causation), called "deficiency of substances," wherein the cause of a specific [expected] result is stated.
It begins with the word "one" (*ekā*), etc.
The chariot has but one wheel; the driver, Anūru, is deficient, being devoid of feet; the horses are uneven in number, being seven. Nevertheless, the radiant Sun traverses the three worlds.

Regarding the prohibition in the maxim, "Seven horses and nine elephants," there is no contradiction here because in the phrase "he traverses" (*ākrāmati*), there is no upward movement (*udnamana*). Thus, the prefix *āṅ* [is used] in the sense of upward movement.
"3 40" means that here there is no deficiency in any part of the chariot and so forth; this is the second [verse].
Due to the presence or absence of substance, even when there is no deficiency [of other factors], this [figure] sometimes serves for distinction and sometimes for non-distinction, as in:
“This shoulder of hers was pressed against my shoulder by the jolting of the chariot;
in this body, one [shoulder] is fortunate, while the rest of the limbs are a burden to the earth. (170)

In this context, the distinction made—even though there is no physical deficiency—namely, "This shoulder has been touched by her; he is truly meritorious, while the rest of my body, untouched by her, is useless," constitutes the aforementioned *viśeṣokti* (poetic figure of specific exclusion), as it is characterized by a cause even when the cause is not explicitly stated. Furthermore, the comprehension of Urvaśī’s excellence in qualities and so forth derived from this sentence is an instance of *paryāyokta* (periphrasis), not *viśeṣokti*.
This refers to the passage beginning with "this," and so on.

"This shoulder, the base of the arm, was pressed by that woman with her own shoulder out of a desire for pleasure; thus, this one part of my body alone is successful and beautiful, while the rest of the body is a burden, a source of weight for the earth.
The word *śeṣa* is derived from the verbal root with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of the object (*karman*) and is used as an adjective agreeing in gender with its referent.
The connection between the words *aṅga* and *bhara* occurs through their non-abandonment of gender (*ajahalliṅgatayā*).
Even though there is here a perception of completeness (*avaikalyadarśana*), this is another type [of figure] because it is a statement of distinction (*viśeṣokti*).

He says—"But as for that which..."—to show that if, by this sentence, there is knowledge of Urvaśī’s possession of specific qualities, then because the aforementioned definition is absent, it is indeed *paryāyokti* (periphrasis).
Thus concludes the examination of the figure of speech Viśeṣa.
Now, the examination of the figure of speech Parikara begins by defining Parikara:

The wise call "parikara" (the poetic figure of circumstantial elaboration) the embellishment of the verb and other elements within the entities of action, agent, relation, the object to be accomplished, and the example.
[Verse 72] Regarding "action":

Action (*kriyā*) is the meaning of a verbal root; the factor of action (*kāraka*) is [the agent, object, etc., such as] the *karman*; the related (*saṃbandhī*) is that which possesses a relation; the goal (*sādhyam*) is that which is intended to be accomplished; the example (*dṛṣṭāntaḥ*) is an illustration; and the entity (*vastu*) is a category-meaning (*padārtha*).

Among these, "ornamentation" (*upaskāraḥ*), "embellishment" (*pariṣkāraḥ*), or "elaboration" (*parikaraḥ*)—namely, the expression of a substantive through an intentional adjective—is the definition of *parikara* (the elaborate ornament).

Among these, the "preparation for action" (*kriyāparikara*) is as follows: "Having communicated his resolve, he was embraced by Sugrīva, who felt joy at having obtained the Wind-god’s sister, while the bees on the lotus garland on Sugrīva’s chest were crushed against his breast. (171)
[He, whose purpose was announced by his resolve, was embraced by Sugrīva, who felt joy upon receiving confirmation from Hanumān, and whose chest was covered by forest garlands that crushed the bees.

Here, because the act of embracing is embellished by the phrases "who felt joy upon receiving confirmation from Hanumān" and "whose chest was covered by forest garlands that crushed the bees," this is *kriyā-parikara* (the poetic figure of the embellishment of an action).
"Having resolved," and so forth:

"He, whose purpose was announced by his resolve, was embraced by Sugrīva— who had attained joy through the arrival of the messenger from Māruta— and who crushed the bees upon the forest-garland on his chest."
"Here, Vibhīṣaṇa is embraced and clasped by Sugrīva;
he is one by whom the intended purpose of his resolve has been made known."
Alternatively, he by whom the matter—namely, the assistance to Rāma which had been resolved upon and intended—had been reported;

by Māruti Hanumān, who had gained confidence and attained trust, [he embraced] so as to bring joy. The two phrases "wherein the bees were crushed upon the forest garland on his chest" and "so that it should be thus" are two qualifiers of the act of embracing.
[Note: *Pratyaya* occurs in the sense of innate knowledge, trust, or causes of conduct.]
Thus says Medinīkāra.
Here, because the principal action is embellished by two adjectives, it constitutes "accessory to the action" (kriyāparikara).
An example of "accessory to the factor" (kārakaparikara) is as follows:
And Janakasuta fell, her cheeks pale from the slackening of the restraint of her hands, as she gasped for breath; her left breast was pushed aside, making her right breast rise unevenly. || 172 ||
[The daughter of Janaka has her right breast unevenly elevated as she pushes against her left.

Here, because the agentive word "Janakasutā" (the daughter of Janaka) is embellished by the phrases "with her cheeks pale from the loosening of the restraint on her hand" and "with her right breast unevenly elevated as she pushes against her left," this is *kārakaparikara* (the ornament of the agent),
as seen in the verse beginning with *paḍiāa*.
"And the daughter of Janaka has fallen, her cheeks pale from the slackening of her grasp, her left breast pressed down while her right breast rises unevenly. Here,
the daughter of Janaka is Sītā, and she has fallen.
The meaning of the word "ca" (and) is that she was not only fainted but also fallen;
what kind [of woman]?
She whose cheek, because the pressure or restraint upon it had been loosened by her hand, was therefore pale and swelling due to the release of the hand's squeeze.

Alternatively, she is one whose cheek is pale due to the pressure of being struck by the hand, yet it swells as that pressure is released; she is one whose right breast is uneven, tilted, and elevated because of her left breast being pushed against it— this movement or pushing of the left breast here indicates the removal of the imminent suffering caused by Rāma.

Alternatively, since a woman’s breast is on the left while a man’s is on the right, it was by that very fact that the word denoting the agent was refined here as the instrumental cause of the act of falling; an example of the "retinue of relations" (saṃbandhiparikara) is as follows:

‘The currents of the rivers, having been uprooted from the mountains, were broken; being lifted up, they flowed straight away; and as they were carried off, they departed along the mountain paths, free from silt. [173]
The river currents, set in motion along the path of the mountains being carried away, stretch out far into the distance.

Here, although the river flows are not the primary agents in the act of uprooting the mountains, they are embellished by their descriptive epithets; thus, this is the figure *saṃbandhiparikara*, as seen in the words "uprooted" (*ummūlitā*) and so forth.

“The river currents, having been uprooted by the mountains as they were being lifted up, became broken; as they were being moved straight away, they became withdrawn; and as they were being led along the mountain paths, they became elongated. Of what kind [of mountains] and of what kind [of currents] were these?

The embellishment (*pariṣkāra*) here is achieved through the qualifiers related to the river's current: "broken" by the shaking of uprooted trees; "drawn back" so as to be straight and not crooked when being lifted up; and "stretched out" and "crooked" due to the force of speed when being carried along—just as in the case of a "sādhya-parikara" (an embellishment of the subject to be proven).
“Despair takes away fortitude, the intoxication of youth takes away modesty, and the bodiless god of love takes away shame; what else, then, can the transformation of fate not destroy? (174)
"What disciplehood can one who has adopted an exclusive position expect, since it is the decline of age that establishes him [in such a state]?

Here, the absence of fortitude, modesty, and shame in one whose youth has passed is the thesis (*sādhya*), which is embellished by examples of despondency, the intoxication of youth, and the actions of the god of love; thus, this is an "ornament of the thesis" (*sādhyaparikara*), as seen in the verse beginning with *dhīram*.

“Despair robs one of fortitude; the intoxication of youth robs one of modesty or self-control; and the bodiless god of love, having taken his exclusive stand, robs one of shame. What remains for that which the maturity of age establishes?
Here, despair takes away fortitude; the intoxication of youth takes away modesty—that is, freedom from arrogance or self-mastery; and the bodiless god of love takes away shame.
The meaning is that he by whom a single side has been exclusively grasped is "adbhuta" (wondrous).

Alternatively, he is one who, within his own essential nature (*svarūpa*), has grasped the one [side], whose nature is the destroyer of all; what transformation remains that he might establish or stabilize? What is left over? The sense is that he takes away everything indeed.

In this context, the embellishment of the probandum by means of examples is the "ornamentation of the example" (*dṛṣṭāntaparikara*), as for instance: "The oceanic expanse, with its mountains situated in its midst, is being exhausted; yet it overflows."

The wheel [of the sun], with its rim loosened by the speed of the sun’s chariot, falls as if it were a mountain supporting the earth situated in its center, while the oceanic circle overflows and wastes away; it is like the tip of a fierce eye that has fallen. 175.

Here, the wheel of the sun’s chariot—which serves as an example for the inserted simile of Mount Mandara and the ocean—is embellished by the qualifier *utkaṭākṣakoṭi* (the tip of the fierce eye) in order to establish the similarity; thus, this is an *dṛṣṭāntaparikara* (ornament of the illustrative example).
[The verse beginning with] *majjhe* etc.:
“The mountain situated in the middle [of the ocean], and the overflowing circle of the ocean, are both diminishing.”
"The wheel of the tip of [Rāhu’s] fierce eye has fallen as if scattered by the speed of the sun's chariot;
here the circle of the ocean is also diminishing.
The word *ca* (and) is used here in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*) with respect to what precedes.
Of what sort was it?
It was where Mount Mandara, the upholder of the earth, stood as a central pivot;
for that very reason, the water had overflowed its bounds and surged upward.
According to Amara’s lexicon, “velā” refers to both the shore and the tide;
what kind of wheel was it, which fell immediately after being jolted by the speed of the sun’s chariot?

"Utkaṭā" means formidable; "akṣakoṭi" refers to the tip of the wheel (cakrāgra), as the *Viśvakośa* states: "The word *akṣa* is used for both a wheel and a die. Here, the illustration is refined with adjectives for the sake of establishing similarity.
An example of the *vastuparikara* (the surrounding context of the subject matter) is as follows:

"May that sound protect you—the sound produced by the collision of their aged, massive bones shattered by the mutual impact of their bodies, which arose when Cāmuṇḍā embraced Bhṛṅgiriṭi with uplifted arms, crying out in joy, 'The Goddess has given birth to a son! O Gaṇas, dance! Why do you stand still?'—a sound that surpassed the deep resonance of the drums of the gods. (176)

And here, because the sound produced from the bones of the hearts of Cāmuṇḍā and Bhṛṅgiriṭi as they collide in an embrace is taken as a concrete reality (vastu) and embellished by the words "The Goddess has given birth to a son" and so forth, this is *vastuparikara* (the poetic figure of the embellishment of a fact).
The phrase beginning with "The Goddess" means:
the Goddess Gaurī has given birth—she brought forth—a son.

Then, having said, "O Gaṇas, dance! Perform your dance! Why do you sit? when Bhṛṅgiriṭi—the Gaṇa named Bhṛṅgin—had his arms raised and was embraced by Cāmuṇḍā, may the sound of those two, Bhṛṅgiriṭi and Cāmuṇḍā, protect you; [the sound] of her by whom words were uttered out of joy, which were the very speech of Bhṛṅgiriṭi.
What kind of sound was it?
It was one whose origin and production arose from the decayed and cracked old thick bones due to their mutual contact;
it was one by which the flow of the dense resonance of the divine drum (devadundubhi), the celestial kettle-drum, was surpassed.
According to Amarasimha, "bherīmānakadundubhi" refers to a specific kind of sound;

here, that specific sound, having been grasped as a substantive entity, is embellished by its qualifiers. This embellishment may be effected through compounds (*samāsa*), as well as through primary suffixes (*kṛt*) and secondary suffixes (*taddhita*).
When it is qualified, they call that the supreme *kriyāparikara* (the embellishment of action).
Just as an action is qualified by means of a compound (*samāsa*), if it is likewise qualified by primary derivatives (*kṛt*) or secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), then it is indeed *kriyāparikara*.
In this regard, an example of [the locative case] used in the sense of "being for the sake of that" (tādarthya) is as follows:

“O Rādhā, you did not wish to leave the water of the Hārikā river when it came from your home; thinking ‘I shall bathe,’ you took refuge in the bower-vines on the banks of the Yamunā; being a cowherd’s daughter, you entered only the forests of Govardhana Hill. Yet, you have not fallen within the sight of the Son of Devakī. (177)

In this context, by rules such as *tumunṇvulau kriyāyāṃ kriyārthāyām* (Pāṇini 3.3.10), it is precisely the action (*kriyā*) that is qualified even when it serves as a secondary word (*upapada*); therefore, this constitutes another "accessory to action" (*kriyāparikara*).
In this same manner, the same should be understood regarding the marks (*lakṣaṇa*) and so forth, as well as the enemies (*śatru*) and so forth. Regarding the words "from the house" and so on:
O Rādhā, you have not fallen within the sight—that is, the eyes—of Kṛṣṇa, the son of Devakī.

Having gone from your home to the river to fetch water, you do not return; thinking, "I shall bathe," you take refuge in the bowers of creepers on the bank of the Yamunā. While acting as the one who binds the cows, you enter only the forests of Govardhana Hill.
*hārikeṃti*: from the root *hṛ* in the sense of "taking away" (*harane*), with the suffix *ṇvul* in the sense of the infinitive (*tumun*).
*Ājihīṣe*: from the root *hāṅ* in the sense of "going" (*gatau*), preceded by the prefix *āṅ*, in the second person singular (*madhyamapuruṣaikavacane*). [Śloka 6, Verse 1]
10. Thus, there is reduplication; [and by the rule] "of *mṛ* etc., *i*" (Pāṇini 7.2.4).

The form *maṅkṣyāmi* is derived from the root *masj* with the suffix *liṭ* (future) in the first person singular; the vowel *i* replaces the *ā* of the suffix by rule 75 (*ityākārasyettvam*), and after the addition of the augment *num* by the rule "the penultimate [vowel] of *masj* takes *num*" (*masjerantyātpūrva*) and the subsequent elision of the letter *n*, the form is established.
According to Amara, "latā," "pratāninī," and "vīrudh" all mean a creeper.
Regarding the term "gosaṃdāyī," *saṃdāna* means binding; it is commonly known as "chānda."
In this context, by means of kṛt suffixes such as *ṇvul*, the action is qualified as being "for that purpose" (*tādarthya*);
thus,
where [the rule] "in the sense of a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) or a cause (*hetu*)" [applies].
The suffix *śatṛ* is applied after the roots *indh* and *dāry* when the agent is one who experiences difficulty.
By this [verse] ending with "lakṣaṇādi-śatr-anta," the action (*kriyā*) is qualified; therein too, the "retinue of action" (*kriyā-parikara*) is to be observed, as for example:
"Having himself gone from the flower to his own tree, he has returned from the fruit," and so forth.

An example with an indeclinable (avyaya) is as follows: “As she playfully fastened a floral ear-ornament to him, its decoration consisting of clinging twigs, some lover pushed her full-breasted one away with his heavy hips, pressing against her breasts.”

In this case, [the phrase] "this [person] pushed him away while pressing against him with her breasts" is, by implication, merely an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*); thus, this too constitutes an *kriyāparikara*.
This should be understood to apply likewise in cases such as the "subsequent employment according to the rule" (*yathāvidhyanuprayoga*).
By this, it is also explained that in some cases, an action becomes suggested (*vyaṅgya*) through its connection with an internal qualifier; for instance,
in the passage beginning with *salīlam*, a certain hero was playfully nudged— that is, impelled— by his beloved with her hip.
Pressing her breasts with her own breasts,
how was he? He was broad-hipped, possessing shapely buttocks, and firm.
By what kind of beloved woman?
By one who, in a playful and graceful manner, was thus placing or fastening a flower-ornament upon him.
Of what sort was it?
That in which the creeper-ornament is attached— that is, bound—
is called *stanopapīḍam*, according to the rule: "And [the suffix *kha* is used] when there is an upapada in the locative case" (Pāṇini 3.4.48).
49. Thus, here the suffix *ṇamul*—being an indeclinable—is the *parikara* (ornamental elaboration) that qualifies the action of pushing.
Such is the case with *evam*.

For in that case, since the *loṭ* suffix and others follow from a particular verbal root (*dhātu*), the subsequent suffix likewise follows from that same root; thus, through their function as qualifiers of the action, they serve as a "parikara" (accessory).
As in the example:
"Those who have been killed lie down on the road, seated in the shade of trees by travelers; in the temples of Śrīkaṇṭha, the righteous people sit in the 'camel-posture' (*uṣṭrāsikā*)."
"O friend, at midday in the summer, in that empty bower of trees, this delightful moment has arrived for those prepared for the practice of meeting their lovers.

(179) In this context, by the two expressions "they sit in the manner of camels" (*uṣṭrāsikā āsyante*) and "they lie down in the manner of the slain" (*hataśāyikāḥ śayyante*), the essence of the state (*bhāvātmā*), which consists of both the general and the particular through metaphorical application, is conveyed by the suffix *ṇvul* itself:
in its general form by the verbal roots (*ākhyātābhyām*), and in its particular form by the two words ending in *ṇvul*.
The plural number here serves to express an excess of contempt;

for there are many kinds of "sitting" (*āsikā*) on the chests of camels that are full of contempt, and there are likewise many "lying down" (*śāyikā*) actions of those who have been slain that are characterized by an excess [of such contempt]. By means of these specific forms, this sitting and lying down—through the apprehension of both difference and non-difference produced by the relationship between the standard of comparison and the object compared—is conveyed by the verbal suffix (*lakāra*) itself as a plurality.

The meaning of the sentence is that "seats are made like dead camels" and "beds are made like those lying in death. This aforementioned *kriyāparikara* (poetic figure of circumstantial action) is exemplified by the phrase "they lie down," and so forth;
on the road, the beds are "made like those lying in death"—that is, they are used as beds by travelers sitting in the shade of trees, as if their sleeping were censured.
In the dwellings of Śrīkaṇṭha, pious ascetics sit like camels—that is, they remain seated just as a camel sits anywhere at all; this is the meaning.

O friend, there, beneath the trees of the bower in that secluded, solitary place, at the midday of summer, a delightful moment has arrived for the well-prepared women going to meet their lovers in the act of approaching their beloveds.

The word *śayyante* is derived from the root *śīṅ* (meaning "to sleep") with the suffix *yak* in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāve*), resulting in *śāyikā*. According to the rule "the suffix *ṇvul* should be stated when indicating the meaning of a verbal root," the suffix *ṇvul* is applied to the root *śīṅ*;
thus, *śāyikāḥ* means "beds" or "reclining places."
Śrīkaṇṭha is Śiva;
as Abhinavagupta states: “Śrīkaṇṭha, Śitikaṇṭha, the bearer of the skull. This is the conclusion.
Regarding the root *ās* in the sense of "sitting," it is stated that the suffix *ṇvul* should be prescribed; thus, *āsikāḥ* means "seats.
As for the word *sajjaḥ*, the author of the Medinīkośa states: "The word *sajjaḥ* is used in three genders in the senses of 'armed' and 'prepared'."

In this context, in order to demonstrate that one who has already lain down or is about to lie down should be prevented from pursuing [the lover], he states the opposite in the explanation. Regarding the phrase "here":

by means of these two sentences, which consist of the general and the particular—"they lie down" (*śayyante*) or "they sit" (*āsyante*) constitutes the general; "one who lies like a slain man" (*hataśāyikā*) and "one who sits like a camel" (*uṣṭrāsikā*) constitute the particular. He is one whose form or nature (*rūpa*) is fashioned or established (*uparacita*) by those two.

In this context, that which is signified or understood by the two verbal suffixes— as in "they sit" (*āsyaṃte*) or "they lie down" (*śayyaṃte*)— is what is meant by "dharma," namely, that which has existence as its essence and the nature of being.
"In a general form" means by way of a general aspect; that is to say, by means of the two words *uṣṭrāsikā* and *ahataśāyikā*, which end in the suffix *ṇvul*.
The meaning is that it is because both the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the qualified (*viśeṣya*) are stated.

If that were so, since the state (*bhāva*) is a single entity, there should be the singular number; how then can there be the plural number, as in "they lie down" (*śayyante*) or "they sit" (*āsyaṃte*)? To this he says: "the plural number."

The meaning is that the plural number is used because the general action is intended to convey the multiplicity inherent in the specific actions; the expression of censure is rooted in this intention. He states that very censure: "For that which... and so forth.
And thus, because of the connection with those specific qualities, there is multiplicity; this is precisely what he says: "by them" (tābhiḥ).

That [entity] in which non-difference is produced through the relationship between the standard of comparison and the object of comparison is [so called] because of the adoption of difference—that is, by virtue of prioritizing difference.
By means of the letter *la* as a nominal suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*),

he expresses the meaning denoted by the letter *la*; thus, in some cases, even an external element in the form of a *kṛt* suffix or having the nature of a *kṛt* meaning serves as an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*) of the action.
For example:

"A hundred times he was addressed with harsh words by my dear friend; a thousand times he was shaken off when falling at her feet; and how many times were frowns knit upon me here—I do not know—but even so, that audacious man does not cease for even a moment from tormenting me. (180)
In this context, the word *vāra* in the term *vārān* is a *kṛdanta* (a primary derivative);

according to the rule *vārasaṃkhyāyāḥ kṛtvasuc*, the suffix *kṛtvasuc* is applied. Both of these [the base *vāra* and the suffix *kṛtvasuc*] serve as qualifiers of the action (*kriyā*) by way of repetition (*āvṛtti*).

But if this is so, since words such as *uṣṭrāsika* ("sitting like a camel") and *vāra* ("turn") function as adverbs of action (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*), would they not also incur the neuter gender just like the accusative case—
as in the examples "he cooks softly" (*mṛdu pacati*) or "he recites excellently" (*praśastaṃ paṭhati*)?
To this it is replied:
Indeed, the qualifier of an action (kriyāviśeṣaṇa) is of three kinds: external, internal, and both external and internal.

Among these, the external consists of the form of the object (*karman*), such as "cow" (*vārā*); the internal consists of specific forms, such as "sitting like a camel" (*uṣṭrāsikā*); and the external-internal consists of qualities (*guṇa*), such as "softly" (*mṛdu*).

Among these, how could the external—qualifying the primary noun which remains unchanged in its own nature through metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*) due to the lack of a relation expressed by "this is that" (*so 'yam*)—ever abandon its own gender? Furthermore, how could the internal—having already adopted a specific gender and number because it does not grasp another particular—ever take on a different gender?

Since it is a quality (*guṇa*), although it lacks an external or internal gender marker, according to the rule "words denoting qualities take the gender of their substratum" (*guṇavacanānām āśrayato liṅgavacanāni*), it must adopt the gender of the substantive, such as "hundred" (*śata*) and so forth.
O dear friend, nevertheless, that audacious man, tormenting me, does not cease for even a moment; he does not become dispassionate.

Having been addressed in such a manner with harsh and cruel words a hundred times, he fell at his feet; and he was shaken and driven away a thousand times with kicks from the heels—that is, blows from the soles of the feet. In this matter, I do not know how many times—how many instances—the frowns were not restrained;
for the word *vārān* [is derived from] the root *vṛñ* in the sense of "choosing" (*varaṇe*), with the suffix *ghañ* in the abstract sense (*bhāve*).
Therefore, the expression "vārapada-āvṛtti" (repetition of the word *vāra*) inherently indicates how many times [it occurs], as in the statement by Abhinavagupta: "It is harsh, rough, and vulgar.
Here, the word *vāra* is a primary derivative (*kṛdanta*).
In the expression *kiyatkṛtvaḥ*, the suffix *-kṛtvasuc* denotes the number of times; thus, it is a *kṛt*-derived form (*kṛdartha*).

Since that which ends in a *kṛt* suffix and its meaning function as adverbs through the sense of repetition (*paunaḥpunya*)—that is, by way of recurrence—they serve as qualifiers of the action (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*). Furthermore, [in such cases] there is neuter gender, the status of being an object (*karman*), equality, and likewise singularity.

Having accepted the view of the learned— that "only an adverb is intended [to be neuter]"— with respect, he raises a doubt regarding the neuter gender of *uṣṭrāsikā* and other such terms with the words "But surely... (*nanu*),
and then provides the resolution with the words "in three ways" (*tridhā*).

Where there is a metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*) between the property (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*), the property, without abandoning its own nature, serves as the qualifier of the substratum—as in the case of "this is that" (*so'yam*) and so forth. However, when gender and number are construed according to their specific forms, how can another gender be grasped in cases such as *uṣṭrāsika* ("camel-sitting")? [The answer is: by the rule "the gender and number of quality-words depend on the substratum," words denoting qualities take the gender of the substantive they qualify.
The suffixes *taddhita* and *kṛtvasuc* have been explained; now those beginning with *thāl* are discussed—as in:
"The rows of deer, having begun to take no morsels of food, their eyes repeatedly hidden by fear, stood for a moment with their necks slightly turned."
These women gaze repeatedly at the sky with faces drenched in tears, so that the water from their wandering eyes falls as if from the tips of mountain peaks. (181)

Here, the first [type] qualifies [the action] along with a verbal adverb (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*)—namely *asakṛt* ("repeatedly") expressed by a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) meaning "many times," *paśyanti* ("they see") expressed by a verb, *valitagrīvam* ("with neck turned") expressed by a compound (*samāsa*), *kimapi* ("something") expressed by an indeclinable noun (*avyaya*), *sthitvā* ("having stood") expressed by a primary derivative (*kṛt*), and *muhuḥ* ("again and again") expressed by repetition (*vīpsā*) in the sense of a primary derivative. The second type, however, while connecting that same meaning through the action "falls" (*patati*) characterized by the present participle suffix (*śatṛ*) in the phrase "as the water from the eyes falls while wandering," becomes a qualifier of the very preceding action itself. Thus, although this retinue of actions consists of a combination of primary derivatives, secondary derivatives, compounds, and indeclinables, it is taught specifically by means of the secondary derivative because of the predominance of the terms *yathā* and *tathā*.
"Uncreated," and so forth:
these rows of deer likewise, in that manner, repeatedly and again and again gaze at the sky with faces whose eyes are filled with tears,
in such a way that the eye-water, as it whirls, falls from the tips of their horns.
Having done what?
Having stood with their mouths making no effort to take a morsel, while their necks were slightly turned and their throats were raised;
being of what sort [were they]?
Those whose eyes were motionless, being covered by fear—such women are referred to here as "tathā" (in that manner); the suffix *thāl* is used here in the sense of a mode (*prakāra*).
The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is that she qualifies [the subject] with this adverbial expression (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*) in relation to the action of "beholding" (*paśyantīti*).

In the word *asakṛt*, the suffix *suc* is applied by the rule *ekasya sakṛcca* (Pāṇini 5.4.19); there is the substitution of *sakṛt* [for *eka*] and the elision of the final consonant cluster (*saṃyogāntalopa*).

Therefore, the word *sakṛt* belongs to the section on secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), and subsequently there is a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*); [in the phrase] "where the neck has moved," it is a locative determinative compound (*bahuvrīhi*).
The *kṛt* suffix *ktvā* [is used] after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) [ending in] the word "muhur" by way of its name.

Regarding the phrase "staying again and again" (*vāraṃvāraṃ sthitvā*), the meaning is that since the repetition (*vīpsā*) applies specifically to the act of staying occurring at the prior time, the repetition must indeed apply to the meaning of the *kṛt* suffix.
Regarding the second [example],
"yathā," it refers to the suffix *thāl*.

Connecting and establishing that very same meaning in its various forms, [the word] becomes an adjective of the primary action (*pradhānakriyā*)—namely, the act of seeing (*paśyantīti*)—which constitutes the preceding action.

Thus, if the *taddhita* suffix is expressed by means of the location characterized as "repeatedly" (*vāraṃvāra*) and so forth, which is denoted by the suffix *kṛtvasuc*, then the *taddhita* comes to have the sense of repetition; in that case, this is a variety of "parikara" (poetic embellishment) consisting of a conjunction (*saṃnipāta*), meaning a state of syntactic connection (*samanvaya*), among the *kṛt* suffixes and others.
By this, the opposite case—that is, the connection with an adjective—is also explained.
For example:
“Just as the night draws to a close, the orb of the moon trembles like the heart of the ocean, which is bewildered as to what it should do and reflects the images of its trembling waves. (182)
"Just as the night comes to an end, so too does the moon's orb— resembling a trembling wave fallen [into the sea], bewildered as to what it should do— tremble like the heart of the ocean.
Here, in addition to being adverbs of manner (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*), the words "yathā" and "tathā" also function as the distributive repetition (*vīpsā*) of that manner.
This preparatory ritual action (*kriyāparikara*) of such a kind is to be understood as follows:
"Just as, just as the night comes to an end, so too [the moon] falls upon the reflection in the trembling waves," and so forth.
"My heart trembles like the moon's reflection in the ocean, bewildered as to what ought to be done;
for here, as the night comes to its end, it reaches its own conclusion through the reflexive passive construction (*karmakartari*)."
In such and such a manner, the lunar orb whirls;
of what sort is it, fallen as a reflection— that is, a reflected image— upon the trembling wave?
"Perplexed as to what should be done here"— the word *iva* (like) expresses a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*), comparing the bewildered and deluded heart of the ocean;
note here the reversal of the positions of the pronouns *tat* and *yat*.
When it ought to be said that "the night is ending as the moon's orb wavers," saying the opposite of what was stated constitutes the application of a qualifier;
this occurs when there is a connection with another adverbial modifier (kriyāviśeṣaṇa) characterized by repetition (vīpsā). Some maintain that even a vocative may be considered an adverbial modifier.
Indication (*lakṣaṇā*) and the other [figures] are indicated by words that are themselves related [to them].
Among these, the introduction of the vocative is as follows:
"O Bhāgīrathī, daughter of Jahnu, wife of the ocean, crest-garland of the Lord of Gaurī, and victory-banner of the festival of Dharma—I implore you."
‘...my life-breaths shall depart as I sit upon a stone within your waters, swaying upon your waves, remembering your name, with my gaze fixed upon you.
Here, the vocative term ‘O Bhāgīrathī’ is embellished by such phrases as ‘the victory banner of the festival of Dharma’;
since any meaning expressed there—even in this manner—does not transcend the status of being an adverbial adjunct to the action, this too is *kriyāparikara* (the embellishment of the action).
"Of Dharma," and so forth:
