Regarding the phrase "by the mine of faults, moving along the path of the stars":

for when one who possesses excessive faults is connected with a king—who is himself a mine of faults and a traveler upon the royal highway—he necessarily causes displeasure and indeed brings harm. Thus, in this context, while the primary meaning belongs to the subject matter at hand (*prakaraṇa*), a second, non-contextual meaning is joined through the differentiation of words; this attains the designation of *bhinnapadaśleṣa* (compound-phrase punning), as seen in the passage beginning with "doṣa" and so forth.
Does that wicked person—whose very nature is to cause harm—not afflict me? Indeed, he does afflict me; for what [harm] could be more disagreeable to him than that which is detested by him?
Of what sort?
One who is connecting—or uniting—himself with the king, the sovereign, in the manner thus being experienced;
the word "himself" (ātmānam) is to be supplied as the object.
In this case, the treatment as if it were an object (*karmavadbhāva*) is not applied because it is connected [to the verb] by way of its meaning;
[the question is] "by what kind of king?"—
by one who is a mine, that is, a locus, of faults, which are corruptions.

The path of the *kṣatra* is the way of the *kṣatriya*; he whose nature it is to abide therein—though there is a subsequent connection with the letter *na* (i.e., "not")—the meaning is: by one who is devoid of the duty (*dharma*) of a *kṣatriya*.
Does the evening—the onset of night—not afflict me, who am separated from my beloved and find it disagreeable? Indeed, it does afflict me;
for what kind of evening is this, being thus joined with the moon, the king?
By what kind of moon,
the maker of night and the source of darkness,
which is by nature situated within the path of the stars— that sky?
In this instance, the word *rāja* (king) is non-different [from its other meanings], while the remaining words are different; thus, it is a "compound-word pun" (*padabhinnaśleṣa*).
An example of a "non-compound-word pun" (*abhinnapada*) is as follows:

‘This radiant king, with his red orb, has ascended the mountain of sunrise; he captivates the hearts of the world with his gentle rays. (227) Here, by stating that this rising moon captivates the heart of the world, the author provides the underlying rationale: [the moon] is a king whose circle is devoted, who rises, whose rays are soft, and who is full of splendor.
For a king who is thus constituted necessarily becomes one who captivates the hearts of the world.

Here too, in the contextual meaning (*prākaraṇika-artha*), the non-contextual (*aprākaraṇika*) element being joined [with it] constitutes a "fusion of words" (*padabhinna-śleṣa*) through the non-differentiation of the words, beginning with the word *asau* and so forth.
That king, the ruler, captivates the hearts of the people with taxes that are mild and non-oppressive;
what kind of man is he?
He is one who has attained and reached an upward course of prosperity.
He who possesses beauty and is endowed with splendor,
whose circle— the region— is red and devoted;
in the other sense, this king, who is like the moon, captivates and wins over the hearts of the people with his soft and cool rays.
Of what kind was he as he reached the mountain of sunrise—
radiant, endowed with brilliance, with a crimson orb and a red disk?
According to the *Viśva* lexicon, "udaya" means both "rising" and "the mountain of sunrise," and according to another source, "maṇḍala" refers to both a "disc" and a "region.
Here, because the words such as "king" (*rāja*) and so forth function through non-difference [of meaning], this is an instance of *abhinnapada-śleṣa* (punning on identical words).
An example of a split action (bhinnakriya) is as follows:
“The sweet, passion-increasing, soft, and honeyed songs of the cuckoos are heard, and the dark-eyed women are embraced. (228)

In this context, the two verbal actions expressed by the pair of verbs “are heard” (*ākarṇyante*) and “are embraced” (*śliṣyante*), which are presented primarily as a conjunction, are connected respectively through the synonymous application of the punning words beginning with “sweet” (*madhurā-*), with the exception of the single substantive word—namely, either “the notes of the cuckoo” (*kokilāgiraḥ*) or “the dark-eyed women” (*asitekṣaṇāḥ*).
For example: which [things] are heard?
Of what nature are the cuckoo’s notes?
They are sweet, increasing passion, and tender.
Furthermore, what were they like?
They were those whose eyes were fixed—meaning seated and rendered motionless—due to the internal experience of joy;
for indeed, everyone who hears a sweet sound becomes one whose gaze is fixed.
And which dark-eyed women with gazes like those of deer are embracing him?
Of what nature are they? They are intoxicated with passion (*madakala*), possessing the voice of the cuckoo, tender, increasing passion (*rāgavardhinī*), and sweet.

Thus, this is called "śleṣa with different actions" (*bhinnakriya-śleṣa*), which is the conjunction of formal objects (*rūpiṇāṃ padārthānām*) belonging to two different actions and having different meanings.
Sweet [songs] such as these are heard from the voices of cuckoos, and dark-eyed beloveds with black eyes embrace their lovers; what kind of women are they?
They were sweet, pleasant to the ear, charming, increasing passion, generating affection, and producing delight;
they were tender, lovely, and possessed of delicate limbs.

Those women are sweet with the intoxication produced by youth, springtime, and so forth; they are also endowed with sweet, melodious voices (*kaladhvani*) due to their intoxication (*mada*), which here refers to the exhilaration of wine.
Having been seated (*āsita*)—that is, made to sit and rendered motionless—their eyes are fixed because of their experience of internal joy. Hearing their sweet sound, one becomes motionless-eyed.
In one sense, they are dark-eyed women;
in another, they are those whose voices are like the songs of cuckoos.
In this context, due to a difference in action, there is a difference in the action of the other words; whereas for those that are non-different, there is the capacity to convey two meanings.
An example of non-different action is as follows:
"Sweet by nature, affectionate, and proclaiming intense passion..."
“Gazes and female messengers, sent by beloved women, draw their lovers [toward them].

(229) Here, because the words *dṛśām* (gazes) and *dūtīnām* (messengers) are applied to the action expressed by the verb *karṣanti* (they draw), there is this specific type of paronomasia (*śleṣa*) called “the identity of action” (*abhinnakriya*).
If one asks: what is the distinction between this and the first two types?
In that case, there is the status of being the primary subject for only one [of two things], whereas here it belongs to both; furthermore,
this [type of comparison] may also have different agents,
as in the verse beginning with "svabhāva" (intrinsic nature).
The glances sent by beloved women act as messengers, drawing their dear lovers toward them; what kind of glances? Sweet and graceful by their very nature and innate disposition.

Thus it is stated in the *Matsaṃgītasarvasva*: "The gaze that is sweet, with its corners contracted, accompanied by a movement of the eyebrows and a smile, and possessing the transformations of passion— that is considered the *lalitā* (graceful) glance."
Glossy and full of luster,
they proclaim an intense, excessive redness;
alternatively, they are naturally sweet.
Or rather, those who are naturally affectionate, tender, and like unto themselves,
who proclaim an excessive passion caused by the effects of wine, or who speak of passion— that is, deep attachment.
In this case, since the single action consisting of "attracting the beloved" is common [to both], there is the state of being a single action (*ekakriyatva*).

He asks what the difference is between this [type of *tulyayogitā*] and that which is expressed by distinct words or non-distinct words: "of the first two," where the word "vā" has the sense of "and" (*ca*).
The answer is as follows:
the meaning is that while in those [previous cases] only one of the two was introduced by the context (*prakaraṇa*), here both are seen to be introduced by the context; this is the distinction.
Furthermore, because it has multiple authors, he states "this" to show that it is also an example of different grammatical agents (*bhinnakāraka*).
An example of a dissimilar agent (*bhinnakāraka*) is as follows:
"Her gait and braid attained equality with the female elephant; her body and thighs with the plantain tree; and her lips and hands with young sprouts. (230)

In this regard, according to one interpretation, because of the metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*) of the property (*dharma*) with the substratum (*dharmī*), the word "gait" (*gati*) is understood [to refer to both gait and the elephant]. Therein, the similarity between the gait and the *veṇī* (tresses) on the one hand, and the *nāga* (elephant) and *ahi* (serpent) on the other; the similarity between the body and the thighs on the one hand, and the *rambhā* (plantain tree) and the *apsarases* on the other; and the similarity between the lips and hands on the one hand, and the *pravāla* (coral), *vidruma* (red coral), and fresh sprouts on the other—these are obtained for the two subjects to be described through the power of *śleṣa* (punning). This is called *bhinna-kāraka* (different-case) *śleṣa*, because it possesses multiple agents (referents), as in the case of the word "gait" and so forth.

The gait—the movement—of that heroine and her braid—the arrangement of hair—were like a *nāga*, both an elephant and a serpent; her body and her two thighs were like a *rambhā*, both a specific type of *apsaras* and a plantain tree; and her hands and lips attained equality with *pravālas*, both coral and young shoots.
As the lexicon of Śāśvata states: "The word *nāga* refers to an elephant and a snake," and "The word *rambhā* refers to an *apsaras* and a plantain tree."
The *Dharaṇi* lexicon states: "The word *pravāla* refers to both a sprout (*pallava*) and coral (*vidruma*).
He says this because of the diversity of its applications;
here, due to having different agents (*kartṛ*), there is a difference in the grammatical factors (*kāraka*).
An example of non-differentiation (abhinnakāraka) is as follows:
“O sweet-voiced one, whose eye—even though devoted to Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna—is yet hanging from Karṇa; how can it be trusted by anyone? (231)
Regarding the statement here, "O sweet-voiced one, whose gaze can be trusted by you?", he provides the reasoning: "Though attached to Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna, she hangs upon Karṇa.

For how could she who is devoted to Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna be one who sides with Karṇa? And who would trust her who is thus divided between both? Furthermore, because they share a single agent, this is a *śleṣa* (paronomasia), as in the phrase "Kṛṣṇa," and so forth. In this case, the words function as non-different grammatical factors (*abhinnakāraka*).
O sweet-spoken one of charming speech, to whom does your gaze convey trustworthiness—that is, become an object of confidence? To no one at all.
The reason for this is that it is dark (kṛṣṇā) and white (arjunā), and reddened at the corners (anuraktā); such is the sequence of its parts.

And she who reaches as far as Karna’s ear, being devoted and full of affection toward Hari on the side of Krishna, yet also partial toward Arjuna Pārtha—that woman, belonging to two opposing sides, how can she be trustworthy?
(According to Amara: *valakṣa* means white, bright, or Arjuna.)

Here, the definition of the figure of speech *śleṣa* (paronomasia) is given as "the state of having non-distinct grammatical factors due to the oneness of the agent," followed by the definition of the figure of speech *bhāvika*.

He states the definition of *bhāvanā* (poetic realization): "The expression of one's own intention, or else the cultivation of another [emotion], or the indication of something else—these they know as the threefold *bhāvika*. (86)
And in our view, there exists no [such] distinction from the perspective of reality;
nevertheless, that [distinction] is said to be threefold, designated as manifest, unmanifest, and both.
(87) "Sva" and so forth...
The expression of one's own intention, the expression of another's intention, and the description of something else are *bhāvika*;
since it arises from the *bhāva*—the poet’s intention—it is appropriately named *bhāvika*.
By the word "regarded" (*mata*), he states the non-difference between *udbheda* (manifestation) and *bhāvika*.
That disclosure (*udbheda*) also consists, among the various types of *bhāvika*, in the expression of one's own intention—as for example:
"She is not abandoned when he is seen; where there is no frown, there is no grasping at the state of being addressed."

Tell me of that pride, O friend, if you wish for my life to continue— [that pride] where a frown is not assumed when looked upon, where no retort is seized when addressed, and where one is neither agitated nor censured when seen by a companion. (232)

In this context, because the intention consisting of the communication of what is undesirable—namely, the knitting of the brows, the refusal to speak, and the casting away of the beloved—is expressed, this is the *bhāvika* known as "the expression of one's own intention.
[The verse beginning with] *ṇāvajjai* etc. means:
"He is not bound by a frown when he is seen, nor is his speech grasped when he is speaking."

"Tell me that pride, if you wish for my life, wherein I am not disturbed when being acted out by my friend. "In this world, tell me that pride, if you wish for my life, wherein, when it is seen, a frown cannot be fixed and is not bound on all sides; wherein, when it is spoken, no reply is grasped; and wherein, when it is being enacted by my friend, I am not disturbed."
In this context, the expression of an unintended meaning is *anyabhāvanā*, as for example:
“[A rope] strong in appearance, firm, binding, long, and well-rounded...”
"In the home of fortunate women, there is a pestle that is bitten by gnats, firm, well-fastened, long, and well-proportioned. (233)

In this context, since the penis has been described as having the form of a pestle through the process of visualization (*bhāvanā*), this subsequent description of other visualizations—beginning with *daṃsaṇa* and so forth—is figurative (*bhāvika*). It states:
"By the bite, it is coiled, firm, well-fastened, long, and well-proportioned."
"In the house of fortunate women, the pestle is under their own control.
In this world, such a pestle as this comes under the personal command of excellent women;
of what sort is it?
In the context of biting, such as the crushing of grain and so forth, *valitam* means "clung" or "stuck";
*dṛḍhakam* means "firm," with the suffix *-kan* added in its own sense (*svārthe*).
"Free from bonds," "long," "well-rounded," and "very thick"—
these [qualities] apply to the penis (*meḍhra*) when it comes to biting and crushing the vulva (*bhaga*). "Wrinkled," "tied," "firm," "free from bonds," "long," and "very thick"—
here, because of the mention of the pestle (*musala*), there is a meditation on something other than the penis.
An example of *anyāpadeśa* (indirect expression) is as follows: “Having eaten with another, take only as much as you need;
O bull, desist now, for the householder’s field is being guarded. (234)
"As long as it was tasted by one who did not know better, so much has been the end of the rice; now, O bull, the householder’s field is being guarded.

Here, under the pretext of warding off a gluttonous bull from another's field, a lover whose identity has long been recognized is turned away; this is the figure of speech called *bhāvika* (the suggestive), specifically known as *anyāpadeśa* (indirect designation).
"Having tasted," and so forth:
"As long as you have tasted [the field] while remaining unrecognized, for that very reason maintain your resolve;
O bull, cease now, having protected the householder's field."
"O bull, having guarded the householder's field here, you may now rest and play;
bind your contentment with only as much as has been tasted by you while remaining unrecognized.
Here, under the pretext of restraining the bull, the warding off of a paramour is expressed through an indirect reference.
An example of what is manifest in the *udbhedas* (emergences) is as follows:

“O Lord of the Gods, honor the world of Jāyā; you who bestow upon the world the nectar of the moon, you who restrain the jewel-tree of the gods, and you who possess a splendor charming to the simple-minded. (235)
"O Manu, you bestow upon me the friendship of Madhumathan; O Lord of the Thirty-three, grant me the jewel of your feet.
Cast aside your deluded nature, O Lord of the Gods, and honor the sight of the Yadavas.
Here, the intention of the deceitful Mahendra has been clearly disclosed by Satyaka; thus, this is a "manifest disclosure" (*vyakta-udbheda*).
He spoke, beginning with the words:
"O Lord of the Thirty-three, you who grant the boon of Madhumathan; bestow upon me this jewel of a foot.
O Lord of the Gods, favor the world of the Yādavas, for they are of a simple nature."
"O Indra, Lord of the Gods, if you acknowledge— that is, accept— the affection and love of Kṛṣṇa, the subduer of Madhu,
then when he offers you the jewel of a tree, the Pārijāta, abandon your foolish nature— cast off your delusion—
and honor and gladden the world of the Yādavas."
In this context, the intention of Indra was made manifest and revealed by his charioteer Satyaka;
it was previously unmanifest, as follows:

"The sandal-paste has completely slipped from the slope of your breasts, the redness is wiped away from your lower lip, your eyes are entirely devoid of collyrium, and this slender body of yours is covered in horripilation."

"O messenger who speaks falsely, you have gone from here to the pond to bathe, not to that base man—since your kinsmen do not know how you suffer. Here, although the messenger's misconduct is revealed by the contextual example "you have gone from here to the pond to bathe, not to that base man," which functions as an *ākṣepa* (objection/paralipsis), it is nonetheless not as explicit as in the previous case; thus, this is an "unmanifest" (*avyakta*) disclosure (*udbheda*).
[This begins with] "niḥśeṣa... and so forth.
"O messenger, you went from this place to bathe in the pond or lotus-pool,
but you did not go to that lowest of men; O speaker of falsehoods, O you who do not know the onset of suffering for those who are dear to you!"
He describes the signs of bathing: "The slope of your breasts has its sandalwood paste completely washed away; your lower lip too has lost its redness;
and your eyes are utterly devoid of collyrium."
Likewise, this slender and emaciated body of yours is covered in horripilation;

here, by the presentation of identical signs of both bathing and sexual union, the mischievous conduct of the female messenger (*dūtī*), which was implied by the context, is revealed, yet its explicitness is not as it was previously described— that is,
of a dual nature— as in the following example:

"O friend, your eyes, as delicate as unfading blue lotuses, are adorned with black collyrium; the paleness upon your cheeks is enhanced by the application of camphor; and let your sighs arise from the whirling of the ball—yet who indeed does not perceive this intense emaciation of your limbs caused by the power of love? (237)

In this context, regarding the application of blue collyrium and other cosmetics by Avinayavatī to conceal the signs of longing—namely, the fading of her eyes, the paleness of her cheeks, and the lengthening of her sighs—even though she consents to them, there is the speech of her friend: “Who indeed would not perceive this intense emaciation of her limbs? By this, her intention becomes both revealed and unrevealed; thus, this is a twofold manifestation (*udbheda*).
These three types of manifestation do not differ from *bhāvika* (the state of being), as seen in the verse beginning with "amlāna" and so forth.
But, O friend, who indeed does not perceive this formidable leanness—the thinness—of your limbs?
For although your two eyes are unfaded, free from pallor, they appear as if newly arisen, tender and beautiful; how so? [They are] such that...
Since [her face] is adorned with blue collyrium,
let the paleness— the whiteness— on the surface of her cheeks be blended by contact with the scattering of camphor;
and let her breaths be born from that very whirling, the circular motion for the sake of playing with a ball.
Of what kind of limbs?
Of those whose nature it is to bear—that is, to carry—the radiance and brilliance of serpents;
the meaning is: those which are lovely by their very nature.
In this case, regarding the unrefined and untrue [speech] of Avinayavatī,
her intention is both partially revealed and partially unrevealed; thus, it possesses a dual nature.
Thus concludes the definition of the figure of speech *bhāvika*.
Now follows the definition of the figure of speech *saṃsṛṣṭi* (conjunction); he states its definition:

The "commingling" (*saṃsṛṣṭi*) should be understood as the blending of various ornaments; it is threefold: manifest (*vyaktā*), unmanifest (*avyaktā*), and both manifest and unmanifest (*vyaktāvyaktā*).
The manifest is like sesame and rice grains, while the other is like a shadow and a mirror.
That [mixture] is unmanifest like milk and water, or like dust and water;
it is considered manifest-unmanifest when combined like a man-lion, and like a variegated color when there is a blending of various ornaments in another [context]. (89–90)
"Commixture" (*saṃsṛṣṭi*) refers to the blending (*saṃkara*) of various figures of speech; it is also called "shading" (*chāyā*).
The meaning is "like a reflection in a mirror";
*kṣīram* means milk,
and *pāṃsuḥ* means dust.
"Citra" means like the colors painted in a picture; "vyakta" means like sesame seeds and rice grains. As it is said:
"The ocean, as if grinding camphor-fragrant sandalwood with the tips of its waves, takes it up and, with its rays, the moon seems to smear it upon the women that are the quarters.
Here, two types of poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) and two types of metaphor (*rūpaka*) are intermingled like sesame seeds and rice grains.

"He grinds," and so forth: the ocean, with the tips of its waves, seems to grind sandalwood-foam; the moon, having taken that up with its rays, seems to smear it upon the women who are the quarters of the sky.
Here, by means of the two words "iva" (as if), there is a pair of *utprekṣā*s (poetic conceits)— namely,
"the foam itself is sandalwood" and "the quarters themselves are women"— and this constitutes a pair of *rūpaka*s (metaphors);
thus, these are mixed together like sesame seeds and rice grains.

Just as there is a mutual commingling of sesame seeds and rice grains even though they are independent of one another, so too here the manifestation is quite evident, like a reflection in a mirror— as it is said:
"The cloudless sky shone with the moon, and the lake gleamed with blooming lotuses."
"But both brothers, their eyes filled with tears, grew faint.

Here, in this mirror-like example of the figure of speech *hetu* (causation), through the comparison of the faces of Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa to the moon and the lotus, a *vyatireka* (distinction) between the similar and the dissimilar is observed,
beginning with the word "nirmala" (spotless).
This [verse] is explained under the figure of speech *vyatireka* (distinction).
Here, since the figure of *hetu* (cause) has been shown by the first half-verse, the *vyatireka* between the similar and the dissimilar is based precisely upon that;
and it is established in the relation of locus and located (*ādhārādheya-bhāva*), like a reflection in a mirror.

The unmanifest [nature] is like milk and water—as it is said: “The splendor of spring appeared like the moon washed in milk, like a blue garment cleansed of indigo, and like the sun scraped by a chisel. (240)
In this regard, I offer a simile and a poetic fancy: just as when milk and water are mixed and blended together, they are not distinguished as "milk" and so forth,
so too was the splendor and beauty of spring perceived by the people.
What kind [of night] is it? It is that in which the moon has been washed with milk,
and that in which the garment— the sky— has been cleansed by being washed with indigo dye.

In this verse, there is a lack of clarity due to the mutual blending of simile (*upamā*) and poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*). [The compound] *ṭaṅka-ullikhita-sūryā* means "that in which the sun has been scratched or torn away by a chisel (*ṭaṅka*), which is a stone-cutter. As Amara states: "*ṭaṅkaḥ pāṣāṇadāraṇaḥ*" (a chisel is a stone-cutter).
This should be understood as follows: because the manifestor of both [meanings] functions with equal status, it remains unmanifest, like dust and water—as in the verse:
"Though her gaze was attached to Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna, it hung upon Karṇa."
"Whom can you, O sweet-voiced one, inspire with confidence? (241).

Here, in the *vyājastuti* (feigned praise), the subordinate relationship (*aṅgabhāva*) of the two [conflicting elements], namely *śleṣa* (paronomasia) and *virodha* (contradiction), which remain unmanifest—just as dust and water [are mixed] in a lump of clay—is understood from the words "O Kṛṣṇa," and so forth.
This has been explained under the figure of speech *bhāvika*;

here, just as there is indistinctness in a lump of clay due to the mutual blending of dust and water, so too, in the context of *vyājastuti* (ironical praise), there is a commingling (*saṃkara*) of *śleṣa* (paronomasia) and *virodha* (contradiction),
which is both distinct and indistinct, like the form of Narasimha.
"Making the sky appear like the surface of the earth with the dust kicked up by horses and the elephants resembling clouds, and making the surface of the earth appear like the sky...

(242). Here, within the Narasimha incarnation, the relationship between the lion and human portions of the body—functioning as the *parivṛtti* (exchange) figure, the *hetūpamā* (causal simile), and the *aṅga* (subordinate) elements—is perceived as manifesting in both manifest and unmanifest forms.
"By the dust," and so forth:
of what sort was he?

Making the sky like the surface of the earth by means of the cloud-like dust kicked up by the hooves of horses, and making the surface of the earth like the vault of the sky by means of the elephants.

In this regard, just as in the *narasiṃha* (man-lion) species there is a manifestation of both manifest and unmanifest forms in the respective parts of the lion and the man, so too in the figure of speech *parivṛtti* (exchange), the status of the cause (*hetu*) and the simile (*upamā*) as constituent parts exists in a manifest-unmanifest form. This manifest-unmanifest nature is like a variegated color; for example: "May the rainy season, resonant with the cries of peacocks and possessing lightning-garlands..."

"Having crossed as it were a great forest, the clouds released their waters. (243) Here, in the figure of *samādhi* (accomplishment), which rests upon the sentence describing autumn, there is perceived a relationship of primary and subordinate elements (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*)—both manifest and unmanifest—among the *śleṣa*, *rūpaka*, *upamā*, and *arthaleṣa*, which respectively rely on words, word-meanings, and the sentence; this is just as the colors blue and so forth, residing in the parts of a cloth, [contribute] to the variegated color (*citravarṇa*) residing in the whole cloth, as in the verse beginning with "mayūra... and so on.
The clouds released their waters upon the great wilderness,
as if it were a vast forest, having passed through the rainy season of the monsoon.
Resounding with the cries of peacocks, she stands there like a creeper accompanied by lightning.

Just as in the case of a variegated color residing in a whole (the *avayavin*) which is based on its parts such as blue and so forth, there exists a relationship of primary and subordinate (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*); likewise, in the figure of speech *samādhi*, a relationship of primary and subordinate—manifesting in both distinct and indistinct forms—is perceived among figures such as *śleṣa*.
Thus, these twenty-four [figures] are, in their respective order, dependent upon both [sound and sense].
The poetic ornaments, beginning with simile (*upamā*), have been explained as they truly are.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Analysis of Both Types of Ornaments," in the *Sarasvatīkaṇṭhābharaṇa* composed by the illustrious Mahārājādhirāja Śrī Bhojadeva.
The total number is twenty-four.
The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "In this manner, these twenty-four figures of speech, beginning with simile (*upamā*), have been described.
Here, the term *ubhaya* retains its original gender (*ajahalliṅgatā*).
The meaning is that they are dependent upon words and their meanings.

A jewel was born as the bearer of jewels, the foremost among the virtuous and faultless; she, the pure Damayantī, also gave birth to this son who is a master of logic (naiyāyika). In the commentary adorned by the multitude of the poetic speech of that author Śrīśa Jagaddhara, the fourth chapter, titled "The Illumination of Both," has come to an end.
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the *Sarasvatīkaṇṭhābharaṇavivaraṇa* composed by the Great Professor and Judicial Authority Śrī Jagaddhara.
The fifth chapter:
Rasa is pride, it is egoism; it is celebrated as the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*).
That meaning, through its presence, causes poetry to attain loveliness.
Born from a particular unseen merit within the inner selves of living beings, it shines forth as the sole cause for the manifestation of the soul’s own true qualities.

If the poet is possessed of the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra), the world becomes composed of aesthetic flavor (rasa) within his poetry; yet if he is devoid of that sentiment, all of it becomes flavorless.
Indeed, in the mere sentence "he sees a woman," no aesthetic flavor manifests.
"It is clearly understood that she gazes at her beloved.
(4) "O maiden, why do you not desire me who desires you?"—this meaning, being vulgar in nature, leads only to a lack of aesthetic flavor. (5)
"O fair-eyed one, let it be that the outcaste Kandarpa is merciless toward me;
by good fortune, he is free from malice toward you"—such is a refined meaning that conveys aesthetic flavor (rasa).
A new meaning, elegant expression, non-vulgar diction, a melodious composition, and clear phonetic texture [are the qualities of poetry].
Both extraordinary meaning and logical reasoning are capable of bringing forth aesthetic flavor (rasa).
The entire domain of speech consists of figurative expression (vakrokti), expression of rasa (rasokti), and expression of natural state (svabhāvokti);
among these, they recognize the expression of rasa as that which captures everything.
Existence, birth, continuity, accomplishment, nourishment, and mixture;
diminution, appearance, tranquility, remainder, distinction, and that which possesses a remainder; separation, and then union—these are its activities and their investigations.
Etymologies, miscellaneous topics, the measures [of love], and the nourishment of love;
the qualities of heroines and heroes, the stages of love such as *pāka*, and the modes of expressing rasa through the combination of various ornaments. || 10-11 ||
Thus, the twenty-four manifestations of the aesthetic flavors (rasas) and their associated elements have been described.
He who knows their true nature is fit to compose poetry.
[Manifesting] from their respective determinants (ālambana-vibhāvas), they emerge...
Rasa, in the form of love and so forth, is designated as "bhāva.
Love, laughter, sorrow, anger, energy, fear, as well as disgust and wonder—these eight are proclaimed as the permanent moods (sthāyibhāvas). || 13–14 ||
Stiffness, horripilation, faltering speech, perspiration, trembling, change of color, tears, and fainting—these eight are known as the *sāttvika* [emotions].
Memory, deliberation, longing, anxiety, restlessness, and intelligence... [15]
Pride, affection, fortitude, shame, dissimulation, delusion, intoxication;
joy, indignation, envy, jealousy, despondency, dejection, ferocity, fear, suspicion, illness, exhaustion, insanity, agitation, and fatigue. || 16–17 ||
Despair, dullness, indolence, sleep, slumber, and wakefulness— these thirty-three states are to be known as the transitory (vyabhicārin) emotions.
They abide for a long time in the mind and are connected with their attendant factors.
Those stable emotions (*sthāyins*) here become *rasas* for those who are awakened.
Here, the mind untouched by *rajas* and *tamas* is called *sattva*; because they arise from its connection with that [purity], they are termed *sāttvika*.
Those which, by their specific influence, cause [the primary emotions] to circulate throughout the body on all sides,
are called the transitory states (*vyabhicārin*), being the causes for [emotions such as] *anubhāva* and so forth.
Or, those which, having once arisen, do not arise again, are the transitory states.

For mindfulness and the other [mental states] arise and do not arise with regard to love and the rest; yet, among all the transitory emotions (saṃcāribhāva) present in sexual passion, only pride, affection, fortitude,
and intelligence are recognized as stable [permanent emotions] in the Uddhata, Preyas, Śānta, and Udātta styles.

By producing an effect (anubhāva) in its own substratum through the intensity of latent impressions (saṃskāra) and other factors— whether it be a transitory emotion (saṃcārī) or a state of being (sāttvika)— it arises.
This occurs when the cause for recollection is made more potent by the excitant factors (uddīpanavibhāva).
The "consequence" (anubandha) is said to be the connection of this [rasa] with the consequents (anubhāva) and so forth.

When there is a conjunction of the determinants (vibhāva), the consequents, the involuntary states (sāttvika), and the transitory mental states (vyabhicārin), its mere production is called "accomplishment" (niṣpatti).

Its excellence and nourishment are said to arise from the objects, the substratum, the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), the qualities (*guṇa*), the natural aptitude (*prakṛti-pāṭava*), and the intensity of the stimulant (*dīpanātiśaya*). [This occurs] when another state arises as the cause for the simultaneous production of power. || 27 ||
Contact with that [other rasa] is declared to be its "confusion" (saṃkara).

That which occurs through the suppression of another rasa or through a different passion, resulting in the decrease rather than the increase of that [primary rasa], they call its "diminution" (hrāsa).
They recognize that semblance of darkness (tamas) only in inferior recipients, in animals, in those who oppose the Leader, and in secondary objects,
when powerful and adverse causes have arisen. || 30 ||
The complete eradication of that [defilement] through its very essence is described as "quiescence" (praśama).
However, its absolute non-eradication—whether by way of its substratum, its nature, or the stability of its formative impressions—is designated as "having a remainder" (saśeṣa). || 31–32 ||

Those who consider the erotic and other aesthetic sentiments (rasas), those which are tranquil or agitated, and the various distinctions such as love (rati) and so forth, to be its specific manifestations;
as well as the determinants (vibhāva), the consequents (anubhāva), the transitory states (saṃcārī), and that which is the substratum (āśraya). || 33 ||
And those [emotions] such as *līlā* (sportiveness) and others which remain for young men are designated as *pariśeṣa* (residual).

That which is the substratum (*āśraya*) from which love (*preman*) and so forth arise— namely, Rati and the like— and that which is the object (*viṣaya*), such as a woman, therein this [emotion] attains its birth.
The manifestation of the objective support (ālambana-vibhāva) is said to be the cause of that cognition;

through that [cognition] in the form of respect and so forth, a latent impression (saṃskāra) arises for it. That [impression] is characterized by being attended to, being sharp, and being repeated, due to the excellence of its substratum and other factors. || 36 ||
For the awakening of that [emotion], garlands, seasons, sandalwood, the rising of the moon, and so forth are the *uddīpana-vibhāvas* (excitants).
Through these, one remembers, desires, hates, exerts effort, perceives, reflects, speaks, and acts. (37–38)
Those which at that time would be perspiration, the bristling of hair, and so forth, as well as joy, indignation, and the like, are to be known here as the transitory (saṃcārin) emotions;
they are born of memory, desire, and effort, and have their locus in the mind, speech, and body. (39)
Those which are the graceful charms (*vilāsa*) of excellent women should be known as *līlā* and the rest:
*līlā*, *vilāsa*, *vicchitti*, *vibhrama*, *kilakiñcita*, *moṭṭāyita*, *kuṭṭamita*, *vivvoka*, and likewise *lalita*. (40–41)
*Vihṛta*, *krīḍita*, and *kelī* are known as the natural-born [expressions] of women;
furthermore, *helā*, *hāva*, and others should be understood as belonging to both women and men.
Scholars consider these to be included among the *anubhāvas* (consequent emotions).
Through subsequent existence and experience, like the attendant emotions (anubhāvas) such as recollection;
and those which are the recollections and other attendant emotions (saṃcāribhāvas) performed by actors in dramas, these are known as abhinayas (gestures/representations). || 43-44 ||
When the state known as love (rati) reaches its highest intensity but does not attain its desired object, it is then called *vipralambha* (love-in-separation).
This consists of four types: love at first sight (*pūrvānurāga*), jealousy (*māna*), separation due to travel (*pravāsa*), and separation through death (*karuṇa*). (45)
Among the various types of men and women, the fourfold division is revealed.
First, a longing arises between a youth and a maiden who have not yet met; that passion, which is delightful through mental ideation, is called the "ancient" (prācya). || 46-47 ||
The course of love is as crooked by nature as that of a snake;
therefore, pride (māna) is said to arise from the expression "I fear" or "No," whether based on a cause or without a cause.
[Verse 48] That which constitutes a long-standing separation between young lovers due to foreign lands and other such factors—
When a lover departs on a journey while passion is either new or fully matured, that is called *pravāsa* (separation due to travel).
When the beloved youth has gone to another world and the beloved woman suffers intensely in her wretchedness, it is then called *karuṇa* (the pathetic sentiment).
Love itself, when fully developed upon the attainment of the desired object, is called *saṃbhoga* (enjoyment-love).
This too is of four kinds, following immediately after *pūrvānurāga* (love at first sight) and the others.
Without *vipralambha* (separation), *saṃbhoga* does not attain full development.
For when cloth and such are treated with an astringent dye, a greater degree of coloration adheres to them.
In the separation of man and woman, there are specific behaviors such as mental agitation and the wearing of ornaments; in their union, there are kissing, embracing, and so forth.
The mutual examinations of love that are specified— occurring through efforts such as pursuit during separation, and through states such as trepidation during union— are called *parīṣṭis*.
[This applies] to the words "separation" (*vipralambha*) and so forth, which are established in common worldly usage.
Etymological explanations (nirukti) are established through the division of roots into their primary forms (*prakṛti*) and so forth.

By relying on deceptive meanings, one should understand that the root *labh* preceded by *pra-* signifies "deceiving," based on the indicative authority (*jñāpaka*) of such rules as "the roots *gṛdh* and *vañc* are used in the sense of deceiving" (*pralambhane*). || 55–56 ||
In the cases of separation preceded by prior affection, they say that taking [the gift], breaking one's promise, the wasting of time, returning it, and deception follow that sequence. (57)
In this context, it is indicated by the prefix *vi-*, which serves to highlight a specific distinction.

For a "promise" (*pratiśrava*) consists of the non-granting of desired embraces and so forth—despite prior affection being signaled by side-long glances and other gestures—due to such factors as modesty and fear. (58–59)
The obstruction of their pride is called deceiving them; or it is the giving of what is not as promised, through such means as false recollection and the like.
In their case, the delay during their absence is clearly understood.
When those who have been away return, beloved women employ these things toward their lovers;
who would not consider this a compassionate act of restitution?
For it is Fate itself that withdraws those very things once they have been given by one's own self.
In the word *pralambha*, if it is used in the sense of mere deception (*vañcanā*) without forming a compound, it is employed for four meanings;
they are, respectively: *vividha* (variegated), *viruddha* (contradictory), and *vyāviddha* (perverse). || 63 ||
And even one who has been forbidden may become attached through previous passion and the like.
(64) In the case of *pūrvānurāga* (previous passion), they say there is various deception by means of bashfulness and so forth;
in the case of *māna* (resentment), they say it is contrary [to that], by means of jealousy and the like. (65)

In the *pravāsa* [sentiment], it is perceived as "disturbed" (*vyāviddha*) due to its long duration; however, in the *karuṇa* [sentiment], it is described as "forbidden" (*viniṣiddha*) by virtue of its very nature of compassion.
Passion (*rāga*) may be simultaneous, subsequent, conformable, or even following after.

In the case of two youths, this unprecedented [love] is designated by the term *pūrvānurāga* (prior love). Alternatively, *rāga* is derived from the root *rañj* (to delight); it is formed with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of either the instrument (*karaṇa*) or the state (*bhāva*).
In other grammatical roles (*kāraka*) or in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*), the rule is restricted by the elision of the nasal (*n*) [resulting in *rāga*]. 67–68.
That by which one is honored by a beloved, or that which one regards as dear, or that which one considers or measures—this is called *premamāna*.
According to the tradition of the author of the *Mahābhāṣya*, what is this [term] known as *anumāna*? 69.
Even when ending in the suffix *lyuṭ*, the word *māna* does not lose its masculine gender.
Where women and young men dwell or do not dwell,
that is called "sojourn" (*pravāsa*) by means of the prefix *pra*, which carries a contrary sense.
That which intensely permeates the mind here through intense longing and the like,
or causes young people to depart, is defined as *pravāsa* (exile). The root *vas* preceded by *pra* should be understood as signifying the act of causing [the mind] to be driven away.
"One should banish him in silence," according to the instruction of the elders.
(73) The root *kṛ* is seen in the sense of producing what has not yet come into being, as in "make a pot";
it is also seen in the sense of uttering, as in "he reviles with the words 'thief! (caurakāram). (74)
Having seen him, she says, "Place this stone for my support," as it is said; and regarding the anointing, she says, "Anoint my feet with ghee.
She utters fainting and lamentations, and sets her mind upon a desperate act.

He who makes the mind suffer is called compassionate (karuṇa). The root *bhuj* is used in the senses of protecting, being crooked, eating, and experiencing; thus one says "he protects" (*bhunakti*), "he is bent" (*bhugnaḥ*), "he eats food" (*bhunakti annam*), and "he experiences happiness" (*bhunakte sukham*). || 76–77 ||
When the suffix *ghañ* is added to the root preceded by the prefix *sam-* and the object *bhuj*, the form *saṃbhoga* is intended to denote either an abstract state (*bhāva*) or an agent (*kāraka*).
This [term] has the sense of "protection" and is spoken of as occurring immediately after "passionate love at first sight" (*pūrvānurāga*).
For once pleasure has arisen toward him, it is maintained by acting in accordance with his will. Having reached that state immediately after pride, she plunges into crookedness for the sake of guile;
how much more so when love is inherently crooked, especially when accompanied by pride?
Immediately following *pravāsa* (separation), its purpose is considered to be *abhyavahāra* (consumption);
for therein, pleasure is experienced like food by those who have fasted.
That which follows immediately after *karuṇa* (compassion) is said to be for the purpose of *anubhāva* (manifestation).
For those who possess confidence in this, only happiness is experienced.
Alternatively, since the word *bhoga* expresses the sense of "union" (*saṃprayoga*),
four specific types attend upon it within the compound.
Whether his practice was contracted, mixed, complete, or characterized by perfect prosperity, he was reborn into the enjoyments taught immediately prior [to his own state].
For in a new union, young people are generally overcome by trepidation and other such emotions.
They employ only abbreviated expressions for the sake of pleasure.

Immediately following the state of *māna* (pride), since the remnants of anger persist through the recollection of past offenses and the like, by whom can their *saṃkara* (admixture) be prevented? || 85–86 ||
For those whose desires are fulfilled, for lovers, and especially for those who were longing for the reunion with one gone abroad, a profusion of enjoyment proceeds;
even when the beloved has returned, it is there that this nourishment of passion occurs.
How can she be described among youths, for there alone lies the restoration of the dead?

The "love at first sight" (*pūrvānurāga*) of the preceding [types] has been illustrated by their respective definitions; the etymological explanations (*nirukti*) of all the subsequent ones follow from that same compounding.

In that case, let the function be either non-abandoning of its own meaning (*ajahatsvārthā*) or abandoning of its own meaning (*jahatsvārthā*); for the meaning of the primary [word] does not cease as long as the primary itself is not modified.
Since the function occurs immediately after the first [word], it is accepted as being non-abandoning of its own meaning.
They know that [the *śṛṅgāra* rasa] does not entirely abandon its own meaning (*svārtha*) immediately after the *māna* [rasa].
However, immediately after *pravāsa*, it is held to abandon its own meaning slightly;
and in the *karuṇa* [rasa] that follows it, there is not even a trace of the meaning of that [former *śṛṅgāra*].

The eighth-day moon, the jasmine of the fourth day, the beautiful spring, the swinging on the fourth day, the single śālmalī tree, the festival of Madana; the water-splashing, the *aśoka-uttaṃsikā* [garland of *aśoka* flowers], and the breaking of mango blossoms. || 93 ||
Puṣpāvacāyikā, Cūtalatikā, Bhūtamātṛkā;
Kadambayuddhāni, Navapatrikā, Bisakhādikā; Śakrārcā, Kaumudī, Yakṣarātri, and Abhyūṣakhādikā. (94–95)
They know that eating sugarcane, playing in water, watching performances and the like, gambling, and drinking honey-wine constitute miscellaneous activities (prakīrṇaka).
[The duties] are classified as constant (nitya), occasional (naimittika), general (sāmānya), and specific (viśeṣavat). || 96 ||
The concealed and the manifest, both the artificial and the natural,
those named innate and acquired, another born of youth, and that born of confidence— these twelve are the loves of great power. (97-98)
Delight of the eye, attachment of the mind, a continuous stream of arising intentions, idle chatter, wakefulness, emaciation, restlessness toward other objects,
abandonment of shame, disease, madness, and frequent fainting. 99.
And death—these should be understood as the stages of the development of love in sequence.
This [term] preceded by *prati* is the *nāyaka* (hero), and preceded by *upa* it is the *anunāyaka* (deputy hero).
This [term] preceded by *prati* is the *nāyikā* (heroine), and preceded by *upa* it is the *anunāyikā* (deputy heroine).
There are twelve types of heroes: the hero, the semblance of a hero, the semblance of a heroine, the semblance of both, and likewise the semblance of these among animals.
Among them, the hero is one endowed with all virtues and who pervades the narrative.
The antagonist (pratināyaka) is one who acts unjustly, is arrogant, and must be destroyed by him.
Then, the secondary protagonist (upanāyaka) is one who is somewhat deficient in virtues yet worthy of honor;
the minor character (anunāyaka) is either equal to or inferior to him. || 103–104 ||
The heroine (nāyikā) may be pervasive throughout the narrative and endowed with all virtues;

she is the cause of [the hero's] jealousy and so forth. The rival wife (sapatnī) is the counter-heroine (pratināyikā). Then, the secondary heroine (upanāyikā) is one who is somewhat deficient in virtues and yet worthy of honor.
The *anunāyikā* (the rival heroine) may be equal to, or slightly less than, [the hero] in some respects.
Their semblances (*tadābhāsas*) are likewise, and their varieties arise from differences in qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth.
Among them, the hero is classified as superior, middling, or inferior according to his qualities.
According to his nature, he may be *sāttvika*, *rājasa*, or *tāmasa*; furthermore, he should be understood as "common" (*sādhāraṇa*) or "of no other kind" (*ananyajāti*) based on his associations.
He is characterized by the conduct of being impetuous, graceful, tranquil, or noble through his fortitude.
According to their conduct, they may be deceitful, impudent, compliant, or clever;
according to their qualities, the heroine may likewise be superior, middling, or inferior; and she may be inexperienced, intermediate, or mature, either by age or by skill. (109–110)

She is "steadfast" (dhīrā) or "unsteady" (adhīrā) according to her composure; she is "one's own" or "another's" because she is not taken as a wife by another; she is "elder" (jyeṣṭhā) or "younger" (kanīyasī) respectively based on whether she was married first or later; and she is "haughty" (uddhatā), "noble" (udāttā), "calm" (śāntā), or "graceful" (lalitā) according to the degree of her pride. (111)
Furthermore, according to their conduct, she is classified as a *sāmānyā*, a *punarbhū*, or a *svairiṇī*.
According to her livelihood, she is a *gaṇikā*, a *rūpājīvā*, or a *vilāsinī*.
According to her condition, eight other types are to be known, beginning with the *khaṇḍitā*. (112–113)
She whose beloved returns in the morning from somewhere with eyes copper-red and heavy with sleep, adorned with the nail-marks of other women, is a *khaṇḍitā*.
She who, out of anger, casts away her lord of her life even when he offers endearing words; ||| 114 || [is a *khaṇḍitā*].
But she who is separated by a quarrel experiences remorse.
She whose beloved has not met her after she has sent a messenger day after day and made an appointment somewhere is known as "the deceived" (vipralabdhā).
She who, having adorned herself and prepared her couch, awaits her beloved in the decorated chamber for dalliance, is known as *vāsakasajjā*.
She, however, whose husband never leaves her side, is *svādhīnapatikā*. (117)
One who is greedy for the savoring of the pleasure of various delights and sports with her beloved is [described as such].
She who, tormented by the flower-arrowed god (Kāma), goes to her lover is an *abhisārikā*.
She whose beloved is in another country is a *proṣitabhartṛkā*.
She whose beloved does not return even when the day of his departure has arrived is "longing due to separation" (virahotkaṇṭhitā); these, then, are the thirty-two types of heroines.
The remaining [characters] are inferior roles: the Pīṭhamarda and the Vidūṣaka.
The parasites (viṭas) and servants (ceṭas), as well as their female companions (sakhīs), constitute their retinue.
[They possess] noble birth, generosity, great fortune, gratitude, and the perfections of beauty, youth, cleverness, good character, and charm.
They say there are twelve qualities conducive to being sought after in heroes: being pleasant in speech, being free from stinginess, and being affectionate toward the poor.
The various stages of ripening, such as those of the grape, the coconut, and the mango, are called *pākabhakti*.
The varieties of passion (rāga) include those such as the dyes of indigo, safflower, and madder;

the varieties of hypocrisy (vyāja) include those that are internal, external, and sincere; and the varieties of devotion (bhakti) include those whose fruits are dharma, artha, and kāma, as well as those whose ultimate fruit is pure love (prema). || 124–125 ||
And just as in individual sentences, wise poets incorporate the blending of sentiments (rasas) and ornaments (alaṃkāras) within their compositions, avoiding all impropriety.
[Such works] are endowed with the four modes of expression (vṛtti) and their constituent parts, and possess heroes who are both clever and noble.
Who would not embrace a literary composition that yields the fruit of the four aims of life?

(127) The wise have declared that there are five junctures (*sandhi*) in a composition: the opening (*mukha*), the development (*pratimukha*), the climax (*garbha*), the pause (*avamarśa*), and the conclusion (*nirvahaṇa*). (128)
The world delights in poetry that is neither too expansive nor too condensed, composed in melodious meters, fragrant with aesthetic flavor, and featuring verses at the end of each canto;
[such poetry] describes cities, groves, kingdoms, and the like, as well as seals and hermitages.
The excellence of setting (deśasaṃpat) serves to enhance the aesthetic flavor (rasa).
Through descriptions of seasons, nights, days, and the rising and setting of the sun and moon, time becomes perfected in poetic works and bestows nourishment upon the rasa. (130–131)
Descriptions of royal maidens, princes, women, armies, and the various maneuvers of their divisions establish the flow of aesthetic flavor (rasa) in poetry.
[132] Gardens, water-sports, drinking honey-wine, and festivals of pleasure— these are the themes.
Deceptions, marriages, and various activities bring aesthetic flavor (rasa) to poetry.
Through counsel, envoys, expeditions, battles, the hero's rise to power, and so forth, the nourishment of human effort (puruṣakāra) showers aesthetic flavor upon poems. (133–134)
The omission of descriptions of cities and such is not considered a fault by the wise,
provided that [the poet] is satisfied by the description of mountains, seasons, nights, and so forth.
Having first presented the hero according to his virtues, [one may then describe] his enmity with enemies...
This path known as "refutation" (nirākaraṇa) is naturally beautiful.
Describing the lineage, valor, learning, and other qualities of even an enemy, and then proclaiming the hero’s excellence through his victory over him, delights us. (136–137)
Now, their definitions and examples:
therein, *rati* (attachment) is the experience of pleasure toward objects that are agreeable to the mind.
That very joy, when its object is no longer in conjunction [with the senses], is called *prīti* (affection). An example of the manifestation of *rasa* in that form is as follows:
"But Hara, his composure slightly shaken, like the ocean at the rising of the moon..."
[He] directed his eyes toward Umā’s face, with its lower lip like the *bimba* fruit.

(1) Here, the particular longing of Maheśvara—inferred from the directing of his eyes toward Pārvatī’s face, which is pleasing to the mind due to its *bimba*-like lips and other qualities—infers only the arising of an experience of pleasure, since there is no production of the *sāttvika* [emotions] and so forth.
An example of birth in the form of that very [pleasure], resulting in the production of the *sāttvika* [emotions], is as follows:

"The groom’s forearm bristled with horripilation, while the maiden’s fingers grew numb; at that moment, their respective physical states seemed as if divided equally by the God of Love between the two.
Here, through the emergence of the two *sāttvika* emotions—perspiration and horripilation—the manifestation of the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) in the form of love (*rati*) is understood.
Birth itself is the movement [of the eyes] at the moment of arising, as for example:
“Their lovely eyes, glancing from the corners and slightly fixed yet withdrawn, endured the constraint of modesty while flickering toward one another. (3)
In this context, the transitory emotion (*saṃcāribhāva*) of shame (*hrīḥ*), as it arises, makes known the birth of the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*);
that very [shame] likewise brings about the emergence of the consequent action (*anubhāva*), as for example:
"Then, at the conclusion of Sunandā’s speech, the princess, having softened her shame..."
"With a gaze pure with serene faith, she received the prince as if with a garland of *saṃvaraṇa* flowers.
(4) Here, the physical manifestation characterized by the "gaze" is the *anubhāva* (consequent emotion), which indicates the emergence of the *rasa*.
Furthermore, the recurrence of one or more *anubhāvas* and so forth constitutes *anubandha* (continuity).
An example of this [simultaneous action] with respect to many is as follows:
“Even the daughter of the mountain, revealing her emotion with limbs somewhat like those of a young kadamba tree, stood with her face turned aside in its great beauty, her eyes cast down. (5)

In this context, the passion (*rati*) that first arose in the Goddess toward the Enemy of Smara (Śiva) is kindled by longing glances at him and by the distinct spring season and other factors; it is then sustained by the involuntary (*sāttvika*) and transitory (*vyabhicārin*) states characterized by horripilation (*romāñca*) and bashfulness (*avahittha*).
An example of this same [passion] occurring repeatedly is as follows:
"By her who was going away, yet repeatedly turning her neck to bear that face—which resembled a hundred-petaled lotus with its stalk turned back—"
"The side-glance of that long-lashed-eyed girl, smeared with both nectar and poison, has been deeply embedded in my heart as if it were driven in.

(6) Here, Mālatī’s love for Mādhava, which had previously arisen, is kindled by the arrival of spring and the display of his specific proximity; it is further sustained by the physical manifestation (*śarīrārambha-anubhāva*) characterized by the repeated casting of side-glances with her neck turned.

In this very instance, Mādhava’s love for Mālatī, which arose on that very day, is ignited by those same excitants (*uddīpana*) and is sustained by transitory emotions (*saṃcāribhāva*) such as joy, fortitude, memory, intelligence, and anxiety, as well as by the verbal expression as its consequent emotion (*anubhāva*).
Thus, the realization of rasa occurs in the form of love itself, as in:
"Beholding him, her slender body drenched with perspiration and trembling, she offered her foot only after it had been lifted."
Like a river agitated by a collision with a mountain on its path, the daughter of the King of Mountains neither went forward nor remained still.

In this case, although Śiva is adverse, the daughter of the Mountain possesses an uninterrupted love for him at all times due to the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of experiences from a previous birth; this love, being kindled by the sudden sight of him—whose union was sought through penance difficult to perform even after long separation—is conjoined with transitory emotions (*vyabhicāribhāva*) such as joy, recollection, agitation, and trepidation, which are characterized by involuntary physical states (*sāttvika-bhāva*) like perspiration, paralysis, and trembling, and with the bodily consequent (*anubhāva*) indicated by the act of taking a step.

Thus, through the conjunction of the determinants (*vibhāva*), the consequents (*anubhāva*), and the transitory states (*vyabhicāribhāva*), this aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) is produced in the form of love (*rati*);
the nourishment of the flavor occurs precisely in the form of love, as in the following example:
"May the lovely body of the Ocean’s daughter, embraced by her beloved—thick-hipped, with a deep navel, slender at the waist, and possessed of very high breasts—protect you all."

With a mind satisfied by the non-injury of his own abode, the Creator—who dwells within the lotus from which Viṣṇu’s navel sprouts—meditates on the welfare of him (Brahmā) whose eyes meet at that very moment.

In this regard, Śrīvatsalakṣmaṇa always dwells in a state of love for Lakṣmī that has arisen from her noble lineage, generosity, steadfast affection, beauty, youth, cleverness, character, good fortune, and great majesty; this love is kindled by the excellence of the excitants (*uddīpana-vibhāva*) consisting of the contemplation of the loveliness of her specific limbs, and it is inferred—despite the presence of Brahmā himself—by the physical manifestation (*anubhāva*) of embracing, which indicates the loss of modesty, the eighth stage of the nourishment of love.
And here, although not explicitly mentioned, other *sāttvika* and *vyabhicārin* states, as well as other specific *anubhāvas*, are perceived;

furthermore, in Śrī, who is the locus of the perfection of all divine qualities, there arises a love for the one marked with the Śrīvatsa that is either equal to or even greater than that [love of the Lord], which—being kindled by the *uddīpana-vibhāva* characterized by the embrace of her beloved in whom affection has grown intense—resorts to the highest stage of the nourishment of love, inferable from the closing of the eyes and caused by all the *sāttvika* and *vyabhicārin* *anubhāvas*.

This very aesthetic flavor (rasa), reaching its highest pitch through the beauty of the object, the nature of the substratum, the intensity of the refinement [of the audience], and the excellence of the excitants (uddīpana), is said to be "nourished" (puṣṭa).

Right here, the love that arises from such objective grounds as "This is the enchanting creation of Brahmā for Śrī," "She is the daughter of the Ocean of Jewels," "She is the sister of the Moon, the Nectar, and the rest," "She is the beloved of Viṣṇu," or "She is the mother of Kāma"—this love, being kindled by her bodily form which does not violate its own abode and by the fear of such violation born from the closing of the eyes; being joined with the transitory emotions (vyabhicāribhāvas) such as agitation, recollection, reflection, madness, delusion, and anxiety arising at that very moment, and with the involuntary states (sāttvikas) such as paralysis and trembling inferable therefrom; and being united with the consequent manifestation of the intellect characterized by the meditation on Śiva—this love is perceived as ascending to the highest degree of excellence.
An intermingling of fear and other emotions within the context of love is as follows:

“Having by chance encountered my beloved, who moves before my face like a digit of the moon seized by Rāhu, as this robber is about to strike her with the fall of his sword—how can my heart behave? It is distressed by terror, agitated by compassion, inflamed by anger, and yet blossomed with joy. (9)

In this context, Mādhava’s love for Mālatī, which had previously arisen, is ignited by excitants (*uddīpana-vibhāva*) such as the sight of her condition; it is further intensified by being intermingled with other aesthetic sentiments (*rasa*)—namely fear, sorrow, wonder, anger, and joy—which are produced through their respective combinations of excitants, ensuants (*anubhāva*), and transitory mental states (*vyabhicārin*); and finally, it is perceived as reaching its highest excellence through contact with ensuants consisting of mental, vocal, intellectual, and physical activities, as well as with *sāttvika* transitory states corresponding to fear and the others.

In this context, the mental application (*mana-ārambha*) consists of the contemplation of the mind’s agitation and so forth; the verbal application (*vāk-ārambha*) is the utterance of speech; the intellectual application (*buddhi-ārambha*) is the thought, "Like Rāhu [seizing] the beloved digit of the moon," and so on; and the physical application (*śarīra-ārambha*) is the act of "snatching away," and so on. Furthermore, the five factors beginning with fear (*bhaya*) correspond respectively to these: "Like Rāhu," "the one moving before the face like the digit of the moon," "having encountered me by chance," "from the range of this robber’s sword-stroke," and "of the one snatching away my beloved. These are the objective determinants (*ālambana-vibhāva*). The contemplations of their specific natures are the excitant determinants (*uddīpana-vibhāva*). The mental states—agitated, hurried, disturbed, inflamed, and expanded—are the consequent manifestations (*anubhāva*). The involuntary physical reactions (*sāttvika-bhāva*), such as trembling, tears, paralysis, discoloration, and horripilation, which correspond to terror, compassion, wonder, anger, and joy, as well as the transitory emotions (*vyabhicāribhāva*) such as delusion, despondency, anxiety, ferocity, and fortitude, when inferred, become the causes for the realization [of the aesthetic flavor].

This commingling (*saṃkara*) of the accomplishment of fear and other emotions, which arise from causes of equal strength at the same time during a state of passion (*rati*), is said to cause a diminution of the excellence of the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) in the form of that passion— as for example:
“Where anger is the knitting of the brows, where restraint is silence, where mutual smiles are the conciliation, and where a glance is the favor...”
"Behold now the ruin of that very love: you roll at my feet, yet for me, a wicked woman, there is no release from my anger.

Here, because the other rasa called "anger" (roṣa) supersedes [the primary emotion] in the woman, and because of his passion for another in the man, a decline in the excellence of their mutual love (rati) is inferred.
An example of a semblance of rasa (rasābhāsa) occurring in inferior characters through the form of love (rati) is as follows:

‘In the month of Māgha, the rustic sells his cloak for an ox, while gazing at the dark mango tree’s breasts in the midst of the glowing embers. (11) [The rustic sells his cloak for an ox in the month of Māgha...]
[Restraining his gaze upon Śyāmā’s breast amidst the rustling of the grass.
As it occurs among animals:
“Behold, the manifest auspiciousness of the young cow in the midst of the herd!”
‘Behold the good fortune displayed by the cow in the middle of the cow-pen as she scratches her eye-socket on the horn of a wicked bull. (12)
An example regarding those who oppose the hero (the rivals) is as follows:
“Arrows released from the hand of Rāvaṇa, having been rendered precious by the touch of Janakasutā (Sītā), produce horripilation upon the body of the ten-necked one. (13)
The arrows of Rāghava, released after being drawn by his palm as if they were as precious as the touch of Janaka’s daughter, produce horripilation on the body of the Ten-necked one.
As for examples in the case of secondary meanings (gauṇa):
‘He bears limbs adorned with the horripilation of new sprouts of grass, as if his body were being embraced by the breasts of the Goddess of the Rainy Season. (14)
Vindhya was urged on by the two breasts of the beauty of the rainy season.
These four are called semblances of rasa (*rasābhāsa*).
Regarding the very same state of love (*rati*), the subsiding of other emotions in the form of shame and anger is as follows:

‘When her beloved was seen, [her pride] was slightly contracted like an eye; when he stood at her side, it was bent down like a face; when he sat nearby, it spread out like horripilation upon contact; when he loosened the knot of her waist-cloth, it became slack like the binding of a sash; and then, as he touched her feet, it departed from the fair-eyed woman like shame, while her anger vanished as she spoke.
Here, by the powerful force of the lover’s affection and conciliation, the subsiding of both shame and anger is brought about.
An example of the remaining state of the aesthetic flavor (rasa) of anger (*roṣa*) during sexual union is as follows:

“When the lover has arrived, the eye of the indignant woman becomes eager; when he approaches, it trembles; when he speaks, it widens; when he embraces her, it reddens; when she seizes his garment, the creeper-like brow is raised in anger; and at the moment of his prostration at her feet, it is filled with tears.
Oh, how the eye of the proud woman becomes so versatile in its manifestations within a single instant once the lover has committed an offense! (16)
In this context, even when pride has been uprooted by intense love, a remnant of it may persist;

these ten varieties of rasa, beginning with *bhāva*, are generally observed even in [the case of] laughter and the other rasas, though they are illustrated here only occasionally for fear of making the work too voluminous.
In that context,
laughter (*hāsa*) is said to be a transformation of the mind caused by physical deformity, shame, and so forth;
the manifestation of the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) in the form of that [laughter] is as follows:

"Victorious is Hari, who, laughing with embarrassment produced by the laughter of his beloved, repeatedly raises up his own luster— which is dark like a fresh rain-cloud— reflected in Rādhā’s breast-mound that is as clear as a golden pitcher, mistaking it for the edge of her black garment.
(17) In this [verse], from Rādhā [laughing] at Hari’s body, and from Hari’s embarrassment, only the mere existence of the laugh is perceived.
Sorrow (*śoka*) is the despondency of the mind caused by separation from the beloved and other such causes.
The production of rasa through that [sorrow] is as follows:
"You have not departed from my heart; you are seen in all directions..."
"O child Rāma, you have gone; you are inferred [to be so] from your anguish.

Here, in one situated at a distance, the rasa in the form of sorrow (*śoka*) is produced—arising from separation from Rāma, kindled by the recollection of his qualities and so forth, and sustained by the commencement of speech—while "anger" (*krodha*) is said to be the awakening of sharpness (*taikṣṇya*) toward disagreeable objects.
The production of rasa through that form is as follows:

“When I, whose mental state was so cruel due to not remembering [her], did not reciprocate the love offered in secret, the bow of Smara was broken by her exceeding anger, as if by the separation of her two curved eyebrows and her exceedingly red eyes. (19)

In this regard, although there is the employment of the word *ati* (excessively) as a cause for intensity in the phrase "with eyes exceedingly red with excessive rage"—which characterizes the production of rasa through the conjunction of the determinants (*vibhāva*), consequents (*anubhāva*), and transitory states (*vyabhicārin*)—nevertheless, anger directed toward a beloved by a heroine of the highest class does not attain such intensity; rather, it is intended as a firm resolve or enthusiasm regarding the undertaking of an action.
An example of the birth of rasa in that form is as follows: [Verse 140]...

Having saluted Jāmbavān with his head, having inquired after the welfare of the generals, having consoled his dear friends whose faces were bathed in tears, and having repeatedly dispatched his messengers with instructions, the swift Māruti, ever mindful of the dust of the feet of the Lord of the Raghus, set out from the peak of Mahendra to leap across the ocean. (20)

In this context, because acts such as salutation, inquiry, consolation, instruction, climbing a mountain peak, and the recollection of one’s chosen deity culminate in the preliminary ritual (*pūrvaraṅga*), they do not constitute excitants (*uddīpana-vibhāva*); and because they lack the nature of enthusiasm, they do not constitute consequents (*anubhāva*). Therefore, this "continuation" (*anubandha*) is neither a completion nor a culmination.
Fear is known as the agitation of the mind produced by the Furious (*raudra*) and other [sentiments].
An example of the continuation of rasa in that form is as follows:

"By travelers here, who mutter the mantras of the Conqueror of Death (*Mṛtyujit*) repeatedly, who meditate on their desired deities with parched palates, whose steps are utterly agitated, who are rendered speechless and trembling—these hamlets are passed, where the barking of dogs, greedy for elephant flesh, is obscured by the thick, smoky haze of buffalo smoke. (21)

In this case, although there is a conjunction of the determinants (*vibhāva*), consequents (*anubhāva*), and transitory states (*vyabhicāribhāva*)—in that the villages serve as the determinants, their two qualifiers serve as the excitants (*uddīpana*), the chanting of mantras and so forth serve as the consequents, and the parching of the palate and so forth serve as the transitory states—nevertheless, because the chanting of mantras and the meditation upon the chosen deity are directed toward a means of escape, the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) is not produced in the form of fear.
For in the case of travelers, if such a flavor were produced, the employment of means such as paralysis, delusion, fainting, or death would be inappropriate due to their lack of fortitude.
Similarly, disgust (*jugupsā*), which consists of censuring and perceiving faults, [is not produced here]. (141)
The persistence of the rasa through that form is as follows:

“O right hand, release the sword upon the Śūdra ascetic for the sake of reviving the dead child of the twice-born; you are the arm of Rāma, who was skilled in exiling Sītā when she was exhausted by her heavy pregnancy—whence can there be compassion in you? (22)

In this context, although even a Śūdra is to be slain by a sage for the sake of preserving the life of a twice-born child—and thus there is no self-reproach regarding his own action on Rāma’s part—nevertheless, compassion still persists toward one who intends to kill an innocent person.
Here, the persistence of loathing should be understood as pertaining specifically to the abandonment of Sītā;
however, in the case of Śambuka, it arises merely from the fact of his birth.
Astonishment (*vismaya*) is an expansion of the mind caused by the extraordinary nature of an object and the like; the production of rasa through that form is as follows:

"Mother, Kṛṣṇa has gone out to play and has eaten earth at his own will many times—is it true? "It is Kṛṣṇa," [the boy said]. "Who says so? "It is the Mace-bearer (Balarāma). "Lie, mother! Look at my face!"
"May that Keśava protect you—he at whose mouth, when commanded 'Open wide! and thus opened, the Mother beheld the entire world and reached a state of wonder.

Here, the child’s mouth is the *ālambana-vibhāva* (the foundational determinant); the observation of the totality of that [world] along with his childhood and so forth is the *uddīpana-vibhāva* (the excitant determinant); and by the phrase "reached a state of wonder," all the *saṃcārins* (transitory emotions) and *anubhāvas* (consequents), though not explicitly mentioned, are understood, as is *stambha* (stupefaction)—the obstruction of physical action caused by fear, passion, illness, and the like. (142)
The nourishment of the rasa by means of that form is as follows:
“His face, with its steady gaze, having lost its natural flickeringness like painted lamps, has become motionless, as if the traveler had departed. (24)
[That natural fickleness of theirs has vanished—like oil-lamps in a painting—leaving them with their luster destroyed, the flicker of their eyes motionless, and their majesty departed.
And this [hero], though robust, because of his *sāttvika* nature, always follows others; thus he is not bound by [the usual] *anubhāvas* and so forth.
Horripilation is the bristling of the hair caused by joy, wonder, fear, and so forth; it is the manifestation of rasa in that form, as in:
"O elephant-woman, this is the thundering sound of the clouds, dense with lightning, echoing against the mountain peaks."
"O you who long for the sound of your husband's bow, why do you vainly bear this horripilation?
This is merely the echo of the thundering clouds at an untimely hour, like the falling of a thunderbolt. [Bandi:

O you whose nature is to long for the sound of your husband's bow, why do you vainly bear this horripilation? This is merely the echo of the thundering clouds at an untimely hour, like the falling of a thunderbolt.]

Because this [rasa] is also characterized by *sattva*, other afflictions such as attachment do not arise; they know that stammering (*gadgada*) is a loss of vocal clarity caused by intoxication, joy, or pain.
The production of rasa in its true form is as follows:
"‘O dear one, give me that wine which is most pleasing, which flows abundantly; quickly, quickly abandon that resounding golden vessel!
Thus the faltering speech of the deer-eyed woman, uttered under the influence of intoxication, was studied by her companions at dawn for the sake of laughter.
Here too, because it is produced through the *sāttvika* state, it is not followed by other [transitory] emotions (*bhāvas*).
Perspiration (*vaprū*) is the emergence of moisture caused by the heat of passion, fatigue from amorous play, and so forth.
The arising of rasa through its form is as follows: “Of women whose lips have become clear with the departure of the cold and whose facial complexions have turned pale... (143)
"The rising of sorrow left its mark upon the decorative paintings on the faces of the Kimpuruṣa women.
Here too, as before, there is no connection with another [emotion]; rather, trembling of the limbs due to passion, anger, fear, and so forth is *vepathu* (trembling).
An example of the arising of rasa through that form is as follows:
“Do not harbor pride, thinking, ‘This cluster of blossoms was written by my beloved’s own hand upon the surface of my cheek.
O friend, is not every other woman also a vessel for such things, provided that trembling—the internal obstacle—is absent? (28)
This too, as before, is not followed by others;
discoloration (*vivarṇatā*) is the change in complexion resulting from despondency, intoxication, anger, and so forth.
An example of the production of rasa through that form is as follows:
"Friend, go ahead; why did I not also go out with him at dawn? For that certain beautiful-faced woman appears in the mirror as someone else. (29)
By whomsoever that certain fair-faced woman is seen in the mirror as if she were someone else—
this very tear, the water welling from the eyes born of sorrow, grief, or intense joy, is likewise not bound by others.
The persistence of the rasa (sentiment) through that form is as follows: “Restrain the flow of tears in your eyes with their lashes upturned, making its connection slack by means of steadiness;
