for indeed, on this path where the portions of ground are unmarked by depressions or elevations, your footsteps will surely become uneven. (30)

In this context, by the word *bāṣpa* (tears), tears residing in the eyes are meant, not the outburst of suffering residing in the throat and other parts; as in: "He lamented with a voice choked by tears," and "Repeatedly sinking in his throat, the tear makes the surface of his breasts tremble," and so forth.
*Pralaya* (dissolution) is considered the cessation of the senses due to intense suffering and the like. (145)
The production of the rasa through that form is as follows:

“When her senses were paralyzed by a delusion arising from the intense assault [of grief], Rati—for a moment—became as if she had received a favor, since she remained unaware of her husband’s calamity. (31)
Here, by the word "moha" (delusion), fainting is meant, not the delusion whose definition will be stated later.
"Smṛti" (recollection) refers to knowledge whose object is a thing previously experienced. An example of the persistence of rasa in the form of that [smṛti] is as follows:

"Having resolved to follow my kinsmen from this rejection, she stood there as her elder brother, who is like a preceptor, cried out 'Stay!'—yet she cast upon me, that cruel one, a glance clouded by a flow of tears; that [glance], which is like a poisoned barb, burns me.
Here, a specific recollection is bound together by both a desire and the commencement of speech.
Furthermore, its [the *vitarka*’s] accomplishments and so forth should be understood as occurring precisely within the accomplishment of passion (*rati*) and the other [emotions].
Since passion and the others are rooted in memory (*smṛti*), they follow its intensification or diminution.
*Ūha* is said to be *vitarka*, which is the investigation of objects according to one’s intelligence.
The production of the rasa through that form is as follows:

“Having fixed in my mind the union with beings imagined [by others], it appears to me as if another jewel among women were fashioned by the Creator through an accumulation of beauty and constructed by his own intellect; this occurs as I contemplate the omnipotence of the Creator and her own body. (33)
Thus, whether unreal or real, this [rasa] is said to be "accomplished" when it culminates in a definitive determination through the means of memory, knowledge, reflection, and so forth.

Regarding the accomplishment and diminution of rasa in the form of longing for the attainment of a desired object, as follows: [147] For instance, the longing that arises when a desired object is not attained, for the sake of its attainment... [147] ...in that manner, there is the accomplishment and diminution of rasa.

“‘Śakuntalā will depart today’—my heart is touched by longing, my throat is choked and clouded by the flow of suppressed tears, and my vision is dulled by anxiety. Such is my distress from affection; how then must householders who dwell in the forest be tormented by the fresh sorrows of separation from their daughters? (34) In this passage, through the conjunction of the determinants (*vibhāva*), consequents (*anubhāva*), and transitory states (*vyabhicārin*), not only is love produced, but longing (*utkaṇṭhā*) is also produced as its concomitant. However, being overwhelmed by the astonishment and other emotions expressed in the latter half of the verse through the very negation [of that longing], it is called "diminution" (*hrāsa*).
And its excellence is precluded by the phrase "for me, who dwell in the forest";
furthermore, *cintā* (reflection) is said to be memory directed toward objects preceded by effort.
148 An example of the excellence of *rasa* through that form is as follows:
‘When her lover was brought to her through mere thought, she remembered her grievances and, quarreling in vain, was wept for by her friends and not laughed at. (35)

"Engaged in a hollow quarrel with her friends, she neither wept nor laughed. Here, through the weeping of the friends, there is a hollow quarrel; from the hollow quarrel, a direct confrontation [with the lover]; from the direct confrontation, anxiety; and through anxiety, the fundamental passion (*rati*) is intensified.
Furthermore, an activity directed toward self-revelation is called *capalatā* (fickleness). 149
An example of the birth of rasa through that form is as follows:
“A certain man whirled a play-lotus, its stalk grasped by both hands, striking the hovering bees with its trembling petals and binding a circle of pollen within. (36)
In this regard, for someone who stands before Indumatī with the gesture of turning a play-lotus,
the determination of meaning through the contemplation of the sense taught in the scriptures is "intellect" (mati);
the persistence of aesthetic flavor (rasa) in the form of that [intellect] is as follows:

"Without doubt, this noble one is fit to be wed by a Kṣatriya, since my mind desires him; for the inclinations of the inner organ are the authority of the virtuous regarding matters that are subjects of doubt.
Here, the *mati* (intellectual conviction) consisting of the determination of the meaning stated in the first half-verse is followed by the second half-verse.
Pride (*garva*) consists of the disregard for others through self-exaltation and the like.
An example of the nourishment of the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) by means of that [pride] is as follows:
"As long as I am armed, what need is there for weapons by others?"
"Or rather, that which was not accomplished by my weapon—by whom will it be accomplished?
Here, through Karṇa’s self-conceit, Aśvatthāman’s contempt is intensified;
moreover, affection that is causeless and irreversible is considered to be the moistening of the heart.
The production of the rasa through that form is as follows:
“This pleasure of mine upon my limbs when touched by this sprout of someone’s noble lineage—what kind of bliss would it produce in the heart of that fortunate man from whose body it has grown? (39)

In this context, the affection (*sneha*) arising from Duṣyanta’s sight of Sattvadamana is intensified by the pleasure of touching his limbs and so forth; being further nourished by longing, excessive reflection, and the commencement of speech, it reaches its full development.
*Dhṛti* (fortitude) is the state of longing reaching its fulfillment upon the attainment of the desired object;
the excellence of the rasa is manifested through that form, as follows:

“Vikramabāhu has been brought under my influence; this Earth has attained equality with myself on the surface of the world; Sāgarikā, the sole cause for the acquisition of the ocean-girt earth, is my beloved queen; and the princess has attained joy through the recovery of her sister; Kosala has been won by the gain of [my] sister—what is there that is not achieved while you, the bull among ministers, are present, in whom I place my hope? (40) In this passage, the fulfillment of all the desires of the King of Vatsa brings about the excellence of his fortitude (*dhṛti*).

The closing of the eyes due to shame, the application of unguents to other limbs, and so forth [are indicators]. (151) When there is an intensification of rasa through such forms, there may be a commingling with anger and grief—as in:
"Of Arjuna, whose fierce wrath was aroused by the slaughter of Abhimanyu at the hands of a base enemy, and who was fainting from internal anguish because he had not yet avenged his foe..."
“Drenched with teardrops, glances fall upon the bow, paralyzed by shame; alas, my son!—these words quiver at the throat but do not emerge from it.
(41) In this passage, the blazing anger and grief arising from Abhimanyu’s unjust slaughter by Arjuna are intermingled with a corresponding shame born of the failure to provide a remedy.
For instance, the eyes and words—which are the objective manifestations (*anubhāva*) of anger and grief—are connected with the qualifying term “paralyzed by shame” (*vrīḍājaḍā*).
*Avahittha*, however, is the concealment of outward signs such as joy when one feels shame and the like.
An example of the persistence of a rasa through that very form is as follows:
"While the divine sage was speaking thus, she stood by her father's side with her face cast down..."
"Pārvatī counted the petals of her play-lotus.
Here—
"Having bowed to Śitikaṇṭha, the gods thereafter..."
"May her feet be colored by the rays of her crest-jewel.
From such words of the divine sage, a form of intense joy arose; yet, out of modesty in the presence of her elders, Gaurī concealed it under the pretext of counting the petals of her play-lotus.
Delusion (moha) is the state of mental bewilderment produced by pleasure, pain, and other such factors.
The production of rasa through that form is as follows:
“When my beloved approached the bed, the knot of my garment loosened of its own accord; my dress remained on my hips, held only by the strands of my slipping girdle.
O friend, this much alone do I know; but as for his embrace, who he was, who I was there, or what the sexual union itself was—I have not even the slightest memory. (44)
Here, the stable emotion (*sthāyin*) of love is intensified through the production of delusion;
intoxication (*mada*) is the blending of delusion and bliss caused by wine and the like. The production of the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) in that form is as follows: [153]
‘With rolling eyes, faltering speech, drops of perspiration, and a causeless smile—
he did not drink in Umā’s face with his mouth for so long, but rather with his eyes.
Here, the rolling of the eyes, the causeless smile, and other such traits, arising from the blending of infatuation and bliss, bring about intoxication (*mada*).
Joy is the clarity of mind arising from the attainment of what is desired through praise and the like;
it constitutes an intensification of the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), as in the following example:
"O child, how many days indeed have passed since you were born, you who are the slayer even of your father, Indrajit?"
"By good fortune, his offspring also abides by the dharma of heroes; thus the lineage of Daśaratha has attained stability.

(46) Here, as the charioteer Sumantra—a friend of Daśaratha from a noble family—expresses his hope for the stability of that lineage, joy arises from the fulfillment of his desire upon seeing the slayer of Indrajit, the son of Rāvaṇa. This joy is indicated by the indeclinable *diṣṭyā* ("by good fortune") even regarding the child who practices the dharma of a hero.
On the other hand, anger directed toward those who have committed an offense assumes the state of indignation (*amarṣatva*) when it becomes steadfast. (154)
The excellence of rasa through that form is as follows:

“Having struck at our lives and our accumulated wealth by means of the lacquer house, fire, poisoned food, and entry into the assembly hall, and having dragged away the garments and hair of the Pāṇḍava women, the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra remain at ease while I am still alive! (47)

Here, from Bhīmasena’s inability to endure even the name "svasthāḥ" (those who are well) applied to the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the resentment born from past injuries such as the lacquer-house plot is perceived.
Envy (*asūyā*) is the intolerance of others’ excellence due to arrogance;
the birth of a rasa in that form is as follows:

‘They are to be revered; let their deeds not be scrutinized—be that as it may! Even in the slaying of Sunda’s wife, their fame remains unblemished. For they are great men in this world, those who took even three steps with their faces turned away in the battle against Khara; or rather, people are well aware of his skill in the subduing of Indra’s son. In this passage, although loathing (*jugupsā*) is produced through the mention of faults such as sarcasm (*solluṇṭha*), nevertheless, that loathing does not merge with envy (*asūyā*), which is the cause of its own production.
They say envy (*īrṣyā*) is the intolerance of honor, gifts, and so forth toward one's equals.
An intensification of the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) by means of that [envy] is as follows:
"Hūm! You shameless one, come here and appease her yourself, from whom this [behavior] of yours comes!"
"Hum! You shameless one, withdraw at once! Go and entreat her alone, by whom this tilaka was fashioned with the lac-dye from the big toe of her foot."

In this context, the *viṣāda* (despair) of a certain woman—who, unable to endure the pride of her rival, felt jealousy when her lover had gone to appease her—is intensified. This despair is first ignited by his prostrations at her feet, which are inferred from the tilaka-mark made with red lac as he fell; it is then further compounded by frowns, striking [her limbs], tossing the body, trembling, perspiration, and faltering speech, which are inseparable from the outbursts of "hum," reproaches, threats, and interruptions. Despair is a dejection of the mind arising from the absence of means or from ruin. An example of the heightening of rasa through this form is as follows: [The verse: "O friend, why do you not speak? Why do you not look at me? Why do you not embrace me? Why do you not kiss me? O cruel one, you have stolen my heart and yet you do not give it back! [Commentary: Here, the *vīra* (heroic) rasa is intensified by the *viṣāda* of the heroine, which is manifested through her lamentation and the aforementioned physical symptoms. The *vīra* rasa is further augmented by the *dhṛti* (fortitude) of the hero, who remains unperturbed despite her reproaches. Thus, the two rasas mutually enhance one another. Furthermore, the *karuṇa* (pathetic) rasa is suggested by the *viṣāda* of the heroine, while the *hāsya* (comic) rasa is suggested by the hero's indifference to her reproaches. In this way, multiple rasas are brought to a state of excellence through their mutual interaction. Thus ends the section on *viṣāda*. Now begins the section on *glāni* (lassitude). *Glāni* is a dejection of the mind arising from the exhaustion of the body or the mind due to excessive exertion, grief, or the like. It is characterized by the loss of luster in the eyes, face, and limbs, as well as a lack of interest in food and drink. An example is as follows: [The verse: "The lotus-like face of the young woman, though beautiful, has lost its luster; her eyes, though large, are devoid of joy; and her limbs, though delicate, are now emaciated. [Commentary: Here, the *śṛṅgāra* (erotic) rasa is intensified by the *glāni* of the heroine, which arises from the exhaustion of her body and mind caused by the pangs of love. Thus, the *glāni* serves as a *vyabhicāribhāva* (transitory emotion) that heightens the primary rasa. Thus ends the section on *glāni*. Now begins the section on *jaḍatā* (stupefaction). *Jaḍatā* is a dejection of the mind arising from the shock of sudden calamity or the like. It is characterized by the suspension of all mental activity and the inability to perceive external objects. An example is as follows: [The verse: "Upon hearing the news of her husband’s death, the young woman stood for a moment motionless, her eyes wide and fixed, her limbs slackened, and her heart as if frozen. [Commentary: Here, the *karuṇa* rasa is intensified by the *jaḍatā* of the heroine, which arises from the shock of the sudden calamity of her husband’s death. Thus, the *jaḍatā* serves as a *vyabhicāribhāva* that heightens the primary rasa. Thus ends the section on *jaḍatā*. Now begins the section on *maraṇa* (death). *Maraṇa* is the final departure of the vital breaths. It is characterized by the cessation of all bodily functions and the dissolution of the sense organs. An example is as follows: [The verse: "The breath has ceased, the eyes are closed, the limbs are cold, and the heart has grown still; the young woman has departed from this world, leaving behind only her beauty. [Commentary: Here, the *karuṇa* rasa is intensified by the *maraṇa* of the heroine. However, since *maraṇa* is a *sthāyibhāva* (permanent emotion) of the *karuṇa* itself, it does not function as a *vyabhicāribhāva* here

“Where even my friendship with the Lord of Monkeys is useless, where the toil of the monkeys is in vain, where even Jāmbavān’s wisdom finds no way, where even Nala, the son of Viśvakarman, is unable to fashion a path for the son of Vāyu, and where even the arrows of Saumitri find no range— there, somewhere, is my beloved.
(50) In this passage, regarding the matter of Sītā’s reunion, Rāma’s despondency is intensified by the absence of any means such as his proven friendship with Sugrīva.
The failure to elevate [the sentiment] due to the abandonment of its essence (sattva), such as in speech and so forth, is called *dainya* (dejection).
An example of the persistence of the rasa (*śṛṅgāra*) through that very form is as follows:

"Having well considered us, whose wealth is self-restraint, and your own high lineage, as well as this inclination toward love in her—which, though brought about by no relative, has somehow arisen in you..."
“Preceded by this general understanding, you must look upon [this woman] as your wife; beyond this, it is dependent on fate, and indeed it should not be spoken of by the bride’s kinsmen.
Here, the wretchedness of entreaty expressed in the first three quarters—arising from affection—is followed by the wretchedness of begging introduced in the fourth quarter.
They know severity toward wrongdoers to consist of harshness of speech and punishment.
The excellence of the rasa through that very form is as follows:

“Since her body suffers even from blows of delicate *śirīṣa* flowers administered in the spirit of playful jest by affectionate friends, may this arm of yours, as you raise it to strike her down, fall upon your own head like the sudden staff of Yama. (52)

In this case, regarding Aghoraghaṇṭa, who has committed a supreme offense against Mādhava, there arises both extreme verbal and physical violence, as well as terror— a striking effect upon the mind— arising from sudden fear and the like.
(157) The birth of rasa takes place through that very form, as follows:

"The sound [of the lute] struck by darting fish, and the glances of the celestial women flickering with terror, reached a state visible even to their female companions, as their sprout-like hands trembled.

(53) Here, the flickering of the glances and the shaking of the hands occur in women due to both natural timidity and amorous playfulness; thus, they are incapable of manifesting [genuine] terror, and therefore no *anubandha* (consequent emotional state) arises.
The wise define *śaṅkā* (apprehension) as the anticipation of the arrival of something undesirable.
An intensification of the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) through that very form is as follows:
“May her beloved’s arrival not be suddenly thwarted for her, who has been emaciated by separation.”
‘Let not the arrival of her beloved be hastily brought about by her, who is emaciated by separation;
for she who has died even from extreme joy is truly dead. (54)

In this context, a certain female companion, observing the extreme emaciation of a woman separated from her lover, out of excessive affection—and despite the presence of an intense joy at the prospect of her beloved's arrival based on the principle that "love perceives dangers even where none exist"—is unable to bear it and thus intensifies the fear of her death.
The mental anguish caused by separation and the like is a disease that brings physical affliction.
(158) An example of how rasa is born in the form of that [mental anguish] is as follows:

"This broad lotus leaf resting upon her breast does not so much declare the internal state born of love as it speaks, through its two circular expanses, of the fullness of her pair of breasts, which are withered by excessive feverish heat.
Here, Sāgarikā’s physical torment is established by the withering of the lotus petal placed upon her breast.

The decline of strength is debility, the source of intense mental anguish and physical disease; the persistence of that state within the *rasa* is as follows: "Like a tender sprout plucked from its stalk, there is a harsh and long-lasting grief that withers the flower of the heart."
"It withers her body, which is pale and emaciated, just as the autumn heat withers the inner leaf of a *ketakī* flower.
(56) Here, languor (*glāni*), which is connected to intense grief, is manifested through paleness and emaciation.
Insanity (*unmāda*) is a derangement of the mind caused by longing, joy, sorrow, and the like. (159)
The arising of rasa through that form is as follows:

“Where [is there] an improper act, and where is the lineage of the bearer of arts? Might she be seen once more? Ah, her face is peaceful even in anger; it has been heard for the sake of allaying faults.
What will those sinless ones of perfected intellect say? That line is indeed of a different kind. O heart, attain composure! What fortunate youth indeed shall drink from her lower lip? (57)
In this case, through the longing and other emotions of the separated Purūravas, a state of madness (*unmāda*) consisting of incoherent ravings is produced due to the intensity of his love;
and because of the excess of his devotion, a mental agitation (*saṃbhrama*) is considered to arise.
An example of the commingling of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) in the form of that [agitation] is as follows:
"Enough, enough! Do not act with such excessive rashness; release this noose of creepers at once.
O Mistress of my life, place the noose of your arms around my neck for a moment, as if to restrain my life that is about to flee.
Here, the extreme agitation born of passion is blended with the excellence of intellect born of that same passion.
Exhaustion of both mind and body resulting from excessive activity is *śrama* (fatigue).
An example of the commingling (*saṃkara*) of this [rasa] with another rasa through its form is as follows:
"It causes your speech to falter, it pervades limb after limb, and it produces beads of perspiration upon the moon of your face."

“O fair-browed one, your eyes close completely; thus exhaustion manifests in you equally with the sight of your beloved. (59) Here, Mālatī’s fatigue born from gathering flowers and her passion born from beholding Mādhava—possessing common attributes through perspiration, faltering limbs, and the closing of the eyes—are mutually blended. Mental exhaustion (*citta-kheda*) arises from causes such as the dawn of knowledge of reality (*tattva-jñāna*), while despondency (*nirveda*) arises from the same. *Note: The term *kheda* (exhaustion) is used here to denote both physical fatigue and mental despondency.*
An example of the remainder of rasa through that same form is as follows:
“Let old age, death, poverty, and disease be as they may; I consider birth itself to be the source of repeated shame for the wise. (60)
In this context, for someone striving for liberation, a state of despondency is understood; it is an incapacity for action, a dullness caused by anxiety, longing, fear, and so forth.
The production of rasa through that form is as follows:
"Having placed his head very loosely and at ease upon the tip of the bow, making the raindrops from his eyes appear like another bowstring, alas,
the noble one— distraught upon hearing the sound of thunder after hearing it again and again— neither moves nor remains still, lost in some ineffable meditation.
(61) Here, the lack of proficiency in action on the part of Rāma, the lover-in-separation, is brought about.
Aversion to action, laziness, and [the state of] being intoxicated by the perception of pleasure [are causes of obstruction]. 161.
An example of the realization of rasa through that form is as follows:
"Of the traveler who was about to depart, but who fell into the bliss of pressing against the full breasts of his wife..."
‘For a future traveler who has fallen into the pleasure of dalliance, urged on by the firm breasts of his wife,
even ill omens, Tuesdays, and days marked by the Viṣṭi yoga bring happiness. (62)
In this context, even for one who desires to depart due to the experience of the pleasure of passion, lassitude arises;
sleep is the turning away of the senses from activity caused by fatigue and the like.
An instance of the persistence of rasa in that form is as follows:
‘The glances of the moon-faced one— whose pupils roll sideways with a languid, drowsy turning due to sleep— are as difficult to endure as the shafts of Kāma. (63)
Even for one who has indulged in love, the downward glances of the moon-faced woman are difficult to withstand.
Here, the downward glances—characterized by a languidness born of sleep resulting from the exhaustion of passion and staying awake—are followed by the rolling and turning of the pupils;
this constitutes "sleep" (*supta*), which is produced by drowsiness and so forth, and consists of the closing of the eyes and other sensory organs. 162
The excellence of rasa through that form is as follows:
“With her limbs relaxed, the daughter-in-law [experiences] a bliss overflowing with the lingering flavor of sexual union, which has surpassed the pain caused by her rivals. (64)
"She sleeps with her limbs relaxed, having experienced the sensation that serves as the antidote [to passion],
and filled with the bliss following the fulfillment of the pleasure of sexual union— [the daughter-in-law].
Here, excellence is conveyed by the word *nirbhara* (filled) itself.
Awakening is the arrival of consciousness caused by the departure of sleep;
it is the persistence of the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) in that form, as for example:

“With her eyes languid from the fresh onset of awakening, she turned away for a moment from the light of the jewel-lamps; heavy with her own efforts, she stretched her limbs with yawns that produced drops of moisture.”

"May the squinting glance of Hari—reddened by the interruption of his sleep, desiring to leave his bed which has the coils of his broad hoods as its pillow, and marked by the Nāga—protect you for a long time.
(55) Here, through the qualities of the glance such as its fresh opening and its sidelong curvature, it is perceived that his awakening is not yet complete;
thus these rasas, beginning with love (rati), have been described according to their various states (bhāva) and other distinctions.
Now, we shall describe certain specific characteristics of some among these very [rasas]:
therein,
the erotic, the heroic, the pathetic, the furious, the marvelous, and the terrifying;

The sentiments (rasas) are the loathsome, the comic, the amorous, the tranquil, the furious, and the haughty. Love is said to arise from nature, from association, from comparison, from spiritual reflection, from union, from pride, and from sensory objects. || 164–165 ||

Love (*prīti*) is also exactly like this; however, in this case, it is not that which arises from sexual union (*sāṃprayogikī*), but rather that which arises from practice (*ābhyāsikī*). Examples of its manifestations in that regard are as follows: "Thinking 'she is dead,' I resolved upon death so that I might unite with her after passing away. (166)
‘How is it that she, that very Avanti, has been obtained by me in this very birth?

Here, through the conjunction of the permanent emotion (sthāyin) with the determinants (vibhāva), the consequents (anubhāva), and the transitory states (vyabhicārin), there is the production of rasa; thus, love (rati) itself is produced in the form of the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra).

Here, the stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) of love belonging to the Lord of Vatsa arises from Vāsavadattā of Avanti, who serves as the objective determinant (*ālambanavibhāva*). This emotion, being further ignited by the excitant determinants (*uddīpanavibhāva*) such as her coming back to life, and being conjoined with the joy-based transitory emotions (*vyabhicāribhāva*) such as joy and fortitude—which are inferred from the verbal expression beginning with "she is dead" and so forth—attains the name of *śṛṅgāra* (erotic sentiment) in the form of a union (*saṃbhoga*) following upon the pathetic (*karuṇa*). [As it is said:
"Without having conquered the earth bounded by the oceans, and without having performed various sacrifices..."
‘How could I become a king without giving wealth to those who seek it? (67).

Here, the stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) of energy (*utsāha*), arising from the objective excitants (*ālambanavibhāva*) such as the conquest of the earth, is ignited by the subjective excitants (*uddīpanavibhāva*) such as steadfastness and courage. When the mental states of recollection, intelligence, and deliberation—which are inferred from the commencement of speech—have arisen, this [emotion] is designated by the term ‘heroic sentiment’ (*vīrarasa*).
[As it is said: ‘For her, even a bed of flowers causes pain because of her delicate limbs.’
"How can the Queen lie upon the funeral pyre containing the fire?

Here, the emotion of grief (*śoka*), which has arisen from the death of the Queen—the objective determinant (*ālambana-vibhāva*)—is ignited by the excitant determinants (*uddīpana-vibhāva*) such as her being placed on the pyre and the flames of the fire; it is then blended with transitory mental states (*vyabhicārin*) such as despondency, exhaustion, and discoloration, which are inferred from the commencement of speech, and is thus recognized as the Pathetic sentiment (*karuṇa*).
[As it is said: "By whom Kṛṣṇā was dragged by the hair right before my eyes..."

"This very wicked Duḥśāsana has been captured; how can he live for even a moment? (69). Here, the stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*)—the anger previously arisen in Bhīmasena toward the objective determinant (*ālambanavibhāva*) Duḥśāsana—is ignited by the excitant determinants (*uddīpanavibhāvas*) of the remembered and witnessed seizing of Draupadī’s hair and other acts. When the transitory emotions (*vyabhicāribhāvas*) consisting of suffering—such as indignation, agitation, trembling, and fatigue—inferred from his verbal outbursts, have arisen, it culminates in the Furious Sentiment (*raudrarasa*). Thus it is produced.
“The garments are the sprouts, the flowers are the necklaces and other ornaments, the fruit is the honey, and the branches are the palaces—such is the nature of the trees of the Nandana grove.

Here, while the natural form of ordinary trees consists of sprouts, flowers, fruits, and branches, for the trees of the Nandana grove, in place of those sprouts and so forth, there are garments, necklaces, honey, and mansions; this is indeed a marvel.

Therefore, from these excitants (*ālambana-vibhāva*) [such as the sight of Indra], wonder (*vismaya*) arises in someone who has attained the state of a god; this wonder, as a stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*), being kindled by excitants such as the sight of his limbs, and being brought to completion through transitory emotions (*vyabhicāribhāva*)—such as joy, horripilation, perspiration, and faltering speech—which arise and are inferred from verbal expressions, is called the "Astonishing" (*adbhuta*).
As in: “This is the thunderbolt of Maghavan, with fire residing in its edge; the mere memory of which is sufficient to cause the miscarriage of the embryos of the Daitya women. (71)

In this instance, the permanent emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) of fear arises in the wives of the Daityas from the "objective determinants" (*ālambanavibhāva*)—namely, Mahendra’s thunderbolt and the fire close to it—even when these are merely being recollected; this emotion is then inflamed by "excitant determinants" (*uddīpanavibhāva*) such as the recollection of the death of the Dānavas torn apart by that bolt, and is further combined with "consequent manifestations" (*anubhāva*) such as the miscarriage of their own fetuses, and with the "transitory emotions" (*vyabhicārin*) such as perspiration, paralysis, and trembling, which are inferred therefrom. Thus, having been brought to fruition in the form of the *bhayānaka* (fearful) rasa, even when described by someone else, it is designated as "the fearful. [As in:
"Drinking again and again the blood of your enemies with the hollows of their palms..."
"The *kauṇapas* (demons) dance together with headless trunks (*kabandhas*) adorned with entrails.

Here, from the demons who serve as the objective excitants (*ālambana-vibhāvas*), there arises in a certain man—proclaiming his victory over the enemy—the latent emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) of disgust (*jugupsā*). This emotion is inflamed by the inciting excitants (*uddīpana-vibhāvas*) such as the drinking of blood and the dancing of headless trunks drenched in streams of blood trickling from severed heads; and when the transitory emotions (*vyabhicāribhāvas*) such as fear, agitation, suspicion, and dissimulation—which are to be inferred from the commencement of speech—have arisen, it is fully realized and designated as the "disgustful" (*bībhatsa*) sentiment.
"O friend, this fresh nail-mark upon the slope of your breast belongs to one whose pride has not yet faded; let it be covered with your upper garment."

In this context, a certain woman perceives her friend—who previously maintained pride toward her husband and whose breasts are marked by his very nail-scratches—as the *ālambana-vibhāva* (the objective basis) for laughter. This laughter, which has arisen in that woman, is the *sthāyibhāva* (the dominant emotion). It is kindled by *uddīpana-vibhāvas* (excitants), such as the recollection of her husband’s previous seizure of her pride; it is brought to completion through the *vyabhicāribhāvas* (transitory states)—such as apprehension, feigned indifference, and faltering speech—which are inferred from the commencement of her speech. This [laughter] is designated by the term "hāsya" (the comic).
[As the verse says: "Whatever pleases me, that alone my beloved does."

"Thus she knows, yet she does not understand that which her beloved does"—here, from the object of affection (the beloved) as an *ālambana-vibhāva*, there arises the stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) of love (*sneha*) belonging to the hero Lalita, who is of a *vatsala* (affectionate) nature. This emotion, being kindled by excitant factors (*uddīpana-vibhāvas*) such as the delicacy of the object, his own nature, and so forth, and being combined with transitory emotions (*vyabhicāri-bhāvas*) such as delusion, fortitude, and recollection, as well as with consequent actions (*anubhāvas*), reaches its full development and is perceived as "Preyas" (the state of being dear).
Furthermore, this very [state] is held to be the fundamental source of both *rati* (erotic passion) and *prīti* (affection).
As they have said:
"There is no remedy for that partiality which is without cause; for it is a thread composed of affection that sews together the innermost vital parts. (75)
"All prosperities belong to him whose mind is content;
for one whose feet are covered by shoes, the earth is indeed carpeted with leather.

(76) Here, in the case of a certain hero of the *dhīra-śānta* (calm and composed) type whose nature is tranquil, the stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) of contentment (*dhṛti*) arises from the objective excitants (*ālambana-vibhāva*) consisting of wives and other enjoyments that have come to him according to his heart's desire; this emotion, being kindled by the subjective excitants (*uddīpana-vibhāva*) such as contemplation of the true nature of reality, accompanied by the transitory emotions (*vyabhicāribhāva*) such as memory and so forth, and followed by external manifestations such as speech and gestures, reaches its full development and is designated as the "Calm" (*śānta*).
Others, however, declare that tranquility is his very nature; yet this is merely a particular manifestation of his fortitude:
"Since she is common property, even another might ask for her hand without fear;
how much more so the great-grandson of the Creator, the conqueror of the worlds? (77)

In this context, the mind of Rāma, who is by nature of a noble temperament (*udāttaprakṛti*) and is inherently intent upon the truth, does not incline toward what is improper, nor does it desist once it has begun to act. That mind, having engaged in the thought, "This Sītā is worthy of being accepted by me," is inflamed by Rāvaṇa’s solicitation and Lakṣmaṇa’s incitement; it is then brought to fruition in the form of the *udātta* (noble) rasa, being conjoined with emerging anxiety, deliberation, bashfulness, dissimulation, recollection, and so forth, as well as with discernment, skill, nobility, fortitude, and other qualities inferred from her timely responses.
"Let there be no fear in your mind that 'I am an offender'; my sword never desires to strike those who have turned their backs.

Here, the sense is conveyed that the pride which is ever-rooted—namely, "let there be no fear in your heart that I have committed an offense against him," and "my sword never dares to strike those who face away"—is what is perceived.
This very sentiment, characterized by pride and termed "the haughty" (uddhata), is as follows;
some, however, [define it thus]:
"When base enemies have been brought under control by relying on steadfastness..."

"The greatness of the great becomes manifest through compassion. (79) Thus, those who place the term *ūrjakhin* (the powerful one) within the category of the *udātta* (noble) cite the previously mentioned example of the height of pride—"As long as I have taken up arms," etc.—as an illustration of its accomplishment; and they describe its natural occurrence in specific instances of passion (*rati*), as follows:

"Disregarding the lords of the four quarters, beginning with Mahendra, this proud woman desires to obtain as her husband the wielder of the Pināka bow— who cannot be won by physical beauty— because of his subjugation of Madana.
In this case, she acts thus naturally due to the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) from a previous birth.
An example of the *sāṃsargikī* (associative) type is as follows:

“O virtuous lady, those winds from the snowy mountain, which have just now burst open the leaf-buds of the *devadāru* trees and proceed toward the south fragrant with the flow of their resin—if they have previously touched your body, I shall embrace them. (81)

In this context, although the winds—due to their coolness, fragrance, and so forth—are sources of distress for those separated from their lovers, they are embraced by the expectation of contact with the limbs of the beloved; thus, through association, this becomes a simile-based [poetic figure], as in:
"Even in this pair of children, there exists clearly that various corresponding trait of Janaka’s daughter which must be inferred through skill."
"Is it not as if that face of my beloved, possessing the splendor of a fresh hundred-petaled lotus, has once again come within the range of my eyes?
(82). This is *rati* (passionate love) directed toward Sītā; by means of seeing an object of comparison for her, it delights Rāma.
An example of *ādhyātmikī* (internalized love) is as follows:

‘“I remember her as one who rejected my advances, not as the sage’s daughter whom I accepted; yet my heart, though intensely pained, seems to convince me otherwise. (83) Here, the love of Duṣyanta—who has forgotten the circumstances of his marriage and so forth due to the curse of Durvāsas—for Śakuntalā becomes *adhyātma* (internalized).’
An example of the *ābhiyogikī* (arising from application) is as follows:

“By the side-glances of the long-lashed-eyed one—glances languid, turned aside, charming, tender, motionless, and slow, with pupils smiling with an ever-increasing internal wonder—my heart, which has no other refuge, has been stolen, cast away, drunk up, and uprooted. (84)
Thus, when Mālatī employs her sidelong glances indicative of an excess of passion, an intense sexual desire (*sāṃprayogikī rati*) arises in Mādhava, as for example:
"When the beloved forcibly raises his face by seizing his hair and kisses him..."

"‘Huṃ-hūṃ! Release me!’—thus the soft murmuring of her who treasures her pride is victorious. (85) Here, because of the very gentle application of words meaning "threatening," "release," and "restraining," the arising of passion (*rati*) during the union of the proud woman is perceived as being based on self-conceit (*ābhimānikī*). For example:
‘This is the fortune in the home; this is an ambrosial balm for the eyes; this touch upon her body is like thick sandalwood paste;
this arm around the neck is a cool and smooth string of pearls—what is not dear about her? Only her separation is utterly unbearable.
(86) Here, the specific inclination is *abhimāna* (self-conceit); from that alone do such forms of love (*rati*) arise.
Regarding worldly [objects], in the case of sound, for example:

“The songs of the women threshing the *kalama* rice shine forth, made resonant by the jingling of bracelets as they slip against one another on their arms that tremble from the playfully smooth, gleaming pestles; they are further filled with a melodic rhythm broken by the forceful quivering of their chests during their low, passionate hums. (87)
Regarding touch, for example:
"Causing horripilation on the limbs, producing bliss in the mind, and closing the eyes—this touch of the beloved proceeds. (88)
Regarding form, for example:
“Drinking in Rāghava with their eyes, those women did not go toward other objects; for the activity of their remaining senses had entered [into him] as if entirely through their eyes. (89)
As in the case of rasa (flavor):
“O charming one, whose mind would this lower lip of yours—not pale as coral, like a desert path—not render thirsty? (90)

Regarding scent, for example: “O you skilled in the work of cooking, do not be distressed; the fire smokes as it emits the fragrant breeze from its mouth, red like a *pāṭala* flower, but it does not blaze up. (91)
"O you who are skilled in the art of cooking, do not be angry! Inhaling the fragrant breath from your mouth, which is as red as the *pāṭala* flower, the fire smokes but does not blaze.
As for what is natural regarding particular forms of affection:

"Blessed are those who, bearing sons who rest upon their laps—sons with bud-like teeth, spontaneous smiles, and speech made charming by indistinct syllables—and who become soiled by the dust of those children's limbs; for whenever love arises, she then feels affection for her sons, or rather, it arises in the form of her sons—thus the natural disposition (*nisarga*) consisting of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) from previous births is brought into harmony. (92) In this passage, the fact that "whenever love arises, she then feels affection for her sons, or rather, it arises in the form of her sons" accords with the natural disposition (*nisarga*) which consists of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) from previous births.
An example of situational (sāṃsargikī) [praise] is as follows:
“The Goddess Earth gave birth to you; King Janaka, equal to Prajāpati, is your father.
O daughter, you are the daughter-in-law of those kings in whose lineage both the Sun and we ourselves are gurus. (93)
In this case, due to the association with Viśvambharā and others, the venerable Vasiṣṭha feels affection for Sītā;
this is an example of *aupamānikī* [affection], as follows:
"The youth, dark and glossy like the petals of a blue lotus, adorned with a topknot, possessing holy splendor, and honoring the assembly of young students with his very beauty—"
“Having become like a child once again, this son of mine, the joy of the Raghus, suddenly—when seen—acts as a nectar-ointment for my eyes; who is this?
Here, Janaka feels affection for Lava because of his resemblance to Rāma.
An example of the spiritual (ādhyātmikī) [type of beauty] is as follows:
"The son of Pṛthā enveloped him on all sides with affection; for even when a kinsman is unrecognized, the mind rejoices spontaneously.
(95) Here, even though he was unrecognized, Vāsava, upon seeing his own son Arjuna, causes him joy.
An example of [the *bhāva*] arising from application (*ābhiyogikī*) is as follows:

“‘This one whose kinsmen are unknown to me is the lord of bears and monkeys; this is the descendant of Pulastya, who strikes first in battles’—having been addressed thus with respect by the Joy of the Raghus, Bharata paid homage to both [Hanumān and Sugrīva], who had surpassed Lakṣmaṇa. (96)

Here, due to Rāma’s diligent pursuit of Sītā and other efforts, the affection of Sugrīva and Vibhīṣaṇa arises as *sāṃprayogikī* (arising from immediate application) in its proper place; an example of *ābhyāsikī* (arising from habitual practice) is as follows:
“Thus, having forgotten his own other duties, the king of men had the burden of sovereignty supported by his ministers...”
"Like a clever mistress, hunting captivated him through constant attendance that increased his passion.
Here,
[the figure is] that which exists outside of words and so forth, characterized by the practice of action.
“Delight arising from habituation is to be known as that which occurs in activities such as hunting. This definition applies to the delight born of self-conceit (*ābhimānikī*), as follows:

“If there is a conflict with those solar kings— who, by granting the gift of fearlessness from the Lord Vaivasvata [Yama], have kindled the fire of their own kṣatriya prowess to burn the arrogant— then it is my good fortune that my bow has its string consecrated by the fierce, flickering rays of the blazing weapons.
Here, Kuśa is satisfied because he has obtained his desired opponent, following immediately upon Lava.
Regarding sounds pertaining to objects (*vaiṣayikī*), as for example:

"Flutes, sweet as the end of night with their aesthetic charms, producing sounds from rows of shells whose openings are blocked by fingers moving in the ancient rhythmic style, and whose breath is softly drawn in—these flutes are being drunk by the ears of the city women, which are slightly drowsy from sleep and possess lips as charming as those of a maiden with a fresh wound. (99)
Regarding touch, for example:

“The breeze, having its heat subdued, gently blowing, and having brushed against the lotuses of the playful women, gave as it were a supporting arm with its taken-up spray, moving within the succession of its waves. (100)
As for example, in the case of *rūpa* (form):

“This mountain, with its lofty peaks dark as a fresh cloud, where peacocks cry out repeatedly in their intoxication, whose trees are thick with nests variegated by birds, and which possesses massive boulders, bestows delight upon the eyes. (101)
As an example regarding rasa (flavor):
“This Phālguna is going [to partake] of sugarcane, the scum of boiled rice, curd, flour-based sweets, and the meat of a boar. (102)
Regarding fragrance—as in:
"Where the fragrance produced by the oozing sap of *sarala* trees, rubbed by elephants to relieve the itching of their temples, perfumes the mountain ridges. (103)
This is merely an illustration;

therefore, from *utsāha* (energy) arise varieties such as the heroic (*vīra*) in battle, charity (*dāna*), and compassion (*dayā*); from *krodha* (anger), varieties such as *bhāma*, *manyu*, and *tprāsa*; from *hāsa* (laughter), varieties such as *smita*, *hasita*, and *vihasita*; and from *supta* (sleep), *pralaya* (dissolution), *mati* (intellection), and so forth, varieties such as dreaming (*svapna*), death (*maraṇa*), and tranquility (*śama*) are produced.

In this regard, although the heroic sentiment of battle (*yuddhavīra*) is described through the phrase "without conquering the earth bounded by the oceans," the heroic sentiment of generosity (*dānavīra*) through "without performing various sacrifices," and the heroic sentiment of compassion (*dayāvīra*) through "without giving wealth to supplicants"—all being manifested in the form of energy (*utsāha*)—nevertheless, each of these is shown individually to be capable of bringing about the realization of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).
Among them, the heroic sentiment of battle is as follows:
"Behold this very spot before you; here, it is said, Hara, while sporting as a Kirāta, was impetuously struck on the crown of his head with a bow by Arjuna (Kirīṭin)."
Having heard this wonderful tale on Mount Himavat, the Lord of Subhadrā very slowly made an ornament for his own two powerful arms.
As for the hero of giving (dānavīra), for example:
[He was filled] with a longing for the side-dishes from the oceans of curds, milk, and ghee.
"In whose great festival of giving the earth itself acted as the *hantakāra* (the sacrificial fee).
An example of the hero of compassion (*dayāvīra*) is as follows:
"Therefore, you must strive to sustain my bodily existence with your own body."
"O Great Sage, let this cow, whose young calf is anxious for the end of the day, be released.

Although twenty-four varieties of pride (*māna*) arise as subdivisions of anger (*krodha*), such as *bhāma* and so forth, nevertheless, because all are subsumed within the categories of the graceful (*lalita*), the ungraceful (*alalita*), and both, only three types are demonstrated therein.
Among these, the graceful anger of women is *bhāma*, as follows:

‘Where lovers, seeking to win back their favor, were made supplicants by the women’s fits of anger— anger that knit the brows, made the lips quiver, and threatened with playful fingers pointed at them.
(107) *Manyu* (resentment), which arises from the suffering born of a beloved’s offense, is as follows:

‘Her gaze, heavy with longing for her husband, falls in many directions— difficult to behold as it rests upon ear-ornaments fashioned from the creepers of the bow-stalks of the *dhana-dhanva* tree. (108)
"The gaze upon the face of the bridegroom is heavy with tears and appears distressed.

Now, one might ask: why is this not considered *īrṣyā* (envy)? It is because here it is not merely the indignation (*amarṣa*) involved in the granting of a formal insult (*māna*), but rather the extreme suffering produced by it. This is like the feigned censure or playful mockery (*utprāsa*) directed toward those such as a beloved, for example: [The verse continues: "O you who have stolen my heart, you who have made me a slave to your glance, you who have bound me with the ropes of your arms! O you who have made me a prisoner, where shall I go? Alas, I am ruined! In this case, the speaker is not truly angry; rather, she speaks thus out of affection for her lover. Therefore, this is not *īrṣyā*. Furthermore, since the term *māna* (insult) is used here, it cannot be classified as *virodha* (contradiction). Nor can it be *praṇaya-kopa* (anger born of affection), because that state does not exist in the absence of *īrṣyā*. Consequently, this is a distinct variety of *māna* known as *duḥkha-māna* (the insult consisting of suffering). Or, for example, in the following verse: "Though he has committed no fault, I shall show him anger; though he has done nothing, I shall abandon him. Even if he were to die before my eyes, I would not weep; even if he were to live, I would not rejoice. Yet, when he departs for another village, I shall surely weep. Alas, the mind of women is difficult to understand! In this instance, the woman is not truly angry; rather, she speaks thus out of affection for her husband. Thus, this is a distinct variety of *māna* called *sādhvasa-māna* (the insult consisting of trepidation). Alternatively, as in the following verse: "O you who have stolen my heart, you who have made me a slave to your glance, you who have bound me with the ropes of your arms! O you who have made me a prisoner, where shall I go? Alas, I am ruined! In this case, the speaker is not truly angry; rather, she speaks thus out of affection for her lover. Therefore, this is not *īrṣyā*. Furthermore, since the term *māna* is used here, it cannot be classified as *virodha*. Nor can it be *praṇaya-kopa*, because that state does not exist in the absence of *īrṣyā*. Consequently, this is a distinct variety of *māna* known as *duḥkha-māna*. Or, for example, as in the following verse: "Though he has committed no fault, I shall show him anger; though he has done nothing, I shall abandon him. Even if he were to die before my eyes, I would not weep; even if he were to live, I would not rejoice. Yet, when he departs for another village, I shall surely weep. Alas, the mind of women is difficult to understand! In this instance, the woman is not truly angry; rather, she speaks thus out of affection for her husband. Thus, this is a distinct variety of *māna* called *sādhvasa-māna*. Or, for example, as in the following verse: "Though he has committed no fault, I shall show him anger; though he has done nothing, I shall abandon him. Even if he were to die before my eyes, I would not weep; even if he were to live, I would not rejoice. Yet, when he departs for another village, I shall surely weep. Alas, the mind of women is difficult to understand! In this instance, the woman is not truly angry; rather, she speaks thus out of affection for her husband. Thus, this is a distinct variety of *māna* called *sādhvasa-māna*. Or, for example, as in the following verse: "Though he has committed no fault, I shall show him anger; though he has done nothing, I shall abandon him. Even if he were to die before my eyes, I would not weep; even if he were to live, I would not rejoice. Yet, when he departs for another village, I shall surely weep. Alas, the mind of women is difficult to understand
‘Men indeed have power over women; what is it here, O handsome one, that you have been so ordained? What fault is there in her noble birth? (109)
What fault is there in noble birth when it is prompted by affection?

Although varieties such as derisive laughter (*upahāsa*) are possible for *hāsa* (laughter), they are nonetheless included within *vihasita*; thus, three of its subdivisions are illustrated here, being only slightly more or less [intense]: among these, *smita* (a slight smile) is as follows:
‘If there were a flower set upon a sprout, or a pearl resting within a bright coral,
then it might imitate her bright smile, which casts its luster upon her copper-red lips.
An example of laughter in which the beauty of the teeth is visible:

“Today you surpass the splendor of the moon with the brilliance of your smile, which is intensified by the clusters of rays from your teeth— a brilliance that acts as a lamp for witnessing Gaṇapati’s performance of the *tāṇḍava* dance, and which dispels the darkness of the night at its terrifying onset.
Such is laughter with specific qualities— as follows:

"May that Śiva protect you, and the Daughter of the Mountain, and that Moon of Play whose body was filled with the rays of her teeth, as the Daughter of the Mountain, with a smiling face, having joined together the fallen crescent of the moon and the bracelet broken in a lovers' quarrel into a circle, said, 'Look!
An example of a specific type of sleep, *svapna* (dream), is as follows:
“I know my beloved was seen by me today in a dream, turned away in anger; weeping and crying out, ‘Do not, do not touch me with your hand,’ she began to walk away before me.
Before I could embrace my dear one and comfort her with hundreds of endearments, O brother, I was robbed of my sleep by that rogue Fate.
A specific type of fainting is death, as for example:

“Beholding that [garland], which was the companion of her well-formed breasts for but a moment, the queen of the king closed her eyes in distress, like the night whose moon has been stolen by darkness.
(114) An example of tranquility (*śama*) as a specific state of mind (*mativiśeṣa*) is as follows:
"When there was ignorance, produced by the latent impressions of the darkness of forgetfulness, then this entire world was seen as consisting of women;
now, for us who have applied the collyrium of superior discernment, our vision has become equalized, and it regards even the three worlds as Brahman.
Other instances of this kind, based on rasa, bhāva, and so forth, are also to be understood in this way.
Now, the specific varieties, the appropriate timing, and the remaining points are demonstrated.
(167) Among these, the substratum is threefold: male, female, and animals, etc. Of these, the male is as follows:

‘It is a marvel that, through the proximity of the spotless moon of the lotus-eyed one’s face, my mind repeatedly falls into a state of numbness, and a liquid transformation is maintained within it by my heart, just as a mountain of natural moonstone is liquefied.
As in the example concerning a woman:

"Then, O Lord, by that heat of her difficult-to-speak words, Sītā— though gentle by nature— attained a state of harshness and blazed forth, suddenly vomiting out rays of speech that were sharp and clear, like a sun-crystal stone.
As for [the expression of anger] among animals and so forth:
"He cries out, sighs, faints, and goes to the bank; from the bank he goes to a tree, and from beneath the tree he returns again to the pond.
In the pond he finds no pleasure and eats not even a piece of lotus stalk—the ruddy goose, indeed, during the nights of separation from his mate.
The objects of experience (*viṣaya*) are threefold: sentient, sub-human, and insentient.
Among these, the conscious [type] is as follows:
“This is she, the one-eyed Lolākṣī, the sole abode of the ornament of the three worlds; and this is that wicked-souled man by whom my sister was wronged.
On one side is intense passion, on the other is the heavy fire of anger; this disguise has been assumed—how can I reconcile this? Thus my mind reels. (119)
An example from the animal kingdom is as follows:
“When her beloved returned, the wife of the desert lands, reflecting on the difficulty of crossing [the wasteland], fixed her gaze upon his face, trembling with tears of joy;
she then respectfully wiped with the hem of her own garment the dust clinging to the tips of the mane of the young camel, who was chewing mouthfuls of *pīlu*, *śamī*, and *karīra* fruits. (120)
An example of the insentient [type] is as follows:

“The lordly elephant did not repeatedly seize the sugarcane stalk thrown before him, nor did he look toward the female elephant who had approached his side; with eyes half-closed, he remembered the great festivals of dwelling in the pleasure-grove at his own will. (121)
Knowledge is threefold: that which is seen, that which is heard, and that which is born of inference.
Among these, "that which is seen" is as follows:
"Even a lotus pierced by *śaivala* moss is beautiful; even the dark spot of the cool-rayed moon spreads its splendor."
"This slender girl is exceedingly charming even with her bark garment; for what indeed is not an ornament for forms that are naturally sweet?
As it has been heard:
"What form does that moon-faced one clearly possess? That is truly marvelous. Is it to incite me to harm another that my sister’s heart is set upon this?"
"Thus my mind, agitated by inner surging thoughts, functions in such a way that even this short path before me seems to stretch into length.
As for inference (*anumāna*):
"This hermitage is peaceful, yet my arm throbs; what fruit can there be from this?"
"Or rather, doors for what is destined to happen exist everywhere.
(124) Conditioning is threefold: respectful, intense, and habitual.
Among these, that which arises from a sense of respect due to the excellence of the basis is the "respectful" [conditioning], as for example:
‘A jewel of a maiden, not born from a womb, belongs to you; and we are seekers of such a jewel. Whatever jewel exists anywhere, it shall accrue to us—even from Śakra.

For the very purpose of a maiden is considered to be the welfare of others. By giving her away, I shall become your kinsman, and Pulastya, Pulaha, and the foremost of the others shall be your relatives.
An example of a sharp cognition arising from a sharp sensory quality:

"Her birth from the sacrificial ground of the gods, her father being a king who expounds the Veda, and her exceedingly radiant form inspire affection in me. That which has arisen through the conviction of repeated practice, by means of the recurrence of knowledge, is called "practiced" (abhyasta).
For example:

"Having seen Mādhava again and again as he wanders along the streets of the nearby city, Mālatī, standing at the high window of her palace's turret, experiences love as if it were new; she languishes with limbs utterly distressed by intense longing. (127)

In this context, although a cognition may be intense due to the quality of the object and yet be weak due to the quality of its substratum— and thus produce both an intense cognition and a weak latent impression (*saṃskāra*)— nevertheless, that which arises through repeated practice as something more intense and most strongly reinforced is called "cultivated" (*abhyasta*).
Among the excitant factors (*uddīpana-vibhāva*), such as garlands, garments, ornaments, and so forth,
the garland is exemplified as follows:

‘She wears an ornament of spring flowers: *karṇikāra* blossoms that surpass rubies in brilliance and draw away the luster of gold, and *sindhuvāra* flowers fashioned into a string of pearls, while the *aśoka* flowers have been cast aside.
As for her garment:
‘With her breasts slightly bending the garment she wore, possessing the hue of the rising sun, she was like a moving, leafy creeper bent down by a cluster of well-formed blossoms.
As for an ornament, for example:

‘The mutual generation of beauty between her neck, which was graced by breasts, and the flat pearl necklace, resulted in a shared relationship where each served as both the ornament and the object to be adorned.
(130) [The factors such as] season, age, intoxication, and so forth; [the factors such as] season and so forth.
Among these, the season (*ṛtu*) is as follows:

“This object of my desire is unattainable, and the five-arrowed god [Kāma] afflicts my mind even at its first onset; how much more so now that sprouts are displayed by the mango trees in the grove, their pale leaves uprooted by the Malaya breeze? (131)

An example of *vayaḥ* (age): “‘Surely you have deluded me, O one of no other birth; let not your mind become thick with defiled transformations,’ and so forth—but here [such a plea] is indeed useless, because both desire, whose qualities have expanded, and fresh youth are present. (132)
An example of intoxication (*mada*) is as follows:

"At that moment, with their modesty overturned, neither wishing to go to bed nor desiring passion, that fair-faced woman became subject to the control of both the Wielder of the Trident and of intoxication. (133)
Sandalwood baths, incense, and so forth refer to sandalwood and the like; among these, sandalwood is as follows:
"Sandalwood has its abode in venomous serpents, and both the moon and wine are siblings to poison."
They cause torment in separation; what more can be said? That they do not kill is indeed a marvel. (134) As for the bath—for example:
"Of those whose eyes are clouded by tears, and whose thighs and hips are revealed by their wet garments..."
‘For the sake of those with copper-hued eyes, whose thighs and hips are revealed by moist garments, and who are accustomed to bathing in the afternoon, does the God of Love not bear his bow? (135)
As for incense—for example:

“In the hair of women, which had been released after being moistened by bathing and was still fragrant from the lingering scent of incense, with evening jasmine flowers tucked therein, the god of love regained his strength, which had been weakened by the passing of spring. (136)
The rise of the moon, the sound of clouds, the recollection of a benefactor, and so forth—these are examples such as the "rise of the moon.
Among these, the rise of the moon is illustrated as follows:
"While this moon, with its light moistened by sandalwood paste, was anointing the faces of the quarters, [the lover] then performed a service for that fawn-eyed woman..."
Tears in your eyes, your face in your hand, your life-breaths in the hollow of your throat, you yourself in your heart, shame on your back, and only your virtues in your speech—you have become thus.

(137) An example of a deep resonance (*ghanadhvani*) is as follows: "Today, as I recall the pleasures experienced with him... [The verse continues: *ajja mae teṇa viṇā aṇuhūasuhāiṃ saṃmaraṃtīe...* (Today, as I am remembering the joys experienced by me without him...)
"Today, as I recalled the pleasures experienced in his absence, I heard the roar of the fresh clouds like the execution drum. [138]

An example of the recollection of a favor is as follows: “That [act] agitates my mind, when, upon seeing me strike with fresh vigor, she—disregarding her slipping upper garment and with eyes as tremulous as those of a frightened yearling fawn—embraced me with limbs as if steeped in nectar. (139)
Regarding the [past] experiences, he remembers as follows:
“Even for a moment it does not depart from my hearts, which suffer daily from the weight of what was given, like a *śyāmā* creeper harboring secret sins. (140)
[Day after day, she of the dark limbs, burdened by the heavy sorrow she has inflicted, does not depart from my heart for even a moment, like a secret sin feared for its consequences.
As she desires:
‘In this very way, having failed to perform meritorious deeds and not having attained my heart’s desire, I shall perish;
even public rumor has not yet arisen regarding that son of a farmer.
(141) ‘Thus indeed, lacking merit and with my wishes unfulfilled, I shall come to ruin.’
Not even a rumor has arisen concerning that son of a plowman.
As for how she hates him:
"Having heard of the overturning of the cart, O dear friend, today on this festive day, my lady..."
“O friend, having heard the slip of the tongue regarding her beloved today, this day and night do not seem like an ornament to her, any more than a garland to a buffalo condemned to death. (142)
He exerts himself as follows:
“Following the daughter of the sage, his forward progress suddenly checked by decorum, though he did not move from his place, it was as if he had gone and then returned again. (143)
For example:
"Her face is like the moon; the taste of her mouth is like nectar; to whom is her passionate embrace, bright with the joy of a spontaneous grasp, comparable? (144)
[Her face is like the moon; the taste of her mouth is like nectar;
to whom is her passionate kiss, brilliant with the impetuosity of seizing the hair, comparable?
It is considered as follows:
"In separation,
she perceives the moon— though it is the lord of the night— as if it were the bodiless god of love with his arrows drawn into a circle, or as if it were a deer that has turned back toward calamity."
In separation, she regards the moon—with its captivating rays—as if it were a calamity that has arisen.
As she says:
"Let no conversation be given, on the pretext that it would be contrary to worldly custom."
‘“Do not engage in conversation with one who is contrary to worldly custom”— making such an excuse, who does not even cast a glance at an enemy when he has come face to face? (146)
It acts as follows:
“Today I must go; even in thick darkness, that dear lady performs the sequence of glances at her lover with eyes half-closed. (147)
"Today I must go, even through the thick darkness; that fortunate man makes me walk through the rooms with my eyes closed, following the sequence of his footsteps.
