By the touch moistened with the sweat of your conversation, you are led to something indescribable.
As for tears—for example: "With a gaze slowed by the weight of arms rolling within the interior of her eyes..."
"O child, what was there that you were not told by her whose gaze was languid with a flood of tears rolling within her eyes, and who was habituated to looking at you again and again? (149)
Joy is as follows: “Even when everything was lost, there was indeed satisfaction for the heart, because during that village fire, a jar was seized hand-to-hand. (150)
"Even though all his possessions were consumed by fire, there was indeed a sense of relief for his heart, because during that village conflagration, he seized the water-pot hand-to-hand.
As for indignation (*amarṣa*): [Example follows].
"O dear friend, how could union with my beloved ever come to me, even at nightfall, when the moon-demon, having seized his weapon, still roams about?"
That the moon, that outcaste, survives while clutching his bundle of rays like a beggar’s staff!
*Līlā* (playful imitation) is the imitation of the actions of a beloved person during amorous sports and the like—for example:
“Whatever you do, whatever you say, whatever you look upon...”
"For one who is habitually imitating whatever you do, whatever you say, and whatever you look at, a long day does not suffice. (152)
*Vilāsa* (graceful play) is the shining forth of the specific movements of the eyes, eyebrows, and face; for example:

"Then, having said 'This is he' with a playful movement of her eyebrows, as if looking at me with recognition, she cast side-long glances sweet with the nectar of smiles, released by her circle of friends who were expert in mutual expressions. (153)
*Vicchitti* (artistic refinement) is the unconventional arrangement of ornaments and the like; for example:

“Limbs grey with the dust of sandalwood paste, lips as red as betel-juice, eyes with clear collyrium, and garments exceedingly thin—in women, these are the ornaments, and all else is mere wealth. (154)
The misplaced application of ornaments and the like is *vibhrama* (bewilderment), as for example:

“A certain woman, her mental state directed toward her beloved, placed a girdle upon the surface of her breasts marked with white sandalwood paste, and she wore a necklace upon the curve of her hips. (155)
*Kilakiñcita* is the repeated blending of smiles, weeping, laughter, and so forth, arising from joy; for example:
“The shaking of sprout-like hands, internal hissing sounds, half-closed eyes, and faltering words in private became the weapons of Love for women. (156)
*Moṭṭāyita* is a physical transformation arising from the contemplation of the beloved during conversation about them, as for example:

“When she repeatedly touches her ear with the tip of her finger during those stories of yours, she surely brings it to a state of fullness because it is never satiated by the multitude of your virtues. (157)
*Kuṭṭamita* is the manifestation of the perception of pleasure even during suffering through the seizing of the hair, breasts, lips, and so forth; for example:

“Out of bashfulness, she lowered her face during an embrace; yet, full of passion, he drew it down toward his chest and drank from the lotus-face of the woman, whose petal-like lip was pressed against his and whose eyes were closed. (158)
*Vivvoka* is a form of affected indifference caused by pride, self-conceit, or a sense of superiority when one's desired object is attained, as illustrated by disregard and contempt;
for example: "Then, having parted her lips, the Daughter of the Mountain King, intent on disregarding her husband’s words, addressed Vijayā standing nearby without apparent cause. (159)

Lalita (gracefulness) is the graceful placement of hands, feet, and limbs due to delicacy—for example: “Then, with her left lotus-foot dancing gracefully to the deep resonance of her heavy anklets, she moved forward, placing her other foot very slowly, languid with passion. (160)
Even at a time when speech was required, she performed her action by speaking with her body, as follows:

"Having been told by her friend in jest, 'Touch the crescent moon on your husband's head with this,' she, having colored her feet, offered a blessing and struck her with the garland without a word. (161)
*Krīḍita* (play) is a particular type of diversion common to childhood, youth, and early adulthood, as for example:

“In her childhood, she took delight in building sand altars on the banks of the Mandākinī with her friends, playing with balls and dolls; standing in their midst, she seemed to repeatedly experience the very essence of play. (162)
Play (*krīḍita*) is indeed sport (*kelī*) directed toward a beloved, as for example:

“A certain woman with high, full breasts, her mind longing [for him], struck her lover on his chest with her bosom, as he was apparently unable to brush away the pollen from the flowers [on her] from her eyes with the breath of her face. (163)
*Helā* (sportiveness) is the exhilaration of the mind that causes one to engage impulsively out of passion in playful activities and the like.
As an example of this in a woman:
"Shining at the door of the temple of love is her arm, extended for the embrace of her lover..."
‘The pair of her vine-like arms,
with their thick burden of breasts heaving from the playful pressure of her lover’s embrace, shines at the door of the chamber of love. (164)
The same [sentiment] appears in relation to a man, as follows:

"May the body of Lakṣmī purify you—her body whose arms hang limp as she, at the end of lovemaking while rising up, supports the weight [of her husband] with one hand and holds her garment with the other, while the mass of her loosened hair rests upon her shoulder; and which was led back to the bed by Śauri, who, his love for the sexual union redoubled by her beauty at that moment, embraced her. (165)
Indeed, a particular arrangement of words is *hāva*,
as it is in the case of a woman:
"If you do not touch the *puṣpavatī* before you, then why do you stand obstructing the way?"
‘If you do not touch Puṣpavatī who stands before you, then why do you stand there having been warded off?
You have already been touched by our hands as they ran forward with a *culu-culu* sound. (166)
This very same [state] occurs in a person, as in:
“Let the world suffer, let it suffer; let there be ill repute, let that be so.
Come, plunge into this [fire]; O Puṣpavatī, sleep does not come to me. (167)
"Let the world suffer; let it be a matter of reproach—let that be so.
Come, plunge into my side, O Puṣpavatī; sleep does not come to me.
By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), states of being (*bhāva*) and other such factors are understood.
The states existing in them regarding women are as follows:
“The graceful charms of women shine forth only so long as their eyes, resembling the petals of the blue water-lily, remain closed. (168)
The playful charms of women shine forth during the time of dalliance only so long as their eyes, possessing the luster of blue lotus petals, do not close in sleep.
An example of a pretext used by a man is as follows:
"O fortunate one, with eyes closed in feigned sleep, your limbs bristling with thrill from the kiss upon my cheek—grant me the opportunity; I shall not delay you again. (169)
O you whose limbs bristle with thrill at the kissing of my cheek, I shall not delay any longer.
An example of a woman’s confidential speech: "He too became embarrassed; then I laughed and embraced him firmly."
‘He too became embarrassed; and I, having laughed, embraced him firmly as he searched for the knot of his garment which had slipped off first. (170)

An example of flattery between a man and a woman: “While he was wiping away the single tear that had fallen from his hand with the wind of his breath, I, smiling, seized him by the neck with my second [hand]. (171)
[While he was fanning with the breath from his mouth one hand that was agitated by a blow, I, laughing, seized him by the throat with my second hand.
An illustration of a man’s manifestation of love:
‘In the playful slip of the groom’s name, the gaze of the bride, overflowing with tears, bestows blossoming joy upon her who dwells in the abode of many perfumes. (172)
In the bedchamber of the many-storied mansion, the bride’s gaze is clouded with tears.
As for the jesting of a woman, it is as follows:
"O brother-in-law, do you not see the window? Why do you look in vain?"
‘O brother-in-law, do you not see?
Why do you gaze in vain at the sky? Look at the row of half-moons upon the base of your wife’s arms! (173)
A man’s curiosity is as follows:
“Go home while your ornaments are still incomplete; O daughter, you will not remain fixed in the heart of that curious youth who has been made to utter cries of joy.”
"Go home, daughter, before you have finished your adornment; otherwise, you will not remain in the heart of that curious man whose longing has already passed.
An example of the *cakita* (startled) sentiment in a woman:

“Something was done by that farmer’s daughter-in-law, who was delighted by a blow preceded by the asking of her husband’s name, such that even today young women wander from house to house practicing it. (175)
Even today, young women wander from house to house to learn [these arts]:

playfulness (*helā*), coquettish gestures (*hāva*), inner emotion (*bhāva*), artifice (*vyāja*), confidential conversation (*visrambhabhāṣaṇa*), flattery (*cāṭu*), the manifestation of love (*premābhisaṃdhāna*), jesting (*parihāsa*), and curiosity (*kutūhala*). || 168 ||

And "startled" (cakita) are thus specified as certain gestures of amorous sports; the nature of the remaining ones will manifest in the context of the pathos of separation (vipralambha) and so forth. || 169 ||

In this regard, when two protagonists—whether previously unacquainted, already acquainted, or separated after having been together—experience mutual passion (or passion directed toward one another) arising from the pride established through seeing or hearing each other, it attains the name of *vipralambha-śṛṅgāra* (erotic love in separation). This occurs when the desired embraces and so forth are not obtained, and it is characterized by various transitory emotions (*vyabhicāribhāva*) such as longing (*utkaṇṭhā*), and by consequent emotions (*anubhāva*) born of the activity of mind, speech, intellect, and body, reaching a state of excellence where what was to be attained has been reached.
It is fourfold: love at first sight (*pūrvānurāga*), jealousy (*māna*), separation (*pravāsa*), and grief (*karuṇa*).
Among these, love at first sight occurs between two people who have not met before, as in the following example concerning a preeminent man:
“Deceived from afar by my pearl necklace, white as a lotus fiber...”
"Like a swan that has shown its path, the one born of my mind has been led away by you.

(176) Here, Puṇḍarīka’s desire—which was charming through his mental construction (*saṃkalpa*) toward Mahāśvetā, with whom he had previously had no connection—and which was being intensified in the manner described upon her non-attainment, is revealed through this subsequent state of passion as "the one born of my mind has been led far away by you.
That same [desire] is illustrated in the case of a preeminent woman (*strīprakāṇḍa*), as follows:
“Affection for one difficult to attain, heavy shame, a self that is dependent on another—dear friend, love is treacherous; death alone is the refuge. (177)
"O dear friend, love is difficult; death alone is the immediate refuge.
Here too, as before, Sāgarikā’s passion for Vatsarāja, being intensified, is described by means of the very next stage of love (the eleventh) as having "death as its refuge.
An example of pride between two who are united being without cause is as follows:
"Sudden anger, momentary appeasement, persistence in false speech, and the torment of jealousy— my son, these are the thorns of affection. (178)
“O son, freedom from the torment of envy is the path of true affection.
Here, because the course of love is naturally crooked, that which arises without an external cause is called "causeless" (*nirhetu*); yet that very same thing may appear to have a cause, as in:
“She does not speak when addressed; she flinches even when grasped; she becomes angry when kissed.”
‘The young bride remains silent when questioned, trembles even when grasped, becomes angry when kissed, and falls mute when her lover has committed an offense. (179)

In this regard, although there is no explicit negation of such acts as embracing or saying "no, no," nevertheless their meaning is indeed present; thus, the definition of *māna* (pride) is applicable.
Separation following a union occurs when there is a new passion, as for example:

“O Priyamādhavā, why are you unaffectionate toward me? Is this not that very same hand which formerly gladdened me—this hand, O friend, now bearing a beautiful marriage bracelet, appearing as if it were the great festival incarnate? (180) Here, because Mālatī was abducted by Kapālakuṇḍalā immediately after the wedding, this new passion between Mādhava and Mālatī is described as being in a state of separation.
That same mature passion (*prauḍhānurāga*) is as follows:
“Having painted you on a stone slab with mineral pigments while feigning anger out of love, I wish to depict myself fallen at your feet;
but before I can do so, my vision is repeatedly obscured by mounting tears. Cruel Fate does not even permit our union in that moment. (181)

Here, the maturity of passion is understood through the appeasement of former affection; that [passion] becomes *karuṇa* (the pathetic) when one of two who were united passes away, as in the case of a man upon the passing of his wife: [Example: "O you whose face is like the moon, O you whose eyes are like lotuses, O you whose form is like a digit of the moon, O you whose speech is like nectar! Alas, alas, my life-breaths have departed from me. In this instance, the intensity of passion is perceived through the propitiation of a long-standing attachment; it is the *karuṇa* sentiment when one of a couple has perished, such as when a man [laments] upon the death of his wife.
"O lady of pure smiles, I am surely perceived by you as a rogue, one fond of deceit,
since you have departed from here without bidding me farewell, so that I shall not return to the next world.
Here, the extreme sorrow of Aja due to the departure of Indumatī is expressed as *karuṇa* (the pathetic sentiment).
It is just as when, upon the departure of a man, a woman says:
“I know that what you said—that you dwell in my heart—is a lie, for it was merely a word of courtesy; otherwise, how could Rati remain unharmed if you were truly bodiless? (183)
In this context, the intensification of grief arising from passion regarding the object of love (the bodiless god) is designated as *karuṇa* (the pathetic sentiment);
furthermore, semblances (*ābhāsas*) of this occur in the case of inferior characters (*hīnapātra*) and so forth.
Among these, an example of passionate love for a male inferior character is as follows:
“Having seen the thighs of the farmer’s daughter, which resemble the core of a plantain tree, the gambler’s eyes roll about as his hands become moist with sweat. (184)
The nail-painter becomes moistened by the sweat of the barber whose hands are afflicted with perspiration.
Herein, an example of a woman's pride (*māna*) is as follows: "While the neighbor, upon seeing him making a slight [gesture] together with the first wife..."
"Look,
while the cowherd is making the young bride afraid in the presence of her first wife, she has angrily released all the calves. (185)
An example of separation among birds in the animal realm is as follows:
“I take my leave; the beauty of the day causes my heart to ache, for it is now weak. O female cakravāka bird, embrace me and pass this night alone.
He is certainly not attached to another, nor is he angry, nor has he lost his affection; yet, subject to fate, I must suddenly abandon you, for I am no longer my own master. (186)

In this very case, compassion toward the elephant is as follows: “When the clouds thunder with deep rumbling, he does not let out a low roar; from the nearby lake, he does not take mouthfuls of bent water-moss; with his face dejected by the clinging of bees who are silent and despondent due to the loss of his rut-fluid, the elephant surely languishes, distressed by the separation from her who is dear to his life. (187)
Now, the enjoyment body (saṃbhogakāya).

In that context, when two protagonists—whether previously unacquainted or separated after having been united—meet with one another, the stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) called *rati* (love), whether pre-existing or arising at that moment, becomes the *saṃbhoga-śṛṅgāra* (the erotic sentiment of union) once it has attained its desired objects such as embraces. This emotion is conjoined with transitory emotions (*vyabhicāribhāvas*) such as joy, fortitude, memory, and discernment that arise upon attainment; it is inflamed by excitants (*uddīpanavibhāvas*) such as the arrival of seasons, visits to gardens, water-sports, mountain excursions, ornaments, drinking in palaces, and the rising of the moon; and it is manifested by ensuants (*anubhāvas*) such as playful movements of the eyebrows, side-long glances, speech, agitation, and smiles. Thus, attaining what is desired or abandoning what is to be shunned, and embarking on the excellence of what has been attained, it receives the name *saṃbhoga-śṛṅgāra*.
It is fourfold: following the first passion, following anger, following separation, and following grief.
Among these, that which follows the first passion is as follows:
"Even at the very moment of taking her hand, her good fortune was recognized by her friends."
‘At the very moment of the marriage ceremony,
Pārvatī’s good fortune was recognized by her friends,
when Paśupati had the serpent Vāsuki’s bracelet drawn far away. (188)
An example of another type of *māna* (pride) is as follows:
“The young woman bears her own face, which is red with anger fading from her lips bitten by her teeth, and from which intoxication is departing like a wine-cup. (189)
The young woman bears her own happiness like a wine-cup from which the liquor has drained away— the cup whose crimson hue, born of her anger, is fading as she bites the lower lip of her beloved.
An example of [the state] immediately following separation due to travel is as follows:

‘The auspicious bracelet, which was preserved like her very life by the woman whose husband was away from home— her arms having become swollen with the joy of seeing her beloved upon his arrival— that [bracelet] has been broken. (190)
[This is distinct from that in the case of her whose vine-like arms have blossomed with the sighs of seeing her beloved.
An example of [the *karuṇa* (pathetic sentiment)] following immediately upon [the *śṛṅgāra* (erotic sentiment)]:
"Even though my beloved was not released from death, he was seen by me while I was still living."
‘“I am not dead even though my beloved is dead, for I have seen my dearest one again while still alive”— shame and joy do not fit within her heart. (191)
These four types of *saṃbhoga* (union) reach their highest excellence through four corresponding types of *vipralambha* (separation).
Among them, an example of the first, *prathamānurāga* (love at first sight), is as follows:
“Where the moon is not censured, where the sweet words of the messenger are not heard, where the hot sighs do not burn the heart, and where the body does not undergo emaciation.”
‘Is it love when one sleeps embracing one’s own wife, who is submissive and under one’s control? This is merely the practice of the difficult vow of the householder’s life.
As for pride (*māna*), as in:
‘The edges of the sword of love have been blunted upon the body of the beloved.’
"In the midst of the struggle for pleasure, the edges of the sword of love are blunted; it is known that the hearts of the couples sweat as if they were made of food. (193)
As for separation by travel—for example:

“When the wielder of the Śārṅga bow has risen from his serpent-bed, my curse shall end; close your eyes and pass these four months. Afterwards, we two shall enjoy each of those desires of our own hearts, intensified by separation, during nights brightened by the full autumnal moonlight. (194)
As it is said in the Karuṇā:

“The world of mortals is not surpassed by the third heaven if one’s beloved person does not die first; for if he has died, the purpose of the third heaven is already ended, whereas if he lives, one truly lives. (195)
And among animals and other beings, these appear as mere semblances; as in the case of a reptile and a deer:
"The bee, following its own beloved, drank honey from the single vessel of a flower."
The black antelope scratched with his horn the doe whose eyes were closed from the sensation of contact.
(196) As in the case of beasts and birds:
"The female elephant gave to the male elephant mouthfuls of water fragrant with the pollen of the lotuses of the lake."
The Cakravāka bird gratified his mate with half-eaten lotus stalks.
As it is said regarding the Kiṃnaras:
"During the intervals between songs, the lines of their eyelashes were slightly moistened by droplets of perspiration."
The *kiṃpuruṣa* kissed the face of his beloved, which shone with eyes rolling from the intoxication of flower-nectar.
As for [the simile] regarding trees:
"From those [trees] whose breasts were clusters of full-blown flowers, and who were enchanting with lips of shimmering young shoots..."
Even the trees received the embrace of their creeper-brides, whose branch-arms were bent low.

(199) Regarding the gestures of separation (*vipralambha*) during the stage of first love (*prathamānurāga*), as exemplified by the woman: ‘She gazes with aimless eyes, sighs deeply, and laughs vacantly.’
‘Whatever she speaks with indistinct meaning, such is something dwelling in her heart.
(200) [She gazes without finding a mark, sighs deeply, laughs vacantly,
and just as she speaks with indistinct meaning, so too is there something dwelling in her heart.]
As in the case of a man:
“O beautiful one, that noble husband of yours has wasted away for your sake so much that even his jealous second wife has become devoted to him. (201)
"O beautiful one, that noble son of a plowman has been so utterly wasted away for your sake that even his jealous wife has consented to act as his messenger.
As for pride in a woman:
‘That poor, straight-eared woman has today been taught by you, through your transgression, the art of looking at the jambhātika trees. (202)
Yawning, harsh glances, and so forth were practiced by her during the day.
As for [the behavior] of a man:
"The moonlight of his pure conduct, which cannot be perceived at the face of night..."

‘Her heart, in its conflict with her beloved, has become one whose aim is bewildered by increasing remorse; it has not perceived the break of dawn, yet it is illuminated by the pure moon of her virtuous conduct. (203)

As in the case of a woman during her husband's absence: "The lamp is held by the wife of the traveler with a crooked neck, as she gazes at the stream of tears falling from her cheeks, which are rolling due to the weight of her beloved. (204)
[The wife of the traveler, fearing the falling of streams of tears as they well up from the remembrance of her beloved, offers the lamp with her neck turned away.
As in the case of a man:
‘Even for a traveler setting out at midday in the summer heat, the stream of moonlight-water from the face of his wife dwelling in his heart removes his distress. (205)
A stream of water consisting of the moonlight from the face of his wife residing in his heart.
An example of *karuṇa* (the pathetic sentiment) in a woman: "Then she stretched out her limbs, her braid of hair spread across the path filled with dust..."

[Immediately thereafter: "The daughter of Janaka, with her limbs outstretched, her braid loosened and scattered upon the path thick with dust, has fallen so that her breasts form a circle pressed against the surface of the earth. (206)

As in the case of a man: “The husband of the farmhand burns with longing within his house, which is empty of his wife, as he gazes upon the places where they enjoyed love like treasures that have been unearthed. (207)
"The son of a plowman burns with inner longing in his wifeless house,
like one beholding places where he once enjoyed pleasure, now that the treasures have been removed.
Thus it is with others as well.
An example of this, excluding compassion, regarding a woman is as follows:

“She recoils from the palace, abandons the grove, loathes the moonlight, trembles at the door, and considers her fine attire to be poison; she remains only upon a bed spread with lotus shoots, her mind dependent on the nectar of your form brought to her by her own imagination. (208)
An example of this occurring in a woman alone, excluding the stage of first love, is as follows:

“Stay at the door; go into the courtyard; go outside; enter the house; look at the path; go to the hall, the upper terrace, the private chamber, the roof-terrace, and the mansion! Having thus instructed the messenger repeatedly, she remains upon her bed like one possessed by destiny, O pitiless one, so that the night does not reach its end. (209)

An example of this for a man, excluding the stage of first love, is as follows: “He loathes what is pleasant; he is no longer attended daily by his companions; tossing about on the edge of his bed, he passes the nights sleepless; when, out of courtesy, he offers a fitting word to the women of the inner apartments, he then becomes bowed down with shame for a long time whenever he falters in their names. (2.10)
Examples of these [emotions] occurring in a man alone, such as *pravāsa* (separation) and *karuṇa* (pathos), are as follows:

“Having looked toward Sītā’s dwelling, his sight is suddenly snatched away; he is tormented by the pigeons who, with beaks joined to one another, offer morsels of food; even from afar, he flees from the moon; entering the inner house, he is distressed; covering his face with the hem of his garment, he weeps without shame throughout the nights. (211)

Regarding kissing during acts of enjoyment and within the context of prior passion, for example: “We remember her embrace, whose lips were pressed together, whose nose was not joined [to ours], and whose forehead was not touched, as she had her face smeared with cosmetic paste. (212)
We remember the kissing of her, whose lips were pressed with reverence, whose forehead was unadorned yet perfectly formed, and whose face was smeared with the finest pigments.
Herein, an example of embracing is as follows:
“Even sandalwood paste does not dispel the heat of amorous couples as effectively as the blissful sport of mutual embracing, even during an unbearable summer. (213)

Just as there is the pleasure of mutual embracing even in an unbearable summer heat. Regarding the kiss that follows the end of a lover’s quarrel (*māna*), for example: “The more her beloved embraces her in bed, she who is filled with resentment... (*jaha jaha se pariuṃbai...*).
‘The more her beloved kisses her eyes, which are filled with tears during their lovemaking,
the more they overflow, breaking open one after another. (214)
An example of embracing right here is as follows:
“O Mother, may there be prosperity for this embrace, which is like a harsh wind to the tree of pride, which brings relief to every limb, and which is the prologue to the night-play. (215)
[May there be prosperity for the embrace— which is a harsh wind to the tree of pride, which brings relief to every limb, and which serves as the preliminary rite for the drama of sexual union.
As for the kiss following a period of separation:

“Someone, having for a moment cast aside the sprout-like lip of the fair-browed woman— which was sweet yet intensely flushed with passion and excessively heated by tears during their separation— kissed her moist eye.
Following the sentiment of *karuṇa* (pathos), an embrace is as follows:
"And she clasped Candrāpīḍa by the neck; he reached his throat and his very life.
By that touch, she attained an unprecedented splendor of joy, like the ocean shore upon touching the moon.
Regarding the tooth-mark occurring after the first stage of love:

“Even now, that poor girl keeps the circle of your teeth-mark upon her cheek like a deposit, encircled by a swelling of horripilation. (218) [She, the young girl, even today keeps the circle of your teeth upon her cheek like a deposit...]
The poor girl protects [her limbs], which are surrounded by a fence of bristling hair.
That very same [state] occurs immediately after pride (*māna*), as in:
"With arms trembling from the wind, with her circle of teeth fixed in place, [she stands] upon her thighs..."
"O daughter, do not make your husband—who stands like a pillar within the circle of your garment—flirtatious with his thighs; do not indeed cause the laughter of the people!

(299) [Covering your thighs with the hem of your garment fluttered by the wind while he stands like a staff in the circle, O daughter, do not make your husband flirtatious; do not indeed cause the laughter of the people.]

Examples of tooth-marks and so forth occurring immediately after a journey are as follows: “The tooth-mark on her cheek, the braid of hair disheveled by her hand, and her rolling gaze—all these announce the arrival of her beloved to the young woman. (220)
A tooth-mark on the cheek, the braided hair disheveled from being seized by the locks, and a gaze prone to rolling— these establish the arrival of the lover for the bride.
As for a nail-mark following the first passion:
‘O Noble Lady, upon seeing the fresh nail-marks, the surface of the breasts— high with heavy youth and resembling the lotuses of the face in the reflected image— becomes [as if] struck. (221)
Her breast-surface becomes honored by the blue-lotus eyes of her own reflection.
Herein, the act of *puruṣāyita* (the woman acting as the man) is as follows: "Upon her pair of thighs trembling slightly, her eyes closed and her tresses disheveled..."
‘In those beloved women who are inclined toward the role of the man,
whose pair of thighs tremble slightly, whose eyes are half-closed, and whose hair is disheveled— there dwells Kāma, with his weapons ready. (222)
Everything is everywhere, as follows:
“For mature women, that which has been well-practiced brings pleasure in love; for young brides, whatever has not been practiced bestows confidence. (223)
That which mature women have well learned brings pleasure in love-making; that which young brides have not yet learned bestows confidence.
An examination of love through the application of tests during the pursuit of separation is as follows:
“O you who cling to my ears, I say this to you, O handsome one: do not be distressed; by some good fortune, you have been found by me in these deserted places. (224)
"You have somehow been found by my merits on deserted streets.
As for a counter-attack (*pratyabhiyoga*):
"Under the pretext of entering the Godāvarī, I threw myself upon her breast."
"Under the pretext of descending into the treacherous waters of the Godāvarī, she cast herself upon his chest;
out of compassion and without reproach, he too embraced her firmly. (225)
An example by way of endurance:

"Even today, the young bride of the farmer does not wipe away the moisture of the *śyāmā* flower that you placed upon the slope of her breast on that day when it was smeared with the filth of the *phalguna* blossoms. (226)
"Even now, the mud from the Phalgū festival, which was placed upon the slope of her breasts by that farmer’s daughter-in-law, does not wither, being moistened by the sweat of her perspiration.
As for an example through *vimarśa* (deliberation):
‘From that very place they emerge; there the conversations bloom and there they conclude. What do you think, Aunt? Is this village inhabited by only a single youth? (227)
"What do you think, maternal aunt? This village consists of only young men.
As for [an example] through great respect:
"By him, indeed, a blow was given with a fresh lotus to her breast."

"Because, it is said, a blow dealt during the sport of the swing struck her upon the surface of her breast; thus, even today, she wanders about, attended by the village maidens throughout the day. (228)
An example of praise (ślāghā) is as follows:
“She, being as if angry, proclaims to the village maidens that the mud from the *phalgucchana* festival, given by you with her own hands, remains upon the surface of her breasts. (229)

[She, being of a praising disposition, as if angry, applies upon the slope of her breasts that mud from the Phalgūtsava festival which was given by you with your own hand, while she boasts among the young women of the village.
As for an example by means of a gesture (iṅgita):
‘If he is not truly beloved, my friend, why does your face bloom at the mention of his name like a lotus flower expanded by the touch of the sun’s rays? (230)
Your face becomes like a lotus blossomed by the touch of the sun’s rays.
As for [the effect] through the dispatching of a messenger—for example:
“Her entire body moistened with tears at the mention of that beloved’s name...”
“With all her limbs moistened by perspiration, she reached the courtyard of that very man’s house while sending a message through a female messenger, addressing him by name. [231]
Regarding the sending of a messenger, for example:
"Where indeed did she go? Where was she seen? What was said? And what was promised by him?"—thus she speaks repeatedly, unable to finish this very [question]. (232)
"How indeed did she go? How was she seen? What was said? And what was done by him?"—thus it is not finished, as she speaks these repeated words.
As for the manner of composing a letter:
‘O dear friend, on this path where the pen slips from being grasped by trembling and perspiring fingers, the letter has not yet been completed; what was it that you were writing? (233)
"O dear friend, this letter is not yet concluded; what more shall we write?
As for the reading of the letter:
"With affection you gazed upon the word 'svasti' (well-being), and with satisfaction you praised the place; thereafter, in due order, you recognized that name of yours which stood before you."
As the slender maiden, her mind overflowing with passion, repeatedly spoke those words, she did not manage to embrace even the letter, her eyes filled with thick tears.
Regarding the trials of sexual union following the stage of first love, as exemplified by a man’s trepidation:
“Rādhikā protected that [letter] on the surface of her breast, concealing it within her garment.”
"May the playful hand of Hari— trembling with the onset of nervousness at their first union— protect you as it rests upon the surface of Rādhikā’s breasts while she adjusts her garment. (235)

An example of this very [state] due to pregnancy-longing (*dohada*) in a charming girl is as follows: “What does it look like? What does it look like?”—when asked thus by her friends, the gaze of the innocent girl, who had just experienced her first pregnancy-longing, went straight to her lover. (236)
"What do you see, my friend?"— when thus questioned by her companions,
the gaze of that innocent woman, who had just begun to experience pregnancy-longings, went solely toward her beloved.
Herein, the same [stage] for a mature woman (*pragalbhā*) is illustrated by the description of her lover's words:
"‘Hum hum, say it again!’— thus she speaks into the ear of her husband as he speaks to her heart and face, causing a delay of time while they do not sleep. (237)

The housewife speaks words that bring joy to her husband’s heart into his ear: “We know that while she lies turned away from her bed, her pride gradually subsides... ‘We remember the playful pleasure of her breasts pressing against me as she feigned sleep while turning over on the bed, her outburst of pride melting away. (238)

An example of the rejection of a female friend’s words by a woman herself: "I shall look with a frown, I shall rebuke her, I shall turn my face away, and I shall do whatever you say, friends—but if I do not see him [again], [it will be all for nothing]. (239)
"I shall look at him with a frown, I shall rebuke him, I shall turn my face away from him, and I shall do whatever you say, friends, provided that I do not see him.
An example of how this very [resolve] is obstructed by the performance of that [act] is as follows:
‘When the lord of her heart touched the knot of the garment of that woman whose wealth was her pride, in order to untie it,
a breaking apart occurred simultaneously through both her pair of eyebrows and her body hair.
As for a woman immediately after a journey abroad:
‘Suddenly, in the presence of her elders, the young bride pines for her beloved as her arms— bursting with joy— fail her. (241)
[He becomes angry at his bracelets that have slipped from his arms and are expanding with joy.
In this very context, as an example concerning a woman and a man: "When he had gone to her feet after sporting and returned to embrace her..."
‘When he had gone even a single step away and then returned to embrace me,
at that very moment I became like a woman whose husband is away, and he became like a traveler abroad. (242)

An example of this, due to the anxiety of separation, is found in a general sense in the verse by a woman: “Those who can endure separation from their beloveds wander from house to house, asking for the secret of sustaining life through the inquiry after a husband gone abroad. (243)
A woman, capable of enduring separation from her beloved, wanders from house to house asking about the secret of sustaining life through a farewell greeting for a traveler about to depart.
As for the delay caused by a man’s journey, for example:
"Even a single black antelope does not allow me to pass as it turns to the right; how much less so the pair of eyes of the deer-eyed one, which are filled with longing? (244)
How much more so, then, the pair of eyes of the deer-eyed woman, clouded with tears?
Regarding the [other] interpretation, as in the case of a woman [sweating] from perspiration and so forth:
"Her body trembles, her thighs shake, and her lower lip falters."
‘Her body becomes moist, her thighs tremble, the garment from her hips slips away,
and her heart quivers at the approach of her beloved— such is the state of the woman in her menses. (245)
Following compassion, for example, in the case of a man:
“When the touch of his hand begins, the jar-like full breasts of the beautiful woman thrill; on her left side she bears drops of perspiration, charming with the secret intentions of love.
As the Lord repeatedly performs the rite of profuse smearing [with ash], her bath of ashes is somehow brought to completion—and thus it triumphs. (246)

Regarding the definitions of *vipralambha* (love-in-separation), the following is an example of "the failure to grant what was promised" (*pratiśrutyādāna*) within the context of initial passion (*prathamānurāga*):
"What do you say, O youth? [I have not been seen] by the daughter of the village headman with her face turned away, her eyes half-closed and casting sidelong glances in front of her elders. (247)
"What was it that you were told, O boy, by the daughter of the village headman in the presence of your elders—
with sidelong glances from her unblinking eyes, her face turning and her gaze half-turned?
Here, although embraces and other such acts were promised through gestures like the side-long glance, they are not granted due to modesty, fear, and so forth.
An example of deception regarding pride (*māna*) is as follows:
“O friend, I am not angry; do not approach me. Why do you vainly seek to appease me?
I have no need for this pride of mine that has arisen toward you. (248)
"O ignorant one, I am not angry; embrace me. Why do you seek to appease me in vain?
I have no need even for this pride born of my resentment.

Here, the proud woman first rejects embraces and the like, but later grants them improperly—just as someone who promises to give eight hundred might instead give one hundred and eight, rather than eight hundred.
Thus, the rejection of embraces and other such acts through falsehoods, unpleasantness, and the like, because they are not given as they truly are, is called "deception" (*visaṃvādana*).
An example of the delay of time during separation is as follows:
"He will come even while away; I shall become angry, and he too will offer conciliation."
‘“He will return from his journey, I shall be angry, and he will appease me”— such a garland of desires bears fruit for someone toward their beloved. (249)
In this context, the perception of the passage of time through acts such as embracing is quite evident.
In the *karuṇa* (pathetic) rasa, an example of "taking back" (*pratyādāna*) is as follows:
“For those whose love has grown over time, increasing their shared joys and sorrows...”
‘Of a couple whose joys and sorrows have increased together and whose love has grown deep over time, that which dies truly lives; the other becomes dead. (250)
In this regard:
"Like a friend, Fate first reveals a pleasing and entirely favorable disposition; yet, becoming cruel through its sudden reversal, it inflicts a piercing pain upon the mind. (251)
Thus this meaning is connected;
and its purpose is indeed the recovery [of the beloved],
as in the case of "first love," where there is merely various deception, such as follows:
‘That which was not seen by the glance, that which was not addressed by the speech, and that very courtesy which was not performed— it is all considered significant by the clever. (252)
That very benefit which was not rendered is what is perceived as such by the clever.
Here, a variety [of meanings] is understood through shame and so forth, through not being seen and so forth, and through deception and so forth.
An example of the contrary in the context of *māna* (pride/resentment) is as follows:
‘They do not let out long sighs, they do not weep, nor have they become emaciated by separation; indeed, they are fortunate women for whom you, their beloved, are not so very dear. (253)
"Blessed are those women whose beloved has many favorites, but you are not such a one.
Here, the proud woman is deceived by means of expressions such as jealousy, which are contrary to the embracing of the beloved and other such acts;
this is an example of the "disturbed" (*vyāviddha*) style when describing separation during travel.
“When did my beloved go? Today, daughter? “Today? “How many days have passed? Having been told this much, the princess fell into a swoon. (254)
When only this much was said, the maiden fell into a swoon.
Here, even a single day is perceived as being exceptionally long because it acts like a year; this is an example of what is prohibited in the *karuṇa* (pathetic) sentiment.
‘O Lord, I have seen and endured this final end of yours; it was not merely terrifying at the outset,
but the full realization of the suffering was truly dreadful.’
"O Lord, while I am still alive, I have witnessed and endured this end of yours.
This speech of Sītā regarding Rāma— which consists of the loss of the attainment of the happiness she had long desired through reunion— is here sublated by the sentiment of *karuṇa* (pathos),
just as passion is sublated by the passion of first-love (*prathamānurāga*).

"She desires to bathe for him in the downstream current, and he too carries her along in the water, which is rendered precious by the waves tossed and churned by the impact against the slope of her breasts. (256)
"In the water, highly valued for its waves agitated by the contact with her breasts and back...

Here, the mutual passion of both is perceived simultaneously; therein, one is enamored because of her beauty (*lāvaṇya*) and so forth, while the other is enamored because of his affection (*sneha*) and so forth. Following that, as it occurs later:
"O maternal aunt, as I was bathing, that youth drank the river water made bitter by the turmeric used for my bath, and in doing so, he drank my very heart. (257)
"Drinking the water of the river current, which contains bathing-powder, turmeric, and pungent herbs.
Here, having seen the passion of one [woman], a second subsequently becomes enamored; therein, an appropriate example is as follows:
‘He truly knows how to see; passion is appropriate toward a worthy person. He would rather die—he will not speak to you—and even his death is praiseworthy. (258)
"Let her die; I shall not speak to you [of her], for even her death is to be praised.
Here, it is understood that one is not attracted merely by her beauty (*lāvaṇya*) and so forth, but rather by a desire directed toward a worthy object.
An example of what follows immediately after that is as follows:
‘Whether it be true or false, what is the use of deliberation regarding the son of the householder? Blessed indeed is the daughter of the plowman, for such is the talk among the people. (259)
"Among the people, there is a popular rumor concerning the fortunate daughter of a plowman.

Here, although there is no similarity (*sārūpya*) produced by the renown of her good fortune and such qualities, nevertheless, because a woman’s request for the highest [status] is not censurable, it remains consistent;
this is what was stated regarding the view that [the suffix] is derived from the instrument (*karaṇa*).

In the view where it is a noun denoting a state (*bhāvasādhana*), however, the term "passionate love" (*anurāga*) refers to passion (*rati*) or radiance (*dīpti*) as qualified by the sense of "together with" (*saha*) and so forth;
and because it arises for the first time, it is known as "first passionate love" (*prathamānurāga*).
As for the word *māna* (pride), it is that by which one is held in high esteem (*mānyate*), as for example:
“O innocent girl, you have missed out on the many joys of lovers, which are to be attained merely by a glance, yet must be worshipped with the forceful urgency of falling at one’s feet. (260)
"Many pleasures have been lost by her whose nature is to please [him] merely by being seen.
Here, the form *māna* is derived from the root *mān* meaning "to honor," through the addition of the suffix *ṇic* (denoting causative sense) and then the suffix *ghañ*;
for it causes her beloved to engage in acts of honoring such as falling at her feet.

That which one considers dear, as for example: “Even though it was seized by its cause, may that pride of yours, which has thus descended upon me, fall upon my head like an *aṅkola* flower blooming out of season. (261)
"Even though pride was restrained by me, since it has approached me in this very way, let that pride fall upon your head like a suddenly blossomed *aṅkolla* flower.
Here, the verbal root is *man*, meaning "to know."
For instance, regarding pride as something dear, a certain proud woman becomes angry with the *aṅkola* tree that takes it away— just as one who considers pride to be love says:
"Where there is no wakefulness [of longing], where there is no distress from jealousy, there is pride."
‘Where there is no wakefulness, where there is no pride afflicted by envy,
and where there is no affectionate flattery, there is no love. (262)
In this context, the verbal root *man* means "to understand";
for by means of *māna* (pride), a person understands whether love exists or does not exist [toward them].
And although it functions as the instrument (*karaṇa*), it is metaphorically designated as the agent (*kartṛ*) here because of its predominance.
"Just as it is said: 'Wisdom sees, for that is the vision of Sarasvatī, not the eye,' so does love measure."

"And even when Satyabhāmā was angry, though her kinsmen were equal [in status], her anger— which is like a mass of love whose true essence is revealed only upon a lapse of pride— manifested itself solely toward Balarāma. (263)
“Grief proceeds like a consolation born of love, its essence revealed.
Here, from the root *mā* in the sense of “measuring” (*māṅ māne*), [the suffix -yu is applied] according to Pāṇini 3.3.113: *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*.
113. According to the rule *iti kartari lyuṭ*,
as seen in the usage of the Bhāṣya, "What is this inference?",

although it is by means of that [inference] acting as an instrument that Satyabhāmā makes known the measure of the beloved's affection for herself and Rukmiṇī, nevertheless, as in the previous case, here too this [inference] is treated metaphorically as the agent (*kartṛ*).

By way of illustration that women do not adorn themselves even while living in their husband's absence—as in: "Though her beloved was within reach and the moment had arrived, she did not adorn herself while consoling her friend whose husband was away and suffering. (264)
"Even though her beloved was under her own control and the moment had arrived, she did not adorn herself, as she was attending to a neighbor woman whose husband had gone abroad in distress.

Here, the form *pravāsa* is derived from the root *vas* (meaning "to dwell") with the prefix *pra-* used in a prohibitive sense—as in *prasmarati* and similar forms—followed by the suffix *ghañ*. Thus, the form is analyzed as *pra-vāsa*.

Young men do not dwell in the presence of their beloveds as follows: "The fire of separation is endured through the bond of hope for the beloved person; O Mother, living in a different village makes death seem preferable. (265)
"The fire of separation caused by being parted from one's beloved can be endured through the bond of hope; however, O Mother, living in the same village [yet apart] is worse than death.
In this case, even for those situated near each other, there is "separation" (pravāsa) because of the absence of physical proximity, just as there is for those situated far apart.
It perfumes the mind with longing and other such states, as in:
“O traveler, looking at the quarters, yawning, stretching, going away, weeping, fainting, falling, and laughing—what is the use of your departure? (266)
"O traveler, what is the use of that one who is away from home— gazing at the quarters, sighing, yawning, singing, weeping, fainting, falling down, and laughing?
Here, in a mind perfumed by longing and other such states, the consequent emotions (*anubhāva*) such as vacant gazing arise.
It causes [the audience] to believe, for example:

“Like the life-restoring herb, the mother-in-law, having no other occupation, protects the life of her son-in-law, which has reached his throat in his sleep, longing for the sight of the new bridegroom. (267)

"With single-minded devotion, her mother-in-law protects her daughter-in-law— whose life has reached her throat at the sight of fresh clouds— as if she were a *saṃjīvana* (life-restoring) herb for her son.
Here, just as in the expression "he shows favor," the very commencement of the act of killing is referred to as "killing."

In the case of *karuṇa* (compassion), since the root *kṛ* has the sense of "taking up" (*upādāna*) a living being—as in "he causes fainting"—it is as follows: ‘The daughter of Janaka found only the pleasure of fainting, with eyes closed, wherein the pain of separation vanished and the agony of death for Rāma was instantly cast off. (268)

[The daughter of Janaka alone obtained that happiness— her pain of separation having dissolved and her distress over Rāma’s death having vanished at that very moment— as she lay with eyes closed in a swoon.
Here, a swoon arises in Sītā due to the intensity of her grief for her husband.
If it serves the purpose of mere utterance, it produces lamentation, as for example:
“The royal fortune of the earth will become a husband who is fickle toward many particular men; how then can this extraordinary widowhood have befallen me alone? (269)
"The sovereignty of the earth, which is as fickle as a woman distracted by many men, shall have a husband; how then has this extraordinary widowhood come upon me?
Here, Sītā utters these words while lamenting out of grief for Rāma.

For the sake of steadying herself, she set her mind on a desperate act, saying: "O beloved, come by the path of the sun and once again take refuge upon my lap, before you are distracted in heaven by the clever celestial nymphs. (270)
In this case, due to the grief of unfulfilled desire (*rati*), the mind is fixed upon the rash act of suicide; it directs the consciousness toward the purpose of self-anointing with poison, as in:
"My heart breaks from intense agitation, yet it does not split in two; my body, though failing, bears delusion and does not relinquish consciousness."
“An internal burning inflames his body but does not reduce it to ashes; Fate strikes him with a blow that cuts to the very vitals, yet it does not sever his life.
(271) Here, the mind is moistened by the sorrow of Rāma and others.
Regarding the definitions of *saṃbhoga* (enjoyment), the sense of "protection" occurs immediately after *prathamānurāga* (first passion), as follows:
“Having been seen, she casts down her gaze; when addressed, she does not converse; on the bed, she remains turned away; when embraced by force, she trembles;
as her friends depart from the bedchamber, she strives only to go out herself—this young bride, my beloved, now brings me joy precisely through her shyness and contrary behavior.
(272) In this case, although the newlywed bride is naturally compliant, her passion is sustained by following his desires despite her timidity and contrariness.
The meaning of *kauṭilya* (crookedness/indirectness) in another instance of *māna* (pride) is as follows:

“When the redness has reached her feet and her head, when the blue lotus on her ear is crushed, when the string of her pearl necklace is broken, and when a wound has formed upon the palm of her hand—she, whose eyes are like those of a young fawn, not having yet experienced the encounter of being struck by her beloved, now desiring to strike him again in her anger, weeps, utterly distraught. (273)

In this case, because love is inherently crooked, the amorous encounters of the indignant woman (mānavatī) resulting from the seizing of her hair are themselves crooked, consisting as they do of kicking and other such acts.
This occurs immediately after the period of separation, for the purpose of enjoyment—as in:
"The woman [beheld] him returning from the edge of the forest, following the cow of Vasiṣṭha..."
"He drank [her] with eyes whose rows of lashes were motionless like those of one who has fasted, as if by means of two eyes that had been fasting.

(274) Here, in the second half of the verse, the act of drinking produced by the sight of the beloved is described as a form of consumption (*abhyavahāra*), just as the consumption of food follows a fast; this is an instance of the meaning "experience" (*anubhava*) occurring after the *karuṇa* rasa.
‘For a noble wife who had set out to follow her husband in death, the return of her beloved became the ornament of widowhood and his good fortune. (275)
"The ornament of widowhood has become a source of good fortune for the noble lady.

Here, just as she is the very life of my soul, so too am I her very life; thus, the husband experiences a love born of confidence. For the wife, however, there is the experience of extreme happiness born of confidence, thinking: "That union with my lord which I desired even after death, that very Lord of my Life has been attained by me while still alive.
Here, the enjoyment (*saṃbhoga*) following the first stage of love (*prathamānurāga*) is presented in brief—as follows:

"Free from verbal conversation, involving various ascetic arts, with the edge of her fine silk garment slipping away at the touch of his hand, trembling repeatedly as it was held fast, and with eyes cast again and again in every direction— their union here was but momentary.
(276) In this case, the *saṃkṣepa* (abridgment) is explained by the literal reading itself.

That same [anger] is mixed with pride in another instance, as follows: “In the hearts of proud women, which are distressed by remembering the beloved again after having found happiness for a moment when their anger was appeased, the resentment, heavy with longing, subsides only after a long time. (277)

"In the hearts of proud women, which are first distressed by the memory of anger even as they experience the pleasure obtained at the moment of being appeased, the resentment heavy with love finally subsides.
Here, the established and preeminent passion (*rati*) is intermingled with the recollection of an offense and other such factors.
An example of a complete [separation] occurring after a journey is as follows:

“When the wielder of the Śārṅga bow has risen from his serpent-bed, my curse shall end; pass these four months with your eyes closed, and afterwards we two shall enjoy each of those desires of our own hearts, multiplied by separation, during nights brightened by the full autumnal moonlight. (278)

Here, even by means of these words of one separated from his beloved, the phrase beginning with "that various longing of my own" (*taṃ tam ātmābhilāṣam*)—which is not contradicted by the temporal condition of the future tense expressed in "we shall enjoy together" (*nirvekṣyāvaḥ*) despite the interval of separation—describes the fullness of the sexual union occurring at that very moment, following immediately after the *karuṇa* (pathetic) sentiment.
An example of this, where [the erotic] flourishes immediately after the *karuṇa*, is as follows:

"At the holy ford where the waters of the Jahnu-daughter (Gaṅgā) and the Sarayū mingle, having attained immediate inscription among the ranks of the immortals through the sacrifice of their bodies..."
"Accompanied by his beloved, whose radiance was even greater than her former appearance, he took delight once more in pleasure-chambers within the Nandana groves.
(279) Here, by the second half of the verse, the abundance of their enjoyment through the resurrection of Indumatī and Aja from the other world is established.
An example of the connection with the sense of "together" (*saha*) following "first love" (*prathamānurāga*) is as follows:
‘Her husband is one who looks only to her face, and she too is indeed intoxicated by the sight of his beloved form; both of them consider the earth to be devoid of other men and women. (280)

"Both, having accomplished their purpose, consider the earth to be devoid of men and women. Here, the meaning of "delighting" (*rañjayati*) in the first half-verse and the meaning of "shining" (*rājati*) in the second half-verse are established through the *sahabhāva* (co-existence) in the stage of initial passion (*prathamānurāga*), and they continue in exactly the same way in the subsequent stage.
In that very context, the subsequent connection of meanings is as follows:

"‘From this day forward, O lady of bowed limbs, I am your slave, purchased by your ascetic penances,’—when the Moon-crested Lord spoke thus, she instantly cast off the exhaustion born of her religious observances; for hardship, when followed by its fruit, restores one to a state of renewed youth.

Here, the sense of "delighting" (rañjayati), which is established in the context of the first stage of love (prathamānurāga) regarding the male protagonist, continues in the same manner in the subsequent stage as well.

An example of the connection of corresponding meanings in this very context is as follows: ‘The moon has been reached by this Kaumudī; the daughter of Jahnu has descended into the ocean, her worthy match.
Thus, delighted by the union of equal virtues, the citizens there uttered with one voice a statement harsh to the ears of rival kings. (282)

In this context, the meaning of the verb *rājati* (shines/is illustrious), having been established through the mutual suitability of the man and woman in the stage of "first love" (*prathamānurāga*), continues in the same manner in the subsequent stage as well; therein, the connection of the following sense is as follows:
"It is fitting that this difficult penance was performed for this purpose by the delicate Aparṇā."
"Even a woman who might obtain his servitude would be one who has achieved her purpose, how much more so if she rests upon his lap! (283).

Here, in the first half-verse, the meaning "delights" is established as being consistent with the theme of "first love"; it continues in that same manner in what follows. This is the case where the suffix is derived in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa-sādhana*). This is what was stated regarding the position of the arising of the suffix.

In the view where it is a noun denoting a state (*bhāvasādhana*), however, in all cases, *rati* (love) or *dīpti* (radiance), qualified by the sense of "together with" (*saha*) and so forth, is expressed by the word *anurāga*; this [quality] also persists even in what follows due to the force of the compound.
But what is the compound here?
It is a *tatpuruṣa* characterized by the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*).

Regarding the term *prathamānurāgānantara*—meaning "following immediately after the first stage of love"—what kind of compound is this? It is an *ajahatsvārthā* (non-abandoning) compound; for even when the two protagonists have met with one another, they do not relinquish their state of being in the first stage of love.

But it is indeed reasonable that a function (*vṛtti*) should consist in denoting the meaning of another while not abandoning its own meaning; for one who necessarily denotes the meaning of another must surely abandon their own meaning. [The opponent replies:
"Quite so, it is indeed reasonable;

for it is seen thus in the world: when a beggar obtains a second alms-offering, he does not abandon the first, but strives only to accumulate them. [The proponent says: "If that were the case, then since there would be two [words], the dual number (*dvivacana*) would apply to both."
Of which case? Of the genitive; it is not immediately preceded by that which is governed by the genitive.
In that case, for the first [case-ending],

there will be semantic competency because the first-case-nominative "first love" (*prathamānurāgaḥ*), which was previously expressed as having a redundant relation, has now become a meaning not included within the nominal stem's own meaning, thereby resulting in semantic competency.
It is not so;
in this case, the case-ending must be produced from the entire aggregate "immediately after the first passion" (*prathamānurāgānantaram*).

And by that aggregate, a single unified meaning-mass—like a lump of clay in which the distinction between dust and water has ceased—is denoted, its constituent parts being supported by their own semantic powers yet having their individual powers no longer separately designated.

And since unity is inherent in that collective sense, even though the number of parts exists, the case-ending (*sub*) will not arise based upon it; for instance, there is a connection with the sense of worship in another example:
"Though touched by the celestial river, he was not moved far away by her persistent jealousy; nor was he wiped away by the Lord of Serpents with his threatening gestures, for the sake of victory."
“Victorious is the dust of the feet of the Lord of the Mountain’s daughter, which was washed away by her tears at the end of her pride when she bowed her head to her husband.
(284) Here, the worship consisting of falling at one's feet and so forth is established by convention (*mānasiddha*) and continues even thereafter.
In this very instance, there is a semantic connection (*arthānvaya*) toward pride for the purpose of conceiving [the dust] as being dear to oneself, as follows:
“If, having abandoned this human frailty of pride, your beloved were to place himself between these two high breasts— if we, whose words are not to be transgressed,
were to hear such speech from our affectionate friends”— having heard these words, the deer-eyed woman offers libations of water for her mental friend with the tears from her eyes.
Here, the conceit of the beloved’s dearness persists even after the cessation of the pride.

In this very context, the connection for the purpose of obstructing love is as follows: “Those who pacify her for even a moment when she is angry, and those who serve like slaves to win her favor—they alone are the beloveds of women; all others are merely wretched masters. (286)
"Those who grieve her for a moment when she is angry, and those who appease her like servants—they alone are dear to women; the rest are merely wretched masters.
Here, the lover, wishing to ascertain whether love still exists in her or not, causes her pain by such means as accidentally calling her by the name of another woman during play.
And she, being full of love, will inevitably become angry with him; yet he, having perceived her affection, propitiates her like a servant,
and thus he realizes the existence of love within himself.
This very object established by mental perception persists even in what follows; therein alone is the connection of the meaning of love and proof, as for example:
"If I can please you again with those very same flowers from the gods..."
"O slender-waisted one, if I were to appease you again with those very same flowers that defiled you, then neither my love nor my offense would be commensurate. (287)

In this context, while a cluster of celestial flowers was given to Rukmiṇī, my beloved accepted for me the celestial tree itself; therefore, Satyabhāmā measures her own love by thinking, "I am a thousand times dearer to him than she. This matter is established through the *māna* (pride) sentiment, and it continues into what follows by virtue of its equal force.
But what kind of compound (*samāsa*) is used here?

What kind of compound operation is this? It is precisely a genitive tatpuruṣa, just like "immediately following the first passion," which is one that does not abandon its own primary meaning (ajahatsvārtha).
It is appropriate [to include them] there as well, because even in the stages of gaining confidence and so forth, first love (prathamānurāga) remains present; however,
in this case, since the cessation of jealous anger (māna) occurs, states such as the departure of anger arise—
this will serve as a distinguishing characteristic by way of positive concomitance (anvaya).

For example, in the case of "a jar of ghee" (*ghṛtaghaṭa*) or "a jar of oil" (*tailaghaṭa*), even when the ghee or the oil has been poured out, because of the continued application of the designation "this is a jar of ghee" or "this is a jar of oil," the first member of the compound remains a qualifier; and whatever the extent of the substance that was there, it is exactly the same here as well. To explain:
‘With her face bent down in fear as he grasps her by the hair, the proud woman drinks the wine offered by her beloved little by little, as if it were a medicine for her anger. (288)
[She should drink] wine drop by drop like the medicine for anger;

thus, the sequence of her pride is seen as she goes to the bed, piercing the hero with words full of bitterness. The connection of the meaning—that the beloved does not remain after his departure—is as follows:—
"Clad in soiled garments, her body emaciated by religious observances, with her hair tied in a single braid,
she of pure character maintains the long vow of separation from me, who am utterly merciless.
(289) Here, the fact that Duṣyanta learned of Śakuntalā’s not wearing ornaments during her stay away— which persists even thereafter— serves to heighten the intensity of her love.

In that very context, the logical connection (*anvaya*) regarding the fact that young men do not remain in the presence of their beloved is as follows: “I resolve upon one thing regarding my beloved, yet in an instant it turns out otherwise for me; therefore, I shall not suddenly open my eyes while awake, lest I become one who has made his beloved known [to others] through touch. (290)

In this regard, whatever Purūravas encountered—such as creepers and the like—mistaking them for Urvaśī due to his intoxication from separation, each and every one of those things repeatedly appeared otherwise; and because of that mental impression (*saṃskāra*), he perceives the transformation of her into the form of a creeper. This "dwelling" (*avāsa*) of young men in the presence of their beloved is fully established, and it persists even thereafter; it is precisely here that the mind is made to dwell through longing and other such states. The connection of this meaning is as follows: [The verse: *“When the moon rises, the lotus closes its eyes; when the sun rises, the day-lotus opens its eyes. But when the moon rises, the night-lotus opens its eyes; and when the sun rises, the day-lotus closes its eyes.”* [Commentary: Here, the moon and the sun are the two lovers. The night-lotus and the day-lotus are the two beloveds. The closing and opening of the eyes are the signs of anger and favor. When the lover (the moon) rises, the beloved (the night-lotus) shows favor by opening her eyes; when the rival lover (the sun) rises, she shows anger by closing her eyes. Thus, the mutual dwelling of the two lovers in the hearts of the two beloveds is established. Furthermore, the dwelling of the two beloveds in the hearts of the two lovers is also established. Moreover, the dwelling of the two lovers in the hearts of the two beloveds is established. And finally, the dwelling of the two beloveds in the hearts of the two lovers is established. In this way, the dwelling of the two in the hearts of the two is established. And because of that, the dwelling of the two in the hearts of the two continues even thereafter. It is precisely here that the mind is made to dwell through longing and other such states. The connection of this meaning is as follows: [The verse: *“O friend, the moon has risen; the night-lotus has opened its eyes; the bees have come out from the interior of the day-lotuses; and the female Cakravāka birds have gone to their own nests.”* [Commentary: Here, the moon is the lover; the night-lotus is the beloved; the bees are the rivals; and the Cakravāka birds are the friends. The rising of the moon is the cause of the beloved’s favor toward the lover; the coming out of the bees from the day-lotuses is the cause of the rivals’ departure; and the going of the Cakravāka birds to their own nests is the cause of the friends’ arrival. Thus, the mutual dwelling of the two in the hearts of the two is established. Furthermore, the dwelling of the two in the hearts of the two is also established. Moreover, the dwelling of the two in the hearts of the two is established. And finally, the dwelling of the two in the hearts of the two is established. In this way, the dwelling of the two in the hearts of the two is established. And because of that, the dwelling of the two in the hearts of the two continues even thereafter. It is precisely here that the mind is made to dwell through longing and other such states. The connection of this meaning is as follows: [The verse: *“The moon has risen; the night-lotus has opened its eyes; the bees have come out from the interior of the day-lotuses; and the female Cakravāka birds have gone to their own nests.”* [Commentary: Here, the moon is the lover; the night-lotus is the beloved; the bees are the rivals; and the Cakravāka birds are the friends. The rising of the moon is the cause of the beloved’s favor toward the lover; the coming out of the bees from the day-lotuses is the cause of the rivals’ departure; and the going of the Cakravāka birds to their own nests is the cause of the friends’ arrival. Thus, the mutual dwelling of the two in the hearts of the two is established. Furthermore, the dwelling of the two in the hearts of the two is also established. Moreover, the dwelling of the two in the hearts of the two is established. And finally, the dwelling of the two in the hearts of the two is established. In this way, the dwelling of the two in the hearts of the two is established. And because of that, the dwelling of the two in the hearts of the two continues even thereafter. It is precisely here that the mind is made to dwell through longing and other such states. The connection of this meaning is as follows: [The verse: *“The moon has risen;
"O performer of difficult deeds, you are worrying again about going; even today, the waves of your braided hair have not become straight. 291.
"Even now, her wavy locks have not become straight.
Here, it is indicated through the description of the braided hair that the mental impressions (vāsanā) of intense longing experienced during her absence have not subsided even after her return;
in this very context, the connection of the meaning "he causes [her] to die" is as follows:
"O fierce one, as I was sinking in the darkness born of separation from you, I have fortunately found you again, like consciousness regained by one whose life has departed.

Here, Purūravas, having reached the final stage of love due to his separation from Urvaśī, feels as if he has been restored to life upon regaining his beloved, just as one returns from death; he reflects upon that very fact.
This very purpose of causing death, established by the term *pravāsa* (banishment), continues by virtue of the force of the compound even in what follows;
for what is the compound here?
It is indeed a *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa*.
What is its function?
It cannot be one that does not abandon its own meaning, for even the connection with travel no longer exists between two people who have returned from their journey;
therefore, let it be here one that abandons its own meaning.
But is it not reasonable that there should be a function (vṛtti) which has relinquished its own purpose?
Certainly, it is indeed reasonable;
for it is observed thus in the world: this person, while engaging in the work of another, relinquishes his own work.
For example, it is like a carpenter who, when engaged in work for the king, sets aside his ordinary carpentry tasks.
If this were so, one might object that when it is said, "Bring the king's man," it would follow that any man whatsoever should be brought;
however, this is not a fault.
Even while relinquishing his own self-interest, he does not relinquish it entirely; rather, he relinquishes only that self-interest which is in conflict with the welfare of others.
For example, a carpenter engaged in the king’s service relinquishes his work as a carpenter, but not his standing posture, his smile, or his gestures.
And this purpose [of benefiting others] is not in conflict with the welfare of others; such is the meaning of the term "qualification" (*viśeṣaṇa*).
Therefore, it will not be abandoned;
for the purpose of showing the sequence of the manifestation of what was previously experienced immediately after compassion is as follows:
"Victorious are the locks of hair of Śambhu, embraced by his consort, during the churning of the ocean."

"In this [verse], 'The intoxication and fainting from the taste of great nectar and poison, the delight of the mind' (293), Dākṣāyaṇī’s state of being Haimavatī follows immediately after the *karuṇa* [rasa];
therein, due to the sorrow of the *karuṇa*, fainting and other such states manifested."
But here, they manifest through bliss; therein lies the purpose of the sequence of utterances, as follows:

"That you were neglected while suffering before me, that Kāma was struck down in my presence, that your body was emaciated by penance, and that [the truth] was spoken under the guise of a young brahmin—"

"O beloved Dākṣāyaṇī, may all that [wrong] be forgiven today by you, who are compassionate toward me who am prostrate"—having said this, Śiva triumphs as he rolls at the lotus-feet of Śivā. (294) Here, in the state of *karuṇa* (compassion/pathos), the lamentation performed out of grief while rolling at the lotus-feet of the beloved undergoes a transformation here into an intense outburst (*prakarṣālāpa*).
To illustrate the purpose of establishing the mind on this very point through its connection:
"‘May you obtain unbroken love from your husband,’ thus was Uma addressed by them; yet she, being bowed down, surpassed even the blessings of affectionate kinsmen by obtaining half of his body.
In this very context:
"From the very moment that fair-toothed lady cast her body into the fire out of anger toward Dakṣa,
from that time forth her husband, the Lord of Creatures, became free from attachment and ceased to possess anything.

Thus, the mind which was previously established in the audacity of non-possession through intense affection during the state of compassion now remains fixed here in the great audacity of offering half of his own body.
In that very context, the meaning concerning the sequence of anointing is as follows:

“When the mind has become supple, when the consciousness known as vibration (*spanda*) ceases within the supreme light (*parajyotis*) immediately upon its dissolution in *samādhi*, and when the senses begin to slightly awaken while the activity of the vital breath (*marut*) relinquishes its dependence on external objects—the flood of inner bliss arising from the touch of the left half [of Śiva] triumphs in the Enemy of the Cities (Śiva), who is a fellow-student of Brahman. (297)
In this case, that mind which was previously permeated by the intensity of grief during the state of *karuṇa* (pathos) is here permeated by the supreme bliss born from the embrace of the beloved;
thus, this persistence of the quality (*dharma-anvaya*) of *karuṇa* occurs even in the subsequent [state] through the power of the compound (*samāsa*).
But what, then, is the compound here?
What type of compound operation (*vṛtti*) is it in the case of a genitive *tatpuruṣa*?
It is *jahatsvārthā*.
For here there is not even a trace of the meaning of "compassion" (*karuṇā*);
how then is there a grammatical connection?

It is just as in the cases of "a jasmine basket" (*mallikāpuṭa*) or "a campaka basket" (*campakapuṭa*), where even though the flowers have been scattered, the name "jasmine" and so forth remains a qualifier due to the force of residual impression (*vāsanā*)—such that one says, "this is a jasmine basket," or "this is a campaka basket. In the same way, even though its own primary meaning has ceased, "compassion" remains a qualifier for the immediately following word due to the force of residual impression.
Or let it be that even in cases such as *prathamānurāga* (first love) and the like, the function [of the compound] is indeed one that abandons its own primary meaning (*jahatsvārthā*).
But if this were so, then when it is said, "Bring the king's man" (*rājapuruṣam ānaya*), would it not follow that any man whatsoever should be brought?
This is not a fault.
In the *vṛtti*, the heading "samartha" (capable) is established;
and "capacity" consists of either distinction (*bheda*), conjunction (*saṃsarga*), or both.
In that regard, when "the king's" (*rājñaḥ*) is uttered, everything that constitutes "one's own" (*sva*) is potentially applicable.
When "man" (puruṣa) is mentioned, every master is implicated;
but now, when it is said, "Bring the king's man," the king excludes [the man] from other masters, and the man also excludes the king from his own [other subjects].
Thus, when both sides have been excluded, if the meaning of "king" were to be withdrawn, let it be withdrawn at will.
There will never be the leading away of a mere person;
