thus, once it is established that qualities (*guṇa*) and sentiments (*rasa*) constitute ornaments (*alaṃkāra*), a sixfold commingling (*saṃkara*) of sentiment-ornaments is possible: the commingling of qualities, the commingling of ornaments, the commingling of quality and ornament, the commingling of sentiments, the commingling of sentiment and quality, and the commingling of sentiment and ornament.

Now, one might object: "The conventional usage of 'commingling' with respect to qualities is not tenable, because even when many qualities are present, the designation remains simply 'one possessing qualities' (*guṇavat*)."
It is not so;
there are three kinds of qualities: qualities of sound (*śabda-guṇa*), qualities of meaning (*artha-guṇa*), and qualities of defects (*doṣa-guṇa*).
Each of these, moreover, is twofold: those that possess distinctiveness (*ullekhavat*) and those that lack distinctiveness (*nirullekha*).

Among the qualities of sound (*śabda-guṇa*), *samādhi*, sweetness (*mādhurya*), loftiness (*audārya*), profundity (*gāmbhīrya*), and so forth are *sollekha*; while *śleṣa*, clarity (*prasāda*), evenness (*samatā*), sweetness (*mādhurya*), and so forth are *nirullekha*.

Among the qualities of meaning (*artha-guṇa*), clarity (*prasāda*), style (*rīti*), luster (*kānti*), and so forth are *sollekha*; while explicitness of meaning (*arthavyakti*), subtlety (*saukṣmya*), profundity (*gāmbhīrya*), appropriateness (*saṃmitatva*), and so forth are *nirullekha*.

Among the defects (*doṣa*) that function as qualities [in certain contexts], vulgarity (*grāmya*), tautology (*punarukta*), meaninglessness (*apārtha*), and irrelevance (*anyārtha*) are *sollekha*; while deficiency of words (*śabdahīna*), confusion (*saṃbhrama*), lack of sequence (*apakrama*), and faulty euphonic combination (*visaṃdhi*) are *nirullekha*.

In that regard, while the designation of "confusion" (*saṃkara*) applies to similar figures when they are clearly delineated (*sollekha*), it is also applied to dissimilar figures even when they are not clearly delineated (*nirullekha*).
For example, among the verbal qualities (*śabdaguṇa*), regarding *samādhi* and the others among similar figures:
"It darts among the fresh sprouts, whirls among the branches, and winds around the mountain peaks."
‘The Fortune of Spring likewise darts among the new shoots, whirls about the branches, lingers upon the tips,
and settles within the clusters of blossoms of the Ashoka tree. (455)

Here, the superimposition of attributes belonging to one thing onto another constitutes *samādhi*; distinctness of words (*pṛthakpadatā*) is *mādhurya* (sweetness); and the grandeur of the composition (*bandhavikaṭatva*) is *audārya* (loftiness). These qualities of the same class are blended together, since even a verbal resonance (*śabdadhvani*) flashes forth in the two phrases "the beauty of spring" and "of the *aśoka* tree," just as a beloved woman moves with grace upon the limbs of some proud *aśoka* tree, so too does she [the spring] move upon this [tree].
Examples of *śleṣa* (paronomasia) and other qualities of meaning are as follows:

“May people, through their merits, attain the state of being water within the ocean; may the clouds, through their auspicious deeds, deposit them in that state within the mouth of a pearl-oyster; and may he [the cloud], through his blessings, reach that transformation by which, O full-breasted one, spreading its luster, it rolls upon your heart. (456)

In this arrangement, the excellence of being well-constructed is *śleṣa* (cohesion); the clarity of meaning is *prasāda* (lucidity); the sequence of actions such as origination is *rīti* (diction); and the state of radiant sentiment is *kānti* (loveliness). Thus, these qualities of meaning (*arthaguṇas*) of the same class are intermingled among the defects and qualities, just as in the case of vulgarity and so forth—for example:
"That woman of beautiful hips is being struck by Smara, the enemy who strikes at the wrong time..."

"She whose every limb is beautiful is being slain; she who speaks so sweetly is being slain. (457) Here, "is being slain" (*hanyate*) has an inauspicious meaning; "of noble form" (*varārohā*) has a vulgar meaning; "is being slain, is being slain" is a tautology; and having already said "she whose every limb is beautiful," "of noble form" is redundant. These four defects, though belonging to the same class, are permitted when they are combined in the speech of someone intoxicated, provided there is a desire to express an excess of compassion or the like—as it has been said:
If some excellence such as compassion and so forth is intended to be expressed, there is no fault in repetition and the like; on the contrary, this is an ornament.
This is the commingling of verbal qualities and semantic qualities that belong to different classes of meaning—for example:

"Who indeed rises up and who sets? Or rather, what is this sun that transcends the worlds, such that when the repository of light undergoes rising and setting, time becomes twofold—divided into day and night?

(458) In this [verse], the following qualities of sound (*śabda-guṇas*) are intermingled: *saṃmitatva* (appropriateness of words to the sense), *audāratā* (magnificence consisting in a well-knit and grand structure), and *udāttatvam* (nobility consisting in the possession of praiseworthy specific excellences). Furthermore, the qualities of meaning (*artha-guṇas*) are intermingled: *prauḍhi* (maturity consisting in the successful execution of the stated matter), *prasāda* (clarity consisting in the manifestness of the meaning), and *taurjityam* (forcefulness consisting in the absence of prideful affectation).
An example of both excellences (*guṇas*) and defects (*doṣas*) of words is as follows:

"Come, come, my child, delight of the Raghus, full moon! I shall kiss you on the head and embrace you for a long time; or, lifting you onto my heart, I shall carry you day and night; or else, I shall worship your two lotus-like feet. (459)

In this context, the qualities of sound (*śabda-guṇa*) are as follows: *bhāvikatva* is the manifestation of speech through internal emotion; *prasāda* (clarity) is the use of words with well-known meanings; and *preya* (loveliness) is the employment of words that convey a pleasing meaning. As for the defects (*doṣa*), there is the tautology in "come, come"; the contradiction in saying "O child" and then "I bow to your two lotus-feet"; and the pointlessness in "I kiss your head" or "I carry you in my heart," where the verb "I bow" is not applicable to such actions, as well as the word "full moon" being redundant when it serves the purpose of an action like "seeing. Thus, defects and qualities become intermingled.
For instance, in cases where the mind is captivated by aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), tautologies and other such features do not constitute faults.
Examples of the qualities and defects of meaning (*artha-guṇa* and *artha-doṣa*) are as follows:
“O cursed gatekeeper, why was this wicked poison-tree—a mango tree—allowed to grow here?
For when it undergoes even the slightest change through blossoming, these terrifying fevers of the madness of love arise. (460)

In this context, the qualities of meaning (*arthaguṇa*) are as follows: *kānti* is the state of having radiant sentiment; *prasāda* is the clarity of meaning; and *prauḍhi* is the carrying out of the stated matter. In the example "This wretched tree is a poisonous plant, a villain," the meaning is vulgar because it conveys an inauspicious sense. In the examples "What is the use of nurturing this? and "Here are the fevers and agitations of love," there is a reversal of the manifestation of meaning (*arthavyaktiviparyaya*) due to the incompleteness of the sentence, which results from the necessity of supplying ellipses such as "for the sake of the purpose of the action" or "for the lover who sees [the tree]," and so forth.

In the phrase "in this [world] which partakes of expansion and transformation," because the word *vikāsa* (expansion) refers to a flower, its application to a tree is considered incapable of conveying the meaning (*avācakatva*), and thus it is a defect. However, defects and merits may intermingle; for instance, while inauspiciousness might arise from a hint of irony (*parihāsaleśa*) that implies a sentiment (*rasa*), there is the principle of supplying what is well-known—as in the maxim "Enter the ball of rice, eat the door"—and there is the metaphorical identification of the container and the contained (*ādhārādheya-abhedopacāra*), as seen in usages such as "the cave speaks" or "the platforms cry out. When employed through such means as contradictory indication (*viruddhalakṣaṇā*), these do not constitute defects. Now, [we shall discuss] the commingling of figures of speech (*alaṃkārasaṃkara*).

Although this [mixture] was previously described as having both manifest and unmanifest natures through distinctions such as sesame and rice, and by way of being either subordinate to the primary element or equal to it, nevertheless, because those [former types] involve the non-commonality of the commingling of *guṇas* (qualities) and so forth, the common type is now stated.

It is sixfold: the commingling of verbal figures (*śabdālaṃkāra*), the commingling of semantic figures (*arthālaṃkāra*), the commingling of both figures, the commingling of verbal and semantic figures, the commingling of verbal, semantic, and both figures, and the commingling of semantic and both figures. Among these, an example of the commingling of verbal figures is as follows:

"haṃsālī bhayataralā sārā sarasā sarāsasārasarāsā ambaramaramārūḍhā sārāsarasā sarāsasārasarāsā"— here, four verbal ornaments are interwoven: the blending of Sanskrit and Prakrit (*saṃskṛtaprākṛtabhāṣāsaṃśleṣa*), the palindrome (*gatapratyāgata*), the *yamaka* consisting of the repetition of words, and alliteration (*varṇānuprāsa*).
An example of the blending of figures of sense (*arthālaṃkāra-saṃkara*) is as follows:
"This is the village within the forest, the location of whose dwellings is inferred even from afar by the drawn-out cackling of roosters perched upon its roofs;
here, in the evening, darkness swirls thick with leaping sparks from heaps of glowing embers, matted with the shadows of swarms of shimmering bats appearing at the edge of twilight. (461)

In this passage, there is an inference (*anumāna*) in the phrase "by the cries of the cocks' age"; a probative cause (*jñāpakahetu*) in the phrase "where the darkness whirls"; and two efficient causes (*kārakahetu*) in the phrases "the thumping of leaps from the heaps of glowing embers" and "tangled with the shadows of the dark-brown bark-garments shimmering at twilight. The figure of speech called *jāti* (generic description) consists in the statement of the nature of an object as it arises. Thus, these four figures of sense (*arthālaṅkāra*) are mutually commingled.
An example of the commingling of both types of figures (*ubhayālaṅkārasaṃkara*) is as follows:
"Indeed, not only did the campaka flowers attain a resemblance to the rays of a lamp..."
‘Indeed, the campaka flowers have not merely attained a resemblance to the flame of a lamp;
by the bees wandering above them, the very function of lampblack has also been performed. (462)

Here, there is a simile (*upamā*) between the *campaka* flowers and others on one hand and the flames of the lamps on the other, based on their form and beauty; a similarity (*sāmya*) based on their functional activity (*arthakriyā*), as both cause the burning of the hearts of women separated from their lovers and illuminate the garden; a "blended" figure (*melita*) because the swarms of bees are merged with the masses of lamp-soot due to their meeting above; and a "combination" (*samuccaya*) based on the relationship of comparison (*aupamya*) and so forth between the swarms of bees and the masses of lamp-soot, which is like that between the *campaka* flower and the lamp-flame. Thus, these four figures of speech are perceived as mutually intermingled.
An example of the intermixture of word-figures (*śabdālaṅkāra*) and meaning-figures (*arthālaṅkāra*) is as follows:

“O traveler, how do you live as you journey through this summer month—when all hope is stifled, when the creepers are scorched, when the deer are ever intent on killing, when the trees are withered, when the bees are faint from lack of nectar, when the roots are greedily consumed at will, when the streams are drying up, when the dust of the earth is heated, and when the waters are like flames, under the fierce radiance of the sun?

In this verse, the *avantikā* style (*rīti*), the *padamudrā*, the *vibhaktimudrā*, and *anuprāsa* (alliteration) are verbal ornaments (*śabdālaṃkāra*); while *jāti*, the *kārakahetu* and *jñāpakahetu*, and *citrahetu* (various types of cause) are semantic ornaments (*arthālaṃkāra*). These are mutually interwoven (*saṃkīryante*).
An example of the commingling of both verbal and objective ornaments (*śabdobhayālaṃkārasaṃkara*) is as follows:
“Little by little, these stars in the expanse of the sky have set; thereafter, the moon, its luster impoverished, goes to the peak of the western mountain.
Then, by the crimson glow of the solar disc whose rising is imminent, even the eastern quarter unfolds, red as the juice of madder. (464)

Here, the *vibhaktimudrā* (the seal of case-endings) consisting of the phrase "samunmīlati," along with the alliteration (*anuprāsa*) in "stokastokam astaṃ gataṃ gacchati" and so forth, are verbal ornaments (*śabdālaṃkāra*). Furthermore, the causal figure (*hetu*), simile (*upamā*), the figure of resolution (*samādhi*), sequence (*anukrama*), and the expression of conjunction (*samuccayokti*) are both types of ornaments (*arthālaṃkāra*) that are mutually commingled. An example of the commingling of both types of ornaments is as follows: "He wears the sky, dark as the throat of a sparrow, as a blanket of clouds; the family of frogs seems to carry out a discussion with their frantic clamor."
"The ground, scorched by the rain, releases a fragrance like that of sprinkled parched grain; the Lord of Light (the Sun), though difficult to perceive, is made manifest by the smile of the lotus.

Here, the figure of speech *jāti* (natural description), *anumāna* (inference), and the two types of cause—the productive (*kāraka*) and the indicative (*jñāpaka*)—are figures of sense (*arthālaṅkāra*). Furthermore, the figures of both word and sense (*ubhayālaṅkāra*)—namely, *rūpaka* (metaphor) and *upamā* (simile), as well as *hetūpamā* (causal simile) and *utprekṣopamā* (simile of poetic fancy)—are mutually intermingled.
By this, the intermixture of poetic qualities (*guṇa*) and figures of speech (*alaṅkāra*) is also explained.

Since the employment of figures of speech (alaṃkāra) occurs only in sentences that possess poetic qualities (guṇa), nevertheless, because the quality is predominant in some cases and the figure of speech in others, the conventional designation of "commingling" (saṃkara) between quality and figure proceeds by way of their relationship as primary and subordinate.

This [commingling] is sixfold: that in which the verbal quality is predominant, that in which the semantic quality is predominant, that in which the verbal defect-turned-quality is predominant, that in which the verbal figure is predominant, that in which the semantic figure is predominant, and that in which both types of figures are predominant.
Among these, an example of that in which the verbal quality is predominant is as follows:
"‘Why would he, who has already attained glory, again inflict upon me that labor of churning? I do not even imagine that sleep, which was previously his, could occur to one whose mind is so restless.
And why does he build a bridge once more?’—as if bearing such doubts, O Lord of all islands, now that you have arrived, the trembling of the ocean appears.

Here, in the expression of a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) based on a cause, the predominance of *samādhi* (poetic identification) is perceived through the superimposition of Viṣṇu’s own nature onto the words "you" (*tvayi*) and so forth, resulting in the attainment of that state.
Now, one might ask: why is this clarity (*prasāda*)—arising from the manifestation of the meaning—not considered a quality of the meaning (*arthaguṇa*)?
For even in this case, there is an excellence of the word’s power (*śabdaśakti*) due to that designation.

Indeed, in such expressions as "in you," "this one," and "of him," the words *yuṣmad*, *etad*, and *idam* have no direct denotation of Viṣṇu; how then, when applied to the object of description, can they express that specific meaning?

It is said: because these [words] denote everything by virtue of being pronouns (*sarvanāman*), for pronouns indeed express all things but refer specifically to that particular [object] understood from the context and so forth; and here, that [particular object] is understood as already manifested by such expressions as "one who has attained glory" (*prāptaśrī*).
Thus, an example where the quality of the meaning is predominant is as follows:

"Victorious for a long time are the dust-particles from your lotus-feet, which are like the powder for subduing the Goddess Lakṣmī; when they meet with the foreheads of men through prostration, they erase the ill-omened letters inscribed there by fate.
(467) Here, although both the figures of speech *hetu* (cause) and *sāmya* (simile) are expressed, the quality of meaning (*arthaguṇa*) is perceived primarily through the clarity of the sense.
An example where defects are predominant over qualities:

“By him the ocean was churned for nectar by gods and asuras, its waters cast aside and the abodes of the serpents laid bare; that very Mount Mandara now shines, bearing the mark of the Lord of Serpents from his revolutions, as if scraping the sky. (468)

In this instance, because of the *jñāpaka-hetu* (indicative cause) in the phrase "marked by the coils of the Lord of Serpents" (*vyāvartanairahipaterayamāhitāṅkaḥ*) and because of the constituent part of the *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) in the phrase "as if scraping the sky" (*khaṃ vyālikhanniva*), the plural number in "by the gods and demons" (*devāsuraiḥ*) is used when the eternal enmity is not intended [to be emphasized]. Furthermore, regarding the accusative case on the word "nectar" (*amṛta*)—based on the rule that "for roots such as *math* (to churn), even among those taking two objects, there is an addition [of the accusative for the secondary object]"—the predominance of both defect and merit is perceived.

Now, one might ask: how can there be predominance of the meaning (*artha*) here, since its subject matter has been superseded by the indicative cause? Even that [cause] is indeed a figure of sense (*arthālaṃkāra*).
And when there is an equality of status between a quality (guṇa) and an ornament (alaṃkāra), it is the ornament that becomes predominant, not the quality;
for ornaments are generally composed of qualities that themselves function as subordinate elements,
as follows:

The Vaidarbha style is held to be that which is untouched by the slightest trace of defects, woven with all excellences, possessing the beauty of the sound of a lute, and endowed with the qualities of vigor and splendor, even when composed of entirely forceful words.
Those expert in the styles (rīti) recognize the Gauḍīyā style as being embraced by a state of looseness yet resting upon an ancient luster;
poets know the Pāñcālī style to be sweet and delicate.
Desiring sweetness and clarity, those of keen intellect do not employ many compound words in the Lāṭīya,
Āvantī, or Māgadhī styles, except occasionally.
Some, wishing to express *ojas* (vigorousness), compose even many [verses] that are characterized by well-known words, are forceful, possess well-knit word-junctions, are clear,
and are self-expressive; such is considered *yamaka* by the learned.

Let it not be that the meaning possesses primacy by virtue of being on the same level as an ornament; but why should there not be primacy for a verbal quality such as *udātta* (the sublime), which consists in its connection with praiseworthy specific attributes? Because defects and qualities possess primacy through their capacity to manifest [the essence] beyond [mere surface], that reputation established by Vāmana remains: "Even today, the envious people indeed continue to strike at the vital spots of the enemy of Bala, who has transcended the heavens."
When a defect becomes subordinate, it shines even more intensely than before;
thus, an example where verbal ornamentation (*śabdālaṅkāra*) predominates is as follows:
"That which wandered upon the tawny mass of matted locks of Hara, which bore the weight of the buds of the rays of ten million moons..."
"May that water of the celestial river (Surāpagā), resounding with the tumultuous *jhātkāra* of its flow against the bowers of the rock-caves of the snowy mountain, purify you.

(469) Here, clarity of meaning (*arthaprākaṭya*) is *prasāda*; excellence of grandeur (*vibhavotkarṣa*) is *udāttatā*; and the absence of unevenness among soft, distinct, and mixed phonemes is *samatā*. From qualities such as firmness of composition (*bandhagāḍhatā*) and vigor (*aurjitya*), the verbal ornament *anuprāsa* (alliteration) is perceived as predominant.
An example where the verbal ornament is subordinate and the figure of sense (*arthālaṅkāra*) is predominant is as follows:

“Young men, embracing women who feign sleep while their cold has been dispelled by the great fatigue of their embrace, and filled with intense joy, sleep with their cotton garments tucked between their feet which are restless due to the shifting pressure of their upward-turned legs.

(470) In this verse, the quality of *jāti* (genus or class) is perceived as the primary figure of speech (*arthālaṃkāra*), owing to its predominance over other qualities such as *bandhavikaṭatva* (elaborateness of composition), which is *audāratā* (loftiness); *ślādhyaviśeṣaṇayoga* (the employment of praiseworthy epithets), which is *udāttatva* (nobility); *vibhavotkarṣa* (excellence of wealth or circumstance), which is *audārya* (magnanimity); and *dīptarasatva* (intensity of sentiment), which is *kānti* (grace).
An example where both types of ornamentation are predominant is as follows:
"The earth was uplifted, the chest of the enemy was shattered, and the royal fortune of Bali was embraced by this powerful youth.
Whatever that ancient Puruṣa accomplished over the course of three births, this youth has achieved it all in a single lifetime. (471)

In this context, the sequence of expression constitutes *prauḍhi* (maturity); the density of composition is *udāratā* (loftiness); the excellence of intention is *udāttatva* (nobility); and the clarity of meaning is *prasāda* (perspicuity). From such qualities as these, the figure of speech *viśeṣokti* (poetic understatement), with *śleṣa* (paronomasia) as its subordinate element, is perceived primarily as a dual ornament (*ubhayālaṅkāra*).

Furthermore, the blending of aesthetic flavors (*rasasaṃkara*) occurs in six ways, just like the blending of ornaments, through the combination of emotions (*bhāva*), semblances of flavor (*rasābhāsa*), and their subsidence (*praśama*), in the manner of sesame and rice, and so forth.
In that regard, the manner in which these emotions [coexist] is like that of sesame seeds and rice grains—as in:
‘This humiliation throbs intensely in my heart like a bolt of adamant; my mind sinks as if into a blind darkness, closed up with shame;
grief burns me because of the calamity that befell Tārkṣya; there is no action whatsoever possible; and yet compassion cuts into my very vitals regarding poor Sītā. (472)

Here, indignation, shame, sorrow, and compassion are perceived as being of equal weight and intermingling with one another like sesame seeds and rice grains, through their manifestation in the verbal expressions of the separated Rāma; they follow the pattern of milk and water, as in:
“‘Proud,’ ‘intolerant,’ ‘excessively clever’—thus, in my very presence, my friends’ reproaches take many forms.”
"Indeed, it is his conduct, smooth with mere courtesy, that surpasses all virtues.

(473) Here, anger toward her friends and envy toward the lover's virtues—though distinct like milk and water—are perceived as merging together through the lady’s preoccupation with the commencement of her speech;
this is the "Mirror-Reflection" type (*chāyādarśaprakāra*). As for example:

"O Sītā! That face of yours, once radiant with smiles that mocked the destruction of your bewildered and wandering kinsmen who were distracted by the weight of pride in their husbands—now Rāvaṇa forcibly makes it drenched in tears falling from eyes wide with terror as he violently pulls back your mass of hair.
Here, within the semblance of anger (*krodhābhāsa*), the semblance of love (*ratyābhāsa*) is perceived as being intermingled, according to the maxim of the mirror reflecting an image.
An example of the Narasiṃha type is as follows:
“O cursed woman at the door, what is the use of this mango tree that has been nurtured? This is a wicked poison-tree;
for when it undergoes even the slightest change through blossoming, the terrible fevers of love break out. (475)

Here, as in the *Narasiṃha-jātaka*, the two bodily parts—the lion and the man—are combined according to the commencement of the description of the mango tree; likewise, compassion directed toward the friend and contempt directed toward the mango tree are mutually blended. For, by the word "O wretched woman of fate" (*daivahatike*), once she is identified as being entirely pitiable under the condition of destiny, it is illuminated that her very skill consists in the cultivation of this mango tree. Thus, you are indeed so struck by fate that you nurture at your own door a poison-tree disguised as a mango tree.

And when the mango tree (*sahakāra*) has been utterly disparaged by the term "poison-tree" (*viṣapādapa*), its status as the cause of the unbearable onset of the fever of love (*smarajvara*) in women during its time of blossoming is conveyed by the suffix *ka*;
as it has been said:
"Whether one is already contemptible or becomes so through being treated with contempt, one is indeed contemptible."
When an object is denoted by its own primary word, by what could that object be qualified?
Furthermore, no contemporary sense of contempt is perceived when there is a difference in words;
for even when something is contemptible, it may be honored, and even when it is praiseworthy, it may be despised.
For example:

"In this world of living beings, there is but one who exists in the form of a living soul, yet is like a beast in human form—he who, like a deer, has not fallen into the snare of the love-noose of those with gazelle-like eyes. (476)
An example of the *pāṃsūdaka* type is as follows:
"Do not harbor pride, thinking: 'The flower-cluster written by my beloved's own hand shines upon the surface of my cheek.
O friend, is not every other woman also a fit vessel for such things, provided that trembling—the internal obstacle—does not arise? (477)

In this passage, a mixture (*saṃkara*) of envy (*asūyā*) and pride (*garva*), which are being rendered indistinguishable like dust and water in a lump of clay, is perceived as a variety of variegated color (*citravarṇaprakāra*). For example: "Hostility has ceased; a sentiment thick with bliss flows forth; my arrogance vanishes somewhere; humility bows me down."
"Upon seeing him suddenly, I have become utterly overwhelmed by something indescribable; for indeed, great beings possess some extraordinary excellence, like sacred fords.

(478) In this passage, the *praśama* (tranquility) of Sītā and the others—which are being eclipsed by the *rasas* of bliss (*ānanda*), composure (*praśama*), and helplessness (*pāravaśya*)—is perceived as being blended with the *rasas* of heroism (*vīra*), arrogance (*auddhatya*), and independence (*svātantrya*). Just as blue and other colors are blended on a cloth, these are found to be intermingled within the occasion of Lava’s speech, which serves as the *anubhāva* (consequent action) and the *upamāpada* (basis of comparison), arising from the power of seeing Rāma and producing an excess of wonder and tranquility.
This is an instance of the blending (*saṃkara*) of *rasas* and *guṇas*.
But surely, just as the elimination of defects, the adoption of excellences must also be accomplished through regulation;
and just as the employment of ornaments, the non-separation from aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) must also necessarily be maintained.
For sometimes the employment of ornaments may even be abandoned, but never the non-separation from *rasa* or the presence of excellences, since these two possess an inseparable connection.
To this it is replied:

where, as in the case of variegated color (*citravarṇa*), the man-lion (*narasiṃha*), or dust and water (*pāṃsūdaka*), there is an arrangement of qualities and rasas within a sentence that cannot be produced by separate efforts—according to the principle of part and whole (*avayavāvayavin*) or the principle of genus and individual (*jātivyakti*)—there the designation of "commixture" (*saṃkara*) does not apply.
For example:
There is sweetness in speech and a presence of aesthetic flavor (rasa) even in the subject matter itself,
by which the wise are intoxicated, just as honey-bees are by honey;
indeed, every ornament (alaṃkāra) pours flavor into the meaning.
Nevertheless, it is precisely this lack of vulgarity that carries this burden to a great extent;
for the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) alone is the sweet, supremely gladdening flavor.
Relying upon poetry composed of that [sentiment], sweetness is firmly established.
In the erotic sentiment known as *vipralambha* (love-in-separation) and in the pathetic (*karuṇa*),

sweetness attains a state of moistness (*ārdratā*), because the mind is more intensely absorbed therein; whereas the sentiments such as the furious (*raudra*) and others, when present in poetry, are characterized by brilliance (*dīpti*).
That which, by abiding in the *ojaḥ* (vigor) of both word and meaning, serves as the cause for their manifestation and constitutes the capacity of a sentence toward all aesthetic flavors (*rasa*),
is to be known as the quality *prasāda* (clarity), which performs its function universally.
Thus, this lack of established distinction (*asaṃkarāprasiddhi*) occurs when the *guṇas* are the originators of the *rasas*;

likewise, it occurs when the *rasas* are the originators of the *guṇas*, as follows: firmness of ego is *aurjitya*; the flow of speech arising from inner emotion is *bhāvikatva*; lack of intensity even in anger and the like is *mādhurya*; excellence of intention is *udāttatva*; the state of being most desired by the subject matter is *preyas*; and the state of having radiant *rasa* is *kānti*.

However, where the qualities (*guṇas*) and sentiments (*rasas*) are introduced into a sentence with equal status—like sesame and rice, milk and water, or a shadow and its reflection—and are accomplished without separate effort, there the designation of "commixture" (*saṃkara*) indeed applies;
it is of six kinds: predominant in quality, predominant in sentiment, predominant in both, non-predominant in either, superior in quality, and superior in sentiment.
Among these, the example of that which is predominant in quality is as follows:

"In the meantime, the Queen—her limbs rippling with the momentum of her stumbling as she was massaged by Lalitahāralatā on her hips—abandoned the bed and went to the inner apartments with the eunuchs, having fastened her girdle-string.

Here, the predominance belongs to the qualities of *artha* (meaning) and *śabda* (word)—namely *arthaprākaṭya* (clarity of meaning) and *audārya* (magnificence)—rather than to passion (*rati*) or anger (*krodha*); thus, it is "predominance of the qualities" (*guṇapradhāna*).
An example where rasa is predominant:

“In this [moment], the hand of the Goddess, whose eyes were tremulous and upon whom auspicious great herbs had been applied, was playfully grasped by the wielder of the Pināka bow with his hand, from which the serpent-bracelet had slipped away. (480)

In this [verse], the excellence (*udāttatva*) consists in the employment of praiseworthy adjectives; *audāratā* (loftiness) is the grandeur of the composition; *prasāda* (clarity) is the transparency of the meaning; and *kānti* (splendor) is the brilliance of the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*). These qualities are surpassed by the flavors of fear, playfulness, passion, and union; thus, it is dominated by *rasa*.
An example of that which is dominated by both [word and meaning] is as follows:
"O you who take pleasure only in the mere sight [of him], why do you wish to cast the seed of the lotus into the pond?"
"Time is the Kali age; this world is ungrateful. O ignorant one, remaining here, he shall seize the very splendor of your face.

(481) Here, there is a specific mode of expression (*ukti*) and a well-constructed arrangement (*saṃvidhāna*), which constitutes the verbal excellences (*śabdaguṇa*) of *śleṣa* (punning condensation). Furthermore, there is the description of the aesthetic flavors (*rasa*) of beauty and charm. Since these are indicated as being of equal status, this is an instance where both [the word and the meaning] are predominant.
An example where neither is predominant is as follows:

‘The wintry breeze, once sweet with the anger of a newlywed bride, has now become harsh from the embrace of simple folk by the fire of dried cow-dung; like the command of one whose wealth has vanished, the radiance of the sun is now faint, and the moon bears the pallor of a woman’s face in separation. (482)

In this [verse], the superimposition of the qualities of one thing onto another—namely, sweetness, cruelty, smoothness, and effeminacy—is *samādhi*. The manifestation (*prākaṭya*) of the four meanings—the anger of a new bride and so forth—as well as sweetness and the rest, which are defined by their respective characteristics, is *prasāda*. The carrying through to the conclusion of the qualifiers and the qualified in sequence—such as "the anger of a new bride is sweet" and "the fire of dried cow-dung"—is *rīti*. The arrangement of the four meanings across the four quarters of the verse with unequal case-endings is *saṃbhitatva*; these are the four *guṇas*. Furthermore, the four *rasas* consisting of love (*rati*), indignation (*amarṣa*), despondency (*viṣāda*), and disgust (*jugupsā*) are perceived as being primarily intended to convey the state of time; thus, both [the *guṇas* and the *rasas*] are subordinate.
An example of one superior in qualities:
“Let there be no birth for me; let there be no fulfillment of all desires. May I neither beg, nor serve, nor endure the humiliation of the wealthy. (483)

In this context, *sauśabdya* (elegant diction) consists in the derivation of nouns (*suptiṅ*) and verbal forms; *arthavyakti* (clarity of meaning) is the completeness of sentences; *prasāda* (transparency) is the manifestness of the sense; and *rīti* (style) is the sequence of actions such as birth and so forth, as in: "When prosperity does not arise, desires are not fulfilled; one whose desires are unfulfilled begs; begging and not obtaining that [wealth], he serves the wealthy; but while serving, he is humiliated by them. As for *rasa*, there is only one, namely *nirveda* (world-weariness). Thus, the former is superior in qualities (*guṇādhika*), while the latter is superior in excellence (*sādhika*). For example:
"A lotus in waterless space, a blue lotus in a lotus, these [all] upon a golden creeper—"
"And yet she is so delicate and lovely—what is this succession of portents? (484)

In this context, *samādhi* is the superimposition of the attributes of one thing upon another—as in "here is a lotus, though there is no water; on the lotus is a blue lily; these [grow] upon a golden creeper. Furthermore, the succession of such striking occurrences, such as "Is this a delicate and beautiful [creation]? constitutes the qualities of *aślīla* (the indecorous) and *amaṅgala* (the inauspicious). *Udātta* is the possession of praiseworthy specific qualities; *udāratā* is the quality of grandiose composition; *rīti* is the consistency of the opening treatment; *prasāda* is the clarity of meaning; *saukumārya* is the absence of harshness; *preyaḥ* is the state of being most desired; and *kānti* is the brilliance of the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*). These are the ten qualities. As for the *rasas*, twenty states—love, excellence, joy, fortitude, longing, impetuosity, wonder, reflection, deliberation, anxiety, fickleness, laughter, enthusiasm, paralysis, stammering, madness, shame, dissimulation, fear, and apprehension—are perceived as the verbal manifestations of a lover engaged in flattering his beloved; thus, this is an instance of the "excess of *rasa*" (*rasādhika*).

By this, the commingling of rasa and alaṃkāra is also explained; for in the case of a great poet, certain objects imbued with rasa and adorned with alaṃkāras are accomplished by a single effort alone. (173)
That ornament whose composition can be accomplished through the impulsion of rasa— being produced without a separate effort— is considered superior,
provided there is no intention to express objects such as aesthetic emotions (rasas) or mental states (bhāvas). (174)
A work consisting solely of ornaments does not please poets.
(175) In that regard, the blending of rasa and ornament is twofold: that which is dominated by rasa and that which is dominated by ornament.
Of these two, that which is described by the experiencer himself is the one dominated by rasa.
For in that case, a sentence possessing an ornament becomes a consequential emotion (*anubhāva*) through the commencement of speech;
therein, there is a commixture (*saṃkara*) of the simile (*upamā*) within the passion (*rati*), as for example:
"In her face, which is delightful to behold, [there is] that produced by the stumbling of her pride..."

Even her anger, born from a lapse in affection toward that lovely face made beautiful by the sight of him, steals away my heart— just as the mud of rutting-fluid, when settled upon the moon, captivates the mind. (485)

Here, by means of the subordination of the simile (*upamā*), in the speech of the passionate Hari—which consists of a verbal expression—the beauty of Satyabhāmā’s anger arising from her seeing the *pārijāta* cluster given by Rukmiṇī is primarily perceived.
An example of a "simile of reversal" (*viparītopamā*) occurring specifically in the context of love is as follows:
"O beloved, that blue lotus which possesses a luster equal to your eyes has sunk into the water; the moon, which imitates the radiance of your face, has been hidden by the clouds."

"Even those royal swans, whose gait imitates yours, have departed; fate does not permit me even the mere diversion of your likeness. (486) Here, as Rāma, separated from his beloved, attempts to console himself by observing the resemblance of her limbs, the simile is perceived as secondary because its power is exhausted in the description of his own nature during the commencement of speech arising from despondency due to the failure of his means of diversion. An example of this same [secondary] nature occurring in the context of passion (*rati*) is as follows:

‘Is it her heavy hips, or rather the weight of her breasts?’— thus, as she was weighed by the tips of the Creator’s palms, her triple fold of skin bears the illusion of the marks left by his sunken fingers. (487)
Her three folds of skin bear the illusion of a path made by fingers dug into the earth [by the Creator].

Here, although the figure of *paryāya* (succession) is primarily perceived through causes of doubt, poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*), and simile (*upamā*) arising from wonder and other emotions born of sexual passion, nevertheless, since this is an *anubhāva* (consequent emotion) of the verbal expression, it experiences only subordination to the *rasa* of love; for *samādhi* (poetic concentration) resides precisely in that *rasa*.

“Having with difficulty passed over her pair of thighs and wandered for a long time upon the region of her hips, my gaze—now fallen upon her waist, uneven with the waves of the three folds—becomes as if thirsty; then, slowly ascending her lofty breasts, it gazes repeatedly with longing at her eyes, which shed drops of water.
Here, the King of Vatsa attributes the qualities of a living being to his own sight, but these subside when the verbal expression of passion arising from the sight of Sāgarikā begins.
An example of *arthaśleṣa* (punning meaning) occurring specifically in the context of love is as follows:
“On your cheek, the decorative leaf-design has been crushed by the pressure of your palm; this nectar-like essence of your lower lip has been drunk away by your sighs;
repeatedly clinging to your throat, your tears cause your breasts to heave. O you who are indifferent to us, it is resentment that has become dear to you, and not we. (489)

In this case, although the conclusion of the sentence is achieved through an implied objection (*ākṣepa*), nevertheless, being primarily expressed by the words "dear one" (*priya*) and so forth, the *śleṣa* (paronomasia) itself assumes the role of a subordinate element (*aṅga*) for the manifesting cause (*anubhāva*) of the lover’s verbal expression, specifically within the context of sexual union.
This is an example of *paryāyokta* (periphrasis), as in:

"Released from her neck, yet held by the slope of her breasts; the height of her jar-like breasts [preserved] by her thighs; the fullness of her hips [maintained] by her thighs; the tapering grace of her hand [retained] by her feet, and her gait [preserved] by her feet."

"O slayer of the elephant [Gajāsura], this hide of yours is indeed hard; what is this obstinacy, O Caṇḍī?"—may the smile of the Noble Lady (Pārvatī) at these words of the Enemy of Tripura protect you!

(490) In this passage, as the Lord begins his speech of flattery, the Goddess’s description by way of synonyms attains the status of a *śeṣa* (remainder). That which is described by one who remains indifferent is primarily an ornament (*alaṃkāra*); for he, wishing to express a mode of the commingling (*saṃkara*) of rasa, bhāva, and so forth, resorts either to *svabhāvokti* (description of nature) or *vakrokti* (indirect expression).
Among these, in the case of *svabhāvokti*, it is *jāti* (genus).
That [joy] by way of positive description (*vidhimukhena*) is as follows:
“Her face has its anger slightly subsiding, its joy gradually increasing, and it possesses a playful charm that is both visible from afar and intoxicating with the essence of passion. (491)
"[Her face becomes one where anger recedes slightly and joy increases little by little, and it possesses a radiance that shines afar, with its charm dependent upon both sentiments.

Here, the *anubhāvas*—such as the downward glance and the brightening of the face—which belong to Satyabhāmā’s departing anger and her spreading joy, are blended together; by means of the phrase "its charm dependent upon both sentiments," the poet expresses them through a positive formulation (*vidhimukhena*) so that they remain exactly as they are.]
An example of the very same birth [of emotion] expressed by way of negation is as follows:

“O steadfast one, let there be no shattering of pride; for one who is truly proud, even when his weight is being lifted on a scale, his heart does not waver, nor does it cling even to a single thing. (492)
"Through fortitude there is the breaking of pride; through the faltering of pride, there begins a heavy display of fortitude.
When weighed on the scale, her heart leaps up; even when one side is steady, it does not settle.

Here, although there is the presentation of a cause (*hetu*), nevertheless, because that serves as an adjunct to the description of her natural disposition (*svabhāvākhyāna*) and is secondary, it is the very nature of the heart's action that is expressed here by way of negation; thus, this is indeed a *jāti* (naturalistic description).
That very same [state] occurs through both injunction and prohibition, as for example:

"Victorious are the fruitless movements of Rādhā’s hands in the sky for a long time—she who, seeing the thinness of Hari’s arm when he had lifted the mountain with ease, reached out her hand to his shoulder, placed her feet at his feet, and desired to become an assistant in lifting Govardhana, yet failed to touch it. (493)

Here, in Hari—the beloved of Rādhā—the states of existence (*astitva*), manifestation (*udbhūta*), activity (*vṛtti*), affection (*sneha*), doubt (*śaṅkā*), and enthusiasm (*utsāha*) are mutually intermingled with transitory emotions (*vyabhicāribhāva*) such as fear, agitation, recollection, reflection, and deliberation. These are perceived within the physical manifestation (*anubhāva*) of the bodily movements occurring during the "illusion of the hand" (*karabhrānti*), which is accompanied by the treading upon her feet (the *ālambana*). They are expressed both through negation, as "not touching Govardhana," and through affirmation, as "they conquer [all others]," according to the theory of *vakrokti* (indirect expression). Among these, the figure of speech *upamā* (simile) is exemplified as follows:

"The thieves repeatedly cast glances, both fearful and longing, like those of a young woman upon the breasts nestled in the lap of her mother, which are like jars of treasure guarded by serpents. (494)
Like a treasure jar well-guarded in the embrace of the bosom of a mature woman.

Here, although there is a commingling (*saṃkara*) of fear and passion residing in the thief, and a description of natural state (*svabhāvokti*), the simile found in the latter half of the verse is perceived as predominant;
for the simile itself is the subject of this commingling with the semblance of rasa (*rasābhāsa*). For example:
"With one eye, reddened by intense passion, she gazes at the sun situated on the western mountain; with her other eye, tremulous with tears, she looks upon her own beloved.
At the close of day, the female *cakravāka* bird, fearing separation from her mate, blends these two sentiments like a skilled dancer.
Here, as it is explained by the literal reading itself, the simile is clearly perceived as the predominant element.

An example of the simultaneous expression of rasa (flavor) and praśama (subsidence) through simile is as follows: “When her beloved was seen, the pride of the fair-eyed woman blossomed slightly like her eyes; when he stood at her side, it bowed down like her face; when he sat nearby, it remained suppressed like her horripilation; when he extended his touch, it became loosened like the knot of her skirt; when he began to speak, it withdrew like shame; and finally, when he touched her feet, it departed entirely like her anger. (596)

In this context, when the stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) of intense joy—which arises from the object of passion (*ālambanavibhāva*), namely the sight of her beloved by a proud woman whose mind was known to be full of resentment toward a certain friend—is kindled by excitant factors (*uddīpanavibhāva*) such as his approaching her side, and while the transitory emotions (*vyabhicāribhāva*) consisting of physical manifestations like horripilation are emerging, and the stable emotion is being elevated to the state of the aesthetic flavor (*ānandarasatā*) through the intensifying expressions (*anubhāva*) of closing the eyes, looking downward, and the loosening of the waist-knot; then, due to the emergence of other powerful conflicting emotions, the simultaneous submergence and predominance of shame and anger—which are diminishing at every moment from those very same causes—manifests as a simile accompanied by a co-utterance (*sahokti*).

However, by the power of figures such as *śleṣa* (paronomasia), poets sometimes even imagine a semblance of the blending (*saṃkara*) of aesthetic moods (*rasa*), though it is not real; this occurs through the combination of metaphor (*rūpaka*) and paronomasia (*śleṣa*), as in:
"Struck in the heart by the unbearable arrow of Rāma-Manmatha, the night-stalker woman..."
"Smeared with fragrant blood-sandalwood, she went to the abode of the Lord of Life.

(597) Here, the sentiment of disgust (*bībhatsa-rasa*) is perceived as if it were intermingled with the sentiment of love (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*), even though the latter is not actually present, by virtue of the power of the double entendre (*śleṣa*) and metaphor (*rūpaka*).
An example of this through a corroboration (*arthāntaranyāsa*) permeated by double entendre is as follows:

"O Goddess, you whose lip is bitten by the stroke of the sword, you cause both your eyes and eyebrows to bloom; O lady with beautiful breasts like blue water-lilies, how is it that you do not produce delusion, you whose glance is so fixed?"
"How is it that she, possessing the beauty of excellent breasts like blue lotus petals, does not produce delusion when not clinging to my chest?

Here, the heroic sentiment (*vīra-rasa*) is blended with the erotic sentiment of separation (*vipralambha-śṛṅgāra*), even though the latter is not actually present, by the power of *śleṣa* (paronomasia).
An example of *śleṣopamā* (simile based on paronomasia) is as follows:

"Cast off when he clung to her hand, violently struck even as he seized the hem of her garment, driven away even as he grasped her hair, not looked upon even as he fell at her feet, and shaken off even as he embraced her— may that fire of Śambhu’s arrow burn away your sins, like a lover who has committed a fresh offense, [as it was treated] by the young women of Tripura with their lotus-eyes filled with tears.

(499) In this verse, the sentiment of *karuṇa* (pathos) is blended with the *vipralambha-śṛṅgāra* (erotic love-in-separation), even though the latter is not explicitly present, by virtue of the power of the *śleṣa-upamā* (pun-based simile).
An example of [the figure] by means of *śleṣa* (paronomasia) and *vyatireka* (contrast) is as follows:

“Having divided the pair of thighs with her feet, having pressed the waist between her arms, having struck forcefully at the sides with her nails, and having bitten the lip with her teeth—even awakening those who were asleep in the forest, does she, desiring amorous dalliance, devour your enemies again? No, no! She is a tigress with a terrifying face. (500)

Here, by the power of *śleṣa* (paronomasia), the non-ultimate perception of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*), being sublated by the ultimate sentiment of the loathsome (*bībhatsa*), produces the cognition of a mutual conjunction between their respective attributes through the figure of *śleṣa-rūpaka*, as for example:
“Wearing bracelets fashioned from entrails, bearing earrings clearly made of red lotuses in the form of women’s hands, and having fastened garlands of heart-lotuses upon their heads...”
“Here, these female Piśācas, delighting in the saffron-paste of blood, gather with their lovers and joyfully drink the wine of bone-marrow from skull-cups.

Here, the sentiment of the loathsome (vībhatsa) is blended with a semblance of the erotic (śṛṅgārābhāsa) suggested by the power of the words, through the figure of speech known as *samādhi*. For example:

"O Kālī! The crescent moon is upon your crest; the moon and the sun are in your pair of ears; the stars are in your eyes; the multitude of wandering moons is upon your breasts; the lightning is your girdle; and the splendors of the twilight are the luster of your garment—this attire of yours, fashioned at the end of a Kalpa, reigns supreme. (502) Here, the *bhayānaka* (terrible) sentiment, being intermingled with a semblance of *śṛṅgāra* (erotic) sentiment—which is suggested by the beauty of the "attire" constructed through the figures of *samādhi* (poetic concentration) and *rūpaka* (metaphor)—attains the status of a subordinate limb (*aṅga*) to the *preyas* (the beloved) sentiment for the listener, and thus it is properly integrated.

Thus, this manifold variety of intermixture (*saṃsṛṣṭi*) should be understood as arising from the blending (*saṃkara*) of *guṇas* and *alaṃkāras*. Even therein, it takes the form of both the manifest and the unmanifest—whether by way of the relationship between primary and subordinate or by way of equal status. Its specific varieties, such as sesame and rice, milk and water, or a mirror and its reflection, are to be understood according to their respective applications.
Should these be mentioned, or should they not? How can they be understood if they are not explicitly stated?

Because they are included within those already mentioned—for instance, in the description of the ornaments of both meaning and sound: in the phrase "khaṃ vaste" (he wears the sky), there is the *vibhaktimudrā* (metaphor of case-ending) in "pārayati carcām" (he completes the deliberation); and in the phrase "kalaviṅka-kaṇṭha-malinaṃ kādambinī-kambalam" (a blanket of clouds as dark as the throat of a sparrow), the *padamudrā* (metaphor of the word) is perceived. Thus, even when verbal ornaments are combined, they are indeed recognized;
so it is in other cases as well.
The two possible modes for characterizing the commingling (*saṃsṛṣṭi*) of figures are: the subsistence of all [figures] in a relationship of primary and subordinate, or their equality of status.
(176) Among these, the subsistence in a relationship of primary and subordinate is as follows:
“O charming girl, the lotuses are vying with the beauty of your face;
for what is difficult for those who possess both treasury and army?

(503)” Here, “the lotuses are vying with the beauty of your face, O charming girl” constitutes a simile (*upamā*), while “for what is difficult for those who possess both treasury and army? is a corroboration (*arthāntaranyāsa*) subordinate to a pun (*śleṣa*).
And there are lotuses complete with both sheaths and stalks; therefore, for them, nothing is impossible, because both the treasury (kośa) and the army (daṇḍa) are the means to victory.

By this, since the paronomasia (śleṣa) supports the meaning that serves as the means [to the conclusion], whereas the simile (upamā) specifies the particular subject under discussion, it is understood that they stand in the relationship of subordinate members to the "corroboration by a general principle" (arthāntaranyāsa).
An example of how all [figures] may be of equal status is as follows:
“Darkness seems to smear my limbs; the sky seems to rain collyrium; like service rendered to a wicked man, my sight has become fruitless.

(504) Now, one might object: since there is equality [of status], would this not result in a lack of connection? How then can a relationship arise among all [elements] with equal rank? The answer is this: when ornaments such as *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) and *upamā* (simile), by virtue of being devoted to the description of the *vibhāvas*, *anubhāvas*, and *vyabhicāribhāvas*, attain the status of subordinates (*aṅga*) to the *rasa* and so forth, then indeed they possess equal rank.

In that regard, there are two poetic fancies (*utprekṣā*)—“Darkness, as it were, smears the limbs; the sky, as it were, rains collyrium”—and a simile (*upamā*)—“Vision has become fruitless, like service rendered to a wicked man. These do not fail to meet the definition [of *dhvani*], because they function as subordinate elements (*aṅga*) by establishing the excellence of the darkness—which serves as the excitant condition (*uddīpana-vibhāva*) of the object of description—through their very equality.
Now, one might ask: why are these three not called similes?
For the particle *iva* is seen in other sentences to denote only a simile.
Do not say so;

for the particle *iva* serves to illuminate the sense of similarity (*sādṛśya*) as conveyed by the words expressing the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*). However, in expressions such as *limpati* ("he smears"), there exists neither a standard of comparison nor an object of comparison such that the *iva* could be employed to illuminate their similarity.

Furthermore, there is no standard of comparison expressed by a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*), because such a suffix denotes an action yet to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and thus possesses the character of non-existence (*asattva*).
Thus he says:

"For comparison is prescribed for that which is already established; since the meaning of a finite verb (tiṅanta) is something yet to be accomplished (sādhya), it possesses no capacity for comparison."
Furthermore, the particle *iva* does not occur only in the context of a simile;
for example, as in the expression, "How will this possibly come to be?

Even if there were a relationship of standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and object of comparison (*upameya*) between "smearing" (*limpati*) and "darkness" (*tamas*), nevertheless, no common property (*tulyadharma*) is observed that would suffice to establish that relationship of standard and object of comparison.
If it is asked, "What else could there be? It is simply the act of smearing; therefore, what must there be [denoted] by the root *lip*?
For the act of smearing cannot exist apart from the root *lip*," [we reply:
Indeed, two things shine forth here: the agent (*kartṛ*) who smears and its object, the act of smearing.
It is not so;
for if that were the case, it would have to be "like one who smears" (*limpatir iva*), and not "as if he were smearing" (*limpatīva*).

Now, just as in the expression "the head of Rāhu" there exists a relationship between part and whole even though there is no difference [between them], so too here there will be a relationship between attribute and substratum (*dharmadharmibhāva*).
Do not say so;

for the relationship between the object of comparison and the subject of comparison is based on the cognition of both difference and similarity. How could he who considers that [relationship] to exist even in the absence of those two not be insane?
As it has been said: "That very thing is both the property and the possessor of the property—no one, not even a madman, would say such a thing."

If it is argued that the agent, expressed by the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*), may then serve as the standard of comparison, [we reply: that agent is subordinated within the verbal word. But how does it become subordinated in the verbal word?

Listen: six meanings are cognized by means of a verbal form (*tiṅanta*): action (*kriyā*), time (*kāla*), voice (*upagraha*), the instrument of accomplishment (*sādhana*), number (*saṅkhyā*), and person (*puruṣa*).
Among these, the base denotes the causes for tense, voice (ātmanepada and parasmaipada), and so forth; the suffix denotes the instrument (sādhana), number, and person.

Since these are for the sake of the action, the action is primary. As for tense and the cause for the ātmanepada, they function as qualifiers of the action; number and person function as qualifiers of the instrument, and thus they both remain subordinate to those two.

Furthermore, regarding the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*): according to the principle that "the base and the suffix express their own meaning together," and by the principle that "even though the 'already accomplished' (*bhūta*) is the primary element, it is taught for the sake of the 'to-be-accomplished' (*bhavya*"), once the action is established, the agent—having already exerted its activity—is subordinate to that action for the sake of another.

Thus, this agent, being preoccupied with the accomplishment of its own action, how could it possibly be capable of requiring another thing as either a standard of comparison (*upamāna*) or an object of comparison (*upameya*)?
If this is so, then the meaning will be understood as follows: "He is like that agent characterized by the action of one who anoints his limbs."
It is not so;
for there is no comprehension of the agent, who is characterized by the action and serves as the standard of comparison, through the force of word-connection.

For a word becomes the cause for the comprehension of a specific meaning only through three modes of operation—primary (mukhya), secondary (gauṇī), and indicative (lakṣaṇā)—which are assisted by factors such as the context and the intended meaning.

For example, the word "cow" (go) denotes an object possessing a dewlap and so forth by its primary function (mukhyā vṛtti); yet that same word, when applied to a Vāhīka or similar person in consideration of his possession of qualities such as standing [like a cow] or urinating, undergoes a secondary function (gauṇī vṛtti).

But when [a word], whether by its primary (mukhya) or secondary (gauṇī) function, is unable to attain the status of a means for the accomplishment of the action expressed, it then indicates another object inseparable from its own meaning through indication (lakṣaṇā). For example, in the expression "The hamlet dwells in the Gaṅgā," the word *gaṅgā*, whose denotative power (*abhidhā-śakti*) is firmly established in a specific flow of water, is unable to serve as the locus for the action of dwelling performed by the hamlet; thus, it indicates the bank, which is inseparable from its own meaning. However, none of these modes of operation (*vṛtti*) is applicable here.
For instance, because the root *limpati* denotes an action, there can be no primary [identity] between the action and its agent;

nor can there be an attainment of that state through similarity between the action and the agent—as in the case of mother-of-pearl appearing as silver—because the qualities of an action cannot possibly reside in an agent, and because the usage is as if it were direct (*sākṣāt*), it is not figurative (*gauṇī*). Furthermore, since an action is itself by nature a property (*dharma*), [it cannot be metaphorically attributed].

The statement "the intellect sees" is an instance of metaphorical usage (*upacāra*), which consists in the superimposition of the attributes of one thing onto another; thus, it is not a distinct type of secondary sense (*gauṇī*).
Furthermore, the word *iva* is observed even in the absence of similarity, so it would not be restricted [to that alone].

For if the word *iva* were to indicate only similarity, then since a similarity between the action of smearing (*limpati-kriyā*) and darkness—which is a substantial entity (*sattvabhūta*)—is impossible, it would imply (or suggest) an agent who is invariably connected to its own primary meaning.

Furthermore, here there are no instances of *lakṣitalakṣaṇā* (indirect indication by implication), *aviruddhalakṣaṇā* (non-contradictory indication), or the like, as in the cases of "there is no redundancy regarding a beloved person" or "he is not seen even after very short periods of time.
Nor do discerning people respect a derivation of word-meanings that transgresses the principles of grammar.

Even if this [meaning] could be established through *adhyāhāra* (supplying ellipses) and other means, nevertheless, one must seek a common ground [for interpretation], for the same applies to the case of conflicting views (*vipratipatti*).

Nor should it be argued that there arises a cognition of a quality identical [to the standard] even for that which is not explicitly denoted, as in the case of "your face is like the moon," where radiance is perceived;
for in the same way, nothing other than the act of smearing is perceived here from the root *limpati*. (177)

Let it be observed that this verb *limpati* (to smear), having darkness as its agent, is intended by the learned to signify the sense of "adhering" (*upaśleṣaṇa*) and the sense of "raining down" (*varṣaṇa*).
[This is indicated] by such words as *manye*, *śaṅke*, *dhruvam*, *prāyaḥ*, and *nūnam*. (178)
Poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) is manifested by words, and the word *iva* is likewise [indicative of it].

Just as in a single sentence, so too in extended compositions (*prabandha*), there occurs an arrangement of the mixture of poetic qualities (*guṇa*) and ornaments (*alaṃkāra*) through the avoidance of impropriety.

In this regard, the avoidance of impropriety (*anaucitya*) is as follows: in the *Nirdoṣadaśaratha*, Rāma was deceived by Kaikeyī and Daśaratha through illusion, not by his own mother and father; in the *Mahāvīracarita*, Vālin was killed by Rāma while he was fighting Rāma himself, not by Sugrīva; in the *Veṇīsaṃhāra*, the blood of Duḥśāsana was drunk by a Rākṣasa fond of blood, not by Bhīmasena; in the *Śākuntala*, Duṣyanta forgot to accept Śakuntalā due to the curse of Durvāsas, not because his passion had subsided; in the *Chalitarāma*, Sītā was made to abandon her belongings and be exiled by two Rākṣasas employed by Lavaṇa after that [deed] was reported, not by Kaikeyī and Mantharā; furthermore, in the *Tāpasavatsarāja*, although Vāsavadattā had been burnt, Padmāvatī was married by Udayana out of a desire for revenge; and when his purpose was accomplished, the King of Vatsa—who did not know of Vāsavadattā’s presence—resolved to enter the fire, thinking, "I cannot live even for a moment without her," which extracted the dart of falsehood from the heart of his beloved; and in the *Vikrāntaśūdraka*, Śivagaṇa, out of devotion to his master, thinking "I shall accomplish my lord's business," abandoned his innocent beloved for the sake of his master's work, saying, "I have lived these many days only for the sake of my master's business; today, having accomplished it, I follow her"; she too, seeing his noble display of love and having her own lover's falsehood concealed, cast herself into that very pyre, distressed by the thought of separation from him—this, then, is the removal of defects.

The adoption of qualities, however, consists in the excellence of the composition through the proper application of those qualities; furthermore, it is endowed with the four modes of performance (*vṛtti*). These four modes are *bhāratī*, *ārabhaṭī*, *kaiśikī*, and *sāttvatī*.
Among them:
that which is primarily speech, employed by kings, devoid of women, and composed in Sanskrit is *bhāratī*.

That mode of performance which is employed by Bharata and named after his own name shall be called Bhāratī; where there are leaps, jumps, and oversteps, as well as cutting maneuvers, illusions, sorcery, and various battles— in such cases, they call this mode Ārabhaṭī.

That which is characterized by delicate attire and special ornaments, associated with women, abounding in song and dance, and featuring abundant refinements for the enjoyment of desire— that they call the Kaiśikī style;
while that which is endowed with the quality of goodness (sattva) as an inner attribute, and is accompanied by generosity and right conduct [is the Sāttvatī].

Intense with joy and having cast off the burden of grief, she is known here as the *Sāttvatī* style of performance. Its sixteen constituent parts (*aṅgas*) are as follows: among them, *prarocanā*, *vīthī*, *prastāvanā*, and *prahasana* are the four components of the *Bhāratī* style.
Among these, *prarocanā* is a statement intended to praise the subject matter to be spoken; for example:
“Victorious is the Self-Existent One, the cause of the universe! Victorious is Murāri, the son of Purandara!
Victorious is the god Hara, whose body is united with the daughter of the mountain, who removes the fear of sin!
(505) This speech, which indicates the occasion for introducing the matter at hand, is the *prastāvanā*; as in the *Ratnāvalī*.
"Even from another continent, from the middle of the ocean, or from the very end of the quarters,
Fate, having become favorable, brings together and instantly unites whatever is desired.
(506) The *vīthī* consists of the employment of the constituent parts (*aṅgas*) such as the *uddhātyaka*, the *kathoddhāta*, the *prayogātiśaya*, the *pravartaka*, and the *avalagita*.
Among these, the *uddhātyaka* (the introductory verse) is as follows:
“Who is victorious? Śarva is victorious! By whom has victory been won?
By the Blessed One, the enemy of Tripura, the burner of the God of Love, whose matted hair is marked by the young crescent moon. (507)
An example of *kathoddhāta* (the introduction of a story) is as follows:

"May that Lord known by the name of Rāma protect you—that Hari who, at the request of the Lord of the Gods, descended of his own accord into the lineage of Ikṣvāku, which was as pure as the orb of the autumnal moon; and who, born from the lotus-born Brahmā, slew the Rākṣasa descendant of Pulastya, the enemy of those who follow the path of the three Vedas. (508)
An excellence of execution (*prayogātiśaya*) is as follows:

“May the playful behavior (*yūthāyita*) of Hari, who assumed the form of a boar while lifting up the earth—his reflection appearing in the thousands of mirrors that were the jewels on the hoods of Śeṣa—protect you. (509)
An example of the *pravartaka* (the introductory verse) is as follows:
“This autumn season has arrived, possessing a pure and lovely splendor, with its bright and stainless moonlight fully attained;

it has uprooted the fierce, dense darkness of the rainy season, just as Rāma, having gathered his kinsmen (*bandhujīva*), uprooted the formidable ten-faced Rāvaṇa after destroying the thick darkness. (510)
An example of *avalagita* (the concealed): "Let this very autumn season be celebrated;
for in it, 'The Dhārtarāṣṭra swans—possessing fine wings, sweet voices, adorned quarters, and beginning their flight with pride—descend upon the surface of the earth by the power of Time. (511)
*Prahasanam* is speech intended for ridicule directed at those such as ascetics who have strayed from their own duty (*svadharma*).
For example:
"The mendicant does not bite the lower lip offered by the wife of his disciple during the act of lovemaking."
"O lotus-eyed one, the eating of meat is forbidden in our tradition.
(512) The four components of *ārabhaṭī* are: *saṃkṣiptikā*, *avapātaḥ*, *vastūtthāpanam*, and *saṃsphoṭaḥ*.
Among these, *saṃkṣiptikā* is the condensation of a subject matter through means such as a great illusion (*māhendrajāla*) or costumes (*nepathya*).
For example:
"Having deceived both Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa by means of a rakṣasa in the form of a deer, he carried off Sītā, his attempt momentarily thwarted by the lord of birds. (513)
*Avapāta* (falling down) is the entry into or exit from actions such as fleeing due to fear and so forth; for example:
"Having abandoned the form of a deer and assumed a hideous body..."
"Lakṣmaṇa is being led by that Rākṣasa into the uncertainty of battle.
The "evocation of a subject" (*vastūtthāpanam*) consists of a collection of all *rasas* and *bhāvas*, whether without agitation or with agitation—
as for example:

"Having by chance encountered this enemy who is about to sever my beloved—moving before my face like a digit of the moon from Rāhu’s jaws—from the reach of his sword-blade, how can my heart behave? It is agitated by terror, hurried by compassion, tossed by wonder, inflamed by anger, and blossomed with joy.
(515) *Saṃsphoṭa* is a violent clash involving various weapons, wrestling, and the like, characterized by furious combat.
For example:

“By that beast who dragged the daughter of the Pāñcāla king by her hair, who stripped away even her garment in the presence of kings and elders, and for whose blood-draught from his chest I vowed to drink—he has now fallen into the cage of my arms; O Kauravas, let him be protected! (516)

*Narma*, *narmasphijaḥ*, *narmasphoṭaḥ*, and *narmagarbha*— these are the four limbs of the *kaiśikī* style. Among them, *narma* is speech or action established in the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) that is accompanied by jesting,
as for example:

‘We are indeed as you have said; what can I say? Yet, all of a sudden in the midst of conversation, he has assumed the shape of a *kadamba* bud. How is it that this girl of noble family is so pure and innocent?’—this is the first stage of union (*prathama-saṃbhoga*), consisting of the description of the new state, the words concerning the occasion of the union, and other such actions, which constitute the playful jests of a woman with full hips.
For example:
"She, the beloved daughter of Vṛṣaparvan, has arrived at the place of tryst; she is like a fresh rain shower, free from clouds and composed of nectar, which sprinkles my limbs.
Do you know? She will surely gladden my tormented mind today; she will turn it back, O friend, like a fierce whirlwind, toward that Devayānī. (518)
*Narmasphoṭa* (the disclosure of a jest) is the sudden interruption of a union between two whose desire and its outward expression have already become manifest;
for example:
"O Princess of Vidarbha, behold these enemies here, whose weapons can be snatched away even by children; you have my permission to look."
"By such martial prowess as this, you are sought after by these [enemies] who have you in their grasp.
(519) The concealment of one's true nature and so forth for the sake of a particular purpose is "playful concealment" (*narmagarbha*),
as for example:

‘Then a certain man with matted hair, wearing a deerskin and the *aṣāḍha* garment, bold in speech and as if blazing with the splendor consisting of the Veda, entered the penance grove like the first stage of life (the student) embodied.
The four limbs of the *sātvatī* style are: the introductory (*utthāpaka*), the transitional (*parivartaka*), the conversational (*saṃlāpaka*), and the composite (*saṃghātyaka*).
Among those [types of *śleṣa*], the "instigator" (*utthāpaka*) is that in which the meanings are mutually related; for example:
"Strike my body first, for I am fond of being struck first; but once I have been dealt a blow, what could you do with another?"
The headless trunk (kabandha), its neck and shoulder-joint suddenly severed by a blazing axe with many wide-spreading flames, [is an example].
Parivartaka (exchange) is the abandonment of the intended meaning for the adoption of another meaning;
as for example: [text follows].

Those women who approached with the desire to bring the sage face-to-face through their quality of loveliness, he himself bestowed passion upon them; for indeed, the course of purposes is difficult to comprehend. (522) In the assembly, mutual censure by various speeches constitutes conversation.
For example:
"How could the hand of Drupada’s son have been forbidden by my father, who was either suffering or afraid?
Today, as you swagger with pride in the strength of your arms, he places this left foot upon your head; hold it there! (523)
The *saṃghātyaka* (composite) type consists of the breaking up of a group by means of tasks, mantras, personal power, fate, and so forth;
for example:
"As if not seeing the Lord, the Gaṇas retreated from the battle."
"For the mind, when seized by agitation, indeed becomes bewildered in times of distress" (524).
By the term "clever" (*catura*), the hero's proficiency in the worldly and scriptural conventions regarding virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation is expressed;
by the term "noble" (*udātta*), the excellence of his disposition and prosperity, as well as his lineage, youth, and so forth, is revealed.

By the statement, "Who would not hold dear a composition that bears fruit in the form of the four aims of human life? it is declared that this composition—which is established upon injunctions and prohibitions, such as "one should behave like Rāma and others, and not like Rāvaṇa and others"—is most desirable for its listeners.
Then, by the passage beginning with "The Opening (Mukha), the Subsequent Opening (Pratimukha)," etc., the five-limbed body of the composition is described;
furthermore, its sixty-four constituent parts, such as the Introduction (Upakṣepa), the Embellishment (Parikara), and so forth, are all included within the Opening and the other [limbs].
Therefore, just like that [example], even a single sentence consisting of five junctures (*pañcasaṃdhi*) attains the designation of a "composition" (*prabandha*).
For example:

"When the beloved somehow drew near" is the *mukha* (opening); "with faltering reply" is the *pratimukha* (development); "by her, emaciated by separation, having made a pretext, an unheeded speech was uttered" is the *garbha* (climax); "with eyes turned aside, full of agitation at the favor of reaching the ears of the impatient friend" is the *vimarśa* (pause); and "in the empty house, a sigh was heaved and they met" is the *nibarhaṇa* (conclusion).

By this, it is explained that even in the case of the meaning of a prior composition, the status of being a "composition" (*prabandhatva*) does not arise merely from what is stated in a single sentence;
for example:
"In the sacrifice of Sagara, [the sons] who were intent on the multitude of horses and who split the earth—even their great-grandfathers, though scorched by the wrathful luster of Kapila..."
"Having performed austerities while disregarding the torment to his own body, Bhagīratha finally caused [the Ganges]—touched by your waters, O Blessed One—to flow forth.
By the phrase "neither expanded nor condensed," the minds of those who fear prolixity and those who dread an interruption in the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) of the narrative are won over.

By the phrase "in a meter suitable for recitation," the weary listeners are refreshed by the completion of the sections (*āśvāsaka*) and so forth; furthermore, in the composition, elements such as garlands and the like are perceived, just as they are in actual arrangements.

By the passage beginning with "In the garden of the city" (*puropavane*) and so forth, the excellence of place, time, and the worthy recipient (*pātra*) is described, thereby expressing the objective excitants (*ālambana-vibhāva*) and the environmental excitants (*uddīpana-vibhāva*).

Through the mention of "pleasure-gardens, water-sports," and so on, the daytime activities of amorous women are indicated; by "the festival of wine-drinking and sexual union," their nighttime activities are expressed;
and by the term "separation" (*vipralambha*), all four types [of love], beginning with "first passion" (*prathamānurāga*), are referred to.

By the term "marriage" (*vivāha*), which serves as an illustration, it is taught that in a literary composition (*prabandha*), the stage of "first love" should end with marriage, "jealousy" (*māna*) with affection (*prema*), "separation" (*pravāsa*) with reunion (*saṃgama*), and the "pathetic" (*karuṇa*) sentiment with resurrection (*pratyujjīvana*).

By indicating that success depends upon human effort through the mention of "counselors," "messengers," and so forth, the excellence of the hero’s character (*sattva*) is revealed through the elimination of deficiencies such as lack of resources.

By the statement, “The lack of description of cities and so forth is not a defect,” and so on, it is established that mountains, seasons, gardens, moonrise, drinking bouts, festivals of love, and the like— along with the employment of ministers and envoys and the triumphs of the hero— are invariably included because they assist in the absence of human goals [in other contexts], whereas the remaining elements are included according to the requirements of the body of the composition.
Furthermore, by first introducing the hero through his virtues and then describing the defeat of his enemies by him,
it is made known that one should be possessed of virtue rather than being a hater of virtue.

By the phrase "lineage, valor, learning, and so forth," it is further made known that only the enemy’s noble birth, arrogance, boisterousness, and valor are to be described, rather than the causes of his downfall, such as righteous conduct and humility;
thus, by the expression "it pleases us," the author reveals his own intention that this very position is superior.
Therefore, one should contemplate the various varieties of this [figure], which is the very essence of the god of love, according to the manner explained above.
May the virtuous in this assembly, their eyes closed in bliss arising from the experience of that [work], attain complete satisfaction.

(526) As long as the celestial river rests upon the head of Dhūrjaṭi, which bears the sprout of the moon; as long as Lakṣmī, adorned with the Kaustubha gem, remains upon the chest of the enemy of Mura;
and as long as the flowery bow of the Mind-born god, potent for conquering the three worlds, endures—so long may this composition be an ear-ornament lotus for those of refined intellect. (527)
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Analysis of Rasa," in the *Sarasvatīkaṇṭhābharaṇālaṃkāra* composed by the illustrious Mahārājādhirāja Śrī Bhojadeva. May there be auspiciousness!
